This game is fantastic!  It's like playing a tabletop wargame on the PC.  You have a puny force of troops pitted against overwhelming odds and you have to tactically maneuver your way across the battlefield to survive.  Closest existing game I can compare to is the Fire Emblem series but the rules are a lot more like your typical hobby shop miniatures game.  There are dice rolls, linear movement without a ruler, simple stats, few abilities, limited debuffs, only a few health points per troop, everything is kept super simple and obvious so you can understand what's going on across the entire battlefield simultaneously.  This isn't one of those Civilizations turn-based games that will information overload you.  It's easy to predict and understand how a fight will go between two units and I found Ogres scary before ever fighting one just by looking at the stats!  Yet likewise I understood exactly how to beat one just by looking at their abilities versus mine.
This is more about understanding your army and keeping units alive.  If you've played turn-based games like Valkyria Chronicles or XCOM then you should enjoy this.  There's even an ironman mode that prevents save scumming so you have to know how to keep your troops alive.  Since there's no way to farm gold between missions you also have to manage your expenses and not blow too much gold too quickly on units or items or potions.
Great game!  Highly recommended!

I normally don't do reviews unless I really enjoyed a game.  I haven't had this much fun playing a tactical, turned based RPG in a long time.  It seems that with modern technology, most developers have lost that charm that RPGs used to have in the 90's and early 00's.  What I love about this game is that you have to think and plan before you make your moves and this game can be a challenge at times.  Especially when you choose the harder difficulties.  This game does have a simple in game tutorial to get you started, but it doesn't hold your hand like so many modern games do.
You can choose sides which consist of the Undead or the Knights, so there are two separate campaigns.  So far I beat the game doing the Sir Edward campaign and I'm definately gonna try out the Necromancer campaign next.  Your main character (hero) is in charge of your own little army of recruits which can be up to 16 units  (Size of army is dependant on level).  With each successful battle you and your army gains XP which can be traded in for new skills, spells, or attribute point increases.
I've been a hardcore RPG fan since the mid 90's and this game is a hidden gem.  I haven't binged on an RPG like this in a long time.  It can be very addictive.  It has that old school RPG charm that cannot be replicated in modern AAA games.  On the surface it may seem simple, but once you get into it, you realize how complex the game really is.  This isn't one of those games where you beat it once and you never play it again.  This game you can play again and again.  I've put about 10.5 hours in and I've felt like I've only scratched the surface.  I highly reccommend Age of Fear: The Undead King as well as its sequal Age of Fear 2: The Chaos Lord.

The fact of this game's popularity is less a sign of its quality than it is of the failure of the game industry - failure to put out good games. This game is not good. It's just "good enough." Its flaws make me want to leave it be. Ultimately, this game is about upgrading your vomit to be the biggest corrosive death vomit that it can be. Sometimes, the vomit twirls, sometimes it flashes and sparkles. I have a sort of cognitive dissonance with this game. Cognitive dissonance is not a fallacious way of thinking; it is a purely rational result of life in a meaningless universe. I like this game - I want to like this game - but I don't.
If you want to stay up to date, this game plus the DLC is $35. This game is not worth $35. It may be worth the base price of $15, but maybe not . . .
Pros
- If you feel so compelled (and many are) you can pretty much play this game endlessly.
Cons
- It's essentially a bullet hell game, personally one of my least favorite genres.
- The atmosphere is incredibly dark. The images, music, and themes will be disturbing. Is this really a place you want to spend 100+ hours in?
People say there is so much content, but really there isn't. There is enough for this to be a respectable sized game, but not much more. Many of the "hundreds of items" just add or subtract a few numbers to your stats - and put a little blemish on your face. Also, the very nature of the game (roguelike) seems to amplify the perceived amount of content. You will fight the same level 1 boss over and over in order to see past it, deeper into the game.
If you want to do well in this game, expect to spend a lot of time shooting every single pile of poop and fire in every single room in order to find spare coins/hearts. It's a bit tedious, as is the backtracking you'll do after clearing out a floor. You'll be tramping around in your newly won, hard-fought, and empty territory. Just so that you can go across the map to deliver a spare heart to a blood bank on the other side.
The fact that on some runs, you can "break" the game, and be extremely overpowered and just have an absurd amount of items or some♥♥♥♥♥♥all over the screen, is not fun for me. Maybe the power thrill is fun for some people, but for me, it is a sign of bad design, and detracts from my enjoyment. The screen can look UGLY. Sprites scaled up way past the size they were originally drawn for, so many objects on screen that it blurs together into . . .
The "hundreds of items" are arbitrary things thrown into a hobo soup that is not in any way elegant. When you begin to collect enough items, weird♥♥♥♥♥♥starts happening. After every 3 seconds in a room, you turn into a rainbow pony and can no longer shoot and instead have to chase down enemies. Where did this ability come from? I have no ♥♥♥♥ing idea, neither do the streamers I've watched dealing with this. Or, every time you get hit with a bullet, you get teleported out of the room, and then you have to go back in and fight all the enemies over again because they respawn when you leave without killing them all.
Why do I have so many hours despite not liking the game? Because I wanted to understand the game (my duty as a game developer) and be part of the huge, awesome community that plays it. All these hours in though, I still don't really get it. I will admit, it is somewhat compelling. On good runs my eyes are glued to the screen, and not all of them do I quit out of boredom.
I've beaten Mom's Heart twice. To my knowledge, I have to beat it like 9 more times to progress further. Yikes. A repetitive proposition, though somewhat reasonable due to the randomization. (And you get a different cut scene each time at the end.)
Or at least it has *some* randomization. Play for just half an hour and you're bound to come across the same room twice - same enemy placements and all. Every time this happens (and it's often), I feel a bit of disappointment for the game. They did not scramble the room layout even a tiny bit to keep things fresh. They could have, for example, rotated each room already built and easily have 4x number of rooms. Then shift a few rocks/pits/fires around, have some logic for that, and that would help keep things fresh. That said, the enemy attack patterns, and bonus effects (e.g. green glow or pink glow, poisonous and charmed, respectively), which are randomized, lend the discrete room chunks back a bit of randomization.
The imagery and themes in this game are disturbing, and might make you feel sick at first. But as you play, for better or for worse you will be desensitized to it, as well as the images changing to simply be symbols on your screen, representing gameplay elements. Duke of Flies still gives me the creeps though. I read
, and although his parents suck, none of what happened to him justifies his sense of humor. He kind of just was a sick kid.
That said, I do feel a slight, genuine awe with some of the commentary this game offers. I felt a feeling of rage while sitting in my grandparents' church singing, "for us, for us, the lamb was slain!!" The Binding of Isaac: Wrath of the Lamb indeed. At first it may seem tasteless and gruesome, but after first impressions it grows and actually contains intelligent messages about topics such as religion. For instance, how can there be a God in a world where there's cleft lip (Monstro)? You'll fight bosses such as greed, lust, pride, wrath, and even yourself.
One criticism I have for the game is how glaringly "gamey" it is. It's like how in Risk of Rain most enemies are stuck traversing back and forth on the platforms they spawned on, unable to jump. In Isaac, you can only shoot in the cardinal directions. The way doors close until you've killed everything in the room is also "gamey"; as is the way consumables spontaneously appear as a reward after killing everything in a room; as is the way rocks, spikes, holes, and pretty much everything are all so tile-based. This issue of "gameyness" goes away, however, when you accept that you're playing a mathematical system, one that almost goes out of its way to embrace established game tropes. This is fine, just expect game logic to replace common sense.
The greatest merit this game has is that tons of people are playing it, and the community creates mods, some of which are actively being pooled into the official game. Why so many people play this game is beyond me, but that's the reason I'm here.

Without getting into the details of the story in order to prevent any possible spoilers, I will end it on this note: I absolutely *love* this game! A great experience of a game and story, with a diverse cast and excellent retro-styled graphics and sound! Give it a shot! :D

To preface, I enjoyed the game. There's a lot of good going on here and I don't regret playing it. But I don't think I could really recommend it to someone else.
Read Only Memories is a quirky, good looking game filled with several endearing characters and some brief dips into philosophy tied together with a good-enough plot. At times the music, visuals, and writing are excellent, but there’s a disappointing lack of consistently throughout the (very short) game. It’s also very keen to represent minority groups, either directly or through allegory, but how the narrative does it ends up feeling ham-fisted on several occasions. The game is quick to chastise you if you are not nice enough on certain topics which ends up severely taking away from the message it’s ultimately trying to put forward.
The biggest flaw of the title is that gameplay is a chore. Dialogue comes in droves and is painfully slow to get through; the two mini games are clunky, and it quickly becomes obvious that you are almost entirely on rails. I think that presenting this as a choose-your-own-adventure interactive novel rather than as a full-fledged game would have been a better choice.
I also can’t agree with this game being categorized as a cyberpunk title. It has many of the staples you see in cyberpunk—crime and counter-culture, dredging through the messes that corrupt corporations make, questions about what it means to be human—but the tone and visual aesthetic of the game are too light to really fit the genre.
Overall, I wish that the narrative had been treated with more subtlety—more nuanced characters and less clear-cut morality on the issues presented—and that the game wasn’t as frustrating to play. Fun way to spend an evening or two but not worth the full price tag.

The game opens up with pretty much your average Visual Novel: you're a teenage boy in high school that doesn't really get along with his father, and he has a rich best friend that doesn't really act all that rich.
Welcome to every visual novel ever.
The thing about
is that it really does its job better than most other VNs, to a point of where you'll remember it for a long time to come.
---------------------------------------------------------------
+ Great, extensive Voice Over
+ Amazing Soundtrack
+ Memorable Lead Character
+ Very Well-Written Storyline
+ Extensive After-The-Story Extras
Seems to Work Great on PC--No Complaints
Slightly Annoying Sound Effects, at Times.
- The Game Might not Start in Your Native Language
- Misleading Tags (Isn't Really CYOA, and Only Has 2(?) Endings)
- (Most) Choices Don't Really Mean Much in the Long Run
---------------------------------------------------------------
Sound: 9/10
- Soundtrack: 10
- Voice Over: 10
- Sound Effects: 8
Story: 9/10
- Characters: 10
- Pacing: 9
- Post-Game Content: 10
Performance: 10/10
---------------------------------------------------------------
Overall: one of the best VNs on steam, in my opinion. 9/10.
---------------------------------------------------------------
One thing that immediately stood out to me was the sound. The game doesn't only have a VO, it actually has two different VOs in two different languages. That stood out to me. (I played with the Japanese VO, and it was very well done). Add on to this the various sound effects that were only slightly grating (looking at you: washing machine), and I think that it hit the nail on the head pretty well. 8/10 in Sound Effects, and 10/10 in VO.
The Soundtrack is beyond excellent. Not too many games make me wish that they came with the soundtrack/had it available to purchase, but this one definitely did. 10/10 in that regard.
The story for this game is incredibly well-written. It plays out at a fairly good pace (I found the ending slightly rushed, but not unbelievably so), and the romantic/"d'awww" moments are aplenty.
Lucy, our main character, is incredibly likable. Innocence is often overplayed in android-based storylines, but it was handled well by the writers. I can't commend them enough.
I will point out, however,
. It has one bad ending, and one good ending, which (correct me if I'm wrong) hangs on only a single choice. The rest of the choices in the game (which are quite a few) are simply for comedy's/role-playing sake. That's not to say it's a bad game, it just is very misguided in representation by the community with the tags.
One of the main reasons why I give the story a 9/10 is the post-game content. After the
ending, you get a few pieces of "what happens after", as well as some lore found in the Extras menu. All of this is done in really good taste, and I think I spent about an hour going through these (much to next-day-me's dismay, as I finished this one at 2am).
NOTE: the what-happens-after content is pretty lore-heavy (as much lore as can be in a 4-hour VN experience, anyway).
I'd give this one a straight 10/10. No problems on Windows 10, nothing to complain about, here.

The game runs super smoothly and overall a great survival experience! Mashing together fun and awesome PVE with PVP elements makes the game truly fun!
The game is very fun with tons of teamwork elements, you have to work together to survive this harsh new world. Miscreated uses a lot of concepts from other games such as DayZ, but presents them in such a way that makes it unique. Not to mention the engine and game itself runs a lot smoother than most other survival esq games like DayZ. Having ran the game on multiple machines to test its capabilities, I have found on even the lowest machines I can still push out about 80-100 FPS on varied settings. Along with the very responsive gameplay and gun fighting, it all makes for a solid experience.
Most survival horror games the PVE is mainly just trivial and not too exciting. However, in Miscreated it is very challenging and could mean life or death for you and your allies (or maybe even your enemies. The mutants that walk around Miscreated are not your typical zombie esq enemies, they respond to the world around them and come in many shapes and sizes. From your normal walker types to the hulking behemoths, these enemies come at your with actual intelligence. Gunshots, light, and other sounds can all attract them, and when they attack, they usually come in numbers so be prepared! I would also like to note, if you can use some items as a distraction then you can lay a trap for enemies.
PVP in this game is like most other survival games, brutal. Yes there are some nice people, and some people who just do what they have to survive, but there is still always those pesky bandits! With the very smooth and nice gunplay, the good melee weapon combat, and all sorts of traps and other weapons, the PVP in this game is extremely fun! You actually feel adrenaline and fear during combat, knowing that every bullet you may use may be your last. Not to mention you may find yourself becoming a bandit rather than a nice person. Along with the dynamic weather, the PVP in this game is superb!

"Pillars of Eternity" is a marvelous game that delivers in spades on its promises of a lore-rich world, engrossing stories, loads of content, and deep, tactical combat as spiritual successor to the Baldur's Gate series. If you've appreciated those games this is a must buy. If you're a fan of cRPGs this is a must buy. If you're a stranger to the Infinity Engine games but love RPGs and are open to methods of presentation and game play that build on older styles then this is probably a must buy for you too.
There's a lot of information available on this game, so I want to focus on the things that jumped out at me as someone who held off buying this game for almost a year after release.
First and foremost, the praise for this game is not contingent on nostalgia. Yes, it is very must an extension of the Infinity Engine games of 15-20 years ago in spirit and function. But it stands on its own. The gameplay is if anything more polished, the lore and writing engrossing, the stories worthwhile. If you're afraid this game is simply derivative of its forebears, don't be.
I was impressed with the many little tweaks in gameplay from the IE games. The possibility of an infinite stash, the camping mechanism, out-of-party companion quests with accompanying stories, the skill viginettes, all add to the experience of story and gameplay. It's clear that the developers have had many years to consider the strengths and weaknesses of the IE games, in that the retained the former while shoring up the latter.
There is an absolute mass of content here. My thorough but not truly complete playthrough of the base game took around 90 hours. Each of the two White March expansions added ~25 hours a piece. Quests are wonderfully varied, ranging from the challenging combats of bounties to story-rich sidequests both humerous and tragic to the engrossing main quest. Quests both major and minor often afford a variety of resolutions, from the violent to the dialogue-based, both diplomatic and otherwise. While the main quests are not overwhelmingly multi-pathed, there are options for who you side with that impact both the story and the rewards. I've found enough variability in this regard to reward multiple playthroughs.
NPCs are interesting and go well beyond the common archetypes. Party banter is done well. NPC sidequests could in general have been better implemented, but they're there to help round characters out all the more.
The mechanics of character building and party construction reward experimentation. There's a lot of replayability from a gameplay perspective alone. After my 140 hour playthrough, I immediately started a new game on Path of the Damned difficulty and am enjoying it just as much if not more from both the gameplay and story perspectives.
In short: "Pillars of Eternity" is highly recommended for RPG fans!

checked the box as i recieved this as a free gift, which in it's own right counts as a good Gesture from the developer in my book on it's own, after 2 hours now spent in game, my review of the title is as follows.
The Undead King is a fantasy turn-based strategy from a indie developer, one i'd not heard or seen anywhere before it appearded in my friends games list here on steam.
RPG elelments like altering your stats and building your units are in right from the start, with a good story to read and play out as you progress, eye candy wise it's not the best looking, but then again it's not the worst either, and more than makes up for it in the play elements, very stable and lots of options in game to choose from.
recruiting new troops or upgrading the ones you have to start with all helps for re playability and makes you progress with different paths if you choose a given set of units, myself i went for swords and no bows, to start with then mixed it later in the game when i had more slots to fill.
can't really comment on the sounds or music in game as it's the first thing i turn off, then listen to my own tbh, sorry.
i maybe would have liked hex's in the game but it plays well with out them, it's just what i'm used to in these sort of games, maybe i'm old school, well old anyway :)
if i had to rate it on a scale, then it would depend on what scale i would use? as it's my first indie game, so can't really compare it to a AAA title either, but if i did, for me it's as playable as the old Dungeon Master, and if you can't remember it, then your too young anyway, as it's all about playability and style and not just looks, and really does well in this respect, looking forward to finishing it and then trying the next one to see how things have progressed and developed from the 1st one, i'd recommend it to anyone who likes the playstyle and format as it's one of those simple games you play for 10 mins every now and then and end up spending a few hours on.
would i have bought it if it wasn't a gift? well to be very honest i tend to not buy many games per year and spend all of my time testing them, so sign up for a lot of alpha's and beta's for some AAA companies, all of which could in my opinion could learn a few simple lessons on forums and replies, listen and feedback, as it's not always what the developers & publishers wants that matters, it's those who buy it, as they are the ones who's feedback needs listening to if you wish for another one to be sold, playability over eye candy and a stable engine is what most want, if you can do it all, then that's all the better...

Now, normally I'm not one for playing games that are this god-awful hard or difficult or with this kind of fixed challenge rating but this is definitely one hell of a game I'll gladly play again and again and again.
The combat system is fluid and very responsive to mouse and keyboard (I would NOT suggest using any controllers, however, because aiming with a mouse is far more fluid and precise) and every blow makes a decent hit. And if you're intelligent enough you can easily take out whatever forces come after you. I myself prefer a more stealthy approach and I was able to literally 'depopulate' an entire region in an orcish stronghold and was able to loot at my leisure before it started to repopulate again.
The mini-boss battles (against the Uruk Captains) is probably one of my absolute frickin favorite moments in the entire game, they're strong enough to where you know if you get more than one of these sumbishes on your♥♥♥♥♥♥you're in BIG trouble! They each have anywhere between 2-4 weaknesses and 6-8 strengths. They are all balanced out, and the higher level they are the more higher quality loot they give you. And by loot I mean runes, the bread and butter of this game.
Because I got the GOTY Edition on sale, it came with a bunch of extra goodies and I was able to make my character look like one of my OLD Roleplay characters who appears to look like a Death Knight, complete with hood, blackened armor, clawed gauntlets, and so forth! There's even one skin where it turns you into a woman, in case you wanted to go Xena-Mode on some Uruk butts!
Lots of lore in this game, LOTS of lore! Almost everything in the game as a description about it that you can read at your leisure, and for an open-world game (which I normally DO NOT enjoy) this game makes me actually EXCITED to go out and start looking for every treasure in every nook and cranny in the game world. Nothing makes you feel more badarse than single-handedly wiping out TWO Captains in a bloody row using nothing more than campfires and explosions!
The story is pretty fleshed out and rather detailed, and you can do any of the story missions at YOUR pace. Don't want to do the story and just want to kill orcs? You can do that. Want to have an Assassin's Creed feel and parkour all over the place, whilst dropping down from above to skewer an orc across the throat or impale them through the head instantly killing them before slinking back into the shadows to assassinate all of their friends without being spotted once? You can do that! Did you want to brand every single orc you encounter with your power to turn them against their own boss so they help YOU kill him instead of the other way around? YOU CAN DO THAT!
There are many other things I can say about this game that I bloody ADORE, but I will finish off this review by stating this: Whatever the Developers did when they made this game it bloody WORKS, keep this formula. THIS is how you make a GOOD open-world Arkham Combat Styled RPG.
I think my only real complaint for this game has to be it has too many damn timed missions, but I always hate those. I honestly cannot find anything about this game I dislike or hate.

Stranded Deep is everything I was hoping it would be since first hearing about the game last fall. It doesn't stoop to modern rules of the survival games by adding in zombies, aliens, infections, etc! Your survival entirely depends on your item managment and your skills, nature is the only enemy (Ok and maybe the annoying sharks lol).
You get a short tutorial in the beginning of the game while flying on what appears to be your private jet, and then you are pretty much on your own to figure things out...I spent alot of time pulling up the Wiki page to find out how things are built and what items I needed for specific builds but it never distracted from the amazing experience. A plus is the fact that you dont have some fancy crafting window (Minecraft), you literally just have to drop or drag everything into a pile and a list of possible build/crafting options will pop up which for me makes it more realistic. The building engine in the game works great, its quite easy to construct a basic shelter and then add on to it as you go. As of now the rain and weather doesn't seem to cause any negative effects so it's a shame that the shelter doesn't really serve any real need as far as staying warm, or avoiding high winds or lightning. The Sharks can be annoying at times, they seem to spawn alot and sometimes to many in a group...once they flip you from the raft it can be difficult to get back into it as they will keep flipping it further and further away.
The game is def worth a play! It was more than worth the $15 asking price!
Hopefully in the next updates the weather will be more of an issue as far as temp and health. If you're tired of the overuse of zombies and other things in survival games, check this one out!

Oh my goodness. I completed all of the story, got all the achievements, and what a ride it was. I've not felt like emotionally drained and hurt in a long time, especially from a visual novel. The fact that the story seems to just take such a sudden turn not once, but twice, got me to the point of tears. Truly a wonderful experience worth the 7 dollars I paid for it on sale.

This is not the sort of story that can be judged after half an hour of reading it.
The pacing is kind of misleading, with a humorous start and, erm, a very emotional climax and various endings.
Overall, it's the kind of story that's quite relevant in this day and age as automation becomes far more widespread.  Will we one day meet people like Lucy?  And how will we respond to the development and maturity of those people?  Sure, Asimov and others talked about those questions long ago, but here's a Korean take on it all.  The Three Laws of Robotics are mentioned consistently and displayed rather frequently, with a few moments that help amplify the situation for the reader, so if you're sick of seeing the same image for a while I can see how some people might dislike it.
There are also limited character poses, but quite a few VNs share that...  Limitation...  No?
But if you look beyond just graphics/art, and quite frankly it's very good art, and perhaps a couple of looping music tracks there's quite a touching story here.  None of the music or art is unpleasant, although there are several scenes that demonstrate the low/conflict-prone parts of the story.  Without spoilers, there's a scene that will bite you in the face if you're grown to care about the female lead.
The game also offers two voices.  I prefer the Korean voice, although the Japanese one is more 'consistent' with her appearance. Beautiful game. I love the lore, the characters, the story, and the combat. The setting is believable, tangible, and breathtaking. I am particularly in love with how many ways there are to play this in the main game alone! Classes, races, origins, there are so many possibilities! You can weave whatever story you want, almost. Obviously there is some guidance, and this comes out sharply with regards to some of your party members. Some conversations are steering the player in one direction, but I can forgive that because there is only so far you can go before your narrative spins out of control.
To start with, this is a standard party-based RPG. Where this game differs from others is that it lets you make adventurers with custom stats at inns if you dislike the NPC party members. However, if you gear your NPCs up well, combat won't be an issue. You also have to travel with NPCs for some quests, which can be annoying if you dislike dialogue with certain people (like that priest). Custom adventurers do better than the standard NPCs on higher difficulties because they can be optimized stat-wise, but if you play your cards wisely with the standard NPCs or with your main character, you won't need to mess with that too much. Now, that isn't to say combat is easy.
While this isn't Dark Souls II, this game is difficult. I recommend starting on Story Mode and then migrating to easy up to normal and beyond. Maybe do a few rounds on Easy first to get your wits about you. I've gotten my kiester whipped multiple times because I didn't strategize right. You will have to micromanage everything. Set up your autopause settings wisely so that you can optimize your strategy. This is crucial for boss fights like the bounty quests you get mid-game and a difficult boss you face later on that I am still struggling with. Your persistence will be rewarded, though. Combat is difficult, but satisfying if you persist with it. Be prepared to learn and soak up the lore because this world is rich with it. I love the story the most here.
Definitely recommend to those who adore fantasy (guilty) and a good RPG with party-based mechanics. Take your time, learn the ropes. Do every quest that comes your way (you need those levels...). Don't give up. Push on and you'll be slaying bosses like a pro in no time. Not going to say much about the plot other than the fact that I thoroughly enjoyed it. One of my fave fantasy stories out there and I've both read and played my fair share. You will enjoy this if you enjoyed Skyrim, the Avernum games, and or Grimrock. Give it a go! :)

Maybe it's because I'm coming into this game in the summer of 2015 and all the bugs are ironed out - I've had nothing but a great experience with this game. The online community is still very much a part of the experience, and UPlay stays out of the way - once I hit "play" in Steam, UPlay loads immediately and then minimizes, the game loads instantly - all this running off of a 7200 RPM HDD.
Gameplay side, the game plays like a fresher Assassin's Creed - it feels more focused and there's fantastic level design. If you've ever enjoyed games like Assassin's Creed or in general third person stealth, you'll love it.

After 40 hours in game now I can summarize that it takes time to get into the game - but if you are patient, it's great. Game mechanics and also lore are unlike anything you have seen before, and it's old school, meaning it doesn't take your hand and explains every little detail just for your convenience. It is not casual play, it is demanding, both for your brain to grasp the game world and for your skill at winning battles, even on Normal difficulty.
GAMEPLAY
Still, it is captivating. If you are looking for a new Baldur's Gate II which is not only a pale imitation nostalgia wise, but a great game merely basing on BG's concepts, stop reading and buy. Because Pillars of Eternity does definitely remember its roots, but excels at some aspects: There is a a function to speed up time, so no random Haste-spell-casting just to get to your next quest location. There's a stash for equipment (some might say that's just bad RP, but hey, it's 2016.) There are two values that bring your characters down in combat, with actually dieing of low health being removed as a core factor of gameplay. No more "Remember that time when I got torn to pieces 20 times during our epic adventure?"
GRAPHICS AND PERFORMANCE
Graphics are o.k. You'll get the pre drawn maps we know from games like BG which are awesome, the level of detail of areas is very high. Characters look a little blocky though and some more work could have gone into them. I've had small lags when opening menus, but they were barely noticable and the game runs smoothly especially when it has to - in combat. Nothing to truly criticise graphics and performance wise, really.
IMMERSION
Just as I said above, it takes time getting used to. Characters will throw words at you and you'll be like... yeah right, but you'll have no idea. But that's fine. Pick up a book, or just run with the story and use your reason, it works just fine. Throughout the game there are tombstones with messages from supporters. During loading screens, you are warned that those break the Fourth Wall, so if you want full immersion, don't read them. I did, though, and my personal high was seeing a message from Gamebanshee which has always accompanied me through BG and other games. Good times.
Quests are all well done and you are not spammed with random, re-occurring tasks like in DA:I. Everything is scripted individually, and side quests sometimes can have a deeper impact on you than the main storyline. Again, legacy of BG right there.
MUSIC AND VOICE ACTING
The important dialogue is voiced and I found it very well balanced to the reading parts. There is much more voice used than in BGII, for example and the voice acting is decent. It fits. Music is background only, don't expect an epic score like they used in Witcher 3. But again, it all works. Some more music would have been nice, but hey, aren't we all spoiled.
GENERAL EPICNESS
People have been calling for a remake of BG as a modern game, and we get a crowdfunded BG style RPG which doesn't give a crap about some of the modern game standards like 1st Person, Superior Graphics, Fully Voiced Dialogue... and guess what - it works. It's a long game, too. And stuff you do really means something. Your choices matter and more often than not you're left with a somewhat sour taste in your mouth after a dialogue completed.
The only downside to this game is that its level of detail can overwhelm you and you might find this and that dialogue to be just a bit too much and the troubles of your companions more a nuisance than a benefit. I recommend just rolling with it and to reduce metagaming like reading guides to a minimum. Especially on Normal difficulty, you'll be fine doing just that.
tl;dr
Tired of going through Irenicus' Dungeon for the 1.000.000 time? Well download a Mod to skip it, or maybe buy Pillars ot Eternity and experience a game that is refreshing and yet takes you back to the good old days of gaming, and the Internet as a whole.
It is a smart and demanding game, it is NOT a casual game. Bring time and be ready to read a lot of text. You may have to start over two or three times, but then it'll be a great run. 8.5/10

It's a no for me.
For some context, I am a gay, nonwhite cismale and when I first heard of this game some time ago I was enamored by the idea of a game that presented a more nonwhite, nonbinary world. Something that is so rare in all media, and especially in video games. Imagine my feelings of luck at finding it dirt cheap in a bundle. But having played through it now, I realize that if I were to buy it full price I would have regretted that choice pretty much within the first hour of play, and even now that I've slogged through the bad parts to the okay parts, I can still only say that what I like the most about this game is how it gives me the hope that other, similarly inclusive games can break onto the scene.
I have so many issues with the game that I'm not sure where to start. On the level of mechanics, the game is a point and click with very little puzzle solving and more running through dialogue trees which are less trees and more bamboo poles. You go in a straight line and the only thing that your choices affect seems to be whether or not characters like you, which affects certain events in the story, yes, but it seems to come up with ways for the plot to resolve itself anyway, making many of your choices utterly meaningless exempting the endings, which are apparently based on whether or not your annoying robot friend likes you. And that's fine. It's a visual novel. I like visual novels. But what I hate is that it puts you at the helm and lets you make choices and then takes them away from you at the moments where you have the most reason to protest. What if I don't want to trust the cutesy bot that just broke into my house and threatened to rip my arm off? What if I think explaining my situation to the associate of the character who has explicitly been stated to be the least trustworthy out of all the characters introduced is a bad idea? What's that? Only one option here? Then the characters act as if I'm the one who came up with this nonsense: "Oh he's so stubborn... he's so dogged and determined... I'm not surprised with your track record hahaha." For a game about identity, ostensibly pushing for the freedom to express certain identities, this game really goes out of its way to pigeonhole who you are so that it can keep the plot running.
Then there's the lore dumping. I get it, the setting is colorful and vast. And truth be told, a lot of it is interesting. But not every single character has to be an excuse to exposit on something. Turing is fine. You don't have to have TOMCAT going on and on about the same technobabble. You don't have to have a coffee shop manager explain to me what moe means with a dissertation about Japanese culture. I got so pleased when it turned out one of the characters I was looking for was dead because it meant I didn’t have to through another 20-30 incredibly slow (even at max speed) text boxes of some minor character explaining something that had nothing to do with the plot.
And what a plot. Every attempt has been made to sugarcoat real world dilemmas in pretty metaphors and good intentions, and you know what, it’s insulting. It’s insulting to have the analogue of oppressed peoples being a subculture that gene splices to become furries. Being born into a world that treats you like less of a person because of something out of your control (being born female, nonwhite, LGBTQ+, disabled; having to abort an unwanted pregnancy that might have been forced upon you) is not the same as choosing to have bunny ears or whining that rocket fists are illegal. That is not the same. It’s insulting to be told the world of tomorrow might be instantly changed by the sudden appearance of a new sapient species and literally the next in game day (your new game plus) having your characters discussing wages for the new robot race like nothing has happened. One of the things real people are still fighting for today and this game believes that the people in power will just hand it over like it’s chewed up gum if you ask nicely. This game belittles the suffering of so many people and it’s gross and it’s stupid.
I want to like this game. I think it’s full of charm and good intentions, and in the end, despite their shortcomings, I came to love the characters. How could I not want a game with not one, not two, but an entire cast of nonconforming characters, to be good? But it really is just a wish-fulfillment sugar plum fantasy wrapped in an overly verbose box with a predictable villain and many minor irritations along the way. And I wouldn't recommend it.

With the D&D universe I know what to expect from monsters, I know that fire hurts trolls and kale kills hobbits, sorry I meant halflings.  In PoE I have to learn the eccentricities of a swathe of all new unfamilar critters with resistances and weaknesses I need to glean from reading through a scrolling combat log while trying to micromanage every idiot step of my reckless party members.  Maybe I'm getting too old, but it was just way too much information for me to have to take in while trying to immerse myself in the overarching story and world.
There are two sides to many PC RPGs, the dungeon hack (loot and levels) side and the rpg side (world building and narrative). When the dungeon hack component requires every ounce of analytical skill in order to "game" the combats into your favour, it's very difficult to maintain immersion.  Theere's just too much going on in the combat as far as I'm concerned and it's stopped me giving this game the time it deserves because it's such a chore keeping my head above water in the combat.
There's so many stats, resistances, classes, and powers, spells, ubiquitous magical items of every conceivable variation, gelatinous cubes in every hue, ARGH it's too much! A product is complete not when you've added everything to it that you can think of but when you've taken away everything that it can do without.
I really hate to poopoo what is clearly a gorgeous passion project, but I only get two choices when rating this game and unfortunately, for what may be for the quite personal reasons above, I can't recommend it....

"Wow." - the first word out of my mouth after beating this game.
I'm writing this review shortly after beating this game for the first time, and I'm planning on doing so again.
I'll preface this review by saying that I went into this game experience blind, and I believe it was for the better. If you are considering playing this game, I highly recommend it. You probably want more details thatn that if you're reading this review still, so I'll provide them, but I'm putting the conclusion up front: I strongly recommend getting this excellent game.
As can be readily apparent from the user-defined tags for this game, the mechanics that should stick out the most are Visual Novel and Point & Click. I'm more of a fan of VNs than I am of Point & Click games, but that's not to say I haven't enjoyed games such as the King's Quest series. The point'n'click mechanics were implemented in a standard fashion, but I feel that they truly shine in how the game presented it's exposition from those interactions. Small, but appreciated quirky details to be found just about everywhere, pleasant surprises, and an excellent sense of comedic timing rewarded interacting with characters, objects, environments multiple times over, and I found myself enjoying experimenting with different actions more than I have in other point & click games. There were enough times were I thought "okay, there's no way the game would let me do this" but sure enough, not only was I able to, but it had a meaningful consequence going forward.
The visual novel nature of this story was truly brilliant as well. This game has highly likable and memorable characters, spot on designs, and an uncertain yet very appreciated weight to your choices and actions that were handled much better than other visual novels. I'd imagine many people who have played visual novels have found themselves groaning over dialogue and action choices that may as well have said "Do you want Ending A, or Ending B". While your own characters tone can often be seen in a clear dichotomy of friendly/trusting vs sarcastic/uncaring, there is a moral ambiguity that is expanded upon later in the game with no clear cut answers. While the game does have multiple endings, it thankfully isn't just good vs bad. There are varying degrees of success and development that can occur with the game's characters, sub plots, mysteries, and overarching story that leave you wanting to explore more, and assuredly get more out of repeat playthroughs.
The game thankfully isn't "just" point & click dialogue exhaustion. I won't give any details for the sake of spoilers, but there are mini-games and puzzles within that help keep a solid pace throughout your game experience. Other than that, I really don't want to say more about the game's plot or mechanics than I already have, as part of the appeal to me was the sheer number of pleasant surprises thrown my way during my first playthrough.
Speaking of pleasant surprises, the audio/visual design of this game was *on point*. Character designs and environments are amongst the most engaging I've seen in such games, and you can really get a sense of emotion and expression during dialogue coming from the main cast. Likewise, a stunning soundtrack and feelgood audio cues stemming from your actionshelped the game feel responsive and immersive. Additionally, the creators of this game have recently announced that a new version is being released that is going to feature more character busts and expanded voice-acting outside of just the narrator, so I'm heavily looking forward to replaying this game once that gets implemented later.
In truth, the only reason I started to play this game was because I heard there was some sort of tie-in, reference, or something along those lines to the recently released VA11-Hall-A. I'm not even aware if this is canonical or just an easter egg sort of deal, but my point is that I'm glad I had the opportunity to play through this game nonetheless.
If you're a fan of Point & Click adventure games, a fan of Visual Novels, or are just looking for a damn good story, this is the game for you.

I went through most reviews here and I can agree with most flaws pointed out like low difficulty (although that was actually a plus to me [yup, I'm a dirty casual]) or badly designed puzzles based on seemingly random patterns or player's character being an observer most of the time (I won't even comment on this "SJW" thing because some people are just hopeless) but I got so invested in this adventure when I was playing, I felt real connection with setting and characters (especially Turing as I really enjoyed their relationship with my character and watching them grow as a person was quite fascinating) and as I said - the game just feels very sympathetic, it has it's charm. Early Access Preview
10 bucks is not a lot of money, in fact to many of us it’s barely an hour out in the local drinking establishment so when offered a chance to purchase the Early Access release of multiplayer survival game, Noct, for a wondrous 10 American Dollars, or around seven quid, I can only suggest you get that wallet out and send some monetary love to the developers.
Noct is billed as a 2D top-down multiplayer survival horror game that blends arcade combat with RPG survival elements and after several hours in the early access beta I can get right behind that description. It also controls sublimely with keyboard and mouse or as a twin-stick shooter, is one of the most atmospheric games of 2015 and will scare the pants off you when you least expect it.
The atmosphere comes in part from its fairly unique graphical look. So OK, there are other black and white games out there but Noct does it in a way that feels special. You control your character through an ‘Eye in the Sky’ camera with various military style filters, think night vision and you will be on the right track. Couple this with some truly brilliant atmospheric audio cues and ambient backing tracks from none other than Robin Finck of NiN and you just know that this game will get inside you and force you to turn the lights back on.
In Noct you get to play one of the unlucky survivors of armageddon, an apocalyptic purge of hellfire and death that leaves you in a barren wasteland surrounded by a ruined civilization, dust storms and a smattering of the biggest, ugliest, death dealing monsters you have ever had the misfortune to encounter, the Nocturnal. Do not despair though because someone, somewhere is watching and guiding you through the ‘eye in the sky’ and is leading you to your salvation, or so you hope!
Noct is perfectly playable as a solo event however the game is designed around multiplayer and as such others can join your world and help or hinder your progress as you are guided by the mysterious stranger who watches from above. The end result is looking to be a vast adventure where you are never quite sure who you can trust or what the end goal really is. Could it be your salvation or your doom? The only way to find out is to play and hope that we are all on the same side come the end of days.
Equip yourself with various guns or a rather handy melee attack and step out into a brooding, dark world of black, white and shadow. Collect items and complete objectives, form lasting friendships or find your nemesis and start your journey in the dark. The Noct are coming for you.

Note: This review is being written after my 2hr play session on the first day the game was launched on Early Access. This is not a future review of what the game could be, it is a review of the game as it stands in Early Access.
The good
- The world and presentation was great. Art, sound, noises, all fantastic and add to the overall mood.
- Multiplayer works, which is not always the case.  No clue if it was cross-platform as I am not even sure what other platforms are supported.
- No tutorial. Dropped in to an unknown world not knowing how to do things makes things get real, real fast. Added to the horror aspect of the game.
- Perspective. Sat nav view of me and the rotating map is something I have never seen done before.
The bad
- No tutorial. The other side of this beast, no clue I had filters or could access a map. Still not even sure what the filters were for.
- Lack of variety in gameplay. The gameplay loop is run to an area, pickup something, shoot monsters/bugs. Rinse and repeat.
- Long open areas between waypoints. There is nothing to do between waypoints execpt run away from monsters.
- Noct monsters. There isn't a point to engage with them if they aren't attacking me or if they aren't surrounding a waypoint.
The Ugly
- Crashes. After two hours I had crashed the game three times. If I can't play your game I can't help you.
- Controller support not listed on the Steam Store page. I honestly almost didn't by this twin stick shooter because it didn't list it on the store page. When I went into the controls I noticed it mentioned X360 controller mapping.
- After about 30-45 minutes I had seen everything the game has had to offer. Plain in simple after two hours of repeating the same content 3 times, I have no drive to return to the game.
Bottom line: It feels like it needs 6 more months of work in-oder for me to be able to sell it to a friend for multiplayer. There just isn't a enough meat on the bone at this stage for it to be fun and engaging gameplay.

I've been making it a point to give a very, very close look to anything Devolver puts their hand to after playing Hotline Miami. I can safely say that this game continues on in the style of that (amazing) game. Devolver is proving that they're willing to put money into polishing/delivering concepts that are stylish and enjoyable.
The atmosphere in this game is awesome, very dark and involved. Personally I dig the overhead, infrared camera style of gameplay, but it won't be for everyone. The music in this game is contemplative, moody, dark, and thoughtful...not unlike Boards of Canada's more minimalistic stuff.
Gameplay is tight in terms of movement, but I must say that in terms of aiming the controls are a bit sensitive. Please bear in mind though that I'm using a mouse and keyboard, and turning down the DPI did help somewhat. While the combat is fairly intuitive, there will be some cheap deaths experienced immediately after leaving a building.
It is important to note though that cheap deaths these days are often just a sign that we're all being spoiled by games that are way too easy. What I'm trying to say is that this game has a whole lot of promise for being in early access, and much like BroForce I have every confidence that Devolver will deliver a very polished product in the end.
At the price point especially...what's not to love?

Do you want a game where the AI can think like a real player? Because this, is, it. Most games don't have an AI that can see through my attempts to lure, know which of my units to target first and how to target without suffering serve losses, or that can beseige defenses that would give veteran players a hard time. And on the harder difficulties these traits can actually give a challenge without giving the AI any special bonuses.
However if you are worried about that making the game too difficult then fear not~! For the game is fairly simple to understand; where the complexity lies is in how to best use your units to out smart the AI. (Which the AI knows how to put to good use of their units.)
So how does the gameplay actual flow?: for the most part you will probably be playing the campaign, which in this AoF1 (This game), which you can choose from humans or the undead. (In AoF 2 you can pick between Demons and orcs, same engine too.) You are given a finite amount of units which depending on your faction have their own roles and quarks similar to chess pieces, however unlike chess, you will be moving units rather freeform state with turns. (Like a general moving units around on a map.) So basically it is like a strategy where you can move units around fairly freely with a few exceptions; the units not being able to magically stand on each other (I am look at you Starcraft), that this takes place in a turn-based style, and a unit can't move through another unit even if friendly.
Okay, as a reader you are probably wondering what kind of bad things this game has, so I will take a break from that to provide you with

First off, this game is made by a poor indie development team who works on the game in their spare time; what that means for you is this: they don't have the money for fancy animations or voicing everying, they can't provide the game with time required to properly optimize the game so the game can require you fiddling with options till things run smoothly as you want, and other small polish related things.
With all that out of the way, I must contridict it a bit. While the developers don't have money for nice assests, they haven't stopped updating the game, and have recently redone the terrain quality from being just passiable to good quality. They are constantly improving the game in their spare time, they have introduced two new systems within my time of owning the game. (AoF 2, both games share the same engine, and are typically updated at the same time.) The two new systems being morale, which makes the combat ever so much more satifying and adds a new dimension to play, and  the other which probably isn't a new system but rather a constant and frequent additions and updates. Which brings me to my next point...
One of the Dev's is a user, just like you :p , name Les that has a tendency to fix any problem as soons as I or someone reports it, answer questions sometimes a few minutes within posting; sometimes even launching an update as well if it can be addressed quickly. (Yes I have seen the game get updated several times a day, yes some of those may or may not have been my fault. )
I am probably forgeting something else that is nice but since it wont probably pop into my head today or tomorrow lets wrap this up with a nice bow, even if it comes without packaging paper.
TL;DR:
Pros:
-Amazing AI that is plays like a player
-Devs actually care about the game, and are still constantly improving it
-Simple to learn but feels good to master gameplay
-Great AI, yes I really like the AI, it deserves to be two bullet points.
Cons:
-Lacks polish
-May run slow
-Poor indie dev problems (Because money doesn't grow on trees, and it does buy nice things)
-Game can have some wierd problems such as sound not working. Consult either the steam forum for the game(s) or Les

Matchmaking/Community~ The bad thing about it is that players with no connection to the internet are a bit out of luck.  The good news is that this game can run on pings somewhere in the stratosphere. Matchmaking is easy to figure out, and you'll almost always have a match to join.  The community is pretty good as well, most people are generally nice, though a grand majority of them aren't particularly talkative.
Gameplay~ The gameplay is essentially a turn based volley of (occasionally) flashy attacks.  The game's physics engine doesn't allow for the floating islands or death-by water of worms, nor does it allow you to take control of an entire team, but rather be part of a team of other players (or go for free for all).
Variety~ The variety is wonderful on all fronts, from the hundreds of weapons, to the dozens of maps, to even a decent amount of varied and fun gamemodes.  The weapons, for the most part, feel very different, and all do differnt things.  The only problem is that some are undoubtedly less powerful than others, so RNG can make the game slightly infuriating at times.  The maps, unlike the Gamemodes and Weapons, can feel rather same-y, which is more a fault of the game's physics engine then a lack of creativity.
Character Customization~ Shellshock has a couple of interesting ideas in the customization department.  Not only do aesthetic options for your tank open up as you level up more, but it has a full fledged skill tree.  You can upgrade four different parts of your tank, those being: crit chance, movement speed and climbing ability, extra health in the form of armor, or luck, which lets you get better weapons in a few different ways.  There are three pronounced skills within each tree, all of which help out in a bigger way.
Story~ There really isn't any story to speak of.  If you're looking story, look elsewhere.
Sound~  The sound design is nice.  The sound effects for firing and landing attacks are satisfying, and the music is fittingly epic, etc.  Another thing the game has is tracks that play after you or your team wins, and they're mostly passable, though some can get a bit annoying.
Why wouldn't you want this game? ~
~ If you need a good story in a game. (1)
~ If your wi-fi is non existant. (2)
~ You don't like the map variety (3)
~ It sounds interesting, but not 7.00 USD interesting.
What to get instead ~
~ As strange is this sounds, there are a good number of flash games that have a decent story and similar gameplay, check out ArmorGames or MaxGames for something like that. (1)
~ Worms Armageddon has a passable single-player mode. (2)
~ The Worms series has a physics engine that better lends itself to varied and interesting maps. (3)
~ I'd again suggest the free flash games (4)

I *love* survival games - you might say I hold an unhealthy addiction to them. Stranded Deep is perhaps the most uninteresting, least-intuitive game I've played in quite a long while. The crafting system is a bit asinine, the carry space one has in inventory is laughably small, and resources too sparse to be vaguely realistic (there are rocks everywhere in the environment, but only perhaps 4-5 usable stones per island.) It doesn't seem possible at this point to craft any storage devices or backpacks.
While it is apparently possible to survive indefinitely on a single island (provided one doesn't chop down all the palm trees, thereby removing the only source of drinkable water I've thus far found,) abject boredom will drive the player to explore nearby islands via raft. Whilst underway, sharks will attempt to dislodge the player, but instead just knock everything overboard one might have been trying to transport. The other reason to explore is to find valuable items... which one doesn't really need at all.
I grant you, I've only given this a few of hours of my time, but couldn't stand anything longer than that. It's pretty and has a good concept, but compelling content is lacking.
I most definitely do not recommend Stranded Deep, and I'm quite surprised the reviews seem to be mostly positive. Perhaps farther down the development line, this will be interesting and engaging.
Rather than slog through this sub-par game, I would recommend... well, almost anything else. For a pure survival experience, The Long Dark or The Forest. For adventure and exploration, ARK Evolved. Even Rising World far outclasses Stranded Deep at this point.

Night in The Woods is an utterly captivating game featuring a colorful cast of anthropomorphic animals on a touching and memorable adventure in a small American town. It tells a wonderful tale dealing with sensitive subjects such as death, friendship, mental issues and more. This game may not be for everyone since it is mostly dialogue with the occasional minigame, but if you are looking for a strong and memorable story then you will not be dissapointed. Highly recommended!!

I enjoyed every moment I put into this game. The sense of humor and charm was constantly surpising to me, and I was excited every time I got to interact with a new thing in the game.
You spend most of the game strolling/hopping through the game's small town, and I was always eager to get back out there and see what everyone was up to. And I was constantly finding new things to look at or places to explore when I went off the expected path to my next main story beat. They also mix up their "minigame" mechanic in a ton of different ways that almost always made me chuckle.
The story structure of the game feels pretty similar to other games you might group this with: something like a Gone Home or a Firewatch. You have a character working through some personal issues while investigating some sort of bigger external mystery. While I think it all progresses and ends really nicely, I could imagine some people are less thrilled with the way it all wraps up. Once I was about half way through the game, I didn't care how it ended: I just wanted to see whatever this game had to offer.
This is a story that feels like it can be really important to you if you're dealing or have dealt with the issues presented in this game. Walking through Mae's mental process about her situation was really helpful in helping me recontextualize some of the things I'm dealing with.
I finished the game with a different sort of view about some things in my own life. And I think that's just about the best compliment I can give a game. Thanks for the journey IF.

Did you grow up in the midwest? Maybe some town you loved but the world didn't?
Play this game.

Within minutes this game is charming. Grabbing a can from a vending machine could have just been a simple button click, but it's this... endearingly clumsy minigame. Moments like this pop up throughout the game and they're all special. I'm reminded a bit of the battle system from Undertale. A simple mechanic being used in a variety of ways, ending up a really powerful way to express emotion. And using Guitar Hero style mechanics is so smart and accessible. For the most part the game isn't leaning on established video game norms to tell its story like lives or respawns or points, which can feel a bit stale.
I love the 'wake, go into town, sleep' game loop. It reminds me a little of 'One Chance' from years back, but it doesn't feel tedious. There's enough repetition that it feels comfortable, so when things start changing, you don't just have to be told that they are, you've experienced it first hand. And even within the sleepy routine of the first half of the game, there's enough variety that it rarely feels like a drag. Maybe a little bit around the start. But I just took a break and came back to it the next day.
I love the disconnect between the player and Mae the character. How you can pick dialogue options that Mae subtly ignores or twists, or is unable to express, a bit like Depression Quest. It's like you're her subconscious.
Technically the game is beautiful, the platforming mechanics feel great, and again, end up serving an emotional purpose.
vague spoilers below but you can probably guess them from the first half of the game. That's not a bad thing, it just has consistency.
Thankfully the story IF decided to tell with these tools is as charming as the tools themselves. It's an exploration of change, depression, and of choosing to continue anyway. It embraces the mundane. I appreciated how Mae isn't constantly 'raging against the dying of the light'. It's not affirming because "no matter how hard it gets, Mae never gives up, blah blah". It's affirming, in a weird way, because at her lowest moment, Mae pretty much *does* give up? Her friends have to save her, despite her refusal, and in the end, it's Mae who has to decide the mess, and the pain, the SOMETHING of life.
Congratulations to the IF team and Finji, seems like this was a real labour of love.

For me, Starbound is a perfect example of love/hate relationship. A game stuck in Early Access hell until recently. A game clearly made with passion. A game made with modders in mind and made so chaotic it turns modders' life into a living nightmare.
But let's get it orderly.
Starbound, in a nutshell, is a sandbox. A 2D Terraria-like sandbox with a distinctive style. So while there is a main quest (arguably, unlike Terraria), it's not mandatory and you can throw it away almost instantly (gear and planet progression has almost no ties to it). In addition to "static" quests associated with the main storyline there are some "static" small ones, as well as "dynamic" auto-generated ones. You can delve into a (rather trivial) main quest, but the real charm of Starbound comes in the amount of freedom it gives you to do what you really like. Explore. Collect things. There are virtually TONS of collectable things, from clothing to pets to recipes to collectible in-game figurines to furniture (some of it you can craft through pixel printer using your money late in the game) to music instruments to food cuisines to... If you have a thing in mind, it probably can be collected. Build colonies from a single block and populate them with NPCs and traders (wiki gives you almost full control over spawning mechanics), then complete their quests and, eventually, hire them as combat companions or ship crew improving your ship. Expand your ship from a small space boat to a massive stellar fortress. Start a farm and grow hens. Search for NPC villages and unique dungeons. Make complex mechanisms using wiring mechanics and logic blocks. Tame poisonous and frigid oceans and build a colony on the seabed. Terraform the whole planet.
The weaknesses are in details and are ingrained in the game so deeply, it's almost impossible to get rid of them. Races, while initially different, now are practically the same - perhaps out of fear to be blamed in "disbalancing". There are no racial abilities, although every race has a distinctive visual style. There is no way to track the place you died at (that is, if you play vanilla Starbound; there are mods to fix that). There is no way to navigate a planet aside from by memory (there is no map or minimap, and that sucks). Bosses's battles are more straightforward and "casual", so don't expect building special arenas like in Terraria (last update addresses that to some extent). Some weather conditions are still frustrating (like sandstorms generating sand to bury your base: unlike water, there is no way to drain sand except manually. Or ash rains burning NPC villages on fire planets). Direct planet progression means you are stuck with fire, frozen and dark planets in late-game, although mini-biomes improve diversity (Terraformer may address that, haven't checked it out yet). Starbound offers many opportunities, but not all of them are explored. For example, while automatic weapon generation system is very interesting, the game offers no ways to customize it, and mods currently barely scratch the surface.
Modding Starbound is a story in itself. While Starbound is quite moddable and doesn't require special knowledge for simpler tasks, chaotic nature of the file structure makes modding a struggle. Dialogue lines are embedded directly into the game files instead of being referenced from a single location, so to translate the game you need to manually transform the file for any item that uses text lines. In other words, being a translator means being in a world of pain. The game directly supports only humanoid models, making non-humanoid custom races difficult (and basically making the whole variety of armor and vanity clothing unusable by them). Documentation is scarce; dig wiki a lot if you want to get some things the community found out through constant dev poking. There is no way to "patch" a game script, so while there can be mods changing the same item, there can't be mods changing the same script. Some things are hardcoded, but there is no distinct border between what can be changed and what can't, this knowledge is mostly limited to the community's trial and error experience (examples include most crafting interfaces and NPC facial rendering order - you can have eye color or eyelids as a separate layer but not both, meaning your custom character may either have colored eyes OR blink them; and if you think to use facial features' layer to do eyelids, you can't since they are rendered UNDER eyes). Overall, it is clear the devs lacked system approach and general view of their work - while the things work as they are, chaos rules over the insides of the game.
All and all, Starbound is a good example of a project where creative freedom rules over project management. Enjoy it as it is. Enjoy it with friends. But don't expect its numerous drawbacks to be addressed (any time soon). As with all things art, such improvements, while probable, will always be a surprise.

The gameplay revolves around clearing waves of zombies and surviving the next and next wave.

You have 5 ammo types to use, quick one, powerful one so on, this adds decision making to the player about which ammo to use when but as they have gone for this approach rather then changing guns implies lazy programming and minimises the possible extremes of which can be offered through the gun system.

The game is early access and has a good skeleton currently but the fate of this game is going to revolve for me around innovation. tl;dr:
good little game, take survivor squad and remove the squad management component for a more hand on action.
It's very early so lot of feature are basic but it got some decent work in it.
The game is pretty much shown in the trailer and demo.
Zombie Horde survival on cramped map with sonar radar and noise. You got different ammo type to help you in your fight
Rapid fire to quickly dispatch weak zombie or group, spread shot for the shotgun enthusiast, power and heavy shot to deal more damage.
The darkness coupled with the narrow field of view will keep you on your toe as you progress through the wave of zombie growing stronger.
Now for the downside.
•The map feel a bit too small, especially if you add more people.
•For now there's no visual difference with ammo type, you have a pistol that can support a wide variety of ammo (maybe in future it will change.) but each ammo type doesn't have a specific trail to help you or other know what you're using.
•You can't rebind the control BUT it support both qwerty and azerty, and it's not a big issue as you only need to move and shoot with the mouse, no fluff.
•The sonar radar seems a bit clunky it work and sometime it doesn't, so dont entirely rely on it to know where the zombie are.
But for 5$ game, it's quite good and well made and fun to play.

Yeah, it's pretty good. Been playing Isaac since the original iteration, and it really is everything it's hyped up to be.
Complaints? Eh, I miss Danny Baranowsky's tracks. (The new tracks are undeniably good and IMO more atmospheric, but Baranowsky's ones are better standalone tracks IMO) Bloat and Mama Gurdy are unfair boss fights. (even though Bloat's BS can be dodged and Mama Gurdy becomes a joke if you get flight) Sometimes, RNG can give you the middle finger.
But Isaac's main strength above other roguelites IMO is the fact that
That's why it rules so much and why it's still the king of its genre. Games like Enter the Gungeon or even FTL are good roguelites, but they don't have this. Isaac is filled with opportunities for overpoweredness. There are multiple item combinations in the game which allow you to become literally unkillable (and yes, this is deliberate on behalf of the devs, it's half the fun of Isaac). You can always play Isaac to reroll items you don't like. There are tricks like Blood Banks + invincibility that experienced players can exploit and use to their advantage, and knowing your item pools/effects can mean you can become ridiculously powerful.
Hell, on the day I'm writing this review, a fairly poor ??? run that I was barely able to get to The Chest had me find Undefined. Because I knew what Undefined does, and what I AM ERROR rooms do on The Chest and similar floors, I was able to utilise it to repeatedly restart the Chest and farm its items, creating one of my most overpowered runs of all time out of a fairly average run. RNG got me Undefined, but knowledge is what got me to the end point of being able to kill ??? in 5 seconds flat.
This game is the face that launched a thousand roguelites for a reason, and it's absolutely worth a try.

This game has a lot more depth to it than you might think, looking at just the screenshots of classic top down sprite imagery.
Not only is there a decent basic storyline to the campaigns, but there are lots of branching options for players; with different results obtained from different choices selected.
The writing is ok, mostly standard classic RPG fare, but good enough.  The campaign alternates between telling the story through text dialogue, and then tactical turn based combats.  the combat system is actually quite good, and lends itself to multiple ways of conquering your enemies.  Use blockers and magic or ranged attacks, or rely on crushing melee charges to disrupt your enemies formations, eschewing the ranged attacks for more risky but often quicker victories.  Some enemies have resistances to certain attacks; for example,  skeletons are highly resistant to any standard ranged attack, so require alternate strategies to deal with them.  necromancers can hang back and continue raising their own dead (or the enemy's!), or use their powers to manipulate the tide of battle dirrectly.  Lots and lots of choices, which makes replayability rather high.
This game is also extremely easy to mod, and even includes a basic map editor.  The unit files and campaign files can be easily extracted from the main .jar files using winrar, and are basic text files that can be edited in any ascii editor like notepad+, and then re-compressed into the main game files.   This leaves the player with endless abilities to modify how units work, making even MORE tactical game-replayability, or you can even write your own campaigns!
overall, game is well worth the price.

Street Fighter IV is the sole reason why fighting games made a comeback when they were at the edge of fading away. If you ask anyone who takes fighting games seriously this game is incredibly important and obviously has a huge following. Its greatest strengths come in finding a way to reintroduce characters from previous games in a setting that dosent screw the story up as bad as SF3 did and at the same time maintain a presentation that has become iconic since its initial release. This game has had WAY too many re-releases in forms of newer versions that that includes the most recent update "ULTRA Street Fighter IV" coming out early next year, but obviously if this game has been going strong for THIS LONG, it must be doing something right. Now, from my own personal opinion, i think a good number of the "new" characters they tried to introduce alongside the classic roster dont really have the same magic as the classics, especially El fuerte and Rufus, but that might just be me. Either way, this game is worth the time and money if you intend on buckling down and seriously practicing and playing as much online and local competition as possible. The online is good, netcode is far better than most PC fighters we get with the exception of GGPO netcode games. I suppose in a way, this game is great for both beginners who get exposure to many of the best classic characters without having to play the older games and its worthy of getting the attention of seasoned veterans. If you look at SFIV's track record, you can argue, but you wont get far. 9/10

Age of Fear is, at its core, a turn-based tactical game about small unit battles similar in feel to Battle for Wesnoth. It has some RPG elements and a unifying story for each campaign, along with the occasional text adventure-like choice to make. The battle system is strong and well balanced. The game is not hex-based and allows for free movement. It takes a bit to get used to how you can effectively use melee units to block access to your ranged/spellcaster units, but once you get the hang of it, it is a thing of beauty.
As a single-player game I found it a bit short; I finished the campaign in about 15 hours on Normal. I would have liked to see more content; I enjoyed each aspect of the game (the battles, the ongoing campaign, text choices, unit recruitment and development, building up my heroes with items and such) but felt that I really wanted to see more of each. The concept and elements came together well, but I was left wanting more. I ended up purchasing this at full price (about $13) after playing through the Age of Fear 2 campaigns; the developers are retroactively updating AoF to match the AoF2 updates/patches, so it was worth it to me.
