I also get why they split the open world into two sections to provide a new set of tougher orcs, but the general lack of desire to return to the older areas and the repetition of these same enviornments in the DLC was quite dissapointing. It felt like a game that strived to check boxes off in its creation of the expected open world without fully grasping what makes exploration fun in the first place. The lack of pay off with the wall symbols as well as the artifacts didn't help either. Kept thinking there would be something, but never was. Just things to collect.
Regardless, the Nemesis system is as always an absolute blast, and there are some standout encounters I still cherish upon retrospect. The designs never failed to surprise, and the voice acting was phenomenal in every regard. Cannot wait to see how it's built upon. Combat is as smooth as a bat, of course, and branding once unlocked changed the game entirely. Shoddy story execution gave way to perfectly paced leveling and challenge. Even at the most overpowered, it's easy to make simple mistakes or plan poorly to where your maxed out Talion could have his face slammed into the mud. Since the Nemesis system doubles as a perfect punishment for death as well, I always felt vengeful at any death. So well thought out.
Don't know why I took the time to write all this, but an absolute blast on the cheap. I feel bad for those who spent full price on that dlc, because The Lord of the Hunt should've been in the base game, but otherwise this is a great package. Snag it on sale.

Shellshock live is a PvP Strategy game in the same vein as the worms series
Matchmaking/Community~ The bad thing about it is that players with no connection to the internet are a bit out of luck.  The good news is that this game can run on pings somewhere in the stratosphere. Matchmaking is easy to figure out, and you'll almost always have a match to join.  The community is pretty good as well, most people are generally nice, though a grand majority of them aren't particularly talkative.
Gameplay~ The gameplay is essentially a turn based volley of (occasionally) flashy attacks.  The game's physics engine doesn't allow for the floating islands or death-by water of worms, nor does it allow you to take control of an entire team, but rather be part of a team of other players (or go for free for all).
Variety~ The variety is wonderful on all fronts, from the hundreds of weapons, to the dozens of maps, to even a decent amount of varied and fun gamemodes.  The weapons, for the most part, feel very different, and all do differnt things.  The only problem is that some are undoubtedly less powerful than others, so RNG can make the game slightly infuriating at times.  The maps, unlike the Gamemodes and Weapons, can feel rather same-y, which is more a fault of the game's physics engine then a lack of creativity.
Character Customization~ Shellshock has a couple of interesting ideas in the customization department.  Not only do aesthetic options for your tank open up as you level up more, but it has a full fledged skill tree.  You can upgrade four different parts of your tank, those being: crit chance, movement speed and climbing ability, extra health in the form of armor, or luck, which lets you get better weapons in a few different ways.  There are three pronounced skills within each tree, all of which help out in a bigger way.
Story~ There really isn't any story to speak of.  If you're looking story, look elsewhere.
Sound~  The sound design is nice.  The sound effects for firing and landing attacks are satisfying, and the music is fittingly epic, etc.  Another thing the game has is tracks that play after you or your team wins, and they're mostly passable, though some can get a bit annoying.
Why wouldn't you want this game? ~
~ If you need a good story in a game. (1)
~ If your wi-fi is non existant. (2)
~ You don't like the map variety (3)
~ It sounds interesting, but not 7.00 USD interesting.
What to get instead ~
~ As strange is this sounds, there are a good number of flash games that have a decent story and similar gameplay, check out ArmorGames or MaxGames for something like that. (1)
~ Worms Armageddon has a passable single-player mode. (2)
~ The Worms series has a physics engine that better lends itself to varied and interesting maps. (3)
~ I'd again suggest the free flash games (4)

Kickstarter has brought us a good handful of smash hits, such as Undertale and Shovel Knight, as well as shigh-profile mishaps like Might No. 9 and Yogventures. Some great games, meanwhile, fly relatively under the (read: my) radar, both during crowdfunding and after release. One such sleeper is MidBoss’ Read Only Memories, a Snatcher-esque adventure game featuring a colorful cast and engaging story, as well as impressive inclusivity and accommodation for all genders and sexualities.
You take the role of a journalist (name and gender up to you) in 2064 Neo-San Francisco, a thriving tech mecca home to bleeding-edge corporations like Parallax, The Augmented Eye, and, never forget, ~Hassy~. After meeting a sapient robot - supposedly the first - you become embroiled in a plot of intrigue and subterfuge. Along the way to unravel its many twists and resolve the ultimate conflict, you meet a number of engaging characters, from a genetically modified hybrid rights lawyer to a pseudo-sapient polar bear, each with extensive, cleverly written dialogue and fulfilling developmental arcs - that is, if you play your cards write. Dialogue choices throughout determine which of the many endings you get; if you’re an♥♥♥♥♥to everyone you meet, there may be no one to back you up in the final push towards resolution. No matter how you choose to play your character, you’re free to explore Neo-SF and hear a considerable amount of well-developed world-building. The writers at MidBoss did their best to explore what several relevant aspects of our society will look like in fifty years, from energy drinks (~Hassy~) to North Korea. Key issues of 2064 revolve around human augmentation, whether it’s genetic or cybernetic; this and other major societal shifts factor greatly into the story’s events. There’s a lot to take in, but ROM doles out the info at a very manageable pace, so you always feel like you’re learning rather than overwhelmed.
As far as gameplay, it controls like your standard point-and-click PC adventure circa 1992. Any interactable you click will give you up to four options: Look, Talk, Touch, and/or Use. You could blaze through the game only using the prompts you need, but there is an honestly vast amount of writing to be discovered by getting creative with your prompts - I highly recommend taking the spoiled milk with you at the beginning and using it on everything possible. Also: talk to plants. Talk to every plant. The game is enjoyable enough when sticking to the critical path, but searching out every optional text and dialogue option is well worth your time.
It’s also worth mentioning that LGBTQ inclusivity was a major goal of MidBoss’ (a good quote from founder Matt Conn: “ Instead of waiting for Sony and other big companies to include gay characters in their games as more than just tokens, we should just do it ourselves”), and they certainly succeeded on that front. It’s refreshing to play a game where such inclusivity feels so normal. It’s never shoved in your face, and none of the characters feel like forced tokens - it’s just people being people.
Read Only Memories is a clever, thoughtful, and truly entertaining game that will leave you wanting more. The world of 2064 Neo-SF is exciting, it’s inhabitants funny, kind, and interesting. I rarely give games the time for repeat playthroughs, but I’m honestly itching to find those other endings. If you’re a fan of classic adventure, murder mystery, solid world-building, or the cyberpunk aesthetic, I can’t recommend Read Only Memories highly enough.

Do you like AI, especially AI that have prominent roles as characters? This story is for you.
Do you like being able to see queer people represented in story? This story is for you.
If you like both of those things, the story is doubly for you.
A brief snapshot: The story starts with the introduction of Turing, a chatty little robot who seeks out your help after the disappearance of your old friend Hayden (Turing's creator). This is Turing's first time being independently apart from Hayden - basically, an important formative stage for them, so the majority of character growth you see is from them.
The main heart of the story is Turing, and your feelings on them are going to probably majorly affect how you feel about the rest of the story.
The story tells of AI development from a somewhat kindly perspective - one that is a bit more focused on the development of an individual than most. It's pretty rare to have stories centered around AI actually focus on them as characters and not the problems of the human who is dealing with them, so I thought that was a really enjoyable aspect of the story.
The game has a nice soundtrack,; it sets the mood for the era the story is in. The characters are pretty fun, and you get to meet a myriad of them, all of who can form different opinions of you by the end game. They range in positions too, from law-abiding detectives to criminals to well meaning people who are somewhere in-between.
If any of those elements sound appealing, I do recommend it. It could do with more options in some places, but I was really happy with the elements it handled that I enjoy, and if you like the kinds of story elements the game advertises  I think you'll ultimately be pretty happy with it.

I’m a huge fan of the show Game Center CX, localized once upon a time as Retro Game Master, where I watch Shinya Arino struggle with difficult old games that I never plan to put my hands on, ever. While watching him, though, I’ve seen episodes where he’s wrangled with games that I’d never heard of; adventure and mystery games that were either rare or completely unavailable in North America. Watching Arino-san play The Portopia Serial Murderer Incident and the Jake Hunter series has left this nerd girl particularly hungry for more point-and-click mystery games neck-deep in story. I want game makers to give me more Hotel Dusk, Ace Attorney and even L.A. Noire.
Read Only Memories tapped right into that desire with such pointed direction, it’s as if MidBoss read my mind. Or maybe there was a demand out there from more people than just me. Not only did they make a story-rich mystery adventure game, they made a cyberpunk story-rich mystery adventure game, inspired by games like Kojima’s long-lost Snatcher. While I’m still waiting for more can-you-solve-the-mystery games, I enjoyed every minute of Read Only Memories and I humbly require no less than a hundred sequels.
The story starts with you, an investigative journalist living in squalor in Neo-San Francisco. After writing a review for the low low earnings of “exposure”, a small robot shows up at your house in the night. Turing is the first autonomous AI, and his creator – your friend, Hayden – has been kidnapped. Turing enlists your help because he knows you’re poor, bored, and a super sleuth. Together, you navigate Neo-San Francisco on the hunt for clues.
Read Only Memories brings forth a refreshing new brand of cyberpunk that isn’t based in the cynicism of the 90s like Snatcher or Shadowrun. ROM takes place in 2064, where heroes and villains are at work through greed, goodness or revenge in equal measure. The purest hearts have prickly exteriors, and the warm and forthcoming may have ulterior motives, and each character is a well-thought-out artefact of the world that they grew out of. The vibe of ROM is more realistic than a lot of science fiction I’ve encountered in some time, and I cannot praise the writers highly enough for that.
As an LGBT+ creator myself I also feel the need to point out to others the levels of inclusion that exists in ROM. Early in the game Turing creates a login system for you, where you identify your name, pronouns of choice, and diet preferences. There are many pronoun options, including one where you can put in custom ones not listed. Detective Lexi Rivers is your sister’s ex-girlfriend, and the two burly male bartenders are in love. One of your main contacts, Tomcat, is explicitly non-binary. Gender and sexuality are a non-issue fifty years from now, but other problems of discrimination have arisen thanks to the times. Hybrids who have adopted animal genes often to remedy disabilities are discriminated against, along with people who augment their lost sight with cyborg eyes and so forth. These things are valuable in an earth-based science fiction story for two reasons:
1. Disabled people and LGBTQA are featured as window-dressing, which is entirely how we prefer to be featured. Our existences by this story’s 2064 has been so normalized that it is no longer an issue and is barely worth being mentioned in the narrative, except that it is there. This is smart world building as well as a responsible storytelling technique that has been executed with amazing tact.
2. This is a perfect example of something I mentioned earlier about cyberpunk realism as opposed to cynicism: while we have won several battles, several more lie before us. There will always be struggles in life, but progress has been made. It is not a dystopia, and it is not a utopia. It’s realistic.
I don’t want to spoil too much about the fascinating measures of worldbuilding that takes place in Read Only Memories. I just have to implore you to play it for yourself, especially if you’re like me and value story in a game above all else. The point-and-click setup of an adventure game is tried and true, and you can take your time to make choices and digest all of the optional dialogue about VR Drama developers in Japan, and Turing’s favorite types of trees, or not. Make yourself a classy drink, curl up in bed with your laptop, and enjoy Read Only Memories like a good book.

A game that old school RPG players waited for a long time. A true isometric RPG in Baldur's Gate style. Fantastic gameplay where tactical combat is more important than fast clicking. For example, the old/new stats system really make you question and forces you to think seriously when it comes to choosing your weapon or armour that grants specific attribute bonuses, or, for that matter, when you are creating you character.
The endurance - health system is also one of the factors you must consider when you enter a battle, because, when you lose all the endurance in the battle you get knocked out. When the battle is over you regain your senses, but you lose health. The only way to regain your health is by sleeping in the Inn, using the camping supplies, and, of course, keeping an eye out on the endurance levels all together, because, when your character health is depleted, he/she will die.
There are so many things you can do in the game and you can easily be side-tracked, but, as it happens, the main story doesn't get lost in the mix. It only expands, whether it is by adding the content and backstory to your companions, or by upgrading your stronghold and solving quests inside it.
All in all, it is a great kickstarted game for the die hard and greenhorn RPGers alike.

I have to admit, I feel little but indifference over this story. I got it because I saw that the reviews overall were positive and the price was reasonable... and it was, in the technical sense, a very well-made game (lovely visuals, nice sound design, smooth running), but nothing groundbreaking, and nothing I would go out of my way to recommend to someone. It's overall a run-of-the-mill kind of experience, and while I enjoyed myself for the time being, had it cost any more than what it did, frankly, I would be quite disappointed.
For pros, the art is quite beautiful (although clearly drawn in at least three distinct styles), the music is atmospheric, and the writing is, even at its weakest, no worse than mediocre... but I've got to say, it didn't leave me wanting to go back and explore the other options, and I'm not sure if I'll remember the details in, let's say, a week's time.
As for cons, the plot is pretty predictable if you've ever read anything similar. The main character wasn't charming or relatable, and not even the hollow shell these protagonists tend to be- in fact he was quite unpleasant, and purposefully choosing the nicest dialogue options didn't seem to change that. (And I also kind of lament the fact that he is a HE, but that's not really a complaint, it would have however been a nice touch to have the option to play as a woman.) The father character was almost cartoonishly evil, and I found myself struggling not only to empathize with him, but also to take him seriously, and Lucy... Well, Lucy is an enigma, somehow managing to be both charming, and mildly insulting.
Simply put, she struck me as a cookie-cutter "yamato nadeshiko" character; a bit of an immature fantasy, but compared to the rest of the cast, quite pleasant in her own way. I was more bothered by how basically every line of dialogue concerning her dealt with every character blatantly objectifying her, and while she IS in the technical sense a literal object, with the game continuously giving us cues to think of her as a person, and giving us a fully (and well!) voiced character and the inserted vignettes about her creation, and in the end, showing us her irrational, devotion... it gains this icky, casually misogyniystic overtone... which would be fine to talk about and discuss, but with the framing of it all, I don't think the game realizes that that is one of the issues it tackles, rather it's just, alarmingly enough, a part of it.
For a casual afternoon's read, it's fine, and worth its price- but, if you're very into either sci-fi or drama, this game will probably leave you disappointed.
(I quite liked the ending I got though, it was pretty unexpected with its cold turkey way of handling loss. It was interesting, if alienating, although I really don't much feel like going back for more.)

- the game mechanics when it comes to battle are a bit too fuzzy for my taste.You don't often get a sense of "whoa, I want this weapon" or "nice armor" that was one of the biggest things in Baldur's Gate series. In Pillars of Eternity it's more like "meh, I really don't know if this is an improvement or not and I don't really know what caused us to win the battle". It is a bit too fuzzy and unintuitive when it comes to battle mechanics. I enjoy more clear systems where +1 means something and you know you don't have enough points yet.
- too many npcs in comparison to party size. I hate it when you have 3-4 characters waiting in line and you want to have chat with each one of them and play the story with each one of them but you can't because they don't fit in your active party. Does a robot have a soul? Especially if it's a kawaii android girl?
This question has been a central theme in quite a few visual novels and anime shows already. Just to name two of the earliest entrants:
and
came out more than a decade ago.
So then, what novelty does Lucy -The Eternity She Wished For- bring to the table? Personally, I particularly liked that the premise of the story was something believable, presenting a very plausible real-life scenario in the future.
The story takes place in 2050s Korea, where everything is much like it is now, except with improved robotics technology. (No mention of North Korea is made. Huehue.)
There is no dystopian setting or over-the-top sci-fi. Unlike
, robots have not taken over the world.
As the main character, aptly named "You", you discover an abandoned android girl in a junkyard. Against your better judgement you decide to bring it home, despite both You, and in particular your father (who was very creatively named "Father") having a dislike for androids. Thus your new life with an android companion begins...
There are no hints of real romance between You and the android Lucy, unlike shows such as
or
. Some people might be disheartened to hear this, but I find the lack of romantic development to be a good thing in this case. It keeps the story focused, not detracting from real-life philosophical issues concerning robotics, such as Theseus's Paradox, The World as Will and Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics. The story actually makes references to these without coming across as pretentious, which is really cool. Who says you can't learn new things from videogames?
Lucy -The Eternity She Wished For- is the first VN I've played that was published by a Korean developer, M-Vizlab. I don't know if it's a issue of certain things being lost in translation, but I found the writing to be less expressive and colorful than
or
. It isn't poor by any standards though - I've gone through far worse writing in some other VNs, even by Western publishers... The art and soundtrack were definitely more than serviceable, on par with good Japanese studios. Lucy is a real cutie, she literally seems to be radiating with cheerfulness!
The story ends on a sad note :( This seems to be a running theme amongst all the visual novels and anime featuring human-robot relationships. The feels trip isn't as hard as
, but you'd have to be a robot to not feel anything during the end.
One shortcoming to note: the game has achievements, but they have not been integrated into Steam. It's a bit of a shame considering how well done the achievement system is, with different icons and descriptions for every individual achievement. Sorry to all the achievement hunters out there :x
If you enjoyed
, by all means you can't go wrong with this VN. There are many parallels to be drawn, but I find Lucy -The Eternity She Wished For- to be a title more grounded in reality, and to be the more thought-provoking of the two.

Forced is a neat little Action RPG puzzle couch co-op game. Maybe a cross between DotA/LoL + WoW + Portal 2. In short you are solving puzzles in a dungeon/instances with your partner while mobs attack you.
Imagine sitting together with your 360 controllers (or on skype) running around avoiding a laser beam while trying to kill mobs that are attacking you. Meanwhile your co-op partner is aligning Balfus (a floating orb) in a straight line towards you and screaming at you to pull the orb so that it goes through a shrine that stops a deadly mists that is slowly filling the dungeon. You pull the orb towards you but just when the orb is about to turn off the the mist your co-op partner gets pinned by a mob he didn't avoid and needs to call the orb back to him to free himself. Now the mist is out of control and your coop partner is low on health. This is a basic scenario in Forced.
The game has several dungeons/levels that you have to complete. Each dungeon rewards a total of 3 crystals. One for completing the dungeon, one for a speed/timed run and one for completing with a special requirement (e.g no healing, not getting hit by a special mob, etc).
Before each dungeon you choose to play one of four available classes. A warrior, rogue, hunter and a tank. Every class has two talent trees: One tree for active talents and one for passive talents. As you earn more crystals you unlock more of your talents.  You get to choose 3 active and 3 passive skills. That means that you have 4 buttons to press: One for basic attack and three for active talents.
This is a game where you can play competitvely and min/max what class and what spec to play for eac dungeon. make a tactic and practice exucuting it impeccably or you can grab a 360 controller and have fun with your girlfriend on the couch.

Edit: I decided to remake this review to be more clear. I'm not much for numerical reviews but if I had to give this game one it'd be a 5/10.
The game is amazing and if you've played similar games and enjoyed them then it may be worth enduring the bugs to play this one. I think it actually shows how good the game is since most other games would be trash if they showed these porting issues, and that makes the issues this game has all the more regretable.
It doesn't have many graphical options. DSFix is basically required but that can add bugs of it's own, like the ladders sending you through the floor that I mentioned in my original review. It can also add game crashes, though this may just be me since I seem to be very unlucky with this game.
Connecting to others isn't great either so I had to use Wulf's Dark Souls Connectivity Mod, and still getting to coop with your friends can take up to 10-20 mins for their sign to appear so you can summon them.
As for the game itself there are a few negatives but they're pretty minor, I don't pvp because I suck at it so this is all PvE stuff. The game is balanced for single player so cooping will shatter the difficulty making even some of the harder bosses simple. The game feels like it favors int builds, magic is ranged (tends to be safer) and can hit hard (with enough int you can peel off 1/5 a bosses health or more with some spells). There are weapons that scale entirely with int (unlike faith) and there's also the moonlight greatsword which has S int scaling and a built-in ranged attack. Lastly, the game is based on offense, this is an issue alot of RPG games have though. It's better to get as much damage as you can to finish a fight fast than to stack any survivability. Plenty of people run these entire game naked, or without leveling, or both and it really makes armor feel worthless.
Watch out for the skeleton dogs...

State of Decay.. Where to start.
I got the demo of this game, when it first released on the Xbox 360, as an Arcade game, and it took me about 15 minutes of gameplay, before i decided to buy it. Even though it had some bugs, and quite annoying moments, the game grew on me, and as i progressed through the storyline, the game got better and better. As soon as you get comfortable with the controls, you'll have a great time with State of Decay.
The storyline is in my opinion really great, i really grew attached to Marcus, Ed and Maya, and only used them, even when i got to the Church in Spencers Mill. But on my first playthrough, i lost Marcus  not long after reaching the church, and eventually lost Ed to Black Fever, which is truly my own fault, and not being to careful. When you progress longer into the storyline, you learn more about Trumball Valley, and some of it's history, and about the Army. I got the feeling, that the Army, were ignoring the helpless survivors in Trumball Valley, and only wanted to find out, what caused this mess. So a feeling of truly standing alone, really helped creating a great and 'scary' atmosphere, which exists in Trumball Valley.
I eventually moved over to the PC version, which in the start were a quite bad port over in my opinion, but the developers managed to get it working, just as good as the 360 version. And when Breakdown were annonced, i couldn't wait to grab it, just to get challenged even more, since this game haven't got a difficulty system.
The graphics, can sometimes be annoying, and look like crap, even on ultra settings, but i can live with that, when the game has so much good to offer. In my opinion it's the best zombie game out there, because of all the great things you can do, and every single action that you do, has consequences in one way or the other. I can't help to grow attached to my favorite, and most skilled survivors, you decide their history once you take control of them, you decide wether they will stick to the homebase, or be the guy/girl who is taking charge of the community, and lead the attacks or scavenging runs. But when the worst possible thing happens, and i can see that my survivor aren't going to survive this encounter, with a zombie horde i get this fuzzy feeling, a truly sad moment, when somebody dies. It's especially sad, when i alone, are the reason for their death...
I really recommend this game, to any fans of the zombie universe out there, sure it has some bugs, and annoying things, but all games have that, and i think that this game makes up for it, in features and atmosphere.
I'll rate this game 10/10, and i hope others will get just as great moments with this game, as i've had.

I actually enjoyed this mode way more than the campaign mode, which was frankly very difficult for me. No points off there, though maybe a controller would make for better gameplay (I have only a mouse and keyboard). This game is the spiritual successor of a genre that has been largely ignored but has come back in a big way, capturing the old fans, drawing in new fans, and everyone in between. I am ChocolatierGames with Computerfiguur’s Network and today I will be taking a look at Shell Shock Live.
Cannon Fodder
Shell Shock Live is a 2d tank game, similar to the likes of Scorched Earth, or if we want to go even earlier… Gorillas. You play as a tank trying to destroy other tanks and sometimes targets. Simple right? Not exactly… SSL is chock full of customization, with items, new bullets, and when playing the multiplayer, various obstacles that appear on each turn. This variation ensures that no two games will be the same, and each fight will be a challenge. The first thing that grabbed me was after each level up you unlock a new weapon, and upon my first unlock it shows you the SHEET of weapons you can unlock, each with multiple stages of power. This was at first a bit overwhelming, but I soon came to look forward to each upgrade.
Whimsy
SSL doesn’t take itself too seriously, in the weapons department, I can launch my standard bullets, or I can launch cats, or I can launch bananas. This is a bit silly at first but then falls a bit flat, as the rest of this game doesn’t match the humor, my biggest suggestion on what they can do is add in the little sort of “damn you” that the tanks give off before they die in Scorched Earth. That would help keep the humor consistent throughout the game, instead of just being an afterthought.
HD neon
SSL steps away from the pixel art style of its predecessors, using smooth edges and semi high definition art, that isn’t on its own too substantial, but there is one factor that makes it look amazing. The lighting in SSL is some of the best lightings I have seen in a 2d game, and it is on everything. The bullets, the tanks, the barriers, the powerups, the supply crates EVERYTHING has this superb glow that makes everything pop, and stand out from other objects. This distinct look is awesome and really shows off how lighting can make a game great.
Ready, Aim, Fire
The game controls fairly well, and intuitively instilling total noobs like me with false confidence (until you get to the multiplayer that is). You control with a hybrid of A and D for your movement and the mouse for aiming. I was concerned that SSL would rely on the arrow keys for aiming, and I am glad that isn’t the case. The early turns will employ a lot of trial and error, as you get your shots dialed in against your partner, and then you will have to account for their and your movement as staying in one place is not the best idea. Some weapons work with this and help you get some damage in early without requiring a ton of skill, and some will reward your diligent aiming with high damage outputs. All of this put together gives a gameplay scheme that feels and looks good to play with.
Wham Bam Alakazam
The Sound effects and music are both good. Wouldn’t say it is anything to write home about necessarily in the SFX department, but the music does do a good job of maintaining the energy. SSL uses metal and rock tracks instead of your standard electronic music, which is a nice break from the norm. And while I can’t see myself downloading the soundtrack, it served its purpose well and was pleasant to listen to.
Better Find Some Friends
The multiplayer for SSL is the main component, and while the single player missions can be fun, you will want to play against others. The multiplayer is very extensive, and multiple modes are available. It is super easy to set up your own match and then you have swaths of customizable options. Things like whether or not you want the wind, how much HP you want all the players to have, and choose the map. The latter one is important, as the default option is a random map, which can end up with you being screwed in a hole for the majority of the game. This is helped after the first 10 turns when, provided you don’t die, the terrain levels a bit and each player get supply crates of weapons. The multiplayer is fun, and the community is decent, considering how other gaming communities are (a cough).
Overall
Shell Shock Live is an entertaining experience. Revitalizing a long dead genre with just the right improvements. The humor fell a bit flat, and the SFX were boring at times, but the art style, lighting, and gameplay were superb. Pack that in with loads of customization and replayability and you get yourself an 8 out of 10 games with a label of “hectic”.

I will admit this is one of the few games I have actually bought right on release day. I'm glad I didn't wait.
Night In The Woods is a fantastic adventure game set in a small nearly dead town, yet has an array of characters you can talk to and learn about throughout the story. It's impossible to get to know everyone and do everything in the first playthough and will require you to play through the game multiple times to learn everything there is to know about these characters. The story is very rich in this game, going far deeper and emotional than I perceived it would beforehand, hitting close to home with the topics of mental illness and just living day to day life in a boring job with no hope of escape, but also throwing in some fun stuff. This game is not age appropriate as i thought it would be. A lot of cursing and dark tones, but very glad this was put in the game. It adds to the matureness of the game and I wouldn't have it any other way.
I will also admit though that there are a couple issues I have that I wanna mention, but they arent gamebreaking and shouldn't push you away from this little masterpiece of a game. There is a lot of talking in this game, and i mean a lot of talking, which leaves the background open to either silence, a bit of music, or a mix of both with outdoor sound effects. There's no actual voice actors in the game, so when the characters talk, its all just reading subtitles, which kinds sucks but isn't a dealbreaker for me. Just a bummer, although I'm confused because you can hear someones voice making certain sounds like groans or sighs and such every now and then which leads me to belive they could have done voices, but it is a small developer team so I won't fault them for it.
Another thing that kinda bugged me was that at times the main character felt like I had no control over how situations went. There are times you can choose a couple things to say, but it can end up spiraling out of control and kinda loses me at times, like why on earth would I say these things? This is a terrible thing to say and nobody in their right mind would say it. Again, not a dealbreaker.
Overall this game is fantastic and is definetely worth the $20. Fantastic story, nice visuals and atmosphere, decently lengthed story as well, a short 6 hours for my playthrough but does have replayability so most likely about 15-20 at least to go through everything, well drawn out side characters and a message that you'll never forget. Just buy the game, it's completely worth every penny.

A satisfying core game with some dissapointing DLC. Get this for the dirt cheap price it gets listed for nowadays though and it is worth every penny. I do hope the more recently announced sequel builds off of the good bits while hopefully learning from the plentiful mistakes this game had, found specifically in the story, mission structures, and traversal.
Story was about as banal as it could possibly be, but hit enough right notes to never fully turn off. Some fun characters that ultimately felt under used and more in place to just move things along. Torvin was fun, but the true highlight for me was Ratbag. Completely underutilized but charming for all he was worth. Traversal was always a pain, as it was nowhere near as refined as the games it mimicked, with plenty of mismatched movement that would lead to some amazingly frustrating situations. As far as mission structures go, if I ever have to rescue another 3 - 5 slaves over some asinine reasoning ever again I will cry. They repeated this structure 24 times with no variation outside of enviornment and dialogue. Miserable, even for a completionist like me. The DLC tried some new things in this regard but they were  both so short I never felt any marked improvement. I also get why they split the open world into two sections to provide a new set of tougher orcs, but the general lack of desire to return to the older areas and the repetition of these same enviornments in the DLC was quite dissapointing. It felt like a game that strived to check boxes off in its creation of the expected open world without fully grasping what makes exploration fun in the first place. The lack of pay off with the wall symbols as well as the artifacts didn't help either. Kept thinking there would be something, but never was. Just things to collect.
Regardless, the Nemesis system is as always an absolute blast, and there are some standout encounters I still cherish upon retrospect. The designs never failed to surprise, and the voice acting was phenomenal in every regard. Cannot wait to see how it's built upon. Combat is as smooth as a bat, of course, and branding once unlocked changed the game entirely. Shoddy story execution gave way to perfectly paced leveling and challenge. Even at the most overpowered, it's easy to make simple mistakes or plan poorly to where your maxed out Talion could have his face slammed into the mud. Since the Nemesis system doubles as a perfect punishment for death as well, I always felt vengeful at any death. So well thought out.
Don't know why I took the time to write all this, but an absolute blast on the cheap. I feel bad for those who spent full price on that dlc, because The Lord of the Hunt should've been in the base game, but otherwise this is a great package. Snag it on sale.

Can’t believe how much Im enjoying this game.  Graphics would have been basic in the late 90s. There's lots of minor UI bugs. Even the story, while very good, is in places delivered with technically poor writing.  E.g. the section for the Faycastle mission has an extra ‘this’  - "The war didn't seem to have effected this them..."
So why’s the game so much fun? The grid free combat mechanics, while not without issue, create unusual tactical challenges.   More judgement than normal is needed to get the balance right between protecting your ranged units while not using such a tight formation that you hamper manoeuvrability.   The unit progression system is great; with individual named units you can upgrade over the course of the campaign. The best thing about the game is probably how all the elements cohere together.  The simple yet nicely plotted story. The primitive but often authentic sounding medieval music, which changes nicely to fit the mood. Basic yet well chosen ambient sound. Even the still art is nicely evocative.
If you’re not too bothered by a few minor bugs and would like a short and sweet fantasy medieval tactical combat game with retro presentation, this game is a great choice.

TLDR: Excellent but minimalist strategy RPG. Some micromanagement. Challenging.
AOF is a turn based strategy RPG. It's not grid  based like other SRPGs, however your units have individual stats that you  manage throughout the gameplay in order to defeat more and more difficult opponents.
Cons:
-No multiplayer matchmaking system, but has too few players/exposure.
-The graphics might be an issue for some. For me, I had a lot of fun. Like they say, don't judge a book by it's cover. This game is deep and can be difficult.
-The girl from the trailer is not in it.
Pros:
-Unit management and advancement requires you to make smart choices in order to survive. You may get to the point where if you've made poor choices, you can't go any further or you lose the level and have to go  back to a last save.
-Good story. A little minimalist, but again, this game is all about the game play.
-Varied and balanced unit compositions. You won't get to the last level and not lose a guy. You WILL be challenged.
Go check out a video and see if you can get past the visuals. If you're a strategy gamer you won't regret buying it.

I got it from Humble Bundle along with 2 other games I wasn't interested in for $1.50 (and donated nearly all of that amount to preserve the Sonoran desert), but it really is worth $20. The main plot, which I can't go into without spoiling, and the elements of artificial intelligence, human/animal hybrids, cyborgs, and robots (ROMs) were really cool. If you'll hear them out, Turing explains a lot of the history that led to the society of 2064, and the backgrounds of various future-tech companies, and it's fairly well fleshed out. And many of the characters were cool too, except Jess but you don't have to deal with her TOO much plus you can be pretty "catty" towards her if you want. Turing is a darling, if a bit too chatty at times, Ollie and Chad (alias "Star♥♥♥♥er") are really good kids, and TOMCAT is sort of hot.  The "gameplay" is actually really fun, a bit similar to Ace Attorney's system of investigating, gathering evidence, and talking with people. There's actually a fair amount of dialogue options, though I'm not sure to what extent they actually affect the plot. I got a good ending, and feel like a made some good friends, although I did not manage to save Wilty the jade plant unfortunately (RIP) :(.

A visually appealing but hollow experience, ROM plays more like an interactive novel than a game. This doesn't make it intrinsically bad, but without well-written characters or voice acting to accompany the interminable dialogue, it gets boring fast. (Does Detective Lexi have a personality outside of worrying about you and pining for your sister? jfc)
Oh, and the "man vs technology" thing is as old and tired as a cyberpunk setting can get. The pro-human group is called the Human Revolution ffs, they must have stayed up all night coming up with that one.
If I had to give ROM some positives, I'd say that the level of inclusiveness is nice (when it feels genuine and not like the developers are pandering to their audience) and the graphics have a gorgeous 16-bit look to them. Then again, if these factors are really important to you, you'd probably have more fun browsing Tumblr and playing Super Famicom games than wasting time on this verbose mess of borrowed ideas.

I bought this game as part of a Humble Bundle deal and started playing on a whim because I liked the art and what semblance of tone/plot I could gather from the screenshots and product description. Almost as soon as the game started, I already liked it - you get to choose your personal pronouns and there are queer* main supporting characters!
In large part, I am an enormous fan because of the player's interaction and relationship with the other main character, Turing. I don't think the emotional appeal of this game would be as strong without them. Through your dialogue choices with Turing, this game deeply explores the moral implications of such topics as sapient AI, genetic modification, human control of machinery, self-identification, among other things. And all of this with a healthy dose of humor!
Turing managed to make me tear up a couple of times and I've become quite attached. It's really hard not to like Turing, honestly, unless you hate the idea of someone exploring the meaning of their identity and existence.
Granted, there are a few cons:
- small plotholes, a couple of which I honestly didn't understand the significance of
- less puzzle-solving than expected (I personally would've liked to have worked harder for certain chapters)
- several under-utilized characters
Every day I take about an hour of my free time to finish up another chapter of the story. I haven't finished the game yet but this has been a very charming experience thus far! I'd play again, I think, just to see what effect being a total jerk would serve, but I think I know the answer to that already. (But mostly I'd play again for Turing.)

The year is 2065. The streets of New-Angeles are riddeled with cri- actually, everything is mostly alright. The world is at the crossroads of three technological singularities. The flames of conflict engulf the peoples and the warring sides settle their differences though democracy and peaceful process.
Needless to say, the author has a very idealistic view of the future..
Read Only Memories is an old school Point and Click adventure, drawing heavy inspiration from Snatcher and Policenauts in terms of its story and presentation. You take the role of a faceless reporter and blogger who wakes up to find a sentient robot sitting next to your bed. Unfortunately, the game doesn't permit you to throw your pillow at them and scream at the top of ones lungs, like one would do in real life.
What follows is a six hour long journey of conspiracies and espionage to uncover the fate of your mising friend with a help of a sillicon companion.
My first compaint with the story is its initial linearity, you are dragged out of your appartment and are nailed to the floor to sit and listen to ten minutes of exposition, followed by another ten minutes of exposition. Though the writing is fairly adequate, one cannot but feel that it could have been compressed or layed out more elegantly.
After that tunel of love, the game finally opens up, both in terms of exploration and the lore. The story takes a turn and introduces three subplots, simply though the player's exploration of the enviorment. Survelance state, radical gene splicing therapy and naturalist movement. Unfortunately, only one of those paths ends up having a propper conclusion, which makes me think that at least some of the content has been cut in development.
However, what carries the story are its characters.
By the time the little bobble head robot asks you about your prefered pronouns and gives you a three page list, you begin to understand what kind of message was trying to get across. The writer was aiming to present a cast of stark diverse characters and achieved this goal quite well. A character isn't defied by their skin colour, orientation, but by their.. well.. character.
Identity politics on the internet are quite a touchy subject, though the creator manages to handle the issue quite well. Most authors tend to get so hang up on creating an inclusive cast that they forget to actually write it, which leads to a room filled with multicoloured department store mannequins or Skyrim NPCs. My personal favourites are the pair of bartenders you meet at the pub and the splicing activist.
After solving a series of puzzles, the game begins holding your hand and then clunches it, like a paranoid mother. After the second act, the exploration ceases and "puzzles" become way too linear. Most players are upset when an adventure is impossible to complete without a guide or pilgrimage to GameFAQs, but this is taking things way too far in the other directions. Usually the puzzle solutions are a few pixels from the puzzle itself. Calling them puzzles would be like calling putting on tooth paste on a toothbrush a "puzzle".
A few minor story branches after, the game kicks you down a corridor for about 40 minutes before the end. There is one scene where your companion mentions where we could get a fake passport and hijack a car. They begins to describe a slum located away from the city, populated by outcast spliced human-animal hybrids.
Following a descrimination bill, many spliced individuals lost their homes and jobs and became vagrants. In order to defend their new home from extremist groups, many established backalley gene splicing clinics and began selling black market military grade mechanical augmentations. Having lost everything, they have shed their humanity in order to become something greater.
So, can we go there? No, instead we just talk to a few NPC's that we have already met and get the key items anyway.
The last ten minutes the game goes full on action, with stealth and shootouts, which are handled fairly well, despite not being central mechanics.
There are multible endings, each doing a pretty good job of wrapping up most of the loose ends. Some are just left hanging there..
All in all, I recommend Read only Memories or ROM (I get it now). A flawed, though fairly endeering adventure that managed to remain short and punchy, despite its linearity and pacing issues. My only wish it that it dug deeper in to the societal implications of radical transhumanism. A sequel, perhaps?
Anyway, I'm off to a gene clinic to get a cool new lizard tale.

For me, Starbound is a perfect example of love/hate relationship. A game stuck in Early Access hell until recently. A game clearly made with passion. A game made with modders in mind and made so chaotic it turns modders' life into a living nightmare.
But let's get it orderly.
Starbound, in a nutshell, is a sandbox. A 2D Terraria-like sandbox with a distinctive style. So while there is a main quest (arguably, unlike Terraria), it's not mandatory and you can throw it away almost instantly (gear and planet progression has almost no ties to it). In addition to "static" quests associated with the main storyline there are some "static" small ones, as well as "dynamic" auto-generated ones. You can delve into a (rather trivial) main quest, but the real charm of Starbound comes in the amount of freedom it gives you to do what you really like. Explore. Collect things. There are virtually TONS of collectable things, from clothing to pets to recipes to collectible in-game figurines to furniture (some of it you can craft through pixel printer using your money late in the game) to music instruments to food cuisines to... If you have a thing in mind, it probably can be collected. Build colonies from a single block and populate them with NPCs and traders (wiki gives you almost full control over spawning mechanics), then complete their quests and, eventually, hire them as combat companions or ship crew improving your ship. Expand your ship from a small space boat to a massive stellar fortress. Start a farm and grow hens. Search for NPC villages and unique dungeons. Make complex mechanisms using wiring mechanics and logic blocks. Tame poisonous and frigid oceans and build a colony on the seabed. Terraform the whole planet.
The weaknesses are in details and are ingrained in the game so deeply, it's almost impossible to get rid of them. Races, while initially different, now are practically the same - perhaps out of fear to be blamed in "disbalancing". There are no racial abilities, although every race has a distinctive visual style. There is no way to track the place you died at (that is, if you play vanilla Starbound; there are mods to fix that). There is no way to navigate a planet aside from by memory (there is no map or minimap, and that sucks). Bosses's battles are more straightforward and "casual", so don't expect building special arenas like in Terraria (last update addresses that to some extent). Some weather conditions are still frustrating (like sandstorms generating sand to bury your base: unlike water, there is no way to drain sand except manually. Or ash rains burning NPC villages on fire planets). Direct planet progression means you are stuck with fire, frozen and dark planets in late-game, although mini-biomes improve diversity (Terraformer may address that, haven't checked it out yet). Starbound offers many opportunities, but not all of them are explored. For example, while automatic weapon generation system is very interesting, the game offers no ways to customize it, and mods currently barely scratch the surface.
Modding Starbound is a story in itself. While Starbound is quite moddable and doesn't require special knowledge for simpler tasks, chaotic nature of the file structure makes modding a struggle. Dialogue lines are embedded directly into the game files instead of being referenced from a single location, so to translate the game you need to manually transform the file for any item that uses text lines. In other words, being a translator means being in a world of pain. The game directly supports only humanoid models, making non-humanoid custom races difficult (and basically making the whole variety of armor and vanity clothing unusable by them). Documentation is scarce; dig wiki a lot if you want to get some things the community found out through constant dev poking. There is no way to "patch" a game script, so while there can be mods changing the same item, there can't be mods changing the same script. Some things are hardcoded, but there is no distinct border between what can be changed and what can't, this knowledge is mostly limited to the community's trial and error experience (examples include most crafting interfaces and NPC facial rendering order - you can have eye color or eyelids as a separate layer but not both, meaning your custom character may either have colored eyes OR blink them; and if you think to use facial features' layer to do eyelids, you can't since they are rendered UNDER eyes). Overall, it is clear the devs lacked system approach and general view of their work - while the things work as they are, chaos rules over the insides of the game.
All and all, Starbound is a good example of a project where creative freedom rules over project management. Enjoy it as it is. Enjoy it with friends. But don't expect its numerous drawbacks to be addressed (any time soon). As with all things art, such improvements, while probable, will always be a surprise.

This is my first time writing a review, so don't expect a full review of the game that encompasses every aspect of it. I will share what I know with you guys (not including any spoilers), and the rest of you can take it as you will.
Now, let's get straight to it. I'll go through a few aspects of the game, and rate each accordingly to my opinion and preference, since this game has it's ups and downs, much like any other game out there.
Writing (7/10)
Most of the writings and dialogues done in the game is well-constructed and has a way of pulling you into the story, and make you feel like you are the protagonist in a real-situation instead of just in a game, since the situation can be very relatable. That being said, there are some parts where it could be better in terms of the writing, but not too bad that I would call it a "sloppy work". There are also parts of the writing what I would call unnecessary. Sometimes, the game tries to describe a situation too much, to the point that you feel it is not necessary to have that particular info. Other than those that I have touched, overall the writing serves it purpose in being able to pull the reader into the story. And, oh, one more thing, there are a few typos, but not a big deal, but since it is a game played by 1,000++ people, one would expect such mistakes shouldn't even be there.
Atmosphere (8/10)
The sound effects, visuals, and voice-acting was up to par. I was particularly impressed with the voice acting. They were really well done, in both Korean and Japanese. I'm not sure about the pronunciation and the technical stuff of the languages, but the emotions and feelings weaved into those  dialogues of Lucy was really well done. The sound effects are also impressive, although there is an issue. From what I noticed, the sounds (continuos sounds, played on a loop) are designed to fade out when needed. However, there are a few situations where it is better suited for the sound to end abruptly, rather than fading out (i.e knocking on doors). As for the visuals, the details of images was well done, but it would be better if the images change to fit the writings. For example, an image of the kitchen. When the writings described food being placed on the table, I would expect that the empty table in the kithen image would change with food being on it. But, alas, it is to be desired. Not a negative issue, but I think it would be an immersive improvement.
Story and Plot (8/10)
And here is the hard part. It's kinda hard to write this section without touching on any spoilers, so I'll be brief and to-the-point with this. The story has it's moments. There are times when you feel like you wanna punch someone, times that you wanna reach for that box of tissues, and times where you just wanna go "Aww
. And I feel that these situations were well engineered, so to speak. They fit the narrative pretty well, without feeling awkward or out of place. However, the choices in the game are a bit of a let down for me. They offer not much else than getting an achievement and maybe getting a few extra dialogues. And then there are choices that is just plain ridiculous. I feel more thought can be put into the choices, to make it feel more realistic and immersive.
Overall (8/10)
It is a pretty ride, with situations riddled with multiple emotions, or even just one emotion multiplied in intensity. One of the good VN's I've played. If you are searching for a laid-back game where you can just sit back and immerse in in without much effort, then I recommend this game to you. I feel players don't even play VN's should try it. For me, it acts as a good example on a good and well-made VN, with a few kinks here and there.

Definitely worth the sale price, and has some good musings on human-like machines - not on-par with "Blade Runner", but a reasonable facsimile of the same argument.  After all, if a machine's responses so closely mimic a human's, then who's to say those emotions aren't "real" simply because they come from electronics rather than biochemistry?

takes place in Korea in the year 2050. The world is much the same as our own, though with androids now becoming commonplace as they are used to help people in various capacities. You play as an anonymous male high school student who stumbles upon a broken android in a junkyard. He manages to activate it by accident and, after having it repaired, starts to realize that its ability to mimic human behavior is truly unparalleled. It is not long before his prior robot-hating ways start to change.
This game is a visual novel, a type of video game that is mostly story-driven. Indeed, much of the gameplay is just reading the story with a couple of choices along the way that change some of the dialogue. There are only two different endings to achieve in the game.
Starting off with the positive aspects, I thought the art was quite good. The backgrounds are very clean and detailed, even if some of the environments, such as a classroom, are more plain. The style used for most of the character sprites follows a rather standard anime style.
After seeing so many positive reviews for this game on Steam, I really looked forward to seeing what the story here had to offer. This is where I found disappointment with this game, especially considering the meat of any visual novel is the story. I looked forward to a game that dealt with themes such as human-android interactions and perhaps some heart-wrenching and emotional aspects. This game was lacking in both subjects. To start off with, the more philosophical aspects of the game are not well explored. There is some debate within the story if Lucy is really feeling things like emotions and having dreams of her own or if it is just an elaborate imitation. But that is really it. I usually avoid spoilers in reviews, but I feel I must include some light ones for this review.
As an adult, I found it difficult to sympathize at all with the protagonist. He often just seemed to come off as a standard whiny teenager. The emotional scenes fell flat because of these problems. I mean, would this story have worked in the slightest if Lucy was not depicted as a standard cute anime girl? Probably not.
Overall, though this game has some really good art, the story was seriously lacking. Perhaps it was too over-hyped with all of the positive reviews, but personally I found this game to be a seriously underwhelming experience.

Zenzizenzic is an in your face action shooter with retro-style shooter game elements that you will recall from the game asteroids. But this is no Sunday walk in the local arcade, but instead, a bullet hell shooter that is as challenging as it is to pronounce the games name! well if you want a challenging game, this is it. When you cannot even pass the first level like myself you know that you are in for a long night of action packed, ultra-addictive fun. As shown on the steam store page, the screenshots are quite the spectacle and yes each coloured box can hurt you, grey boxes give you points. These points are rewarded upon death or level completion and can be used towards upgrades and special abilities which specify how hard the ability is to master.
Fast gameplay is not a flaw as the game runs smooth as silk on my 3-year-old laptop however, I do not recommend playing this while transit or your head will spin. Jokes aside, there is a second mode in the game called Macro Mode which is an open world mode which is entertaining for 20 or so minutes. The Macro mode becomes more difficult as you move along the world, but don’t worry in both modes you can bring a buddy along to play with you locally. Also in macro mode, you can move over chests to upgrade on the fly at a cost. On any level, there are upgrades mid game that drop randomly by killing enemies, easy to talk about, but actually getting the upgrade usually is a challenge due to the slaughter house of bullets ambushing every inch of your monitor. In short, the developer bitHuffel (Ruud Koorevaar) has made a stunning heart thumping title as advertised and is a unique game where you practice endlessly your technique to complete each level.
*Please do note that I have received this game for the purpose of reviewing it*

It is very honest and well executed successor of the Baldur's Gate series, but there are a few things that I find a bit disturbing:
- the game mechanics when it comes to battle are a bit too fuzzy for my taste.You don't often get a sense of "whoa, I want this weapon" or "nice armor" that was one of the biggest things in Baldur's Gate series. In Pillars of Eternity it's more like "meh, I really don't know if this is an improvement or not and I don't really know what caused us to win the battle". - too many npcs in comparison to party size. I hate it when you have 3-4 characters waiting in line and you want to have chat with each one of them and play the story with each one of them but you can't because they don't fit in your active party. But still recommended as the storyline is well written and atmosphere is really close to what made BG series so good. But doesn't get to Planescape: Torment level.

Let’s get one thing perfectly clear straight away. You’re not going to be pouring hours upon hours of game time into Leszek Sliwko’s fantastic Age of Fear series because of breathtaking graphics and incredible surround sound. The game simply lacks that. So if you’re a graphics and sound technology ♥♥♥♥♥ who has little appreciation for other aspects of games then you’re going to want to turn away now and find a game geared more for you. I personally found that the first Age of Fear game to be a fantastic game crying out to be played. It will hold incredible appeal to those of you who appreciate great game play mechanics and those of you who have a likening to well thought out strategy games that begin simple enough to allow you to learn the basics before gradually increasing the difficulty and mechanics of the game to the point that you’re enveloped in the games cocoon.
The game’s greatest strength is its AI. Many people could take pages out of Sliwko’s book on how to program artificial intelligence, well, intelligently. Many games of this nature fail miserably because the computer is not programmed to play smartly with the game often boiling down to understanding the basic idiosyncrasies of the game before they become a cakewalk. This is simply not the case here. The strategy required to be successful starts outside of the battle. You must select your troops and then evolve them – upgrading their talents and abilities – correctly to enjoy sustained success. Otherwise you will find that you are obliterated. The game’s AI is smart enough without the necessity to cheat.
The most significant weakness of the game was the, in my opinion, silly and unnecessary point to make players search for treasure chests after successfully winning a battle. I tried this a couple of times following fights but it is a tedious process that is unnecessary and takes away from the game’s strengths. This isn’t a hidden object game it is a turn-based strategy game where the aim of the game is to defeat your enemy and move onto the next round. While you do not have to find these extra chests it would have been much better to give them to the player for completing the battle or having a random dice roll or something based upon how well you did in combat rather than asking the player to spend extra time on a map following a fight.
Age of Fear: The Undead King is not going to appeal to everybody. However, to those who enjoy it there is a likelihood that you’re going to find yourself returning to it again and again.

Let me first say that there is a lot to like about this game. But. Trying to give AoF a thumbs up or down is like tossing a coin in the air and having it land on its edge instead of heads or tails. It has its good points and bad. The storylines are pretty decent, the background artwork is very nice, the combat is okay but nothing truly innovative. Most gamers will get through the "good" campaign without too much difficulty on the standard setting. But it's when you attempt the dark or "bad" campaign that things become both better and worse. This is because the necromancer plays very differently, has a completely different skillset, and a level path that requires you to take a different but fairly specific approach. Unfortunately, this is where the RNG hits you hard and you will find yourself having to replay levels over and over just because you had bad luck with the rolls or completing them with ease because you got repeatedly lucky. As much as I'm enjoying this game and as much as I wouldn't call it a bad game by any stretch I'm going to push that coin over onto whichever side represents a thumbs down for the simple reason that there are better games in the same pricepoint - specifically Telepath Tactics. This said there's plenty of fun to be had here if you arent too picky. As is often the case I would rather have given this a more neutral vote but there we go. If you grab it in the sale (as I did) you'll likely be happy enough. It's also worth noting that the lead developer cares very much about his games and is very keen with responses to issues in the forums and continues to patch them when he can.
*edit* Recent updates have done more than enough for me to flip that coin back the other way and the game is now well worth its full cost.

Great cRPG.
Story was intriguing, though the main & side quests weren't always as thematically connected as I would have liked. In particular, there's a sort of "twist" at the end (regarding the gods) that's almost never discussed or hinted at - and it really should have been. Still, minor gripe. The characters, while perhaps not quite reaching the level of some of BG2's or DA:O's companions (and the villain coming nowhere close to Jon Irenicus), had interesting personalities and dilemmas. Eder & Durance were my two favorites, though I'm sure mileage may vary.
I was entirely satisfied with the combat system. You'll be pausing a lot (more on harder difficulties) to cast spells, drink potions, and change positions or targets. Aside from Chanter, every class felt powerful and useful, and I often had a hard time choosing between which companion I wanted to bring. What's especially nice is that every stat is useful for every class, so if you want to make a battlemage who's in the thick of melee, that's entirely possible and even encouraged by some of the wizard spells.
I'd be remiss if I didn't mention some great innovations in combat as well. First off, D&D's "attacks of opportunity" are implemented via an engage system. Enter in melee range and you're engaged. Exit and you'll be hit by free attacks. This helps tanks tank, while also making enemies who can teleport into your midst even more dangerous. Second, the infinite-rest problem in other cRPGs is ameloriated by requiring you to spend limited camping spells in order to sleep. Some reviewers have complained about it, but I very much appreciated it. I had to be smart about using my skills & spells. At the same time, I never felt hugely limited. Many skills, for example, are actually usable a # of times per ENCOUNTER (rather than per rest).
One area in which I felt let-down was the magic items. There's not much of a sense of progression. For example, I defeated this bad mafa dragon near the end of the game, but his items were mediocre. And the best 2H weapon in the game (a pike) is bought IN A STORE. Even beyond that, the items and their modifiers rarely felt unique. Nothing like getting Lilarcor or Carsomyr in BG2.
All said though, it's great. I beat it without White March, and, frankly, am glad I didn't. I was ready to move on.
DIFFICULTY RECOMMENDATION: I beat the game on Hard and some fights were quite difficult, especially a few near the beginning (I beat Raedric at level 4, with a party of 3, lawl). But I breezed through many more (especially near the end when I'd hit the level cap and optimized my gear). As such, I wish I had stepped it up to Path of the Damned. Thus, if you're a thorough completionist who enjoys difficulty (e.g. Dark Souls), I'd start with Path of the Damned. It'll be tough, but you're given the tools to overcome that toughness.

I have not played AOF2 since Nov. 2015, thus some points I put here might be dated since devs are constant improving the game. I'm writing this review after such length because I feel I have the obligation to let more people know what this game is good at, to let more to see its great potential as an indie TBS.
Also, as my first language is not English, expect mistakes, misuses and Chinglish and I apologize in advance. I'm writing this in English because review in English will not be filtered. Yes, simple as that.
+decent TBS
-minimal graphic and music
Personal Verdict: Recommend
Age of Fear (AOF and Age of Fear 2 will be refereed as AOF2) came later on Steam than AOF2. However, note that its development was prior than AOF2, so you can understand some drawbacks compared to its squeal.
They are:
Okay, pretty much for its inferiority compared to AOF2. What it's good at, same as AOF2, is:
Great turn-based strategic combat.
Unlike many other TBS games, in AOF series unit size can greatly influence the pace of the battle, and there are no tiles to limit your movement so that you can micromanage your unit position. Unit deployed can block others behind them and affect their movement significantly and hence, when and which unit you gonna move is important, so that you don's screw up. e.g. you may want to have a necromancer to move forward to raise a corpse, but to do so you need to have it exposed to enemy melee units, and you can't get your, say, ghoul, that would originally be behind the necromancer to cover him because it's path is blocked. So it would be up to you to decide, whether to expose a necromancer to fatal peril, or to delay or even abort your plan.
Action per unit allowed executed per turn is limited. It's majorly against casters are ranged units. Most of spells are not allowed to cast after moving and ranged attack the same, and thus you will have to arrange your squad position carefully that your shooters can cover the desinated battle ground, your mages have your targets in spell range and your tank units can cover them, not to leave them to assulters like riders, so that all departments of your army are fully functional.
The drawbacks for AOF and AOF2 in common are:
Above, I recommend AOF. I would say this is an exemplar of how to make an indie TBS: Decent combat, deep strategy. I see some developers put money in fancy graphic and impressive music but the game itself turns out to be crappy, what a waste. Then I wish some people can have more budget to further polish their game. Like this.
You may want to pick up AOF2 and see if you like it, since they don't share a coherent story. And I would like to write more, but there goes my poor memory.

I bought this with a friend, and we had a blast. The payoff here is great; I received immense satisfaction from figuring out puzzles and performing insanely powerful attacks by coordinating with someone else. I firmly believe the best way to experience FORCED is with a dedicated partner or three so that you can complete the entire game with the same group of people.
That being said, the puzzles are not very complicated at all. The true difficulty will be in attempting Challenges (finishing a level while achieving a specific goal) and Time Trials (finishing a level within a certain amount of time). Completing Challenges and Time Trials will require attempt after attempt after attempt. Beta Dwarf could have planned for this a bit better and not put as many long cut scenes in inconvenient places, but you can skip after a few seconds. Nevertheless, Challenges and Time Trials give this title some serious replayability. The game is fun enough to justify multiple (read: dozens of) consecutive attempts. I did not feel like I had completed the game until I had all 75 gems, which took roughly 47 hours.
The online infrastructure can be a little rough. We had to exit out of the game and set it back up once every 1-1.5 hours or so due to game crashing bugs or unresponsive controls. However, it is important to note that the gameplay made it worth it. We kept coming back to it because of the addictive gem collecting and the fun, rewarding combat system. Mercifully, Beta Dwarf has insured that load times are minimal and creating/joining a game are very simple. This means setting up a game is a trivial affair, and the inconvenience of the (infrequent) game crashing bugs is mitigated.
The combat system is the crux of the gameplay. Basic attacks leave enemies with marks. Depending on what abilities your character has, marks can cause special attacks to do more damage.
The abilities you equip your character with (up to 3 active and 3 passive) give you perks and access to powerful attacks. Discovering synergy between passives and actives is one of the most compelling reasons to keep playing the game and adds strategy to what would otherwise be a mindless beat-em-up.
Gems enable you to unlock abilities and equip yourself with more abilities. There are 75 in the game, three for each level (1 for beating the level, 1 for completing the challenge, 1 for beating the Time Trial). Every few gems you score, you unlock a new ability, which adds to the sense of progress throughout the game and encourages you to experiment with your new found awesomeness.
It is important to note that the experience I am praising arose from me from having a friend that was dedicated to playing the game. I cannot speak to the game's singleplayer mode, but I also cannot see it providing the same sense of accomplishment, nor can I see it motivating me in the same way to attempt each level the insane number of times I did. It always helped to have someone to talk to and discuss strategies with. With that understood, I give it...
8.7/10

Easily the best adventure game we've seen in a long time, even if it is half-hybridized with a visual novel.
You will spend a lot of time clicking through dialogue as it scrolls out to warbly noises and an animated portrait, but the characterization and writing is pretty good, and the setting and plot are solid. It kept me guessing, and it kept me intrigued. The puzzles are about half working out what to say, half classic inventory stuff, and are pleasingly logical, if the latter are perhaps hinted a little too hard. Occasionally it throws up a short light-action segment, like Sierra adventures of old. It seems to bend over pretty hard to avoid any unwinnable situations; if you mess up, characters start coming up with backup plans. I'm tempted to do a useless-acerbic-idiot runthrough just to see some of them through.
The aesthetics pretty much nail the '80s/90s transition, with 16-bit era Atari ST-esque graphics, and an ace synth soundtrack. The is retroism celebrating the strengths of the time, not just slapping VHS tracking fuzz on everything, and it fits the edge-of-posthumanism tale it's telling. Apparently plans are underway to fully voice the game, and going by the existing voices in the intro it might work out.
It's good. Really really good. It lacks the big-budget production of the golden age, but the last time we got an adventure game this compelling, LucasArts were still making them.
