Lemme practice on making my reviews short and to-the-point for a moment.
The rest of the Genesis/Game Gear lineup are far more designed for your speed and to get you hurt a lot fairly. They also were not the most replayable games ever, despite being founded upon this, with the exception of S3K.
The later fully-2D games are... huh. Excluding Sonic Mania and Advance 2, pretty much all ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t you a lot but keep *some* stuff to kinda say "yeah, we can do some cool Genesis stuff too!" (though, I really love Sonic Advance 1, don't get me wrong. It does a lot of this very well and holds itself back quite a bit on things it gets is bad.) Oh, also, I literally cannot play Advance 2 without quickly becoming far worse at other games at a proportion due to how all you have to worry about is things that hurt you: if you know how to not constantly walk into a wall and fall into an obvious pit, the game plays itself.
Sonic CD is the one that is all the good things, and also makes it accessible but still difficult, EXTREMELY replayable, even more flashy and rockin', bigger, bolder, uncut. CD technology brings Sonic to some of it's best, removes 99% of all cartridge restrictions (see: the past music being 1/3 done in PCM due to memory limitations, the other fractions being to showcase PCM at all and to make a joke about Sonic's past), and some people find it *the* best. I can really ignore all it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t (which it did cut down on) when I'm having crazy fun, and have a LOT of it, and having some of the most poppin' Sonic music ever, and it's so god damn beautiful with it's effects and pallette and Sonic 1 sprite Sonic is best Sonic and I can play it with a million different routes per character and then enable Debug Mode and do a few challenge runs using that. 27 of my 34 hours of this go to playing it over and over, 1 hour is just AFK time, and the rest come from being a legendary bandwith-less jukebox.
Oh, also, you can both go blazing fast quite easily and win and slow down for something like the Saviour of the Planet run and win even better. I kinda prefer the more exploratory runs anyway though.
...now, if the Sonic 1+2 mobile ports made it to Steam, I probably would trash this review and give it a do not reccomend because hell yes 3 characters in just as big or bigger games and the special stages are far better than their Genesis ones and beatable. (Sonic CD still has the best special stages IMO)

Forced, overall, is a great game, but it has plenty of bugs which can cause major issues when playing with friends.
I bought the four pack, and have had tons of fun with my friends in this game, but I've also suffered through a couple of hours trying to deal with bugs just to be able to play.
Pros:
The spirit mentor mechanic is extremely unique and makes this game a ton of fun. It is challenging because everyone can control it equally, and often all players need to work together and coordinate positioning and timing to complete levels.
The levels themselves are challenging, but easily doable with a little effort. The challenge gems on the levels, which unlock extra abilities for all players, are quite difficult at times and give the game a much harder goal for those who want it.
Each level is unique and fresh, and the game continues to throw new content at the players from start to finish. This makes for an extremely fun game that is made even better when playing with friends.
Cons:
For no apparent reason, some people are unable to join certain game lobbies to play with friends. The only solution I've found to this is to continually remake and have different parties host until it happens to work. This usually takes 5-10 minutes of remaking games for everyone to be able to play together.
Once a level is loaded, there's a chance some players will be unable to move. Sometimes this is fixed by simply restarting the level which takes only a few seconds, but sometimes this bug just won't go away until the entire game is remade, which can make the process take several minutes, especially if there's a connection bug.
For an unknown reason, some players will not be rewarded gems for completeing the level in game. Because the game will not let anyone progress until all members have equipped all their abilities, this can cause major problems early in the game. Fortunately, all gems are rewarded upon making a new game. Once again, this is easily done if everyone can connect to the lobby without any issues, but if you run into the connection bug I mentioned, it can delay your gaming experience even more.
The first two hours I spent in this game, I probably got to play for half an hour. Now that workarounds to most of the bugs have been figured out by my friends and I, it's not so bad. The bugs are annoying, but easily fixed if you have the time to spare. For most games, these bugs would be a deal breaker for me, but because the gameplay itself is so enjoyable and unique, I don't mind. I highly recommend this game, but be aware of the issues it has before going into it.

After supporting the game on Kickstarter (one of very few games I supported), after patiently waiting for two part expansion to get released, I finally played Pillars of Eternity in it's complete current 3.x version and it was an amazing adventure to have. All of my expectations were met and exceeded and not just because we sadly lacked games with truly great stories for the past decade, but because even if there were many, Pillars would be just as great. It's everything you loved about Black Isle, early Bioware, Troika and, of course, Obsidian themselves, but perfected, taken to a new level, despite the very nostalgic interface. It's simple enough to get sucked into it, but complex and deep enough not to be a very fast food-ish feeling game a lot more recent AAA RPGs have become.
So what is Pillars of Eternity with both parts of White March expansion and latest patch? It's an RPG with an active pause and Infinity Engine-inspired aesthetic. But where Infinity Engine felt restrictive in later games, both technologically and storytelling mechanics-wise, where D&D rulesets felt restrictive for the stories BioWare and especially Black Isle wanted to tell, Obsidian made something perfectly suited for their needs. The inteface is highly customisable and smart, technologically the game is much less restricted and the ruleset they created for their world is a joy to play with. You pretty much cannot create a "bad character" unless you try to (and if you do something you regret you can respec easily). All mechanics and ideas complement the concept of you playing the game the way you want and shaping the story the way you want. It isn't as freeform as what Fallout tried to be, but wow it is trying and is much more flexible than even Planescape: Torment. As an example - combat itself doesn't give you experience now, so you never feel like you NEED to kill everything you see and doing things in other ways is perfectly viable. And the idea of very text adventure-like segments that focus even more on your deeds and abilities to do things normal gameplay wouldn't allow is an incredibly smart decision.
The adventure itself is structured close to how the original Baldur's Gate worked (a region where you open new destinations on the world map to go to), but every map tries to bring something new, something unique, something exciting to learn and do. The world lore, the main story, mini stories, companion stories are very fun and try to ask interesting questions and put new perspectives on what you think you already know. In the way how deep and amazing story is, I wouldn't even compare it to Baldur's Gate games, but more to Planescape: Torment or probably a bit of Arcanum. Now, in the White March part 1, story is considerably simpler (and the events take place as an extension of the main story, not as a post-game thing), but part 2 brings back the excitement of the main game topics and questions game asks of you, even if it's still not as great as the main game.
There are, of course, some nitpicks to be had. Loadings for every map, for example, do become frustrating even if it was the only way to preserve the pre-rendered beauty of the backgrounds, especially since as you play longer game seems to start becoming "heavier" for the system. There are rather frustrating AI things as in the fight all party members seem to follow very simple pathing algorithms and can block each other without any logic to go around or shuffle to the side without breaking engadgement with the enemy. The party AI and presets, on the other hand, are very good most of the time, so it's just weird to see pathing being so much of an issue. And there are also some occasional glitches - wrong script triggers, character getting thrown over the path boundries and getting stuck there forever, controls just refusing to work suddenly and even few crashes. These happened VERY rarely, but they did.
These things aside, however, I had fantastic time with Pillars of Eternity and it's two-part expansion and I'd recommend the game to anyone who loves a really great story that you help shape the way you want. One of the best RPGs in a decade, probably best game from Obsidian so far and and adventure to be had. I really wish there will be more games in this universe.

A gem of a game and I enjoyed it thoroughly. I spent many hours sneaking by the Orcs and stabbing them, battling the archenemies spawned by nemesis system. The story is okay in parts but doesn't really give you the feeling that you care about the characters, but gameplay and everything else is what you'd expect from a AAA game
The game gives you the ability to create your own Nemesis, tailored by the encounters in the open world. To tell you the truth, I was worried that nemesis system would just be another gimmick, but it turned out that it was the highlight of this game and has become the games signature feature.
If I would compare Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor to some other games, than my choice would be Batman Arkham and Assassins Creed series. What's more, Shadow of Mordor improves on their fighting and stealth formula, decapitating the enemies is certainly better than punching them (Batman Arkham series). Sneaking and passing the enemies is enjoyable too, and sometimes you immerse yourself in hacking and slashing, sneaking and dodging, that you totally forget why did you come to that area of the map and what the hell do you need to do to solve your quest. Yeah, killing Orcs was never more fun and something you can do for hours on end and not get bored.
So, what is the weak point of this game?
The story.
It lacks the narrative, the thing that will hook you on, the depth you need to feel from a story presented in Lord of the Rings universe. Because of it, at least for me, the game isn't worth a second playthrough.
But, all in all, it is a great sandbox third person action game with RPG elements I would recommend to everyone. The skill tree is such that it takes time to get the really good abilities but not so long that you lose interest in working towards the ones you want.
Overall this is a solid game and a AAA game that is done correctly with unique features and mechanics that keep you playing for hours on end.

Everything about this game seems unfinished or not fully realized.  Were this not 2014, this game might be considered a good production but every aspect of its design seems trapped in a bygon era in which gamers had to settle for products that were limited by the tecnhology of that time.  In 2014 there are things that gamers expect from certain genres of games.  Some of these features include physics engines, compentant AI, clear game mechanics and a user interface that is clear and helpful to the experience.
Conversely, we expect common problems of the past that have been resolved years ago to not make a reappearence.  Some of these failures include simple pathfinding breaks, arbitrary limitations on gameplay, clipping and overly simplified combat.  Content with all of this while playing a "hard core" mode and you have a recipe for dashed hopes and frustrating disappointment.
State of Decay commits all of these fouls and achieves none of the aforemtioned minimum expectations for a game of its genre.  The lack of physics engine collisions is a glaring absense that jarrs the player at every turn.  Because of this and an overall lack of depth, the game world is absolutely static, rigid and non-interactive.  Absolutely nothing a player does in the game world will change the appearance of any part of the single (tiny) open world in a meaningful way.  The only changes that do occur are within one's home base and those (when they don't bug and revert for no reason) are purely cosmetic.  The game is so stubborn with its unintuitive world that there is no way to determine by pure visual inspection whether the outer wall of your home base is able to be climbed over by zombies or not.  Hint: if you don't have enough materials in your base stockpile, those walls that are seem high and appear to have barbed wire atop them will do absolutely nothing as zombies will magically acquire the ability to rock-climb their raggedy butts into your bedroom.
Arbitrary limitations on gameplay: While the player can utilize about 10 different kinds of cars or trucks for personal transportation, there is no system that allows the player to utilize any vehicle for transportation of the supplies that they need to survive in the game.  There are two pickup trucks with massive flatbeds that just beg for rucksacks to be tossed into them and hauled home and yet this wasn't included.  The only way you can accomplish it is via an exploit detailed here
That design choice is just plain stupid.  Adding to the stupid is the penalties that apply when you exceed the maximum number of resources that are able to be stockpiled.  Essentially the idea is that if you gather too much food (for example) than you have proper storage for then it will slowly reduce to the maximum amount that is storable (spoilage), because it's a perishable resource.  That makes sense.  But other resources such as fuel and building materials also are subject to this mechanic and that doesn't make any sense.  When was the last time you saw a cinder block "go bad"?  How about gasoline?  This is a recurring problem with the game as its mechanics seem to be operating in some sort of twilight zone... one where cannibalistic reanimated corpses are to most believable element.
The AI is peculiar in that there's no rhyme or reason for an ally character's success or failures when on a mission.  ISSUE PATCHED.  There are no commands that you can give to your AI tag-along buddies that will control their behavior in any tactical way such as what weapons they should use.  AI companions that are attached to you for a mission will be become stranded if you fail a mission as they will no longer follow you at all.  They seem more than content to stand still in the wilderness until a zombie eats them.  When successul with a mission, the AI companion will run directly back to base, taking always the shortest route possible no matter what hostiles of any level of strength are between them and their destination.  I personally witnessed one particular friendly character jog directly into three fully visible wandering hordes, which pounced on him the second he got into their aggro range.  Oh, and also worth mentioning is that no AI character will ever follow your character on foot along a sloped non-road area.  What I mean by that is that the friendly NPCs' pathfinding breaks when the player moves across any graded surface that isn't a roadway and often get stuck, resulting in a mission failure by restart.  There are a few of these in the game and they're all very helpful to cut down on travel time.  Also frustrating is that the game mechanics are almost a complete mystery.  There's oftentimes no mention of the metrics of resource drain beyond the fact that you're running a deficeit (sp?) so you don't know why you're losing resources until you've run out of them.  Thankfully the game does reveal its specific calculations (of materials, at least) when you drop to zero.  The formula for outpost maintainence is 1 unit of materials per 3 units of whatever resource exists at the outpost, if any.  Unfortunately, the game will not inform you if and when you outpost runs out of the given materials.  At this point, you won't be surprised by such an obvious oversight though.  Additionally, while I've been referring to outposts this entire time, the developers really do need to check their dictionary next time before going to press.  Outposts can function as static resource harvesters to supply the home base with resources, serving as an alternative to the player retrieving the resources from the building in one lump.  Establishing these resource supply chains is continually referred to as establishing a cache. They really should have looked up what "cache" means before using it in one of their core mechanics.  This can be quite confusing when a player is setting up outposts and is being told that they are acting as "caches", implying that no transport is occuring.
Further confusing the player are lack of important item stats and any sort of ability to truly manage the personnel at your base.  When calling for a runner to come pick up supplies, the game chooses which character it will send and the characters never EVER use a vehicle to travel, no matter how far the distance to the target.  While on the subject, the vehicles in the game never run out of fuel despite characters telling the player verbatim in dialogue sequences that they vehicles should be used sparingly due to their limited fuel supply.
More confusion abounds as the zombie AI makes little sense in most situations.  Again according to the orientation dialogue, the sound of firearms and care engines should bring zombies running from a great distance away.  Yet in very few instances did this occur, including when gunning the engine at full RPM, blasing the horn or shooting the loudest gun I could get my hands on.  The only instance where there was truly any sort of mass zombie swarm of any consequence was in response an an artillery strike (which manifests in a rather paltry and unsatisfying sequence of explosions compared to the real thing, I might add).  Even this was poorly executed as the zombies came running to the center of the blast a good ten seconds before the first "shell" landed.  Apparently zombies are most entralled with orange signal smoke over anything else.
Overally, State of Decay is mediocre.  The idea is great, the motivation may have been there but the execution was incomplete and it seems like the development team just didn't care enough to make a complete and fulfilling game.  No wait, scratch that.  It seems that the development team just didn't care at all.

I spent 20 dollars on this. I didn't back it through Kickstarter, but I saw it through some ads and was pretty excited to finally pick it up.
The verdict? Pretty art and beautiful music cannot save a terrible, terrible story.
The first three to four hours of the game are spent doing very mundane tasks around town. During the night, you get cryptic dream episodes that were at first very enjoyable... but have no payoff. The worst part about this whole game was the fact that I kept playing expecting it to go somewhere-- and then it started to! I was finally ready to dive into the story that this game had to offer!
The next chapter? "Epilogue". The game was over. I'd spent 7 hours doing mundane nonsense for a cast of completely unlikable characters (that the narrative tries to redeem over and over to no avail-- the most likable character, Agnus, gets the fewest lines) without the option to tell them off. You're always a total fool.
Also, the dialog? Riddled with syntax errors. Suffers from a lack of commas and oftentimes forgets punctuation at the end of a sentance, making the dialog read terribly.
(Slight spoilers ahead, though I can't spoil much as I didn't even understand the ending.)
But back to the narrative-- as soon as things pick up, which they do about 5 hours into this 7 hour game, they go WAY fast. The pacing? Awful. Suddenly your friend has a crossbow? You're sick? (Why?) There's something after you (what is it??? I literally just wanted to know what it was).
Also, look. I have a tumblr. I can tell this was written by people who use tumblr. I am EXTREMELY liberal, but there was no subtlety to the "screw the police!" and "baby boomers are ruining the world" and "the economy is terrible".  There's not even any humor to lighten what is an overwhelmingly negative message and worldview. Or maybe the way the characters insulted one another was supposed to invoke a feeling a humor? Who knows.
Do yourself a favor and skip this one in favor of Oxenfree. This game is very similar, but it hits visuals, sound, AND story where this one hits two of the three.
On that note, a few positives:
The art direction and sound design of this game are absolutely remarkable! That' why I picked it up in the first place. I wanted to screenshot some of those environments and put them up as my desktop wallpaper! The color theory was impeccable!
I just wish the story had been up to par. Hire a different writer next time, guys! Errors in syntax are unforgivable, come on.
If you want to look at pretty art, go for it. If you want a story, play something else.

A retro throwback adventure title with a rare cyberpunk vibe.  For a cyberpunk game fan, this title shouldn't be missed.  The music is also excellent (!!!) and really set the tone for the 8 bit vibe they were leaning toward.  And personally, when I say the music is good, I mean I would leave it playing and get lost in thought and would frequently jam out to the background tunes.  Very catchy.  Can't say enough about the music.
The dialog is good and thought provoking for the most part.  People have interesting things to say and the writing is to-the-point for the most part.  There are huge number of dialog outputs for combining all sorts of items with the environment.  Additionally there are a large number of interactive items in each scene, each having at least three different dialog outputs.  Lots of reading to do if you want to.  It's great to hear the thoughts of the characters, and feels nicely fleshed out.
It's basically the coolest cyberpunk graphic adventure since Blade Runner for PC.
The puzzles are not hard, the game plays much like an interactive novel and doesn't take very much thought from the player, but the atmosphere and story and music are enough to make me a BIG fan of this game.  I very much hope they can make a follow-up.

I don't really go in for the point-and-click adventure genre (I would never have even thought of playing something like this if I didn't get it in a Humble Bundle), but this one really grabbed me. The story is pretty compelling, the world is very cool and I wish I could play another game set in it because really my only problem with this game is that it's a bit short. Ultimately I was in it more for the dialogue and story than the actual gameplay, but there's rather a lot of dialogue so that was fine.
What I will say in favor of the gameplay was that it wasn't too difficult. The game is good about directing you to the right location -- you're never really expected to read its mind as to where you need to be, and at that point, if you aren't sure what to do, you can just do everything until you get it and it'll only take you a minute.
You get the sense that this game was written by someone who's very sensitive to LGBT issues, and that's nice. You'll encounter plenty of characters who fit that mold, which I appreciate, and even deal a bit with non-binary pronouns, which while not an issue I'm terribly interested in, was kind of different.

There's a few story-content elements to this game that I've seen get discussed a lot.  I think those are important to discuss, but I feel they need to be discussed in context.  For my review I'm separating these elements a bit.  There's the quality of the story, the content of the story, and the gameplay that the story is laid on top of.
As I always wish to point out, this is a point and click game with only a few failstates.
First, performance.  Game had no performance or audio issues that I came across.  I once had a bug with some UI elements in a puzzle not appearing, but reloading fixed it.  The major 'performance' issue of this game that is worth noting is that text does not skip easily, as clicking the mouse button or keyboard to advance text is unresponsive until the text has been on the screen for about half a second and each line of text has a small space of time before it starts appearing.  There is also another facet of the game that combines with this, where character portraits play an emotive animation at a certain point in the text, and often times this animation MUST complete before the text can be further skipped.  This can lead to issues in a few places where you cycle through already-viewed text, view menus with repeating lines of text, or if you reload to choose a different option in a dialogue.  So much time is spent waiting for text to be available to skip that it becomes tedious and frustrating, especially with a particular character who has a long emote animation.
Second, lets talk about the quality of the story.  For point and click adventure games, this is often going to be what defines whether or not the game is fun.  It makes me somewhat unhappy to say that the quality of the story in this game is not very good.  Without going into detail, the intro of the story plays out fine but it accelerates near the end a bit too fast and doesn't really give itself time to develop its grand climax properly.  You went from
to
in the course of a few hours, without giving enough time to make doing so feel right.  Thats not to say that such a story is wrong because it doesn't follow form, but it felt rushed to me.  I needed more time.
You are also forced down a tri-fold dialogue tree which encompasses 'Good', 'Neutral', and 'I'm an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥' themes.  Sometimes that happens because the developers want to plan for certain endings, but the way it is written doesn't give the player much in the way of expressing themselves despite the player filling his-or-xir own shoes in the story.  The player is told his reasons for acting, rather than getting to choose them himself.  I'm not always 'Good' because I believe in goodness for all things like the dialogue option says, and just because I disagree and want to say something opposing usually isn't because 'I'm an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥'.
Additionally, large sections of the game have Turing (the robot you meet at the very beginning) solely talking at length to an NPC, with no voice from the player... and oddly, sometimes vice versa, with Turing having no input in what occurs when it seems like they should.  This is really odd because while Turing is the protagonist (and most interesting character in the story), it is weird for there to be as much dichotomy between who is in focus rather than a more even balance.  It doesn't seem balanced for who should be speaking in the moment, but even saying 'who should be speaking' is weird because the player isn't the main character.  Turing is.  For all the dialogue that has told the player what their motivations should be, they have little in the way of motivation to be in the story, beside Turing being dropped into your metaphorical lap to be a sidekick too.
Third, how is the gameplay?  There's not much to it.  Most of the gameplay is parsing text and moving between location screens.  Interaction is often very minimal,  Puzzles are often very minimal.  The player has items, but more or less doesn't use them.  It certainly never landed on the side of usual point and click games where there's "that one puzzle" that makes no sense.  But there is "that one puzzle" that requires diving a long list of mixed alcoholic drinks to find exactly one that a patron of the bar likes based on a description of taste, and this is required to continue the game.  Outside knowledge of alcohol may be required.  I don't drink.  Combined with the aforementioned sloggishness of advancing text, and this puzzle becomes a failure of good game design.
Last but not least, content.  People have said this game is pretty heavy on 'social justice' topics.  There's a presentation of a setting of discimination against genetic hybrids.  There's a movement for human purity that rejects cybernetics, genetic tampering, and excessive technology use.  The game doesn't really present any direct conflict between these groups though.  You're just told it exists.  These themes are there at the start but don't really keep their part in the story well, and vanish entirely at the end in favor of more
focused topics because of the aforementioned story pacing issues.  The game really seems to avoid any direct conflicts stemming from discrimination
.  Its weird for these topics to be in the story and seem to be centerpiece, but not really matter all that much.
How the game handles 'racial' (genetically modified) issues is odd too.  One of the characters more or less treats you like you are 'normie bigot scum' for lack of a better term, for 99% of the game.  With the dialogue options as they are, you can be a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to her to justify her feelings, or be neutral to positive and have her be a complete ♥♥♥♥♥ to you for no reason other than that you aren't 'one of them,' (meaning she has no outside information to justify her behavior other than your lack of genetic modification).   Sure, its a character.  It makes sense that a victim of racism could themselves be or become very racist.  But it makes the character completely unlikable, and you have no way to dismiss interacting with her because she is important to the story.  Your options are 'help us pls, I'm grovelling at your feet can't you see my normie guilt' or 'I'm an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, racism comes naturally to me.'  I don't like it.  Aside from this interaction with the game's only real racial-issues character, you never see genetic-racial discrimination in the game. Its weird.
As for gender issues, its pretty much a non-topic. The game asks you to select your pronouns (since the game frames the player in the game as 'you!') and gives some default options for contemporary gender diversity as well as the option to enter your own.  Characters in the game might identify as genders other than their appearance but the topic isn't over-emphasized, and Turing (the AI) questions potential gender identity for themselves in one scene that lasts a few sentences and handles it well overall.  Its not preachy or overbearing.  Diverse gender identity is just treated as normal.  From what I've seen people who have non-traditional gender identity seem to really like it, and its not something to be complaining over if you don't.
So, did I even like the game?  No... for the most part.  I very much liked Turing's character.  They were the enjoyable part of the game for me.  I felt attached and drawn to Turing in ways very few characters manage to achieve.  The rest, it wasn't really that great.  Its weird to then say that I do not recommend the game, despite finding something to like about it.

These are based on Miscreated time.
Day 1: I spawned by a house beside the road. There were no other structures in sight. I was scavenging for stuff inside the house until I heard the sound of a car engine. I ran outside and saw a Military truck pass by. I chased it while shouting "Stop! I need help!" And then a feminine voice asked "Hello? Anyone there?" It was this girl with a British accent. She was very nice. She wasn't that well equipped either but she had everything under control. She was nice enough to let me tag along with her. We told each other about where we were headed. I was merely a fresh spawn trying to survive. She told me she used to belong to a group and she is finding her way back to her friends. I asked if I could come along and she said yes. She was a nice person. We stumbled across a small town with a few mutants. I told her we should stop here and take all the supplies we can find. She told me to get down and check each house. I was only armed with an axe that she gave me. She told me to be careful while she circles the town. A few minutes have passed and I haven't heard the sound of the car engine in a while. It got dark and I wouldn't risk getting out during the night so I stayed in one house and waited it out.
Day 2: The sun finally came up. Apparently that server made nights go faster than usual. I decided to ditch that place and go find my friend. I started going around the town on a bike I found. I saw the truck. I quickly ran towards it but nobody was inside. It was badly damaged and it looked like it collided with the house. Either it was too dark for her or Something made her drive off road. I was new to the game and didn't know♥♥♥♥♥♥yet so I just walked anywhere until I saw a sign leading me to a city. I spent most of my time running away from mutants that I encounter on the streets. I met this Chinese dude that told me to come with him. He was the second person I've met in the 2 hours I've played so I assumed he was a good guy. He brought me to the highway and told me to stay. I was in the middle of the road waiting for him to come back and when he did. He had company. There was a car slowly driving behind him. It stopped a few meters away. The Chinese dude came near me and told me it was his friend. He backed away from me and said "Bye bye" then his friend started speeding up heading towards me. I ran in time. Though I got hit, I did not die luckily. I ran and ran so much and so far. I stopped and crouched behind a tree hiding while my health was regenerating. Missing the charm of adventure games of yesteryear, but not the pixel hunts or sanity-defying puzzles? Wish you could play an adventure game that acknowledges that gender isn't binary and that queer people exist as something other than a token character? Check out ROM!
It tackles some genuine moral quandaries, but has at its heart a cast of well-drawn characters. This is a colorful, lighthearted noir romp (as contraictory as those descriptors may seem) through the possible onset of a singularity, but it never loses sight of the people it wants you to care about. It's impossible to overlook that this is a future that, while in some ways perhaps the standard cyberpunk dystopia, is significantly better off socially: queerness is a given and accommodated rather than hated or swept under the rug.
Basically, fans of cyberpunk and adventure games can find something here to celebrate and even be moved by.

So Read Only Memories is a cyberpunk adventure game where a sentient robot named Turing invades your house and pleads for help as its creator went missing. That is all I'm gonna say with the story since it's the big focus of the game.
I really love this game. I consider it one of my favourite indie games now. The story is well written, the characters are all lovable and memorable, the 80s retro artstyle is gorgeous and the music? Well I just bought the soundtrack so take that for what you will.
It's closer to a visual novel with a point and click adventure overlay more than anything. Its puzzles are not really complicated and the real big focus are on your interactions with people you meet. The discussions with Turing is my favourite, it's both adorable and very intriguing to talk to your little robot friend.
This game gets a 10/10 for me but even with that I can't reccommend this to everyone. It's just not that type of game. If you hate the terrible logic puzzles in point and click adventure games then I can safely say it has none of that, they cut the fat off that aspect of the genre. If you want a cyberpunk adventure that's light on the gameplay then I can definitely give this a recomendation to you.
If you're interested then please give it a go. MidBoss have done a wonderful job in creating this world. To me it's one of those games I missed out on during 2015.

Read Only Memories is actually a good non-linear story. And despite its simple puzzle mechanics, it's rather fun to play. The soundtrack is awesome and has great variety. The graphics, while intentional dated, have some really impressive character designs. There's also a wonderful amount of humor both in the open and hidden deep within the game that I didn't expect.
Naturally, most games have their negative moments. Before the boss fight, I was thinking I could rate this game 10/10. But the game mechanics for that encounter were so unrelated to the previous portions of the game and so horrible the first three tries that I'm bumping the game fairly down to 8.5/10.
Don't let the anticipation of a horribly scripted event discourage you, though. I'm still playing this game for good reason. Most of it is fun. So fun, in fact, I'm considering *not* putting this on a "Play and Forget" list after eventual achievement mastery. I relate a lot to a character named Jess, and I just can't get enough of her portion of the tale.
This game is $10 well spent, and I will certainly invest more replay time into it than most other indie titles in my library over the next few years.

In my experience, visual novels are poorly-written, which is a real shame -- the combination of audiovisual cues and written word could really lend itself toward breathing new life into old ideas. Unfortunately, Lucy is yet another example of a visual novel that falls short and leaves its medium under-utilized.
The premise of Lucy is interesting, and I had been hoping to see an intriguing exploration of the problems and ethics behind human-android interaction, and while this does briefly come up in the game, it's only touched on in a superficial and immature way.
Tonally, the game is, quite frankly, a mess. The game can't decide whether or not it wants to have horror elements, which it includes by way of sometimes-startling visual and audio distortions resembling glitches. But if it's not a horror game (and it isn't --
, maybe, but not horror), what purpose do these elements serve? They don't mirror the content of the game by reinforcing its themes. They're distracting and unnecessary.
Lucy has some questionable design choices, and the repeated inclusion of the Three Laws of Robotics seems pretty slap-dash and ultimately proves, quite irritatingly, to be without meaning since
. The voice acting is well-done, and I think the actress breathes life and characterization into what would otherwise be a dull, irritating, and meandering script.
There's a good deal of stilted language in Lucy -- from the way he spoke and thought, I sometimes wondered whether or not the protagonist himself was an android, or perhaps from another planet. That stilted language unfortunately repeatedly spoiled the mood of a scene by taking me out of the fiction instead of immersing me in it. Visual novel writers and translators: I implore you to
get a good grasp of the natural way that people think and speak. Think of it as writing a play, not as writing an essay.
Some other thoughts about the game -- the music was fine, if somewhat forgettable. The UI was well-designed and visually appealing, but the scene transitions were grating. Lucy's character design was good, but other characters seemed out-of-place or just plain weird. I was disappointed to discover that the game had no Steam achievements despite having in-game achievements.
I want to firmly state something about the Three Laws of Robotics, which kept appearing during the game during chapter transitions and in the narrative itself.
Whoever approved that design element should never be allowed to work on visual novels ever again.
All in all, I can't recommend this game to anyone. Maybe it's worth checking out if you get it as part of a bundle, but even on sale at half price, I still feel cheated.

15 Hour Review: 9.0 / 10
If you are a fan of the old Baldur's Gate series or Icewind Dale, you shouldn't hesitate to purchase this game.  It is on sale enough that you can wait to avoid paying full price.  I have just scratched the surface of the game at the point of the review, and I am just as captivated by it as I was with any of the BG games.

I haven't yet finished this game, being the type of person who likes to complete every possible side quest and explore every area in RPG's, but I feel like I have seen enough of the game to write this review.
Pillars of Eternity is a game moulded very much in the fashion of some of my favourite games of all time; Baldur's Gate (I & II) and Icewind Dale, and it definately justifies it's position sitting side by side with these greats.
Being a top down RPG it doesn't have the flashiest or most breathtaking visuals, nor the fast paced combat of many of today's modern games, but it doesn't suffer for it in the slightest. A fascinating, dark and gritty high fantasty world, bursting with interesting and entertaining characters in which you search for answers to a mysterious event from the start of the game set the stage for the telling of a very well devised story.
Like most games of this genre, it features a reasonably well detailed character creation system which allows you to feel that important attachment and immersion during the story, and the voice acting/script writing work is very well done. Expect to be amused, baffled and enthralled in equal measure by the numerous NPC's with which you can party up and travel with (all with their own backstories, most of which I found pretty neat).
Combat-wise the game is solid, being pretty much standard fare for this type of game, but it felt nice and smooth and there is a good variety and diversity of skills amongst the classes. Loot is also varied and interesting enough to keep you constantly on the hunt for that next upgrade or nice drop.
One thing I found very pleasing about the game was the abiluty to acquire and upgrade your own "Keep", which was obtained through a very interesting quest and worked solidly with the main story line of the game, intermingling seamlessly as I quested back and froth between them.
Overall this is a game which borrows, and to a small extent, builds on the solid foundations of prior games in this genre and couples it with a beautiful and detailed world and engaging story. There is nothing particularly groundbreaking added in this game (or at least, what I have experienced of it this far), but there a few new features here and there which fit in very well with the overall experience, without parting too much from the old school feel the game conveys.
Highly reccomended, especially if you already a fan of similar games.

I am not a fan of RPG games and i have very little experience with them, so my review is based on that. After reading all the good reviews i figured i'll try this game out, not really knowing what to expect.
First i have to say i was a little bit disappointed by the graphics after the hype that was created here about them. They are not bad at all, and the atmosphere is good, but i expected even better.
After spending nearly an hour creating my character, i jumped into the adventure (props on the options). The story is interesting and keeps you curious about what will happen next.
However as a inexperienced fantasy RPG player it was sometimes hard to keep track of all the unearthy named people and parties. Further in the story, also the number of quests who are active at the same time, often left me feeling a lack of overview or perspective of why or for what side i was doing this quest again. If i did i probably would have made a few different choices.
What i did love were the conversations with NPC's, where very often you had the option to use a skill for a shortcut or outsmarting manouvre. Also that the members of your own party jump in the conversation now and then, makes them more charming.
The combat system is pauze-command-play style, and simple enough to learn. However in certain situation i felt like some of my characters were not completing the given command for no particular reason(no magic and no obstructions on the path), and if you don't pay attention they just stand idle while the rest gets butchered. That being said i didnt have problems surviving on the normal difficulty settings except for a encounter with a dragon and Raedic 1.
The story ending is clearly explained but a bit abrupt, it would have been cool to really see your keep blossom instead of just to read it has. Also 'The master below' which seemed a interesting and difficult quest to finish. Was not needed to progress to the end of the story and did not seem to influence the outcome of your keep either (wich is something different then what your stewart tells you). So i felt a bit discouraged of completing it still since the story was allready over, and thats a shame.
All in all i still think this game is not bad, it was a nice experience to get more familiarised to this kind of genre. I got this on a 50% off sale so i recommend the game. Although i think a RPG fan will prolly appreciate it even more then i did.

Not bad, but not enough weapons and very little reasons to use a variety of weapons.
Still have the classic FPS bugs such as shooting rails or other objects instead of your target caused by a large collider box and the priority of actions (if you press the assassinate button while being near a closed door, it will kick the door loudly instead of assassinating your target, failing the mission)
There's also the missions spectrum problem, you have access to very hard missions right off the bat, while keeping easy "story-mode" missions locked. Making the difference in difficulty quite astounding, building up frustrations right away.
This is a stealth game, meaning that 90% of the guns you could unlock are completely useless and if you chose to use loud weapons, most missions will automatically fail or you will have to face at least twice as many foes because of "reinforcements"
The aim is not true aim, if you move your cursor fast, there's no problems but as soon as you try to fine-tune on a target (moving the mouse more slowly) the cursor will not move while your mouse does. It's hard to explain but your mouse cursor will cease to move if you move your mouse slowly. Which makes shooting quite a problem, in a FPS game this is quite troublesome.
I also had to edit the engine's files to disable mouse acceleration, because the game offers no such options. This game is not PC friendly, it's obviously a port.
The plane upgrades feels shallow and unimportant, they obviously tried to remedy that problem by adding a modifier that makes you gain more money based on the plane's total upgrades. The best upgrades are to get enemy weapons and prototype weapons which are, based on the genre, not needed at all since you're supposed to stealth and not kill.
There's also no difference between deadly force and non-lethal, other than the kind of points you'll receive from each mission, which does nothing but give you money anyway.
Personally I stealthed missions until I got my full stealth suit with all gadgets and weapons, which was about 5 to 7 missions, on the hardest difficulty. Since then, I just "panther" my way in. (Lethal Stealth)
The "heavy" guards are quite annoying, they are immune to everything but assassination from behind. Took me quite awhile and a lot of frustration to realize that they are simply immune to assassination and everything else from everywhere but their back side.
No reasons to use bombs, electricity, piercing bullets or anything else on heavies.
They feel too simplistic and reduces the array of tactics available to the player, limiting them to a single action.
This game has great potential but basic mistakes makes it a not-so-great title.
Feels like there was more thoughts involved in much earlier titles, despite having a more limited weaponry selection.
Still enjoyable, but a little pricy and a title as great as "Splinter Cell" should be doing much better than this, it's embarassing.

Overall, I'm recommending this game but I decided to write a full review as I don't think any other reviews or descriptions prepared me for this before I started it.  Yes, I think the lore and questions this game brings up are compelling but I wouldn't really describe this as a "point-and-click" game; I think it's much more akin to a visual novel.  There are interactive elements and moments where you can explore your environment with the mouse, but the game is kind of a slog to get through cause of all the long sections of exposition that go on for like 20 minutes at a time.  Sometimes you'll enter a conversation and are suddenly forced to make a choice or move ahead in the story with no warning and no pause point to allow you to go back and accomplish what you intended to in the first place.
What gameplay there is feels largely circumstantial and adds very little to the overall experience - I would even argue they detract from some of the things the game does right.  Gameplay sections appear very sporadically and don't feel well-paced out or integrated at all.  The final chapter features a lengthy portion of gameplay that comes out of nowhere and dooesn't feel like a test of skill or intelligence.  Puzzles are either completely obvious or require a lot of tedious trial-and-error.  Dialogue options often aren't telegraphed well and there were multiple points when I inadvertently made a decision I didn't realize I was making or had a character interpret my response in the exact opposite way I intended.  You have an inventory but it's kind of like when you have an inventory in a TellTale game - it's just sort of there to give the illusion that you might eventually use the things you're collecting.
I kind of like it, but I can't imagine I'll be playing this again.  If everything I said above is your thing, more power to you but I wish I'd known all this going in.

Aight, literally just finished the game and I have a million things on my mind so I'm sorry if I get a little rambly.
Firstly, I loved this game to bits. And while I did enjoy it, no game is without fault in my opinion.
I want to end this on a positive note, so I'll start off with the negatives that I found.
The game is exactly what I expected it to be, however the beginning is really slow. Sure, you could speed through the game but since it is a story-based game, you want to see as much as possible, read all the dialogue, etc. That's why day in, day out, it kind of got a little boring and repetitive running around the entire town, trying to check every little thing that's changed.
That being said, I think the game is rather overpriced for what it is. I'd get it on a sale or something because 20$ for this seems a little excessive in my opinion. I finished the game in 9 hours however the mystery plot only started to move around the 7 hour mark so the majority of the game is really just... running around the town over and over, getting to know the characters, learning about their past, etc (which I still enjoyed, don't get me wrong) but from the trailer I expected a bit more spooky action.
Also a little thing that kinda tilted me was that no matter what, you're gonna miss out on some parts of the game as on some days you just have to choose between hanging out with Gregg or Bea. I'll be replaying it anyway so it's not a big thing but since I loved both characters, it was kind of hard to choose.
ANYWAYS I feel like I've made it sound too bad so now to the positives I go!
If you're an artsy person and you think the trailer was neat, you will love the gameplay.
The soundtrack is 100% on point, the small details in the game are really charming and the overall art style is what makes this game super enjoyable. It's just a really chill game in general, like... You need to go into it with a fresh mind, ready to forget everything else around you and just immerse yourself into Mae's life. It's a really nice mix of "teen humour" but it's also pretty dark and deep at times.
I don't mean to sound pretentious when I say this but from reading the few negative reviews, I realize that not everybody might have the ability to really understand this game. It's deep, it makes little sense at times, but you just... I dunno, you either get it or you don't. And you won't get it if you don't try to, so just.. have an open mind.
The story leaves some things unanswered but I do feel like it's good as it is. It gets you to think. A lot. As said, I really enjoyed this game. I've been waiting probably around 2 years for it and imo it was worth it.
TLDR: Good game. 9/10. Funny and deep. Get it on sale.

I’ve seen a few reviews calling NITW a “do nothing simulator". I’ve seen other reviews saying that a normal playthrough will take you 6 to 8 hours average.
Let me tell you:
My first playthorugh took almost 11 hours, and I definitely missed multiple scenes and only managed to unlock 47% of the achievements. I'll probably clock in at least a few more hours before I feel like I'm done with the game. Take your time with it! The game won't be as enjoyable if you rush it.
The town of Possum Springs might seem small, but there’s a lot to do. As the game progresses, you’ll unlock new areas to visit. On top of that, there’s a ton of locations you won’t notice if you don’t explore. One of my favorite characters is Lori — who you can usually only talk to by exploring the power lines.
In fact, one of my favorite parts of the game is the side characters. After chatting to (and eavesdropping on) my neighbors every day, I found myself genuinely caring about even the most minor of characters. Their significance to the story isn’t what endears them to you — it’s the feeling that every character is a person with a unique personality and backstory caught through snippets of dialogue.
That said, this game is
. If you're looking for a game with puzzles or action, this probably isn't the game for you. It's a step above a visual novel since you have so many choices, a world to explore, and platforming, but most of the gameplay is dialogue.
There are multiple references to the two precursor games — Longest Night and Lost Constellation — and I highly recommend playing these two short games (about a half-hour and two hours in length, respectively) before you start Night in the Woods. Both games are available for free on Infinite Fall’s website!
As for replayability, I'm pretty sure it's impossible to see every scene in one playthrough. I definitely got the feeling that you can’t experience all of the storytelling -- there are many in-game days where you have to choose which character to spend your time with. That said, I doubt I would play the game more than a few times, and Night in the Woods is a very story-driven game. Any minigames or puzzles aren’t going to be prominent enough to warrant another playthrough. The story and characters are the primary reason to buy NITW, and I felt like my time and money was well-spent! Coming from someone who usually only buys games in a bundle or on sale, this game is definitely worth the full price.
A minor issue I had with the game was the keyboard controls. It could be hard to tell which button exited certain menus/screens at times — sometimes it was C, sometimes V, sometimes ESC. The confirmation button also sometimes alternated between C, F, and Space (as well as X in specific circumstances). As you get used to the game, it won’t be a large problem. The platforming is very easy and intuitive. The art style is also gorgeous — the backdrops and dream sequences were some of my favorites. Character animations feel personalized and lifelike, and I found that the style fit the theme well.
The audio in the game is also lovely. The soundtrack for the town screens changes as the game goes on. The game has lyric-less songs that you will play in guitar hero style button-pressing, and they’re easily my favorite part of the soundtrack! Characters are NOT voiced, but there is a quiet sound effect for voices (not unlike animal crossing). The game settings allow you to change the volume or mute individual audio aspects, as well.
For all of my praise, I personally found some of the themes to be very heavy and depressing. If you're looking for a cute, happy game, this isn't it. NITW deals with real-world issues including low self-worth, mental illness, and poverty. Talk about a fun time. The game also  contains some horror game-esque scenes and stressful situations. Thankfully, there are
. Use caution if you have a very weak stomach or the idea of death or mental health disorders bothers you.

If I'm to classify Forced as anything, it's a cooperative MOPA - Multiplayer Online Puzzler Arena ;)
Really good co-op game, with both fun and challenging combat system and clever but not too convoluted action-oriented puzzles, both rewarding you greatly for good teamwork and communication. Since each mission is its own little arena it's easy to pick up and play for a little while with people joining and leaving as they like, although I'd encourage you to play with friends to get the most (screaming and fighting over the shiny ball) out of it! ^^ Each class is tied to weapons and you "level" all the classes at the same time. Classes are divided between players so you can't play the same thing, which also encourages teamwork and letting the best suited for different tasks do their thing, but you can also switch classes freely between each mission. Since you can also skip some missions, it means you can decide difficulty by avoiding harder ones if you really want to, but I for one found the difficulty on an appropriate level. As far as co-op games goes this one is nearly perfect.
The controls feels sharp and responsive, and the skills fairly intuitive. You can fight a boss without taking damage by timing dodges perfectly, or you can die miserably by doing it poorly. There's a nice balance between individual skill and teamwork that you usually (hopefully) find in MOBAs like LoL and DotA, but to me what it reminds me most of is running dungeons in WoW, minus the gear frenzy and hunter pets pulling all the mobs. Overall, I strongly recommend Forced, especially in four-packs.

My main gripe with Dragons Dogma is its absurdly bad level design. The world map is a mess, theres no real fast travel system and your sprint duration is extremely limited, leading to long boring treks across the map. The design of the world map is poor in that youll be running towards the quest marker, and suddenly run into an unpassable cliff. You turn around and trek 10min back the way you came to trace along the cliff looking for a way up. Well it turns out there is no way up in that direction, so you turn around the way you came yet again to try the other direction.
The map in the menu is poorly made, and its difficult to discern what lines are rivers, roads or elevated plateaus. The environment design is also poor, cities feel empty and hollow, buildings have sparse detail; the vast majority are empty with a few barrells and crates scattered around. The world of Gransys is wholey uninteresting, with not a single area being enchanting or breathtaking. Games like Skyrim and Dark Souls never got old because of their varied and intriguing locations to explore.
Dragons Dogma doesnt excell in its sense of exploration either. Theres no real reason to explore areas off the beaten path, as your not going to find any interesting hidden ruins or side quests, or anything of that nature. If you do find an NPC with a side quest, its a lame fetch quest or go kill X amount of this type of enemy for a meager reward, which by the way is halfway across the world. If your lucky youll find a few herbs for the terrible and esoteric crafting system, or maybe a chest that will hold some mundane artifact. The fact that everything looks blah and bland doesnt help much to persuade exploration either.
Ive read reviews on here of people praising the pawns, about how they are so interactive and interesting. I completely fail to see any merit in the pawn system. They are hollow and artificial companions that make Lydia from Skyrim seem interesting in comparison. You cant talk to them, when you interact with them they only spout out one of the few generic lines meant to be tips for new players. 10 hours into the game and theyll still be explaining that you can rest at an inn if your tired... Sage advice pawn, sage advice. They also incessantly repeat korny one liners in combat at a disturbing frequency.
TIS A TROUBLESOME FOE! SEVER THE TAIL! THE TAIL IS SEVERED! SEVER THE TAIL! THE TAIL IS SEVERED! Theres are examples of lines youll hear at least two dozens times during a short engagement. Some of the monsters are complete bullet sponges, and will take 15min of spamming attacks to kill, obviously as a result they will spout out the same lines hundreds of times. Its enough to make your ears bleed.
Pawns can be very irritating. If your trying to trek across the map for a quest, youll run into myriad battle encounters, many of which with trash mob wolves or goblins. Suffice to say they are a waste of time, and your want to just run through and past them. Often times I wont notice they arent following anymore, until one of them dies. That means I must run ALL the way back to revive them, then return the way I was going. This happens repeatedly, making long treks ever more annoying. They wont follow and insist on engaging each and every trash mob.
The lack of a fast travel system is another big problem. There are waystones, which work to teleport you places. Thing is, they are very rare to find and are extremely heavy in your inventory. Once you make the long trip across the map to get somewhere, you can plant a waystone to create a teleport spot, but there goes your waystone, so you cant teleport anywhere else until you find another, and as I said they are rare. If they would have made waystones plentiful, itd alleviate the problem, but alas after 10 hours of playtime your likely to only find one or two.
The combat is good, its Souls like without the difficulty and exhilarating combat. Its a bit dull in comparison, but the boss monsters make up for it. Theres a grapple system where you can climb onto monsters to slash them while clinging on. Its awesome to cling to a dragon or griffon and watch it wildly flail to try and shake you off. The main issue here is that the camera goes berserk and more often than not youll have no idea where you actually are on the monster.  Sometimes the camera makes it impossible to even see the battle from any perspective.
The grapple system is implemented poorly though, movement on monsters is very confusing, I usually end up crawling in circles struggling to steer my character to where I want him. Also it drains stamina to grapple, and at an alarming rate. This means youll be able to hold on for maybe 20-30 seconds before you run out of stamina, are thrown off and need to wait for it to refresh. Compounding the problem is that the majority of your time clinging to the monster, its flailing around to try and get you off. When it does that your stamina gets drained even faster, and you cant attack as your desperately trying to hold on. This makes it where youll spend an entire stamina bar and only pull of a few sustained seconds of hits, with the rest of it spent on getting tossed around like a rag doll. Like I said, its pretty cool, but the utility of it is so inefficient its almost not worth it.
The equipment and progression system are limited and shallow. Levelling has no customization or autonomy. You simply gain a level and some hidden stats are increased at an unknown rate. This takes away the excitement usually obtained from levelling in RPG games. You cant customize what stats to improve, or what specialty to invest in. The skill system is also strangely implicated. You can only learn and assign skills at an inn, which is wholey restricting. So if your in the wilds and want to change a skill, your out of luck and must return all the way to a city and find an inn. Most of the skills are just ho-hum, nothing truly interesting.
The equipment system is very bare bones, and the crafting system is esoteric and confusing. Youll get a plethora of crafting resources, which are very heavy in your inventory. What you do with these items? Beats me, the game neglects to explain what or how these items are used. I havent crafted anything yet, because Im not sure how to, and I dont want to find an online guide and continually minimize my game to refer to it. There should be a detailed guide of sorts to help new players understand crafting.
The games narrative plot is thin and predictable. With cliche moustache twirling antagonists, the typical evil dudes who just want everything to die for mundane and uninteresting reasons and motivations. It borrows yet another aspect from Dark Souls. Your an "Arisen"  which is similar to an Ashen one from Souls. Arisen are meant to... Actually I dont know, something about being the good guy and fighting evil in a archetypal and cliche way. I havent paid much attention to the plot because its so damn uninteresting and poorly written.
The vast majority of NPCs are robotic and bland. No interesting characters with interesting stories,  and they never have anything significant or meaningful to say. Like pawns, they have a tendency to incessantly repeat the same lines, looping ad infinum. The town cryer has been screaming that the Arisen has returned my whole playthrough (so far) and I imagine he will continue to belt it out until the credits roll. They all feel so artificial, like there from a very old RPG game. Thing is, Dragons Dogma isnt that old, but it feels super old.
Overall the game is decent. If your like me, a rabid RPG fan, and have run out of new RPG games to play then Dragons Dogma is worth it. Its cheap now, and it has maybe 40 hours of content to play through. Many of the games systems lack polish and are designed poorly, but that doesnt mean the game isnt fun. I have many many complaints and gripes with DD, but overall its still enjoyable and entertaining.
7/10

One of the best RPGs EVER made.
Dragon's Dogma is hands down one of the best RPGs I've ever played in my life. - As soon as you start the game, you're welcomed to a robust character creation with many layers of different details and things to edit all of which can also be used to create your pawn, your personal traveling companion. - Pawns are your party members and an additional two can be recruited, all created by different players around the world as whichever class as you prefer.
The World of Dragon's Dogma may be small compared to the likes of the Elder Scrolls series but it isn't without it's own wonders. There's always something happening at every corner and after playing for hours on PS3(twice) and PC, I've yet to discover every single open world quest and random activity. - Where the world may lack in meaningful sidequests, the world is filled with epic random boss encounters from Chimeras and Cockatrices to Dragon's and Wyverns that roam the wilds. Even if you may encounter the same bosses, the fights will never be the same.
- in short, it's a great game. buy it.

Things I noticed in game that might help you.
Games very simplistic to any other card game. you have a energy/mana/money/something counter to the bottom left that tells you can summon this cost card that rises with each turn so you can someone more costly units.
Cards have a cost, in the top right of the card and a attack and health at the bottom.
Right click on a card to zoom in on it. the pictures look hand drawn and are really nice. plus you will see if a card has an effect like +1 damage to infantry/mechanical or -1 against received damage from infantry, stuff like that.

Read Only Memories takes place in Neo San Francisco where robots are everywhere and cybernetic and genetic engineering are commonplace. Similar to the San Francisco of today, Neo San Francisco faces a similar crisis where the rich and elite are all in the tech industry. Also similar to current San Francisco is the openness concerning the LGBT characters. In fact in Neo San Francisco, no one bats an eye to see a man dressed as a woman or flinches when a woman says she’s in relations with another woman. Read Only Memories treats its’ LGBT characters with respect, not as running gags or people with lesser qualities unlike many many games that I have played before.
You play as a cash strapped reporter, writing reviews of just about anything to make ends meet. After writing a review for some sweet GX Ultra Beatz headphones, you go to sleep and wake up to a blue headed robot that has snuck into your home. After some brief dialog you discover that this robot named Turing is the first of its’ kind, capable of rewriting its’ own code. Turing tells you he was created by Hayden, a friend you knew a long time ago. Turing explains that Hayden was kidnapped and he fled to find help. It’s your job to find out what happened to the Hayden and the larger conspiracy surrounding his disappearance.
Gameplay wise, Read Only Memories is a standard point and click adventure game. The game doesn’t do anything to differentiate itself other than a few mini-games including one where you have to divert traffic to prevent a cab from escaping and another where you navigate through a maze. I found Read Only Memories easy. Puzzle solving always takes place in the same area and Turing often provides enough hints on what the do so you’re never really lost.
The game goes for a retro aesthetic dividing the gamespace into 3 sections, a menu/character portrait window on the left, the game window to the right and dialog on the bottom. I don’t have the appreciation or the nostalgia for that specific style. I found the small game window difficult to look at because it resulted in pixelated characters and items. I couldn’t really discern if a character is wearing a helmet, a wig or if it’s actually their hair. I also found it hard to read the text because it is so heavily pixelated. The only redeeming quality to the look is the portrait window, where characters are nicely detailed and displayed a variety of emotions.
The audio is good not great. The music is nothing too memorable but fits the whole cyberpunk theme. There is also some light voice acting. It’s completely serviceable, but nothing I would describe as amazing like I would for Supergiant Games’ Bastion.
Overall Read Only Memories tells a great well realized cyberpunk story wrapped in a standard point and click adventure game. I can’t recommend this game wholeheartedly, but if you have a soft spot for old school adventure games and/or cyperpunk stories, Read Only Memories is definitely for you.

Ok so I haven't gotten to the end of the game yet, probably not even half-way there. If something in the later half makes me change my mind, I'll be editing this review to reflect my new perspective.
So this game is pretty charming. Its a point-and-clicker, I guess. I use the xbox360 controller, so keep this in mind with this review.
It has a nice style to it. SImple, nice colours- doesn't go overboard, your eyes are fine and not screaming. Alot of games trying to go for this look tend to make you want to gauge your own eyes out. Not this one.
Side characters are interesting, and recognizable- you won't have an issue confusing them. They aren't over-the-top, but still manage to all be varied in shapes and sizes and colour schemes.
You can take your time, or not. The game does make you feel some sense of urgency, but you can pace yourself without any punishment, as far as I have played.
Idk. Its fun, and the story does bring interest. The side characters are interesting each in their own right, and the game lets you be as polite or rude as you wish to be with them. Some characters like you instantly, others are snappy and defensive (some with reason, some without) and you can approach things in different ways to get your goals.
Personally I like offering gross spoilt milk to everyone and everything just to see their reaction. But thats just me.
I recommend it regardless of the type of gamer you are, its visually nice. Might not be everyones cup of tea, but its good to waste some time, if you aren't really into the story. I am, so I'm willing to play it to the end, but even so its fun just messing around in it.

The graphics are very retro, but don't let that discourage you even if you aren't into the retro scene as the really important content is delivered by the dialog of a cast of characters that you will actually come to like (or dislike).
Recommended for anyone who likes a good story with a good cast of characters. If there is any downside here, it is that (in keeping with the thematic decisons being made) you do need to save manually and there are points where failing to save could lead to a bit of replay. It only happened to me once, so it isn't a huge negative.

Pros:
* Stunning art. The best looking cell-shading since Windwaker
* Great soundtrack. Coupled with the art, this is one of the most aesthetically pleasing games I've ever played.
* Witty writing that presents a setting mixing supernatural creepiness, poignant scenes of a decaying rustbelt town, and the uncertainties of young adult life.
Cons:
* Some gameplay elements could be more responsive. (e.g. Demontower is an overhead Zelda-like mini-game within the game that can often feel clunky)
* Not necessarily a con, but expect to go over the same territory each day to visit and talk to everyone. This is not a fast paced game that takes you right to the action.
Also note that you'll probably need multiple playthroughs to see all the interactions you want. In the first few days in particular, you may wonder how an interaction might have played out differently had Mae made other choices.
If you're not sure whether you want to buy NITW, go to itch.io and play through Lost Constellation and Longest Night from the same creators. NITW will have much of the same tone as the latter and much of the same creepiness of the former.
But I for one was a kickstarter backer who waited three years for the game--and it was worth the wait.

This game surprised me. I had never heard of it before the Steam Summer Sale 2017, but I saw a few people recommending it on Reddit and bought it. That was a great decision. I'm having so much more fun playing this than any other game I've bought throughout this sale, which is saying something.
If you have any doubts about buying this game just because you've never read a Tolkien book, go ahead and buy it. You don't need to have any knowledge prior to playing this game. I haven't read a single page of any of Tolkien's books, nor seen any movies, but I was still engaged by the story and the references are minor in relation to the story. I'm actually going to start reading LoTR because of this game.
The combat isn't particularly challenging, but it manages to be quite fun. The rivals system is interesting, things you do actually affect you later on, but not in a pre-written way. What happens is unique to your playthrough, even the developers couldn't know exactly what was going to happen. This makes for interesting stories and satisfaction at finally taking down a particularly annoying enemy.
I paid $4 for this game, but I'd still be happy with it if I'd paid full price. You're getting so much content it's insane, and it's entirely fun content. At $20 it's a good game for a good price, but at $4 buying it is a no-brainer.

This game is kinda weird for me. It's fun, that's for sure, but when you try to complete it (which you will, it's a classic sonic game) it just frustrates me beyond belief. If it wasn't for the fact that you can just exit the special stages and reset them, I wouldn't be able to get the time stones. The time travel mechanic, while interesting, is frustrating to use, as it's almost impossible to pull if off without finding the special area in the act that lets you do it easily. Again, the game is a mixed bag for me. But the positives definitely outweight the negatives (as seen by the fact that I practically completed it, just missing the "destroy all Metal Sonic holograms and Robot teleporters" achievement).

This is a game I've always known about, because its music is absolutely great and stands out even amongst sonic games which always have good music, but been intimidated to play because of its gameplay.
It definitely takes some getting used to, but having gotten through to the ending with all time stones in hand, I can definitely say it was a worthwhile experience!
Pros: the game is colorful and interestingly designed as heck. Yes it's a sonic game rather than a mario game, which means you'll have to learn the vertical levels and multiple traversal routes and details of the stage through a bit of trial-and-error (which also adds to the replay value), but sonic games make up for that through great unique atmospheric design and incredibly funky music. This game in particular rewards exploration, because 1. you must find signposts and time travel spots if you want to travel to the past, and 2. you must find the robot teleporters and metal sonic holograms in the past to get the good futures and achievements. Because there are 4 possible time zones per level, the amount of variability and unique-design(plus music) per time-spent-to-appreciate-them ratio is quite high, so the game never gets old.
Cons: while the game is a classic, it's not quite as well-polished as newer sonic games, and I'd say a game like Sonic Mania or even Sonic Generations (Classic) improves on the 2D sonic formula in almost every possible way (which is particularly apparent if you compare the Metallic Madnesses from Sonic Mania vs Sonic CD; where imo the best level in one game is the most frustrating in the other, except Wacky Workbench). Unlike Sonic Mania, there is no level select feature, and the game autosaves with each round and special stage, so you must essentially go for perfect runs in one perfect go, unless you want to retry each part every time. And to add to this, Sonic CD does NOT have a retry option in the menu, which means to retry stages you are constantly returning to the menu screen (this even goes for Time Attack mode).
The special stages are also a whole different level of frustration. The UFO hitboxes are deceptively small, and even though they have fixed movement patterns which you can learn after each re-attempt, it's tricky to intercept a UFO's movement even if you know their patterns. I'd say the difficulty in sonic special stages in general revolve around having slippery or gimmicky movement controls, but Sonic CD likely takes the cake; movement and speed control are unfriendly and unintuitive for the most part.
So, Sonic CD is a mixed bag of good and bad, but I'd say its flaws are excusable for being an old game. If you're into Sonic games and you're wondering what Sonic CD is all about (and you're also up for some trial-and-error/exploration gameplay), I would definitely recommend this game!
