State of Decay is a game that fills a niche that many games tried to fill but none did yet.
But it does it in its own unique way, and it does it very well.
You are managing a group of survivors in a zombie-apocalypse. Its something you need to get used to, there are alot of random characters and some plot centric ones that you can get attached to, and mourn for when you loose them to the zeds. There is permadeath, and its cruel. The game can bring out emotions in alot of ways, which is a strong point for it.
There is also base-building in the game on several predetermined locations. The game is a Sandbox, things happen if you are playing or not. As long as you keep morale high and your base secure, you shouldnt have too many suprises whenever you get back to it after you took a break.
The story is told over different mission arcs that you have to follow, to eventually get out of the valley the game takes part in. Overall the story is well presented but it could have been longer and the end is unsatisfying in my opinion. The non-story missions are quite repetitive and can get to be a bit of a chore over time.
Generaly the game felt too easy once you know how to deal with the zeds and have your survivors trained. Yes, you can level your survivors skills and there is nice progression in the skill system. And even tough you might feel like a zombie-slaying superhero at times, as soon as you pay not attention for a moment you can be in dire troubles. If you get reckless you will loose characters to hordes, and to special infected (which are very similar to those in Left4Dead).
The graphics are pretty dissapointing resolutionwise, and the user interface is clumsy and ugly at best. That is because the game was ported from consoles for PC, but generally ist not a bad port. The Devs really tried their best to make the game work for PC. The controls with Keyboard & Mouse where fine (Controllers work too of course). The graphical variety still can overcome the bad texures, so that those only stay a minor annoyance.
I didnt run into any plot-stopping bugs or crashes (seems those where fixed), the game gets still patched from the devs and there will be a second DLC coming out at one point. The first DLC adds an endless mode to the game which is a nice addition.
Its a bit weird to sum up this game with its many small flaws and at the end still say its a great game, but it really is, even tough it could surely have been better in many aspects. Its the whole experience and atmosphere that makes it worth playing. Its a unique game in many ways, and a very welcome and creative suprise in the many zombie/survival games that all feel pretty similar overall.
Everyone should play this, wholly reccommended.

State of Decay is an open world zombie apocalypse survival simulation, made by a smaller studio. As such, some gameplay ideas are not as well formed as they could be and some bugs persist despite ongoing updates & support. Perhaps the studio's vision is slightly greater than their grasp, but the support to date has been great and most major issues have been addressed (aside from few niggles).
Of note, the simulation aspect means that characters in your group will take the initiative & do things for themselves, however the AI is probably not quite up to scratch in handling some of the micro associated with this clever macro idea. If you just don't like any loss of control at all (even when your machine is off!), then this may annoy you a lot - however is is reasonably unobtrusive and does add a degree of SimGame-like satisfaction; if your community is happy and well supplied then it will tick along nicely (the inverse is also true...), and there are endless opportunities for player agency to influence the community's state (!).
The game answers your questions about how Zoey and the team from Left 4 Dead stay so well fed, and where exactly those grenade launchers come from. It is engaging, well thought out and likely to continue to be tweaked and refined.
It reminds me of STALKER + L4D + Fallout Tactics, if that helps. Highly recommended.

Another visual novel inspired by works the likes of I, Robot and Astro Boy, we have a story about an android who makes people question what it means to be human. Whether sentience can be created with circuits and how people react to their existence. In a nutshell, this story is about a boy who finds an android who he, at first glance, mistakes for a person while taking a shortcut home through a junkyard. The player character and the android live and learn together over the course of time through the story, and as you would imagine, this android, being the best of its kind, blurs the line between robot and human. There are ups and downs. There are terrible, terrible downs. But play your choices out right and there is a nice ending. Word of warning, this visual novel likes to break the fourth wall a lot. It grew on me but some people might not like that.
There is not much to say about the characters. The player character never gets a name and his personality is defined by your choices. Besides that, he is a teenage boy with strict parents who are rarely there for him who now lives with a cute android. Said cute android has a personality that is "programmed" to always be happy. To always try to see the bright side of things. The parents are strict ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who are rarely there and are the cause of the problems in this story. The friends are likeable but are not often seen.
The artwork in this game is fairly standard stuff. It looks nice but nothing exceptional. I did enjoy the soundtrack because it was simple, relaxing music. A fair amount of piano and bouncy synth tunes you expect from what is, for the most part, a slice of life visual novel.
To wrap up, this is a fairly short slice of life visual novel with decent artwork and good music about a teenage boy, his android and his idiotic parents.

Let's get this out of the way immediately. If you're not a huge fan of the modern socjus crowd, you probably won't like this game. It has diverse characters as one of the biggest selling points of the game, and it more or less has folks of many backgrounds, ethnicities, sexualities and gender identities. If that turns up your nose, you won't like it. I think, however, that it deserves heaps of praise for doing this. It has managed to put in a large variety of interesting characters with a variety of backgrounds without straying into tokenism or stereotypes (mostly, I'll come back to that).
TL/DR: If you like diamond-in-the-rough well written adventure games, give this one a shot, unless the above applies to you.
Getting that out of the way, the game is generally pretty good, but has lots of room for improvement. I'd like to see the developer come back and do more work, with the lessons this game has taught them, I hope.
Some big gameplay criticisms are: there aren't very many good "talking puzzles" for an adventure game that features a lot of talking. Generally the 'correct' path is very obvious, and there aren't a lot of times where you have to carefully navigate your way through a conversation; this game is very light on the adventure game elements. The solutions, while (mostly) straying away from insane moon logic of older adventure games, overcorrects too far and can be a tad easy.
Some story elements that could use work: while for the most part the dialogue is quite well written, the story relies on contrivances at times. I feel like the writers were worried about tension settling in too long, and so while there's one primary arc that takes up the whole game, each chapter has a number of things that are solved very quickly, and not always in a logical way. Succinctly put, I hope the writer goes back and reads some mystery novels, especially older pulpy ones, if this is the kind of story they're going for. I feel like the difficulty in the puzzles is also reflected in the characters' difficulty in solving the mystery. It could be because of the relatively short length of the game, but I feel like more dead ends, more chances for tension of not being able to solve the mystery would've added a lot to the tension and made the conflict more real. As it stood, I never really felt like the characters were in real danger of not succeeding. I also feel like the story was a tad predictable by about chapter 3 or 4. If you've seen [REDACTED] you'll know exactly what the plot twists are going to be.
Finally, I do have some beefs with some of the characters. I feel like while they did try, and deserve credit for doing so, to make characters of various sexual, ethnic and gender backgrounds, they had a tendency to be a little ham-fisted about telling you about it, and skirted the line very close to stereotype. I feel subtlety would've gone a long way in making this feel more organic and less like the writer's utopian view of the future (a flawed utopia, but still a utopia).
To conclude, if you've made it this far in the review, try the game. It's definitely worth the asking price (and then some), and I've paid more for games I've enjoyed less. Turing is adorable and amazing, and the characters are generally awesome and memorable. It's flawed, but still really good. I'm as harsh on it as I am because I genuinely like it.

A much more rich and colourful view of a cyberpunk future than most I've encountered, a world formed by inevitable decay in certain now vestigial cultural norms but also fallen prey to the same old bigotry just in new shapes. Copyright laws infringe on the rights of person hood for genetic hybrids and neo luddites view cybernetics as diluting the purity of humanity. The style of gonzo journalism is directly referenced in the game and is clearly part of the overall narrative. This game isn't going to dance around issues and ask you how you feel about them; the characters have strong well formed opinions informed by their own lives and will candidly let you know about them.
The game is a fantastic take on the point and click adventure in a style similiar to Snatcher but this game has largely sloughed off any semblance of "pixel hunting" or "rub all of your inventory on a thing until the puzzle is solved." Most of the puzzles occur as part of conversations or as fairly straightforward decisions on how to solve problems. There is still plenty of exploration and you can certainly use your SPOILED MILK on everything to get humorous and entertaining responses but it is hardly necessary.
Lots and lots of world building, extremely well written, straight social commentary on current events through the metaphorical lens of this colourful cyberpunk future. If any of this sounded good than you'd probably be into this game.

Overall quite good, and I would recommend it. There are some annoyances with the UI, namely skipping text you've already seen, and some issues with plot branch mechanics I can't talk about without spoiling anything.
However... It's one of those games you'll think about for a few days after you finish. Which is a rare thing for me these days... Hell, I might even play through it again.

TL;DR
A point and click adventure that is based in neo San Francisco where the world is vibrant and alive, you play as a journalist that delves into the dark side of using technology for humanity's gain.
+Great Aesthetic
+Great Intro
+Great SFX and OST
+Well written dialogue
+Nicely crafted futuristic world
- Hard to recommend to non adventure fans
- Less of a point and click and almost a visual novel game
- Puzzles are extremely simple

As I boot into the game, I am quickly dropped into a introductory cutscene that is very well narrated by voice actor Adam Harrington and I'm impressed by the pixel art that goes along with it. The setting is Neo San Francisco and the year is 2064, where humans have technologically advanced far enough that they now have access to gene therapy which with the help of doctors and clinics can allow them to modify themselves with other species allowing them to become 'hybrids'. This raises moral and ethical dilemmas in the community, where people have risen against and have started protesting this new technology.
You start the game as a starving journalist in a 1 room apartment, from there you meet a cute little robot named Turing. Turing was created as a pet project by your best friend whom you've fallen out of touch with over the years. It turns out that Turing is the first sentient robot and he believes his master has been kidnapped because of him.
You go around investigating for your friend and at the same time are exposed to both sides of the hybrid morality war. You speak with the protesters and learn that they believe that the ramifications of playing God can lead to devastating consequences similar to that of the Atom Bomb which killed millions in seconds. They feel similar to the ideology Brotherhood of Steel from the popular fallout series. They believe that humanity's biggest enemy is humanity itself, lest they are allowed to play with technology that can be abused by individuals in high powers. But as you speak to other humans who have been saved by gene therapy or even just any sort of technological modifications, you wonder how far the protesters would go to stop people from saving themselves.
The Government has reformed mandates to deal with the rising numbers of hybrids in society. There is a limit to how much of a hybrid you can be, otherwise you are no longer allowed procreate. Therefore you must be more human than whatever species you have spliced your genes with to have normal human rights.
After marathoning the entire Star Wars series I can't help but compare the two, with both having AI that are seemingly sentient. One of the most difficult things to do is to create a nonhuman character that doesn't only serve as a progressor to the plot. Especially when it comes to robots who need to have enough 'humanity' in them so that you can empathise with them but not so much so that you ever forget that they are indeed only a robot. Some of my favourite characters in video game history are AIs with unique personalities that serve as companions and not just tools to progress the plot in a deus ex machina type way.
ROM has Turing, which is clearly named after the Turing test used on AI to test whether can be classified as human. Turing seems to be on the cusp of this parameter, where he was programmed to learn from his surroundings and not just rely on his original programming to respond to situations. His programming is constantly evolving where the original programming is all but overwritten at this point by his own learning.
The interface of Read Only Memories stands out compared to most point and click games I've played. It's beautiful, smooth, slick and most of all very intuitive for the genre. Read Only Memories typically has 5-7 highlightable objects per area with huge bright outlines on the items This is to the players benefits as you're never searching for too long and you never feel bogged down by puzzles which can be a problem in quite a few point and click games.
You can interact with these highlightable objects in multiple ways with no repeating dialogue. You can usually get 3 unique responses for each option before the game's dialogue is exhausted, so if you want to talk to a table 3 times, you can, and it won't be a generic 'you cannot talk to this object'.
One of the highlights of the games are the SFX and music to go along with this beautifully constructed world, which has been meticulously crafted by DJ Mello known for his hip hop remixes with videogame OSTs. The music never feels overbearing or drowns out the environment the game is trying to convey to you but brings out the characters you're talking to usually each with their own short theme song.
As a whole I would say Read Only Memories is a unique entry into the Sci Fi genre and is a fine addition with it's vibrant environments and slick interface. It makes the Point and Click genre feel very accessible with animated faces and never bogging you down with tedious puzzles. It just delivers the story which deals with similar themes to the ones we have faced constantly in society only to show us that this too, will pass. But also that humans will always be resistant to change and presents us with the age old question, at what point are we playing God? Does it even matter?

Befriend outcasts and punks in a post-neo-noir cyberpunk setting while dealing with your organic and genotypical privilege and tracking down the shady criminals who have kidnapped your best friend. A rapidly unfolding story of intrigue increases in complexity, wit, and surprising darkness as you proceed through a world more sharply realized than a lot of modern science fiction in that it actually concerns itself with social progress through a modern lens. It's a brisk and thoughtful point and click adventure with some awkwardly-mounted shooting elements and puzzles but nothing to distract you from the true meat of the game, which is navigating social cues with empathy for a world very different than your own.
While the game didn't seem to give much regard to the choices I was making throughout at first, which made it feel a bit shallow beneath the texture of its wonderful cast, the game really is quietly judging you in the background for how you interact with people. As a result, you'll discover one of six different endings depending on how you get on with the citizens of Neo San Francisco, building an army of the people or alone and abandoned to your own arrogance and cruelty.
Great game. 8/10.

Pros:
* Stunning art. The best looking cell-shading since Windwaker
* Great soundtrack. Coupled with the art, this is one of the most aesthetically pleasing games I've ever played.
* Witty writing that presents a setting mixing supernatural creepiness, poignant scenes of a decaying rustbelt town, and the uncertainties of young adult life.
Cons:
* Some gameplay elements could be more responsive. (e.g. Demontower is an overhead Zelda-like mini-game within the game that can often feel clunky)
* Not necessarily a con, but expect to go over the same territory each day to visit and talk to everyone. This is not a fast paced game that takes you right to the action.
Also note that you'll probably need multiple playthroughs to see all the interactions you want. In the first few days in particular, you may wonder how an interaction might have played out differently had Mae made other choices.
If you're not sure whether you want to buy NITW, go to itch.io and play through Lost Constellation and Longest Night from the same creators. NITW will have much of the same tone as the latter and much of the same creepiness of the former.
But I for one was a kickstarter backer who waited three years for the game--and it was worth the wait.

I had this game for the PC when I was younger and it's great that with the help of Christian Whitehead, SEGA updated Sonic CD for mobile ports and other devices. With this version, you can now play as Tails and decide if you want the US or Japanese soundtrack. Overall I think this is a great Sonic title although it's not quite the best in the series.
Gameplay:
Sonic controls very well and the physics are good. The super peelout is a cool move although it's not really that essential to the gameplay so you can get through the whole game without having to really use it. The standout feature of the game is the ability to go to the Past or Future version of each level which is essential to the story of the game. Visually it is pretty decent for Sega CD specs.
The zones all have their own unique character especially the great Stardust Speedway which is the best zone for having fun with Sonic's speed and also contains the classic Metal Sonic battle/race. I'm not too impressed though by Metallic Madness - Act 2 is good but Act 1 is lame and Act 3 is a bit of an anticlimax for a final stage, I'm pretty sure you can get through Quartz Quadrant only using 2 buttons - "jump" and the "right" button on the D Pad.
Bosses:
There are some pretty innovative bosses especially the pinball themed boss in Collision Chaos or the underwater one in Tidal Tempest. Metal Sonic makes his first appearance in this game and it's fun trying to race him to the finish whilst trying to avoid Dr. Robotnik's beam of death. The final boss though is one of the lamest I've come across in the Sonic series to be honest, only takes 4 hits and that's the game finished.
Storyline:
There's a nice almost anime style cinematic intro and outro featuring Sonic showing off his speed and moves. The game takes place on 'Little Planet' which is somehow chained by Dr. Robotnik to the erm...'Big Planet' so Sonic tries to stop him by engaging in a bit of time travel to destroy some generators setup in the past to prevent Robotnik from ultimately dominating the future of the planet. It is a cool concept which is pretty well executed. Amy Rose makes her first appearance and it's nice to have Metal Sonic as a secondary antagonist and one who will reappear from time to time throughout the Sonic series.
Music:
This game features 2 soundtracks - a US and Japanese version which you can select in the main menu. Both are good but for me the Japanese soundtrack is the best and the most coherent and has more of a lively character about it. I love how in each zone you have 4 different mixes of a track depending on whether you are in the Past, Present, Bad Future or Good Future of the stage. As the music was originally composed for the Sega CD so there were less hardware limitations compared to soundtracks composed for the Genesis/Megadrive - as a result it sounds very contemporary for its time in the early 90s with a mixture of rock, techno and rave inspired music.
Conclusion:
I would rate this game 8.5/10. It's good value and a good example of a great classic Sonic game with good physics and some very good well executed concepts which are unique to this game in the series and have been enhanced by Christian Whitehead. It's not quite the best Sonic game as a few stages are quite underwhelming including the ending but there is a bit of replayability and it is fun attempting the Time Attack feature to unlock some more bonus features in the game.

This game is weird. I mean WEIRD. Here are the reasons:
1) You can't sleep in your own bed.
>>> I tried, at least, but it seems you can only pass night time at an inn which, of course, costs money though a small bit.
2) It's not entirely open-world, (it's rather a closed world with an open-world element) and most destructible and collectible objects and enemies respawn immediately upon re-entering the area.
3) No interactale object is owned, meaning you can destroy/take them without ANY consequence.
>>> Thus, there is no such thing as criminal activity even though NPCs do have affinities. This is especially unintuitive for people like me who are familiar with Western RPGs like the Elder Scrolls which have a more practical & sophosticated morality system.
4) On the contrary to above, you CAN attack NPCs.
>>> It won't damage them as far as I can tell, but swinging your blade at them will make them flee for a while, and reduce their affinities towards you. Since you don't need to have your weapons drawn to attack, you can easily attack them by pressing the attack button by mistake while trying to talk to them.
5) All facial expressions are cheap and horrid.
>>> You can see the main character (aka the Arisen) change his/her facial expression during cutscenes, but those animations are like Eviebot's (a notorious browser chatter AI).
6) Character Creation is joke.
>>> Just like Dark Souls games, there aren't many cool parts. It does give you quite a bit of options; however, most of it are shockingly ugly, such as enormous lips and disfigured noses. I mean who would pick them, except those who like to make their character an abomination?
7) (and Finally,) you can kill a BUNNY by simply throwing it.
>>> First of all, who would kill a BUNNY especially if it doesn't give you anything? But most importantly, how would a bunny die from being thrown 4 feet away?

This game is the hardest thing to put into words... This game is the most unsatisfying game I have ever played. I have never wanted more and more out of a game than this one. It feels incomplete, too reminiscent of other games (bad and good), and unpolished.
The graphics are outdated (probably were outdated when the game first came out on consoles too), the UI is horrid, the use of only 3 dagger skills at a time annoys me, the map is small once you realize most of it is mountains you can't climb. All that having been said, I love the game. Even though the map is small, I've spent over 100 hours in the game, and haven't yet completed it.
My complaints are few... but they are large in scope. Unlike Skyrim which was a stroll through a Nordic fantasy land (which I love and always will love), this game I just wanted more and more places to loot, to find big bad beasts in and have fun exploring.
The pawn system is fun and works very well. I have a friend whose pawn I use and we actually help each other... that is a feature I love.
Was this game worth $12? Yes. But it comes at a cost. A cost that you'll find one of the best combat rpgs and have to leave wanting more... feeling unfulfilled.

A game I see myself replaying in the future; a well-crafted classic with just a few snags.
I have come into my own as a gamer playing Baldur's gate II and Planscape Torment and spent good part of growing up with 3rd edition Dungeons and dragons.
Even before this game came out, I enjoyed reading up on the dev's updates and how they were planning to tweak the game mechanics. A lot has changed since BG II and the game presents us with polished and improved battle mechanics that have less exploits and frustrating bits.
That said, the devs did not try hard enough to make the game accessible to an inexperienced audience - the easy difficulty leaves the monsters' stats and battle rules unchanged, which means you still need to understand the mechanics and be able to adjust your strategy with every battle.
On the other hand, the games offers several ways to scale up the difficulty, if that is something you desire.
One of the goals this game set for itself was "mature storytelling" and I think they succeeded well enough. I mostly paid attention to the main story it and enjoyed it, which is rare for me. I tend to skip over text and not care that much what is happening between the banter with my party and all the monster-killing.
One unattractive blemish is the issue of hollowborn children - basically a metaphor for disabled people who are nonverbal and need help with daily activities. In the game, these children are like this, because they are soulless. As a cognitively and developmentally disabled person I did not enjoy reading about people resembling me and my friends being inhuman. Unfortunately this is part of the main plot and as such unavoidable.
The characters, which are one of the main draws of a game like this, were well executed. They range from cute to intriguing to deliciously hateable. Their personal stories are interesting, if a bit short.
What I felt was lacking, was the depth of interaction you have with them as the PC and the interaction they have between themselves. The banter is funny, sure, but I am used to drama complete with hissy fits and threats of leaving the party (now I miss BG II).
All in all - a good staple for those long weekends where you don't feel like doing anything.
P.S.: At the time of writing this, I am almost done with the game. A few days ago White March II has come out, with a patch for the regular game. Unfortunately I can't comment on the changes right now, because there is no time left for me to explore them.

I don't consider myself a person who easily identifies with some pre-phrased choices given to me by the authors of an artificially constructed phantasy. I'm a person of science, never were a believer, and I certainly don't put a lot of value in certainty. Yet this game, with its story about belief, certainty and purpose manages to put tears into my eyes because during its final moments I'm suddenly overwhelmed by this sensation of being understood, because among all the fixed categories I'm given the option to deny categorism. Because while I'm making these choices, my faith in not putting blind faith into authorities is actually being tested. This is a game that has put questions into my mind, and I daresay I normally have very straight answers to the wannabe-challenging issues raised by people with a philosophical agenda. Given this dimension of storytelling, it should be obvious that this game is a literary work with a deep relevance to the questions of our time, and the fact that I can actually discuss it on this level makes it one of the most impressive games ever made. That said, you obviously have to be willing to deal with the game on some kind of intellectual level to be able to enjoy these things. I'm not even talking about technicalities like mechanics or graphics, which are also great btw.
If you liked BG1&2 and IWD 1&2 you will love this game.

I have never played any of the classic RPG’s such as Baldur’s Gate or Icewind Dale (but I know now that this was a huge mistake). So if you’re looking for a Review from someone that isn’t biased by nostalgia, you’ve come to the right place.
I’ve been a gamer for 20 years now, and I can say without hesitation that “Pillars of Eternity” is one of the best crafted games I have ever come across. You really feel the love and passion that went into it. You find it in the story, in the characters, in the beautiful maps and dungeons full of lovingly crafted detail, in the wonderful music and in the voice acting. There is nothing about this game that isn’t great. But let’s get into a little more detail…
First the story and writing. More often than not the stories in PC games are just there to hold everything together as opposed to telling something worthwhile. Not so in PoE. Here the story is really good and worth exploring. It’s dark and sad, has many emotional and dramatic moments, twists and revelations, interesting characters, tons of really good dialogue and a great conclusion. It never feels like the quests that move it along where there first and the story then spun around them. Rather the quests fit into the story very naturally and never seem forced or misplaced. But it’s not just the main story that is worth exploring. You will also find many sidequests, some small, some a bit bigger, that tell all kinds of interesting little stories. Some sad, some funny, some dark, some light, but almost all of them are worth your time.
And then there are the books and the souls you can read. And I really recommend doing this! Yes, there is some redundant stuff there, but you will also find some really great little stories or insights about the world and its history. Especially within the souls you can reach out to. Man is there some great stuff there! Some gave me goosebumps, some made me sad, others where funny, and some unsettling, and I rarely read one that wasn’t worth it. The writing overall is excellent for story and dialogue alike, which is a good thing as there is A LOT to read in this game ;-)
The characters you meet are well designed and consistent, worth talking to and learn their history. This is especially true for the companions that you can pick up as you travel around. The game does give you the option of creating your own party members but I would really recommend against doing that. Yes you can probably create more effective characters than those you will find on your travels, but then you would miss out on so much great content. All companions offer quests that you can follow, additional insights into the world and the main quest and tons of dialogue to explore. And they banter among themselves which at times can be really funny. The developers really did a great job bringing those characters to live. I just can’t imagine playing the game without them as they just add so much to the experience.
As for the game world, again, just excellent work through and through. The world of Eora is deep with rich history and lore. It’s a place of wonder, beauty and adventure, laced with hardship and horror. And the visual representation on the screen is just marvelous. The maps are beautifully designed, filled with tons of detail and are really worth the time it takes to explore every little corner. Sometimes I would just sit there for a moment and marvel at the beautiful landscapes, buildings, ruins or creatures. And all of it is perfectly accompanied by an absolutely beautiful soundtrack that creates a great atmosphere.
The games mechanics are also just excellent. I really love how the classes are designed and how they level. Finally a game where you are forced to specialize and cannot max out everything on every character. Once you choose a class you are stuck with it, once you define your characters attributes, that’s it, you can’t raise them further except through enchantments and temporary bonuses. And skills get really expensive on the higher levels, forcing you to specialize your characters as you will only be able to max 1 to 2 skills on each one. Also each class gets special talents and abilities unavailable to other classes. It really forces you to play each character differently and compose a party out of different classes that complement each other. You will need fighters, you will need a priest, you will want a wizard and so on. Every class brings something important to the party and its really just the right mix that will decide how well your party does in battle. The system feels well balanced and plays very naturally, and exploits are near impossible.
As a result, combat is very complex and tactical. It starts with the right deployment before battle and choosing the right weapons and spells for what you are about to face. Then once battle starts it’s all about timing. For example spells need time to cast, so if we’re talking about area effects you have to aim them where the enemy will be once they fire, not where the enemy currently is. Or casting a targeted spell on an enemy that gets killed by another party member in the time it takes to cast the spell probably isn’t such a good idea either. You will be pausing a lot, give commands, look at all your options, considering the next move and so on. And you will be reloading a lot! Trust me on this, you will wear out the quicksave and quickload buttons on this game, even on normal difficulty. And don’t get discouraged because your party gets utterly wiped out without the enemy even breaking a sweat. It doesn’t mean necessarily that your party isn’t strong enough, it may be just because of flawed tactics or wrong choices during battle. Try again with a different approach and things may take a different turn. I had battles where my party got annihilated on the first try but finally managed to do just the same to the enemy once I figured out the right tactic and got the timing right. And I can tell you it is a highly rewarding experience. Combat in PoE requires a lot of thinking and effort, but it’s worth it!
Is there anything bad about PoE? Well, not really. I can’t find anything wrong with this marvelous game except a few minor things that aren’t really worth mentioning. But for completeness I will talk about them as maybe for some they are not so minor.
One thing I noticed and found mildly annoying is an issue with the voice acting. Now I’m perfectly ok with the fact that not all dialogue is voiced. Hell I would also be fine with none of it being voiced. What annoys me a bit however is that there are a lot of conversations where part is voiced and part not. So a character may say something that is voiced, then the next thing he says is not, and the next after that is voiced again. I can’t really put a finger on the reason for this. It seems that fixed dialogue is voiced and dynamic dialogue is not, but I’m not entirely sure about it. Doesn’t matter really what the reason is, I find it a bit distracting.
The other thing would be loading screens. Since the game is broken up not only into exteriors and interiors but also the world is broken up into many small maps that you travel between rather than just one lager map where you can roam free you will see a lot of loading screens. And the farther into the game you are, the longer you will see them. Now I have a machine which is really geared towards fast loading using high performance hardware and SSD only, and I find it already a little bit annoying at times. So on computers that are less optimized in terms of loading speed it might be a bigger issue.
But as I said, to me these really are just minor annoyances. “Pillars of Eternity” is a fantastic game that I can’t recommend highly enough. If you like roleplaying and are not scared away by an old school approach at presentation and don’t mind having to read a lot then this is really worth your time.

Frankly, I wasn’t expecting to buy this game.  I’d never heard of it before, but boy howdy am I an absolute sucker for pixel games, point-and-clicks, and colorful palette choices. And I have to say if this game doesn’t deserve to be on someone’s GOTY list, then it at the very least deserves an extravagant honorable mention. It’s a really good game!
This is definitely a story where I know the people involved know their stuff about technology and politics. Its cute art really doesn’t prepare you for its rather darker (but remarkably fleshed out) contents. I won’t get into details, but when♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan you will probably be as surprised as I was. Every time. Multiple times. Where it really builds atmosphere is in the soundtrack. It has amazing chiptune and other electronic music featured in the game.
It also features a varied cast of LGBT characters, and while some Steam reviews might complain, it frankly feels natural considering the setting. (Which, honestly, if you think this game is somehow "overrepresented" then maybe this game isn't for you.) The game asks you not what your gender is, but merely your pronouns (some are available as presents, but you can manually enter whatever you want.) It also has a few pop culture references that anyone can appreciate.
As far as gameplay goes, it’s really relaxing, honestly. There’s a few puzzles to solve (that are all easy, even for someone like me who could and has got lost in a Freddi Fish game), 2 mini-games (which are essentially the same), and ONE single combat section which is pretty generous with time (you can actually practice it using an arcade game in the nightclub early on). The game itself is vastly story-focused so honestly its a comfy game that anyone could enjoy. The pixel font might be tough to read for anyone with dyslexia, though.
All in all I would rate this game a 7.5/10.

I wanted to love Read Only Memories in the worst way; it's heavily influenced by Hideo Kojima's cyberpunk classic Snatcher, one of my all-time favorites, and it features some much-needed representation of LGBT characters and gender fluidity in a video game. Unfortunately, its wonderful character designs and great music are squandered on a sterile plot that does a poor job of rising tension, a totally vacuous and unlikable player character whose motivations are forgotten immediately after being introduced, and ridiculously banal puzzles that feel like an afterthought. Then there's the weirdly unnatural-feeling fixation on identity politics that feels like it's pandering, at least when it isn't totally going off the rails and insulting the player or exploring upsetting, half-baked metaphors...but that last part's been discussed ad infinitum in plenty of reviews already, so I'll focus on the game's flaws as a narrative and adventure game instead.
Great games take you on a journey and at the end, you feel like you've accomplished something or are at least left with food for thought. At the end of ROM, I felt like I wasn't sure what I had really accomplished or what the point of it all was. Neo-San Fransisco is too bright and cheery of a setting for its own good; moments of the narrative that are supposed to be impactful simply disappear into the background, a problem compounded by how the characters approach everything with just a bit too much levity. To its credit, the game carries a lot of chuckles and is frequently funny, but unfortunately those moments don't do much for the narrative experience. ROM is also heavy on references to genre classics and cool/obscure games (for example, I caught a groaner of a reference to Deadly Premonition within my first five minutes of playing), which isn't inherently bad, but it seems to be used as a substitute for doing anything truly unique itself. Then there's the puzzles, which add nothing of value whatsoever to the experience, as they somehow manage to simultaneously be lacking in challenge, logic and purpose.
The lack of differentiation continues elsewhere; the design of the shooting segments is a direct rip-off the system in Snatcher, which was not a good gameplay approach in 1994 but was at least understandable for the era. 20 years later, it's baffling. This is similarly a problem with ROM's interface which is clunky and frustrating, and then there's the text that is generally too large for its pixelated design; if you are playing the game on anything larger than a mid-size laptop, you will need to run this game in a window, or the blocky text will give you a nasty headache. Perhaps this is less of an issue for others, but I literally gave up playing this on my desktop after two hours and finished it on my laptop to alleviate this issue, which no other game text has ever presented. There should really be an option to adjust the text size...
I felt really let down by Read Only Memories, and struggle to recommend it. It feels like a pale imitation of Snatcher, the wonderful Konami classic it tries so hard to emulate; meanwhile, Technobabylon is a substantially better modern cyberpunk adventure game that offers a gripping experience without needing to make "cool" references to earn points with the player. I highly recommend you skip this one, and play both of those instead.

When i bought this I did it because it was reccomended to me by a trusted source. If it hadd not been for that I wouldd never have bought this game, because it has been positively SLAM DUNKED by most reviews. And while the game certaintly has its flaws i do not think it is a bad experience. I actually really loved the characters and the interactions you have with them.
Pros
*Very well fleshed out characters
*Nicely detailed enviroments (Plenty of hidden dialogue)
*Because of the way items are highlighted on screen, you will not end up being stuck looking for a pixel
*Pretty good soundtrack (If you're a fan of keyboard stuff)
*A plot that is interesting all the way through
Cons
*If you like to be the protagonist in games, then this game may not be for you as the player character is mostly treated as a secondary character (though you still impact events)
*The game has a habit of putting you into puzzles that seem like they are very important (though some matter less than others) and then not letting you save, meaning that unless you manage to solve them the first time around, you may end up with a worse ending
*Though the use of the highlighted item finding means you will not be caught pixel hunting it does mean that most puzzles that require you to use point and click style problem solving are very easy.
Overall while the game does have flaws i feel that the story and characters more than make up for it, and i thoroughly enjoyed every minute i spent with ROM and its characters.

I picked up this game in a 4-pack in the hopes that I could play through it with my friends, and while that didn't happen, it was still an excellent experience.  The gameplay is beautiful in its simplicity, and hair-pullingly hard as a solo experience, though I suppose I can't say that any of my failures were anyone's fault by mine.
It may seem silly, but I believe that this game truly shines in its progression, which gave way to effective level design. There are no discrete levels, only up to three gems earned in each stage as a reward for completion, completing a special challenge during the level, and completing the level within a certain time limit.  New skills are unlocked after players amass enough gems.  As I earned gem after gem, it rewarded me with new toys to play with because of it.  Because there is no leveling up, there is no stat inflation, and each level is designed to challenge players based solely on the mechanics it presents, and I think that goes a long way toward the game's effective balance of challenge and reward.
Each of the four classes plays differently, which makes replaying levels to earn more gems, or improve a time, or even just for the hell of it that much more entertaining.  With all of those possible combinations, how could one resist experimentation?  It was that process of refining my approach to a level until I had conquered it that truly made the experience memorable for me, and I'd highly recommend it for anyone who's up for that sort of challenge.

Where Sonic 3&K can easily be recommended to any Sonic fan, new or old, because it caters to various rhythms of Sonic, Sonic CD caters mainly to a specific playstyle of exploration much like Sonic 2 caters solely to speed. It can best be described as the black sheep of the series like Majora’s Mask is to Legend of Zelda, and similar to that game it excels over the other games because of its thematic, eccentric gameplay. If you were to ask me which Genesis Sonic is my favorite, SCD would be a close second only because S3 simply offers more levels along with more playstyles/characters, and Christian Whitehead is largely responsible for making CD that good of a game.
To describe this more clearly for people undecided or unfamiliar with the era: If S3&K is the sublime perfection of an idea through rigorous testing, SCD is the haphazard, experimental design that was good enough to be tested. There is clearly one with more polish to an art with purpose while the other mires in its zaniness that it becomes a form of art like stream of consciousness. If curiosity alone piques you to try CD, then you might enjoy it for yourself.
Sonic CD occupies a strange space not only within the overarching franchise storyline but its status as a game to follow S1. The story is well known that SCD was a game made in tandem with S2 by a different team to create a sequel to the original on the Sega CD. Like the game’s emphasis of time-travel, these two games diverged the “official” Sonic 2 into two different existences like a shared multiverse. However, CD was never given a fair chance as Sonic 2 to challenge its rival. As a result of the additional peripheral cost of the SEGA CD, Sonic CD was a commercial flop with critical praise doomed to obscurity.
Enter Christian Whitehead, a man responsible for the excellent mobile ports of Sonic 1 and 2 as well as Sonic Mania, who not only brought CD to new audiences but ironed out a lot of the technical limitations of the CD version. Widescreen support with modern resolutions, Japanese and American OST options, performance tweaks for the 2.5 Special Stages, and small touches and new features like the Sonic 2 spin-dash and Tails as a playable character make Sonic the definitive version. There is literally no reason not to play this over the SEGA CD version due to its technical, gameplay and feature improvements.
Now the perplexing question that comes to mind is not whether CD is greater than S2, rather it’s whether CD is simply a more refined version of S1 as a “remake” of its time or should it be a sequel going its own direction. The problem with the original Sonic was its misguided attempt to space out speed levels from platforming levels. Where Sonic 2 focused exclusively on making speed the most important quality, CD focuses on interweaving speed with platforming and exploration challenges that would become the basis for Sonic 3. Even compared to S3, CD feels like a romp through an actual jungle gym that lets you go wherever (and whenever) you want so long as you make it out the other side intact, bruises and confusion be damned.
There are many words that can describe Sonic CD as a whole: Creative, schizophrenic, multidimensional, purposeless, demanding, convoluted, and perhaps hundreds of other terms that are all correct. Classic Sonic is at his best when levels and storylines are kept relatively simple and straightforward, and the Occam’s razor of game design is to remember the phrase, “Keep it simple, stupid.” This is the pitfall games like Majora’s Mask, Sonic CD, and dozens of other games that use core mechanics like time-travel to take an established formula into an experimental stage that is bound to leave many behind in the past.
Mechanically and thematically, CD is anything but simple on paper, and yet if you understand the ultimate goals of the game it’s perhaps the most stress-free Classic Sonic game to date (once you understand it). Time-travel is relegated to sign posts that will send Sonic forward and backwards in time to altered levels with new pathways, assets and obstacles if the player can maintain Sonic’s speed long enough. Although each post can be used only once, these opportunities do not immediately go away as the ability will disappear over a long period of time or if a player fails an attempt. Players can find simple ways to travel through time at designated “travel” areas like two bounce-pads aimed at each other, or they can try to maintain speed through knowledge of the level’s geometry.  At its core, time-travel is not an overly complicated mechanic but a poorly conveyed one that stresses the player more than it should without a restart button available, though you can save and quit to reset a stage.
However, and this is the important part, mastering time-travel is not required to finish the game. Whereas S2 and S3 used the gatekeepers of Chaos Emeralds to prevent players from completing the game on their first run, CD presents two equally challenging win conditions that caters to both explorative players and speedrunners. Players can travel back in time and find the robot generators in every level, and they will get a Good Future rating—you don’t even need to travel back to the present or the future to win except for an achievement. Or, the alternative, players can complete levels with fifty rings to reach special stages to collect seven Time Stones out of fourteen chances to get a Good Future. These stages are fun, challenging UFO 2.5D arenas that maintain the emphasis of speed. Neither decision limits the player from finding their own means to enjoy Sonic CD, but the addition of a choice does complicate it.
Interesting enough, this addition of a choice based on skill is what saves Sonic CD from being a niche title. Players who only want to rush towards the end can collect fifty rings, which are found in abundance, and reach the end whereas more explorative types can enjoy the challenge of learning the environments to time-travel. This skill-floor makes what could have been a mentally tasking game into a more enjoyable experience, and it’s proof that time-travel, while a novel and unique mechanic, often creates more unintended consequences in the imagination of the player than it truly intended.
In addition to the complexities of time-travel, the environments themselves are not centered around what Sonic 2 would focus on, speed above all else, which creates real playhouses for Sonic to simply revel in his momentum based gameplay. If anything would have helped make CD more favorable, the option of Tails for beginners would have made exploration easier for newcomers rather than a NG+ reward. The time-travel alterations are largely what I believe is responsible for the misunderstood reception of CD as once you play a level enough times every level has as much definition as the other Genesis titles. Now some stage gimmicks can be irritable, yet quirks like how bosses are more environmental based challenges than battles make it only stand out more as it ages.
Fortunately, and somewhat ironically, time has been favorable to CD; it’s a game from another time and place where Sonic 2 was not the pinnacle of the series, and that allows it to bend the established rules not engrained as assumed truths in future sequels. Unlike modern Sonic who can do no right and a lot wrong, CD can be favored for its idiosyncracies.

PROS: Beautiful character art, fun nostalgia inducing music, and compelling story
CONS: Sometimes heavy-handed morals
OVERALL SCORE: 7.5/10
Read Only Memories is definitely a labor of love, filled with carefully crafted pixel art, quirky characters, and a unique story.
ROM is a lovely cyberpunk adventure, and one that has a great number of strengths, particularly in its art and in its storytelling. The art is gorgeous, especially the character art. Whether it's the lanky, butch Lexi or our character's tiny round robotic companion, Turing, the characters all have a unique feel to them. Even the background characters were really cool to look at. The music was also lovely, reminiscent of the old school point and click adventures. It hit just enough nostalgia points for me, and I honestly really enjoy most of the scores. I found myself pausing a lot on the menu screen especially, just to listen to the songs.
Storywise, I thought the game was pretty good. The protagonist is a journalist who finds himself being approached by a ROM named Turing who is searching for his creator - and your old friend - Hayden. Sometimes the choices in the game felt a little unrealistic, but the protagonist is a journalist, so them being willing to do things risky and dangerous did make more sense. Generally speaking, however, I enjoyed the story. The characters are really charming, and you care about their struggles. There's a lot of humor, but there's also quite a bit of darkness, and the emotional moments of the story hit hard. One thing I really enjoyed - the game's twists make sense, but they aren't predictable and I found myself frequently second guessing my plot predictions. As someone who hates really obvious plotlines, I really enjoyed this. It was definitely a fun little journey, especially for someone interested in artificial intelligence and cyberpunk detective stories.
As far as the puzzles, they are mostly clear and logical. There were a few that didn't make sense to me, and some that required digging into the background because the items you needed weren't obvious. Occasionally, I found myself resorting to the age-old strategy of "use every item with everything", but I found that happened less often than using actual logic to solve the problems. In general, there wasn't a whole lot to complain about.
The one major complaint I had was the heavy handed moralizations the game tried to dole out from time to time. The most obvious of this is with the character Jess, who seems to hate the protagonist no matter what they do, and never really changes. I don't necessarily have a problem with characters disliking the player, but the game gives no reason for this hatred. Jess seems to be there to show the evils of discrimination - she is a genetically modified human 'hybrid' that is supposedly reviled in society...except the game never shows this. The only people who hate hybrids are a group of extremists known as the Human Revolution, who are basically seen as a joke by everyone, no one seems to support their opinions. At any rate - all of this wouldn't irk me so much if Jess was a one time character, but she actually makes many appearances in the game, all of which are about as baffling as the first encounter.
On the other hand, most of the characters are quite interesting. All of the main characters had something unique about them, both physically and in their personalities. I'm so used to games with anime styles have characters that all look the same, so I was really impressed by this. There is a lot of diversity in the cast and most of it - Jess aside - is done in a way that makes it seem natural. The game also includes some very frank discussions on gender fluidity that I thought were really refreshing. Even though the game can come off as strong sometimes, there are many beautiful moments of subtlety that make the game great.
Overall, I would say ROM is worth playing, if you enjoy point and click adventures and cool stories about robots. For the price of the game, you're getting an excellent little adventure that will keep you occupied for quite some time.

I found out about this game through the "Games you might not have tried." segment of the Extra Credits channel and they actually do not advertise the heavy LGBT themes that are part of this game, it was presented as a cool cyberpunk adventure. Considering this, I went into playing without any expectations of this and to be honest its presence was not bothersome in the least. Suprisingly enough it is a lot of other creative choices that were made by the studio that ended up demolishing my immersion in the world they have created with what amounted to a narrative sledghammer. In the end I am left very dissapointed because in part I see how much potential the game has and because playing the game like a reasonable person gave me the most boring ending of them all, the one that most people get actually, that is an issue.
### SPOILER WARNING ###
Also there is no TL:DR, you are reading a review for an interactive novel, you know what you were getting into.
Pros:
- The art style for the game is rather great, it captures just the right kind of atmosphere in which cyberpunk tends to thrive in my opinion and modernizes a lot of the fashion and form from the era it was concieved in.
- The music is superb and fits the story excellently, none of the tracks feel out of place with the scenes they are used in.
- Having streamed my gameplay for my girlfriend who is also a sci-fi fan this interactive novel sparked some intense and interesting discussion regarding the social and technological aspects of this established world and the impacts of the various cyberpunk media that came before it.
- The characters are rather varied in the story and it is refreshing to interact with most of them.
Cons:
- The number one con is the massive railroading that takes place in this interactive story and given that it is one it is a bit silly to say that. However, it presents several means for solving different situations but their trigger points are entirely non-obvious and once reached lock you into lengthy interactions you can not skip, even by end tasking the game. I don't know about you but I don't feel like acting in a way I do not expect my character to just because I made one wrong choice in a lengthy dialog tree.
- PC culture is strong with this one. I tried to play this ineractive novel as a nice guy just trying to help out a friend who is in trouble and I tried to engage people in coversation as one would, I was quickly shown that I was in fact playing as the antichrist and I should seriously reconsider my life choices. The game painfully trains you how you are supposed to interact with the story if you don't want to come off as an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with every word that comes out of your mouth.
- One of the greatest sins I can think of in writing a story is to actually snap your subject out of the world they are in with the way you write. There are several instances of this in the interactive novel such as when a robot breaks into your apartment, mucks about with your personal belongings and data, then outright tells you he is not bound by Isaac Asimov's three laws or any other governing structure that would ensure he does not kill you and your reaction is just to roll with it. The breaking point for me was when Jess told me the kind of neighborhood I was going into to help save my friend was so dangerous that without the proper protection from her I could end up in an organ chop shop, that was when I went "Yup this is a game and I am only playing it because its a game, no sane person would do this." given the fact that I had not been in contact with the lad in distress for years and from later conversations in the story its pretty evident why, he's a major♥♥♥♥♥♥ There is also a point where you tell someone that a person's life is on the line and that you need a piece of tat that they own to trade to a dealer to help them and they outright refuse even when someone who knows them tells them its the truth, this leads into a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t segment about sharing and a lesson I was too irritated to learn from the interaction. There are plenty more in the story and its aggrevating to just remember them.
- Another problem I have with this interactive novel is that the authors of it do not have a good enough grasp on the technical and even literary concepts they are trying to convey, it has just enough to keep you interested but for a person knowledgeble and willing to dig deeper you quickly find that it ends at the surface.
- The interactive mechanics of the game are very crude, the puzzles range between too simple and I am just going to rub this on everything until I get a result because I have no idea where to start.
- Also the fact you don't get to play a whole act of the game because you don't sign up for the cyber hippie ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t fed to you in the end of the game about giving all ROMs their own agency which most of them won't be able to use effectively since they are older models in the words straight out of the game, is a low blow.
In closing I will not be playing the game over, the developers have clearly shown that they want to tell a pretty hard sci-fi story but they will only let you enjoy it if you leave your brain at the door and I am not down for that.

Dragons Dogma:Dark Arisen to me is a very underrated game, mostly due to idiots comparing it to Dark Souls. If you expect this game to be a clone of any other game then you would be wrong. Dragons Dogma is a mixture of Devil May Cry, Shadow of the Colossus, and Final Fantasy. This game does have some rough edges, that I can’t deny, but is probably one of the only games to actually reward you for exploring its open world.
I would say that the biggest flaw that has turned a lot of players away from this one, is the pacing of the game itself. It starts out exciting, but after the first hour or two you will be battling mostly against wolf’s, bandits, and harpies for about 15 hours or so, then back into the exciting parts you go. This is where exploring and doing side quest come in, because most of the cool creatures you kill are not actually quest besides the griffin, and the main bosses. You will have to hunt down a lot of the dragons, cockatrice, and hydra’s.
I have seen a lot of people complaining that the game is hard, and they get one shotted by bandit’s etc. This is more than likely due to them not holding your hand and telling you everything you can do. Yes this means you will have to learn as you go, besides the basics. After you learn how to play the game correctly, it will become a little too easy for most, so you may have to increase your difficulty which you can do at any time.
The story itself isn’t the best, and does have some plot holes that never get answered, but it's still entertaining enough to keep you going. I highly recommend this game to anyone who has never tried it out, if your still unsure you can always catch it on sale.

At first, the game feels great. A brand new survival game that actually does what it intends to do; survive. You have your open world, vehicles, large amounts of weapons, scavenging, etc. But if you are looking for a survival game that gives you independence, this is NOT the game for you, and here's why;
This game forces you to be in a group with people as part of some 'campaign' mode, and there is no way out of it if you wish to progress through the game. Now, when you hear it, the group that you join has apparently been surviving for a long time (and doing well). You think that the group can be of help to get your survival going. This, however, is not the case. As soon as you join the group, the group relies on you to do everything that they need. First, you have to scavenge supplies to make the base either better, or to maintain it. Secondly, you have to save the people in your group that are CONSTANTLY getting into messes like being attacked by zombies. Thirdly, you have zombies that you need to take care of yourself (i.e infestations, special zombies, zombie hordes) and the whole game just ends up becoming tedious. Since you are spending all your time on your group staying alive, you don't have much time to actually progress through the game. The resources are also a problem, there aren't enough. Resources that you will find the most of is food, medicine, and gas (which you honestly don't need a lot of). Resources that you actually need though is weapons, ammo, and supplies for building (there are small amounts of these throughout the game).
My experiences throughout the game are based on those, I had no other problem with it, but when I found out that I have scavenged every single building (only having a few upgrades and a low ammount of needed supplies), I was only through the middle of the game, I couldn't progress from there. The game demands too much out of you in a few hours of play.
I only reccomend this game if you enjoy having to do quests every 5 minutes and not being able to progress, because that is how it seems.
EDIT: I also have played +20-30 hours even though steams says only 5 since I usually am in offline mode when playing singleplayer games

It's not your typical shoot-em-up zombie game such as [too many to count], instead there is an emphasis on group survival strategy.  It reminds me of a great little flashgame called "Rebuild" except much more hands-on.  You manage and scout for supplies, look for other survivors, maintain your allies' mental and physical health.  There is also an emphasis of personal survival tactics.  Health and stamina play a large role in your close-quarters-combat strategies, making you prioritize and time your movements.  State of Decay also exemplifies superb zombie detection AI making you think about how much noise you make by running, shooting, driving cars, or breaking windows and doors.
The world state is constantly changing, even when you're not playing, and practically every action in the game has its consequence.  That's not to say that there is no progress or improvement, only that there are many losses and consequences.  There's a feeling of never being on top but it keeps the game engaging and seems to strengthen the concept that your characters are surviving--not winning epically, but surviving by the skin of your teeth against all odds.
If you're a fan of survival games and want something fresh in the zombie genre State of Decay offers a lot of value at a very modest price. I highly recommend State of Decay.

TimeShift is a decent FPS game with a gimmick that isn't seen often: the ability to manipulate time. You can slow down (ok, that is kinda common), pause and even reverse time. This is used to solve numerous puzzles in the game - often the game will automatically highlight the correct action for you but not always and not all puzzles will be solved the same way. But beyond puzzles you can also use the time manipulation to run faster, cause explosions (you can stop time, shoot an explodable container, run away and restore time to actually have the explosion happen), steal enemies' weapons and avoid grenades.
As far as the rest of the gameplay goes, TimeShift is probably closest to Half-Life 2 although not as polished. You get to drive vehicles, travel in a train, fly in a zeppelin and gun down enemies and other set pieces.
Visually the game was very good for its time (it was released in 2007) and personally i loved the overall theme of a dystopian retrofuturistic city. While AAA games have more detail nowadays on their environments, i think TimeShift - thanks to some texture and lighting effects - looks better today than some other games of its time (no, i'm not including Crysis here :-P). Although the human models might be a bit on the repetitive side.

FORCED is an insanely fun co-op puzzle brawler. You play as a slave being trained up to be a gladiator and you are exposed to 25 challenging levels (5 bosses, 20 challenge rooms). After 30 hours of playing the game (it can definitely be completed MUCH faster), here's what I think..
Pros:
- The game is infinitely more fun with co-op partners. The difficulty fluctuates a lot depending on whether you do a challenge solo or with a group. For example, some challenge rooms are easier to do with more people. On the other hand, some boss rooms require a lot more concentration with a full group due to the higher amount of adds. Either way it is a game that does a great job of promoting teamwork seeing as the 4 available weapon-types have a specific role to fulfill.
- The skill variety is ample enough. There are 3 passive and active slots and there are enough skills for all types of situations.
- There is a large variety of different challenges rooms with various objectives. There are 4 acts (or areas) and all of the puzzles are different. No 2 puzzles repeat so you can be sure that the game stays 'fresh' until the end.
- You get to face challenging bosses. Each boss has a speed challenge and a 'self-imposed' handicap challenge. With these 2 challenges, you can't just face-smash your way to full-on victory. Fully completing a boss level requires a certain level of precision and understanding of the room's mechanisms.
- The spirit guide's dialogue is quite well-done. It was entertaining enough to get me through the entire game without getting complacent.
Cons:
- The Camera feels very limited.
- There is currently a glitch that sinks the 3rd player in any group under the floor when entering or re-entering the preparation room. They are currently looking into it.
- High latency can cause issues in some puzzles. These issues can block progression.
All in all I loved FORCED. I haven't had that much fun in co-op since playing Magicka.
I would like to see more puzzles in the future. The bosses were alright but the puzzles felt a lot more satisfying/rewarding when completed.
9/10 and looking forward to sequels and other releases from this developer!

The latest in the Splinter Cell series, where you play the perennial NSA ninja, Sam Fisher.
This is the first time in the series that the voice is not provided by Michael Ironside, which is s shame, but doesn't detract from the game overall.
Also,Sam Fisher seems to have grown younger by a  decade, and also now looks like Doplh Lundgren.
One of the new game mechanics is a broadening of play styles, allowing CoD type players to run and gun, whilst allowing the ninja gamers to sneak through a mission. It's a good idea, and opens up the variety of approaches for redoing missions.
However, let's be clear here, this is less hardcore Splinter Cell source gameplay and more CoD with sneaking, and I suspect this is to cater for the ADHD twitch gamers, who do not have the patience to watch an enemy patrol pattern for five minutes.
The campaign sets a scenario where a rogue MI6 agent is conducting a major offensive against US assests. Your goal is to foil these attacks before each event counts down.
The campaign missions, in true geo-political style, aspan across the globe, and in true Splinter Cell style, almost every high security facility in the world is run by demon accountants, who demand the greatest savings in lighting, giving plenty of shadows to hide in.
Naturally, if they modelled them on real life facilities, the entire area would be bathed in incandescent lighting, and Sam Fisher would be shot dead before he reached the first climable ledge. However, moving on..
Spoiler alert
This time you have a team under your command. These team members are essentially quest givers, with different play styles.
These side missions, along with the main missions will net you money, and can be farmed to get more money, as well as to perfect a play style.
Why do you need money ? Well, you can upgrade both your plane, gear and weapons, all of which is highly recommended.
In additon to the side missions, there are daily and weekly challenges  and Gone Dark missions which are lightweight investigation missions.
The game was released in mid 2013, and as a result the gaming herd has mostly moved onto other games.
There is still a lot of fun to be had in completing coop missions, and if you want to explore that side of the game fully, I'd recommend getting some of your mates to buy the game as well.
Most of the players appear to be US  based, so there is some lag and time differences to take into account, and that brings me onto the lobby system.
It is very much in the CoD interface style of 'hide everything from the player'. Seach for players, and if no one is around, you are given the opportunity to start a lobby for players.
Other than that, the lobby is very basic, so no setting max ping or region based gaming. Furthermore, there is no way to text chat in the lobby - has to be via microphone.
In game, you can both voice and text chat, but there is no history view, often is obscured by a game alert banner and when you are incapacitated, it is removed all together, which completely bemuses me.
The games' origin from a console is obvious, especially when you are trying to complete an action - many of the action triggers use the same button, so you will have situations where you want to open a window, and he flicks off the light switch.
Just for fun, many of the actions are closely grouped together, so when you are trying to move quickly, you get a Benny Hill scenario where Sam Fisher will leap over a fence, leap back, jump up onto a ledge, jump through the unopened window - shattering the glass.
All you want to do was switch off the bloody light.
In one co-op game, my partner was downed, and I had to race to him to resusitate him, leaping over obstacles and dashing forth with courage and valour, under fire.
Well, that was the
Closely grouped actions, panicked button pressing and lag all conspired against me, so rather than a heroic rescue, it appeared my character had suddenly decided now was a perfect opportunity to demonstrate a bracing set of gymnastics, all whilst my partner rapidly bled to death.
Unimpressed, he disconnected shortly after.
Adding to the action hilarity, is that fact the developers have bound some contextual actions to key combinations - but then failed to document them anywhere.
For instance, you are running up to a door, pressing (Shift + W). Once you arrive at the door, rather than stopping to allow you peek under it, Sam will instead kick it in,

Of course, kicking the door in alerts every ♥♥♥♥ing guard in the area, and may well terminate your mission.
The average PC keyboard has 104 keys, and yet Ubisoft have only utilised 2 for action keys.♥♥♥♥♥♥poor effort.
There is a lot to like about this game, but there are so many bugs in this game, I could fill several reviews with the bugs found in gameplay. Most of these issues stem from Ubisofts general disdain for PC gamers, catering to the console market first, and as this is a business policy, highly likely we are going to see the same style of issues in other PC games.
There are also some questionable design decisions (such as, you can't press Esc to skip through the logo loading screen, but once it has loaded, Esc dumps you out of the game with no confirmation; evidently a very clear decision from Ubisoft to say ♥♥♥♥ You)
In summary, it is a good game, and a lot of fun to play.
Given it's age, it can be picked up cheap from a number of outlets, along with the DLC. so, if you can see past the game bugs, it will provide you with a lot of entertainment (and frustration) and is a blast in Co-op.
