== Long Review, No Spoilers ==
It's about time that I wrote a review about this game.
It is about "Binding of Isaac: Rebirth" (BoI) with Afterbirth and Afterbirth+ DLCs.
BoI is a rogue-like "four-way shooter": You control your character either by using a game pad (which I strongly recommend) or the keyboard and view him or her from above. Aside from Isaac himself, there are several other characters with slightly different abilities and stats which can be unlocked throughout the game.
In this review I shall just reference to controlling Isaac but suffice it to say that each of the characters plays quite differently from the others and you have to use different tactics if you want to be successful.
After a short introduction, the game starts in the "cellar" or "basement". Isaac needs to find his way through many different, randomly generated levels to escape from his evil mother. Unfortunately, the dungeons are filled with deadly traps monsters and bosses.
Luckily, Isaac can "fire" tears in a chosen direction to fight off his opponents. He can find hundreds of different items which make him stronger during a "run" and a map helps him find his way through the dungeons.
All in all, the optics of the game bear a very strong resemblance to the dungeon levels of the very first Zelda game on the NES and there are also a few in-game references to it.
As it is common with "rogue-likes", you can proceed to deeper levels and you can save and load your progress. You cannot go back, though, and if you die, you have to start a new run, beginning from the start in a new dungeon with new items.
Anyway, while all this description sounds pretty "standard", the game is not. Though the original BoI started as an Indie Game, it hardly has to hide behind full-priced AAA titles when it comes to game design, difficulty, balance and replay value.
I shall list a few (but not all) of the reasons why I deeply enjoy playing BoI even after > 190 hours.
1) The game is extremely challenging, but you can beat it if you practice your skill. In many other rogue-likes, chance (or the "random generator" = "rng") plays the major role in determining whether you are ultimately "successful" in a run or not. Not so with BoI: In this game, practicing and strategic planning are rewarded and make the difference. I cannot count how many times I was close to giving up on a specific challenge or level because I thought it was impossible to beat, just to pick up my pad again and to realize a few minutes later that I just went about it the wrong way, used the wrong strategy or combined the wrong items.
Do not get me wrong: The RNG still can set you up with an inadequate equipment / item drops but there are enough ways in the game to turn the tide or swap the equipment if you know the game mechanics.
2) Grinding is not required to become stronger in a normal run. Although there are certain mechanics in the game which unlock a starting gear for a character and which e.g. allow improving the stuff the in-game shops have to offer, this is a bonus and not a must in order to successfully complete the game. The "greed mode" is an exception (see below).
3) There are hundreds of items. Literally. While many games feature dozens of similar items which do not really make any difference in the actual game play, this is different with BoI: Though some items have similar effects (e.g. grant you a health container), most items and trinkets (which you also can carry around) have a pretty much unique effect. The best part is, that the devs included some pretty neat and cool stacking effects which apply when you combine certain items. It is a vital part of the game that you get to know the items, know their strengths and weaknesses and know which items are good to combine and which combinations you should avoid.
4) Nearly every challenge or "achievement" you can complete in the game unlocks a new item, character or ability. While this does not sound so impressive at first, trust me, it is: With a total of 339 achievements you can unlock many, many items. The good thing is that this really adds to the gaming experience and still after placing for > 100 hours, you can find new items with new abilities. This also potentially gives you more options in future runs, making you also potentially stronger if you know how to use them to your advantage.
5) The graphics and sounds are retro-style. I like this a lot (while others may not), as it really reminds me of Zelda or Star Tropics.
6) The story is eerie. While not suited for children, I really think the dark mood of the game adds to the atmosphere and it makes BoI stand out from many other "vanilla games".
7) The game has many endings. Don't worry - I will not spoil any of that. Suffice it to say that you can actively choose in which direction you wish to progress and which ending you wish to pursue. You'll find out... :-)
8) Apart from the "normal" game, the devs have added more modes which play completely differently. First, there are "challenges" where Isaac usually starts already with a special set of items and abilities but which often also include certain penalties which make finishing the game harder and which require a good in-game knowledge of items and game mechanics.
Then, there is the "greed mode" in which you can fight waves of opponents in various levels, which drop money you can use to buy equipment and where you can ultimately collect money at the end of each run to unlock new items in the game.
9) You can play coop (2 players) locally.
10) There are many bosses and enemies in the game. Learning how to beat seemingly unbeatable bosses is a key aspect of the game.
11)I cannot emphasize the replay value enough. Though I have literally finished the game > 20 times, there is still something new to unlock and every run is different. I have not had this kind of replay value in any other game I have played before...
After so much praise, I have to be fair and state that there are some aspects about BoI which could be improved:
1) There is no complete in-game description of what items / trinkets really do. Although you can reverse-engineer many effects by close observation or looking at the statistics, I often resort to the wiki pages of the game rather than write down my experiences. The devs could have made it possible to collect this "lore" in an in-game diary which expands by using every new item once in a while...
2) The "greed mode" requires too much grinding as opposed to the rest of the game. If you wish to unlock everything in this mode, be prepared to play *a lot*. IMHO, the devs could have refrained from letting the "greed machine" jam every once in a while as this adds nothing to the gaming experience.
3) Getting every achievement in the game without cheating is extremely hard. So for completionists, this may be frustrating.
There is so much more I wanted to write about this game and so little space...
So let's hear the verdict:
I can truly recommend this game - I have played a lot of games in my lifetime (>500) but this is one of the very, very few which I would rate with a 10 of 10 stars.
If you are even remotely interested in a zelda-reske, rogue-like game with creepy story and tough battles, which requires thoughtful, clever usage of the scarce resources and if you like a challenge, this is your game.
PS: My recommendation is to get the this game instead of the original BoI with "Wrath of the Lamb" DLC, since it features all the items, enemies and stuff of the original game and much, much more in addition.

This game was good, but I couldn't help feeling like it wasn't as good as it could have been.  It feels like editorial mandates got in the way of the story that some writers were trying to tell and gummed up the works.  Quests can feel disconnected and companions occasionally feel neutered by editing, especially those written by Chris Avellone.
Don't get me wrong, the story is fantastic and the companions break the Bioware mold that many RPG's find themselves stuck in.  The world is fantastically realized, being both dark and gritty while also maintaining a sense of wonder not always found in contemporary fantasy.  The lore is also well written and interesting, avoiding some of the pitfalls of other games of the genre by making the lore seem too distant from what is actually presented and giving a real sense of belonging within the game world.
The graphics are another high point, for the most part.  All the backgrounds are well detailed with particle effects that just pop, but the models aren't really consistent.  For an indie game of this magnitude, they do look very good, but if you are expecting highly detailed, AAA models, look elsewhere. Occasionally enemies will have their models go over scenery that they really shouldn't, it is most notable when they die.  Despite those flaws, the overall artistic design is stunning.
Music is okay, nothing really spectacular, but it more than does the job.  For the most part, it is rather sparse and when it does come in it is typically light and unintrusive.  While this can feel immersive, it means that I wouldn't really say any of it stands out.
Overall, it is a really good game, that seems like it could have been better with more time and money.  That said, it is probably the best singleplayer RPG in years and without a doubt the best throwback to the old infinity engine games on the market (although with Numenera looming on the horizon, that may be a better option long term).

Read Only Memories is simultaneously a return to point-and-click adventure glory and a step forward on several fronts. Even in presenting a better future where the gender binary's been chucked out the window and many current equality issues have been resolved, some things never change. Read Only Memories presents an apt metaphor for how difficult it can be for humanity to adapt to social change.
That's really the key thing to remember going into Read Only Memories: metaphor. Are the rights and experiences surrounding genetic hybridization, machine sentience, and cybernetic implants the most apt analogues for issues such as gender transition, body dysphoria, and non-cis/het rights battles? Not entirely. However, the struggles presented in Read Only Memories do present something of a "beginner's guide" look at such issues. Grasping those aspects of identity when you have literally no concept of them can be incredibly difficult, so easing players into that world with a more ubiquitous science fiction context was a good call. Does Read Only Memories succeed in that metaphor? Not entirely, but major points for even trying.
Social issues aside, Read Only Memories is a great game in and of itself. The pixelated presentation is beautiful and consistent, and I loved the peppy, fluid soundtrack. If you can afford the extra expenditure, I highly recommend picking that up as well. The noir undertones of the plot are woven surprisingly well into the bright, colorful version of Neo San Francisco you wander, which makes the looming shades of dystopia that much more impactful when you stumble across them. The characters are all rather memorable, though a few feel criminally underutilized. I expected more from Lexi, in particular, but for the most part she just feels like a nagging conscience, forever whispering about a past you never quite get to explore. I'd also love to learn more about Sympathy, and what made her such a hard♥♥♥♥♥in the first place.
The hybrid and cybernetics rights issues also took a back seat to the core plot, which I feel was a missed opportunity. I'm especially interested in the former, as the cyber side at least tied into the issue of ROMs a bit. Even some tucked-away, extra reading or collectable content would've been nice to look over to learn how genetic manipulation even began taking hold, and why. Midboss has expressed interest in doing more with the world of Read Only Memories, so we may see something to that effect down the line, but again, seems like a bit of a missed opportunity.
And, as a quick aside, I really loved the whole Drinktionary thing, and the variety of drinks presented was both extensive and super-cute. I'm hoping this makes a return in future Midboss games, perhaps with more of a gameplay factor than just passing out after too many. Levels of tipsiness? Interactions changing (for better or for worse) under the influence? There's plenty there to work with, and if nothing else, I just want to see more of Majid and Gus.
In summary, Read Only Memories is a great first foray into what hopefully turns into a wider run of games. It's incredibly charming, and even with a few pitfalls, provides a nice change of pace and a memorable tale. Looking forward to the Endless Xmas DLC, even if it's coming a bit late to be entirely seasonal.

'Underrated' does not properly describe the state of this title. I would take DD over any of the Witcher or Elder Scrolls titles any day of the week and it's not even close.
Dragon's Dogma is an unrealized gold mine; the first company to steal its mechanics and jam them into a better setting will undoubtedly change the fantasy rpg genre forever. Capcom does not realize what it is that they have, here. They'll be beating themselves up, though, when somebody makes a successor before they do.

At the time of writing this review, I'm still exploring all this game has to offer. I've completed the "main story," and I'm entering new game+.
Let's start out with how I see this game. While delving into it, it easily became a favorite. I love the fantastical world of Gransys, and I have to say it's easily more interesting to me than anything like Skyrim of Tamriel (just as an example). The game sets out to make an interesting fantasy land, not a world. The developers didn't strive to explain the relationships between countries, or the politics that lie within, because it is completely unrelated to the character you play as. The world is developed as a small country in which you reside, not a massive land full of opportunity. Let's just say your character is destined for greater things.
When you first begin playing, you'll likely be drawn in with the promise of some fantastic combat and customization. When you're fighting things, you're going to enjoy the game. When you're not fighting things, you're going to enjoy the game.
When I was at this point, I already thought pretty highly of this game. I'm a dark souls/bloodborne fanboy, so finding better combat in an even more lively open world had me pinned. It still wasn't "dark souls-level." I didn't find the story that interesting, although I enjoyed the character interactions. Cutscenes were fantastically done, but I only enjoyed them because the game actually included cutscenes, one of the things I've sorely missed in a lot of other games.
All I can say is my first impression of the story was fairly wrong. Play this game for amazing combat, awesome RPG mechanics, and a wonderful fantasy world. Discover what else it has to offer as you play, because it will take you by surprise.
So basically, if you enjoy fantastic combat, a deep RPG, or dark souls, just play it. If you enjoy a deep story, well, this game has it but it's literally so deep that you can't even see it at first. Good luck! :^)

This game is incredible! Snatcher is one of my favorite games of all time, and Read Only Memories is without a doubt the closest thing I've ever played to a true successor. It uses its cyberpunk setting well and crafts together a really interesting story. The artwork is fantastic and really captures the essence of the era. It's got great music, unique characters, and a plot that will keep you guessing the whole time.
The gameplay itself is pretty straightforward, but there are 6 different endings for you to find, so there is definitely some room for player choice. In traditional adventure game fashion, you can interatct with all sorts of different objects, and if you're like me, you'll easily spend a ton of time laughing at all of the amusing dialogue that comes about from trying to give spoiled milk to people and talk to desks. What trumps even that for me though are the deep characters and overall atmosphere that the game conveys. It really captures the essence of cyberpunk and it couldn't make me happier.
A lot of people are giving this game bad reviews because of the social message that it conveys. It's true that the game goes out of its way to be pro LGBT and call out discrimination, but I personally didn't feel like that got in the way of the game too much. Considering the game takes place decades in the future, it's not too unrealistic that society would be a lot more accepting of these social taboos. The topic may be a bit too heavy for some, but I think it aligns with the setting of the game just fine.
Best of all, Read Only Memories knows how to do demos the right way. Not only is there a free version that lets you play the prologue, but it even lets you play most of chapter 1 as well! And better yet, your save data from the demo carries over to the full game. So if you're at all curious, give it a try. If you're like me, you won't be able to stop there!
Overall, Read Only Memories was one of the best games I played all year. It's a true love letter to not only Snatcher, but classic adventure games and the cyberpunk genre in general. I don't want to get too caught up on the comparison, but since we'll likely never see a real Snatcher sequel, this is by far the next best thing. I couldn't recommend this game more. Check it out!

First off, a disclaimer. I haven't played many visual novels, maybe a couple before this one. As such, I'm not particularly savvy as what makes or breaks these types of games. In fact, I'm not even sure if VNs can be considered games, but that's a discussion for another time.
is a remake of a VN that was originally released in Korea in 2010 and was funded via Kickstarter. The story is familiar enough, boy meets (android) girl, is stubbornly reluctant to bond with her at first, but she eventually warms her way into his heart. It reminded me of
a bit, seeing as that graphic novel deals with the relationship between a human and an android in a world that is openly hostile to the idea of human-like robots (the world in
is less hostile to androids). Unlike
though, this one sticks the landing.
There's more going on in the background with the boy's open aversion to androids, what ties into his family, and, naturally, the question of whether a robot can have feelings is explored, leading to comparisons between a robot's programming and a person's upbringing. While I felt like these questions were deftly explored in this context (as well as another one I won't spoil), there were also a few subjects the VN didn't delve into as much as I would've liked. The already-limited interactivity (by my perceived VN standards) compounded this issue and was somewhat frustrating, particularly when placed in a situation where you wanted the character to be given choices to do or say something. After all, the character's behaviour is, at times, difficult to understand, although he's still a (rebellious) teenager so there's that. In exchange, you are offered alternate responses from time to time (a very long time) that have immediate impact (no ramifications that I can see) and unlock achievements in-game. However, it's only the very last dialogue option that alters how the ending plays out.
I can't shake the feeling that
would have been better served if it had had more time to expand on its story, but then I remind myself it was a small, Kickstarter-backed, project (with a budget of $14,000), what puts things into perspective. There's only one VA in the game and that's Lucy (Korean and Japanese), the rest of the characters are silent, and they're not that many.
Even so, for all its weaknesses,
's story managed to grip me, and move me to the brink of tears through its effective (and borderline criminal) use of dialogue, music, and art. Like
, it blindsided me with a tonal shift I did not expect. Its narrative is cleverly told, so much so that it merits playing the VN a second time around to fully grasp everything that goes on. Like I said before, there are a couple of endings (actually, more like three) that depend on your last choice, as well as an epilogue that I believe gets rewritten if you unlock all the endings.
It took me about 6 hours to complete, unlocking all achievements and extras. It's a beautifully-told, emotional rollercoaster that stands above its flaws and is definitely worth experiencing. I cannot help but think it pulled some punches due to budget constraints. The KS page does mention it has a streamlined storyline so maybe the original is longer and more comprehensive, but
is one VN you should really consider checking out.

Shadow of Snoredor *obnoxious laugh*.
It's graphically appealing; runs smoothly; has good voice acting; the feuds and rivalry thing with the Uruk captains is clever; and it seemed to be setting up a half-decent story (even if Tolkien would be turning in his grave). It made it to the top of many people's game of the year lists, so it must be somebody's cup of tea.
However, an hour in and I hadn't started having fun. Excepting the time when I managed to grab an Uruk and had to repeatedly press X to shank him (which was delightful), I found the combat to be dull and lacking in depth. Just mash X until you see the counter warning, tap Y for a free stun then go back to mashing X. Occasionally tap Y AND B for an execution. Maybe it gets more interesting once you've ground through a bit and unlocked extra combos and finishing moves, but I wasn't feeling any desire to do that, it just felt like a chore. I know stealth is technically an option, but that only feels relevant when infiltrating a fort or something. I'm not stealthing my way across the entirety of that large, interesting, well laid-out, open-world map when I just want to get somewhere by dinner time.
The combat reminds me of Assassin's Creed, but Assassins Creed got away with slash-counter-stab combat because the combat wasn't what you were there for, it was merely the mustard on a lovely parkour/shanking hotdog.
So apparently I only have fun when I'm shanking something. I don't know if that's the game's problem or mine.

The reason for the thumbs down here isn't because the game is terrible, it's just not what I expected going in.  I bought this game thinking "Running around collecting supplies, shotgunning zombies heads off?!  Hell yeah!".  Turns out it's alot more realistic, which could be a good or bad thing, depending on your tastes.
Personally, this game felt like a looting sim.  You run from house to house, grab everything of importance, slowly walk it back to your base, repeat.  Eventually you can call in your fellow survivors to grab the important supplies, or set up a base, but when you do zombies come out of nowhere, for some reason, so there's a good chance they'll die if you don't stay to help them out, and walk them back.
There's also a system in place where the game world continues while you're logged off.  This sounds pretty cool, right?  Well, when you can only play for an hour or two each day, and there's no option to turn it off, you're basically fighting a losing battle.  The NPCs are apparently totally incompetent without your leadership, and everything goes to hell while you're gone.
While I enjoyed the game, and found the open world, as well as some of the mechanics, amazing, the inability to turn off the "simulation", so you can save and the world doesn't continue without you, makes me unable to recommend this unless you are a big fan of simulators, and have a lot of time to play.

The best way I can describe this game is 'meh'. There's signs of a good idea here but sadly it's buried under a tonne of mediocrity. Let me split this into two broad sections: plot and gameplay
PLOT
The premise of the game is that the villain has stolen a prototype suit that lets him travel through time and alter the future so that he is now the great dictator. Now this could have been interesting - alternative universes can offer the devs and players a chance to explore different philosophies and possibilites - but sadly the game wastes all that potential. We never see how the villain came to power, why he did so (not even a "I just want to be all-powerful" speech) and if you weren't told explicitly that this is what happened then you would never figure it out.
The environments are your bog-standard "wet industrial area", "wet bombed out apartments", and "wet military camp in forest" (one of the consequences of altering the timeline appears to be creating a constant monsoon season). They are completely interchangeable and it's almost impossible to distinguish one from the other. Eventually it all just blurs into one dull slog.
Oh and the time-travel that is supposed to be the key feature of this game? Yeah, it barely ever gets brought up. You could remove that element entirely and the game would not change one bit.
GAMEPLAY
While the story at least has the germ of a good idea buried underneath all the mind-numbing averageness, the same cannot be said for the gameplay. It doesn't so much as scream "mediocre!" as mumble it half-heartedly. Guns are what you'd expect - you get  the standard pistol, machine gun, rocket launcher, shotgun, sniper and they shoot alright, I guess. Nothing really special and they seem to lack any kick.
Enemies come in a few flavours: standard grunt, grunt with shield, grunt grunt with a rocket/sniper, and elite grunt with "time travel" (they move really fast). Apart from a skin change from level to level, there is no real variety and you learn pretty quickly how to deal with it.
Your special time-travel powers are also a joke. You have three: stop, slow, and reverse and using each power requires "energy" with slow using the least and reverse using the most. Because of this you'll probably end up using slow the most during combat since it can last about 30 seconds until depleted while reverse only lasts about 10. The only other time you will use your powers will be at set stages in each level where you have to complete a puzzle in order to advance. Again, these are easy to figure out and feel like they were only put there to justify the powers.
COCLUSION
Don't buy this game. It is boring as hell that mistakes having a near-useless gimmick as being comlex. There are better things you could spend your money on

I ran TimeShift on an HP laptop with an NVIDIA graphics card and Windows 10, 64-bit. Further, I also downloaded the game directly from Steam, and did not change any compatibility settings or even download a patch. It was still running Version 1.0 of the game.
And with the above, I
had the game crash or freeze or mess up like many people complain. So I feel very likely that either the machines people are trying are not that good, or maybe it's something like how AMD cards seem to not be as compatible as NVIDIA.
TimeShift is a very fun FPS game, and it's been a while since I've played an old-fashioned one like this, so I enjoyed it quite a lot.
The premise of the game, as the name implies, is your ability to change time. At just about any point, provided your ability has recharged itself, you can: (1) Slow Time, which allows you to move at normal speed while other things slow down; (2) Freeze Time, where you move a little slower but everything else freezes entirely; and (3) Rewind, which simply causes everything else to rewind while you stand where you are.
Without these abilities, TimeShift would be a pretty generic FPS game, but I still would have enjoyed it. I feel like many people who are disappointed with it maybe didn't grow up playing earlier FPS games before stuff like Overwatch became more expected.
Slow Time works for a few seconds and is heavily useful, especially as it lets you regenerate health right away. You can blast a bunch of enemies really quickly, too. Freeze Time is only useful if you're about to die and need to get away. It runs for a shorter period of time than Slow Time, so it's not always good to choose. Lastly, Rewind is almost useless unless you are solving a puzzle in the game. (The only bug I had was where Rewind would sometimes use up the ability meter faster than it should. It "fixed" itself if I let it use up the meter, and then recharged the meter. Then Rewind would use it up slower.)
Because it's an older FPS, enemies seem to take more damage than they should, even with headshots not killing some of them. But it's nothing that breaks the whole game. The only thing that gets a bit annoying are enemies that work against your time manipulation. There are enemies that move extremely fast and are almost impossible to hit, and they spam really powerful weapons at you. You have to Slow or Freeze Time to even get near them. But even if you use Slow Time, they still move faster than you, which is really bothersome. If you run out of your ability meter to use your time manipulation, you are likely going to die if you run into a group of these enemies. And some of the enemies even teleport in and out, popping up right next to you.
But for the most part, the game had enough challenge and was pretty interesting to me. The story is not quite amazing, but it fits the point of time travel.

A fun time manipulation shooter with fun power, decent challenge yet somewhat average in the end.
Before I begin I should post how to run this game on modern systems.
1.- Go to the game menu on steam, right click on the game's name and choose properties
2.- In that little menu choose the local files tab and the button browse local files
3.- Go to the bin folder and look for the exe
4.- Right click on it and select properties
5.- Look for the compatibility tab, check on "Run this program on compatibility for" and look for the option Windows XP service pack 3
And there you go, that shuold run the game with no trouble (but shame on them for not patching that).
Gameplay
It's the standard FPS from that time with a quirk that involves time manipulation in order to beat the game, thus making this game stand a bit out against the rest of the generic FPS. It uses bullet tracers which is always nice to have. And part of the covers can be destroyed.
That being that you have 3 powers in your arsenal and all 3 of them uses the same bar.
Time slow: As the name says it slow time for 12 seconds, giving you a huge advantage over your enemies since not only they move slow thus making them easy to read, but also you go fast and shoot a bit faster, being bear overpowered unless you decide to stand there. This one drains the bar slowly thus making it the one you'll use the most.
(Basically you become made in heaven, which kicks♥♥♥♥♥.
Time stop: As it says it slow time for 5 seconds (yep, just like the world) which gives you a fair amount of time to either steal the weapons of the enemies, move outside their range, avoid enviromental damage, stop movement in the puzzle sections or just plain kill them.
This power is far better than the time slow in many ways, but because the bar drains very quickly you'll only use this one when you really need it and either way you'll use time slow far more times.
Time reverse: As it says it reverses time and it affects everything but yourself and your weapons, however you cannot use it to kill enemies because it will cause a paradox. This one lasts 5 seconds (one second less from mandom) and it's not that useful really because you cannot regain health and it only works on a few puzzles. Avoid it unless you need it.
While in the easier difficulties you can pretty much anahilate the enemies, in the hardest level the time manipulation has to be used tactically if you want to progress. And in some stages certain enemies can use some of your powers (with the exception of time reverse), but once you know how to counter them they'll become a pushover.
The weapons themselvs are very fun to use and they do have a nice variety of them, My favorites being the explosive crossbow, the RPG, the surge gun, the pulse gun and to a degree the pistol and shotgun.
My only 2 complains about it would be if the bar drains completely it takes a while to fill back up, however once it starts filling up you can use it at any time you want. The second one would be that enemies are bulletsponges, which unless you take them out with a shotgun, a crossbow or with explosives they will take a while to kill them.
Controls
The strandard and unchanging controls from every FPS, WASD to move, LMB to shoot, RMB to use secondary fire, spacebar to jump and you know the drill
The only ones worth noticing are V for time slow, G for time stop and B for time reverse. They can be rebindable which is good and they work fine.
Story
The story consists on a doctor who took the alpha suit in order to travel to the past to become a dictator, and before the timejump he bombed the facility. You took the beta suit and thus traveled in time to stop him.
The story is meirely an excuse to use the setting of time manipulation because there's not much details about it and it's shallow. It only exists there so that you can have objectives to follow.
Graphics
Decent, not the best from that time and definetly not the best considering the modern standards. But they do works and you'll probalby won't be thinking about them. But the colors tend to be as dull as the rest of the generic FPS of that time.
Sountrack
Most if not all of it is forgetable and kinda bland, But they do a good job at creating the atmosphere that it tried to make. But many of the songs didn't interest me nor did they made me pump up for a fight.
The only one that I kinda remember is the gauntlet, being the one in the turret section. Which actually made the scene a bit more interesting.
Overrall
To be honest, most of the things in the game are generic as they can be. The only saving grace is that the time manipulation elements are very fun to play with and that the highest difficulty made me interested in using some tactics around it and that the weapons themselves are reliable and some of them are very fun to use due to their destructive power.
Thus for that reason only and because everything else works well but doesn't stands out I give it a 6/10, if it didn't had the time manipulation mechanics it would get a 5/10 for being bland.
But I do reccomed it because it's one of those games you can have mindless fun in being kinda OP with your powers.

This is frequently brought up and for good reason. The story is pretty bad. You almost get killed by a giant dragon, vow revenge, kill everything in your path (whilst helping some people) and kill the dragon.
The open-world is essentially a collection of encounters in an open area with little variation. In addition, the areas presented to the player are not extremely lively (or feel lived in). The only real exceptions to this are the big 'settlement' areas.
However, it is a cool world to explore with some fairly well hidden areas that someone has to really look for to find. Also the world itself looks pretty cool (especially the castles).
This game is not perfect. Yet, I can't help but love it.
I love the feeling of the game. The feeling of fighting enormous creatures with extremely satisfying combat. The feeling of the music. The feeling of almost dying in combat and struggling to get a grip on the situation.
I love the way (some of) the monsters look, looking exactly as how I imagined them and making them look and feel powerful.
But most of all I love being a blood-soaked, monster-slaying, getting-flung-off-cliffs, ravaging maniac who cannot write a concise, well-written review for a game he absolutely loves.

Dragon's Dogma has many flaws:
-Most of the characters are bland and uninteresting, at least for me.
-The story is kinda generic until the last few chapters where it actually gets really good ( No history spoilers but it has some good twists)
-The game doesn't really tell you that some quests can't be completed after you complete a certain quest and you may never get to see some sidequests due to this. (Took me 2 playthroughts without a guide to get all the quests done, missed a lot of them in the first one)
-The english voice acting is so bad that i got the japanese voice over not just for preference but for necessity.
-Some of the end-game sections are re-used a lot ( talking about Bitterblack Isle here) and it actually made me doubt if i was in the same place because they are nearly identical
But these are definitely overcomed by it's pros:

-The combat is just incredibly amazing, i can't even explaing how good the combat system is for a game of this age but i will try. It never got repetitive for me, the grabbing and climbing it's definitely one of my favorites and most used mechanics (if you played shadow of the colossus your will enjoy it a lot), facing a Cyclops? Cimb it. Chimera? Climb it. Dragon? Climb it. Living Armor? You probably shouldn't. Being able to switch between 9 classes which are played in a very different way  gives it a lot of replayability too. (After maxing all the classes i can safely say that they indeed feel different)
-The world: It's really interesting to explore the world even when the stamina limiter for running it's a little obnoxious. Just wandering around the world discovering places and getting ambushed by giant monsters makes it worth for the stamina.
- The paw system: I really wish more games could make AI companions as good as these ones, sometimes i felt like my pawns where doing more than me, they learn as you use them, the best way to kill a mob or the best way to complete a quests, they will learn it. Pawns can be shared throught the online function, allowing other people to use your pawn, they also get knowledge for helping in others worlds, even knowledge that you don't know. Also, pawns can only be 6 out of 9 classes in the game, the 3 basic ones and their 3 advanced forms. ( I believe it is due to the magick archer ability that allows you to sacrifice a pawn for massive damage)

Dragon's Dogma is a highly underrated RPG that any fan of the genre should experience. The area this game truly excels in is the combat, there are 9 unique classes each with a variety of abilities. DD:DA takes this one step further by allowing players to create two main custom characters and decide which class and abilities each will learn. Your second character's AI will also learn and grow depending on how you interact with enemies and the world. while not a perfect game by any means there is a lot here for RPG fans to sink their teeth into, including upgrading gear and reaching the level cap of 200. Farming end game loot is also very luck based and time consuming but rewarding once you finally get the perfect gear. Unfortunately the world map is fairly small and empty and there is very little variety in side quests. The main story is also quite short becasue apparently Capcom had more ambitious palns for this game that never worked out. This is rather dissapointing becasue one gets the feeling this game could have and should have been much more than it is. What is here however is definitely worth your time as the PC port is excellent and mods have brought several quality of life improvements such as unlimited stamina while running. If you are a fan of more fast paced action packed combat systems and don't mind farming bosses/monsters for loot to upgrade waepons this Is the RPG for you.

As an avid Street Fighter 4 player, I consider this game to be one of the best fighting games currently available.  Not only the character roster great, comprised of 30+ old and new fighters from the series to date, but so is the sophisticated combo system that is both easy to pick up yet difficult to master.  I wasn’t particularly a fan of SF4’s visual style and initially reluctant to try the game because of it, yet I’ve grown to appreciate the unique look and feel of each characters and stages that the developers faithfully recreated in this title.
Like many similar games in the genre, SSF4 was initially released on console systems and then ported over to PC.  Luckily, the developer Capcom has done an amazing job, implementing number of customization options for PC, such as support for greater than 30fps and multiple resolutions including 1080p.  In addition, the game also supports many controllers out of the box including XBOX 360 controller and numerous fightsticks.  Outside of Games for Windows Live, game runs smoothly and the loading time is relatively short, so there isn’t much for me to complain about this quality port.
Although brief single player portion of the game is quite good, the multiplayer is where this game truly shines.  Thanks to its improved netcode, finding multiplayer matches are quick and reliable.  Built-in match setups work consistently for the most part and despite it missing my favorite “championship mode” from a previous title, both ranked and endless mode keep the game interesting and fun.  I really like the replay / save feature as well, which helped me to capture and savor those favorite character match ups over the years.
Super Street Fighter 4 definitely isn’t perfect and the game isn’t groundbreaking enough to likely persuade those of you who aren’t interested in fighting games.  If you hold even a little preference over the genre though, this is good as any place to start.  I wholeheartedly recommend this to both casual onlookers and fighting game fans.

I've never been a fan of visual novels. None of them managed to hold me long enough to make it to the end. Then came along Lucy -The Eternity She Wished For-
This game showed up in my recommendations list one day and I saw the "Overwhelmingly Positive" response. Then I started reading the reviews and thought, can a visual novel really make that big an impact? So I decided to pick it up and try for myself.

Once the credits finished and the main menu showed up, there were some jumbled letters instead of the "Start" button. I thought it a bug and restarted the game, but they were still jumbled. Then the REAL ending played. And boy-oh-boy did I gush like a baby at the impact this sequence had on me. I buried my face in my pillow and cried until I could cry no more.
I've not been hit so hard by emotions for a long time and I thank the developers for bringing such an experience.

Preachy, condescending, and incredibly narrowminded.
While there's some interesting music and art, any enjoyment of Read Only Memories is completely snuffed out by some of the most insulting writing I've ever seen in a videogame.  The player character serves only as a dog to be yanked along on a leash by your insufferable robot companion, and gleefully kicked by any of the NPCs who haven't reminded you how superior they are within the last five seconds.  Your constant ally in the game treats you like a petulant child from your first encounter, and relishes every opportunity to express their disappointment in you as a player for daring to explore the dialogue tree or challenge a given idea.  From the outside it may sound funny or like a purposeful stylistic decision, but from a gameplay perspective it's genuinely frustrating.  Even the flavor text you get from examining the objects in the world drips with disdain for the player.
After several chapters of having my character dragged through the mud from every possible direction, I didn't want to play anymore.  The premise is somewhat fascinating, but there's nothing within this package that's not extremely derivative.  This game is what happens when a writer is more interested in forcing their ideas down your throat than crafting a compelling, enjoyable narrative.  I strongly suggest avoiding this game and looking for another adventure.

The game's political overtones are very poorly done, providing only the most grade-school levels of understanding and nuance.
I wanted to like the game. It isn't "bad" in the same way as much of what creeps onto Steam. This is the first time I've really wanted a neutral option. As it stands (and at its price point) I just can't give it the thumbs-up.

Want a fantastic Cyberpunk detective visual novel point-and-click game?  This is it.
You're a journalist who's been reduced to writing reviews for headphones (And just about anything electronic in the game gets a fun reaction from them, try it out!), when a ROM (Relationship and Organizational Manager) robot shows up at your door claiming that his creator (a friend of yours) was kidnapped, and it's up to you to find out who did it and why.  Before long you'll find things are actually on a much greater scope than that...
So you hop aroud the mis-topia of NEO-San Franciscso looking for clues in a city that's bright and vibrant and teched up to the gills, but with a dark side to it.  A corrupt corporate police force.  A movement that thinks genetically modified people aren't "Human".  Murder and kidnapping.  A few bitter genetically modified people who get very touchy and angry when you accidentally slight them.  The implication that the CIA basically turned North Korea into something out of the Fallout games.  And the world's first autonomous self-willed AI.  All this and more piles up on your plate and you have to navigate this minefield to get to the truth.
The game is engaging and well written most of the way through, and atmospheric enough that it legitimately gets creepy at times when the game bares its fangs.
The puzzles aren't that complex, and work pretty well most of the time too.  I only got stuck once for a few minutes near the end on something.  Aside from that one moment, everything went smoothly and dynamically.  There's even multiple endings if you goofed up a puzzle or interacted with people in a certain way.
So if Cyberpunk and point-and-click visual novels are your thing, you'll probably really enjoy this game.

I really want to like this game, but I just think it's too average.
This game is mostly your standard cyberpunk fair. You've got your Blade Runners, your Snatchers, your Ghost in the Shells, your Deus Ex-es and so on. It's wearing a lot of inspirations on its sleeve, sometimes a little too on the nose, but that's fine enough on how they executed it in my opinion.
Fortunately this game also brings its unique style to the table, the environments all have very brightful and cheery colours just like the characters that inhabit them, all of that makes the game unlike anything else in the whole cyberpunk genre. The whole atmosphere is also greatly supported by the beautiful soundtrack that I definitely recommend giving a listen to.
As for the story. It brings a lot of themes to the table, but I felt like it didn't spent a sufficient amount on any of them. It didn't gave me time to think about the questions that I felt the story was asking me to ponder about, and they also lacked weight so they felt like they didn't even matter that much. Personally, I was mostly cruising with barely enough interest on how they'd bring it all together. And that's weird since we're talking about a cyberpunk story, I love this genre to bits but this one just doesn't work for me for some reason.
The pacing is all over the place, I thought it was just bad frankly, because when something impactful happens during the story it's like it doesn't strike hard as much as it should. There's no sense of raising the stakes, there's no tension building up until maybe the very last act. But even then it's a very brief section and then it just... ends.
I honestly thought up until the end that there was going to be some kind of huge ruse, a plotwist that would've changed everything we thought about the story so far, so that then, and only then, the real journey truly began - but no, it just ends and it was just really that predictable and underwhelming as it seemed from the beginning. I don't know, I didn't even had expectations but I was left disappointed anyways.
Another problem I had was with the main character. The MC is supposedly you, the player, but I felt like in this kind of scenario it just sucks. He's just a passive spectator, a weird sidekick to the more interesting characters the story presents to you. He doesn't do much, really. He's a void that somehow the game expects you to fill. Sometimes the game wants you to partecipate to the events happening on the screen, but I never felt like I was that character the game was pointing at.
It's weird to say this, but I think I would've felt more immersed and involved in the story if the protagonist had been an actual established character in the game's universe. I really hate making a comparison here, but Snatcher had Gillian Seed as its main character and he was awesome. And it's not like he was really that cool, he was mostly a naive and goofy guy, but that's why I liked him. I warmed up to him throughout the story, I felt more connected to him as a player than what Read Only Memories has got for a main character.
The gameplay part is fine. They spent a lot of time putting funny descriptions to things you can examine around the environment and I really appreciated that. I love looking at useless things if the game has something funny to say about it everytime. It makes it worth the effort and it adds charm to the game. The puzzles, while cool because they are part of the story, are too simple but I liked how they made them so there's never a game over, so even if you fail one the game just keeps going in a different direction, sometimes changing pieces of dialogues or even entire chunks of the story. That's great and deserves some recognition.
That being said this game is played mainly for the story, it's a narrative focused adventure game and as such my opinion towards the game is mostly based on how the narrative is presented and executed, and the general quality of it. That's why this is a negative review: the framework of the game is fine and you could do some amazing things with it and the artstyle - paired with the music which I again recommend listening to - is amazing, but it just felt mediocre to me. It's style over substance. There are other games in this genre that are more worthy of your time.

tl;dr -
This game is going to forever be one of my favorites. It itself is fantastic, but its underlying message is what truly makes it good. 2064/10. As Turing says, "There is no time like the Present". So why wait for the future to buy this game, when you can buy it NOW?
This is probably one of the best games I have ever played, and will ever play in my entire life. It's hard to explain exactly why, but I think I can break it down.
Read Only Memories has many great things about it, like its Soundtrack, its Art/Sprites, its Colorful Cast of Characters, etc.
But the most important thing about this game is it's Story, which it very well should be considering its a Point-N-Click. The story revolves around the disappearnace of one of your friends, and you assisting his robot, Turing, to find him. Interestingly, Turing is Sapient, meaning they think like a human.
I'm going to stop right here about the game itself, because the game itself isn't exactly why its so great. I mean, sure, the game is funny, heart-warming, sad, and intense, along with other things, and it will make you feel very mixed emotions about the short 5 Hour-Ish story. (That being said, there are multiple endings. As of writing this review, I have only completed the game once.)
The important thing about this game however, is its MEANING. Y'know how in High School and College English classes you have to "Analyze the Book" for it's "Theme and Meaning" or whatever? This game's "Theme and Meaning" is what makes it special and so important for people to play.
The most basic way I can say this, is that playing this game will make you think about societal issues, Future, Past, and Present. The game itself has 2 Issues prominently featured in it. Those 2 issues are Human Augmentation (Whether with Genetics or Cybernetic Implants) and Sentient/Sapient Artificial Intelligence. As the future closes in on Humanity, it will eventually become a real, non-fiction, debated issue. And when you see issues like this in a game, you think about real life, and what issues there are now. What is humanity limiting themselves from doing because it's too dangerous (like Sapient Robots), and what are we discriminating against for no reason at all (Like the Cyborgs and the Hybrids).
It's incredibly difficult to put how this game makes someone feel into words, so instead, I'm just going to tell you to buy it. It's $15, its not really that expensive. If you even wanted to, you could wait for a sale, because it's steam and there are always sales eventually.

I fricken' love this game!  This is what I originally envisioned DayZ(sa) would be like - building outposts, home sites, supporting your community of survivors, meeting other groups of survivors, seemingly never-ending open world.
I understand that this is a single-player game, and so the "supporting your community" and "meeting other groups" is just a bunch of NPCs, but still.
Undead Labs has designed something amazing here!  And it's only going to get better!
I was so dissappointed to discover that DayZ(sa) wasn't much more than a serial-killer-simulator.  I've been murdered so many times, for absolutely nothing (we're talking no gear - a flashlight and a battery is worth sniping over?) that it's amazing anyone gets anything done.  People don't team up?  Or I've just tried the wrong 100+ servers so far, I guess.
Anyways, I am so addicted to this game.
SoD is just a ton-load of fun to play.  Wanna follow the story/missions?  Feel free...  Wanna just roam endlessly and hoard supplies?  That's game too...  Swipe an abandoned car and plow through some zombie hordes, just make sure you don't open your mouth as you turn those zeds into bloody soup!  LOL.
I've barely made it a fraction of the way through the story so far, but I'm taking my time.  Taking advantage of the open-world environment to just build up my home site, and increase my reputation with the group.
I don't even plan on playing the Breakdown DLC until I play through the story at least twice, and there's another DLC in the makings.  Can't wait to see what we get in the next update!  The forums are talking about some awesome enhancements to the game.
Undead Labs is certainly on the right track with this gem of a title...  If they eventually break into the co-op/mmo bracket, they're sure to do amazing things!

Action/Sort-of-RPG
Fight various types of zombies, ammo is scarce. Different survivors, found randomly or through story, have different skill sets, combat and otherwise. Combat skills can be developed to learn techniques (knock-down attacks, better zoom, etc). You have a base of operations but you need to regularly venture out to find supplies (food, medicine, ammo and fuel) by scavenging surrounding locations.You can go on foot or drive. You can also have an AI partner follow you.
Solid visuals, voice-acting (Scout, is that you?) and controls are pretty good once you get used to them.
Although fun for a while, I feel there were some missed opportunities in this game, especially in the potential for customization. I don't just mean characters, but vehicles, weaponry, safe houses or even player-created content. It seems that the developers tried to add many features into the game, but many of those feel bare-bones. This game would benefit greatly from the Steam Workshop. There is a modding community out there that addresses some of the issues the game has, at least.
Overall, 6/10. It's not a bad game, especially for the price. Modding it to your liking certainly adds more, but I feel without the Steam Workshop behind it it stills falls short of its true potential.

This's definitely one of the most overlooked games in the series. Mostly because it was developed for a doomed console, the Sega CD, and it was actually made by a separate team who were originally just going to make an enhanced port of Sonic 2.
I can see even fans of the classic games not enjoying this game. It's much more different and weird than any of the other classic Sonic games, as it incorporates elements never seen in a Sonic game before or after it. However, I feel as if Sonic CD was an experiment for the devs to pour every one of their creatives juices as possible. And in the end, it paid off significantly.
The game plays mostly the same as the other 2-D classic games, what with the fast, frantic gameplay, unique level gimmicks and non-linear levels. However, it is a lot more difficult due to the layout of the levels being drastically different. This game plays more like a Metroidvania-style game rather than a 2-D Sonic game, being that it focuses on exploration, overcoming obstacles and becoming more familiar with the levels. Sure, the other classic games focus on this as well, but Sonic CD does so more than any of the other games due to simply how large and labyrinthine the levels really are. Though even if the levels are bigger, they're vastly shorter as well, making it so they don't overstay their welcome.
The main mechanic in this game, which hasn't been done in any after it, is the Time Travel mechanic. By touching either the PAST or FUTURE signs scattered throughout the level, if Sonic gains enough speed for a short period of time, then he will travel either backwards or forwards in time. In each time period, the visual style of the level has drastically changed, the layout is slightly different, and you'll either have access to new areas or be unable to access previous ones.
In total there's four different versions of a level: Past, Present, Bad Future and Good Future. The present level is how it appears normally, the past has it become much older and become covered by plants and moss, the bad future has it become a mechanized and twisted dystopia, and the good future is the entire opposite with a beautiful and happy utopia. Which leads to an INSANE level of variety within each level.
If you're wondering how there's two different futures, then it's actually Sonic CD's overall best and most engaging aspect, and what makes it feel even more so like a Metroidvania title. Traveling forward in time will automatically bring you to a Bad Future. So in order to cause the bad future of the level to become a good future, you need to go to the past and locate a robot generator, a machine that slowly corrupts and mechanizes a level over time, and destroy it.
However, since the Past signs wear off a lot faster than the Future signs and are a lot more rare, it's much more difficul to get to past than future. This's the game actively challenging you to make sure that you end up becoming stuck in a bad future rather than ever traveling to the past. But in the end, it makes your efforts feel truly satisfying and euphoric since you truly worked for them, and there's no better feeling than getting a Good Future in a level.
There's also a Metal Sonic hologram in each past version of a level as well...but destroying them all will give you nothing but an achievement in modern rereleases of the game, so they're not really worth hunting down unless you're a completionist.
And if anyone would rather simply just go through the level, that's a possibility as that well! You can simply collect the Time Stones as well, which act as this game's version of the Chaos Emeralds. The special stages have you move around in a psuedo-3-D environments while destroying nearby UFOs, and if it weren't for the terrible hit detection they'd actually be quite fun.
Like in Sonic 1, the levels are divided into three acts, with the third one serving as a very short route to the boss. There's Palmtree Panic, Collision Chaos, Tidal Tempest, Quartz Quadrant, Wacky Workbench, Stardust Speedway, and Metallic Madness. Geesh, whoever named these levels sure had a love for alliteration...anyways, each level has different gimmicks and set pieces that make them stand out and feel truly memorable.
Palmtree Panic...okay, it's essentially Green Hill 3.0, but it's still incredibly fun, especially with the perspective-shifting loop in the beginning. Collision Chaos is a very unique take on the casino level, Tidal Tempest is basically Labyrinth from Sonic 1 but actually good, Quartz Quadrant is like the prototype to Lava Reef Act 2 and has switches that change the direction the floor is moving, Stardust Speedway has spring launch pads and winding spring mazes, and Metallic Madness, like Scrap Brain, tests everything you've learned so far and holds nothing back. And it even has two very unique gimmicks, such as being able to move between the background and the foreground and a shrink ray that changes Sonic into a miniature version of himself.
Metallic Madness is actually manageable, believe it or not. But since there's no goal post in sight, you only have one try through the entire level: making it too unforgiving and drag on longer than it needs to.
And of course, this game was the first introduction of Metal Sonic (oh and I guess Amy too.) If it weren't for it, then we wouldn't have had one of the best, most badass and second most recurring villain in the series.
Besides the spin dash from Sonic 2, there's also a new move exclusive to Sonic CD known as the Super Peel-Out. Where if you hold up and then release, Sonic will dash forward in a burst of speed significantly faster than the spin dash. The only downside is that unlike the spin dash, you cannot hurt any enemies in your path, leaving you entirely vulnerable.
The graphics feel slightly outdated, however, and feel like a continuation of Sonic 1's graphics rather than the update given to Sonic 2.
Like with Sonic Colors, the soundtrack has tons of variety to it, being that since there's four different versions of a level, there's four different music tracks of them as well. But the most interesting thing about the soundtrack is that save for the Past versions of the levels, it's entirely different between the Japan (and also Europe) and American versions of the game.
And I absolutely adore the Japanese soundtrack, because it's just...so upbeat, unique and catchy.
While the US soundtrack is...less than stellar. Not only because comparing it to the JP soundtack is like comparing gold to plastic, but overall it sounds forgettable and bland. It just feels like a generic 90's music video since it's filled with nothing but rock and soft vocals.
The only flaws I can think of are Wacky Workbench being one of the worst and most frustrating levels in Sonic history due to the floor being a trampoline that sends you soaring into the air, and hazards being crammed into every corner of the level possible. Though it's at least not on the same level as Metropolis, being that it not only doesn't overstay its welcome like with Metropolis, but Act 2 is at least MUCH more tolerable than Act 1. And getting a Good Future in Act 2 is as easy as breathing air...even if in Act 1 it's nearly impossible.
Then there's Dr. Robotnik's in-game model, because...what in the world were they even thinking? He looks Eggman's redesign in Sonic '06, except for his classic version instead of his modern one.
Even though it has outdated graphics and a naseauting level, Sonic CD is a game that makes you think outside the norm of classic Sonic games with Metroidvania-style gameplay, a unique and fun mechanic in the form of time travel, fantastic and varied level-design, and a mesmerizing soundtrack outside of America.
Despite how difSonic games, I recommend it if you're a Sonic fan just to try it out and see if you like it. Though I don't recommend it to newcomers due to this fact.
*9/10*

You know what else you can replay just as much and get the same amount of enjoyment? A wholesome game of dragging your face in the cement. You can check my hours put into the game. I gave it a solid attempt. I would not recomend this game for anyone looking for "Replay Value" if you're also looking for something fun at the same time. That -IS- what a game should be, after all...
I recently checked a slew of the people who I watch play the game religiously, and most of them share the same views. "Something has changed... It isn't the same... Less enjoyable..." There's a reason there's "Mixed" feelings in the reviews. These were all people who would go on 100 win streaks in the game, now second gussing if the should even waste their time with it on their channels.
I hope this helps save you some frustration. If you decided to get the game, save yourself from Afterbirth+ (Unless you want to mod the game into something that it should have been from the start)

I absolutely love this game. While my time played may be low here, I played it by other means and have beat it many times over. The Uplay version was broken for me, and that was the version I had before I decided to buy it again on Steam where the multiplayer and online functionality actually worked and it didn't crash on me at all. (I have no idea why Uplay wouldn't let me play multiplayer, or even connect, the game would also crash every 30 minutes on the dot, and Ubisoft's support didn't help in any way). Regardless of all the trouble I went through with it, I still recommend it to anyone who loves stealth games.
The story while kind of unoriginal and bland, still held up, and was done quite well. Some characters make their return from previous Splinter Cell games as well.
The game is visually stunning, and looks really good when it is cranked all the way up to Ultra settings. It is also optimized quite well, as I can play the game at a decent framerate on an old HD 7850.
The sound and voice acting are quite good as well. While I wish they kept the old voice actor from the previous Splinter Cells, the new one actually did quite well and grew on me in the end.
The gameplay is a lot like any other Splinter Cell except for in this one, they have 3 different kinds of playstyles that they reward you for. They are Assault, Panther, and Ghost. Assault being gun's blazing kill everyone, and you basically play the game as a 3rd person shooter. While playing it this way isn't exactly my cup of tea, the game does allow you to if you choose to. Ghost is basically the exact opposite of the spectrum, and I actually recommend playing it this way. Trying to figure out guard's routes, and all the different secret nooks and crannies you can hide in or around without being seen is one of most fun ways to play. You are also awarded with more points if you go completely undetected, and  can sneak your way past guards without touching any of them. Lastly, Panther is a combination of both Assault and Ghost where you use stealth, but also kill whoever crosses your path. They did decide to leave in the Mark and Execute from Conviction which is a little annoying, and I think makes parts of the game entirely too easy, but just I chose not to use it throughout my playthrough.
The level design is quite good, and even though I wish it was a little more open, there are still multiple ways to complete missions. Most areas have different paths you can take to get around undetected.
Overall, I put Blacklist in a close second to Chaos Theory. Everything is done really well, and this game was my favorite game of 2013 when it came out. If you are a fan of stealth games, I think it is a must have. I recommend cranking the difficulty all the way up to Perfectionist, and trying to go through completely unseen. It can be frustratingly difficult this way, but it's not impossible, and in my opinion the most satisfying way to play the game. Definitely recommend to anyone that is a fan of the genre.

"Lucy - The Eternity She Wished For-" is a short Visual Novel game with a small amount of decisions, and as a result, next to no story branching, but that's a non-issue for this title.
The story revolves around the main character meeting an abandonned android (Lucy), quickly get you attached to her character and then slowly reveals the Sword of Damocles (aka, a feeling of imminent tragedy).
Lucy's a simple and elegant game, it's cheap and it's enjoyable.

There are multiple pro's and con's that this game has, for example:
When the game boots up, the menu has a small delay when you select certain options.
There aren't many chracters to look into (About five has been drawn fully, with only Lucy being voice acted)
But (and it is a MASSIVE but) the story has made all of those minor nitpicks redundant. The characters that are obviously antagonised you will HATE. And I do mean physically loath the sight of. Not from the great drawing may I add, but because of what they do and how they act.
I will not say anything that may spoil the ending because that is simply one of the best story endings I've ever had in my decade-plus of gaming, (I may have cried a little but SHUT UP)
So, with regards to the absolutely amazing main character, world development (simple slight-of-hand remarks mainly), and with the plot that I can easily see happening in this day and age, I would happy recommended this to anyone that wants emosions galore.
Great work, Mviz lab! I hope you make another tear jerker like this one soon!

The comparison of Lucy, who's only kind because she's been programmed to be, to the narrator, who only hates androids because he's been raised to be, really makes you think about the extent to which free will is tempered by the environment we're brought up in. And for us older players, the story in a whole really encapsulates the entire experience of your first teenage love - how the world changes overnight,  how it seems like you can't go on once it's all over, and how it still simmers in your mind after decades have passed.
Could use some polishing, but it gave me feels all the same.

State Of Decay is a well-made open-world zombie apocalypse sandbox that I can unequivocally recommend to all fans of zombie-stuff and those wanting to get into it. I'll start with the cons, before I get to the good parts:
CONS:
- The graphics are just mediocre, but: who cares?
- The game only saves after a mission was finished (some call this a plus)
- There are lots of generic missions that repeat very often - this is, at times, very dreary.
- Many of the characters appear generic (which they actually are).
PROS:
- Definitely the atmosphere! There are many different kinds of places (towns, farms, a state park, gas stations etc.), a couple of different groups, the feeling of permanent threat (quite real) combined with permadeath of characters, members of your group interacting with you and each other and so on.
- Lots of different items and weapons, all neatly presented.
- Different ressources that have to be gathered by starting supply runs into homes, warehouses etc. - for me this never got boring.
- Upgradeable homebases of different sizes all over the map.
- Many different kinds of cars. Driving them is a lot of fun and the controls were done well.
I probably forgot many things I liked about this game. There is one aspect that I am not sure of whether it's a pro or a con: As the title suggests, there is actually a process of "decay" happening. The in-game time passes even after it was shut down. On the next startup the game calculates a number of events and the consumption of ressources depending on how much time has passed in real life. While this adds to the "realism" it can also be quite frustrating to find out, members of your group have died during the last week and all the medicine  is now gone which led to an outbreak of disease at home... *
Recommended - 7.5/10
*[As a workaround you can always write down the actual time/date after closing the game and set your system time accordingly on the next startup.]

Starbound is an awesome sandbox space exploration game in which you can build bases and explore plants for valuable resources.  When I first played the game, there was no story implemented yet but was still a very fun game.
Since then, the developers have added quite a bit of content to it, including a story driven quest line and story driven objectives as well as more advanced monster AI.  They continue to add to the game as well as correct bugs and the game is still in early access.  I cant speak to the newest additions to the game as it has been ages since I played, but I love what Starbound brings to the table.
Important note, this is NOT Minecraft and it is NOT Terraria but it is in the same genre as these games.  It has enough about it that is different to feel very different to the other two games I mentioned above (and love dearly) but, as you would expect, there are some similarities as well.  The base building is pretty sweet and the exploration is nicely done as well. The game is amazing and I do highly recommend it if your into the sandbox, quest objective, base building type of games!

Let me start out by saying this is not a strait up review of Starbound, simply my impressions of the game and the developers at it has evolved throughout the years I have followed it.
I purchased starbound the day it released on steam in early access. The developers promised so much, and as a lover of terraria it was hard not to get on the hype train. When the game first released, it had some serious fundamental flaws. This was a widely descused topic at the time, the game gave most of what it promised, but it executed it in a way that was so bland. Monsters were "randomly generated" but all of them acted the same, worlds were different but hardly any of them were worth exploring. Building was pointless because you would eventually leave the plannet and never return. And the initial combat and armor mechanics were absolutely terrible. I was worried that these flaws were so ingrained into the core of Starbound that they would never be truely fixed no matter what the developers did. What worried me even more was all the talk of how they wouldn't allow criticism on the Starbound forums and that people were being banned due to voicing their frusterations with the developers. Signs seemed to point to this being another case of indie developers making huge promises, not fulfilling them, and basically dropping the project completely. We've all seen it done countless times before.
But Chucklefish, despite these setbacks, continued to make progress on the game. Over the years, I would go back and play starbound for quite a bit before stopping and not touching it for several months at a time. Each time I returned to starbound, I would be treated to find that the game had undergone massive changes, always being a huge improvement on the last iteration. The other day I, once again, had the urge to pick up starbound. What I had experienced had spurred me to write this review. Once again, Starbound had made huge strides since I had last played it. To the point where I feel it is finally worthy of the all its initial hype. Chucklefish has proven its dedication, and the game is moving in the right direction.
