One Sonic game that I didn’t have in Sonic Mega Collection + was Sonic CD(Since it wasn’t a Mega Drive game). So of course I got it on Steam just to play it.
Story:
A little planet called Little Planet has visited Sonic’s world but Eggman has chained it up and took the time stones that let him take over the past. But Sonic is on the case, but his number 1 fan, Amy Rose has been kidnapped by his most deadly rival even now. Metal Sonic.
Aside from showing a theme that the Sonic series doesn’t explore that much to my knowledge which is technology and nature can live together. There isn’t much to talk about so why not talk about Amy and Metal. Lets start with Amy and I like her. I know most people see her as Sonic’s obsessive stalker but there’s more to her than that. Sure, she loves Sonic but well but her crush aside to help or stand up for her friends, brings the best in people like Gamma and Shadow, and if some messes with her, she’ll smash her with her giant hammer. Like the rest of the main cast she doesn’t need much development and if she written well or in a decent role she can be enjoyable.
Now for Metal. Out of all of Sonic’s rivals, he is without a doubt his most dangerous. Outside of some great boss fights, he doesn’t have much personalty but I don’t think he needs one. His design is one of the most threatening out of all of Eggman’s robots, He’s shown to be cruel to animals in those holograms you can destroy, and even dose a mocking finger wave. And I while I haven’t Sonic Heroes yet I don’t like his design in it. I think he works best as a secondary villain or a main villain for a racing game since his main goal is to beat Sonic.
Gameplay:
This is a bit different than other Sonic games. Yes, you go fast to get the end but you may notice that these levels are pretty short. And that there are Future and Past signposts all over the place. That’s because each level is three levels in one. With these posts and keeping a fast speed, you can travel through  time where it’s the same but different like in the first zone, you might find some invisible platforms in the present and in the past those platforms would be visible. And to make it a bit easier, Sonic has a Super-Peel out which is similar to the Spin Dash only it’s faster but it doesn’t allow you to destroy enemies.
Now there are two ways to get the good ending and while we talking about levels let start with the most unique way this has. Finding robot teleporters. In every level in the past is a hidden RT and when destroyed, all the enemies in the past and some in the present turn into flowers and getting rid of both in a zone makes a good future. While finding the RTs might be hard without a guide, I thought getting to the past was harder since there were more future post than past ones. And while I didn’t mind the level design of the game for the most part except Wacky Workbench which has a nasty gimmick of lunching you into the air and you may hit an enemy or of those electric coils.
And like Sonic 1, just collect 50 rings and get to the end and a special stage awaits. One of the more original ones in he series where you’re in a small arena and have to destroy all the UFOs in a limited time. These are fine for the most part with obstacles to either slow you down, fans that can fly you to the other side of the arena if used well and water that eats away at your time. But there’s one major problem more to due to the time the art than the game itself. Depth perception. You see, you can’t hit a UFO  near you so you need a good bit of distance before you can hit a UFO and it’s easy to overshoot or undershoot the target and land in the water.
And the bosses are the most gimmick I’ve fought in a Sonic game I  played. Yes,  the first and last bosses are two of my least favorite in the series but the rest are pretty good with my two favorites being an underwater fight where you to get the air bubbles to remove a shield and the treadmills where you to keep running til the machine is filed away.
Presentation:
One of the more ambitious art directions they did for the series since they did four different but  same themes for each level. The Present looks the most like a usual Sonic zone with Sonic music while the past looks and sounds more primitive. The future also has two songs depending if it’s good or bad with the good future sounding beautiful and happy  with nature and technology living in peace while the bad future is a techno and miserable and even horribly muted in places like bad future using the happy cheers in an off manner and everything looks like crap.
Now I must say that my liking of the music is for the Japanese soundtrack because I think the American soundtrack is one of the worst Sonic soundtracks I’ve ever heard. I tried to like it but as soon as I reached Collision Chaos, I felt something no soundtrack has ever made me feel. Angry. I was angry of the fact that good music like the fun song for the pinball level was replace by some miserable noise that I wanted to pull my ear phones off. And when I got to the past, my reaction was “Oh, God! the music is good again!” since the past music was unchanged. I heard people say it’s more atmospheric and fits with the levels better and those people will go to hell for lying. The Japanese OST is more atmospheric and if you want proof, listen to both Palmtree Panix’s bad future songs and tell me which one fits with a terrible future of a tropical paradise.
And one final, has anyone notice that all the enemies in this game are bug theme or similar. No seriously. We got lobsters, bagworms, snails, several beattles, spiders, ladybugs, etc.
Verdict:
Bad US soundtrack aside, this is pretty good Sonic game and recommend it for any fan of Classic Sonic or Sonic in general.

This is truly the pinnacle of ports and the only way you should be playing Sonic CD.
In my opinion, Sonic CD is one of the most under appreciated games in the whole franchise and deserves to be compared to the classic Mega Drive games. Stages are large, with more variety thanks to the time travel mechanic, fun to explore and satisfying to complete in as little time as possible when you know them well. Typical qualities you would expect from a good Sonic game. Boss battles also seem more inspired and unique compared to other games, and while I appreciate the change in formula there are times where a more traditional boss battle would've been appreciated (*cough*collision chaos *cough*) The time travel mechanic, while interesting can become cumbersome, since time travel posts can only be activated once and due to the sporadic level designs it can be very difficult to maintain momentum for long enough. This can be problematic since getting the good ending requires you to travel to the past to destroy machines hidden in each level. Luckily the game gives you two chances to achieve the good ending by having more traditional special stages you can enter with 50 rings at the end of the act to collect the 7 time stones. This port includes nice features such as time trails, and being able to play as Tails, with new unique animations and sprites. There is also an option to switch between the Japanese and US soundtracks, which is the best thing ever. The camera has also been panned back for better visibility which did wonders in the mobile Sonic ports and is no different here, especially with the larger and more chaotic level design. So, to conclude, Sonic CD gets too bad a rep and if you have any interest in trying it out buy this port. There really isn't a Sonic game quite like it.

Probably one of the most underrated Splinter Cell games. This game catches a lot of flack because it came right after Conviction, but it really does hold up compared to the original Splinter Cell games. If anything, it's actually improved on the formula. Whether you use Mark and Execute or not (I don't), Sam feels much more fluid compared to other installments. He could do a lot of the same things in the older games, but now you know that he isn't going to jump kick off of a wall into enemies when you just want to climb it. Sam is much more easy to control and the weapons are much easier to control as well. This game has massive replayability and actually rewards you for playing it in each of the different fighting styles. If any of you are upset about Ironsides not voicing Sam, don't be afraid, the new guy isn't too terrible, and the voice acting and dialogue for Grim, Briggs, and Charlie is really solid. The story may not live up to Pandora Tomorrow or Choas Theory, but it'll keep you engaged throughout the whole game.
The only cons I've found with the game is that the PC multiplayer community is almost non-existent, so if you want to play co-op on this, you gotta have a buddy who has it as well. In the entire time I've owned this game, I've only twice been able to enter a co-op game with a random person. Though if you can play Co-op with someone, it is a blast. You'll find yourself co-ordinating shots and takedowns and planning routes. Other cons are sometimes the cutscenes glitch and miss some frames or do other weird things, but overall it's not bad.
Overall though, great game. 8.5/10

I'll keep this simple:
An ambitious and artistic game with a very good, and new, combat system that creates interesting new synergies and a wide variety of playstyles.  I do feel, however, that this depth would have been MUCH better realized and executed if they had chosen to use a full turn-based system.  There is a LOT going on and the 'action' based system simply becomes a chore of 'pause/unpause' micromanagement.
An interesting and well paced story, marred with shallow and nonsensical party NPCs (except for one who is almost TOO subtle).  I liked many of the scenarios that hearkened back to old-school RPGs such as Darklands.  The devs usually presented several paths to the objectives depending on the general skills and interests of the party and player.
Ultimately, the game falls flat on its face for the compromises it had to make to receive funding.  EVERYWHERE there are constant, dissonant and disruptive reminders of the business end of the game.  Almost every NPC that does not directly provide you a quest or a service is a 'backer' sponsored 'ad' ripped from that fan's favorite fantasy novel, game, manga, etc.  Far from contributing to any cogent narrative, their existence in this world simply adds to the overall feeling of shameless marketing on behalf of the publisher.  At least the developers insisted the biographies of these easter-egg NPCs be professionally written, rather than simply allowing a torrent of fan-faction, but it does little to conceal the true motive.  The gravestones also are simply horrible, each one is jammed with dozens of names of sponsors, it turns what might have been a nice gesture toward a few key sponsors into an almost insulting money grab where backers are piled up like wood in a potter's field.
I have adored many of Paradox's titles over the years, but the way in which they conduct business is simply too far a good deal of the time.
I think it bears comparison to Wasteland 2, a similarly imagined and executed project that managed to not lose its way and dramatically mar its artistic vision as this project, unfortunately, has.

In my opinion Dark Souls: Prepare To Die Edition is the best game of all time.
Take for instance the combat system. Fights in Dark Souls are very fast, fun and there are lots of possible fighting styles, not only say a spear, sword or magic: There are so many different types of weapon and magic and a multitude of strategies (and builds) are possible with each individual weapon. Also, how succesful you are depends largely on personal skills and not your luck with rare loot. What I also enjoy a lot is that everyone, except the bosses obviously, (that includes the player) dies from a few hits. That makes fights not like in most MMOs where you stand infront of your enemy for 20-30 seconds and hit each other and the one with better stats wins.
Another great thing about this game is the level- and worlddesign. Every location feels very unique with fitting enemies, lots of items, many places to explore and so on.
The lore of this game is mostly hidden in item description or the dialog of NPCs. Aside from the opening-cinematic you are probably not going to hear much, but if you look deeper into it or watch one of the many videos on youtube that explain the lore (what I really recomend) you will notice how much story is behind every character, boss and location you meet. I personally know no story of any game that I would consider better than Dark Souls'.
Overall I can only recomend Dark Souls to anyone who is willing to invest time into this game, because it may be hard for beginners, but it is a amazing experience.

I started this game on a whim this June, what a ride it was. 10/10
A lot of people have compared progressing in this game to struggling with depression, or life in general.
I would tend to agree. The isolation, uncertainty of which path to take, (for a 1st time player like me) unexplained appearances and disappearances of characters, cyclical nature of the world (not to mention its austere/sublime beauty, I really loved all the ruins), and largely difficult enemies created an exceptionally atmospheric feel that I have never seen before.
What started as a whim to try this notoriously difficult game to see if I, Bravemoof was a true gamer of stout heart and appreciable dexterity of finger, turned into a flaming passion. A passion to kick each boss off their place of power and harvest their souls. One thing I really liked about the game is that I felt vulnerable the whole time. I have played other action titles where by the end I am flying around, disintegrating hordes of enemies, and unafraid of any and all damage (save perhaps the uber-slow and telegraphed mega last boss laser beam, if that). In dark souls my only significant late game power came from myself, (the player) and it was called perseverance. This beautiful game had me playing not because my friends said it was amazing, or for some stupid achievement, but to see if I could surmount the next challenge.
Probably the pinnacle of this game was the fight with Knight Artorias. I had killed a couple bosses on my first attempt before him, and felt the game was coming to a close, when I step through the gate and see his cut-scene. He smites me down before I can even land a hit on him. To go from that lowly starting point, to tumbling past (almost) every one of his attacks and cutting him down was amazing. I threw down my controller, stood up, and unleashed a raspy screech, which probably made my parents shake their heads in disappointment (but that’s another story). That fight and many others embodied what I really liked about Dark Souls. How it makes dying such a key part of the game.
Alright, (insert enemy name) You may have just killed me (again), I may be a nasty withered husk, and my only friend may be an idiotic snake with a mustache. But I will be back ready to chip away at your ankles into you crumble into dust. And in the end, I may be weak, I may be ugly, but I will be all that is left. No flying, no lasers, no invincibility, only the brute will to rise from the fire and sprint once more into the darkness, weapon in hand. All powerful hero? No. Baddass? Very much yes. Again 10/10

Strike vector...
Strike vector could be a good game but the developers ideas at the core of this game don't fundamentally work because games long before strike vector were a gleam in the devs eyes did it infinitely better and it was much more awesome.
Strike vectors problems are -- too much space and the lack of constrained space leads to weapon designs and combat that ultimately isn't interesting.  Not to mention the single player is little more then obstacle courses that are only challenging because the ships controls are so awful.  Obstacle courses designed around crap flight characteristics isn't fun.
1.  The sky gives too much space to run and dodge, so tension of being surprised or hide and seek dropping something like mines behind doors like ancient 360 FPS games like descent is severely lacking
2.  The open sky and too much open space means you rarely if ever get to enjoy the ship models and are aiming at squares and names on screen which leads to ...
3.  Weapons fire fast and the effects really dont get to be enjoyed because the speed at which the jet flies requires very fast weapons which means there's little chance to hide or dodge in interesting ways as you would in an enclosed space.
The reality is Strike vector is inspired by the idea of transforming planes/robots that both fly and hover in mid air, the problem with strike vector is the flight model and level design ideas at the core of this game simply don't work in wide open levels, they need to be rethunk from the ground up because the fast action "up close and personal" that this game is going for simply can't work with weapons that need to move too fast to cross vast distances.
Descent 2 did 3D arcade flight better 20 years ago and the developers tragically are video game history illiterate which is why the controls of the plane are off which is a large part of the reason why their servers are empty.
The problem with their core ideas is -- You are rarely ever close enough to enjoy the graphics of the ships and are always aiming at little squares and names too far away.  This is ok in a game like Ace combat but not in a game that takes after in your face arcade gameplay like descent.  The hybird between a fast action 360 FPS mixed in with 'realistic' flight dynamics at high speed is basically why this game is dead.
The game needed a slower relative movement of the ships /w the illusion of going fast (which can be done via fx) that actually allowed you to enjoy enjoy the combat and be up close with other ships to feel "up close and personal with your big machine", to see the actual player model of the enemy and to be able to see the amazing weapon fire effects.
To have that happen the weapons effects can't be super fast/ or too much instant hit in that there's a chance you can dodge because that leads to lack of tension and excitement because there is no back and forth.  That's what this game lacks... the back and forth fast action exchanges that a human being can manage.  See here "maneuverability as defense"
So the game in multiplayer becomes monotonous run, turn around, look for health and try to kite the enemy from afar and you end up fighting the controls whenever you switch to high speed.
This is the difference imagined physics and rules designed for fun vs trying to apply plane dynamics realistically and not understanding trying to make a plane act like a plane fundamentally breaks 3D combat in an fast action arcade design.
Reality has all sorts of drawbacks (aka aiming at squares because the ship is too far to see) vs a game like Descent 2 where the ship is up close and personal and the levels are confined to mines so the extra 3D space keeps the pace of the game going.  The open space prevents tactics and interesting weapon ideas from being implemented because there's no confined space and too much space to dodge.

In a demanding and high expectation climate of gamers Miscreated stands out as game with several pros & cons, Which outweigh one another is entirely biased. You'll have people who find no reason but to remain in Day Z, H1Z1, Modded Fallout the list will really go on forever.
So to keep this as convincing and straight forward lets just list out what this game has , doesnt ,but... Most likely will
Pros -
1) It runs
I have a 1070 and I've had a 970 and I've had a 760, At all times in my pc gaming life I've been able to run this game on various settings always in 1080. Currently I can run the game above 60fps with my 1070+i5.
2) It runs on Cryengine.
This only benefits why reason 1 is so spectacular, Cryengine will never not shine graphically in any generation of gaming.
3) Scavenging feels real
You don't just find a gun sitting next to a baby bottle in this game, or a pair of pink high tops next to an army jacket.
Using visual clues scavenging feels smart however, this isn't to say in more pvp areas of the map it will feel desperate and you may die starving or dehydrated with pursuers who also... You guessed it, want to blow your head off.
4) Vehicles
Almost all survival games have vehicles but, Miscreated takes it maybe a small step forward. While you wont be operating helicopters anytime soon between various bike types, cars, trucks, uhauls, buses there's quite a selection... Also if your feeling sea savvy...
5) Gunplay
While you may not see much of this unless you truly stack one server with everything you can find gunplay feels akin to Insurgency. Not the clunky prototype feel of a lesser survival games attempt at making guns feel real, but not spinning about counter strike style either.
6) Server Reliability
I've never been without a server that has excellent ping and a good amount of players. Servers allow 32 players which for the map size ( which is large ) feels reasonable.
I've never experienced lag or been randomly dropped from a server unless it's due to my own internet.
7) Weather cycle
There's ♥♥♥♥ing tornadoes
8) Community.
Miscreated not being a giant name like Day Z, h1z1, or Ark the player base has yet to become cancerous. Most encounters if dealt with right can actually become quite the experience and may even lend you a friend. Almost everyone wants to simply get by. It's rare even if someone wants to straight up kill you they wont play a bit with your head before popping it off
9) Town's and Cities
Orca Island truly does have a lot going right for the layout of their towns and cities , all feel real with buildings and small shops, local fire and police departments. From small town to the city of the north as players will refer before seeing how huge it is, Miscreated offers an immersive "lets go shopping and not die" experience on a small side note after a few hours you really understand the map and how to find what you need, using mountains to see distant cities
9) Devs & Potential
To end my pros I'll praise the constant quality updates that add in real game content, this game has come a long way from where it started and I don't believe it's come close to peaking. I'll admit several things are still holding this game back when you focus on them so lets do that.
Cons
1) 'True Survival'
If you're looking for a game where the tempurate and weight of your clothing alone can wind up getting you killed this isn't going to please that hardcore part of you, PVE is extremely weak with little to nothing in the world actually posing a threat except maybe falling off a cliff you didn't (or?) see. Which leads me to my next issue
2) 'The Threat'
Zombies or mutants..lets just call them zombies are kinda laughable concept wise. The three variants either look like a redneck who transmuted into baraka (MK) an alien that got tired of living within Xcom and a giant tumor with endless HP
they spawn thin and if ever they do attack, don't waste time running just take a note from Signs or Indapendance Day and beat that baddy to death with the non breakable weapon of your choice be it a bat or your own fists.
speaking of fists not breaking
3) lack of character conditions
Between smiling bleeding and dead you will find no other suffering and don't expect those bottles of gin you find to have any affect on you neither
4) Base Building
This may be a player base issue more than anything else but don't expect to find any base that looks remotely plausible to being supported by gravity. Maybe you can craft an anti gravity orb in this game but I really doubt it...
5)Crafting
Crafting is a definite miss with almost nothing to offer outside of "well I guess I can make that"
There lies a few shining creations capable of being made but the majority falls next to pointless
That's really all I can come up with, I love the experiences I have and will continue to have in this game, Don't let my cons break the happy train of this review , cheers :v

== Long Review, No Spoilers ==
It's about time that I wrote a review about this game.
It is about "Binding of Isaac: Rebirth" (BoI) with Afterbirth and Afterbirth+ DLCs.
BoI is a rogue-like "four-way shooter": You control your character either by using a game pad (which I strongly recommend) or the keyboard and view him or her from above. Aside from Isaac himself, there are several other characters with slightly different abilities and stats which can be unlocked throughout the game.
In this review I shall just reference to controlling Isaac but suffice it to say that each of the characters plays quite differently from the others and you have to use different tactics if you want to be successful.
After a short introduction, the game starts in the "cellar" or "basement". Isaac needs to find his way through many different, randomly generated levels to escape from his evil mother. Unfortunately, the dungeons are filled with deadly traps monsters and bosses.
Luckily, Isaac can "fire" tears in a chosen direction to fight off his opponents. He can find hundreds of different items which make him stronger during a "run" and a map helps him find his way through the dungeons.
All in all, the optics of the game bear a very strong resemblance to the dungeon levels of the very first Zelda game on the NES and there are also a few in-game references to it.
As it is common with "rogue-likes", you can proceed to deeper levels and you can save and load your progress. You cannot go back, though, and if you die, you have to start a new run, beginning from the start in a new dungeon with new items.
Anyway, while all this description sounds pretty "standard", the game is not. Though the original BoI started as an Indie Game, it hardly has to hide behind full-priced AAA titles when it comes to game design, difficulty, balance and replay value.
I shall list a few (but not all) of the reasons why I deeply enjoy playing BoI even after > 190 hours.
1) The game is extremely challenging, but you can beat it if you practice your skill. In many other rogue-likes, chance (or the "random generator" = "rng") plays the major role in determining whether you are ultimately "successful" in a run or not. Not so with BoI: In this game, practicing and strategic planning are rewarded and make the difference. I cannot count how many times I was close to giving up on a specific challenge or level because I thought it was impossible to beat, just to pick up my pad again and to realize a few minutes later that I just went about it the wrong way, used the wrong strategy or combined the wrong items.
Do not get me wrong: The RNG still can set you up with an inadequate equipment / item drops but there are enough ways in the game to turn the tide or swap the equipment if you know the game mechanics.
2) Grinding is not required to become stronger in a normal run. Although there are certain mechanics in the game which unlock a starting gear for a character and which e.g. allow improving the stuff the in-game shops have to offer, this is a bonus and not a must in order to successfully complete the game. The "greed mode" is an exception (see below).
3) There are hundreds of items. Literally. While many games feature dozens of similar items which do not really make any difference in the actual game play, this is different with BoI: Though some items have similar effects (e.g. grant you a health container), most items and trinkets (which you also can carry around) have a pretty much unique effect. The best part is, that the devs included some pretty neat and cool stacking effects which apply when you combine certain items. It is a vital part of the game that you get to know the items, know their strengths and weaknesses and know which items are good to combine and which combinations you should avoid.
4) Nearly every challenge or "achievement" you can complete in the game unlocks a new item, character or ability. While this does not sound so impressive at first, trust me, it is: With a total of 339 achievements you can unlock many, many items. The good thing is that this really adds to the gaming experience and still after placing for > 100 hours, you can find new items with new abilities. This also potentially gives you more options in future runs, making you also potentially stronger if you know how to use them to your advantage.
5) The graphics and sounds are retro-style. I like this a lot (while others may not), as it really reminds me of Zelda or Star Tropics.
6) The story is eerie. While not suited for children, I really think the dark mood of the game adds to the atmosphere and it makes BoI stand out from many other "vanilla games".
7) The game has many endings. Don't worry - I will not spoil any of that. Suffice it to say that you can actively choose in which direction you wish to progress and which ending you wish to pursue. You'll find out... :-)
8) Apart from the "normal" game, the devs have added more modes which play completely differently. First, there are "challenges" where Isaac usually starts already with a special set of items and abilities but which often also include certain penalties which make finishing the game harder and which require a good in-game knowledge of items and game mechanics.
Then, there is the "greed mode" in which you can fight waves of opponents in various levels, which drop money you can use to buy equipment and where you can ultimately collect money at the end of each run to unlock new items in the game.
9) You can play coop (2 players) locally.
10) There are many bosses and enemies in the game. Learning how to beat seemingly unbeatable bosses is a key aspect of the game.
11)I cannot emphasize the replay value enough. Though I have literally finished the game > 20 times, there is still something new to unlock and every run is different. I have not had this kind of replay value in any other game I have played before...
After so much praise, I have to be fair and state that there are some aspects about BoI which could be improved:
1) There is no complete in-game description of what items / trinkets really do. Although you can reverse-engineer many effects by close observation or looking at the statistics, I often resort to the wiki pages of the game rather than write down my experiences. The devs could have made it possible to collect this "lore" in an in-game diary which expands by using every new item once in a while...
2) The "greed mode" requires too much grinding as opposed to the rest of the game. If you wish to unlock everything in this mode, be prepared to play *a lot*. IMHO, the devs could have refrained from letting the "greed machine" jam every once in a while as this adds nothing to the gaming experience.
3) Getting every achievement in the game without cheating is extremely hard. So for completionists, this may be frustrating.
There is so much more I wanted to write about this game and so little space...
So let's hear the verdict:
I can truly recommend this game - I have played a lot of games in my lifetime (>500) but this is one of the very, very few which I would rate with a 10 of 10 stars.
If you are even remotely interested in a zelda-reske, rogue-like game with creepy story and tough battles, which requires thoughtful, clever usage of the scarce resources and if you like a challenge, this is your game.
PS: My recommendation is to get the this game instead of the original BoI with "Wrath of the Lamb" DLC, since it features all the items, enemies and stuff of the original game and much, much more in addition.
Get the whole bundle please do not buy only this.

First of all, I have put around 45 hours on this game, most of the time on the offline mode. And I'm planning to halt my gameplay with this game until I get my hands on The White March. I'm on the middle of Act II as of now, but since the constantly stellar experience that I have since I start my journey, I have a clear picture of what I think about this amazing game.
Pillars of Eternity is an isometric CRPG, devveloped by Obsidian, the same studio who made Fallout New Vegas, Knights of  the Old Republic 2, and Neverwinter Nights 2 (among others). If you have played, one of their game, you already know what to expect. Yes, a deep RPG mechanic, with excellent writing, reactive world, and freedom of action to bend the world as you will. Give Obsidian freedom, free from the existing storyline, gameplay mechanic from previous game (since they usually make sequels), and "pushy" publisher, and what do you get? It's Pillars of Eternity, an excellent game, made from scratch, with no "restriction" whatsoever, It feels like a game that Obsidian was itching to make from the start, a well realized, polished, ambitious, and nostalgia-fueled (for the better). It's Obsidian's best work so far, at least for me. Let's get more in depth to the individual aspect of this game.
Rich, engaging, moving, and intriquing lore with believable characters. Coupled with a brilliantly written texts and dialogues. A very well paced story where the mystery, back story, and overall lore are slowly revealed over time. Every thing is revealed in the right place, right time, and right amount of it, making the story progression feels ever so intriguing and natural.  A ton of equally superb side quest, that adds even more interesting story behind the land of Eora, and especially Dyrwood, with twist and turns along the way, making it a really great read.
It's an isometric CRPG, akin to Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale, if you're into those kind of games, you will be feel right at home. It's a deep modern RPG, something that has been lost for a decade. An RPG where the number matters, every aspect of the stats matters, and when you're trying to be a jack-of-all-trades, the game will punish you. Not that it's not achieveable though, in fact PoE offers a myriad of different ways to solve a quest. Stealth, frontal assault, backdoor assault, sweet talking, being diplomatc, deceit, it's your choice. And no, you don't get XP from combat, that shows that Obsidian wants you to know that combat can be avoided.
One of the most praise-worthy thing to note on PoE is how it can streamline a complex RPG rule set and mechanic by giving a more straightforward explanation and neat, customizable UI. Both a simplified information of each aspect of the game and an extensive, more detailed manual are there for you to read and learn, in addition of a very customizable difficulty settings.
The depth of this game can be seen even right on the character creation. You get to choose the race, class, birth place, background, and belief/motivation. Each with their own play style, advantage-disadvantage, and special abilties that you can mix and match ranging from the tried and true formula to the experimental one. My first character only lasts 2 hours because I underestimate the importance of those, and ended in an unsatisfying note, the second time (my current one), I  spent around 1 hour, reading back and forth the manual. and learning all those stats, so I can create a character that fits my play style.
The combat is a blend between real time and "turn-based". Well, technically it's a real time one where you can pause anytime to issue command to your party. It's the perfect gameplay mechanic for this game where it can show both the complexity and chaotic nature of PoE. Use trap, ambush, sneak attack, and pretty much everything, PoE has multiple ways to deal with your foes. Dealing multiple effects to the enemy even before combat, you can paralyze, sicken, burn, stuck, frightened a single target, yes, poor lad. It has a flexible rule, and doesn't hold back as long as it's still in the realm of it's rule set.
And then there's the party system. The mechanic itself is your standard party system, up to 6 party members where you can recruit and dismiss. One thing that set it apart is the amazing back story, and personal side quest for each character, and the fact that they are so well crafted, that no one is overpowering anyone, they're diverse, but equal.. Add unique personality, funny banter every once in a while, you'll get a set of memorable and entertaining party system. Oh, and you can customize your own party, like Icewind Dale, where you can fully determine how they looks, their background, role, and their set of skills. They are not as interesting as the pre determined ones, but still a very nice addition if you want to have a complete freedom of how you play the game.
Stronghold is a great feature, though underdeveloped. There's nothing better than seeing your stronghold grow from a haunted ruin to a place where you can rest, hire adventurers, trading outpost, and a safe haven for travellers. But it's nothing more than that, except the mysterious mega dungeon below it. By the time I write this review, the 3.0 patch is released, and it contains improvement on the Stronghold mechanic. This is one of the section where I will revise in the future, So yeah, there's that for the momen.
Art direction, art style, atmosphere, and level design over polycount and how detailed the grass looks, anytime, any day. Graphically, if you mean graphic by the latter, Pillars of Eternity looks dated, OK-ish, IF you do a close up to the character, so does the animation. But, who plays this game on close ups? Pillars of Eternity (and traditional RPG in general) is meant to be played in a farther camera position, widen your field of view, and seeing the beautiful scenery that Obsidian has created. Ah yes, I can't get enough of the scenery, it's an excellently made interactive painting. Every place has their own feels, atmosphere, and personality, strong enough that you know what's going on in that particular place. Creating a world, that is both beautiful when it described on text with a visual representation that can match, and complment it.
It's one of those games that  has an OST which are so great that I care to listen it on YT or through the game files afterwards. The voice acting is also top notch, when there is one. And the effect sounds are great too. It's all around a fine one.
Pillars of Eternity is a  must have for anyone looking for a "traditional", 90's RPG, that is modernized and streamlined in all the right way. It's deep, unforgiving, rewarding, immersive, and intense. A brilliant writing, solid mechanic, an art style that has a lot of personality on it, reactive world where your choice really matters, even if it's just a minor one, side quests that has variety, quality, and quantity, and flexible mechanic that give the player a lot of play style choices, in which you can find a lot of replay value in this one.
It's like the old Infinity Engine RPGs with all of the annoying things removed and lots of improved features added.

As a devoted classical computer RPG player (and book RPG), like Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Neverwinter Nights and Dragon Quest series, Dragon's Dogma, Divinity, Legends of Sword Coast, I can assure you: THIS IS THE GAME YOU'VE BEEN WAITING FOR. Thanks, Obsidian!

Excellent entry to the series. This is my favorite mainly because of the art-style in the cutscenes (only found in the 1999 movie and Sonic Mania, elsewhere), but the gameplay is also challenging with the past-future changes adding a nice twist. I only played the genesis games as a kid, so didn't play CD until recently. Still, it's absolutely one of the classics in the series.

When I was 15 years old, I got a Sega CD for Christmas. While the Sega CD was undeniably a failure for Sega, I personally didn't see it that way as a teen and managed to enjoy a good number of quality games on the addon system for the Sega Genesis. One of those games was Sonic CD, which remains to be my favorite entry into the Sonic series thus far (although I haven't played Sonic Mania yet, which looks great).
I should say right away that I have never been a huge fan of the Sonic games. I enjoyed the first two well enough, but I never caught the passion that the more dedicated Sonic fans out there have for the character. That could be partly why I enjoy Sonic CD so much over the other ones I've played, whereas a good chunk of Sonic fans dislike it.
Sonic CD initially looks and plays like the earlier two Sonic games. Dr. Robotnik/Eggman is up to his old tricks and you have to stop him by getting to the end of each level and fighting a boss battle at the end of the third zone of each area. You'll quickly realize there is a little more to it, though. There are signposts throughout the levels labelled "Past" and "Future." If you touch one and then maintain top speed for a few seconds, you find yourself traveling to a past or future version of that same stage. The designers of the game basically made four versions of each non-boss level in the game: past, present, bad future, and good future. Sonic's goal isn't just to defeat Eggman, but also to get a Good Future. And how do you do this? By going into the past and destroying a contraption left there by Sonic's nemesis.
One of the big criticisms levelled at Sonic CD is its level design. Having replayed the game recently, I can see where those criticisms are coming from. Some of the levels aren't really made with Sonic's strengths in mind. Collision Chaos and Wacky Workbench stick out the most here to me with their verticality. It is very difficult to get through some of those stages without being bounced high into the level. I can forgive this because Sonic CD wants the player to explore the level. You need to find a time travel signpost, then find a place to travel fast enough so you can travel in time, and then you have to find Robotnik's contraption.
I was unaware there were actually two separate soundtracks to Sonic CD until the late 1990s. It wasn't until this rerelease of the game on XBLA and Steam that I finally got to hear the Japanese soundtrack. For years I had been hearing about the superiority of that version compared to the American one composed by Spencer Nilsen. I played through the game twice to experience each soundtrack in its entirety. And honestly, I prefer the American soundtrack, but I have to admit this is probably because of my nostalgia for the game. Either way, you'll always get the Japanese soundtrack for the Past levels because Nilsen never composed the soundtracks for those areas.
This release also features proper widescreen support, and it looks great! You can also play through the game as Tails, which is something that was not in the original game. I haven't tried him out yet.
Anyway, it's a fantastic rerelease of a divisive game. And the price at $5 is perfect.

Truly an awesome Sonic game. The soundtrack is absolutely superb, and you have the option of playing with either the US or Japanese versions. Personally I recommend the Japanese version; it's catchier and simply sounds more upbeat. However, the US version has a more atmospheric feel, and it is definitely not something to disregard. To see what I'm talking about, check out both versions of Palmtree Panic Present. The Japanese version is very happy and catchy, while the US version really sets the tropical vibe of the level.
The level design is pretty good, and mostly lets you "go fast." However, near the end of the game, the levels become less designed for speed and more so for platforming, which may put people off. They also become more difficult, but that's to be expected. Each level has a Past, Present, and Future version, with each being essentially the same except for a change in theme and music.
Sonic controls pretty well with a controller, and I'm sure he would with a keyboard as well, but I haven't played the game using the keyboard. With a controller, I used DS4Windows to play on my PS4 controller, and the default configuration for the controller was strange but usable. The only method of controlling Sonic was with the joystick, and I couldn't use the d-pad. The selection button for the menu was the right joystick button (in-game this was the pause button), but jump was still X (or A) and cancel was still circle (or B). I'm not sure whether you can change the controls in game or not, but I didn't see any way to. Regardless, I got used to them after the first level.
Visually the game looks nice. If you have a 144 Hz monitor, or a refresh rate somewhere around there, you must set it to 60 Hz in order for the game to run at a normal speed. The game itself is fairly short; it can be beaten in about 3 hours. Overall, it's a very enjoyable game, and while it can be frustrating trying to collect 50 rings and reach the goal with them all in the later levels, it's still a fun challenge.

Now im wrapping my head around Capcoms deal here...
Why in the hell would you package a game like this in the way that you did? I got some fans of the game who contacted me telling me to play further; and I did. I have to say I thank them. Its like the more I play it the more acceptable it becomes.
This game WILL NOT hold your hand which is frustrating when combined with the amount of ambiguity this game holds. Why start the game off so odd for the first 3-5 hours? It tries hard to be linear so a newbie can gain footing but I somehow found a way to wander into death level dungeons and quests right out the gate. That being said this game is not without its flaws.
However if you can stomach it.... Wow. This game has some charm hidden deep within. The combat is fun. The variety of enemies does increase as you play and the difficulty does not treat you like a child. For f*ck sakes have dependable heals in your party. I had to restart the game out of frustration of not having reliable heals so I made my main pawn take on this job; you could recruit pawns to fill in this task but its sort of a pain to swap them out all the time instead of having your trusty go to at all times.
There are actually 9 classes in the game; not 3 like I stated above. The world is vast...but again ambiguous as is the questing. I can tell that the more I play this game the more clear things will become and I am sure I will update this again after I make some real progress.
With that being said do not start this game unless you plan on putting real time into it. There is a lot of odd ball mechanics to polish. I still hate the pawns, but I kind of like them to. The ability to change strategies in this sidebar way adds fresh RPG strategy. The game still lacks personality, but its becoming clear that this is because this title is more about quantity of quests rather than quality of plot.
So far 7/10, but I am expecting to be further impressed.

Read Only Memories is beautiful in its willingness to embrace its most earnest parts. Cyberpunk as a genre seems obsessed with the grimy underbelly of technological utopias, social disorder among megacorporation overlords, and the dangers unregulated scientific breakthroughs create for humanity at large. Rarely is it even discussed that maybe there’s room within cyberpunk for more than government induced terror and futuristic narcotics. Where, if I may be so bold, is the cute side of cyberpunk?
In the not so distant future of Neo-San Francisco, AI assistants (known as ROMs, hint-hint; nudge-nudge) have risen to the forefront of the public consciousness, with Parallax single handedly leading the charge in robotic advancement. Vying for news worthiness is the growing disorder among hybrids (which in this sense are primarily anthropomorphic humans) and the rebel group The Human Revolution, who see this kind of bodily modification as an act against God and humanity. None of this is of pressing importance to you, however, as your only preoccupation as of now is writing up tech reviews for a non-paying blog, hoping their promises of “exposure” pay off (it was at this point that Read Only Memories became far too autobiographical and I had to take a moment to calm down). Everything changes when Turing, the first fully sentient AI, shows up on your doorstep (or more accurately hacks their way inside your apartment).
Thanks to the goldmine that was 80’s science fiction, it seems a little too easy to see where this is headed. Uncover the dastardly plot, enlist the help of the cities least wanted, and save the world from a massive corporation that seeks to enslave it. Throw in some futuristic tech and this is cyberpunk 101; easy, effective, and more than a little played out. And this is where Read Only Memories begins to shine. Developer Midboss has taken the essence of cyberpunk as a genre and flipped it inside out, showing the bright and charming side underneath.
Read Only Memories rides the fine line between playful awareness and self-indulgence, letting its humor and love of the 80’s as an aesthetic show through without dissolving into a string of references and in humor. Characters are slyly charismatic and witty, endearing despite their transparent shallowness through strength of writing alone. Read Only Memories might only be surface deep, but it’s an intentional prioritization toward individual conversations over character studies. It isn’t as important who these characters are so much as what they’re saying, an understanding that allows Read Only Memories to mask the simplicity and convenience of its plot by creating memorable encounters which standalone but are no less entertaining because of it.
Words cannot describe how thankful I was to discover how unconcerned Read Only Memories is in wasting your time asking you to solve bizarre item based puzzles. Arbitrary logic-less conundrums are the bane of my adventure game loving existence, but Read Only Memories is far too invested in its dialogue and world building to force you to carry around an abundance of junk which will somehow become useful later on. Even when it seems like the game might be falling into that trap, it immediately flips it back around as a knowing jab at the insanity most adventure games put their players through, despite being almost universally derided for it. Read Only Memories isn’t hands off the way a visual novel is, but it never asked for anything more than for me to care about investigating its world and characters, something I was more than happy to do.
As curious as I was to get at the heart of the mystery which drove Turing to my apartment, it’s the world of Neo-San Francisco and the quirkiness of its inhabitants that caused me to fall in love with Read Only Memories. The synth heavy soundtrack set the tone for a low-scale technological metropolis, charming in its familiarity while still retaining a suitably futuristic vibe. It’s also a wonderfully queer city, allowing LGBT characters to exist without it needing to be a point of discussion. While overt representation is importance, there is a lovely sense of acceptance in how Read Only Memories doesn’t treat being gay or gender fluid as something that needs to be said; it’s just part of who someone is.
Read Only Memories is less subtle in the clear analogies that can be drawn between its hybrids and the social climate LGBT persons face in modern society. There is a rightful anger in many of the discussions concerning the lack of dignity and humanity afforded hybrids by those who see them as less than human, and these moments are perhaps the most raw and impactful. Read Only Memories isn’t really a game about LGBT rights, but that doesn’t mean it can’t become a platform for discussion, or at the very least a notable example of a game that recognizes LGBT people exist and doesn’t treat them like a buzzword to put on the back of the box.
Read Only Memories begins to fall apart a bit as it comes to an end, when circumstances become so convenient as to defy even the limited restraints of the universe they’re happening within. But even recognizing the contrived nature of much of its plot, Read Only Memories never asks that you take it seriously, and doing so would probably only be to your own detriment. This is a game that is at home discussing the implications of mass artificial life as it is asking you to write a deliciously terrible Christmas song for an up and coming pop star. Read Only Memories is adorable and cheesy and holds itself together with an acute awareness of tone and by subverting a genre it clearly loves to death. It might be fluffy and lack a satisfying payoff, but Read Only Memories tries so hard and has such an enormous amount of heart that I’d sooner embrace it than write it off for such comparatively meaningless qualms.

This is a fantastic little game that is a must-play for fans of cyberpunk, or if you just like cute robots.  This game really scratched my itch for sci-fi that pontificates big questions like what it means to be human and all that, but also my need for quirky humor, catchy osts, and bright colors.
My only real complaint is that the middle gets a little tiresome because more often than not other characters will push you forward in the plot rather than teasing out a lead for yourself through investigation.  On the one hand, that keeps you from getting lost and confused as to how to progress, but on the other it pushes it towards being more like a visual novel than a P&C adventure game.
That being said, the gameplay does get shaken up in interesting ways in a few chapters with randomized puzzles, mazes, and even an arcadey shooter minigame.  Also, you are not railroaded into a pre-determined ending; how you interact with people and whether or not you succeed in certain tasks has actual consequences down the line.
Anyway I loved the game, I loved Turing, and I'm eagerly looking forward to anything the developer comes up with next :)

I started this game on a whim this June, what a ride it was. 10/10
A lot of people have compared progressing in this game to struggling with depression, or life in general.
I would tend to agree. The isolation, uncertainty of which path to take, (for a 1st time player like me) unexplained appearances and disappearances of characters, cyclical nature of the world (not to mention its austere/sublime beauty, I really loved all the ruins), and largely difficult enemies created an exceptionally atmospheric feel that I have never seen before.
What started as a whim to try this notoriously difficult game to see if I, Bravemoof was a true gamer of stout heart and appreciable dexterity of finger, turned into a flaming passion. A passion to kick each boss off their place of power and harvest their souls. One thing I really liked about the game is that I felt vulnerable the whole time. I have played other action titles where by the end I am flying around, disintegrating hordes of enemies, and unafraid of any and all damage (save perhaps the uber-slow and telegraphed mega last boss laser beam, if that). In dark souls my only significant late game power came from myself, (the player) and it was called perseverance. This beautiful game had me playing not because my friends said it was amazing, or for some stupid achievement, but to see if I could surmount the next challenge.
Probably the pinnacle of this game was the fight with Knight Artorias. I had killed a couple bosses on my first attempt before him, and felt the game was coming to a close, when I step through the gate and see his cut-scene. He smites me down before I can even land a hit on him. To go from that lowly starting point, to tumbling past (almost) every one of his attacks and cutting him down was amazing. I threw down my controller, stood up, and unleashed a raspy screech, which probably made my parents shake their heads in disappointment (but that’s another story). That fight and many others embodied what I really liked about Dark Souls. How it makes dying such a key part of the game.
Alright, (insert enemy name) You may have just killed me (again), I may be a nasty withered husk, and my only friend may be an idiotic snake with a mustache. But I will be back ready to chip away at your ankles into you crumble into dust. And in the end, I may be weak, I may be ugly, but I will be all that is left. No flying, no lasers, no invincibility, only the brute will to rise from the fire and sprint once more into the darkness, weapon in hand. All powerful hero? No. Baddass? Very much yes. Again 10/10

Read Only Memories is probably one of my favorite pieces of media to come out in 2015. The game is in stark relief to franchises like Shadowrun that deal with similiar concepts, but in all the more gentle way. Much of the grit of the cyberpunk genre is eschewed for a more personal and affecting view of concepts like machine intelligent, transhumanism, and trans-ness in general, and the story is greatly improved by it.  ROM also extends the same kind of care to the player and their avatar, giving them several options for things like pronouns, attitude in conversation, and even religious restrictions on a food diet.
The game's only weak point is that it's ending lacks the personal punch it's been swinging the entire game - instead opting for a Besethda style 'where are they now' epilogue. While understandable in the writing team's long run, I felt this type of big picture ending was determential to ROM's very character focused writing and could have maybe been better served by a playable epilogue where talking to the characters revealed their fates.
Overall, I really cannot recommend ROM enough - it is a game that is gentle and understating in way that is comforting while still allowing for good discussion of the issues it presents. I love this game.

Plus, with the addition of the latest booster pack, (A pack of fan mods and items that comes out every few months) you have the ability to get achievements with mods on, allowing you to use asthetic mods to enhance the experience to your content. Oh, and by the way, the statistics I gave contradict those Edmund gave in the game description. My review reflects the total package of Rebirth, Afterbirth, and Afterbirth+. All and all, this game would land in my top 3 favorite games of all time.

Starbound is an awesome sandbox space exploration game in which you can build bases and explore plants for valuable resources.  When I first played the game, there was no story implemented yet but was still a very fun game.
Since then, the developers have added quite a bit of content to it, including a story driven quest line and story driven objectives as well as more advanced monster AI.  They continue to add to the game as well as correct bugs and the game is still in early access. Let me start out by saying this is not a strait up review of Starbound, simply my impressions of the game and the developers at it has evolved throughout the years I have followed it.
I purchased starbound the day it released on steam in early access. The developers promised so much, and as a lover of terraria it was hard not to get on the hype train. When the game first released, it had some serious fundamental flaws. This was a widely descused topic at the time, the game gave most of what it promised, but it executed it in a way that was so bland. Monsters were "randomly generated" but all of them acted the same, worlds were different but hardly any of them were worth exploring. Building was pointless because you would eventually leave the plannet and never return. And the initial combat and armor mechanics were absolutely terrible. I was worried that these flaws were so ingrained into the core of Starbound that they would never be truely fixed no matter what the developers did. What worried me even more was all the talk of how they wouldn't allow criticism on the Starbound forums and that people were being banned due to voicing their frusterations with the developers. Signs seemed to point to this being another case of indie developers making huge promises, not fulfilling them, and basically dropping the project completely. We've all seen it done countless times before.
But Chucklefish, despite these setbacks, continued to make progress on the game. Over the years, I would go back and play starbound for quite a bit before stopping and not touching it for several months at a time. Each time I returned to starbound, I would be treated to find that the game had undergone massive changes, always being a huge improvement on the last iteration. The other day I, once again, had the urge to pick up starbound. What I had experienced had spurred me to write this review. Once again, Starbound had made huge strides since I had last played it. To the point where I feel it is finally worthy of the all its initial hype. Chucklefish has proven its dedication, and the game is moving in the right direction.

This game is my favorite shooter in the 20+ years since Doom was released on PC.  This game features an excellent story, great coop, and exciting multiplayer.  It even features a type of intelligence minigame that rewards you with score multiplayers in SP and MP.  There are tons of customization options for your gadgets and weapons.  You can: be a heavily armored door breacher that flashbangs then shotguns everything in sight,  be a ghost who uses stealth and gadgets to distract and complete the mission without ever being seen, be a sniper who lays proximity mines for would be flankers, also be an assault rifle weilding/grenade sniping nightmare.  The AI is one of the best out there (but still can be exploited) where the enemy that spots you will run to cover, summon reinforcements, and then they will either: surround you, stack up and rush you, or spread on a line and toss grenades at you.  Increasing the difficulty to perfectionalist will challenge.  The graphics are still great compared to current games.  The combat animations are superb, done with heavy emphasis in krav maga.  The single player dialogue amongst the characters make sense.  It's like jumping into a Clancy novel.  Multiplayer is smaller, sometimes only 2vs2, and you may have to wait a couple minutes for a fourth player to join in off hours (the game doesn't appeal to the COD crowd).  You play as either a stealthy spy, or an armored merc in an objective based game.  You don't get spawn killed in this game, don't have kill streak paladins raining death on you, there's no running around two minutes just to get killed by a guy camping out either.  The learning curve for the spy can be stiff until you understand the maps and how to misdirect and lead mercs into traps.
Not worth that much money, Don't get it!

So now I will give you my full rambled review, I would make it smoother but I am not a big reviewer so guess there is no sense in putting to much time and effort in it. Also part of it will land in the comments because it is way to long:
Night in the Woods is one of the greatest mixxed bags I've ever seen. And this is sad because I really hyped this game to no end. But unlike fallout 4 which delivered even without Bethesda bugothon, Night in the Woods looks like it was made by a student in their spare time.
Now originally it was supposed to come out in fall 2015, of course it couldn't because first of it is was backed with 400% and from ground zero to a full game it takes a while. Oh wait a moment, most of the sprites where already made before the kickstarter. Actually it isn't even that hard to do them, they are simple vector shapes. The biggest thing is that is actually is using vector graphic, so the simple artstyle is legit as. But engines capable of 2D vector graphics are very rare thus they had to program one. Luckily they didn't need to program everything from scratch, just modify the unity engine to do this in a proper manner. But guess what? It doesn't take that long, especially if you work in that field for a while it becomes pretty easy to make. Yes of course polishing is important and the leaves are awesome. Probably the biggest thin to program how the leaves fly trough the air. But guess what, they already finished that development in summer 2015. That means they had the engine set up and the easy artstyle meant easy making of the character and background. So from now on this whole game was more like using rpg maker. It wasn't fallout where you needed to make the models look amazing, have some legit visual effects and that all running in real time, now that is a mammoth of a project to undertake. As a matter of fact I am a 3D Artist myself, yeah just google me. I don't want to act like I am the king of the hill but I am currently making this in my spare time while studying mediainformatic, I am planing on making a small movie which maybe will be very short too. But first it is only one person, in it's spare time, and while I need like 40hours on a singular character, for a NITW one you would only need about half an hour. 3 or 4 people, probably working full time needing about 2 years. Sonic CD... What can I say about this? Not much.
I have mixed thoughts about this, around early 2011, probably when Sonic Generations was first revealed. I remember this game was heavenly praised, now I don't hear much about this game. At first I didn't like the presentation, didn't think much about the soundtrack and just didn't like it. I eventually played it on Steam, and mobile. And while my thoughts changed, it didn't for the most part. Sonic CD was an interesting game, but was just ehh. The level design was much interesting, there was rarely a time where I stop just to look at the level itself, and that's some I always do in a Sonic game, it was okay for the most part, besides the memorable stages everybody knows, the rest was okay. But the structure was a miss for me. For a Sonic game that was released after Sonic 2 that fixed the issues of Sonic 1's level structure; Sonic CD heads back to what Sonic 1 was doing. So basically I see Sonic 1 level structure as two pathways relating to speed, if you manage to get path A which is most likely the best pathway, you'll be awarded with more speed, but with pathway B you'll get less speed and sometimes more platforming. Sonic 2 has multiple pathways that made exploring a big pleasure and had me looking all over the place for hidden secrets, Sonic that Sonic 3 & Knuckles perfected, but Sonic CD went back to what Sonic 1 had and while some acts had multiple pathways, I didn't really bother to explore for the most part. And I didn't like how Sonic controlled, for me he felt stiff, and I had problems making direct jumps while watching my speed when jumping. One main element of the game was the Future and Past goal posts located all over the stages, with this you can get teleported to the future or the past, with this you can find and destroy Capsules and Metal Sonic holograms for a good future. Special Stages are in this game, but with no Super Sonic, I was for the most part disappointed. I like the Special Stages, but not that much. For the most part, Sonic CD was an okay for me, it wasn't bad. But I didn't enjoy it that much.

Like alot of Sonic fans right now, I've been playing tons of Sonic Mania and feeling like a child again, loving every second of the original levels as well as the reimagined classics, after a while I began thinking, I don't play Sonic CD that much and I really should, it's just like the original games, yet I don't seem to go back to it often, so I decided to go through another playthrough recently and well, "Debatably the best Sonic game ever made." is something I often hear when Sonic CD is mentioned, I admit I don't agree with that statement, but I do understand why people would claim it as such.
To briefly touch on Sonic CDs history for a second we have to go back to the 90s, when Sega were trying to make the most out of an unfortunate situation with it's lackluster Sega CD addon for the Genesis/Mega Drive, the technology it sold itself on simply was just too young, the system needed a game, much like the Genesis needed itself when it launched.
After the success of Sonic The Hedgehog 1, Yuji Naka had grown tired of Sega of Japan looking over his shoulder and had taken a good portion of the team to Sega of America (also known as Sega Technical Institute) where they would later work on what would become Sonic The Hedgehog 2, this left co-creator Naoto Ohshima and the remainder of the original team still based in Japan to work on their own Sonic 2.
Sega of Japan's product would ultimately become Sonic CD, built for the system in order to make the absolute most potential out of it's assets, CGI in-game movies, CD quality music and large disc space.
The Sega CD went down under regardless along with the ill-fated Sega 32x addon, but that didn't stop Sonic CD claiming its spot of legacy among the classic Sonic games. Sonic CD would go on to be universally praised regardless of the Sega CDs poor state, the only way people could of played Sonic CD was either through the Sega CD itself, an early pc port in 1996, through Sonic Gems Collection, emulators or the JVC X'EYE.
Thankfully in comes Christian Whitehead, now a beloved developer among the Sonic community, before contracted to work on Sonic Mania, this enhanced Sonic CD port was actually his first ever involvement with Sega, rebuilt from the ground up, Whiteheads version is the definitive Sonic CD experience, super smooth framerate, no collision detection issues, all hitboxes improved and all players now have access to both soundtracks released for the game, more on that later.
So now the plot, our beloved blue hedgehog has traveled to a mystical river called Never lake, where a large world known simply as Little Planet has made its yearly apperance. The sinister Dr Eggman intends to transform Little Planet into a giant mechanical fortress, alongside creating Metal Sonic and kidnapping self-proclaimed blue hedgehog girlfriend Amy Rose, Eggman plans to obtain the 7 Time Stones home to Little Planet to allow passage through time travel. As Sonic it is up to you to travel through all of the games zones, defeat Eggman in whatever contraption he has built for the 3rd acts boss, obtain the Time Stones, rescue Amy and save Little Planet.
To quote another steam reviewer, the best word to describe the experience that Sonic CD offers to fans and newcomers to the series is "Unauthodox", as early as Palmtree Panic you will notice the verticality and width all the stages Sonic CD has to offer, the bizarre platforms, the obsurdist gimmicks, the time traveling element and even the enemy designs and boss battles are as wacky as they are creative.
I'm not kidding, watch Green Hill act 1, Emerald Hill act 1 and Palmtree Panic act 1 side by side and you'll notice it, one is clearly not like the others, but that helps make Sonic CD one of the more unique experiences of the classical formula that so many of us had grown up with. Abstract, intricate yet also allowing for the core momemtum based platforming are brief descriptions of the level design in Sonic CD.
Your ultimate goal in Sonic CD revolves around the time element the game introduces, throughout each zone are posts that read Past and Future, if you can maintain high speed long enough after touching a post, you'll be sent to the corrosponding era, you are to destroy all robot generators in the past to create good futures for every act in the game, if this doesnt sound like your cup of tea, then there is always the traditional sense of collecting the Time Stones by getting 50 rings and jumping into the giant ring at the end of the stage and completing the special stage, which when all 7 are obtained, automaticly create good futures for every zone in the game.
This is one of my favourite things about Sonic CD, except for Sonic 3 and Ks ending (and maybe Sonic 1 even though it's miniscule), CD reacts to your actions throughout the game, depending on what you do in every act determines what happens in it's future and I have to say, getting good futures feels so rewarding, the game shows you the effects of your actions and you feel like patting yourself on the pack saying "Yeah, I did this!" and it's a wonderful feeling, you are the difference between Palmtree Panic becoming a polluted mechanical unsustanable landmass or a tropical healthy landscape, the difference between Metallic Madness becoming a vile rusty fortress of maliciousness or an enviromentally friendly utopia.
It'll be hard for you not to move to the music while playing, but this is an interesting topic, as mentioned there are two soundtracks for Sonic CD, one for Japan and Europe, and an entirely redone one for America, both versions of the OST are vastly different, the Jap/Pal version is much more lively and energetic while the American version goes for a more atmospheric and synergestic feel and there isnt much information as to why this is, if I had to guess, I imagine when Sonic CD was shipped over to America, they had believed the Japanese soundtrack was quite similiar to Micheal Jackons musical style who they were trying to distance themselves from after his scandals became public while MJ was working on the soundtrack for the then in development Sonic The Hedgehog 3.
To better understand the drastic differences, see these links of both tracks for Palmtree Panic present:
JP:
US:
Sonic games are generally considered to have great Soundtracks and CD delivers in spades, but it's definately much more varied here due to...well reasons, on which soundtrack you believe is the better version comes down to preference, personally I'm for the Japanese soundtrack, personal favourites being Palmtree Panic, Stardust Speedway and Metallic Madness.
I've definately grown an appreciation for Sonic CD over the years and do wish I would return to it as often as I do the other classic games, I do recommend Sonic CD to anyone whom is interested, definately the most unauthodox of the series and none the less a great game in it's own right.

If you're using an i3, i7, Intel Xeon, AMD FX 63xx, FX 83xx, or FX 92xx, or an i5 laptop, DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME.
Any processor that supports hyperthreading will make this entirely unplayable.  Shaders will not load.  Polygonal stretching/artifacting is frequent and highly distracting.  Objects will clip out of existence from either getting close or getting far from it, revealing the out-of-bounds areas or making NPCs simply float in mid-air.  No settings will fix the bug and no fix (other than disabling hyperthreading in your BIOS... hell no) is available.  It also has severe stuttering problems, and according to some online sources the bad performance is an AMD specific bug that can't be fixed.
Even more than that, you can't brute-force your way through the game and ignore your problems.  Even when you look past the invisible tiling and exposed out-of-map areas, the true game-ending bug is when your UI breaks and a giant black hexagon covers a good chunk of the center of the screen.  This makes it near-impossible to aim.  Just go play Singularity.
The game itself is interesting and very enjoyable from what I've played, and if not for these shader bugs the Quake4-ish visuals hold up perfectly... but like the original Far Cry or Grim Fandango, the first big challenge is figuring out how to duct-tape the messy, outdated code together, and as of yet I haven't succeeded.  Will update review if a solution can be found.

A game that was pretty unheard of, at least to me, until a few years ago when steam sales were still a big novelty and undderrated gems for $2.99 were must buys. A mish mash of the trending first person shooters around it's release and shameless appropriation of their gameplay mechanics that made it's influences classics.
-Story-
To get it out the gate, the story is nonsensical and largely non-existent. Scientists working on suit, guy takes suit changes future, you gotta go after him... something something alternate universe that is kinda steampunk aesthetic? Something something love interest died in the past... vengeance? Something something villain is a dictatorship? You get these brief, and i mean brief, CG cutscenes of exposition that is hardly exposition but fragments lacking context. The story is not really engaging and serves merely to string the gameplay together.
-Gameplay-
The gameplay is the real meat of the game here. Taking heavy influence from Half-Life 2, Crysis and perhaps even FEAR. You can slow down time; slow down allows you to dodge projectiles, move faster and take out enemies easier.
Stop time; completely stops time which can also allow you to pop a dude in the dome piece or steal their weapons from their hands.
And finally, rewind which allows you to rewind time.
These are all used to move through puzzles outside of combat which gives it a Half-Life feel. I'll say that Rewind I only ever used in puzzles. I didn't really see how it could be that useful in combat but I never tried it. I found slow down to be the most effective in that regard.
The powers are what makes the gameplay incredibly fun and probably the source of it's cult status.
There are various weapons to use. Some really cool like the explosive cross bow, a cannon that fires energy or a flamethrower machine gun. They don't have a lot of kick or feel amazing to use, the more generic guns (machine gun, pistol, sniper) especially but they don't feel completely awful either. The gunplay is serviceable enough.
There's no NG+ or any reason to play through a second or third time.
-Performance-
Rig: i7 4770k, 980ti, 16gb ram, win7
Performance seems to be the biggest point of contention when discussing the game. People failing to get the game working, awful performance on Nvidia and AMD cards even on modern systems and steam running an inferior version of the game.
However, I had very little problems getting it running well. At max settings I ran at rock solid 60 fps the entire game. No bugs or atrifacting that I noticed at least. Nice lighting and rain effects that hindered performance not at all.
The issues I did have though;
Booting it up presents a box saying video drivers out of date or some such. Which isn't true? You can click through it and doesn't seem to effect the game but it is strange and a mild hindrance.
My biggest problem is that though it was 60 fps at all times there was some kind of... jitter? I've had this problem before in Borderlands: Pre Sequel and couldn't fix it there either. The game does have mouse acceleration that you can't turn off. So perhaps that is the crux of the issue but I turned the games mouse sens all the way down and my mouse dpi all up, which seemed to help a little but then the mouse sense wasn't good enough in game. However, this is an issue I've not seen anyone else complain about.
In closing,
It's not a bad game. I'm pretty positive on it, though i think the underrated status is kind of exaggerated.
Stopping time then quickly headshotting 5 enemies, stealing the shot gun out the hands of another, unstopping time, popping dude in the head while he's confused is pretty fun. And there's a lot of fun to be had with that. The puzzles aren't terribly hard and usually a one of the powers is the answer.
The story is not at all the reason to play and hardly the talking point of the fans.
It's not a solid 'buy this full price' reccomendation but during a steam sale, it's worth picking up and getting a fun 8 hour campaign.
