Changing recommend to "Not recommend" and heres why:

-Game tries to be a hobby by using hard earned resources when you are not playing. If you want to actually gain/stockpile resources, you will have to find 2 of each as the game will consume 1 dufflebag of supplies after every REALTIME day. Not every IN GAME day. Dumbest mechanic I have ever seen.

-You are given side missions at a more frequent rate than you are given settlement quests in Falout 4. They are also times and will expire if you don't do them basically immediately. This would be okay if the missions either gave you something for completing them or had no negative impacts in not completing them. They do niether of those things. Side quests give the player absolutely nothing in return and will bear negative effects if not completed, making them seem like a chore that HAS TO BE DONE even though you just want to do the next story mission or loot.

-Looting is the only thing that makes this game worth playing and even the looting has too many down sides. A house can be full of guns/ammo/medical supplies but will be marked as "COMPLETELY SEARCHED" if there are no caches still inside. Duffle bags of supplies can not be stored in vehicles (F***ING WHY?) which makes vehicles only good for personal transport and nothing else. Your inventory space only has like 8 or less slots even with the largest backpack in the game which means after looting half a building you need to head home to drop off all your crap. Also bullets only stack up to 30. That's less than a magazine in some guns. So if you are packing a gun, you have to be overly conservative with bullets all the time.

-Combat uses a stamina system (Yes like Dark Souls), but the player has MAYBE 3 swings worth of stamina that takes ages to regen. Sprinting and dodging also take stamina meaning that if you dodge and attack and swing once, you are out of stamina. And zombies can take up 5 swings depending on the weapon.

It's a case of the classic "Cool concept,♥♥♥♥♥♥poor delivery".

So, so disappointed. I was very excited about this game; I don't have a lot of money for games and usually only buy them on offer, sub-£5, but I couldn't wait for this game and all the hype I read sounded great.
So I bought it full price and played it through. Whilst I can't deny having some enjoyable times - I was a fan of the way the game seemed to persist when you weren't playing, making a base was enjoyable and some of the missions were fun - I was overall very disappointed and felt kind of cheated by the critic reviews and the game developers. The game was just too easy; it felt as though there were no real challenges and that the game was designed so that everyone could finish it without too much trouble. I don't feel as though I am some elitist gamer; I'm happy that the game can be accessed and enjoyed by players of all skill levels but there really is no reason in the world why a game developer should choose not to include a difficulty setting in the game menu.. unless of course they were selling an expansion pack shortly after release which would advertise 'increased difficulty' as one of its selling points.
I haven't bought the expansion pack out of principle and I stopped playing the game shortly after completion, which really does not take very long at all. I delayed finishing the game until I had completed all the side missions but the main story finishes very quickly - another selling point for the expansion. This feels like a rant, but one of the aspects of reviews which made me most interested was the idea of character permadeath. This turned out to be a huge exaggeration and I didn't lose a single character that wasn't scripted (one). To be fair, I was being careful at first, but before long I was wading into hordes with a golf club and coming out unfazed. There really seemed little need for stealth, which took away much of the gravity and tension of the game.
Aside from that rant, another criticism of the game was the zombies themselves - it felt as though effort had been made to aim the game at a younger audience with cartoony zombies with glowing green eyes. In all, maybe buy it on offer but don't pay more than a fiver for it. Don't expect much and you might have a bit of fun.
Tl;dr: can be fun but purposely designed way too short and way too easy, with no option to adjust difficulty. Also cartoon zombies.

I think I've played enough to review it, at least for now.  The graphics are gorgeous.  They resemble anything a major name company could put out.  The interface is decent....the crafting part can get confusing and tedious, as it takes LOTS of wood/lumber to start building things.  The map is quite large, with lots of places to explore.
Besides that, there doesn't seem to be that much to actually DO.  I'm not into the PVP, kill on sight part.  So when you join a no-KOS server, you end up running around aimlessly, searching house afer house for some loot.......and that's about it.  The true survival aspect hasn't been implimented yet, and only time will tell if it ever will.  The mutants and wildlife add some excitement, but encounters seem very far and few in between, at least for me.  I end up spending several hours just running around, filling up my pack with stuff.......then quiting, as there just isn't anything else to DO.  I don't know if it's just that particular server, or my style of play, or what, but it ends up getting very boring.
Maybe in time, the developers will add more to the game, like missions, quests, etc.  "Find this specific loot item", or "kill X mutants/deer/etc", or "find this specific house/vehicle/room/person and do something with it", anything like that can give you something to accomplish.  Give upgrades to clothes, packs, weapons, loot, special items, etc as rewards.  Maybe even an unbreakable crate to store your extra loot in.
As of right now, I'll give it a thumbs up, as the game itself is excellent.....it's just the POINT of the game is a little lacking.

As someone who this game is firmly targetted at, I gotta say, I'm not terribly impressed. The animations and art style are really the only selling point I can think of, other than that it really is just unfun.
I guess my biggest problem is that the protagonist just isn't likeable; the game opens up with them complaining about writing a review for a set of headphones, and goes into how they're "selling their soul bit by bit." This just screams to me of an obnoxious privledged person. Maybe that's the point, to show how they grow as a character, but it really doesn't do you any favors that this is who you're supposed to connect with, especially when you're at the other end of the spectrum.
But the game would almost make up for having a poorly written and unlikeable protagonist if the other characters were actually any good. Turing, your robot buddy, is a smug ♥♥♥♥er who can't ♥♥♥♥ing stop talking about how great they are. There's a cat lady who gets super offended at you when you're forced, by the game, to ask if she's a character you're looking for. Then there's goddamn Tomcat, a guy who is nostalgic for the pre-Civil War south. You know, the south that had slaves. Yeah. He's not super likeable either, surprisingly!
Then there's the plot. Oh my god the ♥♥♥♥ing plot. Never have so many words been used to say so little. Your friend Hayden is missing and your new robot buddy comes to you for help finding him! Oh boy! Excitement! But its all lost in the sea of words, as Turing just keeps talking and talking and TALKING about♥♥♥♥♥♥you legit do not care about. Here's another issue I have: maybe don't have a nameless protagonist and just have the main character be Turing? That way you're never being talked at for what feels like hours and being told how much of an idiot chump you are. Oh and we'd also feel some sort of emotional connection to Hayden (he did create Turing after all!) instead of having a protagonist that just goes along with events because they have nothing  better to do with their time.
Oh and don't even get me started on the comparisons between the LGBTQ+ community and the weirdo hybrids. Not only does this have the most infantitle understanding of how gene therapy would work (sharks can get cancer you morons!), but the oppression the hybrids claim to experience just feels so false. "We wanna have kids!" they scream, "but this law says we can't!" That law is set in place because hybrids would have literal monstrosity babies that would probably die within a few days, because baby octopus-human-fox hybrids could not survive outside the womb. Not to mention the strain it would take on the mother, both physically and mentally. The only actual case of oppression in the game is of a cat lady having some of her non-gene therapy'd eggs being destroyed by racist doctors, but even then the courts side with her and give her a huge pay out! The system works! That's not oppression!

This game is my favorite shooter in the 20+ years since Doom was released on PC.  This game features an excellent story, great coop, and exciting multiplayer.  It even features a type of intelligence minigame that rewards you with score multiplayers in SP and MP.  There are tons of customization options for your gadgets and weapons.  You can: be a heavily armored door breacher that flashbangs then shotguns everything in sight,  be a ghost who uses stealth and gadgets to distract and complete the mission without ever being seen, be a sniper who lays proximity mines for would be flankers, also be an assault rifle weilding/grenade sniping nightmare.  The AI is one of the best out there (but still can be exploited) where the enemy that spots you will run to cover, summon reinforcements, and then they will either: surround you, stack up and rush you, or spread on a line and toss grenades at you.  Increasing the difficulty to perfectionalist will challenge.  The graphics are still great compared to current games.  The combat animations are superb, done with heavy emphasis in krav maga.  The single player dialogue amongst the characters make sense.  It's like jumping into a Clancy novel.  Multiplayer is smaller, sometimes only 2vs2, and you may have to wait a couple minutes for a fourth player to join in off hours (the game doesn't appeal to the COD crowd).  You play as either a stealthy spy, or an armored merc in an objective based game.  You don't get spawn killed in this game, don't have kill streak paladins raining death on you, there's no running around two minutes just to get killed by a guy camping out either.  The learning curve for the spy can be stiff until you understand the maps and how to misdirect and lead mercs into traps.

If you're looking for a solid stealth game with a great story and awesome co-op, this is it.
9/10 Highly recommended!

Okay, I’ve been putting this off for too long.  I’ve got a lot to say about this game (most of it unironically good), and some mixed feelings about the state of the game industry as a whole that Stranded Deep sums up in an eerily succinct manner.
So, first off, this is not some “lol great uninstall simulator” joke thumbs up.  I really do love Stranded Deep.  By pure happenstance, I picked it up just as a big update hit (DO NOT BELIEVE THE PEOPLE WHO SAY THE GAME HAS SLOW DEVELOPMENT, THEY DO NOT KNOW WHAT THEY ARE TALKING ABOUT!!  IT TAKES MORE THEN TWELVE HOURS TO BUILD A NEW UPDATE YOU IMPATIENT DOLTS!!) and as of right now, the only major feature that isn’t implemented is the ability to be rescued.  A big thing to add?  Yes.  Necessary to enjoy this game to its fullest?  Depending on what you want out of it, no.  The game as it is now I compare to a more serious and survival oriented version of Minecraft.  Where Minecraft is about building as impressive a shelter as you can (in theory) with a survival edge to it, Stranded Deep lives on the idea of survival with the ability to build a nice bungalow on the beach just for the fun of it.  The comparison isn’t perfect to be sure, but I feel it at least answers some of the problems the critics of this game (who have a leg to stand on) have.  One of the most common complaints I’ve seen is that it lacks content and you shouldn’t spend money on it until it has more.  This is actually not true.  Because the game is so aimless, I’d put money on many of these people building 1-6 foundation blocks for a bare bones shelter, built a fire spit, collected some crabs and coconuts and called it a day.  The problem with that is the vast majority of the content isn’t just underwater, but also spread out over many islands.  Like with Minecraft, if you don’t give yourself something to do, like building a big shelter, collecting all the easter eggs, constructing a boat motor, killing a Great White or Marlin, or any of the other many things you can do here and there, you’re going to spend an hour on the game, get bored and shelf the game.  If that’s the case, open world games aren’t for you, I suppose.  And that’s fine.  Me?  I spent 20 hours gathering the resources to build the shelter I have in my game.  And it was a fun and nerve-racking and immersive and lonely and atmospheric experience that I will never forget.  And I’m not even close to done with that world yet, let alone the game as a whole.  That said though, I read the patch notes on the 0.01 build of the game and that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s inexcusable.  Had the game been released on the 0.03H3 patch when I got it, I’d put it on the short list of games that did early access right.  Then again, Stranded Deep probably wouldn’t have gotten this far had it not been released when it had.  Add in the fact that, with the number of bugs still in the game (though rapidly shrinking), I have basically payed a developer money to playtest his/her late beta game, this whole early access nonsense has yet again put a bad taste in my mouth.  I hate early access so much that my friend (who has the average amount of hate for early access) wants to size me for a straightjacket every time it comes up in conversation, so you can see my issues with the nature of Stranded Deep’s development.
TL;DR: If you like aimless, open world games with no goal, as of right now and forever more, Stranded Deep will NOT disappoint.  It’s deeply immersive, atmospheric, lonely, and even terrifying at times if you fear open water (as I do).  If you need more structure then that, wait for the ability to be rescued to be implemented.  That may or may not give you the goal you need to work toward to give this game the time it needs to capture you fully.  I got it for the full $15 asking price and never once regretted it (sans the whole early access thing).  If you’re smarter than me and wait to get it on sale, all the better.

Demontower: Part IV - Slaughter of the Blood Thief is a compelling retro-styled hack-and-slash game, sheathed in a rogue-like veneer. Binding Of Isaac players may feel a sense of familiarity playing this game - possibly due to the procedurally generated modular level design, and the linear advancement through differently decorated dungeon floors (each of which climaxing with a boss encounter). However--while the critical comparisons in game reviews to Dark Souls has become cliché (along with reviewers self-awarely calling out the overuse of such comparisons)--the developers have left clear allusions to some of their particular influences, the starkest homage being the "You Died" message typifying every death. And there will be a lot of them.
The dungeon level design may initially make one suspect this is a typical rogue-like (or rogue-lite), but in all senses, it isn't. Deaths don't result in a hard reset, but rather a level reset. This can feel just as crushing at times though; being stuck at a particularly challenging boss will result in having to complete the preceding dungeon all over again, which involves dealing with mob enemies, retrieving a key from an adjacent room, and then locating the boss room. The developers do show a kindness however, in that-though floors are randomised on death-the key room and the boss door will typically remain in a consistent location. This makes speeding through a dungeon to retry a boss less cumbersome.
Mechanically, the immediate contemporary comparison would be Hyper Light Drifter. There are two main abilities your character possesses. For the offensive, there is a melee slash, capable of one-shotting most enemies in the early-game. Spamming this attack will result in the character being unable to attack for a short period, however there doesn't appear to be any kind of visual stamina bar to indicate this, so mastering how aggressive to be with attacks takes some experience. The other core mechanic is a swift dodging ability, useful for escaping enemy attacks, passing through hazards unharmed, and traversing the environment. Unlike attacking, a stamina bar (of sorts) is visible for this ability, and will regenerate relatively quickly after use.
Initially, you feline fighter has 9 health blocks. At first glance, this seems rather forgiving, but this links to the progression system. Again, unlike rogue-like games, there isn't an array of randomised abilities to unlock, but instead, a deliberate progression. After defeating a boss and moving on to the next level, a heart-container is permanently destroyed, while an extra bar is added to the dodge meter (allowing for a larger chain of successive dodges). This type of progression seems to fit wonderfully with a player's learning curve. Newer players who are learning the mechanics are likely to take more damage, and therefore, require the extra health; meanwhile, as a player begins to master the dodge mechanic, possessing a higher stock of chained dodges becomes more useful to them.
While the title might not be revolutionary, it's clearly a skilfully crafted game which iterates upon some of the best modern games, without failing to weave in some unique touches. While some people may have minor gripes with certain difficult aspects of the game, such as how enemy attacks can cause stunlocking, those looking for a sense of accomplishment through mastery will not feel amiss.

In Night in the Woods, you take on the role of Mae, a college dropout, returning to her hometown, only to find a mystery to solve. Needless to say, that mystery becomes much more complicated and big than any of the characters thought would be.
While the main story/mystery is what makes the player's journey so interesting, the characters are the ones that make this game as good as it is. While the player gets one ending, a second playthrough is completely justifiable, because you can get different quests from the characters and you will not be able to do all of them in one go - the game gives you a choice, even if you don't see it at first. Whoever you visit in a store, per se, and agree to go with, will be the player's decision and next "mission". The game is a journey of finding oneself. What you get out of it is entirely up to the player and how they perceive it, especially since it has a sort of open ending. Its the journey of four young adults trying to find their place in the world and accepting the reality of adulthood. For sure, this game is a gem, the hard work and love put into it is more than evident and it shows - I highly recommend this experience.

This is a very challenging action game with a lot of puzzles in the mix.  Not the most difficult game you could be playing but still very difficult, Forced has you playing through a variety of challenges, from puzzles to boss battles to time limits. Keyboard/mouse controls are great, so I did not bother trying out a gamepad, but there is Xbox 360 controller support.  The space key is used for multiple actions, however, and I often had to restart levels because I accidentally called the orb when I was trying to skip dialogue.  Not a big deal, mind you. The game could be longer, and I wish there were more character customization options.  There are no visual customizations, but what I would really like to see are some more skill and stat choices. Timeshift is one of those games that you don't expect to be as enjoyable as it actually is.
The basic plot of the game is that a scientist has stolen a time traveling suit and has become a dictator. You are one of his colleges who has strapped on another version of the suit and jumped after him, leading to your suit getting damaged. From there you join the resistance and go ham on it. The game doesn't really have much more plot than that, just a good 6 or so hours of really good shooting.
Combat is your standard FPS style mass murdering fun, with a twist. You can only carry two guns at any given time, from the standard pistol and rifle, to energy cannons and exploding crossbows. Each and every gun is satisfying, providing a good, hard punch, it also helps that the enemies have fun ragdoll physics. The twist is you have time powers, three in fact. Pause, slow down, and rewind. You are unaffected by the time powers you activate, but everything else? Not so much. It makes for some fun puzzle solving in the game, and adds a nice extra layer to the classic "shoot dude in head" gameplay.
The game looks ok, I also encountered no glitches throughout my playthrough. The only Issue I have with it is the lack of bosses, even the final boss is lack luster, but overall, the experience was satisfying and I certainly recommend it to anyone who's a fan of FPS's.

So, so disappointed. I was very excited about this game; I don't have a lot of money for games and usually only buy them on offer, sub-£5, but I couldn't wait for this game and all the hype I read sounded great.
So I bought it full price and played it through. Whilst I can't deny having some enjoyable times - I was a fan of the way the game seemed to persist when you weren't playing, making a base was enjoyable and some of the missions were fun - I was overall very disappointed and felt kind of cheated by the critic reviews and the game developers. The game was just too easy; it felt as though there were no real challenges and that the game was designed so that everyone could finish it without too much trouble. I don't feel as though I am some elitist gamer; I'm happy that the game can be accessed and enjoyed by players of all skill levels but there really is no reason in the world why a game developer should choose not to include a difficulty setting in the game menu.. unless of course they were selling an expansion pack shortly after release which would advertise 'increased difficulty' as one of its selling points.
I haven't bought the expansion pack out of principle and I stopped playing the game shortly after completion, which really does not take very long at all. I delayed finishing the game until I had completed all the side missions but the main story finishes very quickly - another selling point for the expansion. This feels like a rant, but one of the aspects of reviews which made me most interested was the idea of character permadeath. This turned out to be a huge exaggeration and I didn't lose a single character that wasn't scripted (one). To be fair, I was being careful at first, but before long I was wading into hordes with a golf club and coming out unfazed. There really seemed little need for stealth, which took away much of the gravity and tension of the game.
Aside from that rant, another criticism of the game was the zombies themselves - it felt as though effort had been made to aim the game at a younger audience with cartoony zombies with glowing green eyes. In all, maybe buy it on offer but don't pay more than a fiver for it. Don't expect much and you might have a bit of fun.
Tl;dr: can be fun but purposely designed way too short and way too easy, with no option to adjust difficulty. Also cartoon zombies.

This game is really good for the zombie enthusiast. When it is on sale. While it has a fun, open-world sandbox, there are some things that kept State of Decay from being a smash hit.
#1: No Custom Survivors
If you know enough about editing the game's code files, you could probably in a way make your own survivor, but I really wish that State of Decay would've had something that would've let you, essentially create your own adventure with your own survivors. Customization makes just about any game far more interesting and adds a nice amount of immersion to it, being able to play as and survive as your own creations, create your own story if you will.
#2: The Zombie Spawns are Terrible
This has always been my major complaint with the game. Its mechanics for spawning zombies is atrocious. comparative to a level of DayZ's days on ARMA. Actually that's probably not fair, I think DayZ had an even better system then which was shoddy at best. Nothing is more annoying than clearing off a whole horde of zombies, turning around to get some items from a stash pile, then spinning around and seeing a whole mini-horde spawned in on the area you just cleared out. Very frustrating, especially for hordes that you feel like the game throws in front of you just to spite you and make sure you die. They really should be randomly-generated across the whole map. I know its done the way it is now probably for optimization, but that's just not a good system.
#3: Vehicle Physics are Non-existent
Yep. Your cars in this game are about as light as a feather. The slightest bump in the road at a fast speed will throw you through the air like a tumbling leaf and render your car to nothing more than a noise distraction when it blows up. The vehicles seem to have absolutely no mass or weight, seeming to defy physics. I was taking a back road in Marshal once and, I'm not really sure what happened, I think the rear-end of my vehicle clipped a piece of wreckage and I was shot a good twenty feet into the air, did a few flips, and landed upside-down.

State of Decay brings a new style of gameplay to the zombie game scene, incorporating third person action, RPG and community/resource management into a nice open-world zombie survival game.
In the game, you control a single character at a time and can switch to others when you become friends with them. Each character has their own inventory and stats and traits that may help your community. For example, some survivors might of been a vet or doctor before the outbreak and can use the communities medical supplies more efficiently.
Your community is a collection of survivors who have banded together and found a defendable home to live in, you can upgrade your home base using resources you scavenge in the world and find new survivors to recruit into your community as well as help other established communities and organize resource trades with them.
The game is entirely single player but the developers have tried to give the game a more dynamic feel by making events happen in your game while you’re not playing it. I’m not too sure how I feel about this, it does make things more interesting but I don’t like having that lack of control in a single player game.
Lily, your communities’ radio girl, will advise you about current events and distress signals that are happening in the world. These may include; nearby hordes that need to be wiped out, a survivor in trouble, a community member that needs help with a task, a sighting of an infestation that needs to be dealt with or even a friend at home base that needs help with their depression or anger issues.
While not completing tasks and story missions you will usually find yourself exploring and looking for resources to take back home. Food tends to disappear the quickest, especially when you have a large home population, so building a garden at home or finding a reliable source of food and building an outpost there is a must.
Characters can also specialize in certain fields such as blunt weapons, edged weapons or rifles, etc. Some characters will naturally be better at certain weapons or abilities depending on their traits… the main character I used was an alcoholic and she could not increase her ‘Wits’ stats at all because of that.
Cars are also a big part of the game, after a while of gameplay you will notice that you eventually run out of cars if you don’t start returning them to your home base after you use them. Vehicles can be an amazing zombie killing tool but can get damaged easily after running down a few hordes, so it’s always good to build a proper workshop at home and have a mechanic to repair the good cars you find.
When your community gets too large you will tend to have more problems with survivors not getting along with each other and various mental problems some survivors are having, offenders can be evicted if you don’t feel like having to deal with them and sick or dying people can even be mercy killed before they turn. Finding a bigger and better home is always something that should be on the smart survivalist’s mind when exploring.
The currency of the game is influence and can be spent at community homes to buy items out of their supply locker as well as support while outside of home such as artillery strikes and car delivery. A community with well built facilities will tend to produce more items in their supply locker each day.
When your character dies, you will have to play another character back at home whom you have made friends with – if you have no other player characters you respawn as a new recruit to the community with a few starting items.
My biggest issue with the game would have to be the graphics. It’s not the overall quality that annoys me, but in certain locations with certain lightning I find it very hard to see which was really off-putting for me. I also had quite a few bugs that made my game’s story behave very weird, luckily I was still able to finish it.
The game also has a DLC called ‘Breakdown’ which adds a never-ending gamemode that allows the player a bit more freedom than in the original game, however it should be played after you have finished the main story.
I enjoyed the originality of State of Decay, I felt like I really got attached to the characters I found in the game as well as my own which is rare for a sandbox-type game and I enjoyed being able to play with a community/home management system while also getting to play in an immersive third person action RPG. Unfortunately the graphics were bad enough to make me feel ill at times.

unfortunately, many of the reviews written here give off the wrong impression of read only memories. in fact, they say more about the gaming community than the game itself. ROM is by no means some kind of ham-fisted "tumblr" "sjw" nightmare. what they're trying to say is: "this game is diverse and asked for my pronouns and that made me uncomfortable."
ROM is an obvious love letter to all things cyberpunk, especially
, hideo kojima's underappreciated
, and
. though some unavoidable parallels are drawn between current social issues and those featured in the game, they are hardly ROM's central focus, and the questions it asks are no more offensive than any other cyberpunk work (such as the three i mentioned previously). the writing and characters are consistently entertaining and charming (i love turing so much). the artwork and overall aesthetic is gorgeous, stylish, and detailed. the music is incredibly catchy and groovy and will stick in your head for a while after playing. as far as gameplay goes, if you're a fan of adventure games in the style of
, or maybe even
, you should enjoy ROM. it can feel a bit linear at times, though i know there are a few different endings that depend on your choices throughout the game, but the linearity never really bothered me.
i don't really have many criticisms. ROM can be pretty wordy at times (conversations occasionally carry on longer than necessary, as well as individual pieces of dialogue) and there are some questionable design choices here and there (such as the out-of-place japanese text on some buildings and billboards, which may be there as a reference to its influences). i think my biggest complaint is that the game's length and pacing discourage replay value, which makes achieving multiple endings kind of a chore.
i thoroughly enjoyed it, however. ROM's gameplay and style may not appeal to everyone, but i highly recommend it if what you've seen/heard so far seems like it's up your alley. it's very well-made and clearly had a ton of work put into it, and without a doubt i consider it one of the best games of 2015.

Describing this game as 'a journey of puzzle-solving and exploring' is misleading. ROM plays like a visual novel with very light point-and-click elements.
The highlights of the game are its diverse cast of mostly interesting characters, well written dialogue, and a cool retro-anime aesthetic, that shines despite the lo-fi presentation. The UI is clunky, but serviceable.
ROM’s subtitle promises cyberpunk, but there is very little on offer here. The story is set in the future, it has a big corporation up to no good, and some hacking, but that’s about it. Neo-SF lacks character, it’s a modern day city with some robots as decoration. The social upheaval and strife that’s supposedly happening feels distant.
Despite the criticisms, ROM is worth a playthrough. The 15 € price point is appropriate.

TL;DR: A cyberpunk adventure game that is reminiscent of older games such as Snatcher, while having a well done cast and unique feel all its own.
Read Only Memories really should have more love than its getting. It is a beautifully done adventure game in the vein of older PC-Engine ones such as Snatcher. The story is well done, the choices you make consequential to the various endings and how people react to you. Most importantly, the cast and setting are well done, and left me wanting more media set in the universe it sets up, as you feel the setting is very well fleshed out, and are left wanting more by the bits you hear of the backstory.
While it is probably the least impactful to the actual game experience, lets start with gameplay. The game is displayed in a HUD that pretends to be an in universe computer display. You never see the character you are actually playing, leaving them freely definable (one of the first choices you make after a while is what pronoun you can be called, incluing 'xir'), and moving around consists of switching screens and locations. Interacting with objects is achieved by clicking on them, and choosing to talk/touch/look, or use an item. Notably, you only get an option to use an item if there is some response to it being used, even if it is just text. That alone prevents the rather normal adventure game 'play' issue of 'rub everything on everything to see if it works'. Most play consists of talking to people, investigating surroundings, and the occasional simple puzzle. By simple, I mean its rather logical, without the wierd moon-logic leaps some adventure games take. Your first puzzle is essentially finding a thumb drive, then finding a computer that can read it. There are some more complicated puzzles later on, but nothing that would ever need you to look at a FAQ, and some minor action segments. The game sticks pretty closely to making the game be about the story and characters, not obtuse puzzles.
The story, setting, and characters are clearly the highlight of the game. The cast is varied more so than any other game I have seen, given the setting is a cyberpunk future with DNA-treatments available. The game deals with discrimination against people with cybernetic implants, or genetic therapies that give them animal features (Whether for medical or personal reasons), along with just a general wide variety of people. The game walks that beautiful fine line that so few do, where others might point out 'Look, we included X in our game, aren't we progressive?!' this just introduces you to the characters, and their oddities are part of them, not akwardly bolted on. Noone in the game, other than the one character who could be called the only villain in the story and a faceless corporation, are truly villified. At its heart, it feels like a true noir story, albeit with a journalist instead of a detective. You wander from community to community, investigating while not being a part of it, a sort-of outsider that can choose to react to the various people how you wish, making friends or enemies of differing groups. The setting is well done as well, in that it doesn't throw information at you akwardly, instead you can look at more things to get some more background, and sometimes little tidbits are just mentioned in passing that make it feel more fleshed out because they aren't focused on unnecessarily.
In summation, it is a well done adventure game that focuses more on the story than awkward puzzles, and a beautifully diverse and interesting cast makes it well worth a purchase and play through.

I bought this upon a friends recommendation and have to say, it was worth every cent!
Read Only Memories is a adorable pixel point-and-click adventure with a story that starts out simple enough and becomes both exciting and interesting very fast. If you enjoy games like Ghost Trick, Ace Attorney or the occassional madness of Monkey Island (though not taken to such extremes), then this is an excellent choice!
Here my (spoiler-free) review:
Story:
You live your life barely getting around as a journalist when a cute little bot suddenly appears, asking you to help find a old friend of yours. You agree and meet a lot of interesting people, see what San Fransisco looks like in 2064 and soon become tangled in a plot about self-aware AI, media manipulation and more. Hitting right at the core of todays issues, the world in ROM is believable, relateable and frightingly close to today, taking all of todays events to its logical conclusions and beyond.
Art:
The game is in pixel-style graphic, yet provides quite smooth animations at times. The characters (except for some bots) are all unique and recognizable, the interface is simple and thus easy to navigate and - in stark contrast with a lot of click-and-point games - you rarely have to scan the screen for a teeny tiny object that helps you progress (and even if, all interactable objects get outlines and have a hit box big enough to notice them).
Sound:
The music is jazzy, with a tad of inspiration from Noire detective stories and possibly some inspiration from Ace Attorney music, too. The  beeping sounds from the conversations can be turned off, if found annoying, yet fit this game quite well. The little soundbits that indicate good choices, laughter or similar also keep the conversation sounds from becoming too monotonous.
Gameplay:
A solid click-and-point game which does mostly depend on the player taking the right choices instead of random "Use Can on Christmas Tree to make Phone ring"-logic. While the player has to pick up objects, they rarely are very obscure and even rarer does the player have to use them with something beyond logic (unless finding amusement in the fact that the developers made a lot of interactions unique, thus making it fun to have everything interact with everything for the pure conversations fun).
The main strong point of this game are the many different options that pop up in conversation which can define the amount of information, the relationship the player develops with the character and even the ending. Instead of taking the TellTale Games way of notifying you when you made a relevant decision changing a characters attitude, you have to simply take their reactions for face value though, keeping it realistic and relateable.
Other points that I personally enjoyed a lot:
The developers spend a lot of time in thinking about the world they created. Simply looking at objects, reading the media outlets or talking to Turing will show the amount of work that went into the history between today and the games setting, from world wide conflicts over technology advances to even something like city development. While not necessarily relevant to the plot (its possible to get through the game without knowing anything about the world itself), it shows the love the developers put into the game as well as help understanding the characters that live in it.
Another quite interesting point about this game is that it is really revolutionary in its treatment of sexuality and gender expression. The player is allowed to be whatever they want and get confronted with multiple characters that identify in ways that society might frown upon (such as a lady with beard or a gender-ambigous character enjoying being referenced to as "they"). One can also find one gay couple as well as hints to at least two more, though the latter can differ based on the characters gender expression and the path of conversation leading to the characters being more or less intimate. It never is a actual story point, it is only mentioned with handwaves instead of making it extremely obvious, giving off a very natural and unforced feeling of people like that being the norm, especially since no character (including the player) sees any of it out of the ordinary.
The game further raises interesting questions for today as it deals heavily with racism, even though the aim shifted from non-colored/colored people to 'modificated' people and AI, explaining that discrimminating is apparently in the nature of humans and has to be constantly battled against.
Summary:
Read Only Memory is a fun game that starts out light-hearted and soon dives deep into topics about humanity, conscience and media control. It proves to be a world logical in itself with a strong foundation in todays world and with strong characters that are easy to remember and love/hate. With a good sense of humour, a lot of hidden jokes for meme and videogame fans, an interesting story and dark turns around every corner, it will give you a gaming experience in the wake of Ghost Trick and Professor Layton, all mixed with some nice flair of Film Noir and Shadowrun.
Wether you want to try and talk to cars, put your fingerprints on every window in the city or make all characters hate you to the bone, this game allows it all and makes you love it for what it is.
Can you find the culprit behind your friends disappearance? Will you unleash the secret that caused all the trouble to begin with? And can you become friends with a machine that tries to be human? ROM asks all these questions, you have to find the answers.

is a Action Role-Playing Game heavily pushing a co-op experience.
I would say the weakest part of the game, other than some of the technical issues that some people still experience (see technical) - would be the story. It's a very quick and short tale that leaves a lot to the imagination. I'm not saying it's bad; simply shallow. If  your goal is to find a rich story - you will not find it here.
All players have the option to play one of four classes which are determined in the entrance room to each trial room. It is also good to note that no matter the decision of the class; in most cases you will have healing spells, damage spells, and defensive spells of some kind. Other than the inherit differences between melee and ranged; the developers have done a good job at keeping most everything balanced. The true co-op experience comes into play before anyone even enters a trial; deciding who will have which spell to counter the trial mechanics. This is an element that most co-op games don't have.
Once your skills and class has been chosen - per challenge - you will face 25 trials with increasing difficulty. As one may expect the game starts out in a tutorial manner, teaching players how to navigate the trial and use new mechanics. Balfus (your spirit guide) is an integral part of the gameplay, requiring players to move him to destroy shrines or statues, light the path, assist in damage dealing, or in some trials - used against you!The primary game play is to complete objectives which range from killing monsters, finding the end of a maze, or simply lighting shrines. As a side note I wouldn't say this is necessarily a game with heavy puzzle elements; however there is a degree of puzzle solving.
If you plan on being a completionist, to get all 75 crystals and all achievements, expect to spend some time on this game. At the time of this writing I have completed all achievements in roughly 24 hours of gameplay. Most challenges took my team 1-10 tries; the challenge on the last boss took us roughly 4 hours. If you plan on simply completing the trials to have the experience to play - expect at best half of that. I would not recommend this game if you want to just play single player - this is a game best experienced with friends. Disclaimer: Your mileage my vary, every gamer and team is different you could see significantly less or more gameplay.
I have to peck at the game a bit on this level; there are still a few issues with networking that the developers are actively working on. In addition the game is poorly optimized in terms of graphics use. A lot of the options to effectively reduce load on a computers GPU is non-existant. My system with a GTX570 runs this game fine, but quite hot in comparison to other games with a much higher expectation (100% load in some areas running 70c+). I assume as the game matures further, the developers will continue solving some of the technical issues that some players are reporting as problems; they did not effect my team as much as some but it is important to note that they could come up. Edit: Graphics have been optimized and it's running much better on modern hardware.

I've been playing fighting games for the best part of two decades now and this is by far the most rewarding fg to play. Unlike many games aimed towards the casual player this is designed for the dedicated player who is willing to spend years to learn the in depth game mechanics.

Cons (Since 1.04 Patch):
Ever since the steam transition from the now defunct GFWL, this game hasn't been the same, in terms of online play. Connections are still somewhat inconsistent despite the 1.04 patch, the bars play tricks on you sometimes (green bar really being an orange, vice versa... you get the picture), 1/5 players will rage quit or use some variation of lag switching, spontaneous "disconnects from steam" during matches cause you to lose an absurd amount of points (no longer happens very often after 1.04 patch), aggravating screen freezing/lag while searching for matches/navigating main menu/training mode with fight request (still is happening to me after 1.04 patch, but not for others, seems to be a system specific problem, but I can't find a solution. This never used to happen on GFWL)
Pros (Since 1.04 patch):
Edition Select + Omega mode being playable online makes the game a hell of a lot more fun to play.
Since this is PC, mods for everything are extremely easy to install and raise the replayability of the game by a significant amount, especially if you've been on the 4 series since vanilla.
Lots of mod costumes, hud and other aesthetic mods, custom music, menu art mods... need i say more?
VERDICT - If you're looking for competitive online play, xbox360 is the best platform. PC version is only worth it if you buy during a steam sale, and if you're looking to play the game for fun, with all it's modding glory.

If you replace all the parts of an object one at a time, at what point does it cease to be that object?
Does it ever stop being that object? If so, what happens to the original? If not, what would the old pieces form?
What is there to stop a computer from emulating all the neural impulses that form our thoughts and memories?
Would resulting intelligence be self-aware, or just an indistinguishable fake?
What differentiates an indistinguishable fake from the real thing?
Something tangible? Intangible? If no-one can tell the difference, does it even matter?
Lucy is a visual novel that differs from others in that it chooses to delve deeper into some of the moral, ethical, and philosophical issues that would arise from the existence of Artificial Intelligence, rather than the scenario or events surrounding it. The story is focused around a high school student who finds an advanced android discarded in a junkyard, his changing thought process, and the conflicts he faces with his beliefs, emotions, and family upon deciding to take it in.
What made this novel stand out to me is that I felt it was something that encourages the player to form, challenge, or change their opinions and beliefs on issues that are surprisingly relevant to what technology will achieve in our lifetime. Even if these are things you have never considered before, Lucy is far more thought-provoking of an experience than simply going along for the ride with the average book or movie.
The music and voice-acting I found to be both very relaxing, and while not as long as something like Fate/stay night, Lucy felt like the perfect length for what it had to offer, and not once could I say it felt like the story was dragging out or full of unnecessary filler. For most people who play these sorts of games I imagine you could complete the game in around three or four sittings, but even if you take a more casual approach Lucy is not something that needs to be rushed. Take your time and enjoy what it has to offer; hopefully you can enjoy the story to its fullest and give this game the appreciation it deserves.
I would buy this game again in a heartbeat, and I hope I've convinced you to give it a chance too. You won't be sorry you did.

A current trend in the gaming industry, both AAA and otherwise - is to make games try and appeal and be accessible to as large an audience as possible, partly to secure profit margins and partly under the misguided notion that the broader a game's sphere of influence, the better the game is. Strike Vector is in short, a large triumphant middle finger to that notion. Strike Vector is a niche shooter and is bloody well proud of it. Existing in the 6DoF subgenre, it is a brutally-demanding multiplayer arena shooter that subscribes to old school PC gaming multiplayer-standards as opposed to the matchmaking and progression systems of current games. All weapons and other loadout modifications are unlocked straight away, and there is only a straightforward server browser, meaning that anyone can play against anyone else, regardless of their skill level.
This coupled with the sky-high skill floor of Strike Vector are the main two aspects that make most people refuse to give this game a chance. New players tend to get their asses handed to them very quickly, and only those dedicated enough to put up with the harsh first few hours of play will get any considerable enjoyment from the game; however, those who do manage to ascend the skill floor will find themselves playing an extremely fast, fluid and visceral shooter with a great variety of loadouts, maps, gametypes and veteran players to play against. The matter of fact is that even though detractors claim that this game is dead, it really is not if you are willing to look. There is a small but dedicated community willing to keep this game alive and kicking despite all odds (at least on saturdays).
One of the reasons why this game is so great is because of what I can only describe as "game feel". The speed certainly contributes to this but it is other factors such as great sound design, visceral gunplay and the fact that the player's ship is relatively small, meaning that you can manuever through almost any gaps in the maps, resulting in some great high-speed chases. The movement is made just as fun as the shooting because of this, and it is the main reason why in my opinion, this game trumps similar games such as Strike Suit Zero, where the player's hitboxes just feel way too big relative to the geometry you should be able to manuever through.
This is just the tip of the iceberg too, there are so many little nuances to each of the weapons that even I, who has played 100 hours feel like I still have a LOT to learn and uncover, and I still haven't tried a lot of the available loadouts and playstyles.
These nuances are not perfect though, it does have to be mentioned that Strike Vector is a flawed game in spite of all of its strengths. First and foremost, the server population is indeed low. It seems unfair to blame this on the game, but regardless it is something that can greatly detract from the enjoyment of the game, especially if you are a newer player. Secondly, the weapon balance is not exactly perfect. Most weapons are situational, and are better on some maps than others, but there are certain almost-gamebreaking combinations that can kill the flow of the gameplay, such as dual gatlings with the firerate and range perks, the area of engagement is just too large compared to more situational weapons such as the LMG and swarm missiles. Finally, there is no real means of new players to train for the onslaught they will receive in multiplayer. The in-game tutorial is very rudimentary, and the only single player modes are free flight through the maps on your own, or a few time trials mostly involving shooting near-stationary targets and flying through rings. These can train your movement and accuracy to an extent but not nearly as much as bot matches would, which could also be fun for both newcomers and veterans with the right difficulty configurations. All in all, the shortcomings are clearly prevalent but are not enough to ruin the fundamental fun and good-design at the core of the game's mechanics.
Despite what you've likely been told, it is okay for games to target a niche, instead of going for mass-market appeal and Strike Vector shows that sometimes some of the best games can be made by adopting this attitude. It is true that the game is lacking in server population, and if you are at all interested in this game, you will have to prepare to receive a lot of asskickings and do a lot of reading to have fun, but if you do partake in this, it will almost be certainly worth it when you are able to play alongside veteran players.

What can I say other than the fact that this game is an absolute gem! I waited impatiently for it to come to the PC after reading about it on the 360 - so I jumped at the chance to play it as soon as it came to Early Access (a perfect use of that system too by the way, the game was perfectly playable and only needed a few months to get keyboard support going and to get it properly optimised)
Anyway, the game itself is basic but extremely satisfying for the the cost and the fact that is by no means a AAA title. You start out coming back from some hiking trip, there a zombies everywhere, shizzle goes down and you get contacted by some survivors. From there you are pretty much free to raid the towns, camp sites, farms, trailer parks and just about everything else for resoucres to help maintain moral at your base (which you can move around from a church, to houses, a fairground, a warehouse...), make trades with other groups and upgrade your base and make a few helpful trinkets (molotovs, silencers and whatnot)  A minor irritation to me was everyone will speak to you as if you were the same person no matter which survivor you switch to, but it's not that much of a bother as generally you'll build up a preference for one or two of them you'll end up only using anyway! And that's the other thing - you pour time and effort into survivors, build up imaginary details about their lives (They are relativly bland in the ingame story, but give just enough to get a hint of personality in most cases) only to then slip up and be eaten alive - and it's over. Yep, it's perma-death, you're gonna have to find a new favorite because there's no going back when you loose a survivor. And that's it really, the story is decent, may be a little weak if it was AAA but it's not - it's a cheap zombie survival game that most AAA games could only wish to be (I'm looking at you Dead Island!) For the most part graphics are rather nice here on PC, the animations are pretty basic but completly forgivable. The fighting and sneaking mechanics are solid too. It make you fill in most of the story gaps and lets you create your own attachment to the characters as you wish through the threat of losing time and effort put into each person.
If you essentially want the closest possible thing to a real "The Walking Dead: The Game" this is it!

Like alot of Sonic fans right now, I've been playing tons of Sonic Mania and feeling like a child again, loving every second of the original levels as well as the reimagined classics, after a while I began thinking, I don't play Sonic CD that much and I really should, it's just like the original games, yet I don't seem to go back to it often, so I decided to go through another playthrough recently and well, "Debatably the best Sonic game ever made." is something I often hear when Sonic CD is mentioned, I admit I don't agree with that statement, but I do understand why people would claim it as such.
To briefly touch on Sonic CDs history for a second we have to go back to the 90s, when Sega were trying to make the most out of an unfortunate situation with it's lackluster Sega CD addon for the Genesis/Mega Drive, the technology it sold itself on simply was just too young, the system needed a game, much like the Genesis needed itself when it launched.
After the success of Sonic The Hedgehog 1, Yuji Naka had grown tired of Sega of Japan looking over his shoulder and had taken a good portion of the team to Sega of America (also known as Sega Technical Institute) where they would later work on what would become Sonic The Hedgehog 2, this left co-creator Naoto Ohshima and the remainder of the original team still based in Japan to work on their own Sonic 2.
Sega of Japan's product would ultimately become Sonic CD, built for the system in order to make the absolute most potential out of it's assets, CGI in-game movies, CD quality music and large disc space.
The Sega CD went down under regardless along with the ill-fated Sega 32x addon, but that didn't stop Sonic CD claiming its spot of legacy among the classic Sonic games. Sonic CD would go on to be universally praised regardless of the Sega CDs poor state, the only way people could of played Sonic CD was either through the Sega CD itself, an early pc port in 1996, through Sonic Gems Collection, emulators or the JVC X'EYE.
Thankfully in comes Christian Whitehead, now a beloved developer among the Sonic community, before contracted to work on Sonic Mania, this enhanced Sonic CD port was actually his first ever involvement with Sega, rebuilt from the ground up, Whiteheads version is the definitive Sonic CD experience, super smooth framerate, no collision detection issues, all hitboxes improved and all players now have access to both soundtracks released for the game, more on that later.
So now the plot, our beloved blue hedgehog has traveled to a mystical river called Never lake, where a large world known simply as Little Planet has made its yearly apperance. The sinister Dr Eggman intends to transform Little Planet into a giant mechanical fortress, alongside creating Metal Sonic and kidnapping self-proclaimed blue hedgehog girlfriend Amy Rose, Eggman plans to obtain the 7 Time Stones home to Little Planet to allow passage through time travel. As Sonic it is up to you to travel through all of the games zones, defeat Eggman in whatever contraption he has built for the 3rd acts boss, obtain the Time Stones, rescue Amy and save Little Planet.
To quote another steam reviewer, the best word to describe the experience that Sonic CD offers to fans and newcomers to the series is "Unauthodox", as early as Palmtree Panic you will notice the verticality and width all the stages Sonic CD has to offer, the bizarre platforms, the obsurdist gimmicks, the time traveling element and even the enemy designs and boss battles are as wacky as they are creative.
I'm not kidding, watch Green Hill act 1, Emerald Hill act 1 and Palmtree Panic act 1 side by side and you'll notice it, one is clearly not like the others, but that helps make Sonic CD one of the more unique experiences of the classical formula that so many of us had grown up with. Abstract, intricate yet also allowing for the core momemtum based platforming are brief descriptions of the level design in Sonic CD.
Your ultimate goal in Sonic CD revolves around the time element the game introduces, throughout each zone are posts that read Past and Future, if you can maintain high speed long enough after touching a post, you'll be sent to the corrosponding era, you are to destroy all robot generators in the past to create good futures for every act in the game, if this doesnt sound like your cup of tea, then there is always the traditional sense of collecting the Time Stones by getting 50 rings and jumping into the giant ring at the end of the stage and completing the special stage, which when all 7 are obtained, automaticly create good futures for every zone in the game.
This is one of my favourite things about Sonic CD, except for Sonic 3 and Ks ending (and maybe Sonic 1 even though it's miniscule), CD reacts to your actions throughout the game, depending on what you do in every act determines what happens in it's future and I have to say, getting good futures feels so rewarding, the game shows you the effects of your actions and you feel like patting yourself on the pack saying "Yeah, I did this!" and it's a wonderful feeling, you are the difference between Palmtree Panic becoming a polluted mechanical unsustanable landmass or a tropical healthy landscape, the difference between Metallic Madness becoming a vile rusty fortress of maliciousness or an enviromentally friendly utopia.
It'll be hard for you not to move to the music while playing, but this is an interesting topic, as mentioned there are two soundtracks for Sonic CD, one for Japan and Europe, and an entirely redone one for America, both versions of the OST are vastly different, the Jap/Pal version is much more lively and energetic while the American version goes for a more atmospheric and synergestic feel and there isnt much information as to why this is, if I had to guess, I imagine when Sonic CD was shipped over to America, they had believed the Japanese soundtrack was quite similiar to Micheal Jackons musical style who they were trying to distance themselves from after his scandals became public while MJ was working on the soundtrack for the then in development Sonic The Hedgehog 3.
To better understand the drastic differences, see these links of both tracks for Palmtree Panic present:
JP:
US:
Sonic games are generally considered to have great Soundtracks and CD delivers in spades, but it's definately much more varied here due to...well reasons, on which soundtrack you believe is the better version comes down to preference, personally I'm for the Japanese soundtrack, personal favourites being Palmtree Panic, Stardust Speedway and Metallic Madness.
I've definately grown an appreciation for Sonic CD over the years and do wish I would return to it as often as I do the other classic games, I do recommend Sonic CD to anyone whom is interested, definately the most unauthodox of the series and none the less a great game in it's own right.

Dragons Dogma is a lot like many other open world RPGs. It has the large monster action of Monster Hunter, The sense of adventure and scope of Skyrim and the oppressive brooding dungeons of Dark Souls. Yet despite it's similarities it is something completely unto itself.  For one it's Pawn system allows the player to create his or her own ragtag group of misfits as you run around the world, killing monsters, doing quests or crafting items. And while most of the time they seem mostly brain dead they are a great help in the most brutal of fights. And boy what wonderful fights Dragons Dogma will give you. Every turn around uncharted land gives it a new sense of excitement as you battle everything from Goblins, Bandits, The Undead or a Part Snake, Part Goat, Part Lion Chimeras. Just when you think you've seen it all the game will throw you new challenges, enemies and surprises that freshen up even the most basic of encounters. As well as a fantastic Character Class system that makes learning from scratch on new weapons and skills actually exciting and fun.
The game is a somewhat unpolished gem however. A decent fast travel system doesn't come until ways in, leading to lots of tedious running around. Also the game's lack of handholding can be overwhelming for the first few hours, as you struggle to find out what quests are too high level for you and how the abundance of systems the game run on work.  This a game that will take a while to appreciate. But once everything comes together it's something truly special. You might have played countless RPGs but I promise you that none of those will offer you the surprises and thrills that Dogma can offer you.

This one is a newp. Probably one of the worst games i've played in the recent years.
The environments are nice, reminds me of the Gothic series, the world is pretty large. But that's about the only positive thing i've got to say about it. Combat is... acceptable, provided you are at least 50% overleveled and don't mind the fact that 80% of bow skills are useless, and that any melee class dies in seconds. Magic was ok.
You HAVE to play with a full party of dumb-AI pawns if you want to get anywhere in life. Ok you don't HAVE to, but then your 5 min troll battles will probably become 25 minute troll battles. And 5 minutes for a respawning enemy is already more than what i'm willing to spend.
Fast travel system is nonexistent for a large portion of the beginning. Then after that it's incredibly sparse. You have to keep running through the same areas back and forth, on foot, to get pretty much anywhere, with depleting stamina. Then you have to wait for that stamina to replenish.
Large enemies have "levels" of health, meaning - you get the health bar down to 0 - and then the bar replenishes anew. Then you notice there are dots near the health bar. So you have to deplete the health once for every dot. Wtf is the point of this repetitive grind? And the enemies respawn too. So you walk down the path, fight the stupid troll with 3 health bars for 5 minutes, then 30 minutes later return down this path - and the f*ker is there again!
I think this game was designed to waste as much of your time as possible, without actually teaching you anything new.
If you love being DPS for WoW or FF or whatever raid bosses, and would love to be doing this in single player with horrible-AI party instead of real people - you'll probably love this. You do about the same level of insignificant amount of damage to big guys, so you're basically just spamming the one or two attacks for 5 minutes, periodically changing your position. That's about it.
Yes, there are plenty of battles with smaller guys, but those take so much less effort, and the big guys are so much more painful, that the bad times are all i remember.
Oh, and half the quests are straight out of WoW - "kill 50 boars!" "kill 50 rabbits!" "kill 50 zombies!".
And why on earth are there only 5 different skins for gatherable plants, but 50 different varieties? Was it really that difficult to at least change the color of the flowers or something?

Yes hello, this is Dragon's Dogma, a game about a main character and his army of little girls.
You play as a the Arisen, the person in his village with the largest set of testicles. One day, a giant dragon named Greg attacks his village and starts burning things, so you decide to attack Greg head on even though you're a three foot tall goblin.
Greg beats you up and then steals your heart, making you the Arisen. So you weren't the Arisen before, but you are now. Enjoy not having a heart.
Dragon's Dogma is an action RPG set in the surprisingly small country of Gransys. Outside of combat and exploration there's a big emphasis on custom characters known as Pawns. Pawns are basically emotionless homunculi created by the Arisen to work as a companion character. While you create a pawn for yourself, you can also pick up two more pawns as party members either made by the game itself or made by other players if you're playing online. It's kind of neat just how in depth the pawn system is, but you more often than not end up with a party of little girls.
Pawn population is like, 90% little girls, you're basically a glorified day home employee. A day home employee that murders monsters.
The combat in Dragon's Dogma is really top notch, with a huge emphasis on weight and impact. Every weapon feels good to use, while daggers are about cutting and slashing as much as possible, something like a great sword is more about sending fools flying and crushing through armor.
Each class has a role to play on the battlefield, and all of it feels amazing to use, from Legolas style archers to great sword wielding giants to super wizards that can summon a tornado and the disappointment of the enemies parents.
But this is just for normal encounters with human sized enemies, the game can actually get pretty perilous with what you fight. There are giant enemies such as ogres, cyclops, griffins, your mom, and cockatrices. There are flying creatures like birds with boobs, there are necromancers that can resurrect the dead, and there are even♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ogres. A lot of these enemies you have to climb to kill, and you can even trick them like getting a cyclops to remove its own helmet trying to get you off and things like that.
There are also smaller baby dragons like Drakes, wyverns, and wyrms, who all speak Latin at you before beating you up.
The amount of enemies in this game is actually kind of astounding, and the tools they give you to deal with them is just as numerous. Like magic the enemy is weak to, or the arc of deliverance, which is basically an atom bomb in sword form.
The developers went out of their way to make everything feel grand and epic in combat. Every attack looks like it hurts, every enemy encounter is an event, and every giant monster may as well be a boss in it's own right.
Did I spend enough time saying good things about the game? Okay good, cause I'm going to complain like a little girl now.
You know for something that's advertised as an epic adventure, Gransys is kind of...Lame.
There really isn't much to see outside of random encounters, it doesn't really feel like a place people actually live. Outside of the starting town, a monastery, and Gran Soren, there really isn't much to see. Everything else is either a tent, an abandoned fortress, or some kind of bandit hideout. Pretty much 95% of all of Gransys are bandits, which must be a very lucrative career.
But since most people live inside Gran Soren, who do they rob? Do they rob each other? Is there a circular bandit economy where they just rob gold back from one another?
I can imagine a few outlaw groups roaming around, but these guys are a standing army, they could probably attack Gran Soren and win.
That and Gransys is just kind of dinky. Mixed with nothing really to see save for a few spots, you spend a lot of time just looking at trees or tents. It takes about thirty or so minutes to get from one side to the other, and in that time you've seen basically just a few tents and an abandoned building with nothing in it. Sometimes you get lucky and a big idiot bird lion harasses you,  or a lion and his goat and snake friends who like one another a little too much.
The most exciting adventure is usually going to Blue moon tower, considering it's like Tatooine but with swords. But even then you end up going there like five or so times so that's also annoying.
Throughout the entire game I felt like I was trapped in a tutorial area, or a starting zone for any other RPG. At the very least they give you teleporting items to get around easier later in the game.
Dark Arisen kind of helps with the tedium with a more focused and well put together dungeon, but that will only last you about two hours or so, more if you
I ended up looking a lot into this game because of just how unfinished it felt. Turns out I was right, there were entire areas of the game cut out to make deadline, and by entire areas I mean most areas. There was even supposed to be a journey to the moon at one point, as well as other races such as elves and beast people that you could meet in your journey.
Other things happened like a cut in funding, and at one point developers from Dragon's Dogma had to be pulled away to fix the combat in DmC when they were still making that.
Way to go, Tameem.
Capcom could have had something really, REALLY groundbreaking, but they decided that they wanted it out the door. Its kind of sad, considering how special the game is, how many other games out there let you take down one of the hardest bosses by lighting yourself on fire and latching on to him?
The Pawns also kind of wear on you. Even with all the customization options they're still basically the same, with the same lines of dialogue and quips. Maybe if they let us pick an archetype and then customize that character instead of a pawn. There's even an option to shut them up completely, making your entire journey basically silent.
That being said, it's still a pretty good game for at least one play through. While the adventuring itself may get boring, the combat makes up for it. There are people that can  play this game forever, but I'm not really one of those people. If you can get it on sale, then I say go for it.

Besides having 9 different classes with skills that carry between them, the amount of equipment that can be used by these classes to make a really unique character is overwhelming. While the upgrading of equipment requires some Monster Hunter gameplay (kill enemies to get resources to upgrade weapons to kill more enemies; rinse and repeat), the combat helps to brighten up this repetitive endeavor. From striking the legs of an ogre to drop it to its knees and attack its head, to climbing a griffin to light in on fire so it can't fly away, the maneuvers allowed by the games mechanics bring a lot of variability to every situation. Careful planning and a well thought out team is required to easily beat this game, but it's been fun nonetheless.
