This is a medieval game from capcom set in the medieval realm of gransis. First of, I actually wanted to buy dragons age and bought this by accident, but I had so much fun playing it, that I just couldn't stop anymore. It's really a great game, the setting is wonderful, capcom made a great job capturing the medieval architecture of middle europe in the 12th century.
Gameplay: The fighting style is a lot of fun, while staying realistic. So you're not playing some half demon who can lift a greatsword like a feather, which makes the game so much more immersive and fun to play. There're nine classes, these basically divide themselves in the items you can use and some abilities. Leveling up is much less a deal than in european dragon games. The playstyle alltogether resembles the one in gothic or gothic 2. You kill creatures, grow stronger, kill stronger creatures.
There's no much character specialization, you're character won't be any different skillwise than that of thousand other players. The item's however can be upgraded 6 times and it is fun to go out and kill monsters to get the necesary ingrediants.
The character creation is great in terms of aesthetics. You can create your very own supermodel and even set the muscles of your character. And women with abs do look prettier than I thought, try it out.
The technic of the game is very nostalgic which I like, but most players won't like it. It basically looks like one of these old gothic games with blurry textures and some stiff animations.
Also the narration of the game is different from what you would expect from a dragon game. Basically, there's no big narration with many choices and lots of characters. There's only the capital which is filled with some people and a tiny village, so you won't be part of any guilds like in skyrim and there isn't any dialog. Most options are do it or don't do it.
Capcom did a great job on that one.

I had pre-access to this game but unfortunately Steam hasn’t recorded my full gameplay time! But that a side when you play FullBlast if like me, you will almost have a surge of memories stretching back to those old classical vertical shooters especially from the 80’s and this game is a nostalgic throwback to those days spending your pocket money on Arcade Machines. In the 90’s my games library was taken up with vertical shooters as I made my way through the 16-bit era so I have had some good and bad experiences and went through a fair amount of controllers!
Now the first thing to understand about FullBlast is it isn’t going to suddenly change the genre in any spectacular way but what it does do is update it in a way that makes it a pleasure to play without the sudden impulse of throwing your controller at the screen. You pilot an aircraft shooting at the hordes of alien, insect and plant like foes through 12 challenging areas!
I got through the first three stages with ease but then suddenly noticed the game crank up a gear with bigger threats along the way not to mention the area boss fights, where certain encounters move the game to a rotational perspective all though not new it’s something I haven’t seen in a lot of shooters to date.
FullBlast doesn’t bring anything radically new to the table, but in my opinion it really is a well polished modern styled 3D addictive vertical shooter with the great addition of co-op which seems to be an inclusion that a lot of similar titles leave out! My only complaint is I would have preferred a wider range of weapons!
For the price you will literally have a blast with this game (pun intended) With 12 areas and 3 levels of difficulty, a solid rock soundtrack that does a good job of keeping in with the momentum of the game. It will happily test your reflexes and I think UFO Crash Games have found a sweet spot where games like this are far and few between lately.
It really is a no brainer for gamers who have enjoyed the old classics like Terra Cresta, Air Gallet and Gunbird and are happy to enjoy a little nostalgia on the way! I have added a video of my First Playthrough to give you an idea of what to expect from this great little Indie title!

One of the retro RPG games quite similar to Dragon age Origins. You command created character (you) that travels through the world to uncover deep mystery. While doing so you do many side quest and tasks and find (or create) other companions. You can go with up to 5 another champions in your adventure party (total party size is 6) while others take care of your keep which you are repairing from by enemies infested ruin to glorious castle.
>> Pros
+ Deep characters system (stats, classes, etc.). You even develop reputations (like honest, diplomatic or aggressive) by way you interact with NPCs.
+ Way you created and developped your character is reflected in conversation choices available to you. This means if you create different type of character you can have different experience while playing again.
+ Story is strong and well told.
+ Combat feels balanced and rewarding.
+ Graphics is simple yet nice with no extreme hardware requirements so you can play it on notebook.
+ No internet connection required for play.
+ Several difficulty settings that can be combined. It is not just basically divided into easy->hard options but you can turn on or off several difficulty features as well.
>> Cons
- Sometimes too many text to read.
- Only few texts are voiced (some texts are only part voiced which feels really strange).
- Extremely stupid AI of both your companions and opponents in combat. Characters stucking when available path is just next to them, going somewhere for no reason or just staying idle while few meters away there is battle is shamefully frequnt.
- Poor auto management of characters automatic behaviour in combat. You can't tell what abilities your character can use like in Dragon Age but you can only pick template like "Aggresive" or "Support" which mostly doesn't meet your expectations and you are forced to handle all champions yourself, which is exhausting after several time.
If you like to care mostly only your character, 2 last points above are really irritating. If you like to manage all your champions yourself they hardly matter.
>> Pros or Cons? (depends on your personal taste)
o No free world. You have system of little maps connected by their borders. In the end there is very little of true exploration because on every piece of living space there is something.
o Nothing hold your hand in terms of quests means no arrows, question marks or explamation marks. You must find your quests by talking NPCs around and if you wish to not miss any you need to talk them all through. It's similar to Divinity Original Sin.
o I personally found crafting useless except enhancing weapons which is exact opposite and is necessary.
If you like those types of RPGs it is a good choice. If you like retro type games (no hand holding) do not hesitate a second, you will love it. It is not game for everyone though as it may seem slow and boring for modern type gamers used to Diablo 3 or Dragon Age Inquisition like games.

Game was mediocre. Unfortunately the Splinter Cell series will not go back to it's main roots of SC, SC:PT, and Chaos Theory. This was a good step in the right direction as Conviction was pretty muched a SC skin of 24 (or any typical action drama show).

Been a huge fan of the series since the first Splinter Cell and I don't think we are going to get anything close to it.

The Splinter Cell series are some of the most unique stealth element games. From the same developers who brought you the Assassins Creed series, Splinter Cell is more futuristic-based and incorporates high-tech gadgets as well as advanced firearms. It has introduced more and more new stuff since the first game, and Blacklist is where the pinnacle is at.
Nearly all the different weapons you get can be customized differently to suit your play style. Speaking of play style, Blacklist actually "rates" you based on your play style for every mission. Go full stealth and make as little contact as possible while using only non-lethal methods to deal with hostiles, or be a silent but ruthless killer and leave a trail of death behind you without alerting an entire army. Or you can run in guns blazing and take them head on.
However you choose to play it, Blacklist still incorporates a user-friendly interface. A lot has changed since Splinter Cell: Conviction, yet familiarity remains. Some short tutorials in the first two missions will get Conviction players and new Splinter Cell players alike familiarized with the controls quickly.
The graphics are amazing. On a powerful machine with full settings, it feels like you're watching a live-action movie in cinema. Couple that with the decent sounds, and Blacklist is basically an interactive movie where you get to determine the action that takes place.
The thing about Blacklist is that it does not seem to have a randomization element. Every mission, whether main story or side missions, remains the same every time you start one. Once you have played enough times and grind the same mission over and over again, it actually becomes a "routine". Hostiles will appear and patrol the same few points every single time, unless you disrupt the process by causing trouble of course, but on a full stealth run, it never happens. Very quickly can veteran players do speed runs. Sure, there may be many different methods or paths to complete a mission, but all directions will eventually lead to one destination.
So when the campaign gets tedious, you get to play online in cooperative missions. Much like Conviction, the cooperative campaign features a side story that actually connects to the main story, so this one thing you will miss if you don't have multiplayer capabilities.
When missions get boring, then it is time for some PvP. Blacklist brings back the classic Spies Vs. Mercenaries matches. Although I personally seldom play PvP, I've tried it out and it's not too bad. But don't take my word for it, check out comments from avid PvP players.
Overall, Blacklist is definitely recommended. It's a game that you won't get bored of in a short period of time. It's also fun to compare your playthrough with those of other players and share your tactics.

A charming retrofuturistic romp, packed with cute jokes and adorable graphics in a vividly imagined post-cyberpunk San Francisco that feels both near and strange.
With point-and-click adventures, there's always a fine balance to strike in terms of difficulty. The scavenger hunt-style puzzles here are too eager to hold the player's hand, though there are some decent logic puzzles to break up the rhythm. But winning the game isn't as important as how your choices shape the story, which maintains its light tone throughout (excepting an occasional tonal swerve into some legitimately creepy horror). Multiple endings are possible. The autosave system is unforgiving, so make frequent use of the manual save system in case you want to rethink a decision or take another stab at a puzzle.
The cast is appropriately large and diverse for a whodunnit, and mostly personable. Special mention should be made of Lexi Rivers. A hardboiled police detective with a great, distinctive design, she's definitely the game's MVP and could star in her own noir spin-off.
An entertaining indy game. Recommended for fans of cyberpunk, nostalgia, and point-and-clicks. Try the demo to whet your appetite.

I've been following Read Only Memories for a year before it was released, and once it was released I was not disappointed.
ROM is a point and click adventure / visual novel set in a near-futuristic Neo San Francisco.  Beginning the game as a starving journalist, you are inevitably thrust upon a huge investigation which includes many dialogue choices, puzzles, and a few mini games here and about.  At its core, the mechanics don't bring many new additions to this type of game, but hold up, it gets a lot of it right.
Don't let the faux retro graphics make you think it's a pull at your nostalgia, all of the environments, characters, and even the menus ooze with a techy, 80s like cyberpunk style which breathes a lot of life and character into the game.  The soundtrack (I recommend purchasing it!) and audio fit the theme of the game greatly.  You control the game with a mouse and keyboard or you can opt for a controller (Xbox 360 controller works great with no configuration).  The biggest plus of this game is its story.  There are a group of varied and genuinely interesting cast of characters that really helps pull the story along.  The writing is quite fantastic.  ROM illustrates a believable near future with funny dialogue that'll elicit a sensible chuckle and smart writing that keeps you gripped for the length of the game.
Read Only Memories is a solid tech noir point and click that has great accessibility to anyone who wants an enjoyable story, memorable characters, and thought provoking themes that the game explores well.

Read Only Memories draws its most obvious inspiration from Snatcher, although you can see hints of other works peppered throughout, and truly dedicated folks will uncover a wealth of one-off references and in-jokes that reward the attentive without making anyone not in on the reference feeling lost. It benefits from an incredibly well-written script and a beautiful aesthetic that pulled me in and kept me engaged in spite of what I felt were significant gameplay flaws.
The broad cast of characters is skillfully written to the point where even with a few lines you can really get a sense of the personality behind each character as you're introduced to them. Everyone has a slightly different motivation in helping you out, and their helpfulness is a reflection of those feelings. Regardless of what they may feel for you, the protagonist, appealing to characters' own interests means you're able to cobble together a shaky alliance from people that initially seemed unapproachable or unwilling to help. If there is one weakness in the game it is the highly diminished sense of agency that the game provides; while our protagonist can be highly customized, the choices we make at the beginning of the game have little bearing on the in-game world, creating a few callbacks at best. The player's agency only really shines through on occasion through interaction with Turing; who is inarguably the true main character of the story. It left me feeling detached from the situation -- I wanted the outcome for Turing to be the best possible, and yet the dialogue choices felt not quite right for how I might address the character, and their will made it difficult if not impossible to determine whether I was helping at all. I think this is a good narrative point -- in the game as in life we aren't really able to fundamentally alter the people we associate with, but we can at least hope to be important to them and act as a foil for their own growth.
The gameplay is fairly straightforward but enjoyable; I found myself surprised with the ease of use since point-and-click adventures are notorious for weird logic and frustrating conundrums. This is wonderful in the context of no longer having to fill my inventory with useless items and rub them against terrain features or each other to create solutions, but it doubled back on me at several cases when the ease of gameplay early on dulled my senses to times when I really needed to be more aware of the setting and surroundings. The minigames and puzzles which help progress the story have too few iterations to produce a sense of accomplishment or mastery when finished, giving them the feel of obstacles to be overcome rather than genuinely pleasing and rewarding. The interface feels intentionally clunky - which is effective at slowing the player down to have them experience the game's text, but it also becomes surprising when the responsiveness of the game becomes near-perfect in action sequences. There's a disconnect that felt jarring and took a few game overs to realize that no, there was no bug in the system, it's just that the previous sluggish text/adventuring controls had given way to highly responsive action controls.
What stands out in Read Only Memories is the plot and the worldbuilding. The characters are well-realized and distinct, adding flavour to the setting, but the real star is the mystery that unravels as the player investigates strange happenings in Neo San Francisco. I get the feeling that people who have lived there or visited would be rewarded with familiar sights, personalities, and corporate presences - but as someone who has never been, it felt like a good representation of how San Francisco might turn out in a cyberpunk future unmarred by disaster. The city itself feels like the biggest supporting character, and the plot that unfolds within it paints a picture that is equal parts bleak and uplifting - 'plus ça change, plus c'est la même chose' could be the motto of Neo San Francisco which feels ironically like the San Francisco of today: blissfully ignorant tech giants changing peoples' lives for the better and for the worse with equal disregard, a gathering place for marginalized people where they can be themselves, a city fighting a continual ballet of urban decay and aggressive gentrification. For all the trappings of the future, what happens in Neo San Francisco in Read Only Memories could easily have happened ten years ago or next week in the Bay area.
The game's music is probably its strongest point - the soundtrack sets the scene and seamlessly carries the player through the game. In the middle of mundane tasks I would find myself humming along or bobbing my head, and a stand-out moment happened for me when I helped 4Moolah (an obvious insert of the game's composer, 2Mello) compose a rap. Not only was 4Moolah's rap a good kind of cheesy, but using objects to help him figure out the rap was one of the more amusing and empowering moments in the game. As far as I can tell, there's only one right answer, but the sequence subverted my expectations, made me laugh, and puzzled the hell out of me with a twist ending. I even tested the lyrics and they fit with the background music and was pleased to find that everything fits even for an amateur like me.
At the time of writing, I had only played through the game 1 1/2 times. It doesn't seem to have a lot of replayability but completionists will get a kick out of exploring the different dialogue and path options, and the script is rewarding enough that choosing all-new answers to most questions makes the game novel enough to stick with for another playthrough.
Read Only Memories is a first effort from MidBoss, and as a first effort it is very good. The production values are incredibly high given the funding and timeline. The game is long enough to sit down and play in one night if you're really dedicated but every bit of it is packed with intriguing characters, excellent music, and lovingly rendered pixel-art. It feels like a unique product - an art project whose intent wasn't necessarily to amuse but to engage the player outside the context of the game to think about the world as it is written. It also subverts traditional game thinking by making the player-controlled protagonist a lynchpin to the events of the game without having a strong effect on the outcome. I came away from the experience feeling as though Turing had used me (as the protagonist) but could have easily used anyone in my situation; who I was was irrelevant, I was just convenient. It's unsettling and nontraditional but definitely worth a playthrough or two, and worth the price. I am looking forward to future changes and/or to the release of a second game from this studio. Read Only Memories is a great game - and with a gameplay overhaul, it could have been a masterpiece.

Unfortunately I have played many hours of Terraria before I played this.  I say unfortunattely, because I'm sure my view of this game has been tainted by the king of this genre.  Having said that, what they have here is...fun-ish.
Pros:  I love the soundtrack and ambience during gameplay.  There are alos lots of items and weapons to collect and neat little side mission things to do.
Cons:  The game almost seems pointless, even with the storyline.  I can't quite put my finger on why that is, but when compared to Terraria, there really seems like very little push to move on in the game for some reason.
Second, the digging and ore hunting is TERRIBLE.  You could dig for an hour looking for ore and literally run in to zero enemies underground.  It's very boring, whereas Terraria made it difficult and even entertaining to try and obtain more ores.
Third, the enemies are all the same, just a different look and hitpoints.  They all do roughly the same thing and take almost the same number of hits to kill.
Lastly, the movements are not nearly as precise as they need to be.  It is impossible to get to the edge of any platform because you will fall off.  You can not jump to any small platform because you will jump over it.  The movement controls are quite terrible, and when you try to slightly tap yourself over a bit to get to the edge of something, your guy will dash right off the edge, everytime.  It'll make you insane.
I was excited to FINALLY play this game after waiting for a sale.  Sadly, I wish I'd played this before I ever played Terraria, because Terraria only adds to what this game delivers.  Going the other way and playing this afterwards is only dissappointing.
I know people hate reviews where Terraria and this game are compared, but the sad fact is, they are the same genre and roughly the same game.  So they are going to be compared and that's fine IMO.  Comparing gives a relative idea of how fun another game will be.  I find Terraria much better than Starbound at this point.  Maybe the Starbound devs will step it up and push out some major release that will redo some of the game's mechanics and what not, but now that the game is released I'm not counting on it.  But we'll see...Terraria devs have done that a few times in the past and it almost always made the game better.
EDIT:  Additionally, the biomes are utter garbage.  There is no difference from one landscape to the next with the exception of sand and dirt.  Slime and sand are the same and dirt and other materials are the same.  Aside from that, nothing really changes as you walk the landscape except the look...Very boring and pointless to try to collect items from each biome but for the fact that you get to make different looking things.
And all side missions are the same.  It's either deliver this message there or defeat this guy over there and walk the captive back here.

This early unsung hero produced by Sabre Interactive is a cult classic that would form the basis of the portfolio, get them hired on to produce Halo: Anniversary, and would see ideas put forth in this game recycled by a different developer into the much more successful game Singularity (produced by Raven Software). Unlike that title, which used industry-standard Unreal III graphics and fairly safe gameplay, TimeShift utilized propriety engine technology developed by Sabre themselves that allowed for time manipulation  resembling a beefed-up version of the "Bullet Time" slow-mo effects found in games such as Max Payne. Players could not only slow down time, but stop it altogether or even reverse it, with all physics suspended or undone entirely during manipulation. This allowed for all kinds of neat tricks like stealig enemies' weaponry and replacing them with live grenades, etc. Furthermore, this proprietary tech also made possible then-impressive real-time shadows and bump-mapped textures on par with titles like Doom 3 ; the level of detail in the environments and draw distance on things is still quite impressive.
Sadly, this game was semi-doomed from the start, as the original finished product was rejected and the game was sent back for an entire additional year of polish, which didn't help it contend against heavy hitters like Halo 3 and Bioshock, since the game was mainly pushed on consoles and not PC before digital distribution would be mainstream enough for this game to reach it's proper audience more quickly, Other nitpicks include a somewhat byzantine story that waxes on Half-Life 2 more than it cares to admit, and herky-jerky controls that take more time than some are going to put into the game to make second nature.
However, if one fancies a time-travelling tale wrapped in a futuristic dystopian shooter with some really well-implemented time manipulation tricks and shinier-than-expected visuals for the period, then there literally isn't anything else like this game. Again, Singularity met with more success, but arguably this game did it better.

Summary: Not worth it unless you're in desperate need of some mental chewing gum to get you through a rainy day.

State of Decay comes pretty close to being a zombie fan’s dream game. It expertly combines elements from RPGs and survival horror, mixing in human drama and an engrossing story into a neat post-apocalyptic package.

State Of Decay is a good zombie, survival game. One that many were probably anticipating for years.
You start out in a forest as a man named Marcus in what was supposed to be a normal camping trip, but turned into a fight for survival against flesh eating zombies! You eventually meet up with a few more survivors and make your way into a refuge camp of more survivors. This is the start of your game.
Now it's time to plan and maintain your community and it's morale for survival. You can switch to and play as almost every survivor in your community(after building a good friendship with them) and take advantage of abilities each one has. Some people are strong for fighting, others are nimble for scavenging, some are just worthless drunks, and among many others. Your means of combat is with fists/kicks, melee weapons, guns, and vehicles.
Of course, your home base will require hefty amounts of food, medicine, construction materials, ammo, and fuel. Luckily, there are many buildings in this open world to scavenge to find exactly what you need. Just don't forget to find a high point to survey the land or else you may find yourself in a zombie infested house! Overtime, you may even choose to move your home base. Will it be that farm house far out in the country side? Or maybe even a trucking depot for extra security and space! You decide.
State Of Decay's main story is short, but panned out overtime with many side missions so that you have a long time to play and complete the game when you want to. Overall, I highly recommend this game for anyone who likes zombie, survival, open world games. It's immersive and fun.
-Here's my zombie survival tip: Take care of your vehicles and conserve gun ammo.
Thank you for reading my review and have a good day!

I'm not saying I had tears in my eyes when I heard the menu music, but I'm not saying I didn't, either.
I played KO very early in its lifespan, and even back then the game was very p2win, very hardcore, very grindy. After grinding to 60 on my healer over months, I got invited to join the top guild on my Malaysian server (where I PvPed from Germany on a dial-up connection). My Malaysian guild master would spend his weekly income on cash-shop boosters for PvP and would hook the rest of us up too, even if it meant he couldn't afford food.
It felt great being part of a good guild, swaggering about in our fancy cloaks with our logo on it, I had an absolute blast despite 90% of the playerbase consisting of 12 year old Turks in internet cafes, and 10% being 12 yeard old Malaysians in internet cafes.
PvP was fun and never got old to me, due to animation-cancelling (you could combo in a very efficient way) and sliding (allowing you to stay moving as you attack). I don't know if I would have enjoyed the game nearly as much or even stuck with it as long as I did without those.
The game was absolutely plagued by bugs and poor programming (no leashing, ridiculous threat mechanics, rampant botting and straight-up hacks) and more than once have I witnessed guildmates' accounts being stolen (internet cafes, remember?).
I don't know if this changed since MYKO, but you used to lose 5%(?) XP every time you died (several hours worth of grind beyond level 60), so my friends' compromised characters would often be seen running into mobs face first, in an attempt to de-level the character. Yes, you could level down if you lost XP while below 5% XP into the next level.
It was an awesome, terrible game, and I will always think of it lovingly, with good memories- but I have no idea why anyone would subject themselves to this now...why is this even on Steam?!
I'm gonna faff around in it and maybe even try to level, but I can not honestly recommend anyone play this. Under modern standards, this game is a piece of crap (and the monetization is almost criminal). Just go play Blade & Soul.

This was a surprisingly impressive Visual Novel considering that it doesn't appear to have been written for English as a first language.  There are voice actors for Korean and Japanese as well as English text.  That being said, the English writing isn't nearly bad enough to dissuade someone from reading the story; it was clearly translated and flowed well.
The characters were interesting in the sense that all were pretty evidently flawed, some more than others.  This game is a massive Tearjerker / Heartwarming moment depending on how far in you play, and it will resonate with you for some time after you complete it.  This game questions what it means to be human, and what is and isn't real, amongst many other concepts that will keep you thinking for some time.
The play of the game is pretty solid; the interface was simple and the choices, while not having much of an impact at all, still have interesting comedic moments as well as unlocking scenes.  The free bonus content as well as the
are devastating emotional rollercoasters that kept me on the edge of my seat.  This visual novel certainly does not fail in making you legitimately feel.  At roughly seven hours of content, depending on your reading speed
The soundtrack is pretty nice; there are quite a few tracks that stuck out to me.  That being said, there are also some moments of silence that I didn't really like.  The art is fascinating as well; it isn't a stretch to label it "anime" at all, but that's definitely not a point against it.  For such a short game, there are quite a few CGs and they are both appropriate and well drawn.
The plot was one of the strongest points of the visual novel; most of it is light and cheerful, with appropriate levels of comedy both light and sultry.  It slowly paces towards an inevitable conclusion; you can feel the climax coming and foreshadowing hints at it, but you're still in denial up until it actually happens, and then you realize it isn't over, because the game has three different bonuses to share with you that round off the story more resolutely than anything possible.  If anything, the bonus content
surpasses the tearjerker quality of everything that comes before and after it.
This visual novel will make you feel throughout and think after it, succeeding perfectly in being an engaging and thoughtful play.  Entirely worth the purchase.

Cute little game, definitely recommend it for the low price, especially if you're a Shakespeare fan.

From the title, you may expect a CYOA version of "A Midsummer Night's Choice," and while there are clearly strong elements of that play in the work, it's safer to say that this is a tale that relies heavily on Shakespearean comedies in general.  This game weaves together mistaken identities, tangled romances, and a bit of fairy glamour to create a reactive story that feels like you're playing through one of the Comedies--it's vibrant and familiar, without feeling derivative.
The focus is on the story and your choices, but there is a light stat system that means success or failure in certain events depends on your previous choices, while not constraining you to having threaded a narrow needle to have a satisfying story (unless you're achievement hunting, that is).  There is a lot of freedom to play your role in a multitude of ways, and chances are you will be entertained whatever the result is.  I know that I laughed out loud multiple times throughout play, for example when I seduced [REDACTED].
There is also a lot of freedom to explore queer themes through the choice of your character's gender, and the genders of your companions--as well as even how you feel about having spent time presenting as the opposite of your birth gender.   It's a surprisingly touching approach without getting heavy-handed.
All in all, if you'd like to spend a couple of hours with a reactive text, I'd say that this is a good choice.

It's an action RPG in the same genre as Diablo, Torchlight, etc., but with several twists.  It's much more puzzle based, but combat is still an integral part.  Classes are based on the 4 available weapons, and switching classes can be done with no penalty between levels.  Skills are unlocked by completing levels and challenges (one time and one other per level) to get crystals, which unlock abilities at certain numbers and is not tied to a class.  There's no gear progression, so there's no grinding.  In multiplayer, everyone has to have a crystal for it to be available for that play session, so everyone is on an equal footing.
I picked this up because it was compatible with Macs, and I've really enjoyed it.  I've played with 1, 2, 3, and 4 players, tried all 4 classes and have 72/75 crystals.
Some levels/challenges are significantly easier for either solo or multiplayer (time challenges tend to be more relaxed in multiplayer, but other challenges that require no one screwing up is much easier solo).  Also, the archer seems to be much more powerful compared to the other classes in solo because it is the only class with a ranged basic attack.  Furthermore, once you have 75/75 crystals, I feel there's currently limited replay value, even if you choose a different class.  However, there's a promise for more "endgame" content beyond the current survival mode.

*Disclaimer* I received a key to this game from the developer for review
**TLDR** - Yi and the Thousand Moons is more like a proof of concept that breaks tradition in having its tale told via musical arias and seizes emotion through music. What it lacks in gameplay diversity or challenge, it more than makes up for passion, writing, music, and color. I hope musicals gain a foothold in the games industry.
Yi and the Thousand Moons is a tale of actions and consequences set in the format of a musical.
It's very obvious upon opening up the main menu that this was a passion project because you are introduced to a beautiful, yet melancholy melody set in a backdrop of stars. I must have just sat at my PC listening to the menu music repeat itself for a solid 10 minutes, which is a very long time to me.
If you are looking for an FPS/Action game, then this is not for you, but if you are looking for something new or something different, definitely look into this. The game is, in my opinion, designed to be experiened rather than played. The actual gameplay is simple and straightforward, with little chance for deviation or exploration. It's more like we, the players, are experiencing a dream-like sequence.
Where Yi and the Thousand Moons shines is in its storytelling via music and breaking new ground. The story itself leaves open a lot of plot holes and questions but having exposition and dialogue told in musical is novel and interesting. Hearing story being told via songs and tunes lends more emotional weight it than straight dialogue or reading walls of text in my opinion.
It's not an ugly game by any definition, in fact the basic character designs and simple color palette with simply bloom effects serve to enhance the dreamlike feel of the game that supports the music.
At the end of the day, I would prefer that games like Yi and the Thousand Moons had more time and resources to really flesh out the story, gameplay, and music track. I think this is fantastic as a proof of concept and worth supporting at 5$ per copy.

Have you ever wondered what it's like to see the images of a poem? Well, Yi and the Thousand Moons does so in a mesmerizing way.
Needless to say, this game is sui generis and that's what makes it a great addition to your library. Offering its players a story narrated through music and an aesthetical proposal, this title feels like you are playing a book and watching a musical -with beautiful vocals!- at the same time.
If you are looking for a breath of fresh air and compelling storytelling, you should try out this short, yet charming game.

Yi and the Thousand Moons is a small “art house” game from a new game publisher named David Su that could be best described as an interactive musical. Yi and the Thousand Moons is obviously made with so much passion that I get drawn into it immediately. It has to be said from the beginning of this review: this is a game centered around music, and you should make sure you like the music and singer in the trailer before you buy. The rest of the review is for you who like the music but still aren't sure if you want the game.
The gameplay is basic, a walking simulator with a few instances of simple interaction. The graphics is a mostly empty world populated with a few block people, block houses and a block shamisen. Yet your brain is a pro at filling out those gaps, and the game looks beautiful within the constraints it operates in. And you know what else fills out the world? Music. We're here for the interactive musical ride. The interaction is that you do different simple things to prod the music along, there are no choices or anything fancy like that going on. Yet to me it feels satisfying to release an arrow and hear the characters start to sing when my arrow hits its (non living) mark. The music fills the entire world and sometimes sends shivers down my spine. One song in particular gives me goose bumps every time. The game is short, and I keep coming back to it for replays to listen to the songs again.
I will carry Yi and the Thousand Moons with me for a long time as one of my favorite experimental indie games. I've played it five times, and every time I'm done I'm longing to play the game I feel Yi and the Thousand Moons wants to be, or could have been if the developer had a 10 people studio with him to elaborate upon the parts that had to be down prioritized now. There's so much potential here. While Yi and the Thousand Moons is already great as it is, I'm itching to see what the next step will be for David Su.

Unfortunately I have played many hours of Terraria before I played this.  I say unfortunattely, because I'm sure my view of this game has been tainted by the king of this genre.  Having said that, what they have here is...fun-ish.
Pros:  I love the soundtrack and ambience during gameplay.  There are alos lots of items and weapons to collect and neat little side mission things to do.
Cons:  The game almost seems pointless, even with the storyline.  I can't quite put my finger on why that is, but when compared to Terraria, there really seems like very little push to move on in the game for some reason.
Second, the digging and ore hunting is TERRIBLE.  You could dig for an hour looking for ore and literally run in to zero enemies underground.  It's very boring, whereas Terraria made it difficult and even entertaining to try and obtain more ores.
Third, the enemies are all the same, just a different look and hitpoints.  They all do roughly the same thing and take almost the same number of hits to kill.
Lastly, the movements are not nearly as precise as they need to be.  It is impossible to get to the edge of any platform because you will fall off.  You can not jump to any small platform because you will jump over it.  The movement controls are quite terrible, and when you try to slightly tap yourself over a bit to get to the edge of something, your guy will dash right off the edge, everytime.  It'll make you insane.
I was excited to FINALLY play this game after waiting for a sale.  Sadly, I wish I'd played this before I ever played Terraria, because Terraria only adds to what this game delivers.  Going the other way and playing this afterwards is only dissappointing.
I know people hate reviews where Terraria and this game are compared, but the sad fact is, they are the same genre and roughly the same game.  So they are going to be compared and that's fine IMO.  Comparing gives a relative idea of how fun another game will be.  I find Terraria much better than Starbound at this point.  Maybe the Starbound devs will step it up and push out some major release that will redo some of the game's mechanics and what not, but now that the game is released I'm not counting on it.  But we'll see...Terraria devs have done that a few times in the past and it almost always made the game better.
EDIT:  Additionally, the biomes are utter garbage.  There is no difference from one landscape to the next with the exception of sand and dirt.  Slime and sand are the same and dirt and other materials are the same.  Aside from that, nothing really changes as you walk the landscape except the look...Very boring and pointless to try to collect items from each biome but for the fact that you get to make different looking things.
And all side missions are the same.  It's either deliver this message there or defeat this guy over there and walk the captive back here.

The steady advance of technological progress has brought us many unforeseen challenges. With robotics and AI slowly but surely encroaching on what we used to think of as uniquely human, we are confronted with the question of what makes us so special and on what basis we deem ourselves superior to the intelligent beings we create. Take this cerebral topic and intermingle it with some comedy, drama and romance, and what you get is
.

Set in a mostly contemporary world where robots and AI are ubiquitous and have almost reached the point where they are difficult to distinguish from humans, it tells the story of how a prototype android upsets the fickle balance in a conservative family critical of such technology. A chance encounter has the teenaged main character take "Lucy" from the junkyard, pitting her exuberance against his cynicism and ensuring comedy hijinks as well as drama and tragedy. While his struggles to integrate Lucy into his daily life play out on one timeline, the story intersperses
about the man (referred to as "Doctor") who pours all of his energy into assembling Lucy and protecting her from government interference, leaving the reader to hypothesize early on about how Lucy ended up at the junkyard.
In terms of visual novel mechanics,
packs few surprises. The
packed into its three to five hour main story leads to many of them feeling a bit railroad-y, even though there are multiple endings to be conquered. The visual presentation is crisp and polished, the backgrounds and CGs are of a high quality. While there is nothing wrong with any one character sprite by itself, at times their visual styles are noticeably different, which can make scenes look incoherent (
). The soundtrack is fitting but not particularly memorable. Korean and Japanese voiceovers are provided. The lack of multiplatform support (the VN is available for Windows only) is regrettable. Something that is definitely worth pointing out is the absurd amount of post-game content and alternate endings that bumped my own reading time from just three hours all the way up to five – I am a quick reader though, and looking at the reviews, playtimes of anywhere between 7 to 10 hours seem within the norm. The post-game content also provided the story with some much-needed rounding out, so you will most definitely want to keep reading after the credits roll for the first time.
Thematically the VN attempts to cover a lot of ground. At face value there is the "cute robot girl" story, which would have been easy to turn into clichéd "fated love" schlock, but thankfully the story stays very light on the romance elements and delivers its tender budding affection so subtly that you could almost miss it. Lucy's character itself is less immune to clichés, seeing as she is rooted firmly in the "clumsy, ditzy, caring but naive" tradition of robot girls, and her characterization is at least consistent and believable even if it's not innovative. Most of the situational humor falls in line with what you would expect from this part of anime culture, with Lucy being oblivious of her surroundings and the main character having to clean up behind her.
More interestingly, the story also makes a more than solid effort at tackling the philosophical questions
when robots become almost indistinguishable from humans. For example, part of the story's tension is derived from the question of
if memories as well as body parts can be replicated and replaced as needed (the
is even mentioned by name). As a narrative theme, the idea of artificially created humans has a long literary tradition. VN aficionados will of course tend to notice the many parallels to

, which Lucy's story also reflects in many ways. Now, like then, the question is posed what it is that supposedly makes us humans more deserving of a self-determined life than the ones we create as our servants. The VN is not shy about exploring these questions even at the expense of subverting its own characters (such as when the protagonist shows a  knowledge of Schopenhauer uncharacteristic for a teenager who claims to have no interest in formal education).

, who I suspect is hostile to the point of belligerence towards androids because he identifies so deeply with his work and considers his role as a productive employee the central aspect of his own sense of purpose.
For all its interesting thematic points, there are also aspects of
that I had to grapple with, the biggest one being the general unlikability of the main character. A lot of this can be explained away by his age and familial situation, but with as many external sources of tension as the story possesses, I wish they had relied less on the protagonist's egotism and carelessness as a source of drama, since it tends to strain the immersion. In terms of minor nitpicks, I didn't care for how
was used as a scene transition, since clicking through it every time quickly became tedious.
Overall,
is a very well-written story that profits especially from the aforementioned post-game content. Even though this review is, as always, as free of spoilers as I can manage, I absolutely cannot avoid highlighting the brilliance of the final reveal during the true ending that astonishingly weaves everything together and tempts the reader to start the story over again right away. It's just one moment out of many, but I appreciate the careful construction of the story leading up to it immensely.
stands on the shoulders of giants and it knows it. Its themes have been explored in other works before and the VN has
. However, it is still a worthwhile story on its own that is sharp and polished and has everything a good visual novel would need. If you absolutely cannot stand ditzy anime girls, this may be too much to stomach, but if you're up for a cutesy tale about existentialism and sociotechnical progress, you can't go wrong here.

All I can say to this is "ehhh" - not that good but not horrendous either.
I don't really watch anime (anymore) and this is my first time playing a VN - it's similar to what I expected but at the same time it's not.  I feel for one to become envolped in a story line (of any game) I need to feel some kind of relation to the main character (whether that be enjoyment of slaying dragons or something as simple as sharing a like of super heroes).  With this game, the limit of my relation with the character pretty much extended to that we were both guys - I didn't share any of the values that the main character did which made it hard for me to get emotionally attached to Lucy.
When I came to write this review I wanted to do so with pointing out my opinion of how autistic the main character seemed - but that's a overally harsh.  Trying to think from a view of a ~16 year old and being that age only a few years ago I can understand some of the main characters actions; however for a kid who knows a lot about philosophical theories he seems overly irrational.  This doesn't extend to just the main character, there's a fatal plot hole along with some unanswered questions which basically ruined the whole game for me (I'm extremely nit picky about this stuff but the large majority of people as shown by the other reviews probably won't notice or probably won't even care).  Personally I found the voice acting annoying too but I can see how it would appeal to many other people (especially those who like Japanese culture)
That's not to say this game doesn't have it's merits - rather than focusing on the relationship between the kid and Lucy, it does ask some interesting philosophical questions about indentity, family and robots in general - however it does take a while to get to this stage from the start of the game, and it can get tedious having to constantly read the main characters  thoughts and interactions with other characters in the game.
It's kind of a moot point but if you have played a VN before but if you haven't remember that it's not an RPG - you can't choose as many options as you wish or control your dialogue and you're mainly buying the game to read the text and look at the pictures.  Nothing wrong with that but not my cup of tea.
I have to say though the ending was absolutely brilliant - I saw a part of it coming but it actually surprised me at good it was considering I spent a lot of my time hating on this game.  While the ending was for sure worth $10, I'm not fully convinced the main storyline was.
If there was a neutral option I would l tick that as a recommendation but unfortunately there isn't, and while the ending is a silver lining I personally don't justify the game as a whole being worth $10.

I haven't read Midsummer Night's Dream (I'm an uncultured git), so I can't comment on how closely this is to the original play.  But on it's own merits, I liked this game a lot.  It had a lot of cool choices, and I felt like they actually made a difference in the story.  It's a short game; I finished it in 3 hours.  But it's really cheap, so I definitely feel I got my money's worth.
If I had to complain about anything, it would be the occasionally obtuse stat requirements.  I'm not against stat systems in general, but there were times where I couldn't tell if a choice would use Wit or Charm or some other stat, which was frustrating.  That being said, this flaw is present in most text-based games, so this is more of a complaint about the genre than this game in particular.
Overall I liked it, and recommend it to anyone who's a fan of text games.

I enjoyed A Midsummer's Night's Choice better than some of the other Choice of Games' selections. The writing is quick and jaunts along, much like the game's narrative. If you're looking for a serious story, you might want to turn away from this one. The characters were endearing and it felt like my choices did make a difference in how the story proceeded. I'd have to play another run through to be more sure of this, but there were definitely a few times my choices didn't go as planned because of how my stats changed.
A lot of the choices and selections don't feel as in depth as something like Choice of Robots, but it did not detract from the story immersion. There were some areas that could have been edited to flow better (redundant word usage was also a bit of an issue in certain places).
Overall, this was a really enjoyable CYOA and I'm looking forward to playing it again! If you're looking for some light-hearted comedy-romance, then this would be a fun game for you!

By the time i'm writing this review, we've already experienced what will very likely be the last game in the Souls series, and maybe even the last Souls-like by this developer, so if you're someone who is still yet to find an entry point to the series, i'm here to tell you why this one, the one game that refined everything Demon Souls did, and the one to begin the journey of the undead, is still to this date and in my humble opinion, the best of all of them.
Dark Souls was released on 2011, lacking both the big budget and the hype that its sequels and its brother game, Bloodborne, would later benefit from, yet i would dare to say that on its humbleness lies the true magic and charm that From Software would just not be able to top on later releases.
Players take the role of a chosen Undead, following an ancient prophecy that tells about uncovering the fate for its whole kind in the land of the ancient lords, Lordran, and this is where we will start pointing out the things that make Dark Souls unique.
The world design is, if not flawless, a true example of how open areas should be done, each landscape connects to the next one in a true seamless way, every detail in the background is a place that you will reach at some point, it's a world that expands in all directions and always makes sense, it never stops feeling like you're really travelling through this vast, old and forgotten land, like something out of the most magical fable.
Next is the one feature that became the trademark of the Souls series, its difficulty, Dark Souls is not only challenging, it is sometimes unfair and unforgiving, and while this might sound like something negative, once you experience it, it is  far from it, it is a game that will see you fail, and will dare you to try again, will dare you to succeed on what it has set to make unconquerable...
and then you try, then you try harder, once and again, and then you succeed, and the satisfaction that comes with it, is something that no other series has made me feel yet.
The atmosphere of this game is yet another thing that was done so right, the areas range from gloomy, going through desolate, to absolutely terrifying; while you traverse the land, you will notice the lack of any background music (This being reserved only for its boss battles and the place where you first step into Lordran, the Firelink Shrine, every piece being a magnificent composition by Motoi Sakuraba) but far from making it feel lackluster, it adds to the immersion, to that feeling of being by yourself amidst all kinds of perils.
Every area has just this darkness feeling to it, like you're about to be swallowed by the very land under your feet, and yet for some reason, speaking graphics wise, the next Souls games just didn't seem to get this right.
The last point i will talk about is its very particular storytelling, Dark Souls features very little dialogue from only a small number of characters you will meet during your journey, yet every item, weapon and armor in the game contains a small description about its origins and its place in the world, it is by piecing together all these small stories that a larger narrative is born, and suddenly the world has a background of depths that maybe long cutscenes and hours of dialogue would not be able to equal.
As this review has become very extended, if you have made it to this paragraph, i thank you, and i deeply recommend that you give this game a chance, at the moment i'm writing this the game is on sale, it is a perfect moment to start what i hope is for you, as it was for me, one of the most unique experiences gaming will ever offer.

A masterpiece that falls just short of perfection.  "Lucy" has the highest production values that I have ever seen in a visual novel.  I highly recommend reading "Lucy" on a brightscreen display or laptop.  The artwork was fabulous.  The story was of greater sophistication and depth than I have ever seen in any other visual novel.  The background music was perfect for the scenes.  I was not annoyed at the scenes always ending with "The Three Laws of Robotics."  I, personally, would add a fourth law:  "All androids must prevent unauthorized access to programming by fleeing if possible, and, if not possible, by a series of escalating, pre-programmed defense mechanisms."  "Lucy" presents some uncomfortable truths about human beings.  Lucy herself, because she was programmed by a visionary genius, is so pure, innocent, and full of good will toward everyone that she makes a better "person" than any actual human being.
I mentioned that this visual novel falls just short of perfection.  The reason why is that the future depicted in "Lucy" will never actually happen.  Androids will never be made available for purchase to the public or even large corporations.  Governments around the world will be so afraid that terrorists will hack into androids and reprogram them to carry out assassinations and mass bombings that only government entities and a few government-approved research labs will be allowed to own androids.  Androids will have extreme security mechanisms built in, including self-destruct.  That said, I think "Lucy" is correct that androids will be used in caring for the elderly in the future.  I dread the thought of military use of androids -- except clearing land mines.
"Lucy" is worth every penny of the full purchase price.  This is a "don't miss" and a sure candidate for top ten visual novel lists.  I was certainly not expecting anything this thoughtful -- and emotional.
One nitpick:  I wish that there had been a scene inside Dr. Gears’ house.  Perhaps everyone sitting around a table discussing what political changes would be necessary in the future to avoid a dystopia in which the people who own the robots and androids would own the entire planet and everyone else would be dispossessed, destitute, and desperate.  Robots and androids could create a utopia for everyone, or they could create a hell for almost everyone.  Given current political trends, my money is on hell.

Oh boy, I have to admit, this visual novel is really under rated, not much people have bought this visual novel, although the reviews were nice, it wasn't what this one's worth... To be honest I'm surprised that it turned out to be such a detailed and refined visual novel, at the start I expected a normal robot and human romance story where the end would be sad, either the robot breaks down or it dies in an accident... In fact, it was the robot that chose it's own end, if you're a man of seeking a sense of sadness to make yourself cry to relieve stress, this is the perfect visual novel.
Here's why I like this visual novel and anything it can improve on :
Enjoyables :
-The translation was perfect, it perfectly showed the emotions of Lucy and it was definitely unexpected out of this visual novel.
-Korean vocals recorded by Emily was definitely superior, she had put great effort into mimicing a robot's way of speech, but it wasn't the normal type of robotic speech, although the words were robotic and formal, it was human, you could hear the hesitation when scolded by the master, it's plain and enlightened mood, a really fantastic vocalist!
-Although there were only 6 main characters that's actually relevant to the main story (you, lucy, father, mother that doesn't care about "you", your friend baek and the young engineer that repaired lucy), they were all designed in details, their art was nice, definitely, but what's of more is that their way of speech really reflects the reality of the future society in the story, although they loved and enjoyed robots and andriods, they did not forget the difference between human and machines, which made "you"'s love towards lucy look sinister but charming.
-Music was definitely out-standing, matching the moods properly and bringing the tone of sadness with a sense of calm peace.
-[SPOILER ALERT]The story ended with a sad end with lucy being burned down by father, but there's actually a "true end" towards this where lucy is repaired, even if the story script was set that lucy was "beyond repair", the MC actually spent the next 15 years of his life researching and learning about andriods, so that he could repair lucy and one day, lucy actually remembered the lost part of her memory card, despite the impossible.
^-The end was actually the most enjoyable part, although the twisted end was a scene where you should let your tears fall, it doesn't only bring sadness via sadness, the happy end after the sad end was quite a suprise and you'd cry even harder after knowing that this end was possible ( remember to watch the extra story scenes! ).
Things this game should improve on :
(well I can't really complain about this game, it's truly a master piece and don't expect erotic scenes, it's plain romance and comedy with a twist of sadness, but very very well detailed.)
-Could've made some special events, instead of making daily school life changes as the story.
-There was literally no mentioning about the life with his past mother, whether he forgot about it or the story didn't mention about it, I hope there would've been more hints about his deceased mother.
-Was a dissapointment that the vocals weren't in japanese, but korean vocal is rather pleasing with emily's sweet tone :d
-Wastes a bit of time doing scene changes when you could've just skipped the animation, aka. unnessecary scenery changing animations >:C
That's all I can think of >.< I'm sorry for my inexperience in writing these but I'm writing what I truly think, I hope this helps you into deciding whether you should buy this game or not, it's a game that's definitely worth your money and time, it's longer than the normal visual novels you expect, although it's one of those sad end visual novels, those who are under reality stress, please use this as a relief of pressure, crying or knowing something sad would definitely help you express your emotions better! Lucy - The Eternity She Wished For is definitely worth your money even at full price, although I would highly suggest you to buy it during sales, it would be best to buy it full priced and show support to the creators :D Enjoy and have a nice day!

A very great & faithful, remastered port of the 1993 Sega CD Classic Gem.
I DEFINITELY recommend it, especially if you're a Sonic fan that didn't grow up with the Sega CD (Let's be honest, how many of you guys did?), if you love 2D sidescrollers as I do, or if you just want to own it on another system as I do.
PROS
-It has a very non linear and off the wall level design,
-time travel mechanic is madness and this is the only Sonic game to feature it,
-colors are very lively as usual with a Sonic game,

-the music is awesome and American consumers get the option to officially play with the far superior (in my opinion) Japanese/PAL Version soundtrack,
-the cutscenes are cool, even though they look a little dated and the quality isn't that great but far better than previously seen on the original Sega CD Version.
CONS
Like with all games, there are some flaws.
-The one thing that I don't particularly like are the Special Stages.  While unique in gameplay compared to other Sonic games, it is a little tricky to navigate but at least the framerate is FAR smoother than the Sega CD Version.
-The level design can be a little confusing at times but still fun,
-The boss battles can be either a little lackluster or too much to get through just to only give him a few hits.
There are plenty of extra features to keep the game fresh and distinguish it from previous releases of the game though I don't want to ruin the mystery.

Sonic CD. I tried desperately to enjoy this game, but there were a few things holding me back. Although, the music is quite catchy. This game was supposed to get me ready to play a Classic style Sonic game for Sonic Mania, but it purely made me angry. But... it managed to pull through.
In short, Sonic CD is my least favorite of the Classic Sonic games. This game is obnoxiously unfair. Now, I'll take blame for some of it- I'm not great at this game. But there are some moments where you feel as if you have no control. Collision Choas is a prime example of this. I can't seem to recommend this game simply because it was more of a chore to play through than an enjoyment but... There is a little hope, surprisingly. This game just barely slips past my personal threshold of what makes a good Sonic game.
Now, for the full review.
The story is simple enough, and there's some really neat cutscenes. The game has you going to a bunch of areas, and it's all fine and dandy. Well, that is until you get to literally the second zone. Collision Choas sucks, and it is one of the areas that personally made me dislike this game at first. It took me too long to get through this area because the constant ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t things they throw at you. Randomly going along and they throw a bumber at you, or a random spring, and it's just unfair, especially when it throws you back as far as it does. Collision Choas is a pinball themed level, and while the boss is actually pretty cool, the other two levels just didn't sit very well with me.
Now, I was still looking forward to the rest of this game because every Sonic game has that zone that you simply can't stand, or you dislike, so I was fine with it. The game did improve with the next area- Tidal Tempest. It's a fun water zone that is personally my favorite amongst the Classic Sonics. Other than that, there's not much I can say about it. Quartz Quardrant was the same- I did enjoy it a lot, and it wasn't too bad. This is when I noticed that the game's music and art direction is actually impressive for a game as old as it is.
Wacky Workbench is another area where I got crazy frustrated, and I honestly just ran through as fast as I could here. My frustration didn't come until I attempted the Time Trial Mode for this zone, because that's when I realized that it's not easy to go through here fast. Despite getting irritated, it still proved to be a decent area to play through.
Stardust Speedway was so much fun. I love the music, the visuals, and the race with Metal Sonic was challenging, yet fair. This level lets you speed through it as long as you have some idea as to where you're going, which you probably won't. But that's okay, because the level does eventually guide you back on track. It's a fun level that's going to keep you on your toes, but in the the bad way.
Metallic Madness was a zone I greatly enjoyed. It's got a lot in it, and there's so many parts of each level to explore, and I just found myself really, really enjoying it despite all the complaints I had heard about it beforehand.
So... After my first playthrough, I felt like the game was pretty... Meh. It was fun at some points, but I kinda just went through it to go through it and say I played it. At this point, I decided to check out what else this game had, such as the soundtrack, and Time Trial Mode. The Time Trial Mode is your key to unlocking all the extra content this game has, and that is what sold it for me. I will probably go back and complete this game 100%, but for the casual player who probably isn't going to, I'd recommend this game because the game is fun enough, and the extra content, in my opinion at least, is well worth it.
I'd give Sonic CD a
. It's got it moments, but, for me, at least, I couldn't enjoy the entire game no matter how much I wanted to. It just barely passes my standards for what makes a good Sonic game.
Thanks for reading my review if you did. This one was slightly rushed, but my opinion still stands, and hopefully this review will help you decide if you want the game!

This is the first game I have ever reviewed on steam and for a good reason. State of Decay is easily in my top ten games now and I recommend it to anyone that enjoys video games. While it is buggy at certain points and AI can be a bit silly sometimes the gameplay is still very fun and entertaining. However, the gameplay is not what makes this game great for me. There has never been a game that has made me sad before when a character died. The closest thing being when I nuked Megaton in Fallout 3 and talked to Moira afterwards. The playable characters in the game have some pretty neat stories and something about playing as them when you get them killed really hit me hard but it also makes for some great death. For example, I was going to save some allies that had gotten trapped during a scavenging run and as I was running up the river I heard the loud roar of a feral zombie and turned to see him jumping at my face just in time. Within seconds my character was promptly torn and half and killed. It then dropped me into another character from my community and I quickly gathered some supplies and went back out to not only save those allies but to get revenge on the character that had been killed. After finally finding the feral zombie I wailed him with a pipe in the face when he jumped at me, knocked him on his back and smashed his head in and then proceeded to save my allies after procuring the items that my last character had dropped. I highly recommend this game and give it an 8/10 the only reason it doesn't get those last two points is for some gameplay glitches and a story that wasn't quite as deep as I would like and somewhat predictable.

tl;dr State of Decay is an amazing open-world GTA-style action game.
Undead Labs' State of Decay is a really great zombie apocalypse game that blends a GTA-style (or perhaps a more appropriate comparison: Dead Rising-style) control scheme with a randomized, very dynamic mission system, where missions pop up and disappear every once in a while, sometimes forcing you to prioritize and make difficult decisions. This intensifies as the third major part of the gameplay, the base-building, comes into play. You are part of a group of survivors (and can switch between them), and are responsible for all parts of their survival - which includes ensuring a supply of food, medicine, ammunition, fuel as well as materials to construct defenses from. But due to the unpredictability of the zombies inhabiting the county you reside in, you may end up facing tough choices - do you expand into Marshall at the risk of leaving your base open to attacks from zombie hordes marching in from the north? Do you help a stranger in need or would you rather spend your time clearing infestations? And what if one of your people gets the plague? Can you live with putting a bullet in someone you just spent hours leveling up? Yep, nobody claimed zombie apocalypse was easy.
What makes choices like these even more harrowing is the fact that once someone is dead, they stay dead. That means if you play very badly, you may end up with very few survivors and a close to zero chance of making it through the next night. The fatigue mechanic also makes it impossible to concentrate on a "one-man army" tactic. Even the strongest survivor has to sleep every once in a while.
The biggest problem I've got with State of Decay is that it can end up taking all of my spare time. Personally, I take that as a sign of a really excellently crafted game.
Also, the graphics probably aren't going to win any awards anytime soon, but they're in no way hideous (except for a fair share of texture pop-in).
If you'd like a Dead Rising with looser time constrains (though not by much), a GTA with more zombies or a The Sims action game, you may just find State of Decay to be up your alley. But beware: It just may take up all your time!

This game is excellent. Got it on sale for $9.99 and it's worth every penny. It's what I've been looking for in a zombie game, and while it isn't perfect, it explores some of the things I've been looking for in zombie games. Things like scouting different areas, searching for food and resources in any and all buildings, choosing where to set up your home base, being able to set up safe zones (outposts) in any cleared location, vehicles that last quite awhile (if used properly) and don't fizzle out after hitting five zombies (looking at you Dead Rising 2), and much more. If you aren't much into those things then don't get it. If you are, then go ahead. There are different zombie types (regular, feral, SWAT, juggernaut, screamer, and bloater) which I'm not the biggest fan of, but they are all dealt with easily enough in their own way. Plus, I believe there is a mod to make all zombies the basic mindless type.
Give it a shot. I've easily put in 25 hours so far. Mainly because I'm just doing the missions that are busy work rather than story progression.

This game is sick, got hooked on the demo and I was able to import my save into the full game! Even if the Civil Rights / LGBTQ focus isn't super interesting to you, this game is the best piece of cyberpunk media I have experienced in years. It isn't purely dystopian, it deals with complex social subjects with subtelty, characters are vibrant and endearing, and the world is well realized. While the writing is top notch, the gameplay is incredibly intuitive. You won't ever have to spend 15 minutes checking individual pixels in a room for a key.
While I understand some might write this game off because they think it prioritizes pushing a social agenda before gameplay and adventure, I can say that is absolutely not the case. This adventure game is executed masterfully, and you are cheating yourself out of a great experience if you ignore it.
I don't meant to say having real socially relevant subject matter in games is inherently bad, but I have played some games that are sold more on their subject matter than gameplay, and it would be a crime not to emphasize how well Read Only Memories is put together as a game and as piece of fiction.

By the time i'm writing this review, we've already experienced what will very likely be the last game in the Souls series, and maybe even the last Souls-like by this developer, so if you're someone who is still yet to find an entry point to the series, i'm here to tell you why this one, the one game that refined everything Demon Souls did, and the one to begin the journey of the undead, is still to this date and in my humble opinion, the best of all of them.
Dark Souls was released on 2011, lacking both the big budget and the hype that its sequels and its brother game, Bloodborne, would later benefit from, yet i would dare to say that on its humbleness lies the true magic and charm that From Software would just not be able to top on later releases.
Players take the role of a chosen Undead, following an ancient prophecy that tells about uncovering the fate for its whole kind in the land of the ancient lords, Lordran, and this is where we will start pointing out the things that make Dark Souls unique.
The world design is, if not flawless, a true example of how open areas should be done, each landscape connects to the next one in a true seamless way, every detail in the background is a place that you will reach at some point, it's a world that expands in all directions and always makes sense, it never stops feeling like you're really travelling through this vast, old and forgotten land, like something out of the most magical fable.
Next is the one feature that became the trademark of the Souls series, its difficulty, Dark Souls is not only challenging, it is sometimes unfair and unforgiving, and while this might sound like something negative, once you experience it, it is  far from it, it is a game that will see you fail, and will dare you to try again, will dare you to succeed on what it has set to make unconquerable...
and then you try, then you try harder, once and again, and then you succeed, and the satisfaction that comes with it, is something that no other series has made me feel yet.
The atmosphere of this game is yet another thing that was done so right, the areas range from gloomy, going through desolate, to absolutely terrifying; while you traverse the land, you will notice the lack of any background music (This being reserved only for its boss battles and the place where you first step into Lordran, the Firelink Shrine, every piece being a magnificent composition by Motoi Sakuraba) but far from making it feel lackluster, it adds to the immersion, to that feeling of being by yourself amidst all kinds of perils.
Every area has just this darkness feeling to it, like you're about to be swallowed by the very land under your feet, and yet for some reason, speaking graphics wise, the next Souls games just didn't seem to get this right.
The last point i will talk about is its very particular storytelling, Dark Souls features very little dialogue from only a small number of characters you will meet during your journey, yet every item, weapon and armor in the game contains a small description about its origins and its place in the world, it is by piecing together all these small stories that a larger narrative is born, and suddenly the world has a background of depths that maybe long cutscenes and hours of dialogue would not be able to equal.
As this review has become very extended, if you have made it to this paragraph, i thank you, and i deeply recommend that you give this game a chance, at the moment i'm writing this the game is on sale, it is a perfect moment to start what i hope is for you, as it was for me, one of the most unique experiences gaming will ever offer.

I recommend going as a melee class in this game and just whacking away on stuff. So you can see I put in a couple of hours to this game. I won't get too detailed here, there's enough reviews, I'll only list a few points worth knowing.
The story is both interesting and boring. Interesting ideas, that is, but boring presentation, and it also has one of those stories where the "truth" learned in the last act pretty much makes the rest of the game seem pointless--much of the struggle you go through is just fluff, and plot-wise, could be removed without incident. Characters are very flat, are never in more than a few scenes, and there just isn't much dramatic weight.
But that's not why you play Monster Hunter games, which this basically is, is it? Strangely, I can only thing of bad specifics to list--too easy later on, too many reskins and ways of bypassing enemy strengths, not balanced, requires frustrating min/maxing to take advantage of certain roles and moves, kind of a boring world with too many ruins (even where people are living is usually ruins), last two dungeons are overly complex, etc. Yet, I don't dislike the game at all. It's fun to plan your character, and your pawn, and then try to fill in the gaps with other pawns. It's good to min/max, to explore and find YOUR style. It's fun learning how to pwn your enemies. And then restarting to try a different playstyle forces you to relearn alot of that. Nothing about the game is really and truly awesome and memorable, even the whole "Climb giant enemies to stab them in the neck", but the whole thing is very fun and addictive for a long time.

A brilliant but flawed and ambitious venture into Action RPGs.
The story is inherently forgettable and the world feels somewhat unfinished, but that doesn't really take away the fun that comes from tightness of the controls, immensely enjoyable gameplay, non-restricting progression and overall very high quality of the experience. It's that kind of a game that does enough unique things with a popular formula to feel fresh many years after its release.
The PC port runs wonderfully on weaker machines and it comes with a huge DLC area that adds tens of hours of fun and extra playtime. I wholeheartedly recommend Dragon's Dogma for every fan of the ARPG genre.
