A lot of thought has gone into making it different, there are some interesting challenges and good character interaction - and its not another WW2 game! With shades of HL2 and Crysis this is however very much its own game with a 1984/Orwellian atmosphere and an essential time shift ability this really works as a game. The ability to manipulate time becomes second nature as the game progresses. Slow time to take on the enemy when you are outnumbered. Pause time to walk up and take a weapon, or take on another bloke in a time suit. Reverse time, to go up in a lift that has just fallen. It's also possible to pause time to enable you to step of a runaway train, walk through fire, walk on water etc.

Don't buy it for it's time-manipulation bs - the meter that it lets you control time with is so small a frame that you basically need accelerated senses anyway to slow down time...If your expecting a modern take on Prince of Persia - you DON'T want this.
Also the AI feels a bit scripted instead of natural - case in point: you try to destroy this big yellow mech with allies, the mech heals when you don't shoot it and the allies backing you continuely return to fire and make the same death scene whether you reverse time or not. Basically unless you can 1hit it with inferior weapons and/or make use of the limited time-manipulation reserves you have (something I wasn't able to do) you can't destroy it - however by backing up for cover you also reset the scene so you have to do all this without running back for shelter from it's rockets.
Finally Contrary to popular belief in time-manipulation crowds - you cannnot "undo" a gameover in this game by reversing time.

A good game that was overlooked on release (indeed I myself didn't bother with it). Above all it is
. I'd describe it almost like HL2 with much better shooting/weapon design and less bloat. Indeed they even use the same physics engine (Havok) common to many games e.g. F.E.A.R.
It isn't hard to see why many would write it off as the first two hours or so are rather meh.  Average weapons/shooting (though each gun does have a secondary fire that normally does something fun), bullet spongy generic enemies, so-so level design and the time powers seem like nothing more than a gimmick.
Then it improves. More open levels, interesting level design instead of bland urban areas and you get the first fun weapon (an explosive-bolt firing crossbow). The enemy designs start to vary too from stand and shoot to jetpacks and energy shields. Time powers become important (you're never far from death) and the setting changes from generic dystopia to
sort-of future. It's perhaps best described as similar in style to an 80s or 90s cartoon with its mixture of a serious story and rule-of-cool setting.  Never does it get too silly or too serious, however.
From this point onwards the game just gets steadily better and better until it ends adding more fun weapons, enemies and levels not to mention some vehicle sections (honestly I didn't realise how much I missed them in modern games). Sure it's a little short and another 2-3 hours would have been nice but it leaves you wanting more which is preferable to a game so full of filler you're happy to finish. Again it compares favourably to HL2 which dragged on far too long. The ending levels are, again, in the more boring urban area but it's nice to revisit them seeing the changes you've made with your time travel.
Story isn't amazing but functional and doesn't have any major flaws. It does make some use of the time travel concept but believe me this isn't the type of game you buy for the story. There are also some puzzles that are slightly unintuitive but you aren't likely to have any major problems and if you do google is always available.

Mediocre shooter with porting and technological issues.
The gameplay idea and mechanic is pretty interesting; you control time; slow it down, stop it, or even reverse it.
However, that does not make the game fun.
The presentation is pretty good at places, but the shooting is very generic, unprecise (big crosshair where shots seemed off of the central point), and unrewarding.
Graphics are pretty mediocre.
Levels are very linear, with the occasional wait for trigger or wait for NPC scene.
As for the technological side of things:
The key bindings are totally off - a bad port from consoles.
The game first launched on my smaller, second monitor. I had to fiddle with ini configuration files to increase resolution and make it automatically decide to use the other monitor (good luck if you have multiple monitors with the same resolution).
Especially in the tutorial, I noticed *big* hung-ups when I entered new areas, even rooms, where it probably loaded some data. A bit later, you occasionally slow down, simply walking a lot slower, which probably hides the loadung unresponsiveness. Hung-ups are definitely not something you like to see on a powerful PC.
When launching, it tells me my drivers are not supported, twice, and links me to a dead website.
All in all, I had no fun at all in the little I played (I did press through the tutorial to see if the game itself, with the time manipulation aspect was any fun, but it was not), and with the technological issues, I’m thinking about refunding the game - because I certainly won’t play it any more.
Definitely no recommendation.

If you liked Sonic 1, 2, 3 and Knuckles (and Knuckles), but never had the chance to play CD because only 5 people ever owned a Sega CD, then this game is 100% worthwhile. This port is excellent - it improves the physics engine massively over the original so it feels like you're playing a classic Sonic game, it allows switching between the US and JP soundtracks (both of which have their strong points), and adds Tails as a playable character. If you're in the midst of Mania but never experienced Stardust Speedway in its original form, then this is absolutely worth your time.
Not to say the game doesn't have its downsides. The peel out renders the spindash almost useless. The level design feels like they tried to cram everything into as small of a level as possible, so it feels like you're always running into obstacles and don't get the chance to go fast. The time travel mechanic, while interesting, makes getting the best ending a pain in the proverbial.
Next to the peaks that are 2 and 3&K, CD is dwarfed in comparison, but it still stands tall over a vast majority of other Sonic games.

This remaster of Sonic CD is great on most points. It has basic resolution adjustments and a few options regarding pixel display. Just beware, if you have a 144hz monitor, you will have to cap the game at 60fps using external software; I couldn't find a way to enable a cap in-game. The game will run faster than intended if your monitor is higher than 60hz. Other than that, the remaster is great. The soundtrack sounds high quality as well, and you can choose between the JP and US soundtracks.
For Sonic CD itself and not the quality of its remaster, I think it's a fantastic game. It's easy to pick up and play, but complex to clear, especially on the later stages. Stages are winding with incredible variance from playthrough to playthrough, and it's (usually) a joy to play. The only things going against this game are the occasional hiccups; horrible levels that are just sadistic. The only one that comes to my mind is that ♥♥♥♥ing pinball stage. It's absolutely atrocious. I was stuck trying to get up the tiny corridor for close to 30 minutes. Maybe I was just missing something, but that was infuriating. I actually spent the same amount of time on the final stage of the game, which is just stupid considering how mundane the pinball section was. Anyways, though this level did detract from the experience, I still had a blast and finished the game in one sitting. The fun gameplay and stellar spritework (this game looks great) is all tied together by a kickass soundtrack. Really, the presentation in the visuals and soundtrack are top notch, and the soundtrack has tons of unforgettable pieces.
Sonic CD is a really great experience and this remaster is fine for anyone with a 60hz monitor or FPS capping software. I definitely recommend picking it up to remember this classic franchise (or Sonic Mania, of course).

Review for Sonic CD by Joey
Gameplay 8/10
It's the lovely smooth and fast gameplay you'd expect from sonic, in the original the spindash was nerfed to make you use the super peelout more but this version of the game gives you the less pace breaking original so that original flow breaking issue is gone for those who wish to have what they're used to.
Levels are short in this game but there is a good reason for that, the levels are made very vertically over horizontally  because the objective of each level is to find the signpost labeled (past), jet off super fast till you go to the alternate past version of the stage and destroy a capsule in the level to save the future in that zone (Which you can travel to after and see all the good you did with a brighter look on it and a new theme). When you play the game with that mindset and enjoy the platforming side of it over the dashing speed part you'll enjoy the game more. (It's of note you can get the time stones which is this games chaos emeralds to get the good ending without once destroying a pod)
If I had to give this game downfalls, they would be the boss fights which include (wait till he attacks and hit him 3 times in a row and win, play an easy game of pinball, not drown by attacking the boss and 4 hits of the easiest to avoid / counter attacks in history) with the only good boss of the game being the featured Metal Sonic.
Special stages in this version of the game are fixed to be fun this time, not lag fests making it impossible to judge speed in.
Graphics: 9/10
Everything in this game looks so colourful and bright that it just screams fun while you're jetting through the levels or searching for rings or pods, also a big bonus to this version is the special stages no longer have the god awful lag that they originally did making them look as great as they should have done in motion all those years ago.
If I had to say something negitive for a CD game it doesn't look the best but for a classic sonic the improvements are clearly there and I can't deny that.

For my review I had the JP ost and it's great, every tune is enguaging and hype, if you have no plans to play the game I hope you'll at least take the time to listen to the JP OST, it's a great listen.
Overall: 9/10

This open-world survival horror is an interesting hybrid, borrowing elements from other games while maintaining a unique style. It begins quickly and with little exposition: the first player character, Marcus returns from a camping trip to find the world he once knew is now his worst nightmare. You must fight to survive in a post-apocalyptic setting, securing supplies and reinforcing safe houses and areas you will secure as you progress in the game.
The game will cleverly deliver both experienced and inexperienced characters making the way you manage your characters key to the survival of your safe house and those in it.
While there is a story running throughout State of Decay, it wisely plays second fiddle to the open-world exploration and survival aspect of the game.
Game play in State of Decay is no joke, you have no second chances, so when you screw up, it’s on you. A character dead is a resource permanently lost, and may and will be devastating. So never act or play in a rush, make your choices carefully and plan ahead. Do nt rush it, never rush in this game or you will pay dearly. And even though this may sound like a "con", this is what makes this game so exciting. Whatever happens, it is for real.

Lucy - The Enternity She Wished For is a great entry-level Visul Novel. If you haven't played a VN before, this is a great place to start.
Keeping short at probably just under 5 hours ( I tended to pause and go AFK while the game was open) the game isn't as full-featured as many other VNs out there (Katawa Shoujo for instance). Nevertheless, the game is a great way to introduce someone into the world of VNs. Having spent over 25 hours in Katawa Shoujo, and having touched on other VNs and the like, I still enjoyed playing this game. It has a great storyline, fantastic art, absolutely spot on voice acting, and enough different paths to take that the replay value is valid another couple of times. I didn't find any part of it slow or boring, nor did I ever think it was dragging on.
Lucy - The Enternity She Wished For is a great way to get into the world of VNs and appreciate what they are. While not the most full featured VN out there, it provides a great base for getting a feel on the world of VNs. If you're looking for somewhere to start, this is the perfect place. Well worth the price, congrats on getting funded on Kickstarter and Greenlit for this, I'm glad it made its way to Steam and I found it, it was a nice experience and I look forward to future projects from the developers behind it.

Obsidian have reinvigorated my CRPG love with Pillars of Eternity.
The game has been designed to generate nostalgia whilst showing a way forward for the genre.

No where is this more evident than in the sound design: everything just sounds like adventure done right, right down to the clang of swords on armor, expert voice acting and epic musical score.
The writing is deep, lore-filled and witty: everything you would expect from master storytellers Obsidian.
The art direction is straight fantasy for the most part, but there are plenty of ways Pillars differentiates itself from the common fare: little touches of detail and beauty even in the ugliest of evil monsters... it's isometric done right.
Overall, I can't recommend this enough to anyone who likes RPGs in the slightest... you'll get lost in an amazing world, and be much happier for it.  You must gather your party before venturing forth, and what a party it is in Eora.

A great take on games like Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale, the most recent game I played like this would be Neverwinter Nights two. (Note I am very nostalgic for Baldur's Gate 2 so this review is probably biased, I found an Easter egg in the game referencing something in Baldur's Gate and freaked out.)
The game knows what it wants to be like and lives up to the older games quite well while still trying to be somewhat original. The game has its own separate lore and world. Its classes while similar are different enough to not be generic but not so strange as to be confusing. One thing that is totally different however is the combat system, a point which I have seen in a few of the negative reviews. It is a bit weird when you first start and isn't very similar to the older games however I found the different mechanics very interesting. Does it not make sense that having a giant shield on your arm will decrease your accuracy? And that you attack slower the heavier the amour you are wearing? I just decked out one guy with both and made him a meat shield, he does less damage than the priest but then again he doesn't need to, he just needs to protect my ranged damage dealers and support, works fine for me.
This game's characters however are somewhat of a contradiction, while each has their own background and quest they really become near totally opinion-less once in your party, not to say that having them speak up all the time would be a good thing but I never did anything that so disgusted or conflicted with a character that it caused them to leave or have some other penalty like in Dragon Age making them feel like automatons.  There is no opinion system for each character and most of the time they don’t seem to react to your reputations. Additionally you had to ask most of the characters to join your party instead of them being forced with you are through a point of convenience which was annoying for me as by the time I met most of them I already had a full party and didn’t really want them. The fact that I can create my own full party of customized characters from scratch really stopped me from using the ones you could recruit, the only downside to them being that you didn’t get any of the extra dialogue.
That being said the game can end A LOT of different ways, based upon the quests you do and the factions you aid, the ending of each character also being a large part of that. A single character can have around half-a-dozen different endings. While some of them are rather obvious, (complete their quest to make them happy), other times simply choosing the wrong dialogue option in a conversation can lead to a different ending, which chafes a bit seeing as you could only guess at the outcome your words will have on their future and you want to act in character, something the game usually rewards you for.  From what I hear there are only six characters of which only four I found and recruited, I only used two for the majority of the game preferring to make my own companions.
The only truly huge thing I hated about the game and which made me rage at my screen is that sometimes the movement and attack AI for the characters is far worse than the original games that his one takes after. The graphics might be a new take on a classic but the AI seems straight out of some of the older games with a few tweaks to make them more infuriating. I can’t say the number of times I’ve yelled at a character for doing something stupid. Everything from standing around doing nothing apparently taking the sights during battle towards actually contradicting the commands I give them as they are executing them, “You wanted me to go over there? Eff you magic hand in the sky, I’m going to go over here and get myself killed!”.
The pathing is also a big problem, out of combat a character can pretty much walk through a rest of the group with ease, in combat however the rules change and all it takes is a single character in the middle of even a large door way to block the whole rest of the group, and while bottle-necking is a really useful strategy you usually want to bottleneck the enemy not your own party…  Additionally the AI has a habit of going after a single enemy with reckless abandon. This can manifest in anything from a character going all the way around the battle lines to attack an arbitrary enemy when there is a perfectly good one to attack right next to them, to a character glitching out and heading off into the fog of war alone to attack a enemy even I don’t know is there, and which certainly isn’t part of the current encounter. All of this being said I can forgive quite a bit of it as you are supposed to micromanage your party, I just got lax and was angered at their incompetence.
Well now that I got that off my chest I can say that still quite enjoyed the game and would recommend it to anyone who enjoyed similar games like this. It may have felt a bit short and I was a little disappointed that by the time I got a party I liked all together, equipped, and specialized, the game was over. Additionally I do have a grief about the Endless Paths however the review is already way to long…

I started playing this game because I wanted an RPG to play when my D&D group couldn't meet. I've never played a crpg like this, though I did play the first Fallout a few times, and tried (but didn't finish) Fallout 2. I've also played Fallout: New Vegas, and really liked that.
I got what I expected: a challenging, interesting rpg that kept surprising me with how detailed and thorough the developers were. Every time I've sat down to play, I've been pleasantly surprised to find something interesting or unexpected, to experience a funny (or tragic) piece of dialogue, to be drawn in by the narrative--and often just the exposition--or to discover an interesting use of a familiar mechanic.
Pillars of Eternity is tough, though. It forces you to think about placement, pacing, and specifically how your characters interact on the battlefield. It's killed me many times, and frustrated me enough to turn it off several times. But each time I hit a wall, I learn something, much they way you're supposed to in an rpg like this. My biggest frustration is that the rules are very, very similary to D&D (I'm most familiar with 5e, but I have some knowledge of 3.5 and 4, and I have a feeling it's far more like 4e than any of the other editions, given the sheer volume of stats). That leads to situations where I expect something to happen, but it doesnt, because the rools deviate in an unexpected way. It's something that only happens once in a while, but when it does, it's like getting a sliver from your favorite rocking chair. A cruel an unexpected betrayal.
Also, Kana sucks.

Usually I'd love this sort of game with the great fantasy elements, and as much as I'd love to say graphics and such don't matter, they really do for this sort of game, in my opinion anyway, especially on character customisation, which can be a massive part of the immersion. It isunfortunate that Capcom seems to want players to roleplay as a potato-beast.
With this game from Cap in particular, it felt like we'd been thrown back to Dragon Age: Origins, in terms of graphics and animation quality, whereas even that got customisation well done, and also had very good voice acting. I like good graphics and such, and I can usually overlook them when they're awful if the gameplay and such else is captivating, and I do really like the SotC vibe of climbing on everything, but SotC was acceptable for the time and was much smoother, but this plays like your stock JRPG. Everything is rigid, every animation is robotic, the 3D models, meshes, textures, and clipping is all god-awful, and that's not to mention the voice acting, it doesn't help that NPC's constantly talk over one another and if you have subtitles on to try and catch what they're saying, the UI takes up half your screen.
I was really expecting to like this, but I got a feel for the gameplay within the tutorial area, and knew it wasn't going to deviate from that at all. It has a set formula it follows to the damn T and sticks with it. The switching styles on the fly to adapt to combat was a nice element I enjoyed and thought 'I could get into this', but that one niceity is so overshadowed by everything else.
If you like boxcut JRPG's, you'll like this. It's a 'tried and true' type that people seem to love but it's not my cup of tea and I'm not sure why it's so engaging to others when it's really not engaging the player whatsoever.

This game is too much fun:
Graphics
The graphics are good if you turn them up and have a decent computer (mine is pretty damn good) for a 2013 game (this is being reviewed in 2015).
Story
The story was OK, but it was quite short (compared to most games), depending on how you played the game would either be 5-6 hours long, or 12-15 hours long, and thats quite a big difference.
Gameplay
If you are into textbook stealth mechanics with cover systems, a choice between lethal and non-leathal weapons and gadgets and good assault gameplay, this is definetly for you.
Co-op
The co-op makes this game infinitly more fun, throwing dudes of buildings, almost getting caught, getting caught, last minute choices, and if your playing with random people online it makes it even more fun.
Multiplayer (Competitive)
The multiplayer is fun, mainly for me being the spies is more fun, as you have more agility than Sam Fisher (the protaganist), therefore being able to reach higher places. And the Mercs are basically armoured dudes with guns trying to stop the spies. The spies are in 3rd person mode like the story and co-op, and the mercs are first person, like you will experience playing one or two of the story missions with Briggs.
Customization
The customization of your character for the story and co-op (Sam Fisher) and Spies VS Mercs are all together quite good. There are multiple choices of loadouts, from Panther (Stealth kills) and Ghost (Stealth knockouts), to Assault (Non-stealth kills) and a combination of all three. And the more you customize, the more badass you look.
All together, I would give this game an 8/10.

Not counting hours offline, or hours from Xbox...this game has become one of my all-tme favorite games of recent memory. The amount of hours cannot speak enough for how much this game has tested me. Good and bad, I suppose.
This gloomy-yet beautiful world is full of danger - the undead, the supernatural, the unknown, and even people just like you (albeit online invasions, fighting bosses together, and covenant-related objectives). The story in question is vague and perhaps for good reason, having you try and piece out the lore of this world in order to overcome all that's in your way, or at least when deciding how to conclude this game. That, and Wikis really help.
The game has aged since released, but still stands out as a world to be both invested and swallowed in. From the array of enemies (undead soliders, black knights, skeleltons, drakes, towering armored guards, friendly chests that may or may not try to eat you upon opening them, etc.), the scope of how you want your character to be - a typical knight, mage, thief, pyromancer, among others. The world as mentioned again is unforgiving, but almost fascinating enough to push forward, only to see a greater challenge ahead. To put it simply without giving away too much detail - it's a hard game, but it's a game you'll love because it's hard. Dark Souls is known for being challenging for a reason, and it still remains a game I can jump back into, with a few dozen deaths here and there.
All I can say is that it's worth giving a try, and once you become invested in the game, the world only opens up further.
P.S. - I highly recommend downloading the DSfix mod for this game. It'll allow the use of editing the game in order to have it run on your own preferred settings. Unlocking the framerate drastically improves this game for me.

Imagine you are playing half life, but only with the crowbar. And without the save system. And every time you die, you are starting in a different level. Now, there are pickups along the way to make it easier/more interesting for you. But sometimes, those pickups transform the crowbar in a giant dildoe, sometimes they stop you from sprinting. Sometimes they make the crowbar shoot flames all over the enemies, sometimes they grant you the noclip power. And regularly, you can see very helpful powerups placed out of your reach. As for the enemies, well, they are randomly generated, in totally inconsistent quantities/order: sometimes you have three headcrabs in an open space, and other times you find fourty two Vortigaunts in a confined corridor.
With such mechanics, one easily understands that winning/losing is much less influenced by the average player's skills, and much more by the RNG. To the extent that said skills become utterly irrelevant, and most people who think they are "good" at the game are essentially only being lucky: the only way to progress is to buff the character enough to compensate for the difficulty increase (modulo your skills - but don't be fooled, only very few humans have the skills to consistently beat the game without a single powerup) as you go deeper; but not only the powerups (or downs) are random (fair, it's a roguelike), they also regularly placed out of reach... So that when you win; you are perfectly aware that the game "lets you win".
I truly wish I could recommend it because it is otherwise a very solid game; and aside from its main shortcoming, does the original TBOI justice more than well.
But unfortunately one of the major elements of game design, the reward system, is really broken. It might be that some people feel rewarded after a win, being oblivious to the fact that they only won because the RNG was favourable to them, and not because of their actions; but for those of us who are aware that the game does not present the player with the mechanics needed for choice making and has zero strategy involved, there is no reward feeling, even for winning. One of my friends even told me: "the only thing this game rewarded was me stopping to play it".
The problem lies with the fact that what makes a game fun is that it rewards intelligence, and learning, by giving the players the tools to change the outcome of situations with adequate reactions to stimulis, which have a
logic behind them; no matter how complex. This game does not allow for learning, as one cannot learn randomness (or crypto wouldn't even be). This is actually a rather common flaw in rogue likes, where random generators are replacing most of the game design, when they should only drive it; and TBOI:R is far from being the only game affected by that problem. However, it is one of the most interesting of those problematic games, and this is why I wrote a review for it, and not the other ones.
This could be strongly mitigated if the game design allowed the player to bet on the items they find or commit sacrifices for the items they need (more or less in the way banks and loans work): if you have 53 pennies in the first level, but zero key, you could for example sacrifice some of it, or your health, to obtain a key and unlock the shop's door. Or if you see an out of reach "full health pill" (that you know to be so because you already discovered it), taking a damage blow while being at one heart would kill you, unless you decide to pay that one heart with a few seconds delay, so you have the time to get the pill and use it before taking the damage. Or giving temporary flight at the cost of sudden-death to access a powerup impossible to reach anyway because it's surrounded by half a screen of unbreakable blocks and you can't fly. Or having the RNG settings consistent, by making the difficulty of the monsters depending on the current loadout (so you don't end up with flight + blood barrage against small bouncing worms while you previously had chocolate milk and a speed-nerfed character against black death).
As for myself, well, I still play it, mainly because I am attracted by its undeniable qualities; but I found myself arbitrarily starting a new game while playing more often than not. The reason for that is that I do not wish to invest so much time and effort into something arbitrarily aborted by a RNG.
In short, TBOI:R could be a fantastic game; but is too simplistic in its design to properly leverage the abilities of most players. So unless you are a hardcore fan of reflex-only games taking the "decisions" for you, you probably will not enjoy this game for long.
Due to the reaction of numerous people to this review, I would like to make things clear: while TBOI:R is a hard game, it is NOT VERY HARD. Difficulty comes from challenge, and challenge comes from something you can overcome. Lifting one ton of stone with your pinkie isn't hard, it's impossible. This game, and that is the entire point of the review, does not do "hard" correctly. It does it randomly, which sometimes happens to be correctly, sometimes isn't hard at all; and sometimes is plain impossible (as I brought up in the comments to the first version of this review; I ended up in situations that had very easy bosses spawn flies literally faster than I could
tears).
To be completely honest, this ish is too fast for me but I got it for free so I'll recommend it if you can get it for free.

Much like the time manipulation gameplay it's based on, Timeshift is a window into time. A time when games had to try and be as familiar as possible, but still contain a gimmick to attract any sort of audience.
Superfically the gunplay of Timeshift is very reminisicent of F.E.A.R, Timesplitters Future Perfect and Star Wars Republic Commando. The art style is painfully reminiscient of Gears of War. And the timeshifting gameplay itself is taken straight from Prince of Persia: The Sands of TIme.
Something you may have noticed is all of these games released years prior to Timeshift. As dated as Timeshift is right now, it was dated even when it came out. The game is painfully linear, the art style is very generic and colorless, the storyline is laughably generic and sounds like half a dozen other shooters and the time shifting gameplay feels too much like a gimmick. I end up just not using it at all because it makes the game too easy even on the hardest difficulty.
But I still recommend this game for people who like first person shooters. The game is still surprisingly competant, and its multiplayer was a halfway decent attempt at mimicing Timesplitters Future Perfect. But you have to go into it knowing that it's very generic and unimpressive. It does a good job at being a clone. Much like the time manipulation gameplay it's based on, Timeshift is stuck in the past and never moved on.

I had high hopes for this game when I backed it, and I was thrilled to play it when it came out.  I have my complaints, but the enjoyable experience far outweighs them.  This game is fun.  The story is intelligent (it just doesn't go as deep as I'd hoped.)  None of the puzzles are particularly mind-bending, but they still leave a feeling of satisfaction upon completion.  The dialog is great.  Most of the characters' lines are a perfect balance of corny and heartfelt (though I could have done without 4Moolah).  I've played through twice and enjoyed both experiences.
There are a couple of spots where the game forces me to make a decision I don't feel is in line with what the characters would choose based on information they had.  I get that this is used to keep the story on its rails, but in at least one case it was done so unsubtly that it gave away a huge plot point.  It didn't detract too much from enjoying the game though, and really just limits the scope of the story to save a little time.
Absolutely play this game if you enjoy the point and click adventure genre.

After too long, we finally have another retro-SF adventure game for the ages.  Its retro graphics are perfectly designed and laid out for today's widescreen displays, and its pixel art is just blocky enough to call back to the days of yore while being simple enough to be workable when it releases on smartphones and tablets in Q1 2016.  Its music calls back to 80s retro-futurism with catchy tunes that you'll have difficulty forgetting, especially the memorable credits track 'Love Me Better', so I'm really glad I decided to get the bundle with the OST.
The only thing I didn't like about Read Only Memories was its length - I played through it once in 6 hours with no walkthrough, and I'm really missing the sights and sounds of Neo-SF already :(  It's probably the best flaw any experience could have, though.

Catchy soundtrack
Retro graphics
Classic adventure game gameplay
CONS:
Length
Not enough uses for the Spoiled Milk

The game dos have a problem with explaining certain elements, with much being learned through trial and error and very little knowledge from the game, but the game is actually fun. Four different class options, with enough similarities and differences to be able to find a build for any number of players or any play style. You do have to play through the levels many times to unlock your key skills for your prefered play style, and the levels do not change. but the puzzle elements,bonus challenges and the challenge to beat the level within a  cartain time IMO do balance it out. Story wise, it is lacking a bit, with a very simple story that does not do a great job with immersing you in the game, but it does add these little spots of humor every now and then. Combat consists of repeatedly pressing a button, with a few abilities that are modified depending on the marks on your enemy, which are added every time you land an attack on said enemy. Modifications usually include a cooldown reduction, more damage, or a larger knockback radius. There are also a selection of passive abilities that add a bit more customization to your character, allowing you to make him more unique. This game currently has two game modes: A story mode, which allows you to go through the levels and increase your characters power, and survival, which allows you to face wave after wave of enemies using the abilites unlocked in story mode. The game supports up to four players, with the difficulty scaling to the number of players currently playing.

This game has an unfortuantely rough start. You're tromping all over a large area with no real ability to fast travel and, if you're doing side quests, doubling back through areas that are no longer challenging. However, once you get a little ways into the game, and can place a few of your own fast travel beacons, the game starts to really open up. When you first start, I'd recomend getting a list of the missable quests and then following the main story as quickly as possible, until you can get to Hill Figure Knoll and pick up your first port crystal (don't forget to pick up your eternal ferry stone from the inn in Grand Soren). I also recomend hitting up the Bitterblack Isle as soon as you're comfortable with it, since it removes all of the tedious wandering around and has some absolutely gorgeous scenery.
Once you get past all of that though, the game is like a mix of Dark Souls and Elder Scrolls, with the ability to climb on monsters. It also has some rather interesting classes and the ability to freely swap between them, at inns, so you can change up your build pretty much at will.
Lastly, on a personal note, please look up what pawn inclanations do. They're actually important.

Quick review
I like it... with caveats.  The game has a very nice combat system - fluid, fast-paced, and highly interactive.  The downside is that you will be using it mostly against waves of low-level filler monsters, whose purpose is to slow you down on your long treks between places of actual interest.  The story is a tolken effort as well.  However, it's all worth it (for me, at least) for the battles with the larger monsters, which can get pretty intense and exciting.  These fights are very engaging as you climb all over them to hit weak spots or cut off pieces of armour as they react to your movements.  It feels like how a fight with a giant mythical monster would go down.  To get your greatest enjoyment out of the game I recommend:  tracking down texture upgrade mods, playing as one of the hand-to-hand classes, and being willing to be patient with the tedium.
Conversation
FIrst and foremost: explosive red barrels.  Can we not, please?  Any emergent tactics they provide are overshadowed by the damage they do to my immersion.  Unless a game is the long overdue tale of the guy who keeps placing these in radom locations - along with the tiny items in smashable, over-sized, novelty crates - I don't want to see them any more.  Thank you for your consideration.
The next overdone cliché I need to bring up is "the prophecy".  Player characters are always rising above their humble beginnings after being told that their coming has been foretold by legend, and the fate of the world blah, blah, blah.  Let's call this out for the lazy writing it is.  It is a ham-fisted, in-game excuse for why the player is playing the game so that a plausible player personality doesn't need to be established.  It gives all of the NPCs something to call you, so they don't have to actually use your custom name.  By the by, you can use a pre-determined actual name, I'm okay with that.  Proper epics start with a pastoral, but why can't any of our characters adventure because they have always adventured?  Instead, a talentless fisherman just ups and leaves his life and is now personally responsible for everyone with a tentacle♥♥♥♥♥♥monster in the basement, every army that needs a siege broken on their castle, every villager that hasn't seen another villager all morning, and every anonymous bounty placed on... 45 rabbits, what?  The legend cliché is a way of telling you that what you are doing is important to the world rather than showing you.
Open world gaming is more ambitious than linear story arcs, but that don't necessarily equate to a better gaming experience.  Dragon's Dogma is a very large world, with imposing castles and varied landscapes and it all feels so empty.  And that largeness becomes a chore through the numerous A-to-B-and-back quests.  And now someone wants to be escorted to B, because reasons.  And someone wants you to run around and shoot 25 crows, or collect item drops from monsters for reward, or collect plants for the lame alchemy system, etc.  This is all a MMORPG set of mechanics that is designed to be addictive rather than fun.  It's totally the wrong model for a game like this, as it is designed to eat up player time.  But the game makers make the same amount of money on the game if I play the game every day for ten years or buy it and never end up installing it.  So it's not helping them.  As a player I want to see the exciting content and not sit around killing 45 skeletons in such-and-such area.  So it's not helping me.  They are doubling down on the least interesting parts of the game, rather than focusing on the epic fights that the game does well.  If it were a more linear narrative and setting they could have maintained a finer control on the pacing and this could have been a smoking hot game.  And, seriously, if you want your game world to feel large you need to put more people in your towns.
Thoroughly into pet-peeve territory is monster ecology.  My dad was a wildlife biologist, sue me.  Imagine, if you will, a long trek through the back roads takes you on a long, winding mountain path.  There, you have heard tell of an ancient temple hidden behind the water fall.  You squeeze through the narrow passage behind the falls to find the temple is located through a cavernous maze of puzzles and traps.  The zealots of the old god have left their treasures behind, set up their traps, reset all of the puzzle locks blocking the passages, and buggered off - as is the custom in archaic religions.  So why, when I get to the heart of the temple, why do I find a dozen large lizards and a 10m tall cyclops?  Did they all find and squeeze through the narrow opening behind the falls?  Does the cyclops get along with the lizards?  Is this waterfall-based society surviving on the "small rank fish" that is only source of food in the temple?  Are they resetting the trick bridge and re-hiding its control lever as they go back and forth?  This sort of set up has always bugged me, but in a game that really should be about it's big monsters, it describes a wasted opportunity to be a bit more "Monster Hunter".  It doesn't have to be elaborate, but if I believe in the setup I believe in the world.  If track down the cyclops based on where they like to live and what they like to eat then I am engaged with the monster.  I am interested in that monster.  Instead its always so very random, and it feels like such a waste.

"Oh, it's just another Pocket Tanks clone" you might think. Well, you're wrong then.
Yes, ShellShock Live shares many concepts with Scorched Earth, Pocket Tanks and all the other old-school tank-duelling games, but it doesn't make it a rip-off, rather a spiritual successor.
is done, in my opinion, just in a way such a game should have. There's a chance for you to get almost any weapon during a match, but you mostly get the weapons you already unlocked. Levelling up unlocks more weapons, and all the weapons are upgradable as you deal damage with them. This means that you are free to experiment with a wild range of weapons even at lower levels, but you still have a purpose to do better and level up. You don't have to grind for exp, levelling up doesn't take long at all.
The game isn't free, but that is very much a positive thing, because it allows to get rid of any sort of in-game payed features (yes, even the cosmetic changes can only be bought through playing the game) and minimize the amount of cancer.
are quite nice, both somewhat simplistic and high-quality at the same time. The sound is also good, albeit sometimes a bit too loud. The game is pretty much stable (on Linux at least), it crashed only once.
The best thing about this game, however, is how flexible it is in terms of gameplay. Not only the frightening number of different weapons and maps to play with, but the number of different game modes as well, from simple deathmatches to sniping competitions and soccer. You can also play the game with basic ballistic trajectories, or make it increasingly harder by enabling wind and putting different restrictions on used weapons, whatever suits you best. These changes are balanced by increasing the multiplier on recieved XP and raiting gains.
Now, the raiting system at this point is kinda useless, apart from deciding if you really want to play with a team of low-rated people.

You like sneaking through shadows? Waiting for your enemies to make a mistake and strike? Or do you like to run and gun? In Splinter Cell Blacklist you can do both or a way between it.
I admit that i didn't expect much of the game as i bought it. Somehow i played every Splinter Cell game till now, but it never really got me hooked. I always liked the sneaking tho. The same happened to me with this game. But hold on. This doesn't mean the game is mediocre.
The story is decent enough. Easy to follow, but not really impacting.
The characters are good. Some known characters like Grimsdottir are  on board as well as new ones like the CIA Agent Briggs. The first time you see Briggs you know that he was mostly included to offer a partner for co-op gameplay, which is part of the game as well. Nonetheless i liked Briggs at the end. He showed a lot of character and the development of not only him, but all characters is very well done.
The mission design is the usual Splinter Cell formula. Hack computer system, defuse bombs, rescue hostages, kill HVT's. Nothing really new, but still enough to never get boring. Aside from the Single Player missions there are also 20 side missions. 5 for infiltrating and hacking, 5 for assassination, 5 co op exclusive missions and 5 last stand missions where you have to hold of against an ever increasing number of enemies. The side missions are good enough. Offer a bit of plot even if not that much.
The game has really good mechanics. The sneaking feels great. The "stay in the shadows to not be spotted" is great and is really accurate. The game calculates the chance to be spotted very precise or so it feels at least :) The climbing is abit limited because of the amount of spots you can climb but still enough to create a lot of opportunities to sneak by your enemies or or engage them from different angles. The cover system is solid. You can take cober at basically everything. With a press of a button you can switch covers or leap over em. Pretty solid work in that regard.
The AI is good. On higher difficulties they spot a bit too fast and easy, but it was never really unfair to me. Most enemies have their patrol route and like in every splinter cell game. you have to be silent and study their routes. Especially if yo uwant to be as sneaky as possible.
The animations look okay for the most part. Only the sprinting looks a bit weird. Sam looks like he♥♥♥♥♥♥his pants. Other than that the movement animations look good. The facial animations not so much. SAm and all the other characters look like they are not allowed to open their mouths when speaking. Also the faces look like out of stone.
The graphics are decent. Nothing really astonishing, but they are good to look at.
The amount of gadgets and weapons are massive. Each weapon customizable with a lot of different attachments. Gadgets are a lot too. For every situation there are gadgets that feel good to use. Being more sneaky or more action oriented? Doesn't matter. You have either sleeping grenades or frag grenades.
Each item has to be bought from ingame cash you gather during missions. You can achieve extra cash by doing some hacking inside each mission or capturing high value targets.
So that should be it. I really liked the game. I have not really much to complain about. The game is good. Bought it on sale for 5 bucks and i have to say it was worth it. The game is entertaining.

With all this hype for Sonic Mania, I thought it'd be fitting to go back to Christian Whitehead's first official work with Sega. To put it bluntly: He did a really damn good job with Sonic CD. I've barely played the original version (and even then, it was on the Gems Collection for Gamecube), but I can still tell where Whitehead improved the game. The physics and collision detection feel much more in line with the other old-school 2D games. As for what's retained from the original game, the time-travel gimmick is an interesting way to switch things up (take notes, Sonic 06), even if destroying the robot generators is a little cumbersome. But, hey, you can also get the Time Stones to fix the past! And I would, if I could get a feel for the special stage controls. Anyway, going back to stuff I like, the audio for the game is fantastic, with the option of choosing either the original Japanese soundtrack or the American version. The bonuses are also pretty nice, like playing as Tails after beating the game and bringing back the old sound test screens (Fun is Infinite, anyone?) Overall, I hope you don't get the idea that my nitpicks keep me from being a fan. I do like the game, and the things that Christian Whitehead added are just icing on the cake.

Hey so I've been playing Sonic games ever since I was 6 years old and while it is not the best Sonic game I have ever played (that goes to Sonic 3 and Knuckles). It sure is a classic.
Firstly, the gameplay is what you expect from a sonic game. It has a complex physics engine that rewards players for going fast and makes it more enjoyable. However, the level design can punish players for going too fast because Sonic is in the middle of the screen making it difficult to detect in coming enemies. Also, the time travel mechanic is neat but could be improved because I found myself getting close to going back in time but then a random wall or enemy pops up and completly stops my momentum.
The Graphics aren't by far the most advanced in comparision to 2017 standards, but my god, this game is very colorful and charming and still holds up today. It might be the second best looking sonic games of the classic era. Levels pop out and have a great color scheme which is impressive because this came from a sega cd originally.
Lastly the music is still great, the opening intro, "Sonic Boom" is catchy compraed to the Japanese counterpart and all the levels stick out to me with catchy music. Again like the graphics, the music fit each area perfectly and give it a distinct feel.
Now I didn't want to be biased for this review because yes I am a Sonic fan. But I don't like a lot of Sonic's games, "Sonic 06", "Sonic Boom", "Sonic Lost World", "Sonic 3d blast" or "Sonic Adventure" to name a few. But I still believe this is one of the greatest Sonic games out there and this remake just makes it even better. While yes the level design is still not quite polished or maybe you wouldn't like sonic's movement, but to me, the game is holds up. Definatly check this game out.

TimeShift succeeds in being one of those games where it's required of the player to pay attention to detail if they want to understand the ending. Because the ending can be confusing if you weren't following along with the cutscenes or any of the dialog spoken by Krone during various instances.
Before I get into the game itself, a few things you should know if you want TimeShift to run properly on your system:
1. Find the TimeShift.exe in the install folder and change the compatibility to Windows XP (SP3)
2. Find and install patch 1.2 for the game as Steam/Activision only have it updated to 1.0 and you'll have a slew of problems.
I'm pretty sure those two cover it, the game will run much more smoothly and won't/shouldn't freeze on any loading screen or when paused.
I can't say I enjoyed the overall story in TimeShift, the whole stop a madman from ruining everything in a dystopia seemed rather generic. I did like that the protagonist stays unnamed and has ulterior motives when he jumps into the past to save the future. The gameplay was rather repetitive, running and gunning, going through vast buildings, pushing buttons, sometimes driving, using a turret, climbing up and down ladders. That's pretty much it. The saving grace with the gameplay is the time manipulation ability that comes with the Beta suit that the protagonist has. It's really cool, being able to stop time and seeing rain just frozen in mid air. Or reversing an action if you messed up. Or slowing down time/being able to move really fast.
I guess my biggest complaint was how uninspired the story seemed at times. There's hardly any background as you're just thrown into a situation. I would compare the whole situation of a dystopian world and you're the hero to Half Life, but at least in Half Life, there's context given and side characters that explain the situation. The side characters in TimeShift are so minor that I actually thought they were expendable and was surprised when the small crew you're with for a large portion of the game survives. Granted, you're not actually with them; most of the time, they'll stay behind and let you do all the work.
At least the graphics are still pretty good. Obviously a bit dated being 8 years old now but the whole world had an atmosphere of 'wow, this place is really falling apart' and added so much to the overbearing dystopia. Sound design was pretty great too.
Anyway, while it has a number of flaws, TimeShift still proved to be fun after I got it working.

By the time i'm writing this review, we've already experienced what will very likely be the last game in the Souls series, and maybe even the last Souls-like by this developer, so if you're someone who is still yet to find an entry point to the series, i'm here to tell you why this one, the one game that refined everything Demon Souls did, and the one to begin the journey of the undead, is still to this date and in my humble opinion, the best of all of them.
Dark Souls was released on 2011, lacking both the big budget and the hype that its sequels and its brother game, Bloodborne, would later benefit from, yet i would dare to say that on its humbleness lies the true magic and charm that From Software would just not be able to top on later releases.
Players take the role of a chosen Undead, following an ancient prophecy that tells about uncovering the fate for its whole kind in the land of the ancient lords, Lordran, and this is where we will start pointing out the things that make Dark Souls unique.
The world design is, if not flawless, a true example of how open areas should be done, each landscape connects to the next one in a true seamless way, every detail in the background is a place that you will reach at some point, it's a world that expands in all directions and always makes sense, it never stops feeling like you're really travelling through this vast, old and forgotten land, like something out of the most magical fable.
Next is the one feature that became the trademark of the Souls series, its difficulty, Dark Souls is not only challenging, it is sometimes unfair and unforgiving, and while this might sound like something negative, once you experience it, it is  far from it, it is a game that will see you fail, and will dare you to try again, will dare you to succeed on what it has set to make unconquerable...
and then you try, then you try harder, once and again, and then you succeed, and the satisfaction that comes with it, is something that no other series has made me feel yet.
The atmosphere of this game is yet another thing that was done so right, the areas range from gloomy, going through desolate, to absolutely terrifying; while you traverse the land, you will notice the lack of any background music (This being reserved only for its boss battles and the place where you first step into Lordran, the Firelink Shrine, every piece being a magnificent composition by Motoi Sakuraba) but far from making it feel lackluster, it adds to the immersion, to that feeling of being by yourself amidst all kinds of perils.
Every area has just this darkness feeling to it, like you're about to be swallowed by the very land under your feet, and yet for some reason, speaking graphics wise, the next Souls games just didn't seem to get this right.
The last point i will talk about is its very particular storytelling, Dark Souls features very little dialogue from only a small number of characters you will meet during your journey, yet every item, weapon and armor in the game contains a small description about its origins and its place in the world, it is by piecing together all these small stories that a larger narrative is born, and suddenly the world has a background of depths that maybe long cutscenes and hours of dialogue would not be able to equal.
As this review has become very extended, if you have made it to this paragraph, i thank you, and i deeply recommend that you give this game a chance, at the moment i'm writing this the game is on sale, it is a perfect moment to start what i hope is for you, as it was for me, one of the most unique experiences gaming will ever offer.

Having been unaware of the Kickstarter for this game, the first thing I thought when seeing the gameplay screenshot on the Steam new release page was 'that looks a bit like Snatcher'. Quite fitting as the term 'that's a bit like Snatcher' could be applied to approximately 90% of Read Only Memories.
It's just as well that Snatcher was one of the most under-rated games of the mid 90's (or 80's if you're going back to the original chibi sprite MSX version) & it's surprising that more adventure games haven't taken inspiration from it before now. So, in similar fashion, R.O.M. has the same 16-bit-esque pixel art/EGA look & letterbox game interface that Kojima's game has.
Unlike Snatcher, the main protagonist is left undefined for you to project yourself in their place. The game interface is also far more akin to a point & click adventure than just a visual novel with objects in the environment window to be interacted with in a latter Lucasarts period SCUMM style interface.
The story & character writing is exceptionally good. Your robot companion Turing (again think Little John) who're you're introduced at the start of the game being particular affable as he discovers what it means to have true independent sapience. There is also an ecleptic cast of other supporting characters and while it is unfortunate that they are not voice acted, their personalities are delivered in the text dialogue adequetly to get a feel as to how to approach them.
It's worth pointing out that developer for the game is the organiser of the GaymerX convention (infact Turing is even currently in the website banner logo). As such there are multiple LGBT characters and themes throughout the game.
While it's refreshing and a great step forward to see inclusion in entertainment media such as this, one criticism might be that there was an unrealistic ratio of both throughout the game. Of course, it's hard to say what the RL ratio is with social pressures & bigotry that still exist, but it felt a little skewed in one direction of the kinsey scale none the less.
The other criticism being that by not giving the protagonist an actual character to play, you form these friendships with people by making appropriate dialogue choices that don't actually go anywhere. I was hoping that the story would develop in a way where you would be able to take things further with either TOMCAT or Jess, providing an option for whatever pronoun you've decided to be refered towards at the start of the game. But alas, this wasn't to be.
Throughout the game there's also a real lack of urgency or tension until perhaps the last hour of it's 8-9 hour span. Even in several occasions upon entering a darkened room, there's no decapitated Jean Jack Gibson here to really drive home the seriousness of the situation. Almost all the point and click style puzzles have the solution in the same location and are therefore trivial & feel like padding to prevent R.O.M. being purely a visual novel with dialogue choices.
The Snatcher homage is even perhaps a little /too/ closely adhered towards in that the game has a grid based light-gun section & more importantly that if you've previously played the Kojima game, you can already guess a character plot twist waaaaay before it happens.
Criticism aside, it's still a fantastic title & with multiple endings & dialogue choices you can perform it encourages repeat playthroughs. Though it would be hard to make a sequel seeing that the story is self contained and definitely reaches a climax, anything else containing Turing would get an immediate purchase from me. Probably my favourite character of 2015!

In general i really liked it. For me ROM feels more like a 'casual' version of Snatcher. by this, i mean that there really isn't a way to fail or loose at ROM that i have found (execpt near the end). In fact you can mostly just sit back and just read the story they are telling you with small little puzzle breaks here and there. Some people may like this, others may not. I don't know if ROM is really a game or just an interactive novel because of this. Other games like the Ace attorny sereies actually have  'lose' conditons or have you puzzle things out more. Again, it's not a flaw, it's more of a design choice. they really wanted this game to be very casual gamer friendly. if you have never played an adventure game before this is actually a really good first game to pick up! ROM is really forgiving ;-) If you like it try to find an emulated version of snatcher (it's basically ROM on hard core mode :-)
Okay so now for my negitives which are really just nitpicks. One, I guessed 'who done it' by chapeter 2 and was correct. really the game doesn't try to hide it too well and alot of in game text (if your good about reading everything) from chapter 2 down just reinforce it.  the good thing though is that even though i knew who did it i totally didn't know HOW they did it so the reveil at the end was still satisfying to me. Two. GOD! your inventory is just jacked! usually in an adventure game you can pick up things to solve puzzles and what not. And some things you pick up are just useless. they are just red herings to get you to think about the puzzle. In ROM your inventory constently shifts! sometimes you will see items you picked up before and other times you don't. I think this was a design choice to limit your options so you don't get confused or frustrated but i found it way to hand holding and also confusing when you ask "HEY! where did item X go?" only for it to reapper in your inventory later when it's more 'puzzle convient'. again, this isn't broken, you can progress fine but it's another one of those design chocies for more casual/ first time players.
So should you buy it? Oh yeah! totally! It's a fun little story that kept me intrested just don't look for deep game mechanics or a big challenge. It's an  easy, breezey, and beautiful casual game. :-)
last note. one of the BIGGEST thing i love about this game is that it's VERY LGBT inclusive! I mean it's based in san fransciso! Anybody who worries that they will be playing as a 'gay' need not worry. the game just have alot of LGBT people in it just living there lives, no one comes on to you or throws their 'gayness' in your face. it's just treated as a basic part of life and the story just moves on without blinking. which honestly its the way it should be. I will say though that if your not use to other gener identies some pronoun usage might get a little wierd but you get over it really quick. (i'm looking at you TOMCAT, love a hon!  your a doll! ;-)

Read Only Memories is very much a well crafted adventure game in every sense. You follow the developing plot in the role of a down on his luck journalist assisting your newly befriended self aware A.I. companion Turing. Deciding to set out on a quest together. In order to try and unravel the mysterious sudden disappearance of Turing's creator. Set in Neo-San Francisco in late December of the year 2064.
You're placed in a world where humans and implant enhanced hybrid humans share a shakey coexistence. Here you will encounter ominous, shady, corporate entities, a "pure human" activist group, along with a varied cast of other rough and tumble characters. Ranging from a young detective to some even younger street punks who can help aid you along. Helping to further fuel the intrigue and assisting Turing and yourself to piece together the puzzling  situation as you progress.
This all unfolds in a beautiful art style, that I would kind of describe as a mix of 80's and 90's anime, robo, sci-fi inspired awesomeness. The immediate influences from movies and gaming like Snatcher, Phantasy Star, Gabriel Knight, Akira, Bladerunner and even Deja Vu are very clear. This game isn't a bland clone however and stands worthy on it's own two legs. I consider it a very excellent first entry by Midboss into such a lofty kingdom of fondly remembered cult titles of the past from which it invokes. The beautiful pixel art, not to mention the fantastic mood driven synth music and creative sound effects makes it a pleasure for the eyes and ears.
The writing has alot of humor and offers tons of dialogue if you chose to interact with your surroundings thoroughly. Alot of attention is given to even small details. Which helps to give off a feeling of truly being immersed in this shadowy world. The menu system is very much like that of Snatcher. Pixel hunting is never really a problem, since you can usually use the keyboard itself to run through all the background to find things to interact with.
One of my favorite things this game includes, is that it allows you to try just about every option when interacting with the environment. Many times yielding some pretty hilarious results. Alot of games would take the lazy way out; just by repeating the same line over again about that doesn't work. While ROM on the other hand, makes an effort to reward your curiosity to keep making you want to explore. Of course much of this is optional and not required if you're just looking to cover the main story quickly.
David Fennoy and Adam Harrington do a fantastic job of lending their voice talents to this project. The voice acting comes off very professional and adds some good personality. My only real complaint would be that they weren't used as often as I would have liked to have heard. In fact one of the few real complaints I have with this game would be that it could use more voiceover work. I'm guessing that budget an time constraints might have played a role in that matter.
Aside from that complaint. The only problem I have with the game at the current time of writing this are with the few bugs and crashes that I've encountered. Some of the puzzle sections can present bugs which render them impossible to complete. Reloading the game seems to fix these bugs that can come up. At least on the one puzzle bug that I did encounter. Most all of these I believe the developers are aware of and working to fix at the moment. However these things can make it rather hard to gain the achievement for finishing the game in a single attempt, without having to continue or reload a save. Not to mention making you lose alot of playtime hours if you didn't manage to create a save before hand.
The game features multiple endings scenarios. The main deciding factor on how you obtain these is through how you treat certain characters. This doesn't just change the endings, but also bits of the dialogue and story as the chapters progress. Offering a good reason to replay it again. It throws in a few puzzles as well, that offer a bit of challenge, but are fairly easy to grasp. It even features a few shooting portions very similar to the grid style shooting scenes in Snatcher.
As you can probably tell from the length this review ended up becoming I was very impressed with this game. All in all I found it to be a great game and would recommend it to anyone who likes a bit of that detective noir spun in a futuristic dystopia setting. Even if you're a newcomer to genre, I think this game offers enough to keep you entertained for many hours.

This is a pretty cool game, with some annoying issues. You (and a few others if you play online) must complete a series of challenges to advance. You're afforded the choice of four different weapons - they all play quite differently and come with their own set of abilities and buffs. And each challenge gives you up to three crystals, and when you get a number of crystals, you get new abilities.
It's a pretty unique take on this type of game, as you can't really 'grind' to level up, at most you can get a couple new buffs to help yourself out, if you master previous challenges. Because of this, it comes down more to strategy and skill, and can become quite fun in some segments.
Sometimes, however, things can be a pain in the butt. Certain challenges or bosses seem to combine the most annoying parts of the game all in one, in seemingly unfair ways. And though the game says that it's balanced for either 1-4 players, more players simply make it easier in so many ways.
That said, I really enjoyed the game, when it wasn't being irritating, and would recommend it to others who are looking for a challenging title to play along with friends.

Recommended for the great control and game mechanics. The controls are on par with, or even succeeds, the best in the genre (which would be Diablo III I suppose)... they are very snappy. Ok, maybe calling the orb to your location could be smoother, that is the only thing I don't like.
FORCED differs itself from every other ARPG by not having any grinding... and also not having equipment or experience points. If this is good or bad, I don't know, but it makes for a different game.
You unlock abilities by completing trials. Each trial is a level with monsters and sometimes puzzles.
You get one point for completing the level.
You get one point for completing the level within a specified amount of time, and
you get one point for completing a unique challenge for each level.
However, by not having the grind, there is a burden on the developers to provide a lot more content than normally in the genre. You finish each area much faster, and there is no value for the player in going back once the trials are completed... and the amount of content is OK, but not great.

Dragon's Dogma is at once both an amazing game and an awful game and let me tell you why.
This game is so much fun. I struggle to think of games that I've had more fun just
it. The climbing elements of this game are something RPG fans wish to see in just about every game with large monsters. Oh, sure, I could fling fireballs and arrows at it, but what if I want to climb it!? You do just that in Dragon's Dogma. It's a constant challenge and a lot of fights require you to train and think.
The character creation is rich and can go very in-depth. Let's just say that Monster Factory had a really fun and easy time with it. It also has some relevance to the story if you do NG+ which I'd heavily recommend just for the ending and difficulty.
My last big point about Dragon's Dogma is the soundtrack. It has amazing composition. I played Dragon's Dogma originally on the Xbox 360 when it first came out and I still listen to the soundtrack from time to time. It's not the greatest soundtrack ever composed, but to me, it's iconic and a lot of the tracks on here are simply memorable and enjoyable to listen to.
--
But Dragon's Dogma does suffer heavily from a few oversights by Capcom. The most glaring issue this game has is the story. As a narrative, it had so much potential. It's a hopeless cycle of life and death and that point definitely caught me by surprise. I don't mean that in a good way, unfortunately.
There's very little building in most of the game. No character building, no world building, nothing. Whatever you get out of the characters you meet and areas you visit are just that: it's whatever you get out of it. It could mean something to you, it might mean something to other people. For me, the world was cool to traverse but a lot of the characters were shallow and unimportant to me. Until the end of the game.
The main point Capcom doesn't capture until the very end of the game is that this is a quest about and for
. Mostly the player character, but also the player. You push through challenge after challenge and probably die to every boss a couple of times, some more than a couple of times, but you push through it.
.
I swear the true ending of this game is one of the most memorable experiences that I personally have in gaming and it's a shame that it's lumped in with the rest of the story.
If you're wondering why I regard it so highly and don't care for spoilers:
--
If you get into it just for fun, believe me when I say you'll have it. The story will at least keep you interested enough to keep going and not suffer through it. You'll likely be pleasantly surprised like I was at the ending with the dragon and the one after the dragon.

Splinter Cell: Blacklist is Third-Person Shooter. It's also an awesome comeback of Sam Fisher. Plot? We have seen this a lot: terrorists are threatening America, so we send special unit to destroy them. Luckily, game is much better than its plot.
After events from Conviction,  Fourth Echelon is formed to neutralise threat for The Engineers. Guess who leads it? Yeah, good ol' Sam. With other members of the team (Grimm, IT genius Charlie and soldier Briggs, who sometimes helps Sam on the mission) and Paladin crew they have to trac down and eliminate Engineers Leader. But what is Paladin? Your new Hq, Paladin is a military grade plane - where you spend time between missions. It offers weapon customisation (game offers quite a few guns), plane upgrades (like sonars enabling minimap while on mission, and things like that. All improvemnets are done mid-air), and chat to crew or Sam's daughter. And of course access missions, both story and e4 ones (could be played coop or solo, all except Briggs ones).
Finally missions. You visit some places, like Middle East, States, Britan or Guantanamo. Most of them aren't much diffrent. Blacklist introduces playstyles for Splinter Cell, each one with diffrent score (and money) rating. Ghost is something for veterans - challenging sometimes, but extremly satisfying. It rewards avoiding enemies, and quiet KOs and shocking instead of loud approach. Most challenging, but also most rewarding. Panther style is a lot like Ghost, but it focuses on quiet killing and leaving no witnesses. Gives around 75% of Ghost rewards. And final one, Assault. Created for people who love CoD, so they can also play Blacklist. It obviously focuses on blazing into the room, tossing a frag or two and killing everything that moves. Personally, I use Ghost style at the beginning, but after some time i gave Panther a try, finishing the game with this one. Better finishers with melee, and ability to use sniper rifles and pistols won :) Good thing is, that with upgrade of Paladin you can change your loadout on supply cases - nice idea when you grow bored of quiet approach and want to shoot something. To be honest it's good idea to have 2 loadouts - one for Ghost and Panther, and one for Assault, regardless of your preffered style. Why? One of Blacklists minuses is that sometimes it forces usage of one playstyle. Like Ghost only in Guantanamo, or full Assault during Plane takeoff (after one mission) and Charlie's missions.
To sum up, Splinter Cell: Blacklist is great game, no matter whether you look for some sneaking, or trigger happy shooter. Enemy AI isn't making stupid mistakes, and variety of gagets (there are a lot of them, like frags and  incendiary granased for assault, tear gases for Panther, or Sleeping gas for Ghost. And some universal ones, like sticky EMP or noisemakers) will help you a lot. Playing it was a pure pleasure, and it's likely that i will come back to it in future.
P.S: Game features Multiplayer and Coop missions, but to be honest, i haven't played them.

The last one is Perfectionist, for those who seek mastering the game or going for achievements.
Co-Op: I haven't played it much but the co-op missions have same distinct features, other one plays as Sam Fisher and the other as Briggs. Most of the missions are considered fun but somewhat challenging. However the game doesn't tend to be annoying at any point.
Multiplayer: It's a classic team deathmatch with spies against mercenaries, I did like it even tough it gets annoying sometimes when you face sudden death haha.
