It's okay. It wasn't as exciting as I thought. The campaign leaves an open-ended scenario where the Engineers (the antagonists) are still operating throughout the world and 4th Echelon's mission is to find and stop all the 12 nations who are funding the Engineers.
Overall, it feels like they copied the Splinter Cell brand but delivered another game instead. Like a sequel meant to milk money from the fans by dumbing down the technology in-game, so they have less to deliver.
COULD NOT PLAY ONLINE. NEGATIVE.
PROS
1. Mission Objective Marker
Very useful. At least you know where you are going.
2. Execute
Not bad. I like the way Executes are carried out. Instant headshots for up to 3 enemies within range. It even works on enemies standing behind you. Doesn't work on those with helmets though.
3. Knockouts
I like how stealth KOs drag the terrorist towards your position, so you automatically hide the body. Very realistic.
4. Stun Gun/Crossbow
Instant KO without the mess of a corpse. I like.
5. Dogs
This is pretty good. They sniff you out if you are within range and add a new element to the game.
6. Mixes
Grimms First Person perspective mission looked pretty good. Controlling the Paladin's rockets and cannons and aerial sniping  were fun too.
7. Tri-copter
Not bad. Fun to play with. Replaces the old stick camera. Allows you to see everything with a birds-eye-view in many maps and helps you to get rid of terrorists. Really silly to restrict the mission boundaries though.
CONS
1. Story
Was okay. It was not exciting. No climax or an interesting development.
2. Lockpicking
Removed lockpicking from the Splinter Cell. With all the "best" weapons/technology in the world, you can't lockpick a door.
3. Weapons
I find the purchasing of normal weapons with earned credits extremely silly. You are a top-tier government spy agency and you have to function like a mercenary group?
4. Technology
A step backwards from Splinter Cell : Chaos Theory. You used to be able to listen in on conversations and hack computers from a distance. Now you have to manually walk up to them and press buttons. Your pistol used to be way more advanced too.
5. Interrogation
They removed that too. Now holding a terrorist hostage is only for bullet shield purposes.
6. EMP
They took the EMP pistol away and used EMP grenades, which have to be purchased.
7. Sonar / Night Vision
Used to have thermal imaging to find guards. Now you have Sonar which only works if it pings and there isn't a drone controller blocking. Somehow, even Night Vision is messed up by a drone controller, who can influence the infra-red spectrum of light.
8. Last Known Position
It is extremely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to see the AI shoot a white after-image of yourself.
9. Aiming/Scope
Absolutely horrible. 4 lines that don't even intersect. This is lazy.
10. Aerial KOs
Why do all the aerial KOs have to stomp on the guy below? What happened to neck twisting?
11. Stealth Movements
Clunky. You can't stealth move smoothly around a crate. If you press Q and stick to the wall, you can't round the corner unless you move the camera and press the Spacebar. While I appreciate hugging the sides, it is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to see that a box is the only thing preventing a terrorist who is standing up from noticing you.
12. Weapon Caches / Dead Drops
What the hell? Who placed the weapon caches under electrical circuits? Dead drops on the edge on wall on the 3rd-storey? It's almost a random drop design. Not to mention that terrorists seem to have all the equipment that 4th Echelon has as well.
13. Wall Climbing
Lots of wall climbing. Up and down and left and right. So much wall climbing, I thought it was the Prince of Persia and I would need to wall-run.
14. Lights
Everywhere. No EMP pistol, you have to shoot them or play run-and-slide with the terrorists.
15. Railroading
You either take the hard way or the easy way. Through the front door or the back door. Not much of an open-word concept here. No free exploring since part of the maps have invisible walls.
NEUTRAL
1. Zipline
I do not understand why you would put a zipline that does nothing cool. It only brings you from the top to the bottom.

I'd recommend you pick this one up if it's on sale like 75% off or something, it's a fun shooter, there are about 9 weapons or so and most of them feel great, my favorite being the shotgun and they have alternate fire modes too, usually being a more powerful "blast" that consumes more bullets
Then there are the time bending mechanics, you can slow time, stop it altogether or reverse it, consuming your suit's energy to do so, granted it regenerates quickly so no need to worry all that much about saving it, it's pretty satisfying to kill your enemies in slow motion and you can do fun stuff like grabbing their weapons and see them running around in fear as you do so and there are a few really easy "puzzles" throughout the game using these mechanics aswell
The problem with the combat however, is that it can be quite easy and become a bit repetitive as the game goes on, basically you slow time, blast some fools and then run to cover to regenerate your suit's energy / your health and repeat the process, some enemies try to charge to your cover location but it really doesn't matter all that much since you have your radar and you can see the red dot coming by which ends up making things even easier for you
Story wise it's pretty darn forgettable, an evil scientist dude steals the "Alpha Suit" and travels trough time so you grab the "Beta Suit" and "time jump" to go after him in an alternate reality in the beginning of the game but it's pretty hard to care for the "resistance" or the villain at all, he barely shows up, maybe twice at most in the game and I don't think he even has 1 line of dialogue in it, then you get these 2 second cutscenes every now and then which are like flashbacks that try to build some semblance of a plot, and then there's this pretty annoying resistance leader guy who keeps shouting at you constantly throughout the whole game to do everything, "Hurry press that button" "Cmon soldier! Do this!" "Do that" "Hurry" "Go! What are you waiting for?" "We need fuel!" which all culminates in a pretty anti-climactic and confusing / sequel bait-ish ending
And that's one of the other issues about the gameplay, all your objectives are really boring, it pretty much consists of pressing buttons or pulling levers all game, and there's no exploration at all, when I started playing I looked at every nook and cranny like I usually do in games but quickly learned that it was a pointless exercise, you have regenerating health and ammo is plentiful too so you pretty much never run out of it, so you're just going level to level, waypoint to waypoint pressing buttons and killings dudes with combat that turns repetitive after a while and in the end you have a very easy and disappointing final boss
Plus if my playtime's any indication the game's 5-7 hours long at most and multiplayer is dead for this game, so combining  all that you can really see why this game wasn't initially well received in the first place, and after I read a bit on it apparently it had a really rocky development cycle, changing publishers a few times and even it's story was scrapped and completely reworked a few months before release
So in conclusion: like I said in the beginning of this review it's still a fun shooter with some interesting mechanics that weren't quite fully realized but at the end of the day is not really worth it's full price, just wait for a sale and you'll power through it in a few hours

BetaDwarf guys decided to do something we haven't seen in a while; create a new genre, and they did it really good! Ok, not exactly new, it's more a hybrid between classic ARPGs and puzzle games, but it plays very differently from both...
Actually, you play through many different "arenas" (trials) trying to pass their main challenge thus providing yourself a crystal (something like leveling)... Each trial, has 3 crystals, one for completing it, one for special challenge within it, and one for completing it in a specified time frame... Completing a trial is the part of the game you will have problems with, but completing the special challenge and time frame is almost impossible, and you will often need to level up (gain more crystals) and come back later to do it...
Gameplay consists of classic hack-n-slash, fast reflexes for dodging and puzzle elements. Puzzles are not hard, but you're always multitasking, killing monsters, running and using a spirit Balfus to activate everything you need (be it healing, damaging or puzzle element)...
Story is not spectacular, but it makes sense which is not easy for games like these, graphics style is nice and colourful (the latter can be a problem sometimes) and gameplay is interesting, dynamic and often frustrating...
And, that frustration can sometimes be the biggest problem this game has... It is hard... extremely hard! Unforgiving, and painful... But, for the same reason really, really rewarding!
Another downside is the necessity to use online feature even for local co-op?! Very bad :(
Either way, it's a fantastic game, and easy recommendation!

While I’m not normally a huge fan of point-and-click adventures something in Read Only Memories drew my attention. It might have been the graphics, or the fact that I’m familiar with some of the voice actors, but it could just as well have been the story. Or maybe just a combination of all of these things. So: is Read Only Memories the game that has finally managed to win me over? Will I start playing more adventure games from now on? Let’s head over to the next paragraph!
The game starts off with you hanging around in your own apartment. While you are tired and want to go to sleep you suddenly remember that you first have to write a review for some kind of new headset. After all, you still have to pay for the rent and you hope that this will be your big break, to finally make it as a journalist. After having written the review you decide that it’s finally time to go to bed. Suddenly, however, while you’re asleep, a robot silently enters your apartment. Upon waking up you are confused, a bit scared even. What does this robot want, what is it doing here? After a lengthy conversation it seems a friend of yours – who is also the robot’s creator – was being chased that very same night, by something or someone, and has suddenly vanished. Was he taken, did he run off, or..? What happened? That is the big question you keep asking yourself. Ultimately you decide to accompany this robot named Turing and try to find out what exactly has happened.
I just described to you the first 15 minutes of the game or so: it was more than enough to pull me in.
All the aforementioned factors were a part of this. The writing is excellent and witty, the music and voice acting are superb and the gameplay… well, the gameplay is pretty much the same as many other point-and-click adventures out there, but it’s absolutely solid. It’s a well-oiled machine, with every little part of it functioning as it should. You can clearly see the passion that was put into this little gem from miles away. Simply brilliant.
With the risk of possibly spoiling the game I’m not going to dig any further into the story, though. You will just have to experience this for yourself. I
tell you that it keeps you interested and intrigued all the way through its six playable chapters, although it tends to drag for a very short while about 3/4th into the game and the ending also felt a bit rushed to me.
I’ve already mentioned that the gameplay is exactly what you would expect from a point-of-click adventure. If you’ve ever played a point-and-click adventure in your life (and let’s be honest; who hasn’t?) then you know exactly how things work here. You point your mouse (objects you can interact with will then be highlighted) and click.
Click on an object and the game will open a context menu that gives you the option to push/touch, look/read, talk to someone or use an item. Other games sometimes have the habit of putting actions or objects in annoying - extra - little submenus, but not here, though. And while Read Only Memories doesn’t do things wildly different; it all works effortlessly, without hindering me as a player or giving me the feeling that it’s interfering with my progress.
The puzzles themselves aren’t the most difficult puzzles I’ve ever laid eyes on. They’re more of the casual, anyone-can-solve-this-with-a-little-brain-activity sort of puzzles. They’re relatively easy to solve and the solutions can always be found in the same area or level. For me personally it’s ideal because I hate having to solve frustratingly hard puzzles while also trying to understand/follow a story (I easily lose track of the less important things), but I do wish there were more of them. In total I think there are 5 or less actual puzzles, and with its casual nature I personally think there should’ve been more. They’re just too easy to solve to really feel like (complex) puzzles. On the other hand, the puzzles blend in seamlessly with the story and this results in them not feeling forced or tacked on.

There’s not a whole lot to tell about the audio that I haven’t already mentioned before. The voice acting is amazing; everything is wonderfully and professionally narrated. But unfortunately it’s limited to only the intro and outro, and that amounts to roughly 5-10 minutes in total. So it’s just a small part of the game.
The music itself is similar to the games you used to play back when you were young, so there’s a lot of electronic music, but also sound effects. If you’ve ever played Mega Man then you should have a general idea of what it will sound like if you play it. At least, that is how I experienced it.
I can be really short about the graphics, too (but I really don’t want to). The graphics use a retro style and are shown in pixelated 2D. The colors are used well, there’s a very cool atmosphere and everything is nicely animated. It all gives off a very polished feel.
A lot of detail has gone into the graphics; from the character portraits during conversations to the environments: they did a tremendous job creating all of the art.
Since this is an adventure it’s highly likely that you will play it just once. I personally don’t mind, though, as long as it’s a fun experience, which it is. In total it will take you anywhere between 7-10 hours to complete, depending on how easily you can solve the puzzles the game throws at you and how much you explore. There are six chapters in total and each one will take anywhere between 30-90 minutes to complete.
Even though I normally don’t play a lot of point-and-click adventures I am really glad that I gave Read Only Memories a try. It has become a to-the-point adventure, with a lot – if not all - of the fat trimmed off that you normally find in many other point-and-click adventures (please note: I am mostly talking about the puzzles here). It managed to keep me entertained and intrigued all the way through, despite its somewhat rushed and convoluted ending.
Anyway, for a little over €1 per hour you get an excellent story-focused adventure and that’s not a bad deal at all in my opinion.
Pros:
+ Magnificent – but limited - voice acting
+ Beautiful retro graphics and music
+ Solid point-and-click adventure gameplay
+ Intriguing and focused story that pulls you in and manages to keep you interested all the way through (well, mostly)
Mixed:
+/- Too few puzzles and they’re also too easy to solve, but on the other hand: it does keep the story going and they seamlessly blend in as well
Cons:
- Drags just a little around 3/4th into the game
- Maybe a tad too short
- Ending feels a little rushed and convoluted
(Ratings aren’t calculated based on a formula, but on my personal feelings)

Read Only Memories was interesting enough for me to finish it, and the inclusiveness of its setting gave me a lot to think about. However, playing it is wading through passive-aggressive, condescending murk and it's not an experience I would recommend to other people.
I feel that the story of this game would be better served by being setting it up as a visual novel with Turing the robot as the explicit protagonist rather than the point-and-click adventures of their bumbling sidekick. You are very much Turing's sidekick. Turing drives the story and it's Turing's journey that the game is ultimately about. Your role is to piously "witness the world’s first sapient robot learning to grow and live," absorb info dumps, serve as a punching bag for constant anger and threats, and to provide comic relief by talking to inanimate objects. I found it tedious.
If you don't want to play quite so reverently, there are a lot of dialog options where you can be a jerk for no reason, but really that just gives the game ammunition to treat you even more like a total schmuck so I didn't bother.
Also, prepare for glitchy, poorly explained puzzles that pop up out of nowhere, keep you from saving when they appear, and may not affect the story at all or may downgrade your ending if you mess them up.
If you want a game that explores meaningful choice, I would recommend Life Is Strange.
If you want pixel art and an awesome story with awesome characters, I would recommend Undertale.
If you want an interesting experience where you are not the protagonist, I would recommend The Beginner's Guide.
If you want a cyberpunk game, I hear that Shadowrun: Dragonfall is pretty good.
If you want the most inclusive setting, then and only then I would recommend this game.

Like most cyberpunk stories, ROM has a bit of Blade Runner and a bit of Neuromancer at its core, filtered through all the games that have aped those settings over the years. It's a lengthy adventure(I spent about 8 hours on a first play, and then 4 on repeats) with a lot of dialogue puzzles, a smaller amount of inventory puzzles, and a few one-offs involving shooting or hacking things/people.
The plot is primarily a mystery story in which your faceless, hard-up journalist main character assists Turing, the first sentient robot, in solving the disappearance of their creator and the story behind their origins. Like in any good noir, the lines between good guy and bad guy are blurry, the protagonists are unknowing pawns, and people who are too close to the truth die. And like in good sci-fi stories, the stakes hinge on ethical consequences of future technology, even as they retain analogues to the present day.
If you are wondering about the "queer content" of the game - you don't need to be very invested in it to follow the story.  Many of the characters are composites of cyberpunk tropes against gender and sexual minority identities, but your character interaction doesn't revolve around those aspects, as the setting normalizes them into background flavor. Instead, choices to be nice or jerky are transposed to the new topics of 2064: the situations and rights of hybrids, cyborgs, etc. The game won't shame you too much to stay on the "good" path(you'll just feel bad if you have any conscience), and in fact it's a decent challenge to explore the game enough to find all six endings on your own, since they depend on character interaction throughout the game, not just in the final sequences. There's also plenty of alternative paths that don't affect the endings. ~4 hours times ~6 plays = good replay potential.

If you like cyberpunk, future science fiction, or robots, you'll like this game. If you also like cute likable characters, mysteries, or compelling narrative with choices, you'll love it. And if you also like old-style adventure games, retro-graphics, or great soundtracks, you'll adore this game. It's well-worth your time.

Admittedly the lore of the game is dense and you will be at least 10 hours into the game before you really start feeling like you understand the world. When you want to read lengthy dialog between characters because it is giving you a more detailed understanding of the world, you have transitioned from the reading being a chore, to being part of the game.

This game has me in its claws. It has me hooked like so few games have ever done. Dragon's Dogma has most of the things that keep me playing. It has modding. It has great mechanics. It has character development that's paced just right.
Your character's weight and height actually affect your gameplay. It has freedom. It allows you to craft your own saga. Imagine the wonderful Shadow of the Colossus mixed with Dragon's Age mixed with Dark Souls. Fighting a giant beast that seems difficult to harm? Climb on it and find its weak spot. Tired of the class you're playing as? Go to the capital city and change it whenever you like.
The game features different game modes: Easy mode, normal mode, hard mode, speedrun mode. Hard mode makes the game more Dark Soulsy, speedrun gives you a timer. For your first playthrough, I recommend normal mode.
Perhaps my favourite feature is the pawn system. This little sub-multiplayer mechanic is the system the whole game revolves around. You create your own pawn, shape how they act in battle as well as out of it, gear them up and let them loose into other people's games. They learn as they follow you and the people who choose to take them with them. And they will use that knowledge to help you. They learn enemies' weak spots. They learn how to progress in quests and give hints to alternative ways if they've learned about them from others. They learn about the places you visit.
There's also a ton of potential for creating your own stories. Want to play as a group of kids out to take on the dragon? Sure. Want to be a giant ready to crush anyone? Why not. There are many stories like these and I found them in this recent
.
The article also brings up a good critique about the game. The world is generic. It's so generic that if it didn't have all those features listed above, it would never be able to suck me in like it does. Also its graphics are aged. But that can be solved by simple modding. I'll list the mods I use to make the game prettier without affecting gameplay at all below:
To sum up: Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen is a great and involving ARPG with wonderful mechanics and great possibilities. The equipment has all the looks and synergy one could ask for. The story is good, albeit generic, but it takes off after the beginning. The pawn system is wonderful and works great for people like me, who mostly play singleplayer games. I recommend it to anyone who likes fantasy RPGs and the Souls games. Also, you can climb big monsters and throw people off cliffs.
It is a bit of a learning curve when you start out, but it is great fun once you get the hang of it.

::: Game-Related :::

You have several equipments your disposal, which affect your playstyle. AI is nice, although it not that smart, but it is challenging enough to keep the game in its pace. You cannot sit in the shadow, looking into enemy's eye at almost arm-length. You can be spot if you cross its LOS.

Apart from the (great) game itself, there is a critical flaw, Uplay.

Splinter Cell is a series that has gone through some troubled times. While the first three games were made relatively quickly, Ubisoft decided to get creative with the fourth entry. While it's next-gen release was met with mixed response, it would be the follow-up that would redefine what Splinter Cell was.
Old fans were shocked to see a game with a more combat heavy approach being braned with the Splinter Cell moniker. How could this be the same game they followed for years? While I thought Conviction was one of the best in the series, most fans wanted a return to form; a game that would allow them more approaches to tackling situations apart from "Kill everyone."
Enter Blacklist, a game that not only attempts to bring in the old crowd, but appeal to everyone at the same time. While the results are mixed, as far as the campaign is concerned, the entire package is a pretty nice deal. You get the standard mixture of co-op and competitive modes, but the redone Spies Vs Mercs mode combined with the sheer quantity of co-op missions available makes for a great package that stealth action fans shouldn't pass up.
Co-op takes many different forms with a requisite horde mode, regular story based missions, stealth style predator missions and some objective based ghost areas. These all require a good deal of teamwork on the hardest difficulty, though the game lacks a lot of challenge if played on anything lower.
For starters, the AI just isn't that great. While you will spotted from time to time, escaping should not be so simple. Often times, I ran for cover in the same room and my enemies lost the trail. To make matters worse (and more gamey feeling), the enemies eventually start donning heavy armor and riot shields.
I suppose enemy variety was never a strong suit with Splinter Cell, but does everything need to follow in the footsteps of Call of Duty? There is also a single-player level that is comprised of half third-person and half first-person gameplay. I know the Spies Vs Mercs mode has always featured this, but when did players want a Splinter Cell game in first-person?
For that matter, why are there so many scripted events? The beauty of the first two levels is the freedom offered to the player. You can go guns blazing or sneak past everyone and each option has more than one viable path. You never really get filtered into a specific corridor, leading to levels that feel massive and rewarding.
I get that certain points need to have tighter direction, but how many times are we going to get a train level? How many times will we need to escape an exploding building? Ubisoft seems to have cherry picked the best scripted events from the past decade and thrown them into a series that never excelled with pre-calculated chaos.
The big elephant in the room has to be the new voice for Sam Fisher. While I have no problem with changing an actor (and Michael Ironside may have declined the role, for all I know), I will not forgive changing the actual personality of a character. Sam Fisher went from a wise cracking, easy going gent to a snarky, stuck up and incredibly one-dimensional jackass.
Even his crew is loaded with stereotypical people. You have generic hacker guy (complete with modern lingo), faceless black grunt and ♥♥♥♥♥y superior officer (who happens to be a woman!). The enemies are also no better, though the main baddie has some solid voice work.
As with most Tom Clancy based games, I got lost with the plot after the 6th mission. Things just become so generic and predictable that I shut my mind off. I was more intrigued with sneaking past people and not trying to kill anyone. Those moment to moment interactions with the enemies more than make up for any failings the plot may hold.
Splinter Cell has never really been about plot, either. The games have always allowed you to be a ghost behind enemy lines. I guess with Conviction, you could know become a ghost and a gunslinger, but I'm not sure if mixing in action oriented, mandatory scenes works within the confines of Splinter Cell.
At least if you only grab this for multiplayer, you will be well served. Spies Vs Mercs is a great return to form after the travesty with Double Agent and co-op is fantastic. It removes any of the limitations the campaign has that serve the story. You are given free reign of the environment and minus a few hidden load screens (DOUBLE LIFT DOORS, HO!), the levels are your oyster.
So to wrap this up, if you are a fan of the series, you should be pleased. Sam may be a total jerk now, but the game does feature a lot of classic gameplay. If you aren't a fan, I think you would be better served with going for Chaos Theory or Double Agent on Xbox/PS2. Those games represent the highest potential that a stealth game can achieve. Blacklist is mostly a melting pot of industry conventions with a few clever mechanics thrown in.
7/10

Timeshift is one of those games that was mostly overlooked and forgotten, and it's a shame because it's actually a pretty neat game. It gives you the power to rewind, pause, or slow down time, and while you can just play the game by slowing time, shooting everyone to death, and then moving on to the next fight and doing the same thing, it's pretty boring that way, and the game gives you room to be somewhat creative with the powers instead. You can freeze time and grab enemies' guns out of their hands, and they'll either try to maneuver to a nearby gun if it's on the ground or just surrender to you. If someone throws a grenade at you, you can rewind time until it's back in their hands and shoot their arm, causing them to drop it at their feet. Most of the weapons feel satisfying to use (the assault rifle is the main exception, since it's pretty weak against most enemies and is only really good for the grenade launcher secondary fire), and most of them have unique secondary features like flamethrowers or laser cannons. The game uses a 3 weapon limit system, which isn't really ideal, but at least gives you the opportunity to have a close range weapon, a long range weapon, and a fun weapon, instead of just being limited to the standard shotgun/assault rifle combo that most games with two weapon systems force you into. It slows down a bit near the end and has a few levels that feel like padding that don't give you as much of an opportunity to appreciate the time powers, but otherwise it's a generally fun if somewhat basic shooter campaign.
I wouldn't say it's worth immediately going out and buying for $20, and since it's an Activision game you can pretty much bet on it not dropping except for the occasional Activision sale, but when that sale does come around and Timeshift drops down to $5 again I'd pretty easily recommend it. It's worth mentioning that the Steam version of the game is 1.0 and it lacks the 1.2 patch, so if the game doesn't work for you (It worked fine for me, but maybe I was just lucky) you may need to follow one of the guides on Steam on how to install the 1.2 patch.

One of the best games I've played in a while, and definitely the most realistic zombie game.
Unlike other zombie games, State of Decay is a sandbox zombie game that has a strong focus on community building.
It has the usual scavenging for items, but it also has recruitable survivors who have varying personalities and traits.
Some of them are skilled in important areas like medicine, mechanic, cooking and you want to look for these people to make your home better.
The survivors have a mind of their own and they will go out to scavenge for items, and some of them may require your help in bailing them out. If they get deathly sick, you have the option of giving them a mercy shot, where you kill them before they turn into a zombie. A survivor that has gone missing may either be dead or still alive hiding in a building where you have to bring them home safely. The random events tell a story of their own in this sandbox game, though the base game does have a main story that you can complete.
The survivors also have moods which can improve or worsen depending on random events and whether you successfully solve problems. Ignore the problems and some people may leave due to low confidence.
There is base building where you can build facilities such as a medical area to house your sick people or else they may spread it to other people, a garden to grow food, a watch tower to snipe incoming zombies, and cooking area to prevent food contamination. There are not enough space to build everything so you have to choose carefully.
In addition to scavenging for personal items, you also need to scavenge enough things for your home, like food, medicine and ammo, for home consumption and to keep home morale up.
This game has no multiplayer, so it is a single player game.
The nice sandbox features, community building and random events of this game ironically make it closer to the Walking Dead TV Series than the Walking Dead game itself. The community building is a breath of fresh air for this genre, and this game is strongly recommended.

A very addictive hack-n-slash game, if you are into one-man-army kind of game and are also interested in "the romance of three kingdoms" era of chinese history.
In this installment, we have story mode, in which you can play the routes of different faction. The storytelling is pretty accurate to the novel "romance of three kingdom", which in itself is somewhat fictional. And if you fulfill some conditions in certain battles, you can unlock a IF route, basically a storyline which tells a whole different, purely fantasized developement of events.
In free mode, you can replay any battles you have unlocked in the story mode, even as the opposite faction. You are free to choose the character you play with, his/her equipment and everything.
The ambition mode is the most fun thing for me. In this mode you pick one character (you can switch later anytime you want) and start your own base, your goal is to gather materials and more characters through random generated battles, to further expand your base. Whenever you return from a battle, you will have options to upgrade your weapons at the blacksmith, purchase food items that will enhance you abilities in the next battle from the diner, or send troops to other areas and they will come back bringing you random loots/weapons/support animals. You will get the chance to recruit all the playable characters in this mode, and freely switch between them, or bring up to 3 of them with you into battle and raise friendship with them (unlocks new skills and dialogues).
And the character's level, equipment, the upgraded weapons are all also carried over to the story mode. So the ambition mode serves as a good place to casually level up some chars, or to grind some nice weapons, which will make story mode battle for a fresh character much easier.
Besides the battles and story, the game also offers detailed biography, historical information about events, characters. So whenever you wanna relax for a bit, or get curious about one character or event, you can just sit down, enjoy the relaxing music and read through the archive. There's also weapon exhibition, wallpapers for you to collect by leveling up characters.
Compared to most previous dynasty warriors games, the character is no longer bound to his own weapon anymore, there are as many weapon types as playable characters, and you are free to give a spear user a bow, a whip, or whatever you prefer.
About performance, I'm very satisfied with this game. My computer is pretty low-tier, many games would make it overheat and the computer would shut itself down without any warning, thats how bad it is. And i can play this game all day long and nothing happens, and the gameplay is very smooth, no lag in any situation.
About control, out of habit, i have always played dynasty warriors games with just keyboard, i re-map the keys in a way that i can do most things easily and it's totally managable.
All in all, i enjoy this game a lot, currently i'm maybe only finished with half of the story mode, so plenty hours still await me.

It's got a lot going for it, I like the action combat and how ammo is scarce so you have to get good with the melee combat, but once you master it the melee is devestating and there are so many different weapons.  Plus there is RPG like advancement of your main character and the other 'party' members you recruit along the way as each has a variety of skills and each skill advances as it's used unlocking further skills and special attacks/abilities.  It also has a very nice open world which rewards exploration as pretty much any location you find out of the way will have some nice loot to scavenge (better weapons, backpacks, etc.).  You also build yourself a base/community and have to manage various resources and personalities.  Helping out strangers opens up trade options and if you help them enough they'll be friendly and ask to join your community, but it's still up to you whether you want to add them and support them through play or no.  There are also more things to do than you can possibly get done timewise so you have to choose who to help and what to put priority on; but I've found gives me that sense of just one more thing and then I'll quit... awww just one more...
If you like the game then the Breakdown DLC adds a new game type where instead of following the story of the main campaign you have a minor story just the framework of survival for the world but gives RPG like goals in accomplishing certain things like using certain weapon types, or other accomplishments which unlock hero characters you can recruit where they don't start with minimal skills but instead have special items and upgraded skills.
The one complaint I have is that it's very hard to maintain a clear zombie free area.  Seems like more often than not you only get a few steps away from a building you've cleared and zombies are right back into since the zombies seem to mostly spawn right around where your current character is, and I wish I could just lock some of my party/community members in our home so they'd stop going off on their own and getting in trouble within minutes of my rescuing them from one thing they are back out looking for trouble again.  Also for some missions which have a limited time to respond it would be nice to know what those timeframes are or see some color scheme like green, yellow, red so that you'd better know which ones need to be prioritized without having to keep track of when they showed up relative to the other available missions.

Read Only Memories brings to mind games like Snatcher and even Deus Ex in its cyberpunk future, mixed in with a healthy dose of anime cyberpunk influences as well (Think more Appleseed than GitS).  The game is played like most classic point and click adventure games, with an emphasis on choices (both dialogue and in terms of actions taken) having impact on the relationships and eventual ending you can get.
Writing and aesthetics are the two strongest parts of ROM; the art is crisp and very colorful, and really takes the 'dinge' out of the usual cyberpunk games that focus on dreary, dark futures--ROM instead uses somewhat colorful pallettes of neon tones and primary colors to build character and personalty; individual characters have their own color schemes, and they reflect their personality.  The music is excellent too, on a somewhat natural level (it reminds me of the best tracks of games like Phoenix Wright, which really draw you in to the game through the aural atompshere).
As for the writing, all of the characters are distinct, and each choice you make has weight, meaning that the way you choose to have your character speak draws specific outcomes, and allows for you to act however you feel your character would; the game is even considerate enough to include options to select preferred pronouns (even custom), and (as what seemed like a joke), your dining habits, to help you flesh out your character.  I found this to be really engaging, because point and click games rarely care about the "character" of the PC--you're generally just a pointer that talks, but ROM really made it feel like I had created a character with existing relationships and preferences that I could work into my choices, instead of just hammering "Good" "Evil" or "Neutral" options.
If you're a fan of point and click mysteries, cyberpunk works, or even visual novels you may enjoy ROM; it really works to build an organic world that you get to interact with, and doesn't spend copious amounts of time on pseudo-science, instead using the setting to tell a great story, rather than use a setting to simply drop world-building dialogue and techno-babble.

Of course, I dislike things about the game, but I'll just let those things slide in this review for now.

Dragon's Dogma is an action game with RPG elements in an open world that is so boring and bland to explore that it isn't worth it in the slightest. It is nothing but filler and has no reason to even be there. It's a grinding game disguised as something else. There is no skill required to beat bosses, you can buy infinite healing items and use them as much as you want, wherever you want, in an enemy's grasp, while swinging a sword, wherever. People have called this game difficult when the only real solution to overcoming obstacles is "just grind more".
Story in this game is quite obviously not important in the slightest, despite the game trying to make you care about certain characters and their interactions and feelings in cutscenes. You can safely ignore it and you would be fine. There are no story options that change outcomes, no matter what decision you make at the end you go into NG+ anyway, similar to DS1.
The combat is fun but the stuff you're doing, for the most part, isn't. The only enjoyable parts are the big health beast fights but they are so few in differentiation and in terms of when you'll see them that you'll be spending more of your running around an almost empty world getting ambushed by the same enemies over and over.
The beasts themselves are few in terms of diversity, in my playthrough I discovered around 4 kinds of beasts that were actually unique. Some would use the same models as others and even the same attacks. It's quite underwhelming, especially only one is truly entertaining to fight as it has multiple different body parts that have varied attacks and moves. At least the dark arisen expansion was responsible for fixing that a little bit.
There are multiple classes you can switch between during the game and the only ones I thoroughly liked were the ones that you could dodge and strafe with. This helped the game feel like a little more like an action game and not like a bethesda where the only suitable strategy is backpedaling because you can't dodge moves.
This game would work 1000x better as a boss rush game similar to the dark souls games or hollow knight or binding of isaac. The open world is not worth trodding through just to get to the next good part of the game, so why even have it in there? It's bland, empty and a waste of resources.

I'll make this very short - this is an excellent game that is very much worth your time and money. If you have some to play it with, that is - ideally someone sitting with you in the same room.
The game consists of a disconnected series of "trials" (aka levels) with an overarching, persistent upgrade system and four classes you can change between at will between runs. After finishing six of the 25 available levels, I can say that thinking up and implementing strategies for achieving each level's extra goals (finishing it within a given time limit, plus one level-specific goal) is really satisfying.
You will be running the same levels over and over again, but there's no grind - you will be trying various approaches, or attempt to perfect the execution of a strategy you thought up (it's not the hardest game in the world, nor does it try to be, but it's decently challenging for your average gamer, so that will happen sooner or later).
It's not the Greatest ♥♥♥♥ing Thing Ever, but it's a splendid game you might spend tens of hours on and thoroughly enjoy it, and it's an excellent co-op experience. As a fair warning though - one of the game's core mechanics makes it highly troll-prone. Only play with people you know and/or trust to do fine, and as I've said before, ideally with people sitting in the same room.

I've been playing the classic Sonic games lately. So far I've replayed Sonic 2, played through Sonic 3&K for the first time and revisited CD (I have no idea how many times I've played it) and I really feel like it's time for a review.
Now I gotta say,
This game is very short. I tried to time one of my runs and it was only a little over an hour long. However, the short length is one of my favorite things about the game. Because of that and it's very balanced difficulty, It's easily repayable. The game also has a time mechanic, which lets you go to the past, present and future of each stage, which changes the look, music and designs of them. On top of that, the game has two great soundtracks, all adding to the replayability.
One thing that's different about CD than previous games is that... it's different! Mostly when it comes to the level designs. The stages are pretty short, and are designed a bit differently compared to previous games. The levels are a lot more "weird" (take that as you will). Some people love it, some people hate it. What I like about CD's level designs is that you can get through them super quick, but you can also easily explore them as well (most at least), which makes it not so tedious to get a good ending, which you can do by either collecting all the Time Stones from special stages, or by doing some in-game exploring to destroy hologram projectors and robot teleporters.
I don't know what else to say other than that I really recommend this game. It's a short, sweet and seemingly never ending adventure for me, and I hope it is for you as well.

Ah, Starbound. Such a great sense of wonder packed inside a small file size, and hours of fun to be had for 15 dollars. But is it worth it? I've packed over 100 hours into the game, but over a span of years. I'll explain things in retrospect.
When the game first came out, we actually pirated it and played it for hours on that copy until the weekend arrived and I was able to afford a copy. The game had an effect similar to Minecraft where its lack of story and content actually added to the adventure. There was a sense of whimsy when I was exploring the different worlds and learning how to play the game as I went, I felt lost in a big universe. Eventually I explored the game beyond my friends' interest and once I reached the end game of whatever version was out in late 2012 or early 2013, I stopped playing for a long time. I believe I clocked in at 60 hours on Steam at that time. I was disappointed with the lack of any real end game, and I left it alone for years feeling ALMOST satisfied with whatever I put into the game.
Then the game actually released. I noticed there were many improvements made. The game ran better, there was a story, there were more biomes to explore, tons of cool mods to goof around with, it gave me a sense of adventure again as if the current version of Starbound according to the review date was a brand new game again. I started with a Felin character, put 15 hours into it goofing around, and then lost it somehow. Then I decided to go witha Novakid and within a few days I packed in 35 hours into the game and beat the main quest. Of course, I was working on a farm for a good third of that time and building a huge house, as well as overmining planets of their resources, but that doesn't mean the game lacks content in the main course of the game... The story progression!
The game feels like a lootfest, but there's too much loot so I'm constantly stuffing lockers full of goodies. Too many weapons I'll never use, too many bars I'll never craft things with, too much money I'll never spend. I feel like after beating the game I've lost all sense of wonder in the single player. The side quests aren't too intruiging aside from being able to upgrade your ship and there's not much to explore after finishing the main questline. Nevertheless, I still had fun. Goofing around with friends is an entirely different aspect of the game and can help encourage creative building. Other side goodies include playing music and murdering each other... I'm not sure you can still do the second one in this version.
Either way, this game has something other games don't seem to have, other than Terraria. A grand sense of scale and adventure that seems nearly endless in its dawning hours. The difference between this game and Terarria is that the Starbound will feed your sense of adventure to the brim instead of providing a challenge with every encounter. But it does weaken the sense of reward you get when finding certain ores.
I kind of forgot to talk about the graphics and music. The graphics are decent enough but the game still runs like garbage if you play for a while. The music just makes me either bored or sad so I just turn on my own tunes. The music's still good, just not anything noteworthy.
This game gets a solid 7/10. Wonderful execution, but the excitement fades the deeper you get in. There's still lots of creativity to be had with the game and all sorts of things to do on the side, so the game is still solid. I think I'd rate my experience with the game an 8/10 if I were to put together my time with the game altogether across various versions. I say you should give it a buy!

This game is amazing technically.  It looks great, the controls are awesome, and even if you are terrible, it is a joy just to fly around.
The ability to hover and strafe is amazing too.  Overall, RageQuit have made a very impressive game that should have become super popular, even a staple for the Steam community.  However, I feel it has one fatal flaw:
It's too goddamned difficult.
I know the game wasn't designed to appeal to everybody, or become the next Hat Simulator 2.  I know RageQuit prided themselves on creating something that elite gamers from the classic multiplayer era of shooters would appreciate.  All the same, the difficulty curve is jacked.
Really, there is no difficulty curve.  It's a friggin' difficulty wall.  You'll be playing gainst people just as bad as yourself and still struggling to topfrag with 3 kills after the time limit is up.
The reason games like TF2, DOTA 2, and CS:GO developed such substantial followings is because a new person can pick it up and still somewhat try to contribute to their team, plus learn little by little along the way.  When a new player has 2 kills and 15 deaths in CS:GO, they feel like they can eventually learn and aren't discouraged.
Psychologically, there aren't enough payoffs here.  You may never kill anyone.  A lot of the weapons need to be led, and both you and your opponents move not across planes like a ground-based shooter, you're floating in 360 degree space.  A lot of the hitscan/locking weapons are too weak.  It's frustrating as hell, and not because your opponant is more skilled; they might not even know they evaded your attacks as you fly into yet another wall.  In fact, you might die to crashing more than anything else.
What's hilarious about all of this is the game gives you visual rewards for EVERYTHING, Call of Duty style.  That's a game designed for console users and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, hardly the ultimate proving ground of FPS skill that this game claims to be.
I'm not a total baddie as far as FPS's go, and early 2000's is my favorite era for shooters as well.  All the same, I would rather face the best player in the world in Quake 3 than one moderately practiced player in this game.  At least I might get lucky with the railgun once in awhile.  At least Q3 had an audible hit indicator, plus not every single weapon required the precision of an industrial robot to use.
I would like to see this game re-released easier to use wepons, less penality for colliding with walls, and maybe environments where everything isn't the same dingy color has your opponents.  A bot mode would have helped too.  This game could have filled a very unique niche, but as it is, I can't find anyone to play on the servers.  ANYWHERE.  No one else had the patience to weather the crazy difficulty curve,a nd those who did probably got tired of waiting around for hours to play NOBODY.
Like I said, it's got potential, it's just not accessible yet.

After finishing this game, my impression is that it is neither particularly excellence nor is it particularly awful.
First off even though you are in a high tech time traveling super suit, you are still very fragile. Don't think you can just do a run and gun waltz towards a group of enemies, they will tear you to shreds. Of course you aren't meant play like that, you have to use your time manipulation powers to deal with the baddies.
Speaking of baddies, there is a lack of enemy variety as almost all of them are based around a human holding a gun. You won't find any hostile giant insects, hungry zombies, or evil robots in this game. Still, there are a few specialized enemies that will require the use of time manipulation to deal with time.
In terms of weapon variety, the guns are pretty standard. Assault rifle, shotgun, sniper rifle, rocket launcher, etc.
As for the environments, there isn't anything else particularly interesting or memorable about the setting. Still that doesn't mean that the game is lacking in the variety of level environments.
Finally, the story and backstory are rather thin. Perhaps the setting can be fleshed out some more if a sequel is made.

Yes. I recommend this game for anyone who remembers the 2002-2007 era First Person Shooter games with warmth. This game is filled with a bunch of cliches, bad dialogue, flat characters and an uninteresting story, but my damn if it isn't worth a playthrough.
The game's general design incorporates the usage of time manipulation: slow-mo, stop and reverse. You are definitely not being dragged down by the storyline, but are instead left alone with you, a bunch of enemies and your powers most of the time. The strength of this title is definitely in those time abilities, as it doesn't get old to go into slow mo, shoot eight guys in the head with the shotgun and then go back and watch them fall to the ground instantly.
It's not a very long game and it's not too difficult. It's a good thing in this case, as variety isn't a featured element. Yes, there are a few vehicle and turret sections, but they're very short and, well, a little boring.
On the surface this title is far from perfect, but beneath it's got it's own charm. And unlike most TV shows it quits before people get bored of it.

I recommend this game and their is more to be said, but these are the things that stuck out most to me. Also note, I haven't played the game that much.
The GOOD: Probably one of the most realistic zombie shooters out there. The game delivers something new and different. Not being in a city or a mall (Dead rising), but merely settled in a few towns , farmland, mountains and a very small "city". It's very diverse, and you can really fortify your base making beds, small medic stations, etc. That is cool. The graphics are really good when you set to Ultra High. Ed, Maya and a few others can fight for themselves, it makes you feel like you are not babysitting all the time.
The BAD:  Dialogue is mediocre. I end up only really like a few characters.  ALAN is my least favorite. You meet him in the Chapel and he strictly tells you to not drive any cars, or shoot guns near the Chapel, although the guy is shooting zombies from the watch tower, leading zombies to the Chapel and getting in. It would be fine if most of the survivors could fend for themselves. I mean, come on, the Pastor got killed by one zombie and no one would help them. Also, I get that the game is realistic, and once you loot a house or restaurant that it is gone forever. I get that, that's awesome. But what happens when you loot the entire game? So it's over? That's not fair! What if I really like the game? I don't want to start over. That is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Why has there only been one DLC? I want more.
The UGLY: I heard that this game is based under the "Perma Death" system or whatever the hell it's called.
So what that means is that the longer you are away from the game, the worse off you will be.  Supplies like food and medicine will deplete, zombies will start attacking your base more, and survivors will end up dying.  So When you have a busy schedule like me, and you can only play video games once or twice a week, you will end up having to deal with that. What a load of horse♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm sorry that I can't play a ♥♥♥♥ing game every damn day to keep up with it.
So that is my small review.  KEEP IN MIND. This game is really good. For twenty bucks, you really can't beat the price. I happen to get it on sale for ten bucks. To me that's worth it.

I expected Read Only Memories to be an inclusive, loving homage to Snatcher. Perhaps with a few nods to Tass Times in Tonetown, Mass Effect... and Bob Ross? Yes, ROM hit all those notes, but it also surprised me with the depth and nuance it brought to its characters and world. ROM may seem like a point and click adventure/visual novel, but it also asks the player to listen and pay attention. Conversations matter. People you may have written off matter, sometimes negatively, but sometimes in delightful ways. There are stakes, but they feel organically earned.
I also can't say enough about ROM's aesthetic. The artwork is clean and vibrant. The character portraits are wonderful and full of life (especially Turing, the AI that steals every scene). The music right from the title screen is stuck in my head. And I want the sound effects on my phone! They're just perfect.

The dialouge is entertaining and hillarious, the characters are fleshed out, and the whole game has a unique charm to it. Not to mention, Turing, your robot sidekick through out your adventure, is one of my personal favorite video game characters to date. I can tell this isn't a game for everyone, but if you like the Ace Attorney or Famicom Detective Club franchises , this is definately up your ally. If you're still on the fence, I'd recommend at least trying the free demo.

First thing first:
If you've played Hideo Kojima's Snatcher before, you'll be right at home with this game!
Read Only Memories is a really neat cyberpunk adventure game that does a banging job on hitting the familiar feels if you've grown playing MSX, PC Engine & Sega CD games. Top notch low resolution pixel art, really groovy chiptune vibes and the sound effects are a fantastic throw to the back in all the good ways! Also I like the way how the characters are really expressive even with such little frames and all!
Another banging note I wanna bring up is the level, and amount of writing in this game! Pretty much everything is interactable and examinable, and instead of non-descriptive "You can't use that with that", you get unique responses and really funny ones as well! There's so much of choice dialogue sprinkled everywhere and I genuinely enjoy talking with the characters I meet in this game!
Speaking of characters! It's really refreshing to see genuinely wide cast of vastly different kinds of folks in this game, with unique looks and personalities and such! It's also really inclusive game, and they've done pretty sweet job of recognizing LGBT folk and preferred pronouns and other really superb stuff - oh and don't worry! There's no force-feeding of any agendas here, which is also super cool in my opinion!
While I can't say too much about the plot and overall run of the game yet, as I'm still working my way through it, the plot has gotten me pretty hooked up and I can't wait to see what kind of wild ride this game is going to turn out!
Oh, and extra note! The Midboss devs are like super SUPER nice and cute people and they're really responsive and just nice folks in general! You should definetly try out the demo and if that feels like your thing, give this game a shot! I'm sure you're going to dig it a lot!
I'll edit this review later once I've finished this game to add my final thoughts!

Forced is a very interesting and fun game. It's quite different from anything I've played before, requires a lot of synergy between the players and even after dozens of consecutive failures trying to get a challenge done or killing a boss, you still keep trying because the combat and puzzles are fun, you know you can kill the axe dude faster this time, there's still hope that your friends won't screw up (again) and you just can't go to sleep until you unlock that next skill... and when you do, you must try it out, even if it's 4 a.m.
Each of the 4 characters are also very different from each other, if you are not doing well at the moment, get another guy and everything changes. Each one has several different skills, and you choose 3 active and 3 passive ones before going into an arena.

The moment where a promise prevails over any sort of command or order, where this fierce, burning passion yields to nothing short of the desired goal.
Time and time again, stories that revolve around androids has never ceased to amaze me no matter how many times I have seen similar themes being handled; they continuously give a nudge at one's heartstrings. Almost as if reading this visual novel is the same as playing a harp with each string representing a different emotion that is then played at various frequency, duration, and intensity to develop into a string of notes turning into a vibrant melody all coming together to become a feast of emotions filled with enough diversity to fit into each and everyone's need. The conductor guiding the flow of the story's ambiance into unison and therefore, producing a single, bittersweet product that is masterfully handled.
Lucy -The Eternity She Wished For- is impressive in all respects: the art, voice acting, music, story and many more are to be desired of, given the fitting beauty in many scenes of the story, although seemingly simple, the story is intriguing, touching, and all in all an enjoyable work. As the story unfolds itself, one can't help but to sympathize with the characters and become immersed in the story of just what it means to become attached to someone; whether they are human or not, or blood-related or not. Someone important is simply someone important, nothing more and nothing less.

The game Lucy asks the question: can an android  be human?  Or maybe even what is important for humans to accept another human. What you'll have from this story depends largely on yourself. How much you want to think about it. What you want to believe. And what not. Even the good ending can be a distopia depending on your beliefs.
So it's a pretty adult and merciless  game. In contrast to that Lucy is what you expect her to be. Innocence on two legs you want to protect even if it cost your own life. The game designer used all the tricks so that we'll feel sympathy for her. And we have quite early huge trouble to just see the machine in "her". The father plays a keyrole and I would recommend to put yourself at least for one playthrough in his shoes. See Lucy and the whole situation from his perspective. Think about what he tells you. Also what your friend tells you. It's important to fully understand the situation you are in and the true meaning of your decisions.

So, at first this game had a lot of promise, and it still does if you are only looking forward to a small game with your friends. However, when you start devoting more and more time to this game, you realize that the amount of content being distributed by the developer is pretty miniscule. Most of the updates are features that the game should've had on release, such as more features when creating a lobby or other quality of life improvements. In terms of the experience system, it feels pretty great at first from 1-81, but after that, the amount of experience required to level up starts to increase dramatically, so much that you question the worth of actually leveling up. You don't even get weapons for some of those levels, which is just ridiculous, considering how much devotion it takes to get them. I should also mention, that every time you level up you get a "Tank Token" when you put into one of four sections, which are Chassis, Gun, Luck, and Tracks. At first, the upgrades are miniscule but as you level you start getting checkpoints which help. This feels pretty lackluster, but combined with the weapons from 1-81, leveling isn't that bad. The developer is adding weapons for lower levels instead of catering to the higher levels, which is a continuously growing portion of the community. I understand this is just my opinion, but thank you for taking the time to read this review. At the end of the day, it's not a bad game, but don't be looking forward to new content after 200+ hours of playing the same content, as I learned that myself.

Miscreated is a lot of fun but there are problems that become apparent. Some of them are major.
- Zombies are rare, restricted to outdoors and are usually glitchy.
- Food/Water is all over the place.
- Vehicle damage system is buggy. Bicycle goes nuts when you get off and usually glitches when you get on.
- Lots of kill-on-sight due to lack of PVE.
- You will run around and generally find empty places. Feels like a lonely running simulator.
- No character customization or progression. You spawn as the same dude but with different clothes.
- Blueprint (if you can even find any) and building system is basically worthless.
- No prone or auto run
If most or all features above were fixed, this game would be fantastic compared to what is currently out there. I think Miscreated is going in the right direction but it is currently not worth $20. Definitely get it on sale if you can!

Where to even begin. This game is a narrative trainwreck, which sucks because a lot of it has so much potential that you can see rotting on the vine.
First off, this game doesn't handle multiple monitors very well.  I've had to turn off my side 2 through nVidia control panel to make it play nice. Every time the game starts up, it opens a little pop up saying I've got incompatible drivers and sends me to nvidia's homepage to download the latest drivers which I already have. Older game, hard to program forward compatibility, but whatever, I can deal with that. Not impressed, but not enough to kill it either.
Gameplay: This is a generic linear corridor shooter with a gimmick of limited time control. You can slow time down, stop time and reverse time.  And that's about it. It's not even as much fun as it sounds. What would have been more interesting is an open level approach with multiple solutions, instead of forcing the player down a single path and having the only option to be to shoot everyone. The time control features are introduced within 5 minutes of the opening level, and other than some weapons, that’s about it. The weapons themselves tend to flip flop between underpowered pea-shooter and BFG9000. There’s no character customization, only about 6 weapons total, a few have some alt-fire which is easily ignored and forgotten.  A better way of doing this would be a leveling system that lets the player choose how they want to accomplish their objectives: perhaps some would like to do things stealthy, others like the time manipulation tools, still others prefer to load up on heavy armor, big guns, and shoot friends and foes alike until there’s nothing left but smoking ash. Some variety.
The AI is forgettable. They mostly just stand there, or get into poor cover while shouting about what kind of gun you have, request reinforcements, or repeat the same few canned lines again and again and again. They make up for their stupidity in sheer numbers and by killing you in a few shots.
Story wise, don’t even bother. You’re dropping into an alternate timeline around 1939, but might as well be 2100 with all the future tech running around. There’s the generic evil empire vs the good rebels, but I constantly found myself asking “Who are these people and why should I care about any of this.”  You see some of the present in flashbacks, but don’t expect it to answer any questions. It might have raised a few questions, but by then I didn’t even care.
Do yourself a favor and pick up a copy of Deus Ex or Dishonored instead.

Competent, yet completely average and uninspired shooter. Ultimately, Timeshift feels just gimmicky - and it exhausts it's bag of tricks very fast. I had fun shooting an explosive bolt into a guy's head with time frozen and watching him suddenly become inert gibs. A couple of the weapon are very interesting, regardless - a submachine gun with incendiary rounds and attached flamethrower was different enough to become a favorite -, but their designs are, again, uninspired (What the hell is that assault rifle?!), and the audio and feedback lacks any punch (though the shotgun WILL send people flying... after maybe two or three shots at close range.)
The game quickly devolved into slow-motion dashing through cover while waiting for the limited time-resource to recharge.
In the end, Timeshift didn't offer enough freedom to abuse my timepowers nor enough challenge or solid gameplay to constitute a good shooter - in this regard, it didn't achieve either a sandbox I could blow steam off in nor a challenging game I could be engaged in. Instead, it forced me to play it like a shooter with a fun-but-repetitive gimmick I could enjoy every forty seconds - and it doesn't have enough foundation as a shooter to force me into that. F.E.A.R. provides a far more enjoyable experience - in which the time effect, while not as varied - supports a much better game - and one that stands on its own without the gimmick.

Shadow Of Mordor was well worth the $3.99 I paid. The story line is engaging and deeply seeped in the LOTR mythos. I won't spoil any of the story line, except to say, it is "precious".
The gameplay is great. Fluid combat that gets it ques from games like Batman: Arkham series and Prince of Persia. It also has added elements that makes the combat intuitive and unique to the game. You really feel like a Ranger of Gondor as you plow through Orc and Uruk strongholds. Archery, swordplay, and fisticuffs are the name of the game, and there's plenty of enemies on which to dole out the pain. Pick your style, run in and terrorize the enemy or stalk around their camp picking them off one by one. The stealth aspects of the game are great, much less frustrating and time consuming than other entries into the open world/chain-based multiplier combat genre.
Another unique element of this particular game that makes it stand out from the rest of the genre is the fact that when you die, there are consequences. Staying alive (ie running your ranger butt off away from the enemy) will benefit you in the long run. Although the game makes dying so important, it still throws you a bone in the form of XP everytime you take a shank or arrow or thrown axe or spear in the heat of combat.
Shadow of Mordor is a fun, open world, multplier combat game that really delves into the LOTR story. I'd recommend it for all gamers, and espeically LOTR fans.

It took me 50 hours to play it through in a rather slow and calm kind of way. While it obviously cannot nearly keep up to the amount of content of a Baldur's Gate II, (lenght of the campaign, amount of optional quests, interesting storylines), it yet does some things better than its predecessors.
It is in every sense indeed a game for adults. Dialogues are very well-conceived and sophisticated, and so is the whole background of the story and this new world. Prepare yourself for a LOT of careful reading, if you want to really understand what's going on and take some insights from this game. If you don't, there is still a very good tactical fighting system to explore, but that's obviously not the major purpose here.
You find yourself confronted with truly hard moral decisions, where you really have to think about what's right and what's wrong. That is so because the game gives you absolutely no hints where things might lead you or what is now the "good character"-choice. Sometimes I found myself staring for five minutes on some dialogue options before i chose one, thinking really hard what to answer. The game, in its way, rewards you for the effort, building plausible consequences even on the nuances of how your character behaves and what he says.
There is no black and white and grey like we are used to from the fantasy genre. Every situation is unique, and sometimes several or even all options lead to consequences that you can't morally justify, but yet you have to come to a decision!
It's just like in the real world.
That's why i liked this game.

I haven't written a review before but honestly felt compelled to write one for Stranded Deep.
I was on the fence about whether to purchase this game or not for quite some time now. Going by the trailers and screenshots, it looked absolutely amazing. However, going by some of the reviews and the general expectations of most Early Access games, I held off on buying it.
I'm not sure what it was that made me take the risk, but I decided to give it a try.
I have been incredibly pleased with my experience so far. It's all far from finished and that is quite clear, but my word does it have some charm to begin with!
The visuals are where it's at for starters. At full settings, It looks stunning! There are some tears and graphical glitches... but when you take in your first sunset, they seem trivial at most.
The crafting system is a refreshing change to the overused 'Minecraft-esque' table. It feels more physical and you can't carry 64 pieces of wood around in your pocket. Being able to physically drag and move items, really helps immersion and that's the strong point that Stranded Deep should emphasize even more.
There's basically zero combat, going by my experience so far. I really enjoy this to be honest. I've grown tired of survival games that make you battle fantasy based enemies. I've wanted to play a survival game that pits the player against nature. There isn't enough content to say that Stranded Deep is that game, but it's one of the strongest contenders that I've come across so far. I love that I can hang out on my beach at night time, beside my campfire, as I take in the world around me. I'm not under siege of groaning zombies or trying to take down a T-Rex with a mallet. I'm just watching a tiger shark swim back and forth, as I chuckle quietly... safe from the comfort of my beach.
I do recommend this game BUT... I highly encourage anyone who approaches it, to do so without researching the gameplay too much. I didn't really watch any playthroughs or gameplay footage, before I started. I had no idea how to craft and/or what items were craftable. This gave me a real sense of washing up on a desert island and having to figure things out myself.
This game doesn't really hold your hand or walk you through what needs to be done. It's immersive and requires you to pace yourself.
I cannot wait to see Stranded Deep grow into something fantastic. From what I understand, it seems that development has slowed down and some folks are worried that it may go the same road as many other 'open world/survival' Early Access games. I sincerely hope the development continues and generates a bigger following because this could be amazing.
-Pros-
+ Stunning Visuals / Lighting
+ Immersive Crafting System
+ Player defined pacing and progression
+ Sharks are scary
+ Fresh and interesting take on survival games
++++ NO ZOMBIES!!!
-Cons-
- Visuals need some care (Graphic tears, Draw distance is annoying, Lighting glitches)
- Needs more content
- Audio feels unfinished and empty at times
- Needs more content
- Slow development
- Needs more content
