The gameplay of Strike Vector is mightily interesting.
Some of the interesting points of Strike Vector :
While it seems that all aerial combat games that we played are indeed high speed, the thing that differentiates Strike Vector is the ability to transform from flight mode to hover mode. On flight mode the aircraft has greater speed, agility, and evasion, while at hover mode the aircraft has better accuracy, and of course, easier to control to fire the weapons. Like all flight games, all players must watch what goes above them, below them, and around them, creating a fight on 3D space that is very interesting, and deadly.
The maps are nicely made. The maps also bring good narratives to the game, for example huge ships and huge floating cities. The maps are quite detailed, and fun to fly around and shoot around. The maps have various characteristics too. Some maps are very open, allowing long range duels, like the map in outer space, but some maps have very cramped, like the map where the dogfighting occurs inside a refinery. Some maps also have combination of both. Some parts of the maps are cramped, and some are very wide. The maps, are nicely done.
Frankly, this is a weakness. With no AI bots, we will depend on the availability of the servers, and the number of existing playerbase. This will be covered later.
The craft that we have could be customized, starting from the look, to its weapon system, to its characteristics, and its special weapon. You could create a "long-range" craft that have homing missile, and equipped with system to allow better detection of enemies "vector" (crafts) and mines to protect your place. Or, you wanted a "melee" craft, that is equipped with carbine and gatling gun, with system to better track fleeing enemies, and ghost system to make your vector invisible for a short while. Or, you wanted a "stealth" craft that is equipped with plasma and shotgun, with system to make your vector harder to detect, and defense system to make your vector tougher. So many options. So many option. So many tactics. This is a very great thing in the game.
You got XP and medals for doing some things. Like 3-kill streak. Or kill somebody when you are dead. Or when using your flaming, dying craft to make a final kill. Or when you successfuly kills the person who kills you. A lot more. A great flavor to the game.
A major concern here. The game is easy enough to understand. After all, it's just another flying game. But the hard part is how to apply those flying skills in combat. Not to mention that this game has lacklustre, and sub-par tutorial. In the tutorial you are told to do this and that, without even told what is the key to do that, or why we have to do that. We are told that going through booster rings makes our vector goes faster, but no tips at all, to survive PvP combat.
This game is fully multi-player. No bots at all. The devs made a vague promise, but that's all. The devs is working on another game, so usually this game will not be developed much. The developers still came and care for the game, for example releasing new maps, but I think they won't be releasing an AI. The devs has stated that it is difficult, and I agree with them. Sadly, there are only a few people willing to play this great game. Even after released in Humble Bundle for a cheap price, only few people are playing this game.
This game has a lot of servers around in the world, from USA to Singapore. That means all regions are covered well, and no one should have large pings, but the problem is the lack of the players. But if you are playing this game, don't worry, although most servers are empty, there should be 1-2 servers that have players there. A major gripe here is also that some people (they called themselves veterans) that are good in this game will trumps new bloods easily, thus creating an aura of elitism, and kicking new bloods out. Some veterans are good, but some are bad.

Stranded Deep is a game that hit's everything I want in a good survival game. Atmosphere? Check. Good Textures? Check. Terrifying Creatures? Check. Lonliness? Check :D. This game installed a fear into me that though I may be on land sharks are still swimmin' waitin for me to go into the water.

Even though this is still a very early alpha at the time I am writing this (Version 0.03) it is already my favorite game. The term "survival" has been stretched a lot these days, most people think of Zombies or other players shooting you on sight when they hear the term.
However - "Stranded Deep" is different.  If you ever watched the movie "Cast away" you already get a feeling what it might be like to be alone on an uninhabited island and how hard it is to survive - but this time it's all up to you.
The game is not even overly exciting, it's more of a trip into your inner self and after a while you understand why Tom Hanks was starting to talk to a volleyball in that movie. Now you experience loneliness, desperation and fighting for your life first hand. Incredible how happy one can be just to find an old machete in a sunken shipwreck deep down on the ground of the ocean. Or the joy you feel when you built your own primitive hut from sticks and palm leaves.
No matter what kind of games you played so far - good chances that this one is unlike anything you ever played.
At currently 15 bucks definitely my best buy ever.

Absolutely terrible onboarding process. Logs are the only language accepted in this game and new players will have an absolutely miserable first half dozen games until they figure out the shorthand required for log taking and they will still be unable to play evil classes without having had a chance to see pretty much all of the good classes so they can fake logs. The community guides are all wrong, either pertaining to outdated versions or suggesting "easy" lies that are so obvious to the playerbase that claiming them truthfully will get you killed half the time. And that doesn't even count the enormous numbers of edge cases you have to memorize to make decisions.
Get past that, and you can see I got my money's worth, incredibly addictive for a while but a flash in the pan like PUBG and for similar reasons. You can play 20 games and you'll maybe see 2 good ones that are down to the wire where something actually interesting happens. 10 of those you play classes that are a simpler flow-chart than Ken, who literally have no plays other than "grief someone randomly" until late game and then their flow-chart is just the same action over and over and whose only contribution to the detective game is dying and hoping when their logs spill out of their corpse that "Couldn't grief this random guy due to blockage" is the last evidence the sleuths need to crack the case. And about 16-18 of those, the good mob or the evil mob will throw the game on a boneheaded play or through miserable random chance. Maybe the rare good game is worth it, but I play games, not slot machines or gacha.
The only memorable moments I can even name, the only times I remember winners and losers having a sportsmanlike cheer/groan of a well-fought battle in this game are when the Fool makes a strong play. And the Fool's only goal is to trick everyone into executing him. In most every other game I'm infuriated at my allies or feeling pity for the moronic play of my enemies.
So it's like PUBG, there's a lot of tension, when you're past the newbie sinkhole and into figuring out the tricks and you're figuring out the rules of the game and it seems like there are so many possibilities ahead of you, it's a buffet you can't get enough of. Only then, a dozen or two plays later, you realize you're faffing about blindly half the time and going through the motions the other half and failing at every action and getting sniped out of nowhere in the third half... you burn out just as fast as you started, from 0 to 100 and back to 0 again. I can't say I didn't get my money's worth out of both PUBG and ToL but a point comes in both where you just don't want to play it any more and can't understand anyone who still does.

In Town of Salem you get AFKers and leavers that leave the game to the chance the sheriff will find the killing factions.  In Throne of Lies, its completely different.  Each role feels to make contributions to their faction.  The presence of neutral roles creates additional people for both Blue Dragon and killing faction to be on the lookout for. Shellshock Live is that classic 2D tank game you probably know of…but with online Multiplayer and a crazy weapon selection that surpasses even Worms. For the most part, the gameplay is turn-based where you move your tank a small distance each turn, then put an angle and set power into your shot, then hope you calculated it right and it hits the enemy. The huge weapon variety prevents it from being stale, though, as you may have to plan different strategies depending on what weapons the crates give you. There’s not much to describe, but I assure you it’s fun and easy to get into, especially with friends.
There are a few flaws, though. The biggest flaw is the upgrading system. As you play more, you can upgrade your tank’s health, movement, etc. This can create unfair discrepancies between you and friends if one decides to play alone or if someone’s new. You pretty much have to reset tanks at that point. Also, you unlock weapons and the player with the wider weapon pool is usually at an advantage. The game has a few ways to try and balance this, but I think it would’ve been more fun and easier to pick up with anyone if everyone had the same tank stats and all weapons unlocked.
Otherwise, I think this game is definitely worth a shot. If you can get your friends in on it, I think that’s definitely the route to go…as long as you all stay leveled near each other.

An example of a re-release done right, and a great opportunity for people to experience an otherwise underrated classic Sonic games. Firstly, this release includes choice of Soundtrack, with the Japanese one being my personal favourite, partly due to consistency with past music, and partly due to feeling a lot more lively. That being said, the US soundtrack is by no means bad, and makes for a more atmopheric and environmental experience, The inclusion of Widescreen is also a great addition, really complimenting the side-scrolling and fast-paced gameplay. The option to choose from 1 of 2 spindashes (classic Sonic CD vs. Sonic 2) is also a nice addition. Finally, its nice to have a classic character like Tails thrown into the mix also. One minor drawback, is that the Japanese opening does not have vocals (but this is forgiveable given every other feature present here)
As for the game itself, it is a nice and unique Sonic game all on its own. While time travelling can be a tad tedious (given a requirement for speed + duration + an appropriate time-period sign collected), the idea works rather well, and it's interesting exploring the different time periods of each zone, all of which have strong similarities throughout each of the periods, but with interesting subtle differences (e.g. the conversion of the factory like setting of Wacky Workbench, into what resembles more a lighthearted toy factory for example). A lot of classic Sonic elements are still within the game, and this is also the introduction of the one-true Metal Sonic and Amy. Boss fights themselves (taking place in the future) differ when compared with other Sonic games, often taking only 0-4 hits, rather than the standard 8, and usually involving a strategy other than direct spin attacking.
One final interesting point, is that there is essentially 2 different ways of achieving a good ending in this game. The first involves a more traditional method, utilising the collection of Time Stones (i.e. this games Chaos Emeralds). A second method however, involves exploration and time travel. Rather than collect Time Stones, one can simply travel back to the past in each Zone (the equivalent to Act's in othe Sonic games), and destroy Robotnik's robot creation machine. Destroying both in each level, destroys all past badniks, wipes out a chunk of the present day badniks, and essentially creates a good future. Destroying every one of these machines in the game also leads to a good ending.
The unique differences in this game may perhaps feel a little foreign to some die-hard Sonic fans. That said, the game can otherwise be enjoyed and played through like any other Sonic game, ignoring the need for time travel should one just want a linear and straight forward playthrough of the game. Not only is this a great Sonic game, but it's exactly what near perfect re-release should look like. There are minor differences in physics from the original, but these do not really hurt the game in anyway. A definite recommendation here.

The binding of isaac is a fantastic game in it's own. The remake rebirth was truely a work of art, now that it no longer suffers from the low frame rate and is fully fleshed out. This game is filled with thousands of items, combinations and synergies alike. I can be certain that every single run is different and packed with excitment. I've only been playing it for a few dozen hours and I still have an unreal amount to unlock and challenges galor. It's really a game for those who enjoy lots of challenge and the sweet rewards of unlocking new things in return.

The point of the game is to get to the boss of each floor and move on to the next, with 10 floors total (after you have unlocked them all). Half of the gameplay is a bullet-hell style combat, where you can shoot in 4 directions with the arrow keys, and the other half involves the strategic element of the game. There is actually a lot of complexity with regard to choosing which items to take and how to manage your bombs, keys, coins, and health. For example, you can only hold one active item and one trinket, so you must sometimes decide whether to give up your current one for other ones you come across. You must decide whether to use bombs to look for secret rooms, blow up skulls and mushrooms for potential items, open stone chests which can only be opened with bombs, or save them to use on the next floor. Then there's the strategy involved in shops and devil rooms where you can give up heart containers for powerful items. Sometimes randomness can mess up your run, but even if you get unlucky or make a wrong decision, you can try and make up for it in skill.
Anyway, BoI is one of the funnest games I've played in a while. I've played 80 hours (at the time of writing this review) and still have a bunch of things to unlock and some challenges left to do.

so as far as the singleplayer is concerned there are a few things that i think are improved. Primarily the gameplay is improved in all ways and more fun than Conviction. The budget and production values are severely diminished and the new Sam Fisher makes the presentation jarring. However the gameplay itself is far improved and the story works as a continuation of Sam Fisher's double agent mission.
The multiplayer is the best it has ever been and as usual is an improvement over the last game's multiplayer. Conviction didn't have any versus modes so it's good to see it come back. As a player of the versus modes since Chaos Theory i have a few comments.
Spies vs mercs is back however it is a perfect combination of all the  versus modes until now. So here is how i will break it down.
Terminal hacking begins like in chaos theory by hacking the terminal directly as in chaos theory, a discontinuation from Double Agent where you hack the terminal completely remotely. However the once you have begun the hack you can hack remotely away from the terminal ala Double Agent.
As far as the spy gameplay they have the predatory techniques of Chaos Theory, with some of the more pacisfist techniques found in Double Agent (360) being removed. However unlike any multiplayer mode yet the Spies themselves can actually fire real weapons and not tazer darts. So the attack power of the spies is higher than ever. So in a combination of the spy technique from Chaos Theory, the remote hacking techniques from Double Agent (360) and the spy's emphasis being on shooting ala Double Agent (Xbox original), the multiplayer ends up being a perfect combination of all game modes before it.
The mercenary gameplay is exactly what you would expect which is a strong basic shooting gameplay that is perfect for the series Versus mode.

In the end everything about this game is a perfect sequel of the previous games, however the Versus mode returning it s what really stands out for this iteration. So if  you've always been a fan of Splinter Cell's versus mode, or if you want to experience a unique gameplay that has never really been impersonated. I can reccomend this game solely for the multiplayer.
However i haven't had a chance to the test the co-op, but this has been one of the strongest features of the series since Chaos Theory.

this game is one of those that just flies under the radar.  its really cool and worth multiple playthroughs.
there are three time powers you can use:
reverse time: you wont use this much besides a couple of plot puzzles. the only real use for it in combat is when you get hit with a sticky grenade. it'll send it back and give you a brief window to avoid getting hit again.
stop time: this one is also used in a number of puzzles but its actually useful in combat.  you can stop time and get easy headshots or you could use it to stop enemy fire and recover your health. of course because its so overpowered it doesnt last very long.
slow time: this one is by far the best.  it lasts the longest too.  you move at normal speed but everyone else is really slow.  its a lot of fun running around getting headshots on everyone.

overall a great game. i definitely recommend it.  of course with all the other games available you should probably wait for one of the big seasonal sales to buy it.

What a breath of fresh air or more acurately a breath of old air...Thats not stale. (Actually, forget this metaphor, its not working.) A masterpiece of old meets new. Old school gaming interface with new graphics. A very atmospheric game with a  fantastic storyline. If you are an older gamer...ahem, like me, then you will remember all the things you enjoyed about PC gaming from the likes of Gauntlet, Balders Gate, and Neverwinter Nights, with a hint of the new, such as Diablo 3. This game was worth the wait, I backed it on Kickstarter for twenty in order to get the retail version for free and waited three years for them to finish it and here is why it is so good.
First off, if you enjoyed Baldurs Gate, Icewind Dale, Neverwinter Nights, or any other game like them in the genre you will enjoy this one as well.
To make it short and sweet, this game ahs everything like its predecessors but to me has more strategy built in and character placement and saving are even more important than before. I remember playing Baldurs Gate and just rushing into rooms and saving before each room, and this title does it just as well.
The biggest Pro to take away from the game is that your whole party has to be whiped out in order to lose a battle unless your character dies, but don't worry, because it's very clear whether or not your characters life is in danger depending on how many times they have fallen in combat so far. This is a big plus because the old system benefited casters and range and really hurt those players who wanted to make tanks. Of course your tank is gonna die here and there. A lot of the time your tank survives long enough for your damage to finish the boss in games like this and PoE doesn't hinder this playstyles progression.
So all in all, PoE is a great game that revitalized a genre that isn't seen very often anymore. For those who haven't played the genre, what are you waiting for, give PoE a try.

When I think of what makes a truly great RPG, it all boils down to one question: Would I play it again (and again and again)? And for me, that question comes down to two primary factors: choices and classes.  Pillars of Eternity nails both of these.
Even after multiple playthroughs, you will still find yourself with plenty of "roads not traveled" to explore.  For example, on one playthrough, I made a choice that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off a leading family in one of the major cities.  Their response was to start sending assassins after me.  After getting annoyed by the random assassin attacks, my emotionally mature decision was to go and slaughter the entire family and all their soldiers/servants.  Of course, in doing so, I forfeited an entire quest line they could have offered.  What if I played nice with the jerkwad family next time and beat up some goodies, instead?
There are a great variety of classes in PIllars, and thus an enormous variety in potential parties.  Via companions you pick up along the way, you will get to play with most of the classes ... but not all.  You'll need to create several PC's to get the full experience! I ended up running around most of my first playthrough with a fighter (PC), paladin, priest, canter, wizard, and cipher.  Even a cursory view of the forums will tell you that is not an OP party; I just happened to relate to those companion characters the best.  Next time, I'll try something completely different.  Variety is the spice of life and of CRPG parties.
In my opinion, Pillars of Eternity is the frontrunner among the new generation of CRPG's coming out.

If you pine for the days of Descent and triple-A title arena-style shooters like Quake 3 Arena and Unreal Tournament, you should just go ahead and click the "buy" button now. It blends the core elements of both these game types in a fast-paced Arena FPS environment (although you can play in third person as well). The levels are gorgeous and range from wide-open space-style dogfighting environments to the sort of claustrophobic passages and chambers that were commonplace in descent. You can get around both with level flight for dogfighting and instantly switch to a hover mode for face-to-face FPS-style dueling. There's even left/right strafing and powerups thrown in for the arena FPS junkies. The musical score for the title/configuration menus and sound effects is awesome as well. What's amazing about all of this is that it wasn't created by a large or even medium-size game studio. The game's website notes a total of eight people who worked on this game, yet it's extremely well-polished for what it is.
Of course, the game isn't flawless. There's a bit of a learning curve for flying mechanic of the game; it's simple, but you fly fast and need good reflexes (as you would in most FPS games) and you'll crash very frequently while trying to get the hang of it. However, the biggest problem by far is that virtually nobody is playing this game at the moment. It's a tragedy that the 8 people putting together this game didn't have a marketing budget to draw more people into it, but it is what it is.
If you love arena FPSes, do your part; try this game out and play it!

Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen is a masterpiece that suffers from a lot of problems. The story is your standard fantasy affair, and while it does have some interesting and intriguing plots, it never fully delivers on any of them. The character design and voice acting is average and lip syncing is practically non existent. The soundtrack has some amazing scores which you'll rarely ever hear since most of your travelling is spent in areas that the best pieces don't play. The UI is cumbersome and annoying, the game is filled with fetch quests and kill x amount of enemies, and while the open world boasts some rather impressive vistas and locales, they all start to blend together between the plains and forests.
So why do I consider Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen as one the best Action RPG's of all time? The combat is incredible. This game absolutely nails the gameplay. You will fight massive beasts that continually challenge you as a player. Creature design is amazing, and how you fight and play is left completely up to you. There is no right or wrong way to play this game. There are 6 classes to choose from and 3 hybrid classes unique to the player, and all are equally as viable and satisfying. If you want to play the whole game as a Strider with daggers climbing on top of your enemies or targeting their weakpoints from afar with a bow, go for it. If you want to play as a Sorcerer conjuring tornadoes and meteor showers down on a group of enemies? You can do that. You are not locked into a playstyle. If anything, the game actually encourages you to play as different classes and experience different approaches to combat. You could play 50 levels as a Fighter with a sword and shield and switch to a Mage and after a little training be just as strong.
The game also makes use of a unique game mechanic called the "Pawn" system. You create a "Pawn", an ai companion bound to serve you who will act as your constant companion as you play. Your Pawn is completely created by you, you can have a massive tank of a man, or play with a short little kid. The Pawn can be any of the 6 main classes, and can be changed at any time. The Pawn will grow and develop as you play, becoming more proficient at fighting as they learn about enemies and areas. Your Pawn can be even be rented by other players to join their adventure in their world, and you in turn can hire two other player's Pawn's as well. Hired Pawn's don't gain experience from playing in other player's worlds but do earn Rift Crystals, a form of currency in game, and can be gifted items and equipment by other player's if they liked your pawn. Pawn's also gain knowledge of different places, enemies, and quests while playing with other players. This system completely changes the dynamic of Dragon's Dogma from a single player rpg to a multiplayer coop-esque experience, where creating the perfect party is only possible through cooperation with other player's pawns.
Dragon's Dogma has problems, but almost all of them are surface level things that while annoying at first can be looked past in time. As of writing this review, I've put 44 hours in, but I've put 50 hours in on an alternate account, and well over 150 hours in on the 360 version years ago, and it still is just as fun to play. No other game comes close to the amazing completely unscripted events that can occur in this game that make the combat so exciting, and I highly suggest giving it a chance yourself.

Lets be honest, this game's success is largely due to a fan base that simply loves hack and slash games, or simply Warrior-styled hack and slash. For that matter, hack and slash is a somewhat rinse and repeat genre, so I wasn't expecting anything that suggested otherwise. Personally, I find it generally satisfying hearing your hero make a reference to being the greatest warrior in the Three Kingdoms (1000 K.O.s). It's a good game, and probably one of their better installments; however, I really wish the game had steam cloud. At one point, I reformatted my computer, and lost the data. Fortunately, I only played through like 3 battles of the Shu campaign, so it wasn't a big deal. In fact, I pretty much finished it up, and backed up all of my data ever since.
Another thing: expect some exploits that make the game easier. Remember the days when playing on the hardest difficulty meant dying to like almost anything? In this game, not so much, because there's a few exploits. We already know musou's your trump card, but weapon switching is like your ace in the hole. It provides you with invulnerablility on use, which is pretty OP, considering I managed to sweep through the hardest difficulty using this and the musou exploits. In fact, sometimes, your weapon switch ability can provide you with crazy weird mobility (Guan Xing's literally makes him dive all over the place like a land dolphin, and I think it's much faster than going by horse. I don't remember the requirements to do it, but I think you may need to max out your weapon mastery or something).
Visually, it could use some improvements; granted, it was made for the 360, PS3, XB1, and PS4 as well, so it would not surprise me if they didn't care enough to enhance the graphics for the XB1 and PS4. On the plus side, this also means that the game plays really smoothly. On my PC, it's probably the best DW experience I've had, but on PS3 and 360, I remember it was somewhat laggy and load times were pretty annoying. Load times are still a thing on the PC, but I honestly think it's far more tolerable than the game's console counterpart.
Anyway, I went into this game expecting what I would of any game from the series: a repetitious beat 'em up that retells the events of The Romance of the Three Kingdoms with some accuracy and inaccuracy. I will say this though: It's still an improvement on DW6 (**** the renbu system), and builds on DW7's system of improvements.
Personally, I wouldn't buy the game at its full value. I never thought any game in the DW series was worth its full release value of $50-$60, so I generally draw the line at $30. When I got it, it was $25, but I played through it in its entirety. I honestly didn't care much for the Xtreme Legends portion of the game; however, I will say it's nice that they bundled it together for a change. In fact, this is the only time I ever got Xtreme Legends.
Ultimately, if you like the DW series, then I don't think you'll be disappointed; on the other hand, I wouldn't go into this game expecting something overwhelmingly unique compared to its predecessors. Fortunately, we may get that experience in DW9. I heard DW9's going to be open world, so it may be the DW that branches away from the game's history of repetition, or it could be really bad. Time will tell...

Sonic CD is the third main installment of the Sonic series. Released in 1993 on the Sega/Mega CD, it is one of the many games that splits the fanbase. Most people love it, but there are some that don't like it. Heck, the two different OSTs split the fanbase. Sonic CD's gameplay is almost exactly like the other Genesis/Mega Drive games, but there is a new mechanic that was added. Time Travel. Time traveling involves Sonic passing a sign post that either says "Past" or "Future". He then has to run at high speeds to go to the past or future (by the way, never use a future sign post). When Sonic goes to the past, he can search for a roboticizer. If he destroys it, he destroys all badniks and ensures a good future in that act. If he gets a good future in the first two acts, the boss will take place in the good future, meaning that the blue blur has made a good future in that zone. You can also get a good future if you collect this games emeralds, the Time Stones. You can obtain these by collecting 50 rings and completing Special Stages that can be found by entering a giant ring at the end of an act, just like Sonic 1. If Sonic doesn't destroy all roboticizers or collect all of the Time Stones by the end of the game, a bad future is created, a future where Dr. Robotnik wins. The level design is kinda "eh". Some zones like Palmtree Panic and Stardust Speedway allow you to go fast, but others like Wacky Workbench and Collision Chaos sometimes punish you for it. Overall, the levels encourages players to be cautious. As mentioned before, this game has two soundtracks. The US OST is more rock-based, but the JP/EU one is more pop-based. I love both soundtracks, but I like the JP/EU one just a tiny bit better. It defines Classic Sonic for me. This game introduces two well-known characters, Amy and Metal Sonic. Amy's design is very, VERY different from her current design, so it may be hard to tell if it's her (not really). The Metal Sonic race is a defining part of this game.
In short, Sonic CD is a fun game with two killer soundtracks, but has some odd level design.

An excellent installment for the DW series. I haven't seriously played a game since 5 and this has been a really great experience so far.
I love that the story mode lets you switch between characters for each battle (something that I don't recalll from earlier games. You played through the entire story with the same character, and if you wanted to lvl up another character from the same kingdom, you just did the story over and over and over again. It got veeeery boring after awhile).
Character levels all carry through in story mode for most of the warriors that you're able to select before each battle, so if you decide to play as Guan Yu five battles into the story, he won't start from lvl 1. I haven't gotten through an entire story mode yet, but this is the best format that I've played through so far.
Ambition mode is completely new to me. You can pick any character you want and you start a new camp up from scratch so you can try to get the Emperor to join you. Go into battle to gather materials from boxes, gain allies and fame, and upgrade your camp's blacksmith, tea house, barracks, etc.. The tutorial explains it well, and it seems relatively easy to pick up. I just started playing with the bodyguard system and that has also been a lot of fun. I frequently stop during battles so I can assign different tasks to my guards. Rather than spending the entire time running around, mindlessly killing soldiers and generals (I'm not complaining, but I like the variety of adding in fire attacks, poison traps, defense, ambushes, etc..). It seems like there's going to be a lot more in Ambition mode that I haven't figured out yet, but so far, I really love it.
I'm using a PS4 controller in Big Picture Mode and I've having zero problems with it. So far I've only had one series of crashes everytime I tried to go into a battle, but I restarted my computer and it was fine after that.
For $15.00 during the summer sale, I'd say this is veeeeery worth it if you're a fan of DW games. It's been years since I've played and I'm having a blast. Happy to be back. :)

A terrible port of a game many love, the PC version of Dark Souls is a sad state of affairs. I've played the game on PS3, and the PC version is a poor, poor shadow of what the PS3 version has to offer. How so? Well, the graphical settings, mouse/keyboard controls, and mouse/keyboard prompts are all wrong by default. A user had to make a multi-step guide that I've spent about an hour total between two separate attempts at getting the fixes that person designed to work, and despite being pretty darn anal and trying to follow each step, I still had the controller button prompts instead of the mouse/keyboard controls displayed on screen. It's entirely possible I missed a step, and I don't blame the person who made the fixes. They deserve money from the publisher and developer for making their game a bit more playable to increase PC sales. If you must get this game, I would recommend getting it on a console if you have one. If not. you'd better hope the fixes work better for you than they did for me. Even some of the files for the fix say they may not work for you. =/
As for the game itself, if you can get it to play, chances are you will either love it or be genuinely uncomfortable playing it. This game could be called "Masochist Tester 5000," because I am certain many people who had not yet realized that they are masochists learned it from this game. This game is very difficult, and unless you enjoy being killed again and again and again in a game with plenty of time and effort lost (think of Diablo 1's death system, but it's specifically only in regard to your experience and currency (souls are both, so  i.e. if you die, you can go back to where you died and get your dropped souls back, but if you die on the way back to your souls, they're gone for good, no matter how much you had built up.
Making progress in the game either requires a lot of skill, or a lot of grinding and some skill, so unless you're amazing, be prepaed to sink lots of time killing the same enemies that spawn in literally the same spots for a few hours. This game is going to kick the crap out of you, and if you enjoy a game being a total pain to play and potentially making you feel uncomfortable to press ahead, simply because instead of thinking "man, this is fun, I want to keep going," I'm thinking "man, this isn't fun, and I know that the further I get, it's going to get even more difficult and less enjoyable." If I'm already not having a great time because the game is so tough, I'm sure not going to enjoy it when it inevitably gets harder. I got all the way to Blight Town on the PS3 version, and since I already knew I hated poison really, really bad and this place had lots of baddies wielding it, I finally just gave up and felt better for it ever since.
Not only is the difficulty a pain, but the game does not contain a map, which makes it difficult to know where to go or what to do. Just wander until you find enemies that don't kill you almost instantly, and you're probably in the right area. Keep wandering. That was acceptable in most 8-bit games because the technology was simply difficult to make, and prior games did not exist to set a gold standard for maps back then. I "dealt with it" because there was no choice when I was a kid. Then along came the SNES, and games like Super Metroid and A Link to the Past started putting in pretty freaking useful maps. Heck, eventually games like Descent III even came out quite some time back, which had fully three-dimensional, rotatable maps, and that was a game you could literally face any direction in the game. Then we get a game like Dark Souls, and they don't bother putting a map in. Was this feature left out because it costs money to make them? Maybe. Or was it done because it makes the game more of a pain? Could be. Heck, why not both?
While masochists may enjoy this game, I also need to mention braggarts. Some folks aren't masochists, but they will enjoy the game because they know just how well-known it is for being difficult, and if they can complete it, they can brag about being able to complete it. I gripe about the map? These people will brag about how a person doesn't need a map and it's better not having one. It's better because it doesn't have a feature games with moreso open environments have had since the 1990s? Suuuuure. Want difficulty levels for players who aren't as good as everyone else? No way! Being exclusionary for the sake of being exclusionary is for the best, in many such folks' minds. If I could beat Dark Souls, they wouldn't be able to feel so smug about themselves, after all. These are some of the people who directly or indirectly brag about themselves by defending the game's difficulty or lack of features when someone says anything negative by putting down a player who has a tough time, because doing so implies that they were able to get through the game despite whatever is giving you a tough time.
I never got stuck, or even really came close to it. The game is just frustrating and doesn't feel fun for me at all. "Git good" is  portion of the community's mantra concerning these games. Don't complain, just get better. I got good enough to get as far as I did and wasn't stuck, despite me generally being crappy at games. I'm not proud of myself, though. In fact, I'm disappointed in myself. I let other people's love for this game convince me to play it on PS3 as long as I did, and to waste time on PC trying to get it to work right as well, despite knowing long before I quit playing that I wasn't enjoying the game at all. Heck with that. I'll be happy and just "git gone" from the game. I'm not a masochist, I'm not a gaming braggart, and this game just makes me feel generally unpleasant most of the time I play it. I'd be insane to continue trying to play what is a miserable experience, and cannot recommend it as such (especially with the pains of getting it to work right on this PC port).

I play lots of TD, and I like hunting achievements to 100%.
Garden rescue is a good but not great tower defense. Without looking at the pricetag and can't remember how it got in my library I'd say its worth $5-$10 (but everyone's wallet is different). The levels are very nicely balanced on harder difficulties but failures can be rage inducing since rounds are slow and the differences between 2 and 3 stars earned is miniscule.
Bad:
* No keyboard shortcuts. (Pfff. is this a PC-game or what?)
* The speed up button is not doing enough.
* Tower Upgrades/routes are lackluster at best. No meta-upgrades or meta-game at all.
Good:
* The powerup system works well, and it's almost a puzzle game more than anything else in how to use/abuse items so you can use your money on the "income-towers" as early as possible.
* Nothing is left up to chance. Every round is identical down to the last pixel. Often there some elements of chance in tower defense,  When you get that last monsters last 3 hp seemingly by luck just before it exits tower range? Here it can always be reproduced - and it's very satisfying to find "the perfect build" for the first few rounds. (Not that I think RNG is bad for TD's generally but the fixed numbers works very well for this game.)
* Very challenging (on hard and sometimes for 3 stars on normal).
* I think the length of the game was just right as well - more and it would have gotten obnoxious.
Achievements however can all be taken on easiest setting, so no thrill there.

I'll set the stage.
Bought the game for $9.99 on sale, Christmas day.
Download and jump in...
I spawn in the middle of nowhere, it's dusk, and the sounds hit me, immersed to my bones.
I cautiously explore a nearby house, finding a few bits of loot. Backpack, Baseball bat, a soda and some peaches.
I feel confident, and strike out to locate a lucrative spot to collect all the things a growing survivalist requires.
My shoes pound the pavement, echoing through my ears as I scan both sides of the road for any movement.
In the distance, a sign, and a town...
I scavenge the buildings, cars, finding precious little that I need.
Suddenly, a roaring sound fills my ears, my heart rate doubles. Switching off my flashlight, I hide inside a clothing store, hoping to look like a fugly, badly dressed mannequin.
Then a voice cries out, and I hear the horn... Friendlies, offering a ride to a cozy hotel, with rooms, electricity, even a working elevator!
Stepping out, I wave my hands and announce my peaceful intentions. Then I see it, a lumbering 6-wheeled beast, rolling down the street with two guys in the cab.
I decide to take my chances, hoping not to be brutally murdered in the street. Guys in the truck tell me to hop on in, that there is room in the back. There is, as well as a few other folks.
We get to chatting, everyone seems very nice, likeable, and funny. Gradually we find more, and more people, soon, the truck is full. 10 deep we are rolling through, laughing and joking, making plans and speculating.
After a long drive, we arrive at the hotel, a 9 story building in downtown Hayward.
Some skilled hands and the right tools, then lights, power, and a huge sense of accomplishment.
I'll always be one of the Hotel Boys, and I've made a few really good friends already in this game.
9/10 - Highly recommend at the current price, or even full price.
I've gotten my money out of this purchase multiple times over already.

I've put in over 250 hours into the game now so I feel like I can write an educated review of the game
First, I think the game is amazing for where it's at in its development. I normally don't like PVP or survival games all that much but, for whatever reason, I really enjoy this one. Here's the review:
There are three major types of players in the game. People are usually one of the three or a combination of all of them:
1.  Wanderer: They loot up and PVP until they die and start again from scratch. This player might hide a plot sign and a stash somewhere in the trees and hope it isn't found. He doesn't care about guides or collecting anything permanent. I think if you're this type of player, the game would get stale rather quickly as there's nothing permanent to keep you coming back. You have limited storage, and PVP on a populated server will find you sooner rather than later. If you are good at PVP, it might hold your attention a bit longer.
2. Base builder: This person wants to build the grandest base possible to secure his/her stuff. Unfortunately, there's a 250 item limit and there is no snapping of parts which can cause gaps and some weird layouts. If you build on a hills, you won't be able to place some of your bigger pieces without some creative thinking. The best pieces are in crafting guides which need to be looted from houses or off of the Brutes. Only wood structures can be made currently which can be hacked through by one person with an axe in 5-15 minutes depending on base piece. Once the base is found, it will get raided continuously until you have nothing left or you manage to build your base well enough to make it not worth their time. Even then, every once in a while there's that one person (or three) who seems to have time. Base building can be frustrating if you don't have the patience to collect guides and stress out when your stuff gets stolen (which it will). It is very rewarding once you get to the point where people stop raiding it continuously because it's too much work to get to your stuff.
3. Base Raider: This person/group of people like to go around hacking at a wall for 10 minutes plus hoping that there is good loot inside. Most of the time there isn't or the stashes are floating and not accessible. However, it's a great feeling when you find a stash that is loaded and not floated (very rare)
Personally, I play the entire game. I have a 250 piece base, I have multiple cars, I have two stashes, I've collected almost every guide (missing curved). I PVP when I feel like it, and I avoid it when I don't. I raid bases. I think if you only do one of the things I listed above, you will get bored or frustrated quickly. It's nearly impossible to build an impenetrable base that isn't floating. There are better base building games out there. Just PVPing means that there is no permanence to your character. The only persistent things in the world are your base and the crafting guides you learn. It's the only progression you have. To me, base raiding is the least efficient way to get gear. It's fun to look for cars or tents in bases, but I wouldn't count on stashes that worth anything being reachable.
If you’re someone who likes to play all parts of a game, this game will keep you entertained for hours. If you understand that you WILL lose gear, you WILL die, you WILL be raided, you WILL be KOS'd (even on PVE only servers) and don't stress out about it, you will have a good time.
As far as performance goes, I run an I7 GTX960 and the game runs fantastic. I've never had it crash unless the entire server crashes or is restarted. I lag rarely when car spawns render on my screen. Here are some notes for prospective buyers. I see lots of complaints from people who have tried the game and give a bad review due to some of the following items. Sometimes the complaints are correct. However, most of the time, it's a lack of understanding of how the game works. I will try to address some of these things so that, if you are looking to buy this game, you don't make a bad purchase:
1. You cannot locally host a server. If you want to admin a server, you need to rent one from
2. There are official miscreated servers that are administered by the game company. Any other server risks being shut down if the owner doesn't feel like paying the bills.
3. ALL servers are PVP servers. Some servers might say PVE on them, but you can and probably will be killed on them. The admins of those servers can try to set rules and ban people who break them, but they can't stop it from happening.
4. Guns are easy to find, but not easy when you first start out. They blend into the background at times and aren't always out in the open. As you learn where stuff spawns, you will have more guns and ammo than you know what to do with. However, don't expect them to fall from the sky upon first logging in
5. Melee weapons are effective. The best time to be really aggressive is when you are a fresh spawn. Grab a knife or a pickaxe and rush/trap the first geared person you see. If you die, who cares, you have nothing to lose anyway. If you kill him, then, congrats, you are fully geared.
6. Server restarts/crashes happen relatively often on populated servers. It's almost always day when it happens, which then turns to night. It's annoying, but what do you do. If you don't like the night, join a no nights or a fast nights server.
7. Nights can be DARK depending on your monitor. There are no in game setting to change the gamma. Just because the game is dark for you, doesn't mean someone else can't see so be careful. You might not be as hidden as you thought.
8. Base building is limited to 250 pieces. A plot sign lasts in the world for 48 hours without interaction. Each additional base piece adds 12 hours up to a maximum of 2 weeks.
9. Vehicles last 48 hours without interaction. You must turn on the lights/honk the horn within that time period or they will disappear.
10. Crafting guides are relatively rare. Some are rarer than others. If you want any hope of securing your base, you need some of them. Walls 2 and Platforms 2 are the most important IMO. The gatehouse is a good one as those doors can be used as walls and are the toughest to break through. I've played 250 hours and am still missing one guide. This can be a grind
11. There are numerous bugs in the game:
i. Headshots don't work on some servers.
ii. When you place a stash on uneven ground or in bushes, sometimes the loot disappears in certain slots. It's still there (just invisible) so don't pick the stash up. Instead, place another item in that slot and the first item will appear back in your inventory. This happens often with ammo, food, and other smaller items.
iii. Sometimes when you get out of a car in your base, you die randomly if it is a tight space (the bug I hate the most right now)
iv. Rarely when you log out and back on, you will be naked (yeah that's fun)
v. There are more, but these are the most annoying bugs for me right now
12. I mentioned KOS before but I'll stress it again: YOU WILL BE KOS'd, no matter what type of server it is and no matter whether you are a fresh spawn or not. Would it be nice if everyone met up and talked first? Yes? Is that going to happen most of the time? No way. If you care about that, then you are going to be frustrated.
13. It doesn't seem like it when you first start playing, but it is incredibly easy to gear up once you understand where the loot is at. More importantly, gear mostly doesn't matter. You can kill someone with just a knife (even if they have an AK, though you might not want to run straight at them), you can base build with just a hatchet. More slots are nice, but not essential, and the rest of your clothes do nothing besides change your look.

A cute but difficult tower defense game with a christmas theme. It looks and feels like the mobile port it is. You don't place towers, you drag them into position. The maps are designed with a lot of micro-management involved, simply placing towers isn't enough, you may need to sell them to get money, which then allows you to place another tower elsewhere. You need to time the placement, upgrading, and selling of towers, with the amount of resources you have to ensure you have enough free resources to place the exact tower you need to beat/finish off that particular wave. (It's actually simpler than I'm making it sound here.)
What is tricky is the timing, which you only achieve through experience. Your defences might have held against the previous wave, but even just upgrading what you have might not beat the new one. You might have to sell some towers and/or exchange them with others depending on the wave.
Overall, I didn't particularly enjoy the micro-management and found it frustrating to get a long way into a level, only to lose because I messed up the timing or placement of a single tower. However, the graphics, sound, and gameplay were solid and it's very cheap. If you like micro-management and time management, then the game might appeal to you, but check out the gameplay on youtube first!

:Strike Vector: is the funnest, most competitive, and fastest multiplayer shooter I have ever played.  Nothing tops this game's multiplayer.  It looks awesome, it looks fun, but in reality... its very, very, VERY niche.  I'm gonna tell you right now that this is probably not a game you want to play.
It has wonderful graphics and runs like a charm on my rig.  The game has lots of customization and weapon loadouts, and everything except cosmetic stuff is available from the start.  The weapon loadouts are endless, and of course most outperform others, but there is more than enough variety to always keep the game fresh.  Of course, its not much work to unlock the costmetic stuff either.  Skill really shows in this game, and if you are good you are rewarded for it in spades, and if you can't keep up its painfully obvious.  This game has no hand holding, everything you do in this game is via your own skill and you knowledge of the game mechanics.  Being good at this game is something to be proud of.
BUT, this game has one glaring, stupidly big flaw.  The game is so competitive and the skillgap, even if tiny, has such a huge impact on gameplay that most people don't even stick around to play because they simply cannot keep up.  Generally, most of the newbs and unskilled players only last a few days before they get bored or permanently ragequit from getting roasted by the much fewer, yet better players.  However, most of the better players quit because there aren't many people left to shoot.  As such, the game has largely killed itself because its TOO competitive.  This is not a game for casuals in any sense of the word.  Please keep in mind that of all the 100+ thousand people who bought this game, less than a tenth of a percent of them are still playing to this day.
Reviews give the impression that this game is undesirable because it has low population, but this is misleading.  The gameplay is actually BETTER on low population servers.  Its not a typical shooter where most firefights end up relying on confusion and teamwork.  This is a very personal game, and much of the gameplay is just that; personal.  You will literally be dogfighting individual players 90% of the time you play this game.   This is what the game was designed for and where it excells.  High population servers ruin this however, namely because the combat degenrates into nothing but confusion and nobody can finish kills.  That is not to say it could benefit from more population, because it could, but the low population isn't what is killing the game, its the competitiveness of the game itself.
Of course, the game also has other flaws.  If you don't live in East Europe or the United States, chances are your ping will be above 100 when you try to play on any of the sparsley populated servers.  Anything above 100 ping is generally unplayable as you will find enemies teleporting all over the map and you yourself rubberbanding all over the place and randomly crashing into walls.  Likewise, generally anything under 50-60 FPS is considered highly detrimental to this skill based gameplay, especially considering how fast-paced this game is.  Your rig has to be up to date for you to play this game properly.
I highly, highly recommend you only play this game if you have played similar dogfighting games.  This is a very new experience, and it is painful to learn.  The learning curve is MASSIVE.  Its a cliff to most people.  It introduces new playstyles and is very, very fast.  But if you like competitive, fast shooters and are GOOD at them, then this will probably be the funnest multiplayer shooter you will ever play.

I want to like this game, plenty of love was obviously lavished on it, but for me it's an ugly mess.  I mean ugly, as in the graphics (while technically proficent enough, polished even) lack any sort of artistic feeling.  The game also lacks feeling - it's a plodding sort of adventure in a perfectly vanilla fantasy world, utterly unmemorable, a place where there is minor animosity between the Tolkienesque races, the church worships some kind of crystal dragon jesus, the barbarians feel vaguely celtic, you fight slimes and spiders in the beginning, and the nobility is somwtimes evil and corrupt.  This lack of feeling or ideas would be forgivable if the game was mechanically interesting, but it's not - character creation  and leveling are a tangled mess of far too many tiny variables, with skill trees that grant minor this and that, but don't really change much, and combat was generally a sort of a clunky mess.
All that said, if Pillars of Eternity had a good story, a novel game world, or fun mechanics - any one of the three - it'd be a good game.  Sadly it doesn't though, everything creeps close to decent, might even be decent, but nothing stands out making for an overly crunchy, dull looking game experience with a trite cliched story.  I really can't recommend it - maybe people who really like number crunching will enjoy the character development, maybe players who enjoy very predictible fantasy worlds and narratives will not be bored by the story, but for me it's not enjoyable.

I bought this game in the steam summer sale, and it was good for the price I bought it at. It's very fun to figure out, and survive, at least initially.
However, updates are slow right now, and the current state of the game is quite repetitive. Even after only four hours of gameplay I started a new hoping to find some variation. Currently for me, the game always goes like this:
I'm on an island, I craft a spear, find the items from the shipwrecks, then have to move on when I run out of coconuts to drink from. So then I stock up on fish, and take my raft on the journey to the next island. There is no real progression, and surviving isn't that hard.
I would like it more if there was a natural progression of items that I could get, or craft, and then the 'endgame' would be being able to stay on one island. Right now, I see no progression, and more importantly no endgame. At this point, there is no way that I have found to stay on one island for more than a couple of days because you need a constant supply of water, which comes almost exclusively from coconuts.
Pros:
Graphics and overall look
Crafting system is well done

Good fishing
Realistic islands/travel
Cons:
No progression
Lack of renewable water supplies (I think)
Falling every other time I climb a palm tree
Repetitiveness

Hey guys, hope this review helps you out.
I just purchased the game on Friday, March 13th.  Do to Steam's "Ubisoft Weekend" I was able to get the Delux Edition for only $9.99.  I cannot in good conscience recommend it due to the fact that it is barely worth that amount of money and the price will go back up on Monday, March 16th 10 a.m. PST.  But I lucked out and I don't think it's a total waste of ten bucks, but it would be a waste of eleven.  Let's do this
PROS
-Good action and combat gameplay
-Very good graphics, though they could be a tiny bit better (will re-explore in CONS)
-Acting is performed admirably
-Stealth gameplay is good, though this too could be better (and less goofy, will re-explore in CONS)
-Story line itself is very good, lots of kudos on creativity to the writers
-Ability to choose equipment became ALOT better, though could use improvement (will re-explore in CONS)
-Gadgets are really freakin cool
-An over all PRO is the fact that Splinter Cell always sates our appitite for esionage, even though it fails in many ways to be a good game over all, we're left with few other options as far as spy games
CONS
-First off our options are limited in how we get a job done, you'll see alot of places you should be able to climb, jump, and drop to and be disappointed when the option to do so is not there.  ESPCIALLY in a coastal environment.  Really Ubisoft???  Sam Fisher can't swim or drop into the water???  HE'S SUPPOSED TO BE AN EX-NAVY SEAL FOR CHRIST SAKE!!!!
-Ahem....moving on.  Collision detection should have had more focus than it did as far as graphics.  When I climbed out of the back of a truck, the rifle on my back passed through the back door all ghostly like.  In real life that would have made alot of noise and resulted in my demise.  Stuff to think about
-While acting is good, and I understand Michael Ironside's inability to do this latest project, you picked the WRONG replacement.  Eric Johnson is a good actor, but he is NOT a Sam Fisher.  He doesn't have the gravely voiced battle-hardened saracasm, or worse yet, the age of Sam.  Sam's old.  Mid 50's old.  You can't just take any guy in his mid 30's and slap on some grey hair and call it good.  Stupid move.
-While stealth gameplay has considerably few drawbacks, as well as alot of realism....the LIGHTS!!!!....on your kit showing you are HIDDEN!!!...in the SHADOWS!!!!  WHAT THE HELL!?!?!?  Have you people at Ubisoft just stopped trying???  You've had everything from HUD indicators to transitioning to black and white to show that the player is hidden and you threw that ALL out for something THIS STUPID!!!!
-I digress....anyway, your equipment options.  Dangling items in front of our faces to get us to register on your website is stupis.  It's low.  And personally, I find it to be an INSULT TO MY INTELLIGENCE.  We will not stop hating Uplay, or the rest of your software.  GIVE IT UP GOD DAMNIT!!!!
-Composure, composure.....sorry.  Last but not least while starting every mission from the same location was a kind of clever idea, it being an enormous plane Fourth Echelon uses as it's HQ, it makes the game less adventurous.  But of course you probably did it FOR that reason, because you're lazy.
In closing, what makes this game so bad?  Ubisoft, of course.  I love Tom Clancy.  The games, the novel adaptations, the film adaptations (apart from Ben Afleck) ALL of Tom Clancy's material is good stuff.  I really hope someone eventually takes away Ubisoft's rights to wipe their♥♥♥♥♥with his material one day.  I can hope...  I can dream....  At any rate, don't pay any more than ten bucks for it.  But if you see it for ten or less, that's a decent price given the quality.  Out.

So it's been almost a year since I first reviewed this product and felt it was only fair I gave an update; since the developer has been working so hard on it. The game has improved a lot since I first tried it and many of the problems I had with the game have been changed or fixed.
In this game, you own a PC repair shop and have to diagnose faults with the desktops brought to you by clients. You will also have clients that come to you just to buy specific components, if you don't have these in and on your store displays, you still have the option to order them in, so as to not miss out on sales early game when you have little money.
Faults with a PC can be anything from a faulty set of RAM to a virus infection. While the RAM is easy enough to swap and send back to the cilent, the virus removal will require you to boot it up, download and install an anti-virus, run the scan and then after that's completed, you may send it back to the client.
The desktop side of things was not introduced when I first played and reviewed the game, I feel this helps to make the game more interesting and entertaining. Before with a faulty GPU, it was a simple diagnose, swap and return. Now you need to ensure any old drivers are removed and the correct drivers for the new GPU are installed.
While I feel there is still much that could be added to this game to make it better, the devloper has shown they are commited to keep working on and improving it.

Can't recommend until they add mouse support, as it might end up being a deal breaker for me as for the rest of the game it's exactly what I wanted and expected from the Dynasty franchise. First paragraph is my lengthy complaint about lack of mouse support, otherwise the rest is an actual review of the game.
No support for mouse whatsoever. It makes playing the game very very hard, for some you may be able to get used to using only the keyboard, they use keys like j for the attack and can be remapped to whichever key you want, but for people like me I would just rather have mouse support. Otherwise if you played these games before then this is more of the same (which isn't a negative, just same as expected and what I wanted but with mouse support). If you however have a steam (or any other controller) you can use it to play the game similar to how you would on the console. I'm assuming this is what the developer intended (and assuming it allowed them to be lazy porting it over from console). I'm mean how hard is it to add mouse support, out of the hundred(s) of computer games I've played I haven't found one with out mouse support since late '90's early '00's. Especially if it's more than a side scroller or text based game, even the most basic computer games come with it. Debating whether or not to just get my money back. Trying to positive, I guess it does give me a reason to use the steam controller that bought a while back and pretty much never use (have the steam link too).
Now that I got that complaint out of the way the rest of the game  is similar/same as the others in the series, so if you've played one in the past you'll get the same/similar experience here. For those who have never played Dynasty Warriors I would recommend the game however some people complain that it's just a button mashing game, which it can be to a certain extent. As the boss's get harder and/or you adjust the difficulty level up you need to use at least some skill to defeat them.
Essentially it's fighting mechanics is simple enough that anybody can jump in and learn it within minutes as it has three attacks and one block. You have a regular attack, strong attack and special attack you can also jump and do some basic attacks from the air. Different weapons allow you to have different attacks so each character has their own uniqueness to a certain point. The most stand out feature is the story telling for each character and I believe this is more of what the game is about.
Keyboard or Gamepad controls only. No mouse functionallity at all. No thanks.

Absolutely cracking game. Bought the original on Xbox and played for many an hour; but as I began to move onto PC gaming I enjoyed the experience so much that I re-purchased State of Decay on Steam; along with the Breakdown DLC (typical that both were half price a couple weeks later... Such is life)
There are a few really in-depth reviews on here but I shall be fairly brief. Through all the zombie games I've played over the years, this one is by far the closest I've ever found to 'that game' you have in your head when you want one with zombies. The game is by no means perfect; but by every means points the genre in completely the right direction - the fear of danger with the perma-death system; the scareness of ammo causing every shot to count; the ability to commandeer every car you see, the aspect of stealth, resource management, multiple survivors in a team to increase chances of survival... So many golden aspects that lead me to believe that if and when a State of Decay II comes out, it will undoubtedly be the best zombie/survival game there is. Despite this, I sometimes feel that the zombies do not quite pose a big enough fear or threat for the player (although this is almost solved in the higher levels of Breakdown) but perhaps a higher volume of zombies in denser groups but with slower movement speeds would be an alternative for the future... Or maybe that's just me.
To be frank it's all the little things that make this game worthwhile - forgetting to suppress your pistol and bringing in 20 nearby zombies with the sound caused is one of those moments that brings this game alive. If you are in any way considering the purchase - go right ahead and I promise you will not be disappointed.
One more supply run. Oh, I guess its 6 am now. I should probably get two hours sleep so I can play state of decay for another 16 hours.

So you've really not got much to lose trying this game out and at the time of writing this review, the price is 30% off making it less than a fiver (£5).

This game focuses heavily on story, depth and immersion. You got to be ready to read for this game but the story is a work of art. The big name reviews are right - this is the best hardcore RPG of the last few years. And I do mean hardcore. The level cap is low, I think 12, and that isn't because the game is short - it's because you will WORK to get those levels. This is a story driven RPG - your addicted because the plot, because the world, because the curiosity of whats in that cave there. This is not a shallow derpy RPG that we all know and love that sacrifices any form of coherent story telling to get you addicted to the sounds of dings and purple tinted armor icons. Put this game on normal difficulty and you will be challenged, put it on hard and you will spend more time on the pause screen issuing orders and working on your parties positioning, trying to ambush the enemy and lead them to traps, working to form a shield wall, strategically using your abilities. (Or turn it to easy and relax, enjoying the story, it'll still bite your hand off if you stop paying attention in combat!)
This isn't WOW, this isn't Rift, don't expect a game like those that constantly rewards you by raining down levels and gear. Play it because the story is one of the best this year in ANY medium. Also the combat is some of the most brutal, challenging and epic

It's impossible to review this game without comparing it to Town of Salem, so I'm not going to even try. Most reviewers seem to be of the opinion that Throne of Lies is a through and through upgrade on that title; my opinion is that it's a bit more complex than that.
Let's start with the aspects where Throne of Lies is an improvement over Town of Salem:
* The interface is much, much more usable. Information is easier to access; everything is more intuitive
* All roles are more fleshed out. In Town of Salem, many roles are given impossibly difficult objectives, and no tools with which to complete them, having to basically rely on providence. Some roles are just plain boring to play. In Throne of Lies, it's a rare day when your character doesn't have at least one interesting play at his or her disposal. Most roles have more options than their equivalent role in Town of Salem
But now we get to the stuff Throne of Lies does worse than Town of Salem:
* Game balance. The number of characters in each of the two main factions fluctuates wildly from game to game, especially since the king can be aligned to any of them.
* There's a lot less deductive reasoning. Every rule in Throne of Lies has so many exceptions, and the initial setup has so much variance built into it, that it's almost impossible to deduce anything. Roles that had been "confirmed" can be converted the following night. You never know who killed whom.
In Town of Salem, I had so many of these "Eureka" moments, where I initially scratched my head at something that seemed plain impossible, only to then have that epiphany about its only possible meaning, and go all L like over the opposition. In Throne of Lies, that never seems to happen. The only mode of play in Throne of Lies is closer to what in Town of Salem would have been the "All Any" mode.
* There's a certain sense of futility to it, thanks to questionable design choices. The main "evil" faction is capped at 3 members, and they can convert "good" members. Successfully executing enemies very often merely means that they get to convert more from your faction. When all is said and done, you rarely feel like your actions had any sort of impact on the match's outcome.
Now about the stuff both games are on even ground with each other:
*Both are butt-ugly to look at. :D
Yeah, it's a minor complaint, but I have to say it anyway.
So you might be asking, he's still recommending Throne of Lies despite everything that he just said? Yes, because even though it won't blow your mind, I do feel it's still a worthwhile experience for the asking price. And the developers are still making frequent changes to the game, so who knows. In a year or two this might have been polished into a top contender in the (admittedly very small) genre.

The map is fairly easy to learn, and with the scenery of the game it makes every place look different from the last. The weather of the game consists fog, torrential downpour, and clear. Something that i personally enjoy that they included in the game is that tornados will appear in different places on the map. While i can not say that these tornados kill you, i got close to one but it crossed a river and i determined i would never catch up, it is still terrifying to first spot one of these, especially in the middle of a field. It is an obvious art choice to make your world seem abandoned after a disaster, something DayZ has yet to do. Lots of potential to be a great little management game, right now it's got a good base of ideas, but I would like to see it expanded upon in a few different ways. For example I would like to see people come in with different problems other than "my computer doesn't work, find out what's wrong and fix it." Maybe you could have people wanting to upgrade their PC for example. I can tell that the developer has plans for future updates as there are certain things in the game right now that don't really do anything, such as the specs of the components (which I'm sure there is a lot to be done with this), and people's reactions to the condition of their PC as right now there are meters that essentially make it so you have to give back their PC or better or they won't take it. Still lots of fun to play around with, but I think I've seen everything that this game has to offer in it's current form, although as it recieves updates, I will update this review.
Bugs that I ran into:
- turned on mouse edge collision (or whatever the menu calls it) while on windowed mode and my mouse got stuck outside the window and I had to delete my config.bin file to fix it (this would have been a game breaking bug had I not figured out a way to fix it for myself.
- Clicking and dragging items is frustrating as you have to drag up before you can drag to the side or it won't register that you want to drag the item.
- Dragging things into their sockets on the computer is hit or miss, and RAM is particularily finicky.
- The game makes you use way too much thermal paste
- There is no real reason to ever not be paused in the game other than when inspecting items waiting for customers, I would maybe like to see the pause feature taken out and then maybe just reduce the frequency that customer come in.
- Used HDD's and other broken (burned) parts can sell for >$20 in this game for some reason
Things I would like to see in future updates:
- More parts! I love the 3D models of each part that exist, and more would always make the game better.
- More scenarios to deal with (like I said above, more than just replacing parts, for example, upgrading PCs, building PCs to order for customers from scratch, etc)
- Better UI (more readable text, higher poly sprites for character as well as the shop
- Upgraedable shop
Conclusion: If you have a passion for computer hardware like I do, then you will probably love this game, but keep in mind that it is at a very early stage in development and you are buying an incomplete product. I would normally say that it is too early on to justify the price tag, but at only $8 on sale I would recomend it as even in the form it is in now, it's lots of fun, and I'm sure future updates will only make it better.

This is a really early access game, so all I can recommend is getting it and seeing if you like the idea and premise itself, and watch the refund clock. Gameplay is really basic at this moment, but there's a huge potential for a good time management game here.
