*** See the updates below ***
Early-Access Game at the time I made the purchase, one of the best-looking games available.  It took a little while to figure out how to craft certain things, but once I figured that out, survival got a whole lot easier.  It's still challenging, and my map-making skills still need some work, but there are worse ways to waste away the day.
Since the game isn't finished, I'm not expecting to get rescued any time soon.  Talk of multiplayer has me a little concerned, though, as some items took forever to find and I'd become a bit disgruntled if another player helped themselves to my stash while I was out exploring another island or abandoned oil rig.  Minor glitches with the interface, but for the most part, a well-polished 90% complete game.  Really looking forward to the full version, whenever they get there.  Thanks to Generikb on YouTube for some very informative and entertaining Stranded Deep videos.
UPDATE 5 AUG 15:  They ruined the game.  Someone decided to update the graphics (new artist?), as well as the game engine, and it looks like sh*t.  Period.  Taking the graphics level up a notch or two makes the game lag, and the bloom effects... probably not compatible with any graphics card more than 3 years old.  This used to be a visually impressive game.  Not anymore.  Save your money.  Wait until they unf*ck themselves before buying.
UPDATE 16 DEC 15:  They salvaged the game.  Kinda.  I've become a fan of Generikb on YouTube, and happened to catch Season 3 of his Stranded Deep videos, and it was enough to persuade me to give the game another chance.  The graphics are beautiful on an SLI graphics platform.  For the gamer on a budget, you'll never see those beautiful graphics.  Before the big change, I thought the graphics were really good enough - and could be appreciated by a wider audience.  Now, unless you have a higher-end system, you will not be wowed by the graphics, and you might even think things look worse than before.  And you'd be right.  But... some of the flickering graphics issues on Mac systems have been resolved, and the game is in fact playable, again.
At the time of this update, the game is on sale.  It's still considered early access, and it still needs a lot of work, but it's available for half as much as I paid for it.  This could be a sign that the devs are done, they gave up, and it will soon fall into the abandonware category.  Or, maybe they're trying to get more beta testers while making a little money in the process.  Programmers have to eat, too, right?
With the lower price, it's less of a gamble.  If you have a robust 3-year old or younger system, you should be able to play it without too much trouble.  Anything older or less robust, and it'll probably play, but it won't look as good as it did.
UPDATE 20 NOV 16:  Not sure what they did, but it's playable again, and it's as good as when it first came out.  Thanks guys!

Dynasty Warriors 8 is what you get when a unique series of action games reaches its very best.
Along its lengthy history, the Warriors games have always been about one (wo)man slashing through entire armies. The Japanese name of the game, "Shin Sangoku Musou", literally means "The Truly Unrivaled One in Three Kingdoms". This satisfaction is on its own well worth the price. But Koei Tecmo has always been able to come up with more and more ways to make it even more fun and perfect.
Rest assured, Dynasty Warrios 8 is definitely not a "press button to win" game. In the past they relied on numbers and stats to increase difficulty, but things are much better now. In DW8, there's a weapon effectiveness system around Man-Heaven-Earth, which works like Rock-Paper-Scissors. Since you can take 2 weapons, you need to constantly assess the situation to switch to the more effective one. That's some real-time strategy already.
There is also strategy involved on a larger scale. In almost every battle you have a base or general to defend, so you cannot just go in whichever direction you want, because enemies may slip into your base when you are busy fighting elsewhere. You need to be aware of everything happening on the battlefield and choose the correct action that best boosts the morale of your side. Failing at this may make your allies extremely weak, the enemies extremely dangerous, and the battle almost impossible to win.
But all these strategy elements take just so much time that the focus is still on the slashing action, and there's a perfect balance between the two. This results in the game feeling much more authentic, as if you really are that officer on the battlefield writing history, instead of some blind killing machine.
Speaking of history, DW8 is also brilliant at telling history. Different from earlier games, DW8 sticks close to what really happened in history. If Wei really lost that battle in history, it won't be the other way round in the game just because you are such a good player. (The story does branch into fiction if you choose to, though.) Also for the first time, DW8 featured entire campaigns around Jin and Lu Bu, so now you finally know how the Three Kindoms Era ended, and what Lu Bu really did besides being killed by Cao Cao.
In conclusion, whether you are an action gamer or history lover, Dynasty Warriors 8 is a unique experience not to be missed. Unless you are so hardcore that only Soul games are difficult enough for you.

+ Great balance between action and strategy

Pillars of Eternity a throwback back to the days of proper Role Playing games. Where character sheets and making actual dialogue decisions (coinciding with some stat checks, I don't believe there are dice rolls) were par for the course.
An only slightly more modern take on Balders Gate or Icewind Dale.
The game pretty quickly drops you into the action and tells you you're very important. Its up to you what to do with that or how to react. Combat takes place in real time. With each action using a cooldown to activate in order to avoid an interrupt, aside from movement. A sort of active turn based variety of combat.
Character creation is extremely in depth perhaps lacking in physical customization but the character traits, stats, class and narrative background are all available for customization.
There are many many many classes to choose from to fill out your 6 person party.
Perma Death is a real thing on higher difficulties. The green bar on the character portrait is Heath, the overall status of that character. The portrait itself, when taking damage fills in red, this is endurance and when depleted is what will knock someone out of battle. If someones Health is depleted entirely. Bad News Bears I'm afraid. You'll run into characters that have quests associated with them and require you to take them on your journey. These characters are also voice acted as well as some important NPC's. Though not every line has a voice over as this was a kickstarter game (as the loading screen is very apt to point out) That's simply not a realistic goal for something with as much text and dialogue. I should mention that though another character can interact with NPC's you are making the dialogue choices based on your base character for any stat checks that may occur in conversation.
You can re-spec any character at any inn for a relatively inexpensive price if you've made a terrible judgment in choosing traits or some other facet that would otherwise make your current quest more difficult. You can 'hire' a new recruit at any inn, by which I mean you can just make the exact type of character you are missing from your party. More money equals higher starting level.
Fairly early on, you arrive at a place called Caed Nua, which becomes your own stronghold and fairly integral part of the game. You can upgrade it, repair it and use it as a place to rest and receive bonuses from. Depending on how much prestige you and your party have as well as the overall status of your stronghold it can be attacked by bandits (or by other groups) in which you are given the option between hiring some mercenaries and auto-resolving from afar (they can help in a manual resolve as well) if your travels have taken you too far away to make it back in time before they strike or you can travel back yourself and manual resolve to defend your keep. There is also a rather extensive side mission available here among other things.

After many years, the prodigal son has returned! I loved playing the first few Splinter Cell games on my Xbox back in the day. They emphasized stealth, provided multiple routes to complete each mission, and offered a plethora of cool gadgets to use to distract or take out your enemies. Then Splinter Cell, like a rebellious teen, lost touch with his roots and went down a strange run-n-gun, action-heavy road for many years, always leaving longtime fans like myself wondering whether Sam Fisher would ever be the stealthy bad-a we originally knew him as. Thankfully, Splinter Cell: Blacklist finally brings Sam back home, and he even brought along a few action moves that suit him quite nicely.
This game is awesome because its design allows you to play however you like. If you're a patient player and enjoy figuring out how to go over, around, or under each enemy without being detected, you'll like this game. There are lots of gadgets to use to distract and confuse your enemies so you can slip by them, and there are always alternate paths and multiple routes to reach each destination. They call this the "Ghost" playstyle.
If you liked Sam's rebellious teen years and want to tear through your enemies without caring as much about being stealthy ("Assault"), you'll like this game. There are gadgets, grenades, and lots of guns that are loud and very satisfying to use.  The only issue I have with the game in this respect is the fact that you can only equip one primary weapon apart from your pistol. There were several missions where I wanted to have both a sniper rifle AND an assault rifle, for example, but I could only carry one of them. Oh well. At least you can unlock the ability to change your loadout at the major checkpoints of each level.
If you like to be as stealthy as possible but enjoy doing takedowns ("Panther"), you'll really enjoy this game. You can do all kinds of lethal and non-lethal takedowns (from above, from below, from behind, out a window, etc.), and there are numerous silenced weapons and gadgets that facilitate it. I felt that the mechanics and level design generally work best with this playstyle, and it's how I spent most of my time playing.
Overall, this is a really awesome game, and you should buy it! The gameplay is smooth, the takedowns are always wonderfully satisfying, the graphics are fantastic, and the story is actually quite good! I wish it had more choices/consequences a la Mass Effect, but it does what it does very well.

First off I understand it's a survival game and I understand there is some realism it has to have to make it considered a survival game to those hardcore survivalist out there. Ok sure it doesn't need to have like a instant spawn where a player wants, but maybe a bed spawn, or spawn in a certain area would be nice. Say if I died in a town, it would be nice to spawn close to that town again, and not end half way around the map, spend around 30 mins(yes 30 mins) going back to that town to meet up with my friend. Ususally if you die while going on an adventure with a friend, it wouldn't be worth it for them to wait for you as it would take ages to meet up again. The last thing was base buidling, which is not as good as games like Ark, or Rust. Not going into detail about this one, but theres nothing new about base building that's not in any other survival game. Honestly I felt like out of the 16 hours i spent, only 3-6 hours were the "this is so fun" moments. When I went exploring the city with my new friend for the first time and died to the miscreated, another time was when I was in Sultan and there was a firefight breaking out at night and I hid in the bushes. Also building a base with some random guy I met was cool. Overall I would still recommend this game as I enjoyed playing the game, even for only a little bit. I will not play it anymore because there are much better games out there right now, but I might return in the late future to check out if there are any new updates. I hope this game does improve!
Anyways thanks for reading my review, best of luck if you plan on checking this game out,

This game is probably my favourite FPS released this year (and maybe in the last couple of years).
It's a twitch shooter with a lot of classic elements that you don't find in modern shooters - projectile weapons, health pick ups, ability (and need) to go really fast and manevre a lot. Basically there's everything that I want from a shooter.
Most of game modes are also equally classic - there's a team deathmatch, simple deathmatch and ctf.  This game is doing a really good job at scratching that "old school" itch for me.
It also happens to look beautiful and has some really great levels.
There's however a big problem with the game - it's just not popular enough and has a very small community. The skill level for entry is a bit too high for a mainstream user, it's too easy to crash into things or be wrecked by experienced pilot. It takes a few hours to learn but it alienates most people who just want to jump in.
So this game is pretty much dead outside of steam sales. It does come to life during those periods though, if only for a week.
I can recommend buying it, but only if you are willing to play it while the sale lasts and then just wait for the next sale.

Throne of Lies is a thoroughly addicting and charming social deduction game. Every single game feels fresh and exciting and I feel like my mind gets a mini-workout each game, regardless of what faction or class I am playing (except when I play Court Wizard; ♥♥♥♥ that class).
I’d like to touch on a couple of things that I haven’t seen mentioned much in reviews. ToL has quite a steep learning curve for such a “cutesy”, casual game, and there will be games where you will get flamed for not knowing mechanics and how the different classes interact with each other. Keep your head up, read up each class on the wiki, and watch some youtube/twitch videos.
The other issue I’d like potential buyers to be aware of is that you may get into games where you get flamed for not doing something “popular” (but you’re not breaking any of the game rules). For example, the extremely powerful class known as the Prince generally doesn’t reveal himself, for safety reasons, however, I was in a game where the Prince outed himself immediately, asked his faction’s teammates to keep him healed/guarded, and to feed him information each day. I felt bad that he was flamed for doing something “different” – as long as what you’re doing doesn’t go against your faction’s goals and the game rules, I’m all for weird and unconventional strategies in this game.
Just be aware of this, and this is my heads up to you that I have almost 80 hours invested so far, and most games have been enjoyable and flame-free. There will be some “blah” games with some very childish people, but as far as online communities go, it’s solid and generally mature.
I think if you’re at all interested in deduction and/or social games, don’t care at all about the graphic style, and are willing to invest some time into learning the mechanics, you’ll discover a true gem of a game, with endless possibilities, combinations, and a variety of personalities in your respective teammates (and enemies). In some games, you’ll want to punch kittens due to the ridiculousness of it all, and in other games, you’ll legit get out of your chair, point your finger at your computer monitor, and roar, “GET DEDUCED”.

Having loved the Baldur's Gate Series I had high hopes for Pillars being just as awesome. The game does not disappoint, in fact it vastly improves upon the combat mechanics and gameplay to make it much easier to play but without limiting the tactical options available. For example, there is no limit on items that you can carry, so you don't need to worry about selling loot to free up space or trying to find bags of holding. It's also much harder for your characters to permanently die which leads to less frustration than BG. The graphics are much improved too - all in all this is a much more enjoyable game to play than the BG Enhanced Edition versions.
Like Baldur's Gate there is a rich world to explore and many interesting side quests, most of which present difficult morale decisions that the player must choose from. For example , there are missions involving stealing items for an NPC you usually get a choice of whether to steal the item for the guy who's paying you, or betray him and help the victim. It's really up to you how you wish to behave and the game does certainly test your morales like a true RPG should.
My only disappointment is that the NPCs which I have encountered so far are not quite as memorable and entertaining as the likes of Minsc and Boo, Edwin and Jahera from BG (but I suppose they tried!)
Be warned if you are trying to play this on a 32-bit system as I experienced frequent crashes when loading new areas. Apparently this is quite common to Unity games. Since upgrading to  64-bit Windows 10 I have had experienced no crashes , running with 4GB RAM.

Starbound excels as a crafting and exploration game, as a 2D platformer with varied and engaging combat, and as a Zelda-esque story RPG with a detailed world and memorable alien cultures to interact with. The sheer volume of different kinds of locations to discover, items to craft and build great structures with, and flashy ways to vanquish aliens prevent any part of the experience from getting boring quickly. It can feel overly punishing and time consuming, particularly in the first few hours. But the freedom to uncover the secrets of the galaxy and make its worlds your own is worth the wait, and the expert fashion in which Starbound binds all of its facets together makes it truly special.

Unfortunately, the controller support for this game is non-existant. The native controls of the game also seem like they would be difficult to try to learn, so I would deem a controller necessary for most players familiar with the series. I had bought this after I noticed they updated controller support for Samurai Warriors 4-II, but it seems that this game just doesn't have the support. I am using a standard PS4 controller, and was able to get it to properly work with a controller driver, so it can be playable, but the controls are still not as fluid as they are on the original system.
As far as the game itself goes, based on playing it on other systems, it is definitely a fun game to play, and seems to return back to the play style of 4 and 5 for general game play. While the story mode isn't as fleshed out as those games, you still get a very interesting take with the "What-if" scenarios, and the length of the stories for the individual kingdoms are a lot better than the previous two titles. It is a standard Hack-and-Slash title with an amount of good features. However, from what I've seen on my limited time playing, as well as other reviewers, I do have to agree that this is a port done poorly. I do wish that there was more support for this game, but being the most recent addition to the series and seeing a 2 year gap in the major updates, with the most recent one not really being significant to the game play, that should have been a warning sign.
My final verdict: If you do decide to get this game, and do have a PS4 to play it on, I would recommend the system over this port. It was made for that system, and I would understand why a lot of people say this is a money grab. I can recommend the game, but be cautious when you are buying it. Some controllers may work, while others will take a good amount of third party support to get to a functional level. While I am considering a refund at the moment, I will play for at least another hour or so before making the call.

I could have made this sweet and short, and just say: You'd never have a dull moment, with this amazing beefed up Assassin's Creed and Batman influenced games, as well as the beautiful and interesting story locked onto The Hobbit and LOTRs.
But nah man, let's continue..
Shadows of Mordor is a fantastic gameplay experience with an underwhelming story, which is sad since it is set in the famous Lord of the Rings universe. Its gameplay foundations are built on the Assassin's Creed series free running and stealth and the Arkham series combat mechanics and it adds to these with the very impressive "Nemesis" system. However the story is rather weak and even the combination of Troy Baker and Nolan North couldn't redeem it.
Taking this into account Shadows of Mordor is still an incredibly enjoyable experience. The system of manipulating and watching the interaction between different enemy captains and war chiefs is a marvel to behold. It is so incredibly satisfying to make a bodyguard betray his war chief, assist in the battle and watch as the bodyguard is crowned the new war chief, who you now control. The combat in the game feels fluid and fun, it takes everything from Arkham and makes it thoroughly gory. It is complimented by slowing time while using a bow, which is very much like playing out your Legolas fantasies. Also it makes it much more difficult. Ever play Assassin's Creed and feel like you can cut through everyone? Well even with wraith powers you still feel mortal in any close fought battle and I have personally died several times, even when playing it cagey. The game still retains a feeling of power and finesse but displays this constant tension, that death is only around the corner. One of the best parts of this is when you are killed, the Uruk that killed you will either increase in power or be promoted. It gives every battle a certain motivation that cannot be found in other games. They will even remember your last encounter and often taunt you!
The enemy captains and war chiefs have their own individual traits and abilities that can be found out by gathering information form other Uruks. This adds a good amount of strategy to the game, as charging in and finding out that an Uruk captain is invulnerable to combat finishers, is not a solid strategy. It feels in game like Assassin's Creed should have felt, and every victory is so much sweeter. It sounds simple but making the highest ranking enemies both, the hardest to kill and the hardest to plan for, is a sound design choice.
Unfortunately if you bought this game because you want to see some big name Lord of the Rings appearances, you're out of luck, as the game is set between the Hobbit and the Lord of the Rings trilogy. It's very unusual that a game studio would pay for a well known license and almost avoid the main content that makes LOTR what it is. However there is a fair amount of fan service in this game with references to the LOTR universe everywhere. Saruman is mentioned, Sauron is the unseen antagonist and of course Gollum makes an appearance, even if it isn't Andy Serkis. So I suppose it hits the spot if you're into the universe itself and not its main characters. Which is still an enthralling world to be immersed in.
The main character of the game is Talion an "Aragorn like" ranger who is murdered along with his wife and son in a blood ritual. His fate is intertwined with a wraith who is clearly of elven origin but has lost his memories. Talion is banished from death and the only way to break the curse seems to be to help the wraith in finding out about his past which ties in to the very making of the one ring and Sauron's rise to power.
Most of the gameplay consists of planning to kill a target or complete an objective then sneaking into a stronghold and carrying this out. There are quite a few side challenge missions and a few missions that require you to tame a certain beast or find an artifact, but there is not much in the way of variety in this game. Perhaps if the developers had another year to write a compelling story and add more variety in missions it would be a contender for game of the year. Overall Shadow of Mordor is a game that feels a little under its potential but the gameplay at its core is so satisfying that you'll find it easy to forgive. Go sink several hours into this compelling universe.

If I could sum this game up in one word it would be: Frustrating.
I have literally restarted two different missions at least two dozen times.  I spent over three hours doing a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ side mission.  Why?  Because the game designers have decided that instead of going with a smarter AI approach, they're instead going to make enemy mobs that are 100% impervious to any gadget attacks in the game.
Oh and with a gas mask, helmet and 200 lbs of armor on, they can also magically hear you sneaking up behind them for a stealth kill.  I have 100% stealth armor, the navy camo upgrade for night missions and I've carefully shot out every light within a 10 mile radius.
None of this matters as you approach him from the rear while he stares pensively over the railing of a ship.  He can hear a feather fall onto a cloud from 10 miles away inside his gas mask.  Which is utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  I spent the better part of a decade in the Army and I've worn gas masks more than David Caruso wears sunglasses.  You couldn't hear a Harley Davidson driving through a jet engine with one of those things strapped to your face.
They can't be electrocuted, they can't be gassed, they can't be snuck up on and God help you if you decide to shoot them because it will take more ammo than was used in the entire siege of Stalingrad just to knock their helmet off.
Also, the game now forces you to go 100% down one of three paths for each mission.  Personally I like to use the entire toolbox of gear that I bring on Sam Fisher when doing missions.  However, this is penalized as some gadgets will automatically incur a Ghost kill while you're trying to go 100% panther route.  Don't like it?  Can't use that gadget, then.
Oh right, the Sniper Rifles.  This one kills me.  No literally, my sides are splitting open as I slap my knee and guffaw at how idiotic this is.  Sniper Rifles are about as powerful as a large handgun.  The only bonus they have over other guns is range and control.  In the real world, if you built a military grade sniper rifle that couldn't penetrate a helmet at 100 yards, then you'd scrap the design and go back to the drawing board.
Not only do Sniper Rifles not penetrate helmets, it takes 2 shots or more just to knock the helmet off.  This is pure garbage and designed to further frustrate the player.  It's almost as if the devs have taken extreme pains to ensure that you have to tediously crawl through every mission choking out everyone with a helmet.
Lastly, Sam Fisher must have Parkinson's disease because he can't hold a pistol or assault rifle steady to save his life.  If I ever had a soldier on a firing lane that wobbled that much while holding a rifle, I'd rod him off the range and administer a breathalizer test.
Yet again, the developers making the game artificially difficult for no reason.  I mean I get that Sam Fisher is in his 50's at this point, but hell my 55 year old mother can drill out the center silhouette of a target at 10 meters with her stock Glock 17.  I'd think Sam Fisher, one of the most experienced field operatives in the world, could hold a heavily modified special forces pistol rock-♥♥♥♥ing-solid-on-target for at least the first 10 seconds he's aiming it.
It's more than just this, there's a good half dozen other things that just irritate the crap out of me about this game such as the climbing and movement models still being tied to extremely specific pieces of architecture.  How long has Assassin's Creed been out now and Spinter Cell is still sticking to the early years of mobility limitations in game engines?
Sigh, so so much wrong with this game.  Not even sure I have the patience to put up with it much longer.

As someone who grew up with a sega console and had played Sonic The Hedgehog as his first game, I loved the 2D highspeed series and everything about them, the music, the intensity of the levels, the backgrounds. All just absolutely amazing. But the one 2D sonic game I hadn't played and had only discovered recently was Sonic CD. Now, as someone who has played all 3 and a half Sonic games originally on the Genesis, allow me to give you a pros and cons list on this ORIGINALLY very hard to find installment. (Thank god for ports and remakes, am I right?)
Pros:
-The music is frigging phenomenal. Whether you be in the present, past or future, the music will change to fit the environment you're in and I find this to be pretty damn sweet. Plus it's all just written so well it's nothing but a treat for the ears.
-The graphics are absolutely wonderful, from Sonic's sprite to the level colors, background art and the way it scrolls with you as you move. It all comes together well in a way that just feels comfortable.
-Bossfights are just difficult enough not to make you want to toss your controller down on the ground and huff in anger. They feel rewarding and get you excited to move onto the next zone.
-The good future / bad future systems are interesting, but more on that later.
-Every single set of acts with different settings and music tracks make this really feel like a good, authentic and exciting adventure, although it be a short one.
-You can also unlock and play as Miles / Knuckles. That's pretty cool and give the game some replayability.
Cons:
-Going to the future in this game really has no use for your story progression at all and is a pain in the behind, so you really want to go to exclusively go to the past, that is if you can get there because of the past signs being so rare and in strange places.
-The timestone collection bits are really bad if you don't know the exploit to allow you to redo the special stage over again, the later ones just feel unfair.
-Metal Sonic seriously sucks to fight, although the music during his parts are cool and the fights seem really action packed, they suck due to having to learn his attack patterns fast, and if you don't you're as good as dead.
I'd give this game a solid 7.5 / 10.
It's really fun, but it's got it's flaws. Still worth a buy though for only $5!

Ah Sonic CD, the Classic Sonic game I haven't had much experience with. Honestly I enjoy this game greatly, it's heavy focus on exploration is something I find more fun than say Sonic 2's levels which had exploration but didn't really focus too hard on that.
Now to break down the rest of the game.
The game's main gimmick of time travel is actually pretty cool. You start in the present and need to hit a Future Sign or a Past Sign and run at decent speed for a long enough time to time travel. There's also 2 futures, a good one and a bad one. By default all futures are bad and you need to go to the past to fix that. In the past is a robot teleporter and a Metal Sonic hologram that once both are destroyed you get the good future. The Metal Sonic hologram isn't needed for the good future but they're all easy to get and free the animals of each stage so I recommend going for them. You can also get all seven
Time Stones to instantly destroy all robot teleporters (thus getting all good futures).
The game has 2 soundtracks, a Japanese one and an American one. The soundtracks are great in their own respects, I prefer the Japanese one but some of the American tracks are pretty damn good too. Each track does a good job giving the "emotion" of each stage and what timeline of the stage you're in.
The level design, now I know this get's criticized a lot but I like CD's level design. What I don't like about it is the enemy placement. I've had so many times where I hit a spring and found myself bashing into an enemy I had no way of knowing was above me, currently I almost only play in the good futures which have no enemies so that problem is kinda worthless
If you go for all Time Stones then you will suffer from the enemy placement.
The graphics look brilliant, especially the good futures. I've never had a stage that bored me or bothered my eyes when it comes to visuals (except Special Stage 6, that one is seizure inducing).
Replayability is also present (pun intended). I have 2 complete save files, one with Sonic and the other with Tails. Once you unlock stage select you can select any of your save files then go to stage select and replay the game with whatever percentage of completion you have. Meaning if you have all good futures or all Time Stones (or you can do what I did and get all Time Stones and all Metal Sonic holograms) and replay any stage in the good futures.
I recommend this to more explorative gamers, but that being said I still think anyone can enjoy at least some of this game.

Let me first confirm all the noise about the Strike Vector community:
It's dead. Which sucks.
If it wasn't true at the time of the previous reviews, it sure is now.
That said, the game itself is a fantastically well-crafted dogfighting game, one which - as a game designer myself - I feel very much inspired by. The level of effort put into making this game what it is, can only be a result of great passion by the developers, which I can respect.
If only more of that effort had gone into advertising.
Most of my friends have never heard of this game - even the flight sim addicts - and I only barely stumbled on it in during a sale. This is very sad, because this game deserves recognition.
The flight controls are very responsive, and switching into hover mode for a surprise kill is extremely satisfying. The levels are well-designed (and often claustrophobic, in a good way), and the visuals are stunning, especially for an indie title. The sound effects are intense, and the explosion you make when you pilot your crashing vessel right into an enemy ship feels like revenge done right. Top that off with a simple-but-effective loadout system (albeit with a few unbalanced combinations), and you have a very solid space-shooter that just feels right.
The main reason that I recommend this game (aside from the fantastic gameplay) is that the community is still salvageable on a smaller scale. It's on sale pretty often, so pick up a 4-pack or two, and get your friends in on it.
The maps cap out at 16 for the most part, so turn it into a social thing with your gaming buddies.
Great game, unfortunate example of the importance of advertising.

This game is fantasic. Having had it not only on PC, I've gathered around 60 hours on the Binding of Isaac Rebirth and Afterbirth Plus. The point of the game is that you're dropped into your randomly generated basement and have to horde off monsters from all shapes and sizes by crying on them with your tears, until you get to the end of your run, where at the start you beat your Mom, and other end bosses that come afterwards. The thing that makes this game so good is the randomisation of every single run. You never, ever know what you're going to get with this gem of a game. One run, you might destroy every enemy in a room in seconds, with a massive laser, and another you may have tears similar to a machine gun, but with poor damage. This game with all the DLC included has over 600 items, and 1000s of room types. This game can suck up 100s, if not 1000s of hours of your time. I completely recommend this game to ANYBODY.

As of the time I have written this, Isaac Rebirth has recieved both of its official DLCs, Afterbirth and Afterbirth+. I reccomend Rebirth to roguelike fans and classic Isaac players alike and I reccomend the Afterbirth DLC even more. However, I do not reccomend the Afterbirth+ DLC unless players are one of two things: Hardcore gamers or Completionists.
Here is a basic run-up for newcomers. You play as a little boy named Isaac who is running from his mother who wishes to sacrafice Isaac to her god. From there the story becomes purely up to interpretation and very rough to understand.
This game is the most roguelike of roguelike games. You control Isaac in a top-down shooter where every room has enemies and treasures around every corner. Each floor has a treasure room where you can get an upgrade (Both physically and in your appearance in-game) as well as a shop to spend coins and a boss room guarding the exit leading deeper into the depths.There are also a few other kinds of rooms to discover and solve within the endless RNG floors of the game. With each successful win you unlock more and more in-game content to find in later runs. But don't think that getting those wins will be a walk in the park, this game is quite difficult and there can always be times where you find nothing but bad upgrades which ultimately ruin your run.
As I stated earlier, I reccomend Afterbirth because it adds new layers of fun to what was already a fun game, new levels, new modes, new upgrades, new everything. Afterbirth+ on the other hand...
Let me put it this way: The game was already pretty hard, but even bad runs were winnable with enough determination and skill. Afterbirth+ adds a whole new shabang of content just like Afterbirth did, but the new enemies and bosses and mechanics are so blindingly difficult that even veteran players who completed the base game and Afterbirth were thrown into a bed of difficulty spikes and just couldn't complete the game for the final time. The only silver linings for Afterbirth+ are the community-made mod support and the only actual "Good" Ending in the game.
Rebirth: 10/10
Afterbirth: 9/10
Afterbirth+: 4/10

The best Dynasty Warrior games seems to be in multiples of 4.
The 4th in the series was one of the best with tons of content and lots of characters.
The 8th game in the series continues that trend, only more so. There is a insane amount of content to be had in here, and a PC port to boot (Dynasty Warriors was traditionally a console only series, though Dynasty warriors 4 Hyper was a pc port). The music is top notch (par for the course for DW games though).
I'll be frank, there are some issues. Slowdown at points (mainly due to Vsync ♥♥♥♥ing up the framerate). Some characters are overpowered to the point of making the game a stupidly easy cakewalk and are unlocked from the start (*cough*Lu Bu*cough*). Another is the frankly painful pricing of it's actual game and DLC. Had the game been knocked down a extra 10 bucks and the dlc normallized to 5 dollars for skins, 10 for level packs then i would far kinder to it and give a higher rating but I can't. TK's pricing on their stuff is frankly insane compared to other games. Sodding Paradox has better dlc practices.
Also, the cutscenes are awfully stifled with the english audio. I guess the voice actors were told to speak like that to match the pace of the cutscene's animations but i don't know. It just looks bad.
Despite everything bad that I said. Dynasty Warriors 8 CE can keep you entertained for a very long time. If you see this game on sale I recommend you pick it up. The DLC you can pick and choose though in all honesty you can avoid it without any loss to the final produce (unless you badly want more stuff to do in the game).
TL;DR - 8/10, Buy on sale.
PS: Use a controller. It's the way DW is meant to be played

My main concern is the difficulty of scavenging things from various shipwrecks. Often times, I would die before I could find the materials for a bandage or a motor. Parts are hard to transport and collect, and wood is nonrenewable, which only adds to the difficulty since one is then forced to relocate to other islands, leaving behind all the work they had previously done. Sometimes making something too realistic makes it unenjoyable to a point. However, I won't ding the game too hard for that because that's kind of the entire point.
In conclusion, I love it and can't wait to see what more is added in the future, especially with the items I keep finding that currently don't have a use. 9/10

If I could sum this game up in one word it would be: Frustrating.
I have literally restarted two different missions at least two dozen times.  I spent over three hours doing a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ side mission.  Why?  Because the game designers have decided that instead of going with a smarter AI approach, they're instead going to make enemy mobs that are 100% impervious to any gadget attacks in the game.
Oh and with a gas mask, helmet and 200 lbs of armor on, they can also magically hear you sneaking up behind them for a stealth kill.  I have 100% stealth armor, the navy camo upgrade for night missions and I've carefully shot out every light within a 10 mile radius.
None of this matters as you approach him from the rear while he stares pensively over the railing of a ship.  He can hear a feather fall onto a cloud from 10 miles away inside his gas mask.  Which is utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  I spent the better part of a decade in the Army and I've worn gas masks more than David Caruso wears sunglasses.  You couldn't hear a Harley Davidson driving through a jet engine with one of those things strapped to your face.
They can't be electrocuted, they can't be gassed, they can't be snuck up on and God help you if you decide to shoot them because it will take more ammo than was used in the entire siege of Stalingrad just to knock their helmet off.
Also, the game now forces you to go 100% down one of three paths for each mission.  Personally I like to use the entire toolbox of gear that I bring on Sam Fisher when doing missions.  However, this is penalized as some gadgets will automatically incur a Ghost kill while you're trying to go 100% panther route.  Don't like it?  Can't use that gadget, then.
Oh right, the Sniper Rifles.  This one kills me.  No literally, my sides are splitting open as I slap my knee and guffaw at how idiotic this is.  Sniper Rifles are about as powerful as a large handgun.  The only bonus they have over other guns is range and control.  In the real world, if you built a military grade sniper rifle that couldn't penetrate a helmet at 100 yards, then you'd scrap the design and go back to the drawing board.
Not only do Sniper Rifles not penetrate helmets, it takes 2 shots or more just to knock the helmet off.  This is pure garbage and designed to further frustrate the player.  It's almost as if the devs have taken extreme pains to ensure that you have to tediously crawl through every mission choking out everyone with a helmet.
Lastly, Sam Fisher must have Parkinson's disease because he can't hold a pistol or assault rifle steady to save his life.  If I ever had a soldier on a firing lane that wobbled that much while holding a rifle, I'd rod him off the range and administer a breathalizer test.
Yet again, the developers making the game artificially difficult for no reason.  I mean I get that Sam Fisher is in his 50's at this point, but hell my 55 year old mother can drill out the center silhouette of a target at 10 meters with her stock Glock 17.  I'd think Sam Fisher, one of the most experienced field operatives in the world, could hold a heavily modified special forces pistol rock-♥♥♥♥ing-solid-on-target for at least the first 10 seconds he's aiming it.
It's more than just this, there's a good half dozen other things that just irritate the crap out of me about this game such as the climbing and movement models still being tied to extremely specific pieces of architecture.  How long has Assassin's Creed been out now and Spinter Cell is still sticking to the early years of mobility limitations in game engines?
Sigh, so so much wrong with this game.  Not even sure I have the patience to put up with it much longer.

Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell Blacklist (SC6)
Just a little disclamer: I am trying to be as balanced as I can be but I am a huge fan of the Splinter Cell francise from Day One, i am also a fan of many other Tom Clancy games, including Ghost recon, Rainbow Six and Hawkx.
I am just saying if you feel inclined you may want to take this review with a grain of salt and make up your own mind.
To start this review without comparing this game to the rest of the Splinter cell series would be BLASPHEMY!!! So i will start with just that.
Blacklist gives a whole new aspect to the steath genre by incorparating many of the amazing things the previous games brought to the plate, for example: SC chaos theory's differant ways to complete missions, a free roam aspect but without as much hand holding as there was in Conviction. It still contains convictions assualt attitude but you can choose whether to be "Ghost"(Super stealthy, no killing) "Panther" (Still very stealthy, but with gunplay) and of course, "Assault" (All guns no stealth).
You earn more points in differant areas for the behaviors, but over all you earn more skill points for having a "ghost" style.
A lot of people think Chaos theory was the pinnacle of the series, I agree, but with all the experience Ubisoft have gained over the years of making Splinter Cell, they have really changed my opinion on the "best game" of the series. This is a serious contender in my opinion.
The multiplayer.
I never really got to play the multiplayer in the first games as by the time i had got round to playing them the multiplayer was abandoned.
This game heavily incorporates multiplayer. But its done well.
Amazing Spies vs mercs, i just can't describe how it just works so well. The teams are nearly always balanced,
(I was worried about this as many online games have this issue and also, Ghost recon phantoms, a F2P title is sliping into a game i don't like, with the unfair teams and lagswitching.) and the way the game is layed out it just plain works.
There is just one thing i am worried about, the fact that in a year from now the multiplayer will probably be deserted and the game will lose a huge chunk of it mechanics in the doing so.
Great for the steath fans, brutal takedowns and a true contender to the top spot of the series.

This game has a lot going for it: beautiful graphics, a wonderfully magical world, a nice hint system, and a nice map showing you where you still have stuff to do.
Unfortunately it has the worst fatal flaw a P&C adventure can have: dead end issues. At least that Is what I am assuming it is. The hint system merely states "There is nothing to do here" - and it reports that no matter where I go. I visit each of the locations where I still have stuff to do, but there is nothing I can do to advance the adventure. I googled the issue to find I wasn't the only person stuck in this fashion, and there were no known answers to the dead end.
That's the most important thing a game like this has to avoid - and it unfortunately is a game ruiner, for me.

Amulet of Dreams is a point-and-click puzzle game following the story of a boy named Aiden who is attempting to save the life of his sister Alison, who has been beset with a grievous illness. Dimension hopping follows. This game wasn't necessarily bad, it just wasn't that great. For one, the story itself, if you could even call it that, was inconsistent and made little sense. Likewise, the puzzles weren't so much difficult as they were unclear, prompting ample use of the hint button. With a weak story and puzzles that seemed to be based more on luck than logic, I didn't leave this game angry so much as underwhelmed at its quality.

Buggy crappy crap.
In at least two locations, if you don't take some necessary objects in the correct sequence, they close and you cannot get there again, having to restart from scratch. And these locations are almost in the very end.
... And while the graphics/animation are rather well done, the whole thing feels like just slapped together with no rhyme or reason, some worlds feel like authors ripped off famous games/movies just for the sake of having no imagination of their own.

The graphics of the game are nice. The story starts off promising, but after the first world you seem to end up in 6 random other worlds. After the last action of the game, there is a 5 second cut scene explaining how the story ends, but to me it doesn't make much sense.
The puzzles were okay'ish, but definitely not good. It regularly happened that when I clicked an object, I got an explanation what I needed to do much later in the game. There was no need to explain it that early, it would be nice if the hints appeared at the appropriate moment. Also some puzzles didn't make sense and even after using the hint button I didn't understand the logic. The "use" actions also seemed to be a bit random. Sometimes it was accepted if the object was used in the right area and sometimes you needed to put the item exactly in the place of the cog. But with one or two puzzles (e.g. the one with the basket) you had to make sure the cog wasn't visible, otherwise the puzzle wouldn't work. Very confusing.
The Steam achievements seem to be just a "tick in the box". You get them every time you move to a new world, so if you finish the game, you also get all achievements. The descriptions of the achievements are also poor.  It would be better if they were left out (or improved a lot).
It took me 4 hours to finish. It's an okay game, but I definitely wouldn't pay much than a few euro for it.

By far one of the weirdest HOG's I've ever played. It reminded me of Alice in Wonderland as storylines go. Totally illogical in every aspect imaginable. As if the developers were on some type of mind altering drug whilst in creation of this game. For what may seem to be a hint or object for one thing is something else. Once you get past the bizarreness and battle of your wits to the visual chaos, the game unfolds into a fantasy realm with twist and turns to keep even a seasoned player amused.

Weird casual adventure game that is just a bunch of neat backgrounds barely tied together with a sprinkle of story. The puzzles aren't horrible, but they are far from great. You will end spamming the hint button a lot as most of the solutions are quite obscure. Not to mention the amount of puzzles that can only be solved using one specific item even if you have another item that does the same in your inventory (you have a saw in your inventory and you need to use a sawfish or you have one kind of vice in your inventory, but you need to use another vice).
The background music doesn't fade in and out, but rather is just switched on when you are in a location where it is supposed to play. Then it doesn't start from the beginning but rather just continues like it was playing muted in the meantime. I just mention it because it is rather disturbing.
The hidden object scenes are okay, but nothing special. Overall the game is just bland both from the story (which there is very little of) and the game play. I spend a bit over 4 € on the game and I wouldn't recommend getting it for this or a higher price. Get it with a big discount or in a bundle.

Strike Vector deserves much praise for making a unique mutliplayer shooter about jet/mech combat while not being FreeToPlay. Yet there's next to no reason for me to talk about the game's positives simply because of one excruciating fact, the community is dead. It may be possible to find games at certain time of day or on certain days. You may be able to coordinate with other players and fans to set up a game. It's possible you may join an empty server, and wait around so other players can see the only server with a single player and join you.....yeah, that is the extent you may have to go to in order to play a round.
The contols and combat also has a steep learning curve that also turns off potential new players. I'm not sure if it is bad persay, but I definitely suck at it and it didn't help when the jet slightly veers off your aim, or when your target is in a awkward location in the map (that damn 4 tutorial map). The game prides itself for not being F2P, but sadly, this game may need F2P with transactions just to make it cost back (if it hasn't already).
From my minor first impression, Strike Vector has a great base game that is made mostly pointless due to being multiplayer only with no players available. You can mess around in training/challenge missions if you so desire, but at best you will have stationary targets to shoot. I will probably launch it a few more times to see if there are players and to get my card drops. But Strike Vector is a definite no to purchase, unless you can verify that there are other players to play with.
If the gameplay mechanics interest you, I'd recommend taking a look at Strike Suit Zero and Strike Suit Infinity. I haven't played enough to make a review, but it has the same flight transformation combat.

Largest downside I found to the concept of the game is it's "Persistent Universe", where even as you log off for the night the game 'keeps playing'. If missions left incomplete or threats to the base unresolved depending on your characters / survivors skills the next time you log in you'll have anything from minor supply loss above your daily rates, or once I had the misfortune of losing three of my four stored vehicles, my favorite character died, six survivors defected, and (probably just a glitch) I logged in to find a horde inside my base. This just seems to punish you for stopping the game since no matter what I did, I never received a positive outcome. The illusion of Artificially Intelligent survivor companions living their lives with or without you is lost when I become the only possible force keeping a pack of zombies from ruining everyone's day.
I greatly enjoyed the game even with it's minor technical quirks and glitches and would recommend the game for sure. Especially with it's low price point and high time to beat. But without a dedicated daily time to allot to it to replay, I haven't gotten around to more then a single play through.

I'm slightly on the fence over this game. It's fun the first time through. It'll take you about ten hours to get through the entire main storyline IF you take your time. It took me twelve hours to beat it and then I didn't want  to play it anymore; however, the DLC makes it much more playable for repeated runs.
Y'see, the problem with State of Decay is that it just repeats scenarios, over and over. You wind up doing the same thing so much that you start losing interest. Sometimes tedious little quests will pop up that you don't want to do, but you have to, otherwise, the game will end before you get to the end. And that sucks, trust me.
The good things about it, though, is the strange array of characters that you can gather. Most survivors that are in your group you can play as and each survivor has a different set of characteristics (some traits make the character better. Some traits make the character worse). If a character in your group gets infected, you can ask them to leave, let them stay and do nothing about it or kill them. You have to keep track of your supplies too. You can't survive a zombie apocalypse without any food, so, if you have the materials for it, you can actually build a garden for a steady supply of food at your base... Farmville rip-off (THAT WAS A JOKE, DO NOT TAKE ME SERIOUSLY!).
It's a good game. It's not amazing, but it's worth at least checking out.
If you get State of Decay, I highly recommend that you also get the DLC (Breakdown) as well. It's basically "endless mode" for the game, rather than stopping when you hit the final mission. Unless you're only looking for about ten hours of gameplay: the DLC is a must!
Is it worth twenty dollars? Probably not. Is it worth ten? Yeah, I think so.

There is some residual beta-like wonkiness this game never truly escapes, but I have to say, it is the closest anyone has ever gotten to the perfect zombie game. It's open world, you can pick among a variety of safehouses and fortify/upgrade them, and go rescue/recruit other survivors. The map is nice, the combat is fun, and the expansion pack adds a TON of replay value. Assuming it's on sale, as it so often is, and you can get both the base game and the DLC for $20 or less, it's a great deal, and you probably won't end up furious about the minor glitches you encounter along the way. It's also gotten fantastic support from its devs, with frequent updates and fixes, so it gets a little better every few weeks. I also give them points for having a lot of strong, fun, female characters, which far too many games ignore, considering it's now 2014, not the mid-1800s.

I have played a lot of other games. I had not previously played Town of Salem before I picked this game up. Town of Salem is better and it's free on browser. I see this as a Town of Salem clone but they made it worse.
The tutorial is very short and the community is toxic. They clearly came from Town of Salem and already understand the way these games work. I'm trying to learn and I get accused from everyone that I am throwing the game and they are going to report me. So it's reporting for cheating by witch trial.
There are so many different classes and things that can be done, this game is honestly just a roll of the dice if you win or lose no matter what you say or do. Then if you win, you get a few coins that you can spend on a small amount of cosmetics.
I'm truly disappointed to write this review. I'm done for now but may check again in a few months to see if things have changed. I do think the devs are active and care, but it remains to be seen if they are able to make this game good.

A great and innovative RPG.
This game's mounting mechanic is an incredible addition to an already well-beaten and tired genre.
One game after another, year after year RPG's continue to have you bash the monster's ankles until
it dies, well that changes here, and they do a damn good job at it.
Aside from the exciting combat, the game's character class system is a really well designed approach
as well, offering variety in playstyle and different approaches to  an encounter, although some classes
outdamage others by a gross margin (looking at you blast arrow ranger). Each subclass comes with
its unique set of skills that really change their playing style.
Other than combat and the different classes there's very little else here. The world is pretty
empty, the characters are forgettable with a very small roster of voice actors, the quests
are really boring with a vast majority being monster kills, gathering, and Gaben forgive me
for uttering these words: escort quests!
Even after saying that I'd still recommend this game to any
RPG fan as a breath of fresh air with it's unique combat style.
Come here, when you've finally moved on from Skyrim. It'll fill the void and so much more if you lend it the chance.

In this Hidden Object/casual adventure game you play as a boy, Aiden, who wants to rescue Alison and to do this, you have to solve various kinds of puzzles in multiple worlds. The puzzles range from object combining to hidden object to some simple logic puzzles.
The various locations are beautifully illustrated with limited animation on most screens, and in the hidden object parts everything is correctly labelled and can actually be found.
There is some voice acting, which is reasonably well done. It's not professional but doesn't distract either.
Rounding out the presentation is a relaxing music soundtrack and some effect sounds.
The major downside of this game is that it relies on 'moon logic'. On multiple occasions I had absolutely no idea what to do or where to go next, even with the assist of the in-game map. At these times I simply had to use the built-in help to proceed and even with this, it wasn't always clear exactly why something worked that way.
Making it worse, a few of the puzzle solutions do not make any kind of sense. Why can't I cut vines with a sword I already have in my inventory, for example, but I must use another cutting object found elsewhere?
There is quite a lot of backtracking in this game, even across the various worlds, so you'll either need to be very persistent in trying every single object everywhere, or regularly rely on the help function like I had to.
There is also some inconsistency in the story. Aiden and Alison are referred to at friends at certain points, and as siblings at other points. The story also ends rather suddenly without any epilogue or other kind of aftermath.
These gripes do not make it bad game, though. The overall experience I had was a good one, and the game does not contain any scary moments so it is also suitable for very young players.
However, since it does rely on a lot of obtuse logic in places, I can /only/ recommend this to die-hard Hidden Object / Casual Adventure fans who aren't annoyed by getting stuck,

In my opinion, this is a good game. I only paid fifty cents for it (less whatever I recoup from trading cards), but I doubt I'd regret the purchase at a lesser discount, even the very low full price.
The game is good, but not great or amazing. The devs are not the next Zun or Cave. "Best bullet hell experience" feels like a bucket of baloney, but then, my idea of a good bullet hell experience alway includes a focus button, or at least an equivalent that's always on, which this doesn't. You're always zipping around the screen way too fast, like the devs didn't realize that pinpoint dodging is hard when you move like a hummingbird.
That's my biggest complaint. Early on, it has an appropriate level of bullets for normal mode of a no-focus-button game, and it uses fast shots instead of screen-coating. (In other words, it keeps you perpetually overwhelmed and reacting at a higher level of intensity than touhou does. It's not all reflexes, but you usually don't have time to stop and plan your dodges before executing)
But bosses use attacks that would be ever-so-much easier if I had a way to transition to more precise controls. The final boss is legitimately challenging on normal, but it would be less so, and more fun for me, if I could forcefully slow down my ship's movement speed. One pattern, in particular, is sadisticly challenging when your movement speed is in screens-per-second but would be, if not trivialized, at least easier if you could make it a speed of "hitboxes" per second on command.
Still, I've had at least an hour's fun out of it. If and/or when I get bored of the other bullet hell games in my collection, this'll be a good way to practice the faster-moving genre and movement options.
The other stuff the game offers isn't bad. The wide variety of shot types and bombs is nice- bombs here are not touhou-style panic buttons where the attack is secondary, but merely a superweapon that does nothing of value except damage.
To compensate for this, unlike most bullet hells I've played, taking hits is expected- you have shields that heal over time. I generally find it fun, but I'd feel cheated if I spent ten bucks for it.
It's not properly conventional, only half of its unconventionality is an improvement, None of it is ikaruga level of novel-fun but I enjoyed it. Still, it's probably replacable, and if bullet hell games weren't so hard to find at times, it wouldn't do so well.
Pros:
- Fast-paced, intense gameplay (at least for someone who can't clear all touhou on normal, with the difficulty set to normal)
- Attack patterns aren't novel, or at least not productively novel, but they're at least interesting.
- Wide variety of guns that you can mix and match.
- Interesting multiplier system with benefits not limited to points.
- Plot feels like a marvelous suble parody of general "Aliens are invading, you're the hero we need you to save us" plots, as you refuse to accept surrender even after you've taken out entire planet's worth of infrastructure in return for a failed attempt of invading a single planet. To add fuel to this obvious jest, they continue to talk about how they're saving earth- nevermind that they could have had a surrender on favorable terms without taking further risks.
- eighteen levels probably falls here? I'm not sure.
Cons:
- If the plot isn't a parody, the plot is terrible, and worse, it's the kind of terrible that drags down other mediocre works in the future.
- No focus button.
- Game allows for a lot of getting hit per level, and occasionally pulls BS out to mess with you- like enemies showing up behind you, weak enough you could easily kill them if they weren't behind you in a game with no backwards shooting!
- No focus button
- Weapons select only works after you unlock them. Apparently, that's quite a while.
- A few levels (a mid-game one involves lots of undodgable attacks that you have to kill before they reach you.) are total BS, or require unintuitive knowledge (friendly fire is allowed, and stops projectiles, for instance). In the same manner, some bosses have inconsistent difficulty, with their hardest patterns showing up after their easier ones.

Getting this out of the way first: As of me writing this I've beaten the game once on normal story mode, so anything I say will be based on that.
EDIT: I've tried out the other game modes as well and have written about them below.
I'm not the world's greatest shmup player, but I still love playing them, be it regular or bullet hell. From what I found on the net this game was made by a bunch of vikings. I got it for 50 cents, but honestly I'd readily pay 5 or even 10 bucks for it. They did a great job.

>he plays games for the story
Joking aside there is a story mode to this game, but I didn't really pay much (read any) attention to the story and I generally don't unless I'm playing an RPG. Between each mission you get a briefing where the old talking heads from Starcraft 1 tell you things. If you want more on the story look through the other reviews, I'm positive there's at least one down there that bothered to describe what the story is about. Far as I'm concerned you're a ship shooting down progressively bigger ships until you find the biggest one and shoot that one down.

Graphics wise the game looks like most early to mid 2000s Windows/PS2 era shmups (think Ikaruga or Touhou 06 and up) and honestly I'm perfectly fine with that. The visuals and effects are nice and clean and don't get in the way of the action which is vital for any good shmup.

I'll be honest here, I was about to mute the game when I first heard some background wubbeth in the main menu, thankfully I decided to bare with it and BOY AM I GLAD THAT I DID.
The music is the highlight of this game. I loved the entire soundtrack from beginning to end. It's like the composer infiltrated my brain, found out what I loved listening to while growing up (and still do) and made a soundtrack based on that. We have FM Synth, late 90s/early 2000s electronica, some truly intense symphonic metal boss tracks and plenty of other goodies all taken from an age when you didn't have to dig all the way to China in order to find good music.
Even if you don't like these types of games you owe it to yourself to check out its soundtrack. It's amazing.

I'm not gonna bother explaining the basics of gameplay. If you're reading this chances are you already know what a shmup is. Instead I'm going to tell you what this game does different from most other shmups.
EDIT: This only applies to story mode. The other game modes play more like a typical shmup. You still have your shield, but the hull no longer has hp nor can you repair it. You have lives instead. You get points by killing enemies and collecting the things they drop (touhou does this as well). You pick a ship preset at the beginning, but you can't change your weapons midgame.
Difficulty wise I found the game pretty balanced at least on normal. It's pretty intense, but it doesn't quite reach the insanity I've seen in most bullet hells. I plan to try hard and above at some point as well.

I bought this for 50 cents (it costs $1 normally) and I got a pretty good bullet hell shmup with an amazing soundtrack. It's cheap as f*ck, so if you're even remotely interested in shmups (it doesn't even have to be bullet hell) I highly recommend you get it. It's a very neat little game made by our viking bros.

Now this is a game that severely needs players' attentions.
Strike Vector is an extremely fun, fast-paced, multiplayer, action, dogfighting game between transforming aerial vehicles called Vectors. These Vectors have two modes, a Vector and a Harrier mode. While in Vector Mode, your vehicle's default mode, you can fly at extremely fast speeds allowing you to easily chase escaping targets or easily escape and outmaneuver an enemy if you so happen to be their target. While in Harrier Mode, your vehicle basically enters a hover mode allowing you to turn faster and aim easier. The downside with using the Harrier Mode is that while you can still strafe at a slow speed, you're basically a sitting duck, allowing other vectors to easily target you and take you down. Knowing when to switch modes is a key mechanic to master in this game in order to be successful; using Harrier Mode for example, while being chased, to quickly turn around and switch back to Vector Mode to try to outmaneuver your chaser is a pretty nifty trick to use once you get the hang of things.
Player progression doesn't come from unlocking stronger weapons or loadouts as you level up, as per standard by other games. Instead, all of the weapons and equipment are already given to the players at the very start of the game; the only things you unlock as you level up are different cosmetic items to change to appearance of your Vector, unlockable art, etc. This makes the game a lot more skill-based as opposed to level-based, a design philosophy which I highly applaud.
One may think that in order to play this properly, you're going to need a joystick. Well, to you I answer: Nope! Controlling your Vector is actually pretty easy and intuitive with the keyboard. There's your standard [W][A][S][D] keys for directions with [W] for forward/boost, [S] for backward/brakes, [A] for strafing left/rolling left and S for strafing/rolling right and transforming is done very easily with the [space] key. You move your camera around with your mouse and you also aim this way. You then shoot whichever weapons you have equipped with your left and right mouse buttons. That's it for the very basic controls and if you are somehow unhappy with the control scheme, don't worry; each key is rebindable.
Now, I've been going on about controls and mechanics but is the game actually fun? To put it simply, HELL YEAH! and very much so. I've mentioned before about the game's fast pace and from the very moment you try it out, I'm sure you will feel it too. The Vectors move very rapidly especially in Vector Mode and this may make flying a bit difficult to those who aren't used to it yet resulting in many crashes/suicides. Don't be discouraged however as once you start to get the hang of things, flying in this game will start to become one of the most satisfying things to do, be it making those sharp corner-turns or threading the needle multiple times. Now add to that flying, multiple other vectors each with the intent to kill each other, a variety of gorgeous looking maps, the variety of different weapons and equipment you can equip on your vector and you've got yourself one adrenaline-pumping, ridiculously fun, multiplayer dogfighting game.
I did mention at the very start of this review that this game needs attention. Why is that? Well, it's simply because unfortunately, not a lot of people play this game. Perhaps we can blame this to poor advertising or players simply being uninformed about this game's existence. Whatever the case, this is an extremely fun but overlooked game that clearly deserves more players than it currently does so play the game and help spread the word! :D

Movie-quality presentation and immersion combine with frustrating gameplay.
This is a game that, for the typical gamer, likely plays out in one of two ways.
1) You tried the stealth approach because it seemed like the best idea, and you failed.
2) You have given up on the stealth approach and now everyone will die.
The good news is that for the most part, Blacklist understands that you will just not get people to stick with stealth when it's this stupidly annoying, so you have 3 paths available to you in many cases.
Sometimes, though, just like the "stealth" missions in Assassin's creed, you are forced to avoid detection, and those can be nightmarish, controller-throwing, descents in to infuriation.
And yet, the whole game is so well done that you can almost forgive it for this.
Almost.
Most likely though, you will play the game with trepidation, hoping that just shooting everyone is an acceptable path through the mission and push forward to enjoy the storyline before it inevitably decides that it's time for a pure-stealth exercise in repetition and futility.
Some will say that this is all a deficiancy in my ability to play the game - maybe so - but games should be quite forgiving to the player that wants to enjoy the story and experience, and well, Blacklist just isn't. If you aren't great at pure stealth, then no difficulty setting will save you.
So do I recommend this game? Absolutely! It's fantastic - just, practice all your techniques for controlling stress, and remove breakable items from your general vicinity if you aren't the greatest at sneaking around in a game that isn't forgiving.

Ubisoft presents Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Black List by Tom Clancy published by Ubisoft and played by me is pretty cool I guess.
As some people may know, I am a big fan of the Splinter Cell series, being dragged into it back in 2005 with Chaos Theory. But being a fan of a series owned by Ubisoft is like having your lover fart in your mouth. Yo that is foul as ♥♥♥♥. After the mediocre Splinter Cell: Conviction, Ubisoft Montreal decided to stop being like the stuff I find in the back of my box, and actually try and make a Splinter Cell game. The problem with this is, they still need to meet publisher quotas, or atleast that's what I've been told.
You once again play as Sam Fisher, but now he sounds like he could be my big brother instead of my actual dad. The game revolves around a terrorist cell known as the Blacklist who commit to attacks every week the United States doesn't pull it's troops out of every country in the world and send them back to America. We, of course, cannot have this, so instead the president lady has Fourth Echelon (That's one more than Third Echelon) go on a mission across the world to hunt down Blacklist and it's leaders and be home in time for apple pie.
The gameplay works, it's like they wanted to make Chaos Theory again but had to use Conviction elements. Now you can go in non-lethally like the older games pre-Conviction, and you aren't put into set-piece like arenas where you have to end the lives of everyone who came into work that day. The game's levels, while not as open and expertly crafted as prior games, give you enough freedom so that you aren't bogged down by memorizing enemy patrol patterns to get past them unnoticed. It cuts down on the frustration and stop me from resorting to abusive alcoholism.
You get money after each mission that you can use to buy new stuff, such as suits, or guns, or gadgets, or a girlfriend. And if you're lacking money for that new hug pillow with Rise-Chan on it, you can always go on sidequests that you can bring that one friend you actually have along with you. Which is neat so when I eventually do mess up, I can blame on them instead. Good job, Mark.  Although these missions have less of a variety as the story missions, they still manage to be open and free enough that you can go about it your own way instead of having to follow a beaten path, which means you have time to get that wedgie out of your crack because your OP suit is riding up like it's asking you to prom.
If you're returning to the series, you'll notice some noticable differences in the characterization. Sam is nowhere near as snarky or as comedic as he was in previous installments and since
most of the charm of hearing two friends screw around has really hurt both the tone and the likability of the lore and the story. Michael Ironside is gone and replaced with a guy who I didn't bother to remember, who makes Sam sound like he's a fresh young member of the agency rather than a grizzled old veteran. The change in tone from Conviction onward has honestly hurt the series, further proving that Conviction is like that other guy that lives beside your box but insists on spooning with you because "We have to stick together."
If having feel-good fun time with your friends doesn't tickle your pickle
, you can always go online in the Spies vs Mercs mode. In this game mode you play as either Paul Blart mall cop in first person or Frankie Muniz from those Agent Cody Banks movies in third person.
So what you have are Mercs in defense, where you move around and♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants because a spy could be around any corner ready to steal the colonel's secret recipe from you. Or you play as a spy while you move around and♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants because a merc can come around any corner and fill you without enough holes that it's both a war crime and a sex crime. Dirty.
While not being as pulse pounding as Chaos theory's or Pandora's Tomorrow's multiplayer, it's still a rather fun diversion and may keep you around if you enjoy both competitive and stealth gameplay. Don't expect anything revolutionary, though. They're video game developers, not miracle workers.
But should you play Splinter Cell: Bar Bouncer front gate?
It's fun. Not 30 Canadian Funbux fun, but you'll get some enjoyment out of it. It's certainly better than the fifth game in the series, but nowhere near as good as the second or third.
