In this review I’ll be focusing on the single player experience.  This review will contain minor spoilers.
Starting off I played with the Realistic difficulty and for whatever reason could not stealth the first real mission so shot my way through with ease.  For a few missions after that I stuck to the Panther playstyle but soon got the hang of stealth and starting doing Ghost on Perfectionist.  Ghost seams easier than it should be to be honest.  A few segments are tough but most of the game is easy to ghost through.  Even Brigg’s first person segments (which you’re not even supposed to ghost through anyway) are easy.  As a side note, I tried Assault on Perfectionist and that can be very hard; much harder than Ghost in fact.
The gameplay is very fun however, I will complain that there are segments where they force a certain playstyle on you and I really don’t like that.  I think it defeats the purpose of tracking how much the player sticks to a certain style if at certain parts of the game you’re told you have to play a certain way.  The three parts that annoyed me the most are as follows:
These sequences don’t ruin the game by a long shot; they’re just annoying.
The story is decent but I don’t like Sam’s new voice or that the main characters like being jerks to each other.  I do like that you can talk to the main characters between missions and call Sarah.
Splinter Cell Blacklist has what I consider to be very advanced AI.  At the very least the AI is far better than its predecessor Splinter Cell Conviction as well as Hitman: Absolution and Assassin’s Creed IV: Black Flag.
The AI in Conviction had a lot of potential but felt underdeveloped (but still not as bad as Black Flag).  Blacklist takes everything Conviction’s AI tried to do but does it in a much improved way.  The last known position is still a part of the AI’s decision making but they respond to it in a smarter way.
In Conviction the AI pretty much always assumed that you were trying to draw them out and found cover near the last known position and shot it until someone ran towards it and figured out you weren’t there.  In Blacklist enemies will become suspicious over different things and actually try to search for you and will dynamically form searching parties and then break those up as need be.  They respond to different things like lights turning on or off or doors that were closed being opened really well.
Unfortunately, their patrols, when they don’t know you’re there are often easy to avoid.  However, they sometimes require a frantic mix of waiting in an area very patiently and hoping to not be caught and quickly moving forward, towards and past enemies that are often too close for comfort because staying still will get you caught.  These situations require very precise timing.  On rare occasions, areas did seem unfair but mostly, it was because I was being a complete idiot and missing the too-easy path past all the enemies right in front of my nose.
Throughout the game the AI did various things that impressed me such as, enemies noticing that their buddy I had knocked had vanished and then trying to find them.
The game still had a few of what I’ll refer to as “Black Flag moments” which are when the AI acts so incredibly stupid you have to wonder how no one noticed the flaw and fixed it.  The two main complains I have in this regard are:
I’m not the biggest stealth fan out there but this is easily the best stealth game I’ve ever played with the exception of Hitman: Blood Money (but that’s like comparing apples to oranges).  It has some issues but it is still really fun.  It also runs well performance wise and is an excellent port in terms of quality.  Obviously, Uplay is stupid and should not be allowed to exist.  I give this game an 8.5 out of 10; loosing points mainly for sequences that force a certain playstyle on you.

This is as close to MMO you can get without being a MMO. Some people find it to their liking, however, foe a single-player game, it is a flaw, rather than a merit.
All of the quests, except for the main one, are generic "kill X enemies of a certain type", and the rewards are given automatic, so you can slay a dozen of wolves in a forest, and suddenly get a sword spawned in your inventory. The main storyline is nothing to speak of as well. I haven't learned any names, locations, or managed to follow the narrative, as everything is very much the same. Nothing memorable.
Crafting is just confusing. You throw things into a pot and something else appears. You will have no idea what resources you will need if you want to craft something, and thus, you'll be following sheer luck.
Interface takes a good chunk of your screen and messes with it all the time. Not to mention, it's confusing, lacking hotkeys - you can only open your inventory in the game, while to get to the map or quests, you have to pause the game (ESC key), and choose the option needed from the list.
Speaking of which, import to PC is awfully inconvenient - it's confusing to play it without a controller because of the key bindings you have no ability to change, and really confusing  mouse options - at some interface places you can use it, at some you cannot.
Combat is very simple and very dull, with little variations to what you can actually do during it, so it gets repetitive pretty quickly. Your enemies basically vary by their HP, so you're just click spamming them to death. Only the beginning of the quest in, and I already avoid combat, because it's just so dull.
I'd speak of low graphic and animation quality, but, considering the year of 2012 it was made in, I cannot blame DD:DA for not being up-to-date. It's an OKish graphics for a five-year-old game. Not good, just OKish.
Most important, THIS IS NO RPG, there's no role element at all in this game. It's just a third-person action, so don't be fooled by the tags.
All and all, I do not recommend it. It's an MMO without other players, and only other players is what makes MMOs so interesting. This specific game is plain dull, and not in an atmospheric "Gothic" or "Morrowind" way, where games have certain feeling and slow pacing, but win via RPG element or mechanics, this one is just
. Fourteen hours in, and I cannot find anything good to talk about for this game. I do try, as telling something good is always on my mind when I write a review for film, game, or a show, but there's virtually nothing innovating or plainly interesting in it. I'm just disappointed I've spent money on this product.

The idea behind the mechanics is cool: switching the gravity axis to find your way into a volumetric maze, that's neat. But there are a bunch of unpleasant problems:
1. slow jump, slow walk, slow everything. Your character is a snail that has as much control over its jump as you'd have over Superman 64. A platformer with a timer where you don't feel like walking around because it's too slow and unwieldy feels like a game that should be patched up.
2. arbitrary "fall damage". It feels as though the paths you can walk on are restricted, even though nothing visually says so. You'd use your physics bending powers to go to a platform, but your screen turns red, you hear a "argh" and it's a fail state. Why? Did I fall from too high? It didn't seem higher than the jump I made 2 seconds ago...
3. arbitrary controls. You don't have any control over the input. See, the game expects your brain to work similarly to its developper and associate "left button" to "go left", but mine associates "press left button" with "push from the left" (thus "go right"), so everytime I need to use these controls, I have to take 2seconds to think about which button I should press. You can figure it's frustrating as hell.
These are all major complaints I have for now.
Asking for a refund, but I'll keep watching out for patches and updates that would fix those issues.

So far so great; first impressions.
Miscreated can be easily passed off as another clone of DayZ and i do agree with this to a certain degree but it is very nice to play a game like this that gets it's core gameplay correct. It's impossible for me to not compare it constantly to DayZ (which i put many hours into in mod stage and standalone) as i began playing this game but find myself often thinking how much better it has done certain aspects of the style. Straight off the bat it's nice to have full control of your movement and mouse control that feels natural. While i understand DayZ aims to be more tactical and slower paced it is constantly frustrating when simple things become much harder to do because of forced realism that generally ends up showing more bugs than anything else. Despite this so far Miscreated definitely lacks some of the atmosphere and intense situations that are present in DayZ but still excels with its own style that you would defintely say is a more arcadey experience. DayZ has a massive scope and a much bigger map but it feels spread very thin in relation to how the game has developed. Miscreated somehow has quite a lot more features already but definitely has a more focused approach with it's smaller map and less unique locations.
But to me that's not a bad thing and it is refreshing to play a survival game like this that is created in a good engine. Miscreated nails the simple things when it comes to gameplay. Movement and shooting feel smooth and responsive. Vehicles are in the game and have worked fine so far with simple enough systems in place to get them running(including boats which was a surprise). I think it's important to note that this game is not made by a big company and probably does not have massive funding which for me puts it in a different perspective. Because of this fact i think Miscreated punches well above it's weight and surpassed the expectations i had when going into the game. It is mind blowing to me that they can nail many simple things that a game like DayZ cannot which tells me that the developers have focused on the right things when they set out with the development roadmap.
I think it's important to note that i find the PvP experience completely fine. People are going to kill you for no reason, its a matter of fact in these games and i have no problem with it. In some cases it makes situations much more tense which is really the experience i'm looking for in a game like this. It's part of the experience and even so i have ran into quite a few people already who were friendly already which was surprising. I just think it would be unfair to quickly judge this game based on a interaction you've had in a game with another player if it comes down to simple things like player choice. That being said perhaps this game is better suited to at least playing with one other person.
The performance is great for an early access game and it looks quite good too thanks to cryengine. Looting in houses with a torch feels much more immersive than other games and the loot system seems to work quite well so far. It's nice that all the simple things just work, no worrying about picking up loot not working or nothing ever spawning it seems. Bugs have been minimal for me so far besides some glitchiness in AI behaviour of wolves but nothing too serious. The infected in this game do have a presence but it is not overwhelming. I would not mind if they increased this in the future as the combat mechanics are consistent enough to deal with them. Melee feels reponsive and reliable which is a nice change while you do still take damage and it's not a total pushover.
There is quite an array of loot as well and i'm sure it's going to improve. Interestingly after 15~ hours of gameplay i've found items i haven't seen before which i think is quite good. On top of all of this there is an easy to use crafting system that contains many items and so far it has worked very easily.
Something i cannot completely cover yet is base building and the mechanics of it. However i have encountered others bases and it's pretty cool to see some stuff others have built and being able to explore it.
For me i feel like as long as this game is continually worked on it is only going to get better and better. Some of my early encounters have already given me a similar to feel to what i have experienced in DayZ with the difference being that i felt in control the entire time of what my character was doing.
The northern most part of the map is a great change from the rest and the small city area seems well crafted. If more areas like this exist in the future it will be a massive improvement.
I expect the major negatives for me could come in the form of getting bored of the much smaller map, however it is too early to say if this is true and the gameplay is still very enjoyable and it helps that it looks pretty good too. [Update 2014-10-07: When playing with an Xbox360-compatible controller, there seems to be much more control of the camera angle than with the mouse. This removes my primary irritation with the game.]
[Update 2014-10-12: When playin with controller, shortly after I got two people following me instead of one, the game very frequently popped up a prompt to Taunt/Cheer/Agree/Disagree. Nobody had said anything, so the last two don't even apply! The buttons to answer the prompt are the same as buttons you need to do melée, finishing strokes, searches, open/close doors. This means that I randomly was unabled to attack, defend, or close a door in time. Sometimes I could work around it be quickly pausing, unpausing, and immediately pressing the desired key before the Taunt/Cheer/Agree/Disagree prompt got in the way again.]
You can control many different characters and improve their skills, such as with a particular weapon. However, they all seem completely unable to handle themselves without you present, regardless of purported skills. Keep in mind that when you close the game you are not considered present, so the next time you open it you may find that a nice situation has become dire, or that a desperate one has already been turned into failure.
This is not a game you can play "from time to time", but rather one that requires you to frequently come back to make sure that things haven't collapsed while you weren't playing. And if you have to exit the game during an in-game crisis to deal with real life, you may have to do a lot of rebuilding, healing, and recruiting of new characters when you return. You may even have to start over.
[More Update 2014-10-07: Although they did eat all the food and use all the other supplies in the months that I left this title alone (and the window barricades mysteriously disappeared without the window glass being broken), nobody died--not even the one supposedly in critical condition. Now wishing I could change my "Not Recommended" mark to "Don't know if want".]

I honestly say that I tried to enjoy this game. It seems like a fun game but there are a few issues that cause me to not want to play any more than past the 3rd level. Keep in mind i used KB/M for my experience.
-Bugs. One specific one I've noticed is in level selection. You go in, can't select your level, exit out, go back in and can select it again. Easy bug to go around, not a big deal but on top of other things it's quite annoying.
-Incorrect tutorial prompts. One specifically that tells you to use Shift+Space to wallrun, coming from Cloudbuilt, that makes sense. In reality to wallrun all you have to do is have shift held when near a wall. If you try to press space when around a wall, you'll immediately jump off, caused quite a few unnecessary deaths. Admitidly so, it is partly my fault for not fixing my habits, but the game tells you how to do an integral part of the game incorrectly.
-Camera. The camera work is absolutely terrible. For the three levels I did play, it felt like I was constantly fighting the camera to see where i wanted to look. I even changed my mouse's settings for max DPI and it still felt like the camera was constantly trying to snap back to where I wasn't trying to look. It's hard to explain, but it felt like it kept pushing back towards the MC's line of sight. With lots of corners and trying to move fast, fighting with the camera isn't something I want to have to do.
-Respawn. I have three points with this one, the first is that there is no quick respawn. You have to wait for the whole scene for the MC to die, even if you know you've missed a jump, you don't have a button to just respawn. The second is that there is no key locking while respawning, after the screen turns dark you can move from the respawn point, changing the camera angle, and changing from red to blue or vice versa. Lastly you keep the same camera angle that you had when you died. If you took a 90 degree turn before you died because there was a corner before the next checkpoint, you respawn facing a wall or a cliff, if you missed your jump and tried to salvage it because theres no quick respawn and you end up dying facing the wrong way, you start facing backwards. Minor complaint, but on top of fighting with the camera, it's quite annoying to come back like that.

I was willing to give this game a chance after the horrible nightmare that was Splinter Cell Conviction.  Interviews with the devs highlighted a game that they promised would go back to some of Splinter Cell's roots while still moving the franchise forward, which is fine by me.
The execution of the game however still lingers like acid reflux that no amount of tums can put down.
The uncomfortable:
Long gone is Splinter Cell alumni Michael Ironside, the voice of Sam Fisher for the 6 other (I think 6) entries in the franchise.  This is such an immersion breaker for me, and I suspect anyone else like me, that is a long time fan of the series, but not the direction it took in Conviction.
Michael Ironside IS SAM FISHER, the choice to either not hire him on purpose or for whatever reason is such an alienating mistake for long time fans of the franchise.  But here's the thing, Ubisoft does not care about the old fans of this series, they care about getting new fans and competing with call of duty.
The EXTREME:
The game gets in your face, granted in a bit more subtle way than Conviction did, but there's this intense Monday night drama!!!!!! feel to the game as you're introduced to your new base, your team, and your goal to protect the world from the most extreme bad guys ever by going to the limit!
Promises broken:
I was interested in the 'ghost / phantom / whatever' game play mode, one that emphasized a pure stealth approach to the game, because that's what the old Splinter Cells were about, because Sam wasn't equipped for extended combat.  So the idea appealed to me, as well as the insistence that there were multiple ways to clear an obstacle...
Which there are, to a degree.  Movement is still totally linear, it would be nice to have this game take some lessons from Assassin's creed and give you a bit more of an open world to use in your approach to a target.  I understand a narrative needs to have some degree of linearity to move a story to a point, but the "alternate paths" feels like:
"You approach the bad guy, do you want to close one eye, both eyes, or have both open?!"
Everything leads to one point, and if you are trying to play a zero kill playthrough there are moments where they do their hardest to make that improbable.  You have to exploit the AI to make it work.
The missed opportunity:
I'm done with this franchise, I'm done as long as they are going to use Sam Fisher and Anna Grimmsdottir.
The new guy playing Sam is just plain terrible at voice acting and has no shred of the gravitas that Michael Ironside brought to the character.  And why is Grimm suddenly this extreme beeyotch of a boss?  She was never like that in the original run, she was an operational advisor for Sam.  I could see her succeeding Lambert, but not in this way.
Honestly, if they ditched the old characters but still called it Splinter Cell, I'd have less of a problem with it.  Give me new characters in a Splinter Cell world you want to redefine, my brain won't reject it as much.
Because I grew up playing Splinter Cell, I knew Splinter Cell, and this game is not Splinter Cell.
Conviction was a terrible turning point, they invalidated amazing character choices from Double Agent.  Sam's daughter is killed in a random accident and Sam hits rock bottom, taking on an absolute zero success chance suicide mission to infiltrate the JBA.
Hey, guess what, his daughter is alive, because feels!  It was a setup so bad guy number 7 could get to him and enact Independece Day Initiative!
Sam is so deep undercover, the only man who knew he was is dead, Sam's on the run as a wanted terrorist, he may have to straddle the line just to survive and clear his name!
Nope, never mind, let's throw him in some cliche plot where the world is in danger and he must auto murder people and explode helicopters to do it.
Blacklist is more of that, it's more from people that just don't get what Splinter Cell was.  Which is fine, if you didn't grow up with Splinter Cell, or better if you stop trying to hang on to the old guard.

Being an amazing and always evolving series, I couldn't wait to get my hands on Splinter Cell: Blacklist. And god, after the enormous changes the previous game (Splinter Cell: Conviction) made, I was hoping this sequel to come back in a slightly more classic way.
And here it is! Blacklist is the perfect balance, in my opinion, between the Splinter Cell "older" gamers know (from the first to Double Agent) and the changes made in Conviction. The result: a stealth-action game with fluid gameplay, badass movements and giving you a certain degree of freedom in your approaches. You can sure as hell go all gun blazing, but this is not the recommended way to go: being sneaky is still the best approach.
The only (maybe) downside to this game? Well, I guess that is the main character, Sam Fisher, who looks like in his 30-40's, when he is supposed to be approx. 60 years old according to the story. I'm playing with french voices, so the change of voice actor does not affect me.
I really hope to see a sequel to the series, or a prequel; but in the first case I think this would be better to make Sam Fisher a secondary character (example: he would be the new playable character's instructor).
Conclusion: Splinter Cell Blacklist is an amazing game, who made the good move to head back to its roots without doing a complete 180°. The only thing I'd like to see is some consistency in the universe, but that's about it.

If you are unaware, Keen Dreams is the black sheep/prodigal son/forgotten chapter of the Commander Keen series. It falls somewhere between the end of Invasion of the Vorticons and Goodbye Galaxy, so that effectively makes it episode 3.5 or some such nonsense. Since then it’s floated around like a chunk of loose cat hair, with an Android release in 2013 by Super Fighter Team and now this crowd-funded re-release for the PC by Javier Chavez. This includes not only the source code, but an updated port of the game for Windows, Linux, and Mac OS computers. Pretty snazzy in concept -- and in reality!
This isn’t a complete overhaul or anything, this is just a port with a few extra thingies. Thingies like modern gamepad support, widescreen and windowed mode graphics options, cloud saving, achievements, and even a switch for CGA and EGA mode right from the main menu.
As for the game itself, well, it’s the same pared-down Keen experience as it was before. The story is that Keen refused to eat his veggies one night, then has nightmares about it where vegetables are torturing him in the land of Tuberia. Dressed in pajamas and armed only with hippy-fied flower power seeds, it’s your goal to collect enough boobus bombs to eventually defeat the giant sentient potato, King Boobus Tuber. Most notably, you don’t have a pogo stick, which puts it up for debate as to whether or not this is even a Keen game at all without his trademark power-up. Some other things are missing as they were in the original DOS release, like any music whatsoever, the ability to look up and down, and grabbing onto ledges while jumping. Disregarding the sparseness of features, the gameplay itself is similar enough to Goodbye Galaxy that it doesn’t completely suck. I had a lot of fun with this as a kid, and I still find it to be a unique challenge, with its non-linear progression and the challenges of using flower power due to the arc you throw the seeds at.
So while the gameplay itself is as "meh" as ever, this is just awesome if you ask me, because games like this don’t deserve to be forgotten. Even without my own nostalgia for this title, I’m just glad this is getting some attention, because no matter what Level 32 of Doom II says, Keen will never die.

Pillars of Eternity is a RPG game developed by Obsidian Entertainment, releasing on Steam in March 2015. This game is a spiritual successor to the game series Baldur’s Gate and Icewind Dale. The game was kick-started in September 2012, with the highest ever funding at the time of over $4 million.
Game play in POE is very much like the other games in the series, the tactical combat with your party of adventures, and an overwhelming amount of choices in terms of stats, equipment, skill points and attacks.  The game play does get easier the further into the game you get, as you characters grow in strength and you just become more tactically aware of your surroundings and you will work out how to get the most out of all of your characters. The game is has a heavy amount of dialog, if you don’t like reading then this game is definitely not for you. The game starts off very slowly and for the first three or four hours, you will spend the majority of that time reading text and getting started with the story. Throughout all of the dialog choices, you also get plenty of important decision that can change the outcome of certain events as you progressively get further in the game, such as siding with different factions etc. Whilst the outcome of your choice is not always very clear, the game does a very good job of masking those decisions without you realising how important they actually are.
Right from the character creation screen, you will see how in-depth this game goes, there is an abundance of choice and options for you to make whilst creating your character. I was a little disappointed to see that I actually reached a level cap towards the end of act three, so almost half way through the game, I couldn’t progress my character any more. This in turn made the rest of the game seem somewhat imbalanced as I was able to just waltz through the enemies without batting an eyelid.
POE whilst it doesn’t have super amazing graphics, the environment and locations that you find yourself in still look gorgeous. The way the world is presented makes you want to explore it inch by inch. The UI is the most important part of this game graphically; it is smooth and functions perfectly. You are able to find all the information you need within a click or two – believe me, there is a lot of information in this game you are going to need!
This game is basically a novel inside of a game. The story is often criticized by some people, but I for one was completely intrigued and loved following it right from the start. The story is deep and moving, with plenty of cliff hangers, twists and turns as you progress.  On top of the main story line, you can follow plenty of optional side quests which add so much more immersion to the world you are in, it allows for extra character development and more choices. I actually really cared so much about my characters at the end due to what they have gone through, I spent more time than I would like to admit pondering over dialog choices. Like I said above, there is a lot of text in this game, whilst a good portion is voice acted, another good portion is not. So you better be prepared for some reading. Normally I much prefer my games to be completely voice acted; it helps me get more immersed in the story and I am probably a bit lazy, but I was completely happy to read everything this game had to offer. I honestly thought I was reading a book at times.
When you begin the game, the difficulty level is fairly challenging. You have to really think about your adventures’ next actions and movement, but as with most games, as you become more familiar with how the mechanics actually work, you become more and more Intune with it, allowing you to breeze through the game at points. The end boss is somewhat of a challenge, which required me to retry a couple of times. Once you get a few bits of high quality equipment, and your characters become over levelled due to the amount of experience awards in the game, you won’t find any point to be impossible to conquer though.
I finished my play through of POE in just under 60 hours (not sure why Steam says I only have 45?); this was doing the majority of side quests and exploring the world quit sufficiently whilst also taking the time to enjoy the dialog in the game too. I have seen some people put well over 100 hours into this game, and I suspect that is because of the game’s high replay ability factor.  One of the main elements which makes the game replay able, would have to be the in-depth character creation, you can create a brand new character that plays completely different to your last one, making your gameplay experience different too. Personally I don’t think I would do a second play through of the game because I feel I have got all I can out of the game right now, but those that really want to drill down this game for every inch, there is definitely a high amount of replay ability on offer.
The game runs like a dream too; I was able to play on 4k resolutions with the graphics turned right up. At times I did attempt to use the Steam controller, but the mouse and keyboard is the much prefer method for this type of game. The game did release with a few bugs and glitches, but after the first patch, these have all been cleaned up so I was able to play without any problems.
Pillars of Eternity is any classic RPG fan’s dream. If enjoyed Baldur’s gate, or want a completely immersive in depth role playing experience, then you need to be picking this game up. Steam’s price of £34, 99 to me seems a bit excessive, but you can pick this game up for almost half that on external websites if you shop around.  For me this is a stunningly good game, that I would consider a must play.

I'll start out harshly and say that I view this game as a failure, given that the mission-statement was to create a spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate.
Now that doesn't make this a bad game, but the comparison is not too evident to me.
I'd actually say Pillars of Eternity is a very good game, but let's focus on the negative first:
The game is incredibly dialogue heavy - sometimes unnecessarily so. Avid readers will definately enjoy this game - but the massive contrast between the grindy combat, the occasional hard encounters that require a keen tactical eye and then hours of page-long dialogue is just too much that the game ever really feels homogenous.
Sometimes Pillars feels like three different games all in the same package, and once you've gotten accostumed to the grindy combat for a bit, it becomes sincerely difficult to sit through multiple pages of dialogue describing abstract imagery and metaphorical representations of thoughts and emotions.
Pillars also has a very "strange" (as in, non-generic) game-setting that can be very difficult to relate to. It's hard to draw any parallels to game-worlds we're used to, or the real world for that matter.
After playing the game multiple times, I'm still not quite sure what their atlas would look like, and most of their cultures are incredibly (and unncessarily) obscure. It feels like the authors were trying to create an unnecessary layer of diversity, only to have this competely missing from the actual game.
Now the good:
Apart from the bouts of extremely abstract dialogue, pillars does have some of the best dialogue options I've seen in a roleplaying game in a long time. It is absolutely awesome how all of your character-building decisions matter on  some level.
The game has some excellent tactical combat, and if I may say so, the game mechanics are so much better for a roleplaying game than traditional D&D - the lack of any proper tutorial makes it initially difficult to see how it works and how it is much better than the game mechanics in games of the same genre, like Baldur's Gate.
You can enchant just about anything, you can  collect ingredients for crafting in the world, inventory space is not necessarily a problem, carry weight isn't a factor to be worrying about and you do not need excessive amounts of resting and healing after each battle!
The endurance/health system means you character can fight many battles before you need to rest, but you can't just rest all the time either, because you need camping supplies to rest!
An excellent way to get rid of that constant heal-spamming.
Powers are limited to a number of uses, a cool down, a number of uses per encounter, a number of uses depending on some sort of class specific statistic or a number of uses per rest. This means a character tends to remain useful far beyond one round of combat.
All in all, I feel like there are some issues in the game that the developers could address with some better tutorials, some better material and perhaps a way to summarize long needless dialogue about abstractions of emotions and feelings, but I'll gladly recommend the game.

It's hard to explain how much I've fallen in love with this game. It really is the RTS for everyone. I was never an RTS fan -- there's too much focus on crazy clicking and not enough on strategy. Also, most RTS games are heavily focused on economy, causing both monotony and spending time micromanaging things that aren't really interesting. This is a different kind of RTS game. The economy is there, but it's minimal - reduced to the minimum necessary to get you going - and not weighing you down with repetitive management. Instead, you're free to focus on the actual strategy -- how novel! You don't need X actions per minutes to compete, and you don't need to keep clicking around the map, because everyone's limited to the same view around their leader. It's a beautifully designed game -- minimalistic, strategic, easy to pick up and hard to master, just like a great board game, but in real-time, so it only takes 10-15 minutes per match. Did I mention you can use your controller to play? Did I mention you can play 4-player local multiplayer on one machine? The graphics and music are also excellent and round out a wonderful package.
Get this game. Play it. Get it for your friends. *Especially* if you haven't liked RTS games so far.

I picked this up on the basis of  another review saying the game might be good for someone looking for something different. In hindsight I ought to have paid more attention to the fact that the reviewer had only clocked up about 15 minutes recorded gametime, and also the boast that the game was developed by the same guy who brought us "back to life 2" and "back to life 3" (check out their reviews). But I'm a sucker for something "different" and it was on sale for £0.79 so I thought what the heck.
Well I think there's the germ of a good game idea here but it would need w-a-a-a-y more work to make it enjoyable to play. Where to start? First a general comment about the production values. Put it this way; the initial screen containing the configuration info for the main game contains a facility to alter the default key bindings - but guess what? There are a dozen actions listed none of which correspond to the game that is about to be launched!
Next- the inadequate instructions. "The aim of the game is to save a number of prisoners in the maze of each level and bring them to a save point placed randomly within the maze, and to do this you have to group them  and bring them to a save point placed randomly within the maze".  We are told that key "E" "groups the prisoners near the selected point", and we have mouse control over the "protagonist's" direction, mouse click to move and spacebar to shoot the nastys, "You can only group the prisoners near the 'group point' i.e. those who are inside the large coloured target".
Clear so far? No? OK let me fill in the gaps. The mouse controls not only the player's direction but also the position of the "large coloured target" which is a blue hexagon I initially thought was there simply to help the player aim. The player moves by keeping the LMB depressed while steering with the mouse. When the "prisoners" are found (a group of small cubes like lego bricks) you put the hexagon where you want the prisoners to move to, and press the E key. All the time you have to be alert to the enemies (large green cubes) which require blasting by aiming at them using the mouse, and pressing the space key. So there are 3 keys (E, space, and LMB) each of which produce directional effects, but only one aiming device. That's the first big problem with the game mechanics: if you want to fire at an enemy which isn't directly ahead, you need to stop, turn and stop leading your prisoners. I suppose this could be seen as part of the challenge of the game, but the challenge ought to be enjoyable and wrestling with the control system isn't.
Then there's the fact that you are shooting enemies in narrow corridors when your prisoners are very fragile themselves. Almost inevitably what happens is that while you are trying to lead your prisoners to the save point you will find them between you and an enemy. What do you do then? Unless you are close enough to move past them in time, when you shoot at the enemy, you destroy all your prisoners in the process. There's nothing else you can do to stay alive. And the prisoners move so slowly that the basic gameplay involves stopping and starting your own movement constantly to let the prisoners catch up, remembering to stop your own movement and your prisoners movement when you have to change aim to shoot an enemy.
Finally there is the random element. Yes it's fun to have unique levels generated every turn, but you might find your save point next to 9 prisoners and you can win by just pressing the E key, or you might find it right next to an enemy spawn point making it almost impossible to deliver your prisoners safely.
All in all I suspect the gameplay would get repetitive if I had the patience to stick with the game long enough to judge but I haven't. So I'm sorry to say this but for me it was not a good purchase even at £0.79

This is as close to MMO you can get without being a MMO. Some people find it to their liking, however, foe a single-player game, it is a flaw, rather than a merit.
All of the quests, except for the main one, are generic "kill X enemies of a certain type", and the rewards are given automatic, so you can slay a dozen of wolves in a forest, and suddenly get a sword spawned in your inventory. The main storyline is nothing to speak of as well. I haven't learned any names, locations, or managed to follow the narrative, as everything is very much the same. Nothing memorable.
Crafting is just confusing. You throw things into a pot and something else appears. You will have no idea what resources you will need if you want to craft something, and thus, you'll be following sheer luck.
Interface takes a good chunk of your screen and messes with it all the time. Not to mention, it's confusing, lacking hotkeys - you can only open your inventory in the game, while to get to the map or quests, you have to pause the game (ESC key), and choose the option needed from the list.
Speaking of which, import to PC is awfully inconvenient - it's confusing to play it without a controller because of the key bindings you have no ability to change, and really confusing  mouse options - at some interface places you can use it, at some you cannot.
Combat is very simple and very dull, with little variations to what you can actually do during it, so it gets repetitive pretty quickly. Your enemies basically vary by their HP, so you're just click spamming them to death. Only the beginning of the quest in, and I already avoid combat, because it's just so dull.
I'd speak of low graphic and animation quality, but, considering the year of 2012 it was made in, I cannot blame DD:DA for not being up-to-date. It's an OKish graphics for a five-year-old game. Not good, just OKish.
Most important, THIS IS NO RPG, there's no role element at all in this game. It's just a third-person action, so don't be fooled by the tags.
All and all, I do not recommend it. It's an MMO without other players, and only other players is what makes MMOs so interesting. This specific game is plain dull, and not in an atmospheric "Gothic" or "Morrowind" way, where games have certain feeling and slow pacing, but win via RPG element or mechanics, this one is just
. Fourteen hours in, and I cannot find anything good to talk about for this game. I do try, as telling something good is always on my mind when I write a review for film, game, or a show, but there's virtually nothing innovating or plainly interesting in it. I'm just disappointed I've spent money on this product.

I seriously wanted to like this one; it's a shame that this honestly has too many flaws associated with it. Rudimentary bugs that anyone could find suggests that this game was either QA-tested incompetently, or not at all. The story isn't great either, all you have to do is to rescue crystals and relics from some evil guy, and the ending is a complete cop-out. It's also hampered by a lousy stock font.
Levels aren't really designed that great either; you cannot really seem to maintain a nice flow of running and platforming because some elements are designed in such a way that it kills the flow. There's a ludicrous amount of precision required to solve specific challenges, and the fact that the checkpoint system is also inconsistent makes this a rather more irritating experience as you go along.
I was pretty happy when I finally finished it, because the last few levels were the most annoying of the lot, where all the problems I have were exhibited to the fullest. Plus, the game never ran particularly well on my own computer even at lowest settings, making all these a lot worse. It can usually handle other games at 60 FPS on lowest, but this never comes anywhere close.
That said, I love the soundtrack and hope to get it later on. The oriental Chinese flavour to it as well as the instrumentation gives it some fantasy epic feel to it, saving it from almost complete mediocrity. That and the relatively fast 100% achievements (I took only 2-3 hours to beat it, and that was after one of the aforementioned bugs made me start the game from scratch after about 1 hour in, and 2 hours of card idling time).
I don't regret my purchase a lot since I was lucky to snag a 90% off coupon. If you want to get it though, get it on sale. The short length means that it isn't worth $10.

Some complain about to much trivial combat, there is some certainly, but it isn't bad, comparing it to MMO grinding, it's a walk in the park. Their new combat system with agro and tanking I thought worked well. Really the only bad thing I can say about this game is sloooooow loads.

Overall, PoE is an enjoyable experience. I get a lot of enjoyment out of discovering new things in games, so any time a game introduces new systems that I've never seen before AND they're actually good, I'm probably in for a good time.
I think that PoE didn't have enough fresh stuff going for it though because once I figured out some of the better builds and party setups, the game lost a lot of its appeal for me. I've played and enjoyed all of the Infinity Engine games, so it shouldn't come as a surprise that this is a potential risk for any game that mirrors the old classics as closely as PoE does. It may seem fresher for those who haven't seen it all before.
I've logged a lot of hours into PoE for such a lukewarm recommendation (200 hours at the time of writing), but most of that was actually spent trying to find a class for the main character that I really liked. I restarted the game several times before settling into a Cipher, only to play up through Act 2 and restart again. There's something a little disappointing and unfulfiling about each class I've tried.
But the game is perfectly functional. The writing is very good, but not SO GREAT as to warrant the excessive, self-indulgent volume of text. The companions are a lot like the classes - mostly good, but something a little disappointing and unfulfilling about each one of them. The graphics and art direction are great. Combat has some cool never-before-seen mechanics, but it too is flawed with an extreme oversaturation of melee enemies and lack of interesting "mage duels" beloved by so many in the classic Infinity Engine games.
Overall, I recommend PoE. It's actually better than the classics it's inspired from in some (perhaps many) ways, but it suffers from a lack of distinct personality of its own.

What is Stranded Deep?
Stranded Deep is a game where you are a passenger sitting on a plane, when all of a sudden a storm comes on, and the plane crashes, you then have to get to the life raft and set off and find and island to survive on. You start with a Lighter and a Pocket Knife, you must use these to gather Resources and then make other tools and things that you need to survive. You even have a Survival Watch that tells you the current temprature, time, and how many days you have survived for as well as your Hunger, Thirst and Health. Stranded Deep's are randomly generated each time you play, so you won't need to worry about playing the same world over and over again. While exploring your world, you can find sunken boats and ships containing containers and cases which may sometimes contain resources you can use, you can find old rusted sea forts and find more resources and things to help you, you can craft tools, items and other things, there's sharks, crabs, fish and ive even seen a whale! Really, the possibilities are endless. The game is very well detailed with great sounds, music, and gorgeous graphics. The game is currently in Early Access which means it is still in development and you will get new content and features as the game is updated. I paid $9.89 for Stranded Deep when the Summer Sale was on, and i am defenitly getting my money's worth. Even at $14.99 i wouldn't complain as it certainly is tons of fun to play and explore the world. Really looking foward to seeing this game progress.

This game takes mafia/werewolf to a whole new level. If you enjoy those games but don't enjoy the setup, explaining rules and gathering people then this might be for you.
Some might compare this to Werewolf, EpicMafia or Town of Salem/SC2 Mafia but its really unique in its own sense. It brings the best elements of all those and puts them together with a very active development/balance team. If you've played them and are afraid that this game won't be fresh, let me assure you that it is VERY fresh and you will enjoy it immensely if you've played previous titles with the same theme.
For some examples of great things that this game brings along. This game offers slightly longer day time for more discussions, it offers a leading role in all games (mayor known in other games and King in this one), all roles have abilities which leads to more complexity and limiting math solves until the very end. The only time it should and is feasible to fully rule out who is evil. In addition neutrals have very strong powers to help them stay neutral and similar to Town of Salem, the sound track is amazing. I cannot recommend this game enough.
Now I mentioned it took the best elements of mafia games to bring together, what else does it bring? Well it brings new character screens and animations. Each character has their own night scene depending on their role, there are a couple death scenes so dead (town) court members don't just show up dead in front of their house the next day. It gives better immersion in my opinion. Town of Salem and Epic Mafia was meant to run in a browser but this game runs on a game engine. That means the possibility of more custom day and night scenes, custom execution scenes and a customization options that not only make you look better but have an effect on your animations. Town of Salem only had your death animation, this has the executioner's animation instead which changes based on your weapon. Its amazing.
Don't take my word for it, I highly recommend you try it out. If you don't like it then you could always refund it but its dirt cheap anyway and updates are coming in quick and fast. Its worth the price and I recommend it.

This game is truly a masterpiece among games, but before you judgers go and try comparing it to things like Terraria, I must tell you that NO IT IS NOT JUST TERRARIA IN SPACE. Although they have their similarities, notably the ability to build, 2D platforming, generated worlds, and Fantasy-like 2D combat, they also have their differences. Give me some time to explain this to you:
Generation:
Terraria has a single generated world that is very finite on resources and has a limited space. It is generated based on certain needed structures and essential biomes in one. It generates chest loot based on certain objects in the game that are always the same in every aspect.
STARBOUND has infinite world generation across whole solar systems and galaxies! It procedurally generates infinite worlds AND creates procedurally generated weapons with different stats every time. There are different generated dungeons and structures in each world, giving more variety to your universe!
NPCs:
While Terraria may have a nice and faithful cast of characters that give you exactly what you'd expect from them, it doesn't really give you a feeling of true civilization. You just look like a weird motley crew colony in the middle of Cthulhu Hell.
Starbound, on the other hand, also has a wide capability for generating NPCs. There are merchants, there are guards, there are citizens that give a nice and properly populated atmosphere to the whole game unlike Terraria's super specific NPC system. What's more is that you can even perform quests for NPCs, let tenants move in to the houses you build for them, and even hire some of them as your ship crew.
Other differences include your own ship that you can decorate, upgrade, and fly through space to different planets and even act as a central hub for teleportation around the universe where you mark places to beam down and teleport to. Most importantly, Starbound has an actual story that drives some of the game if you decide to delve into those wonderful things. I promise you there is a good present in store for you if you ever decide to follow the story instead of bore yourself by aimlessly darting to and from each world. Starbound even has a REAL Hub called the Outpost that serves as your main area for important items you can buy from different market stalls,
.  Terraria doesn't have all that wonderful stuff.
Now for the standard tiers of progression through the game, it's a given fact that a good game formula provides the player with progressing tiers to work on building up to the end, and of course the best way to obtain all this progress is through looting and crafting, which both titles provide, but Starbound still does it in a more refined way.
In conclusion, Starbound generally has infinitely more, giving a sense of true depth in the game that the alternative can't offer you. While I will admit, I do like Terraria for its own content that it has to provide, I don't think anything can quite beat the merit that Starbound has as its own indipendent title.

This game has really nice art and an interesting setting, but at least as far as the single player campaign it's brought down by the actual gameplay. It starts off fairly reasonable and teaches you stuff about the meta and whatnot. Essentially Tooth and Tail is a simplified RTS where you control the faction's commander, who acts as the cursor. They respawn if killed, meaning you can scout safely, which I like. Maps are also fairly tiny, so games don't go too long, and there's no tech tree or multiple resources to worry about. Those are all fine, and the game does start reasonably enough, teaching you things you can use in multiplayer.
But by halfway through the second faction's missions it feels like it stops being a strategy game and more about getting lucky or sort of cheating. A good example is a level where you have to defend meat merchants from enemies, who get to spawn units in around the area when you're not looking (which is a pretty terrible way to go about difficulty, but I digress). The most efficient method agreed upon in the forums is to search around with your initial forces, smash one when it pops up, and then put a turret down there, and just repeat until the whole level is being watched by them. Obviously this isn't a tactic you'd ever use while playing against another person, so why have a level where it's the most practical tactic?
I actually brute forced a level just because I didn't want to deal with its gimmick, which is a swarm of aerial units that spawn in to attack your base every couple of minutes. If you're lucky with the generation the initial batch of stealth melee guys you have is enough to bum-rush the enemy base and blow it up right away. Though in my defense, that's the strategy regardless of how long you spend in the level, since they're the best unit to use for it, and there's no reason to use your whole army. Whether you had ten chameleons or thirty the end result would be the same. I could have stayed and done the level as I assume they intended, but I wanted to get it over with. Not really a good sign of your game's quality.
I don't really mind trying to make an RTS more bite-size, and some of the levels are interesting puzzles, or at least I can see how they'd be if better tuned. But overall the single player, at least a decent portion of it, isn't fun for very long and may not reflect well on the multi-player experience. Some changes to the campaign are supposedly coming, and if they're good I'll edit this.

Great game - lovely art style, did a great job of implementing an RTS control scheme that, while relatively simple, is perfect for a gamepad and can still provide a surprising amount of depth. The story and setting is a delightfully dark blend of Animal Farm and the Bolshevik Revolution.
I have one major criticism though, and that's that the procedural map generation can really make or break a mission. It can be very hard to tell where exactly is traversible on the terrain, and sometimes a map is created that has enemy turrets shooting straight into your resource production from the very start.
I just finished playing a Civilised mission I was attempting to get the Heroic objective on, in which I had full control of the map save one corner that had only one entrance filled with water, and all resource production. I sent wave after wave of my max allowed army at it, but could never get enough units to survive the approach to do any damage. I eventually starved out, despite having numerous campfires and the enemy having absolutely no food production.
Moments of extreme frustration like this can be common, and I would love to see the developers patch the map generator  so these situations don't happen (or at least change the lose conditions for some single player missions so you can't starve with several thousand food stockpiled and more coming in via cookfires, while the enemies can spawn units for free with no food production). But despite this, when the game works it WORKS.
TLDR:
8/10, procedural maps are mostly good but can really let it down sometimes.

The RTS genre is a barren wasteland, and Tooth and Tail brings a morsel of something juicy and fresh. It is different from most RTS in that you only control a banner-bearing leader, which serves as your cursor, builder and scout all in one, waving the flag around to order your troops into formation.
The true beauty, however, is in the story and characters.
Tooth and Tail tells the story of an industrial society of 'civilized' animals that refuse to eat vegetables (even the herbivores!), seeing the practice as lowly and barbaric. Only meat will do.
But since every animal is both sentient and part of said society- what do they eat?
do they eat?
Whoever
, of course.
The game has four factions:
*The Longcoats, wealthy capitalists who believe the free market should dictate who gets eaten.
*The Commonfolk, unwashed masses who believe democratic vote should decide who gets eaten.
*The Civilized, religious followers who believe a lottery should decide who gets eaten.
*The KSR, secret police wishing to maintain order and the status quo over who gets eaten.
Each one of their leaders is chock-full of personality, and their in-between-mission banter with their respective armies is a delight to read through. In truth, though the gameplay is enjoyable enough, I found myself just wanting to get to the next scrap of lore and worldbuilding. It is that good - juxtaposition between anthropomorphic animals and an essentially cannibalistic society is quite enjoyable!
If that sounds good, then pick up Tooth and Tail.

the combat is somewhat similar to assasins creed (especially in the beggining), but whereas i did not find the combat of assasins creed enjoyable, i found the combat in this one interesting for the most part. however, there where some boring parts after combat drain is unlocked but before branding is unlocked. you can perform instant kills on enemies if you get multiple hits without taking damage. you can get upgrades to increase the strenght of your finishers or to make it so that you need less hits in a row to use a finisher. you can also drain enemies to get bow ammo (or,later in the game, brand them) instead of using a finisher. the bow was quite interesting. while using the bow, headshots instakill everything except for captians. time is in slow motion while aiming the bow, but you only have a certian amount of slow motion time before you run out. you can get upgrades so that you have more arrows, so that you have more slow motion time, or so that slow motion time is replenished by headshots or stealth kills.

Do you like inaccurate controls? Do you like overpowered enemies? Do badly placed checkpoints appeal to you? Do you like annoying trial & error passages? Do you like dealing with tons of bugs? Congratulations, this might be the perfect game for you.
The single player mode is boring. It has some nice moments, but the story is predictable and only few of the missions are really memorable. The coop mode is nearly abandoned, but if you're lucky and manage to find a teammate you'll most likely end up crying in front of the game because he's unbelievably terrible. The PVP-mode isn't fun at all.
Blacklist was promoted with different playing styles: Ghost, Panther and Assault. Well, it just feels like a downgraded version of Hitman: Absolution or Deus Ex: Human Revolution. You're in a big area and you can either take out one enemy after another or you just draw your gun and shoot everyone. Neither of it has an impact on the game, you only get a different score for highscore-hunting. You can't find any information or interrogate enemies like Sam used to do, you try to reach the next door and it doesn't matter how you do that.
You can also buy lots of weapons and upgrades. However, after at most 30% of you game you should have earned enough money to buy all the equipment you need. You'll end up with millions of dollars, not knowing what to do with them because everything you can buy will be a downgrade.
I played each Splinter Cell game on the highest difficulty multiple times, including Essentials and the Old Gen-version of Double Agent. This isn't going to happen with Blacklist.
Please, Ubisoft, let the Splinter Cell franchise rest in peace. Either develop a decent stealth game like Chaos Theory or a decent third person shooter like Conviction, but don't deliver us some half-hearted piece of trash such as Blacklist.

I never write reviews for games. I'm only writing this review out of love for Strike Vector. Despite that love, I will give it a fair review:
Strike Vector lacks polish in a lot of ways and it excels only in it's multi-player gameplay. It's hard to get into. There's no adequate tutorial, the single player is uninteresting, you simply die a lot when you play multiplayer--mostly because there's only ever one server to play on due to the small community. After about a month and 50+ hours of playing, it seems like a solid small community but it leaves a difficult gap to cross for those with no experience to those with a lot. I don't expect a lot of these issues to be fixed either. So, here's what you do get: In, my opinion, the best aerial combat simulator ever. The numbe of situations you run into are always fun and engaging. You could be chasing someone whose takn your flag at breakneck speeds through logic defying industrial cityscapes at one moment and in a 3 on 3 dogfight in the skies at another. You will crash a lot and probably never stop crashing a lot but, to me, it's almost always hilarious. There's a lot of fun to be had.
Unfortunately, the community is so small. It's really why I'm writing this, so that hopefully some people will find what myself and a few others love so much. As it stands, it's hard to get into because you get simply slaughtered by veterans. There's a newbie server but since there is only ever enough people to fill up one server at a time, everyone just goes there. Too bad a review isn't really publicity but at least I'm trying. Come play! 7.5/10 overall, 10/10 multiplayer.

A fun, fluid Platform game. I tried it at an event, and bought it on the spot I liked it so much.
The game is based around a simple mechanic - shifting between two different colour dimensions, red and blue. You can only interact - for better or worse - with anything in the same dimension as you. Built on top of this is a parkour platformer, with fluid, intuative controls, and a wonderful "Lost World" asthetic.

...castle with the so-called "endless" dungeon underneath, I got annoyed and stopped playing. Now, don't get me wrong. I don't have a problem with dungeon crawler games per se, and I own a few rogue-likes; sometimes you just want to beat up some monsters. But this is supposed to be a story-based game, and a 15-level dungeon filled with a menagerie of monsters with no cohesive fictional basis for being there completely breaks any real immersion. Ogres on level 3! Vampires on level 8! Oozes! Beetles! Undead!
Can you imagine a 15-level dungeon filled with 22 different kinds of monsters underneath King's Landing in the Game of Thrones universe? Under Mount Doom in Middle-earth? It would feel silly. The "endless" dungeon in this game screams "filler content to artificially increase play time", not "great fiction." That gets my thumbs-down at the current price point of $45, as well as the $22.50 I paid. This is a thoroughly average $10 game.
Not sure if I like the price politics of the Publisher, but the game itself is realy good.
This is truly a spiritual successor to the PC Baldur's Gate games: great dialogue, interesting NPCs, good storyline, high fantasy, create your own character. But no romance options.
Side quests in this game have more fleshed out stories and characters then most AAA releases nowadays. I absolutely adore this game.

Baldur's Gate I and II and Planescape Torment are among my favorite games of all time, Icewind Dale was not great but still a lot better than this.
The world feels very lifeless, the first town is full of completely unconnected NPC background stories and nobody other than a few quest givers to talk to.
The party system is badly balanced as choosing a class that can't survive and fight on its own makes fights much harder than they would probably be otherwise (in my case I picked a priest). This is compounded by the fact that there is a limit to how often you can rest with the available supplies.
There is a lot of lore and system information to remember but the explanatory popups work only in some of the places where e.g. the names of gods or skills appear.
Most of the areas I visited so far are just your regular old wilderness spot with evenly spaced enemies and a few plants to collect, making for a very boring gameplay.
If you are thinking of buying this game because you enjoyed the old Infinity Engine games I would strongly recommend against it. It is nothing like them and does not make up for it for having either particularly strong writing or engaging combat.

Pillars of eternity review
I'll start with the negatives, since that's typically why most folks read reviews:
1) Story is slow and more intellectual/philosophical.  Not a bad thing, but does not lead the player into curiosity.  I think it's more the storytelling than the subject matter.  Since it's philosophically-driven, I'll contrast it with Plansecape:Torment vs. Baldur's Gate 2, which was character- and adventure-driven:  If Planescape was a 10 for you, I'd say this is about a 5.  It's still a good story, just nothing to write home about.
2) Music is very good, but uninspired.  BG2 music was thematically-/geographically-perfect in that it actively added to the overall experience.  The music in Pillars of Eternity is not distracting or bad by any means, it is just mediocre.
3) The absolute worst mechanic in the game is the "engagement" mechanic, which is their take on "attacks of opportunity" from DnD.  It really needs tweaking (see the wiki for how it works), but can lead to you taking damage from unrealistic attackers (visually too far away to make the attack).  It started as a good idea, but it needs a nerf.
4) While casting spells (priest or wiz) can still be done pre-battle, they put limits on spells such that you can only pre-buff with a few, and the durations are rather loe.  Either they overdid it a bit in trying to preclude cheesy tactics, OR (and this could very well be the case) the fact you're no higher than level 12 is affecting my perspective.  It's just a little unbalanced for those of us used to pre-buffing before battles.
5) Voice Acting - mixed bag to decent.  Some are very good, but most are just adequate.
6) Characters - only like two that are memorable, and even then they were just "good".  BG2 fans - think Cernd-level of charisma as the majority of these characters, with the two good ones who were more like Mazzy-level of memorable.  Not a single Minsc, Jaheira, or Jan in the bunch.
The good:
Mechanics - both in and out of combat are very good (minus "engagement" above).  I credit the Unity engine for the massive improvements over even the EE versions of BG/BG2.  Interesting take on stealth and time within the observer's line of sight.
Visuals - fantastic for the genre.
Pathfinding - thankfully, Unity has really improved this!
Interface - very good - I play turn-based with autopauses for complex battles, but their implementation of auto-slowing means people who play action-style can do so MUCH more smoothly than we could in the Infinity engine.
Performance - very good - occasionally has longer load screens than necessary, but I am unsure if that is a side effect of Steam Achievements checking or the game itself.
I DO highly recommend this game, regardless of the criticisms above.  As has been the case with so many, it cannot touch BG2, but it is still worth playing.  I would liken it to Icewind Dale - very good game, just not a terribly memorable and exciting story.  If I had to assign a subjective numerical rating, it'd be 7.5 or 8 out of 10.
Edit:  I almost forgot the BEST part of this - stable native Linux support!

I remember playing this when I was much younger, back when it was only an online flash game. Since then, it has developed significantly. As the pinned forum thread says, there are many reasons why this stands out beyond other similar free games.  The main one is the amount of content regularly updated into the game. Since I originally received it from a friend, there have been many weapons added, balance fixes to weapons and missions, fixes relating to overall gameplay and graphics, and changes to achievements to make them more manageable.
As for the gameplay itself, there is a very rewarding sense of progression. Hitting the level cap takes very dedicated playing, so there will always be more to get. Every single weapon has upgrades that you can unlock by using it. Your tank will become stronger through leveling, and you can respec your upgrade paths every once in a while to try different strategies. The gameplay may be somewhat repetitive, but it doesn't get boring. There is a surprisingly large amount of single player missions, ranging in difficulty from shooting practice all the way up to rng-dependent challenges.
The dev does a great job of keeping the game up to date considering it's just one guy. The game might be simple, but it's definitely worth throwing a few bucks at it.
It reminds me of some games I used to play back in the day. Really fun, great throwback, totally interesting. I stayed up too late playing it.

Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen occupies that sweet spot in between fantasy RPG and action game. It caters to fans of the fantasy RPG genre with its setting, lore, characters and interactions, and things to unravel. It really does feel like a tabletop RPG campaign as the story unfolds and the stakes get higher and higher.
On the flipside, its a very solid action game. Tight controls, lots of tactical options to combat, and good environments for fighting are all important elements to this game. If I had to sum it up, its no Bayonetta, but its infinitely better than most 'real time combat' solutions a lot of RPGs had when this game came out (cough skyrim cough).
You can dodge, parry, climb enemies and stab their weak spots, use a varied moveset to deal with lots of different types of enemies, making the game feel much more like an action game than a typical fantasy rpg.
And it really is a blast to play. Moves feel like they have a great weight to them, whether it be the slamming of an axe into a griffin, pulling the string of a greatbow all the way back as you aim it at a cyclops eye, or calling down lightning onto a horde of goblins. The effects associated with dealing and taking damage, as well as the sound design, really make the player feel like they're doing the associated action, rather than just hitting buttons and using abilities.
With the robust character creator, pawn AI learning and sharing system, incredibly customizable class system, there's a lot of depth of customization here. I think every player will find something to do once they get the hang of things.
I do have to dock the game points for not having a lot of different enemy types, the everfall and grinding for gear in BBI or the base game in general, as well as how the whole romance thing works.
Warning for anyone who plays the game: figure out who you want to romance very early, and then look up how to do it on the internet. The game will just decide "this is the character you like the most" at some point in the game and then it can have implications on the rest of the game if it chooses a merchant or quest giver or something.
Other than those things, this game is a great game to just immerse yourself in: the sound, voice acting, well made environments and depth of things to do in this game will be a great way to spend a lot of time.

In this strategy game not-so-subtly inspired by the Russian Revolution, animals fight one another in order to avoid becoming food. There is a twist, however: You aren’t just a mouse, but the
. By waving your flag, you rally your troops, tell them to attack specific targets, or move them across the randomly-generated maps. This is the most major way Tooth and Tail toys with the standards of the RTS genre, but a lot of other tweaks have been made. For example, your production structures activate automatically once you gather enough food, with each acting as a population building and barracks all at once. Instead of matches taking upwards of 20 minutes, the median time is roughly 7, and a starvation mechanic kicks in to make sure things don’t drag on excessively without collusion.
This probably sounds horrible. In practice, though, it’s great. As a veteran of countless strategy games, being able to see what your opponent is focusing their attention on opens up a new and unique level of mind-games, and being unable to effectively manage multiple forces at once allows every unit and tactic a chance to shine. As for the campaign, I cleared it in about 8 hours before a patch reduced how hard some of the most difficult missions were (Howling Veil, The Hungry Face a Stiff Wind, and one of the last missions in the game whose name escapes me being the biggest standouts). It is a story with ups and downs, and while it’s a little paint-by-numbers, the finale is an excellent payout that echoes the reality of civil war. Returning to a hub between missions allows you to gain insight into the game world, a setting which definitely has merit enough to be explored further. When you’re done with the campaign (or choose to skip out on it), split-screen and online multiplayer are available, allowing you to test your mettle in FFA, handicap matches, team games, and traditional 1v1.
With a meta that continues to evolve with several semi-regular tournaments and consistent balance patches, accessible gameplay that can appeal to everybody from those who grew up on Age of Empires to gamers who have never built a base before, and a surprising amount of character, Tooth and Tail really surprised me earlier this year. I certainly got my money’s worth out of it, but if you aren’t sold just yet, it’s probably better to wait for a sale.

If I were to give one reason for why this game is dead, it's because of a lack of a campaign. I don't care much about story, but a campaign introduces you to how the game plays. Sure, a community can be as nice as possible to help you learn the game, BUT IT SHOULDN'T BE THEIR JOB. It's the developers! It's not fair for either the noobs who have no way to get a grasp of the game other than relying on other players nor is it fair to the pros who have to restrain themselves and take time out of their enjoyment of the game to play teacher. Sure, being a guru of the game has a nostalgia factor, but it quickly stops being enjoyable when EVERYONE has to ask you questions because the developers expect you to do their job for them.

In conclusion, the developers did not do enough to give players the opportunity to learn the game before they were mercilessly slaughtered by those who obviously had an abnormally large tolarance for suffering to get good at the game.
