NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Rising Islands is a third-person 3D platform game from a new indie development team.
You play an unnamed heroine with assumed responsibility for saving the world from chaos as a corrupted guardian attempts to use three relics for his own selfish means. By taking the power of dimension swapping and using various acrobatic feats to traverse the broken landscape floating in the sky, your goal is to retrieve the relics and restore their protection to the world. Or at least, that's what I've been able to pick up from a few hours of play, anyway.
Graphics - Rising Islands' graphics vary considerably. The game uses cel shading to achieve a cartoon-like look, but even then, some of the textures are quite bland and the terrain geometry is uninventive and a bit boring, looking rather blocky and dated.
The character graphics are a mixed bag, too. The main character model is very good, but the textures aren't great. The corrupted guardian model and textures, too, are not that impressive, but the other guardians are quite creative, reminding me of Okami, for some reason.
The main character animations are really good, but even then there's a bug where they get stuck sometimes and you end up 'flying' around the level, stuck in the jumping animation instead of the sprinting one. The death animation is not that great, though, and the automatic camera sometimes gets stuck, making the screen bounce around like crazy.
The special effects when changing between the two dimensions and dashing are quite nice. Oh, and the title screen looks very nice, except for the broken model intersections that make it look like the grassy rise on which the character sits is swallowing her. This happens sometimes in game, too; I've had to restart levels because I've been stuck in terrain geometry or fallen through the floor.
Cut scenes are pretty bad, with a whole lot of seemingly slow motion animations and a lack of good sound effects or voices making them seem very unprofessional when compared with the rest of the game.
Graphics options are relatively standard for Unity, with a single detail setting ranging from 'Fastest' to 'Fantastic', resolution and windowing options, and anti-aliasing. I encountered a few minor performance issues on some levels on an old gaming laptop, but any new gaming machine should cope very well.
Sound - Sound effects do the job, but are basically forgettable. There are no voices. Music is great, with a nice oriental theme, but there seems to only be one track through most of the game (and title screen), so it wears thin after a while. The other track (on relic levels) is okay, too, but not quite as impressive.
Gameplay - Rising Islands plays like a typical 3D platform game: run, climb, and jump as you navigate through each stage from start to finish, collecting sometimes-hidden gems along the way. Each stage provides you with a power crystal, which is eventually used to open up a route to the next of the three game worlds, at the end of which you restore one of the protective relics. Each world of five stages includes a timed stage as well, but I found these more frustrating than fun, particularly the second one.
Right at the beginning of the game the primary gameplay 'hook' is introduced, albeit poorly, and you are given the ability to swap between two dimensions: red and blue. This gameplay hook is then used for nearly every platforming challenge in the game.
There's no real in-game explanation for the dimension-swapping ability, however, or for the guardians' choice of the player character, or her ability to run up walls, for that matter. It's unfortunate, too, because providing more information on the character and the game's lore would have added to the experience immensely. Contrast this with something like Prince of Persia (2008) and Rising Islands feels hollow and superficial, with no emotional investment from the player.
Controls are simple and work reasonably well on both keyboard and controller, with full controller support. I played with keyboard to begin, just to test out the controls, but if you have a controller then use that; it's definitely a superior experience. Unfortunately they're a little bit 'loose', and you'll probably find yourself running off some ledges to your death when you're sure you pressed the jump button.
There are a few problems with the mostly good level design, too, with some challenges being very frustrating and based at least partly on the uncontrollable camera angle, and some others being easily circumvented (e.g. the first switch puzzle doesn't actually require you to use the switch at all). Prepare for very high frustration levels and rage quitting -- I've found it frustrating enough that I haven't yet been able to force myself to finish it.
The game includes Steam Achievements that you'll gain by carefully completing the game (with one requiring collection of every hidden crystal), and also includes a time trial mode to increase replayability.
Pros:
+ It's mostly pretty good fun
+ Some graphics are very good, including the main character animations and title screen
+ Full controller support or useable keyboard and mouse controls; both work well
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- Camera, control, and level design frustrations hiding a relatively short game
- Game background and lore is minimal, but what is here has some grammar errors and could use a bit of work
- There's really only one hook in the game, so it gets a bit boring more quickly than it should
- Some graphics look rather dated, and there are lots of geometry intersection issues

There are some negatives as well, a game is ever perfect, however the following points really bothered me;
- The game contains lots of text, that in itself is not a problem, but there are many typos or inconsistent use of punctuation. I'm not a native english speaker, and i could find multiple spelling mistakes. A few more read-throughs are still needed to fix this.
- Some parts of certain conversations are also voice acted, but not everything. Tesla Effect or how to become addict to a game (and a character).
I wasn’t familiar with FMV until I started playing Tesla Effect. In fact, the idea of a mix between a movie and a game was seducing enough for me to try it.
I got hooked straight away!
- The characters
Most of them are just brilliant, you can feel that the actors had a lot of fun impersonating them and as a result, they don’t look out of place in the game at all.
Oh, and there is Tex Murphy of course. He his totally worth it. In fact, you should get the game just because it’s Tex…
- The atmosphere
Take an old-fashioned P.I. from the 1950s and send him in a futuristic and almost post-apocalyptical San Francisco. It gives a proper atmosphere to the game, one that is the trademark of the Tex Murphy universe. I really enjoyed the way technology meets old fashioned comic books!
- The story
When Tex suffers from a major memory loss, he is forced to investigate to discover what happened to him. The fact that I didn’t know Tex before Tesla Effect actually helped me connect to the character and the story. Tesla Effect is story rich and despite finishing the game once, I know that I’ll start it all over again to enjoy all the narrative possibilities.
Investigation, humor, action and sci-fi are packed in Tesla Effect. I would recommend it to everyone who looks to play a game that it is also the movie you wished to make!

A poorly designed nostalgia trip for the hardcore fans.
Sets are not exactly what i would call "interesting". Pretty bland. Atmosphere is absent.
Pointlessly scattered objects that are stuck in walls. Parts of sets are oversaturated with details you can interact with, but walking a few feet further will get you to an absolutely empty part of the set with nothing in it. This makes you feel like somebody forgot to finish that part of the set, a feeling that is confirmed by objects sticking out of walls and other objects jittering insanely.
Dialogue mechanics are impossible to follow. Cutting every couple of seconds to let you choose the next prompt makes conversations incomprehensible. The promts that you can choose from don't make any sense. If you thought the dialogue prompts in Mass Effect were bad, Tesla Effect makes Mass Effect dialogue prompt selection look like a masterpiece. At least there you were given a hint as to where the conversation might lead and what the character might say when selecting prompts.
Outdated clunky pop-culture references made simply for the "oh, I remember that" effect, which seem quite out of place.
(Looking at a street "Where we're going, we... yeah, we'll need roads" - all the while it's been established that all cars are flying in this universe. So what was the point of that reference?)
Poorly designed sets that are lacking atmosphere; unbalanced interaction areas; incomprehensible, impossible to follow dialogue mechanic; pointless P.I. point system; a storyline that has not been able to draw me in after 40  minutes of gameplay.
Conclusion: Unless you're a hardcore fan of the series, I don't think you will find much enjoyment out of this title. However, as far as the hardcore fans go, judging by the reviews, I am glad to see the studio made them justice. Unfortuntely, I don't feel like they made the genre any justice.

I originally got a physical copy of the game for Windows 95 years ago.  Back then, it struggled in anything other than 256 color mode, but... it still rocked.  I didn't have a Genesis, Sega CD, or ANY console... but I had this.  It was amazing and played through it until my fingers bled.  I still have that copy but it hasn't worked with a computer in years.
So when they reintroduced this semi-remastered version, I knew I had to pick it up.  And lo and behold... it was pretty much exactly what I remembered.  Sure, some small differences in menu layout, but you get both the American and Japanese soundtracks, as well as a couple bonuses that everyone knows they want, even if they won't admit it (go player 2!)
Now, let's give this an honest review, taking off my rose-colored nostalgia glasses.
It's Sonic 1 graphics with Sonic 2 controls.  That's actually pretty cool.  Also, two different spin-dash moves: traditional, and a "figure-8" which gives you faster speed but leaves you vulnerable.  I'll take it.
Level design is pretty good.  I am passive on this because you have a mix of inspired design, like in Palmtree Panic or Stardust Speedway, but then you get to things like Wacky Workbench which will make you tear your hair out oh god I have hated this level for 20 years please make it stop already why won't you just let me be happ... *cough*
Okay, I'm fine now.
The time travel plot seems cliche now, but this is the game where most of those cliches originated from, so it gets a pass.  It's cool to seek out the differences in the Past, Present, and Future.  Also, the "good future" Eggman/Robotnik battles are pretty cool looking.  Also, first appearance of Amy Rose, so all you furries out there should pay this game some proper respect. First appearence of Metal Sonic, too.
Everyone complains about the special stages, and yes, they're difficult.  Not impossible though, and once you get the hang of them, it's an extremely rewarding feeling.
I will admit disappointment in the final boss battle.  For such a well put-together game, it's a bit of a disappointment.  I know that's kind of par-for-the-course with 2D Sonic final battles, but... I wanted more.
How does it run?  Perfect on every computer I've tried: from a high-powered gaming rig to a potato netbook, it all flies.  Lovely.
This is by far one of the best 2D Sonic platformers, if not THE best.  If you like the traditional Sonic games, you'd be doing yourself a disservice to NOT have this in your library.

Having played most of the mainline Dynasty Warriors games, this entree in the series is by far the best. There are over 70 characters including a character creation with a huge variety in maps and story missions. The "Complete Edition" includes the base game combined with the Extreme Legends Expansion that provides a substantial amount of gameplay to be had. Although this is the so called "complete" edition it in fact DOES NOT include all the DLC, go figure. The extra DLC includes such items like extra skins, missions, maps, music, and weapons at a disgusting price point. Not recommended unless you really love certain characters and the game as a whole.
Story: The story is yet another retelling of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms but in a modern anime style. It's very entertaining as it has the right amount of seriousness and cheezy anime flare. You can go through the storys of the Wu, Wei, Shu, Jin, Other, and Lu Bus very own story path separate from "other". Within these Story paths include the so called history accurate branch and a fun what if path depending if certain conditions in the missions are met. The stories of course intertwine and give a telling perspective of each dynasty and their struggles as they conquer as much of china as the can. There are many moments of victory, humor, and tragedy. It can be very depressing as times when you have to witness some of your favorite character die off but also satisfying when they overcome great struggles.
Audio: The game includes DUAL audio of both English and Japanese. Ironically there is still no Chinese language option but I can only assume finding Chinese voice actors for over 70 characters is probably pretty difficult. The voice acting ranges from pretty good to god awful in both English and Japanese, however for some of the bad voice acting you can probably get some nice laughs from it as it can be "good" in a campy sort of way. For anime fans there are many great notable voice actors you will recognize from the Japanese side. For the music it is a unique mix of hard rocking tunes with some more classical chinese melodies. Great soundtrack with the songs fitting the missions and scenes very effectively; conveying the mood accurately. The option for more music through DLC is bitter sweet as there are some great tracks from previous games but bitter because you have to buy it.
Gameplay: The gameplay is the traditional hack and slash action that the series is known for but with some new additions to it in order to keep it fresh and different from the rest. My favorite addition is the ability to actually equip each character with two different weapons as well being able to switch weapons on the fly which can make for some fun combos. Now the main complaint of the series is the same old song and dance of how the ai just stands there and don't attack as frequently as you would want. This still holds true through each difficulty and varies depending on difficulty, however it is important to understand how the game actually plays. Usually in these warriors games you arnt going around just killing everything in sight. As therapeutic as that is, the main flow of the game includes going around the map completing sub missions and killing the officers. This in my opinion is the meat of the game, fighting the different officers as they can provide a good challenge. There are smaller peons around that are really just there for the player to kill and gather upgrades as well as be a huge nuisance when fighting officers as they will attack you in order to break your combo and disrupt any action your doing. Just something to keep in mind as most people that go into these games expect the smaller units to be a threat when they truly arnt suppose to be. (Unless they are archer units, ♥♥♥♥ those guys.)
As a side note, some players have been experiencing poor performance in the game. I for one havent had any issues really. And another important note is the game has mostly the PS3 textures and assets with the character models having the PS4 models. Pretty lame but since its on the pc you can play the game much more stable at a solid 60fps which the ps3 and ps4 versions do not which imo offsets the ps3 textures setback.
All in all great game for those that want a more casual and laid back experience.

One of the best single player RPGs I've played, and one of the strangest. It took me several tries to get into this game, but eventually it clicked and now I'm hooked.

I have never written a review before, but it had to be done for this one.  People need to be warned before they accidently play it.  This might be the worst piece of white hot garbage Ive ever suffered through.  You ever play a game and see a feature that makes you think "Why the hell did they do it like this?"  Thats 85% of this game.  Theres the crap you already know about, no fast travel, pawns never shut up (even when youve told it to), every third enemy being an unbreakable damage sponge.  Its all true and its much worse than youve heard.  Even the features everybody brags about arent very interesting.
I made my pawn a mage cause I wanted some heal support for the long road.  It took every pack of enemies about 10 seconds to murder her, if she was VERY lucky she could get a spell off but most of the time she would stand there and try to channel a spell over and over till she got swarmed.  And theres not much you can do to help her, you have to hunt down the archers that are constantly shooting you with an ability that knocks you to the ground, there will be at least 4 archers in every bandit pack, have fun on the ground.  Even during boss fights when you have the boss' undivided attention most of the time she would just stand and watch me fight, not even try to cast a spell.  Pawns are less than useless.
As far as the large mosters that everybody seems so happy about being able to climb up and kill, that strategy only works about every 1 in 5 times.  Usually when you grab the monster it starts to shake like a wet dog until your stamina is depleted and you fall or jump off, now youre standing at the giant monster's feet with no stamina.  If it does manage to stop shaking long enough to get some damage in, chances are you wont be in the same place.  I jumped onto a dragons chest to beat on his heart, by the time he stopped shaking I was tucked into his armpit.  Poor execution on a good idea.
Theres an achievement to get to lvl 200 so I already expected a grindfest, problem is theres none of the benefits of a normal grind.  There seems to be alot of gear in the game but every piece of gear you pick up will be worse than the piece you bought from the vendor in town.  I think I upgraded gear 3 times when they got new stuff.
Most of the quests are boring and lifeless BS like 'Bring me 66 skulls'.  That is an actual quest.  Or escorting a guy to a spot halfway across the world.  Then theres the quests that it turns out you cant complete because you did another completely unrelated quest first, I got a bunch of these.  Tabbing out to consult the wiki became a way of life.
I could honestly go on all day but this has gotten pretty long.  I HATED this game pretty much from start to finish. I gutted it out till the end because Im stubborn but Im not even going to attempt the Bitterback crap.  Seriously people, if youre looking at reviews before you decide to buy this or not, save yourself the money and headache.

This game is wonderful. I’m old enough now to know that tastes change, experiences change us,sometimes we lose ourselves and sometimes we regain more than we expected, and that we aren’t the same person we were long before our last breath. But if I were ever to say a game was my favorite, Dragon’s Dogma would be it.
This game is an RPG and a sandbox world. You create your character--the hero of the journey--but you also create  a second character, who is your Pawn, someone to help and guide you through the story that lays ahead. You and your Pawn can be joined by two other Pawns, who are creations of actual people. This is a fantastic mechanic, as you can “rent” out your Pawn to other people, who will not only come back with a reward from an appreciative player, but also with knowledge of foes and quests that the other player exposed to them. Your Pawn, and other pawns, are constantly talking to you (unless you ask them not to) and guiding you through this world. It’s amazing, it’s funny, it’s annoying.
The world itself is fantastic. The story is engaging. My first few playthroughs I couldn’t get into the game. It felt alien and weird. The game doesn’t hand things to you, so I found myself wandering around irritated that I didn’t know what I was supposed to be doing or what was going on. I’m an Arisen? What the hell is that? There’s a dragon waiting to kill me, why don’t I go straight to it and fight it, why am I stuck in this place? Then, as I was walking the streets to somewhere, I heard an NPC talk. NPC’s talk all the time, making comments to you or to another NPC. And while it wasn’t obvious they were talking about you or the game you were playing, the situation you found yourself in, they WERE. And it clicked. The game was about how you face your life, no matter what is thrown at you. The NPC’s came alive, I wanted to talk to them to see how they were handling this terrifying ordeal. Some were afraid, some wanted to check out, some wanted to fight, and some just didn’t see a change in their lives since they aren’t the ones who fight dragons. I found quests which reflected these interactions, and I discovered all the quests reflect them, and even the last battle itself. When faced with a horrible, impossible choice--who am I? What kind of person am I? What will I do? Will I take the easy path and lose that which are close to me? Or will I take a risk and not only win myself my life back--but also change the lives of others around me for the better? The game is very philosophical and I love it.
The combat itself is good. You have classes you can level up (and change whenever you want), and each class has special skills. You can use those skills, you can also grab and hold enemies so your pawns can beat up on them. You can also carry an enemy and throw them off a cliff if you want. There are giant monsters you have to face, and you can use the grab mechanic to CLIMB UP THEM. I always enjoy climbing a cyclop’s back and wailing on their head.
Also, there is a love mechanic, the game doesn’t tell you, so you’ll want to do some research before your girlfriend is a 12 year old girl or a big, sweaty, hairy blacksmith, because you can’t change that, it happens when it happens, you’re stuck with that. So….yeah.

What a game! I can't remember when the last time was i put so many hours into a single game.
It's just plain great. When playing it, i had the feeling that this game had everything i missed from the 'Enhanced Editions' of those re-released Infinity-engine games. Don't get me wrong, those are excellent games on their own, and still worth playing even after finishing PoE. But PoE has a fresh look, it's more shiny, clearer, beautiful and adds so much more. I never understood why the 'EE' editions never cleaned up their graphics, or rerendered cutscenes, they just look horrible today, their graphics washed out and grainy. You can hardly call them enhanced, but rather an update or a patch.
Enough of the games PoE is always compared with. If you are an RPG lover you simply must get and play this game. In all those hours i never got bored, there is so much to do, there are so many different things to do. Playing the game, the controls and mechanisms feel very familiar, but at the same time things are different enough so that it all feels fresh and exciting.
Saving is important as death can happen at any time, and you never know when you run into a bug (see bellow). I have found no bugs in the story however, when i was hit by a bug i could simply reload and try again and almost always the bug would not reproduce itself.
There are some negatives as well, a game is ever perfect, however the following points really bothered me;
- The game contains lots of text, that in itself is not a problem, but there are many typos or inconsistent use of punctuation. I'm not a native english speaker, and i could find multiple spelling mistakes. A few more read-throughs are still needed to fix this.
- Some parts of certain conversations are also voice acted, but not everything. And so it is sometimes very strange that you get into a converstation with a character which will speak some lines, not the speak the next lines, but then suddenly continue speaking again. If you like to immerse yourself in a game, something like this doesn't really help.
The voice acting itself isn't always very good. In fact there are perhaps only 2-3 really well done voices in the game. The rest are OK'ish, but combined with above issue i was really cringing at times.
- Bugs are to be found as well, sometimes a slain enemy would spin out of control of the screen. You can get stuck in battle mode and some items didn't have a name and would be listed such as 'item #5412', very helpful!
- Buttons in menus would disappear at random, but they become muscle memory soon enough and clicking on where the button supposed to be, still performed the action.

I've been playing the old isomorphic D&D RPG's like Baldur's Gate (EE) again recently, and compared to Pillars, they still are way superior.
It comes down to world building, basically. In the old D&D RPG's, you'd have hundreds upon hundres of NPC's you could talk to and would have funny conversations or possible side quests leading into other side quests; and so on and so forth. That made the world seem real and created an immersive experience.
In Pillars however, the number of NPC's who will actually interact with the player are so limited, you're reminded all the time you're playing a game. Same with maps. They're so repetitive and foes are so predictably scattered, it's signaling all the time: 'You're playing a computer game'.
Not immersive; boring. If you're looking for this type of game, go play Baldur's Gate I & II or Icewind Dale. They're vastly superior.

I really liked State of Decay. Unforunately, like a bad relationship, things seem very rosy for the first couple of hours until you really get to know the person and you realize there isn't much too them. State of Decay is pretty much that. You start off scrounging for supplies, not really knowing if it's safe to go between buildings, wondering what calamity is going to hit you next all while hordes of undead are roaming around making everything miserable. The gameplay system is very shiny as it tempts you with character flaws/traits, boons for managing supplies and building your own zombie-proof fort! How cool is that?!
Really cool, for like 20 minutes. Then you realize that you don't really need to try at gathering that many supplies, or when you do, it's just a unchallenging grind. You end up glossing over most of the stuff you find because it really doesn't matter if you bring it back to the base or not. All the cool boons you get for having friends i rarely used (except for the
). Having your map point out where everything is was actually kind of a letdown in a way, as you knew exactly what you needed to do everytime and that is a huge benefit when you can just avoid parts of town/country you don't want to go into.
Ultimately, State of Decay was not that thrilling of a survival game. It was more of a "survive then thrive" kinda scenario, where it was hard going in the beginning but once you get past all of that, there is really no point to playing the game anymore other than to have several different hunting rifles in your cabinet you're never going to use. If you like the simulation aspect and you like action/RPGs, then i would still urge you to pick this up (on sale as of Feb.25/2014!) but don't think you're going to play this game forever. If you think you want to play this game forever, grab the DLC to give it that little bit of replayability (DLC, also, huge letdown: let's give you the exact world you were just in only you start one the other side!).

This is going to be a somewhat long review/explanation, so make sure you have the time to read this thourougly.
This game may not be for everyone, but it sure is for people who like a game that looks complex at first and is complex at its very best allthewhile being simple.
I don't have much experience in explaining what's good or bad about a game, so I'll just give you the run-down on how runs go:
(When you play a game it's called a run btw)
How the game will go normally(for
runs):
You start out on the first floor, get a few items, beat the boss, go to the next floor, and then repeating this untill the last boss.
How it REALLY goes(for first(ISH, and I really mean it!) timers):
You start out on the first floor and:
a) Die because of a lack of potential skill or knowledge (which can be achieved with enough playtime)
b) Get extremely lucky and get good items
c) Get sub-average to bad/useless(maybe) items
d) Find something secret
e) Die to the boss (I'M LOOKING AT YOU, RAG MAN!)
f) Go into the shop and find out there's not much you can buy
g) Find a tourture room (room with a spike in the middle) and skip it, or die from the spike(from curiosity)
h) Follow 'normal' run protocol
Next floor(s):
a) Follow first floor protocol
b) Find some arcades
c) Find yourself in a Devil/Angel room, with either trolls, items that you don't know what they are, yet they are op, bad(sometimes), or just do something which you don't know, chests, or some pickups
d) Follow 'normal' run protocol
e) You might repeat this to the end(I say might because I most likely missed something).
As for people with experience, I will do a brief summary.
When an experienced person does a run, they do either the right run( in short detail, starting floor is 'good'), or stick with the run their given(when they are streaking(completing runs in a successful fashion). After this, they decide how their run will go either before/after/as they get items or pickups of a few sorts. Then they use their knowledge of the game to do certain things, and here's two examples of those things:
1) Complete the run in a relaxed or speedily fashion
2) 'Break'(use knowledge of the game to push it to its limits) the game
Both of these are fun to do, and even watch. To gain lots of knowledge and practice on this game, I recommend watching a livestream or youtube videos.
Some suggestions for these are ones that I've watched like:
CobaltStreak
(Streams 5pm to 11pm central time every day, doesn't always play this game, but nearly every day he does if he feels like it. He also has a youtube channel)
Northernlion (Is on twitch.tv, also has a youtube)
BrainTM (Is on twitch.tv, he speedruns this game)
At the end of all this, I wish you good luck and may RNGeesus favor you.

If you want a game that combines the fluid and paced combat of Batman Arkham City and the stealth and climbing of Assassin's Creed, then this is your game. Once you're used to the controls, you become a one man army. Uruks (the orcs you kill in this game) will fall by your blade so easily that you can probably do it with your eyes closed.
The gameplay is split into two different systems. The general combat (with the counters from B:AC) consists of you getting a high enough combo to execute different "actions" of your choosing. You want to execute an orc in brutal fashion? Press the button. Wanna brand him to make him fight your buddies? Go ahead. The other is to go into a sort of bullet-time bow & arrow where you can kill as many Uruks as you can until you either run out of arrows or the slowdown runs out.
A note: The game's Nemesis system is amazing. It works like this: the game has Uruk captains that you have to defeat. However, if they defeat you, they will gain power and will remember you the next time you fight them (they will comment about how much you suck and such). The more you die, the more powerful he gets. Essentially making an enemy you want to defeat/avoid. The captains can also run away if they feel pressured or scared and will reference it the next time you meet them. Each captain also have distinguished titles and personalities that make them more memorable then your typical boss enemy. They also have certain strengths and weaknesses you can exploit whenever you fight. It is simply amazing and I hope more games do similar stuff.
Story is decent. But it's not a Telltale game. It is there and is mainly in the interest for Lord of the Ring fans. The characters you meet aren't going to be by your side for long and will just disappear once you do a mission or two. But they serve their purpose within the game. Although the dwarf is so humourous that a DLC is centered around him.
Graphics are good. It's pretty.
The game runs pretty well. I run an i5-6500 with a GTX 1060 and it runs at a stable 60 fps with no dips anywhere for the three playthoughs I had for the game.
Overall, the game is a blast to play. Hell, I turn the game on here and there to sooth my stress with a complete genocide of orcs because the gameplay is that satisfying. It does a great job of making you feel like a badass right from the start and makes you a god towards the end.
Somewhat important note: The game becomes easy once you get the controls down. So I recommend, if you want a challenging experience, to keep everything to a bare minimum. Skills, weapon upgrades, etc. If you don't, you will cut through Uruk captains like they're playdough.
If you like Lord of The Rings or Assassins creed, Buy this. Its good.

Got this game in a bundle and I'm liking it. A rendition of the classic shoot-em-up game in space as you fly a plane filled with unlimited ammo, but a limited quantity of secondary weapon (special).
I've played a few in the 90s and while the graphics for savior during gameplay is above average, all the other graphics are below average. The pilots are just creepy-looking, especially when you want to read the text for the story, but you have to also stare at the images to do so. During gameplay, I stuck with easy-mode at first and the game can be completed without much skill (just need to follow the game prediction of where the enemies will come and you'll be fine). Increasing the level definitely is where the fun comes in as you get more things to shoot at to maintain your burst gauge. Also, the game is still enjoyable where you can still keep track of everything you need to dodge, while keeping track of your plane during gameplay (which can be hard as some games do a poor job at this). The perks aren't at first very clear on how they can help you, but I find the first two perks being the most valuable as they increase damage, rate speed, and spread. A large variety of weaponry for you to choose from and some levels definitely benefit from you choosing the right combination of weapon. For example, one level was a boss battle where the boss is predominantly in front of you. So I chose the weapons that state high damage + focused on shooting in front of me only. Cleared the level much quicker than choosing the weapons that spread out more + do less damage.
Overall, the game is decent and has value in its gameplay for one to enjoy. Will have to try the co-op one day to see how that fares. However, enjoyable game to come back to every once in a while. 7/10.

Finally, an RTS I can play from the couch with controls that are heavily worked away from genre conventions. I don't feel like KB+M was handicapped or ignored to make room for gamepad players the way Halo Wars and similar console RTS games did. Split screen multiplayer is a huge plus if you have a big TV and spouse to play with. The campaign is solid, I don't normally play the campaign in RTS games but the writing alone is entertaining enough for me to play through this one. However, multiplayer is where the real
of the game is. Matches last about 10-15 minutes even at the lowest skill levels, unlike StarCraft where beginners end up stuck in 30-45 minute matches. Plenty of viable and interesting strategies despite the game's apparent simplicity. This game is pure elegance -- with some cannibalism thrown in for good measure.

Was nervous about the ammount of depth this game offered with unit variety and was pleasently supprised. Short match durations make losses easier to stomach, and reduced micro requirements enhance accessability. Being able to take only 6 units into each fight forces you to adapt units to new situations.
Split screen is great, and makes teaching the game to friends easier, before pummeling them into the ground until they master the fundamentals.

Sonic arrives at Never Lake where the fabled Little Planet (also known as Miracle Planet) is said to appear on the last month of every year. Sonic arrives to find the planet tethered to a mountain by a chain and completely mechanized.  Sonic realizes this is the work of his nemesis, Doctor Robotnik, who had set foot in this island to transform it into a giant fortress. Upon discovering Sonic's presence on the island, he dispatches Metal Sonic to kidnap a young female hedgehog called Amy Rose, who followed Sonic to the mystical planet. Sonic must collect the Time Stones: seven jewels capable of altering the passage of time itself.
You Controll Sonic from left to right, collect rings, defead enemies and try to reach the goal post. While Sonic is running through a level, he can touch several "past" and "future" post, which allow him to travel through time, if he manages to get enough speed. Each level has a Present zone, Past, Bad future and a Good future. To achieve a Good future, Sonic has to either travel back to the past and destroy a robot-generating machine. Should Sonic be able to destory the Machine in both acts, he will create a good future in act 3. The other way to create a good Future is by collecting all the Timestones. By collecting 50 Rings, Sonic can enter a giant ring at the Goalpost, from there Sonic will enter a Special Stage. Sonic has to destory a number of UFO's while avoiding the water and other objects. Should Sonic be able to destroy all UFO's before the time is running out he will be awarded with a Timestone. Should he collect all the Timestones, he will create a Good future whenever he travels to the Future and will recive the "Good Ending" of the Game. Should the player decide to destroy EVERY Generator in the past and not collect all the Timestones, he will be rewarded as well with the "Good Ending".

You can also select the Japanese Soundtrack or the American Soundtrack, so you can have the best of both worlds.

Great, fun and well designed. Blacklist doesn't look like much on the outside but once played, the experience you get is a near flawless one that gives you delightful fun and fulfilment.
Taking the new gameplay mechanics from Conviction while also bringing back the stealth aspects most notable in past games, Blacklist manages a good balance between this combination that ultimately proves successful.
This time, you're given the freedom on how to truly play, with a ranking system that judges your performance based on three playstyles: Assault (shoot and kill, screw alarms), Panther (get detected but still go silent) and Ghost (total stealth, nobody knows you were ever there). Ghost, of course, gives the most points, thus being a good incentive to follow but albeit a challenging one. The game however, often assumes the path of Panther as its default, which can be quite an annoyance; seeing some scenarios play out like soldiers charging out of doors in search for you even when your existence shouldn't even be known if Pure Ghost is played. Makes no sense, but nevertheless, the player is forced to go along with it either way.
Customization is vast: you're allowed to choose each piece of apparel on you, ranging from boots to even the color of the lights. There's also large assortment of gadgets to choose from, ranging from the silent to the loud. Lethal weapons like sniper rifles may be more advantaged over others but this advantage is held back by the points system that awards no-kills over kills.  It may sound discouraging, but you will eventually find the game flooding you with so much money anyway.
Levels are smartly laid out and designed with a focus on non-linearity to give for multiple entryways, shortcuts and routes that different players will take. Settings and environments are never always the same, allowing for more variety and change in scenery. The first half of the game takes place largely in the Middle East though, a fine differiation from Convictions cramped building maps.
The story follows Sam Fisher finally taking up the reign as a official covert operative once more, now in a newly formed Fourth Echelon tasked to take down the bad guys who are some bunch of generic terorrists... obviously.
The premise is typical of the esponiage genre but fitting in bringing back nostalgia and comfort in the good ol' days of Chaos Theory.
Sam Fisher is no longer voiced by the familiar Michael Ironside, which makes him sounding a little softer in tone. But seriously, who cares about how these characters talk?
The plot is a rather straightfoward one, from start to end, but proves sastisfying enough but with an ending that might leave scratching your head.
One new feature in the game is the complete lack of a proper main menu. Instead, your flying ship, the Paladin,
the main menu. It's the place where you get to run about silly and free, and customize your s**** , select missions and stuff. An innovative move, clearly taken in inpsiration from Bioware's Mass Effect series.
Overall, Blacklist still truimphs as a true SC game, once again bringing back the glory and origins of the franchise.  It can definitely be regarded to me as one of the, if not,
most refined stealth game of the 7th generation.

This game doesn't have modern first person shooter graphics but it doesn't intend to.   It's an old fashioned dungeon crawler like Ultima or Bard's Tale.  I thoroughly enjoyed those games and I'm liking Pillars of Eternity just as much.  There are lots of barrels, chests and other objects to loot. There is one annoying little bug where the ACCEPT and CANCEL icons are sometimes missing when you manually save a game but all you have to do is remember to click on the lower left of the box for ACCEPT and the lower right for CANCEL.   The saves work fine like that.
I've got 24 hours in this game and since there are many areas of the map I haven't visited yet, it looks like I've got a lot more playing time to go.   I don't regret buying this game at all.  I like intricate character building and equipment upgrades.
If you are looking for an action game, you will be disappointed.  If you want a fantasy role-playing strategy game, this one is excellent.

Pillars of Eternity is now one of my favorite crpgs of all time and it exceeded all my expectations. In particular, I found the character development and combat to be enjoyably deep. Most of the recruitable npcs were well written and interesting and I appreciated the polish of the game world.
I particularly appreciated how flexible and customizable the gameplay experience was. Many HUD and combat elements have multiple settings. Also, there are multiple difficulty levels and modes, which I found hugely entertaining. This flexibility allows Pillars to be both highly accessible for those less familiar with the genre, and punishingly difficult for those seeking a challenge. I also found the flexibility in the central plot and many side quests expansive enough to warrant multiple play throughs, especially when coupled with different party compositions and origins for the main protagonist.
Impressive game.! Although a bit tough in the initial stages to transition from rpgs like Diablo/Titan quest to Pillars of eternity the game is gripping and very addictive.

If you have the time to invest in it, Strike Vector promises to be a lot of fun. Bear in mind, though, that it is not a laid-back, "pick up and go" sort of game. It's challenging, it takes practice, and it will test your patience...and that's just in solo training mode. Honestly, I didn't even get to multiplayer before the weekend trial ran out. But despite the difficulty - or perhaps because of it - the game
to play, sort of like a 90's arcade game that was ported to your PC.
Now that being said, here's a couple tips for would-be purchasers:
- FULLSCREEN MODE IS NOT A GOOD IDEA. As of this review, enabling fullscreen causes a bug that will lock you out of the game on relaunch. I had to go into three separate game files and make manual adjustments to get the game to run correctly again. Ragequit knows this is a problem, and the fix for it is a pinned post on the Steam forums; but having to play in windowed mode kind of kills the sense of immersion.
- Mouse: if it feels like you're dragging your mouse through quicksand with every turn, it's probably because you are. I'd recommend using the first two or three training sessions to fiddle with the mouse sensitivity (found in gameplay options) until you strike the right balance between smooth steering and accurate aiming.
- Keyboard: default controls are okay, but I found flipping quick-turn to 'Q' and 'E' and special action to 'Z' to be more intuitive.
As much as I enjoyed the weekend demo, I've decided to hold off on actually buying the game until the kinks are worked out. If you're willing to look past those, I recommend Strike Vector 100%.

I pre-ordered the original FMV Tex game Under A Killing Moon despite my favorite magazine at the time (PC Gamer) giving it a truely terrible score of 30%. That was how much I loved the idea and look of this game and my gamble paid off. I fell in love with the series and eagerly both all subsequent games. When the Kickstart for this game appeared I jumped on the chance, funding the game and I'm very glad the result was seriously worth it.
This is a return to form - it's very similar to Pandora Directive (which already ironed out some of the annoyances of the first game) but even more streamlined. The FMV is clearly far superior but the dialogue is still well written, the acting ranges from average to great, the puzzles are mostly very logical and fun to solve with no obscure solutions and exploring is still the best part of the game. (you got to love feeling like an actual detective).
There are some remarks, however. They don't stop this from being a great game but see it more as ideas on how to improve further Tex games:
- I miss the ability to duck - in the earlier games this was great for hiding
- The graphics were designed to run well on even low end systems (just like the original UAKM which ran on a 386!!) but even then, they should have put a little more effort in how it looks up close. Some textures are worse than in Pandora Directive.
- the logic puzzles are quite boring - they're mostly the sort of stuff you'll find in other puzzle games and not that interesting to solve. I don't mind a few being in the game but there were at least 10 of these if not more and that's a bit too much for my taste
- some parts of the game felt like they received less attention - especially the  Tesla Society HQ. Despite how huge the place was, there was almost nothing to look at, nothing to interact with except for things directly related to puzzles - it's a missed chance. I felt like a kid in a candy shop until I realized all the candy is fake plastic and can't be eaten.
- The traditional system of talking to the neighbours on the street didn't work as well as before because the game wasn't laid out in a similar way. Asking the topics only works if you slowly uncover new evidence but the game worked more on plot progression outside of the street meaning there was no need to return.

Small price tag for a game that will yield a far-above average amount of hours even without DLC.
An all-original free-form survival game that focuses on the growth of a group rather than the goals of a single person.
Where do I start - base building, a large open world map, character traits, firearms, epic combat, etc.
State of decay is an open-world, 3rd person, survival, group-management game that will definitely leave a mark on your ability to enjoy any other game that resembles it.
The player progresses through the game by managing their group and their base. Keeping your group up to date with supplies, keeping your survivors from going insane, and keeping things mellow, are some of the tasks the player upholds when they first start their game.
The player does not play as a single character, or a 'god' that overwatches the community, but rather the community itself. The base concept is that you gain enough trust with a person to befriend them, at which point you can switch back and forth between the characters you have befriended to take advantage of everybody in your friendgroup. There is no single main character, although the player can choose to concentrate on a single person. The twist here is that when characters die, they are dead forever, and won't come back.
When playing the game, the player upholds a third person perspective with whatever person they are playing as. You can loot and scavenge, clear areas, set up outposts, scout out areas to add icons to your map, and much, much more.
This game is one of those games that will leave you in doubt considering how much content it actually has versus how much you would think it didn't from a distance. There is so much going on in this game it is easy to miss the minor features here and there. From a distance, one may think it is just a third person combat-based shooter.
you would rethink your entire perspective in a single matter of visiting the base management screen.
What I'm trying to get at is that the game does not start strong with the story mode. The game gives you the illusion that you are playing a game where you just follow a line of missions where you just go from mission to mission until eventually beating the game. Until you reach the church (The base and group the story mode gives you to start), it will seem like that. The game does not provide convinient tutorial on the game's content, leaving it up to the player to realize that they aren't playing a linear game maybe 3 hours since they started.
There is a 'random bank' of survivors to ensure that the player will not end up with the same people every time (unless they are counting the story characters from story mode), there is no set spots for certain items to spawn, and every game playthrough you go through will be noteably different.
The game generates missions based on what is needed or if the player hasn't tended to a growing problem. If you leave a guy to wallow in his anger for a long time, he will be at risk of snapping, giving the player the option to try to talk them down from their bad mood, or ask them to leave, as an example of this. Other survivors you aren't playing as can ask you for help, or you can even ask them for help as well.
The game does not use money currency or anything like that, you use your influence in the group to make descisions and take things. This also means that you definitely do not start in the decision-making ranks, meaning that you will have to play it for a little bit before you gain the trust needed to make the big move to the bigger compound, stop that zed hunt, etc. Influence can be gained for sticking around for a while and doing a lot of influence-gaining tasks. Be involved with your group, and your group will be involved with you. It's not a game where you can screw around and hope your bros will survive.
That's the one bad thing - you can't really screw around when driving that car off a cliff will destroy it permanently or the fact that ammo is really rare. It depends on what your motives for playing are.
While I recommend this game, I must warn you that it requires time and goes off of a real-time simulation. Survivors will gather little supplies daily, or you might get lucky, but there is daily rates of consumption of each material depending on what your setup is. Maintenance may be required, but usually your group will make it. It's nothing you can't handle.
Get this game if you have the time. If you are looking for something combat-based that you can play in an hour and not have to worry about anything, go play something else.

This game is wonderful. I’m old enough now to know that tastes change, experiences change us,sometimes we lose ourselves and sometimes we regain more than we expected, and that we aren’t the same person we were long before our last breath. But if I were ever to say a game was my favorite, Dragon’s Dogma would be it.
This game is an RPG and a sandbox world. You create your character--the hero of the journey--but you also create  a second character, who is your Pawn, someone to help and guide you through the story that lays ahead. You and your Pawn can be joined by two other Pawns, who are creations of actual people. This is a fantastic mechanic, as you can “rent” out your Pawn to other people, who will not only come back with a reward from an appreciative player, but also with knowledge of foes and quests that the other player exposed to them. Your Pawn, and other pawns, are constantly talking to you (unless you ask them not to) and guiding you through this world. It’s amazing, it’s funny, it’s annoying.
The world itself is fantastic. The story is engaging. My first few playthroughs I couldn’t get into the game. It felt alien and weird. The game doesn’t hand things to you, so I found myself wandering around irritated that I didn’t know what I was supposed to be doing or what was going on. I’m an Arisen? What the hell is that? There’s a dragon waiting to kill me, why don’t I go straight to it and fight it, why am I stuck in this place? Then, as I was walking the streets to somewhere, I heard an NPC talk. NPC’s talk all the time, making comments to you or to another NPC. And while it wasn’t obvious they were talking about you or the game you were playing, the situation you found yourself in, they WERE. And it clicked. The game was about how you face your life, no matter what is thrown at you. The NPC’s came alive, I wanted to talk to them to see how they were handling this terrifying ordeal. Some were afraid, some wanted to check out, some wanted to fight, and some just didn’t see a change in their lives since they aren’t the ones who fight dragons. I found quests which reflected these interactions, and I discovered all the quests reflect them, and even the last battle itself. When faced with a horrible, impossible choice--who am I? What kind of person am I? What will I do? Will I take the easy path and lose that which are close to me? Or will I take a risk and not only win myself my life back--but also change the lives of others around me for the better? The game is very philosophical and I love it.
The combat itself is good. You have classes you can level up (and change whenever you want), and each class has special skills. You can use those skills, you can also grab and hold enemies so your pawns can beat up on them. You can also carry an enemy and throw them off a cliff if you want. There are giant monsters you have to face, and you can use the grab mechanic to CLIMB UP THEM. I always enjoy climbing a cyclop’s back and wailing on their head.
Also, there is a love mechanic, the game doesn’t tell you, so you’ll want to do some research before your girlfriend is a 12 year old girl or a big, sweaty, hairy blacksmith, because you can’t change that, it happens when it happens, you’re stuck with that. So….yeah.

This is really hardcore, really fun and really compelling. It takes time to build your confidence and your supplies, but when you start to venture out and dive for loot you will start to really enjoy the process. With a minimalist interace and an intuitive crafting system, this game really immerses you in the experience of being a castaway. At first you will stay on the first island you find, but as your resources dwindle you will have to venture out onto the open sea in search of another island to plunder. With limited room in your backpack you will need to make hard decisions about what to take on each voayge, and more importantly, what to bring back to your home island. Without the ability to navigate at first, you will have to get creative so as to avoid becoming lost. I made sure that I chopped down a palm tree on each island I visted and pointed the trunk towards my home island. This saved my bacon a few times when shark attacks spun me around so many times I lost my bearings, and when fog completely obscured my view whilst at sea. When I found the compass on one lucky dive I began mapping my environs on paper and now have a detailed map of many islands and wrecks. I can't really describe how much fun this game is. There are no goals beyond staying alive through eating, drinking and maintaining your health. The slow trickle of items you salvage will add to your resilence and allow you to mount focused missions with specific tools. It's a sandbox experience that you control.

I got bored of this game really fast. It's better than the terrible Arkham games and Assassian's Creed 3, but falls short for a few reasons.
1. All of the fights are either too easy or too hard for all the wrong reasons. Generally, the only enemies that are worth worrying about are either archers (since their attacks are difficult to notice and dodge) and higher-ranking members of the army that have enough strength to one-shot you. Everything else can be cut through like butter if you're willing to mash Y or A at the right opportunity. For some reason, the game has a built-in easy mode skill named "Storm of Urfael" or something along those lines that lets you instakill a bunch of people for no real reason. Even Arkham didn't have something like that.
2. The nemesis system is cool until you realize that you won't die enough to use it. The only generals that have killed me come when I get wounded and leave right after poking me with their sticks.
3. Open world that's empty. I honestly can't tell if the missions repeat or not since most of the ones I've done involve stealthing around the camp and freeing a bunch of slaves. The rest either compound how bad Arkham-style combat systems are or let you shoot arrows at still targets in slow motion (which gets easier when you have the skill that replenishes focus on headshots).
4. The story has one interesting idea wrapped up into a plot that feels like a circleclique of LotR lore. Basically the whole plot revolves around you trying to find out that the Elf Lord is, in fact, the Elf Lord. Although the idea of an immortal man wishing to lift his "curse of immortality" so he can die and join his family is incredibly interesting to me, none of the characters felt that they had any personality aside from Gollum who was already pre-established in LotR so no props for that.
5. The game is, in the style of Arkham-likes, trying to be too many things at once and failing at most if not all of them. Does it want to be a game where the world evolves on its own if you don't come to intervene by using Sauron's Army? Does it want to be a stealth game where you sneak around attempting to free slaves without a trace? Does it want to be a beat 'em up where you go around slashing the heads of thousands? Does it want to be an exploration game where you go around finding beauty in the Land of Shadows? All the mechanics are almost as if they were made /just/ fleshed out enough to avoid any internal contradictions, but weren't expanded upon anywhere past that (i.e. in stealth, the guards will notice bodies but won't notice you crouching within their line of sight.)
Want a game where armies and generals create a world around you, waiting for someone to tip the scales in their favor? Play Mount & Blade: Warband
Want a game where you attempt to stealth around unnoticed? Play Thief.
Want a game with a big open world waiting to be explored and plundered? There's actually a lot of those around that fit the bill better than this, you can find them with a google search.
Want a game with the best usage of Arkam combat in a while? This one actually fits the bill, it rarely feels ridiculously forced and stupid. Often you can be surprised about the creative useage the powers are given in the middle of combat.
tl;dr it's not as bad as the arkham games but also isn't that good

This is my third time purchasing this remake of Sonic CD. This remake of the game is the definitive way to play Sonic CD.  One of the best Sonic soundtracks by far, with CD quality music and two different soundtracks to chose from (An exclusive feature to the 2011 Sonic CD by the way). Sonic has a new feature really only seen in this game: The super peel-out. It's really fun to use and the spindash is customizable from the original (Has a long charge time to use) and the sonic 2 styled spindash which is turned on by default if I remember correctly. Seven zones, with 2 acts and 1 boss act each with different variations on the level by using the time mechanic that allows you to go into the future or the past. You collect time stones, so no super sonic unfortunately, but the special stages are really fun, so they're still worth collecting for that alone. The time stones help you get the good ending as well, but you could also get the good ending by destroying all of the machines in the past. Beating the game in this version will unlock tails, who wasn't playable in the original game. This version is also in widescreen and the loadtimes when traveling through time are very quick. I can't recommend this game enough, and if I were to give one complaint, it would be the boss fights. They are really underwhelming for the most part. Some of them are really easy and others just take alot of time to defeat. I do wish that the features in the sonic 1 and 2 remakes (That aren't on steam which is unfortunate) were this game. Knuckles isn't even an unlockable character, and you can't use tails as a combo character in this game. Regardless, this is an excellent version of an already excellent game. Buy it.

So the tl;dr for the lazy people, it is a spiritual successor of games like Baldur's Gate and manages to live up to and even surpass its predecessors. I got really bored and wrote a review for my friends on facebook and decided to copy and paste it to here, minus the game name and steam store link of course.
Pillars of Eternity is the child of a Kickstarter by Obsidian Entertainment to make an old school rpg, more specifically the well regarded Infinity Engine games of their past. Obsidian is essentially a descendant of Black Isle Studios which created Icewind Dale, Planescape: Torment, and Fallout 2. They also were involved with many early Bioware projects (notably the Baldur's Gate games). More recently they were the developers of Fallout: New Vegas. Obsidian sought funding to make a game heavily inspired by these games and free of the influence of a major publisher which would almost certainly attempt to "modernize" the game beyond recognition. The support they received smashed all goals, landing just short of their final stretch goal. They had over 77,000 backers pledging just short of $4,000,000. With this money, Obsidian set out to make one of my favorite games in recent memory and the game is filled with tributes to the backers who made it possible (sadly I was not one as I lacked a proper PC back then).
The game they produced feels like a classic Infinity Engine game but streamlined. Annoyances are removed, features added, systems refined. It looks, not surprisingly, much much better as it was made using the Unity Engine (yes, decent developers can use it too). The game has a wonderful sound track and a lot of voice acting in addition to pages and pages of dialogue, description, and texts (this is not a game for those who shy away from reading). The game does not shy away from sensitive topics such as slavery,♥♥♥♥♥♥ religion, genocide, etc but rather explores them in a fairly serious manner making the world seem more real for it.
The party members (you can create generic ones that fit your needs but for obvious reason the premade, voice acted ones are far more interesting) are generally interesting. Some endearing, some grating. They all had their charms. What you say and do will shape their fates and they can die if you are careless in battle. They provide interesting interjections in conversation as well, along with occasional and amusing conversation with each other.
The story is interesting. I can't explain it in too much detail because spoilers but it is thought provoking and reasonably well written. The real meat of the game is of course in exploration and side quests though. If you are a main story only kind of person this is not your kind of game
The combat is as one might expect; it is essentially D&D in video game form (heavily based on 4e I think). You control up to six party members along with any animal companions or summons you might have. There is a ton of equipment and ability variety and generally a good amount of flexibility within classes as to how you want to play them as equipment rarely has any restrictions on use. Obsidian clearly has a bit of a hard on for the estoc though as some of the coolest and best weapons you can get are estocs. That said, pretty much all forms of weapons and armor have plenty of high end options. The classes themselves feel fairly unique. You have, of course, the classic classes but also the unique Chanter, who passively chants phrases with minor effects to actively use much more powerful invocations while fighting as well as the equally unique Cipher, a psychic that can read and manipulate souls through focus which is gained by damaging enemies. Enemies run the classic gambit from trolls to ogres to undead to dragons. All in all the combat exactly what I expected (and wanted).
Now for the bad, as little as there is. Bugs. There are a few. From occasional missing descriptions to quests that won't complete. They are few and far between but still present. That said, nothing I saw was game-breaking. My only other complaint is the somewhat murky consequences at times. You sometimes have choices with completely unforeseeable consequences far down the line which, while neat, can be extremely frustrating when they screw you over over a seemingly minor detail (the mere act of accepting a given quest can alienate multiple factions for example) and your disposition or reputation can sometimes suffer changes that don't quite seem to fit the situation.
When all is said and done, Obsidian promised a classic experience with a modern makeover and boy did they deliver. They created their own world and breathed life into it, giving a game that feels both old and new a the same time. It is a wonderful experience that I wholeheartedly recommend for dozens of hours of entertainment.
As a note, the DLC is equally recommended. It provides a decent amount of new content, new areas, two new full companions, and a TON of new items. It is part 1 of 2 for now with the second half coming out in January making for roughly one expansion in total.

Let me start by saying, this game was recommended by my friends, so I figured, why the hell not.
At first, when I started playing, I didn't realize how fast you have to forage for supplies, so I ran from door to door trying to find food, weapons, and anything that wasn't nailed down on the floor. This is when I realized that I needed more space for items. Now, at the time I didn't know that certain clothing and bags can outrank the others. After my friends told me about this, I started searching for suitable clothing in hopes to survive better. I did, along with my friends. There was 5 of us in total. We figured, with a big team like this, what could possibly go wrong?
Well....Everything.
A person showed up, not a gang, not a couple of people. Just. One. Person. He also had a gun with him so it was pretty tense. But I figured, 5v1, we'll be fine. Keep in mind this was my first interaction with a stranger, so I had not a clue on how he'd react. I walked up to him...
Yeah, he drew the gun pretty damn fast. It was a .22 luger, I think. Not much, but still a gun nonetheless. So, I started running for cover, and my friends started wondering why I was freaking out (they heard the shots but didn't know who shot them). I started running, more gunfire was happening from all around, atleast that was what it felt like. I still had the thought we would be fine because we had more gunfire on our side. But, all of that changed fast when one of my friends started to flip at the sound of lots of gunfire, and people all around him (the people was me and my friends). He started opening fire at all of us, killed us all, one by one, completely missing the actual baddie, then ended up gettign killed himself. We lost everything, since I finally realized permadeath wasn't to be taken lightly in this game
And that, was my first experience. Full of regrets, mistakes, and fear. 10/10 would play again.

Okay, jokes aside. Overall, despite its massive flaws, I really enjoyed the game. I haven't played precedent games prior to this, but it was a blast nonetheless.
Cons
-Story for each path is too short, can be completed in mere 1-2 hours time.
-Controls on the Keyboard are weird... I recommend playing with a gamepad/controller.
-There were times that the camera was so intrusive, as it automatically rotates whenever you lock on to a target.
-Speaking of targeting, the lock-on tends to bug out especially when you enter Spring Harvest Mode.
-Selling and Buying items tend to be a huge chore.
-Confusing Menu UIs, you would have to get used to it first.
-The torture mini-game is such bull!
-Not enough customization options for female protag, and why is it that it has to have to be locked in completion walls?
-Not enough Gun, Spear, and Dual-Wielding Swordstyles and especially Hand-to-Hand Combat Styles.
Pros
+While the Story Paths for each faction is too short, it has its moments. Especially when you're gunning for the True Ending Path, which was a blast.
+The radiant quests/fetch quests are not as much as a chore as I thought it would be, which surprised me. Basically, you get a random quest from a random NPC, then move to your target then once you dealt with it, instant completion. No need to run back to that said NPC to finish the quest.
+Disregarding the clothes, face and hair customizations, the Accessory Customization was really decent. Reminds me of Soul Calibur's where you pick your accessory then place it wherever you want.
+The combat gameplay is really fluid and dynamic, various stances and various swordstyles to choose from. Each had their own strengths and weaknesses. From the unpredictable and lightning-fast Iaijutsu, the devastating and aggressive Jo-Dan, to the unconventional One-Handed swordstyles.
+The skill tree is simple but engaging, some styles share same movesets but each of them had unique learning curves and special moves to be fulfilled in special conditions or via scrolls.
+The enemy AI is surprisingly smart and unpredictable, you do not want to underestimate a run-of-mill thug. Duels and battles can be either casual easy, to mind-numbingly intense. They can parry, block and even out-maneuver you if you're not careful. For the best challenge in gameplay, I recommend playing on Hard Difficulty for a more satisfying run.
+Spring Harvest is very satisfying to use, especially when you're surrounded by Enemies 10 to 1. Basically you just drop everything and go Dynasty Warriors--or in this case Samurai Warriors up theirs then watch as your character sheathes his/her sword with all enemies dropping dead with a click of the blade. Badass.
+Sword Customization is a huge + for me. Although simple, at best, it was nice to craft my own sword with my name on it.
+The sidequests are entertaining, the 4 subfactions of the game. The Homeless, The Yakuza, Thieves and Constables. Complete all of them and you get to do an epic quest finale for them and unite the 8 samurai to go up against the foreign invaders. It was better than the main questline IMO.
+The Yobai or Nightcrawling is just a meme-worthy mini-game. Basically you have to go flirt with any female npc's (although the main NPCs require special conditions.), then when they accept you, you go sneak up on them in their huts and find them to get your sexy time. It's funny and sometimes rewarding, as they always leave an item after a session.

I played this game's campaign and was having quite some fun up until several missions. They seemed nearly impossible but through RNG map generation I manged to get by them, up until a single mission named "vacancee downfall." This mission alone has brought a new meaning to Tooth and tail. Its about fighting the impossible AI's that you just can't beat. Several of these campaign missions are pretty much impossible without extreme luck. This mission has you starting out with the bare nothing, while the enemy has fortifications and farms all around the map. The heroic quest for this mission is to scout everyone on the map within 1:45. Sounds easy enough right? Well heres the thing, maps are random and can put you anywhere, next to like 4 foritications or in a corner. You'd think a corner is good until you realize the next mechanic of this mission, wind. Wind will blow you around and it seems to target the player negatively almost all the time. After going through hours of finding the right spawn and seed and completing theh heroic quest you now have to win... against 3 ai's who never run out of food, while you are stuck with nothing cause you had to scout the entire map at the start. Explain to me how this is possible. I manged to get a map where i was lucky to scout the map out and managed to get a good foothold on half the map, but was pushed down by the countless enemies which I could not fight off. I ended up starving and tried to expand. I sat in there for nearly 10 minutes with the enemy spamming units and dying from my fortifications, while they seem to never run out of food the entire game. Cheating AI, or poorly designed AI. Another cool looking RTS which brings whole new mechanics to the game only to be ruined by impossible missions designed for cheating, and poor AIs. You will probably love the game against players but I couldn't go out of my way to even try to play against players since I was trying to learn on the missions a bit, but from rage inducing missions I just strait up quit this game. I wonder if the developers have even tried playing this missions, cause I would like to know how some human is supposed to beat them without insane luck. I heard that some of these missions may have gotten nerfed a bit to make them easier, and if that is the case then I would like to know when it was a good idea to make impossible missions. And if your curious, only 2% of the population of the game has even beaten the heroic quest, which only supports my statement even more.
I honestly wish steam had a neutral vote as I can see this game being extremely fun for a lot of people who like fast RTS and grandomly generated maps. Along with that the music is amazing and I love it a ton. The controls are bit weird and I would love being able to set groups 1-9/0 so that you can control different groups. Its annoying moving every single unit of a single type when you need at least one somewhere else. It seems to be a very limiting RTS and could use some heavy improvement on the controls of moving units around, also the economy needs some impovement since sometimes when you happen to want to build something a unit gets built instead when you desprately need a farm.
