Atmospheric game with good setting and limited strategic options.
I bought this game right after its release. It looks amazing on screenshots and video so I expected a lot of fun hours. I played 30 minutes and didn't touch it for 3 months because I had more interesting gamed in my library. I gave this game another chance and played for some more hours. Anyway, I deleted it from my library an I will tell you why.
It's kinda innovative RTS game. It breaks usual rules. You can't make different groups of units here. There you can make only 1 army which is controlled by a leader. Actually, you even can't control this army, you just control a leader. You can command him to move him anywhere and you have three extra options 1) attack with unit type 2) attack with all army 3) retreat.
I don't know why devs decided to do this, but I think the game with such limited options couldn't be called Strategy. Probably, it could. Anyway, Tooth and Tails is the most casual strategy I have ever played. Is it good or bad? Let's talk about it.
I have started playing campaign. I was a little frustrated with controlling of units for first 2 missions. Then I understood how it works. I completed first campaign in 36 minutes and stopped playing it for next months. Yeah, devs tries to make missions diverse, but come on, all you need to do is 1) build farm 2) wait until your army is growing 3) destroy everything on the map. You gets different units, but every mission was the same for me.. Also, I played on hard and didn't feel any challenge... just wait, wait more, and... mission completed.
I reinstalled the game last week. I forced myself to play little more, actually I wanted to close the game after 2th mission of 2th campaign, but I forced myself to complete second campaign. I expected something new. But... no. There were 2 missions with special requirements (sun hurts outside of territory and wind slows your units), but even they didn't change anything. Just mass army and go fight or survive for X minutes.
I finished playing a campaign at the first mission of third campaign. And I went to PvP.

PvP Engaged me for.... 5 battles.. When I understood how to win here and.... I got 9 win streak.. Then I made a guide about it... played some more games with other strategies to prove my theory... then I deleted the game and was writing this review now.
The huge positive side of PvP in Tooth and Tail is what it is super fast. One game usually last 2-10 minutes. It was pretty fun to play until I tried all units and found most of them useless. I found the best set and then I found 2 good strategies which allowed me to make 9 win streak with no chances of losing.
So, there are huge balance issues at the current moment. The game is 3 months alive and I don't understand how devs doesn't see it.
There are armor/attack types. I think this is must have option for good strategy game. It gives a lot of ways to make counter actions on any enemy actions. There is not... Every unit is effective against any other units. Yeah, AoE units are effective against small units and range units can attack air units, but that's actually is all. In this game, you can win just massing 1 unit type.
Also, I hated a lot random generation map. I confused me a lot and always give disadvantage to one player. I would prefer to see hand-made symmetric maps. And I had lags every 5th game.. Nothing critical but it's not a good feature.
Also, it seems that the player base is getting low (less than 500 players online), so multiplayer is gonna be prety dead soon. When I played it took up to 1 minute to find a game (it's ok for now).
There are 4 commanders in the game. I thought eacn one has special abilities and units.. I was wrong. They give no bonuses. It is just 4 visual styles of the unit. Come on, Devs. You could add small bonuses and the game would become more interesting. For example: +25% food gathering rate / -50% unit production time / +20% unit health / +1 unit max stack for each barrack. And add at least 1 unuqie unit for each commander. The idea "all units are avaialble for everyone' is bad. Could you imagine Starcraft with only terrans?
I understand why you decided to implement such units control. Because you made the game for consoles. I would like this game if I were played consoles. But play PC games and I want to use all my strategy skills and abilities. Making the game with such controlling is "One step back in strategy genre".
Pros
- Very cool setting with animals and World War I weapons
- Cool pixel graphics and awesome 2d art
- Innovative RTS mechanics
- Not bad story. Anyway, I skipped it :D
- Could be great for casual players
Cons
- Mechanics is very limited for experienced strategy players
- Random map generation whic confuses a player a lot and brings disadvantage in PvP
- Commanders gives nothing special. Every player could take any unit.
- I found some balance issues in PvP.
- Only 15 units. A lot of units are useless and noone uses them.
- No armor/attack types
- Every fourth PvP was lagging. Every 12th had lags which slowed the game by 3 times (=impossible to play).
My final thoughts are closer to negative, because there were a lot of things I didn't like. But this game is well done and could be interesting for a lot of people, so I give this game a positive review because we need to engage people to RTS game and motivate devs to make more quality RTS games. It's pretty dead genre now. I hope, devs will listen to players and will make the game better.
If you are OK with the main gameplay idea (controlling 1 leader instead of controlling different armies) than 20$ price tag would be fair.
If you are primarily casual player and don't like play hardcore game, thinking hard, planning your moves than you should try this game. This game would be welcome for newcomers in Strategy genre.
If you played any strategy games in the past and especially if you played ranked 1v1 in WC3 or SC2 don't buy this game, because you will find it really limited and boring.

Let's be frank. This is a GTA-esque adventure game with zombies. The one thing it has going for it is that it allows you to control an entire enclave. You can add different structures to your holdout, like a library or machine shop, that give you assorted bonuses. You can send your fellow survivors out on looting runs or help them with their zombie problems. But it's still a GTA-esque adventure game, seeing you drive through an abandoned rural county for missions to progress the story.
The problem is it doesn't do this well. The entire game is a standard zombie trope. You start a few days into the infestation not knowing what the hell is going on, and your goal is to get out of town. You help (or not) survivors in other enclaves along the way. The writing is lackluster, and the plot, twists and all, can be found in any b-rated zombie flick or book.
The worst part though is the insane number of bugs, and the horrid console port. Keyboard controls are lousy, and I found myself switching to a controller because the game felt not quite as crappy that way. The Options menu is poor. More often than not I had to restart my game because a bug either killed my character or made it impossible for me to continue. NPCs love doing stupid stuff (I had to chase an escort npc across an entire freaking map, then push it back to where he started to get him to reset). Cars get stuck on *nothing* and flip when you're driving them down an empty road. And there's no sign these bugs are going to be fixed. Occasionally a patch comes along, but they don't seem to fix important issues.
The only reason to buy this game is if you're a fan of the zombie survival genre looking for a game that lets you control an enclave. Because quite frankly this types of game is rare. If you do buy it, get it on sale and be prepared to fight the bugs more than you fight the zombies. Otherwise, avoid it entirely. Hopefully someone will make a cleaner game that blows this out of the water.

Remember those old papers thrown on the ground with a slight brown/yellowish tint that you've seen in every game ever? Yup, those are here.

The novelty wears off and it becomes a nuisance rather than a plot device. The game is simply not fun or engaging.

The fact that it was released early 2015 might be the cause for all these gripes I have with this game. Just keep in mind that Amnesia was released in 2010, Outlast around 2013 which contributed to the steam greenlight boom of forgettable Horror survival games using the same engine, same dull storyline and copy pasted gameplay elements.

Tex Murphy is a decent little adventure-puzzle game, with some well done green-screen FMV scenes and a sense of humor about itself. A nice entry into the detective genre with a minimal reliance on violence as a game mechanic. The main character is a likable, goofy private eye who gets amnesia (trope alert!) and investigates their missing memories and girlfriend.
It's not a flawless game, by any means. The graphics are stylish, but not terribly realistic, the characters are well-acted without ever being terribly deep or developed, and the story has an interesting premise that doesn't really get explored to its fullest. The game can be funny, but the jokes aren't really integrated into the story as much as they are just asides the main character makes to himself when wandering around San Francisco. I almost feel like the developers couldn't quite decide on making a serious or humorous detective game, and so tried to do both in different areas of the game. It is clear that a lot of thought and love went into making the game, and that helps to smooth over some of the rough edges, but with a little more polish and stronger plotting, it could've been a lot better.
Overall, it's a good game, 7/10 if I had to give it a number. I won't play it again, but I got it in a bundle for 12 bucks and I am very happy with it for the price. I would certainly not pay 20 dollars for it, as it has little to no replay value, but if you like detective stories, or you want to relive the era of FMV cutscene storytelling, pick this up when it goes on sale.

Disclaimer: This is the first Tex Murphy game I've played. Before this game I knew nothing of the character.
This is a difficult game to review. When I started, I found it rather poor. As I played it, I began to enjoy it. Overall, it isn't a good game... but the story and comedy make it worthwhile.
This isn't so much a game as it is an interactive movie. Most of the game is watching cutscenes.
During most scenes you'll get several chances to choose your dialog. Much like Bioware games, you'll get 3 dialog options. Unlike Bioware, it isn't good/evil/neutral. Instead it's vague/vague/vague. Instead of getting options like, "I don't know what you are talking about" you get "be cool". In fact, almost all options are 1-3 words. I often find myself being mislead by them. If you get an option like "be cool", there's no telling what will happen. Tex might make a calm statement. Then again, he might make a sarcastic comment. He could even become defensive and tell some to "be cool". You never really know.
The other problem with the dialog choices is that it often seemed like Tex, and whoever he talked to, were having two completely different conversations. The characters' reactions to Tex frequently didn't match the mood of the discourse.
When you aren't watching cutscenes, you're walking around looking for things to click on. If you play on the easy (casual) setting, you'll get hints and clickable objects will sparkle. If you play on normal (gamer), you don't get either of those. That's the only difference. Without the sparkle, some of the objects are difficult to find. While playing I sometimes wouldn't know what to do. All I could do was walk around looking for things to click upon.
Some objects, when clicked, will load a cutscene from a past Tex Murphy game. I guess these are supposed to be fun easter eggs... But I've never played a Tex Murphy game before. Most of them have nothing to do with the plot of Tesla Effect. For me, they seem random and out-of-place. The strangest part is that many of these objects are found simply lying in the street. This game is set 7 years after Tex's last adventure. Why are these objects just sitting outside? Why would a guy hiding from the NSA leave an ID of the NSA officer he escaped...
?! This makes no sense. He might as well put a sign outside that reads, "Come arrest me".
Themematically, the game is full of contradictions. At times, Tex is serious. During these times the story seems very much "detective noir". That never lasts long. There's lots of slap-stick and wacky characters. A lot of effort went into giving the appearance that the game takes place in the 1940's. However, the game is set in the future of 2050. So you have people that look/act as if they are from the 1940's, but also sci-fi technology stuff. I don't understand it, but the characters make it fun.
The acting ranges from passable to terrible. Surprisingly, the best acting isn't from Tex's actor. Instead it's two bit characters. One is severely handicapped and confined to a wheelchair. The other is a 7'4" transexual. These two actors took their roles seriously, even though both are ridiculous. Their dialog seems genuine and believable.
The biggest problem I had with the game was bugs. I found ways to jump ahead in the story several times. I often triggered dialog that would assume that I already knew certain things. Which would reveal facts I had no way of knowing. Once this happened, I didn't need to do as much to advance the story, but it was also confusing.
To sumarize, the game isn't that great, but the story is. There are many flaws, but there's something good in there. Totally worthwhile... but I wouldn't recommend paying full price.

The first time I played Sonic CD was this "remastering," and growing up with Sonic the Hedgehog 2 on the original Genesis, I have to say that this game is a Visual and Audible step-up from the standard Genesis. The folks at SEGA really tried to take advantage of the Sega CD's hardware advantages, and it shows. This remastering improves various flaws with the original, and I warmly welcome those changes. Included is the ability to switch between the original Japanese and American soundtrack, and how the spindash is executed, allowing the player a limited form of customization. Lastly a warm welcome has been added to this remaster; by beating the game, Tails (who is absent in the origina game) can be unlocked, and functions similar to his Sonic 3 counterpart.
Unfortunetly, there are a couple issues with this game. It is roughly the same length as the original Sonic game from 1991, the time-traveling concept is underplayed (and difficult to execute at times) easy bosses, and feel easy for the duration of the experience. If you don't have the cash to buy a physical Sega CD console and Sonic CD game, or want to have an experience outside the cartridge-based Sonic games, this might be the choice for you.

For me the appeal of these games is combat and strategy and it just wasn't enticing enough here. I got so bored towards the end that i rushed through everything, skipping through every dialog.
On an unrelated note i thought it was funny that they had that combat music that's pretty much straight out of De-Arnise keep (BG2). And Twin Elms had a theme that was very Kuldahar (Icewind dale).
Pros:
Baldur's gate gameplay.
Story is not stupid and cheesy.
You can create your own party and not have to use official companions.
There is a bit of that keep management stuff (although not much).
Decent amount of content.
Some interesting combat ideas but read on for cons because those mechanics get meh further into the game.
Party members have decently unique personalities. Even the bland♥♥♥♥♥elven mage was spiced up with a secret.
Cons:
Wayyyy too much reading: paragraphs and paragraphs of text on every dialog. That may be a pro for some people, but i've read enough in my lifetime and i'm tired of it.
Combat mechanics too complicated (too many different defenses/resistances/stats/conditions, it may not be more complicated than modern d&d rules but d&d rules have been building up slowly for a long time, while this game just jumps straight into complicatedness.) And i either never found much explanation on how stuff works as far as damage application goes, or i found it and it was more paragraphs of text and i got bored reading it.
Party members join up too easily and will never leave you, so there wasn't that much roleplaying with them, and also no alignment thing that dramatically restricts how the world perceives you, (yeah yeah there is reputation with different factions but i didn't notice much gameplay difference with that).
Unique items: that's one of the main complaints i have. They weren't amazing enough or hard enough to get. I want stuff like Carsomyr +5 (BG2). You had to kill one of the hardest enemies in game for it, and only a specific class could use it, but once you get it - it makes a huge difference, (and then you can go after Kangaxx! :P). Here - i got so many clutter drops from enemies and every once in a while there was a small upgrade but it never really made a big enough impact.
Anyway, overall this is not a bad game, and if Steam used a number rating i'd give it a 7 out of 10 maybe. But i didn't love it, i have no desire to replay it, and i wouldn't recommend it to any of my friends. It was like going to steak and shake late at night. Nothing else is open, and the milkshakes are good, but the service was mediocre at best and if I had a choice - i would have gone somewhere else.

So a little background. To get it out of the way yes, I am a fan of the Warriors series games. I have been for around 10 years with Dynasty Warriors 3 as the first of the series I played on the original Xbox. This is quite a lengthy review (and it doesn’t even cover everything about the game) so there is a section titled “Final Thoughts” which summaries my review for you as well as my own final opinion. Now onto the game itself.
For the newcomers to the series Dynasty Warriors is a series of Hack-n-slash action games which draws its story and ideas from the historical novel set “Romance of the Three Kingdoms” believed to have been written by Luo Guanzhong. The series of books tell the story of the epic struggle between three great warlords and their followers. The game is set after the fall of the Han Dynasty and through the Three Kingdoms era of ancient Chinese history from 169AD to the eventual reunification of the land in 280AD.
Now for those who know about the game most of you will probably know what you are getting with this. It’s the standard Dynasty Warriors hack-n-slash formula many of us have grown to love about the series but now ported to the PC. I’ve made headings below to structure my review and to help you decide on whether this is worth purchasing.
With the Xtreme Legends edition there is a large roster of over 80 playable characters in the game to choose from each with their own unique move sets. Each character now can level up with experience which can be gained by defeating enemies in battles as well as collecting EXP scrolls dropped by generals. There is a much stronger sense of progression in this game than previous entries with more moves and musou bars becoming unlocked at higher levels. As to the individual characters themselves many retain their distinctive animated personalities from the previous entries to the series and the chemistry between the old and new officers is a welcome addition.
Story Mode follows the history of the different warring kingdoms of the era. With the previous game it works very much like Dynasty Warriors 4 where each kingdom has their own story rather than following individual characters. The main kingdoms are those of Wei, Wu and Shu as well as Jin introduced in Dynasty Warriors 7. In Xtreme Legends there is also the Lu Bu Story Mode and the return of an “Other” kingdom Story Mode.
Story Mode now follows a linear system following the events in chronological order with some stages offering branching paths depending on whether certain requirements and events were completed. This can simply be that an officer will appear later on which they otherwise would historically not have appeared in or even unlock a hypothetical timeline for that kingdom where you can rewrite history. All conditions for unlocking this route are secret until they are completed or until the campaign is completed. There is also a separate timeline that plays out as a series of “What If?” scenarios which take place at various turning points in history during the Three Kingdoms era.
Free Mode has returned allowing players to choose any map from the Story to play with any officer they want. Players also have the choice of which difficulty, bodyguards and animals they wish to have as well as various other settings. Of particular note the AI has also been significantly improved so that players who help their allies increase their army's morale and can help turn the tide of battles in their favour whilst those who ignore their allies will be punished and are more likely to lose allies as well as allied morale.
Ambition Mode is a new twist on the previous Conquest and Legend Modes offered in the previous game. Here you are in charge of building up a settlement from simple foundations into a thriving city fit enough to attract the Emperor enough for them to visit and invite them to join your cause. There are various missions which are short and aimed at acquiring material, fame or recruit allies to increase the size of your city. Famous officers can also be fought and recruited to join you as bodyguards to take into battles offering support in addition to forming bonds with your playable officer outside of combat.
There are numerous buildings which can be built which feature weapons and item shops, farms, a barracks to send soldiers out to other provinces to return with materials and other rewards. The blacksmith in particular allows the player to buy better weapons with increased blacksmith rank as well as the facility to create custom weapons using 40 different weapon attributes with use of the tempering system similar to the Warriors Orochi series. Weapons can be tempered (combining attributes of two weapons into one) or reforged (combining 3 different weapons to create a new randomised weapon).
The weapons system is very similar to Dynasty Warriors 7 but gender restrictions have been removed and players can no longer change weapons during battle. Two weapons can be equipped at a time and each character has an EX weapon which are the signature weapon of that character. These weapons have extended special moves when equipped with them e.g. Zhao Yun and his Dragon Spear. There is also the new addition of the new affinity system where each weapon has either an affinity of Heaven, Earth or Man. This works like rock, paper, scissors whereby each affinity is superior to one and inferior to another. This is all explained in-game during the optional “Tutorial” section of Story Mode with one Tutorial stage for each of the 4 kingdoms/factions.
As I have posted at the start of the review this was one of the first PC ports of the Dynasty Warriors game for the PC. One of the issues many players have mentioned is the downgrade in the graphics. Although being a vast improvement over previous games they have been locked at a lower resolution and quality similar to those offered to the previous generation of consoles rather than the current gen. There is also a lack of online multiplayer support unlike the console versions which can be a deal-breaker for some. However the game does have split-screen multiplayer available.
Another issue raised by many players is the controller support in the game. Keys displayed in-game remain as those for the keyboard controls rather than changing to controller buttons when a controller is used. This can be confusing but I personally found it manageable once I had re-binded the keys for the controller.
DYNASTY WARRIORS 8: Xtreme Legends Complete Edition is a brilliant addition to the Dynasty Warriors games with lots of new features for fans to enjoy whilst still maintaining the revered hack-n-slash nature of the previous instalments. This is a must-buy for long-time fans of the series on the PC if they are able to look past the locked graphics and controller hiccups.
For new players I also think this is a great first game to join now with the inclusion of the comprehensive tutorials and hints for almost all the new concepts to ease players into the game. I thought the new Ambition Mode and the return of Free Mode extends the replay value immensely and has even gotten me to nominate this game for the “Just 5 More Minutes” award (seeing as I spent a few nights up still playing this game and creating my own weapons!) and the "No apologies" award (because despite its flaws I still love it!). However those looking for a game requiring lots of strategy, accurate history telling, immersive storylines or role-playing mechanic there are likely to be more suitable titles elsewhere.
Thank you very much for your attention! I hope you enjoy your day and have fun!

Miscreated. For me personally, the hardest game ever to review, because this game has huge potential and my ingame hours might tell that I enjoyed this game a lot for some time. At some stage I was a dev-tester for Entrada and the base I built can still be seen on Miscreateds store page (second screenshot). For the last year or so I had a positive review up here and as much as I hate it, I feel like it doesn't do the game justice anymore. But still - if you're into these kind of games it might be worth the money for you, but prepare to be let down once you get deeper into this game.
So I got this game pretty much just after its release late in 2014 and it was quite a rough start. Very small map, huge performance issues and not much to do. But right from the start this game and its devs were different. It looked pretty, the devs were (and still are) very active and patched this game frequently. They solved a lot of performance issues, added a lot of new content and kept talking to their quite small community.
Sometime in 2015 they released a freebuild-basebuilding system that alows you to create very unique bases, as every part can (and has to) be placed and adjusted individually, so no snaping baseparts like in Rust, H1Z1 or pretty much every other game in this genre. I loved this basebuilding feature so much, that I spent about 70 hours to build a single base, which even made it into their store page screenshots. The system had it's issues, but I thought to myself "hey, this is early access, it'll improve over time, just like other stuff they fixed before".
Then a lot of sales started, it felt like half of the time in early 2016 the game was on sale for 9,99€, which finally got the devs what they wanted and of course every game needs - a large playerbase. And from this point, it all went down pretty fast and and this game got ruined.
It seemed and still seems like the majority of (young) players are only looking for one thing: Destroying the gaming experience you have and kill everything that moves. If you were not on a strictly PVE server, everyone in this community, which was back in the days so special and friendly, would just kill you on sight or betray you by pretending to be friendly and shoot you in the back. I know this is typical behaviour for a lot of people who play online, so why do I blame the devs for this?
Because they encourage this behaviour in any way they can! The last couple of patches have just been filled with guns, grenades and other PVP stuff, even though this game has so many guns already and desperatly needs survival content, which just isn't there. There is literally NO challenge in surviving in Miscreated. Mutants are no threat as they are stupid, most of the time slower than you and usually don't appear in a group, supplies are a joke (in over 800 hours I wasn't close to starvation or dehydration once!) and there isn't anything to do when it comes to survival (sicknesses, temperature, personal character development etc.). Why should I hunt a deer, collect it's meat and build a campfire to cook it? There is food around everywhere, why bother? This is not a survival game, this is a giant deathmatch arena.
Another example of how the developers encourage "bad" behaviour: To get into a base and destroy baseparts, you only need a melee weapon(!!), which you'll find in less than 2 minutes after spawning. You can only build wooden walls/gates and they are not strong at all. So even if a person needs to break down multiple walls to get to the storage box of someone else, it'll still be way faster to just do that and steal all of their stuff than actually going into the cities and scavange. So what's the solution 3 out of 4 players come up with to protect their stuff? They build floating bases. Cause once a base part is placed, you can remove the parts under it without the upper part falling down, so no gravity. By now about 85% of the bases on regular servers in Miscreated look like♥♥♥♥♥♥ because they are floating in mid-air or are abandoned because they've been looted and destroyed multiple times a day. Instead of fixing issues like that, basebuilding just sits in the game and is not focussed on at all.
Half of my steam-friendlist contains people I met in Miscreated, mainly from the earlier days. So many good people, such great adventures we had. This is all over now, I talked to a lot of these players and most of them have the exact same opinion. I guess that the problem these devs will have to face is, that once people get bored of their endless deathmatch-rounds they will move on, whatever that means for Miscreateds playerbase. And please don't get me wrong, I like intense PvP fights, it's part of a survival game. But it's supposed to be just a part, not the entire game and all there is to do.
When I was a dev-tester I was connected to the dev-team through skype and of course I won't tell anything out of these conversations. But I want to say one thing: Most of them seem like really friendly, down to earth people. But whenever I mentioned these problems I didn't get an answer or they just didn't agree, which I can not understand as these issues concern core elements of a survival game. Of course I accept their opinion, it's their game and if they want to go that path I wish them all the luck in the world and I really mean it.
But my high hopes for an intense SURVIVAL game have turned into a huge disappointment from a plain deathmatch simulator with nothing but PVP elements.
This game rocks. Buy it. Buy it now.

Good art, good music. Story is a bit mediocre at best, and other than the units, factions don't feel like they differentiate themselves from eachother too well lore-wise. But god, the gameplay.
This is made for controller. Now this isn't necesarrily a bad thing, other games like Halo Wars make it work, but this feels awkward. There is no free camera roam, it's locked onto your moba-esque leader the enitre time. As an RTS veteran going back to Dune, I found this totally annoying, especially considering that the enemy can attack from multiple places at once, and that you can't micro all too well. About 5 missions in I lost 5 times in a row and that was me already decided not to torture myself anymore. Sorry, the gameplay just isn't fun. There's little penalty for your leader dying, so the AI just constantly yolo into your base and Army, and while the game has a basic tutorial, I think an advanced one woud do a great deal better. But I'm guessing because the gameplay is so shallow that's why there isn't one.
An RTS that you can pick up and learn all the basic controls in the space of 30 minnutes means that there's little to master there. All it comes down to is figuring out what units your up against and countering. The most basic of RTSs do this, and most do it far better.
Base management is simplified to the point where there's little sense of satisfaction to doing it well. And your economy buildings stop working altogether after they've generated a certain ammount of recources. While this works in game, because you can have high tier tech by then and go bulldoze your enemies, the end game here from what I've seen is jsut getting spammed to death and then repaeting the level. Commanding units isn't fun or satisfying. There's no vetrancy (As far I know), because again, this is a shallow real time strategy.
Good work on the score and the art, but everything else just isn't to my taste, and many RTS vets will probably find it the same. Dissapointed to say the least, I was expecting a lot more.

Tooth and Tail isn’t your typical RTS, instead of a rare breed: those who attempt to take the RTS format and adapt it for controllers. Surprising to absolutely nobody, this never works out as well as you’d think and you end up having to cut features and simplify your gaming experience so that it’s accessible for the controller. If you try and keep all your features intact with little to no simplification then you end up with something a little like halo wars, which was an extraordinary RTS but I feel would have been inarguably better had it stuck to a normal control scheme. I feel similarly with Tooth and Tail, though I will admit that the way they adapted it works really well with the game’s theme, as well as with the changes they made to RTS gameplay. That’s what kinda bums me out, there’s endless potential with Tooth and Tail and I feel that while the developers realized a majority of said potential, they hamstrung themselves by trying to build the game for controllers. A perfect example of this is how indescribably frustrating the attack controls are. Since they built the game for controllers they had to absolutely eviscerate the controls, now only giving you two real controls for your soldiers: left click for giving orders to one unit type, and right click for ordering all units. This seems great, as if they found a way to successfully simplify RTS controls, except since you can’t use the mouse they had to find another way to allow you to perform actions like attacking. Now it gets rough, because you can only order your units to attack highlighted targets, and the targets that are highlighted are selected based on distance from you. So if you want to attack a turret, you have to stand close enough for it to be selected and then hit right click, which means that it’s impossible to attack one specific unit in a crowd of enemies because the highlight is too unpredictable. This isn’t the only problem that Tooth and Tail has, there’s also the issue of how the campaign levels are generated. Every mission in the campaign has the same objectives, but each time you play it generates a new map seed, meaning you’ll never get the same map layout twice. This is a unique idea that I haven’t ever seen done in an RTS before, and now I know why: it creates a chasm of unpredictably fluid difficulty. I’ve had missions that were extraordinarily easy, then gone back and replayed those missions only to get curb-stomped because the enemy AI got a better spawn this time. I’m kinda mixed about this because while it creates problems with difficulty, it also means every level is a new experience and adds just about endless replayability. Having this unpredictability also means that if you’re having trouble with a mission, you can just keep trying and eventually get a map that may allow you to finally beat it, which takes the pressure off on some of the tougher missions.
Understand that I love Tooth and Tail, I just feel like the RTS genre is absolutely not for controllers, and trying to force that in only weakens what otherwise is an absolute gem of a game. Now that I’ve finished with all the negatives, the eviscerated control scheme, the poor system for giving orders and all that, I’d like to get into the treasure trove of fantastic features this game has. The one you’re going to notice right off the bat is gonna be the artwork, good god the artwork is so incredible. It’s definitely not easy to manage an appealing pixelated look, but I can tell you for a 100% certainty that they flawlessly pulled it off, every battleground is a work of art, every unit a masterpiece. Every RTS has its share of unique units that manage to leave a lasting impression on you: the Thor and Ultralisk from Starcraft II, the Avatar of Khaine from Dawn of War, the priest from Age of Empires II, all of them memorable. Tooth and Tail is no different, except in the fact that every single unit is memorable, not just a few of them. Having animal units opens up so many fun options to make unique and memorable units, like grenade-firing gas masked skunks, or trench-club wielding chameleons, even ferrets hefting massive artillery cannons on their backs. That may be my favorite part of Tooth and Tail, the animal warfare theme makes for an unforgettable RTS experience that provides a fresh take on strategy games. Not only is the art direction absolutely flawless, the music is extraordinary too. I was surprised to be hearing a AAA quality soundtrack in this small indie game, one that perfectly fits every scenario, from resource building to the down and dirty battles. On top of the solid art direction, the gameplay, while suffering from the aforementioned control simplification, is action-packed and extraordinarily enjoyable. I haven’t really delved too deep into the multiplayer, so I can’t speak as to its quality, but I can tell you that there seems to be a significant community around this game that’s keeping the game living and matches easy to find. The campaign is quite a bit of fun, Tooth and Tail is not only unique in its controls, but also in its approach to game length, with most games lasting 10-12 minutes at the absolute most. This means that each game is significantly more action-packed and has less down time, something that I think works well with all the other changes introduced. Overall, while I do have a massive problem with how they handled the controls, every other aspect of the game is beautiful and the campaign, while short, is an exceptionally enjoyable RTS experience.
Even with the controls having been gutted, Tooth and Tail is a refreshing take on RTS games with some of the best unit and general art design that the genre has to offer.

Tooth and Tail is a fun RTS game that's easy to learn and hard to master. I'm one of the better players out there (maybe top 5%) and I can tell you that it was no easy feat getting to this point. This game is sure to last you hundreds of hours, with a fun story mode that challenges even the best players and a nice multiplayer mode, with Ranked, where you earn points with each victory and lose points with each loss in competitive 1v1s, and Unranked, where you can play 2v2s, 2v1s, 3v1s, and 3 and 4 player FFAs. To make it easier for you, I'll just make bullet points of pros and cons for you.
Pros:
-Little to no lag on most computers
-Amazing soundtrack
-Interesting storyline
-Random map generation (This makes more diverse games, and while most of the maps favour one player above the rest, this forces you to improvise and honestly, I believe it adds to the intensity)
-Lots of strategy diversity
-Fast gameplay (Lessens the blow of losing and means that most games can be turned around in mere seconds)
-Interesting language
Cons:
-Random map generation can sometimes make you super♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥if you're having a bad day (Bad spawns happen. You're not alone.)
-Ranked matchmaking system: A person that is Rank 5 could face up against a Rank 40 player.
-Pixelated graphics that some may dislike
-Some story mode missions just seem impossible to do
Overall, I definitely reccommend Tooth and Tail if you're looking for a decent, low priced, fast-paced RTS.

Tesla Effect has it's ups and downs. On the ups, are some great mood building with lighting and barren-like set design. The FMV sequences play out like your usual 90s borderline cringe, but the plot makes up for it all. For the most part, the plot device of Tex Murphy's amnesia works well, it gives newcomers enough reason to not know what's going on, but I feel it lets down seasoned Tex Murphy fans in a way, as Tex is always playing catchup with everything, rather than being full on Tex.
Puzzles in this game swing wildly between "what, this thing moves way too fast and the graphic design of this puzzle gives me a migraine" to "flip some switches randomly and you'll get it". Interactive bits and bobs you pick up around the environment are sometimes pixel-thin and hidden by the environment, either caused by badly textured or poorly art-designed props. It's really unfortunate this Tex Murphy has transcribed the "pixel hunt" problems from 2D adventure games to a 3d environment.
Yet, despite the hair-pulling wobbly quality standard applied to puzzle and art design, there's a fun game here, with characters I found to be quite charming. Tex's attitude is just the right blend of serious and blundering detective PI that I like and his amnesia does allow for some choice observations. I only would have wished more time and effort could be put into fleshing out the street level, possibly building out the level to have more tiers of puzzles on the block, rather than mostly running between shops talking to the store owners.
Overall, if I had to score this one, it would be a
, it's a fun romp through the story, but is not consistent in the level of quality it gives gameplay wise.

This game is a must for any character creation fanatic like myself.
The color choice isn't the greatest, but you can make some truly unique avatars in this game to fit any sort of theme you imagine.
And the fact that you get to fully customize 2 characters you can truly plan or come up with some very fun duos. Whether it's your own little backstory, or just a pair that look/work amazing together.
Now for the gameplay.
The controls are easy and intuitive for the most part.
Every class (vocation) has it's own unique playstyle and I'd say there is a class for everyone (I myself am a fan of more stealth/ranged based combat). The skill system is easy to use and offers a good variety in play styles even within individual classes.
Leveling and progressing are never really an issue since a good hour of monster hunting will almost always be plenty to make significant progress along your class.
As for the combat itself, it's very reminicent of games such as Monster Hunter and Darksouls. With each enemy having it's own weakness/opening for you to exploit and unique fighting style for you take into consideration, the combat is varied.
The bosses make for some great fights as well. As I've said it's very reminicent of Darksouls and Monsterhunter, meaning they can be quite the challenge. Most bosses have attacks that can flat out one shot you or nearly do so, and are almost invulnerable with very specific weaknesses or hit zones.
However the best thing about the bosses is that they are FAIR. No matter what level you are, if you are good enough or persistent enough you CAN defeat any boss. At the same time, you can't just yolo farm for 4 hours and come into a boss fight without a care in the world. They don't have any "BS" moves that you can't avoid and are not completely imune to damage. You can always damage them if you know where to hit, and you can dodge everything if you pay attention.
As an example I defeated an Ogre while I was only level 8 (Not tricking it to falling of a cliff either, just kept shooting it full of arrows for over an hour)
The graphics are alright. They look good where they matter, but they don't have an INSANE level of detail.
The sound track is great and defintely sets the mood, whether you're chilling on a road or going face to face with a Griffin.
Finally the open world part of the game is truly great. You never feel as if you only have one choice, or that you're forced to do anything. You can just walk around, clear dungeons and craft gear at your own pace.
Also the "random" events that take place. While they only happen in specific zones, you never really know when they're going to happen. So it just adds an extra layer of unpredictability to the game.
I still remember nearly sh!tting myself the first time a Griffin showed up out of nowhere.
All in all, it's a great game for anyone who feels like spending a good couple hours just doing their own thing.

There's Terraria, which is a great game.
Then Starbound came along to be greater in all respects. There were amazing promises about all the features and so on and it sounded like it would be like Terraria, only better. The problem is that Starbound never got even good at what it wanted to be. Even worse - they changed their goals, tweaked them and so on. The development seemed extremely unfocused and so it went nowhere.
In the mean time Terraria got patches over patches and got better then Starbound at pretty much anything. Starbound was very ambitious, but never reached any of its goals. It took years and years between meaningful updates and even through those the game always just got something added which changed the game, but it didn't enrich the game.
The combat is very ambitious, but it never quite worked. The idea with various planets with various perils and dangers and things to discover is a great idea, but ultimately it's different colours for the very same biotopes over and over.
I gave this game a go several times, and it never was much fun. It disappointed in all things which were meant to elevate it over other games of the genre and what was there for basics other games did better. I don't suggest buying this.

Once you build a community you have to go out and gather ressources to survive, and don't be careless out there because you will get overrun and killed. The fighting system is really simple and fun wether you choose to go melee or use guns. You can still sneak around them, especially in the dark and score a few stealth melee kills wich is always nice. I also like how you can choose to build your community by finding more survivor, controlling certain characters to level them up and get them to learn new abilities and be stronger. You have quite a big map to explore as well, a lot of scavenging to do. You have to be carefull to keep the zombie population in check around your home base so it doesn't get overrun. The gameplay is really fun and well done. And of course, among all of that, you have a nice little quest story line that gets you to learn about what  happened and what caused all this. Ugh, i really wanted to like this game, but it's not for me. I've been a huge Baldur's Gate fan since forever ago, and i'm really happy that the genre legacy continues (since stupid Dragon Age keeps moving further and further away from it, i'm glad at least someone still tries making these types of games). But I just couldn't get into this one. I think if you're into hardcore d&d and read a ton of that kind of literature - you'll love this. For me the appeal of these games is combat and strategy and it just wasn't enticing enough here. I got so bored towards the end that i rushed through everything, skipping through every dialog.
On an unrelated note i thought it was funny that they had that combat music that's pretty much straight out of De-Arnise keep (BG2). And Twin Elms had a theme that was very Kuldahar (Icewind dale).
Pros:
Baldur's gate gameplay.
Story is not stupid and cheesy.
You can create your own party and not have to use official companions.
There is a bit of that keep management stuff (although not much).
Decent amount of content.
Some interesting combat ideas but read on for cons because those mechanics get meh further into the game.
Party members have decently unique personalities. Even the bland♥♥♥♥♥elven mage was spiced up with a secret.
Cons:
Wayyyy too much reading: paragraphs and paragraphs of text on every dialog. That may be a pro for some people, but i've read enough in my lifetime and i'm tired of it.
Combat mechanics too complicated (too many different defenses/resistances/stats/conditions, it may not be more complicated than modern d&d rules but d&d rules have been building up slowly for a long time, while this game just jumps straight into complicatedness.) And i either never found much explanation on how stuff works as far as damage application goes, or i found it and it was more paragraphs of text and i got bored reading it.
Party members join up too easily and will never leave you, so there wasn't that much roleplaying with them, and also no alignment thing that dramatically restricts how the world perceives you, (yeah yeah there is reputation with different factions but i didn't notice much gameplay difference with that).
Unique items: that's one of the main complaints i have. They weren't amazing enough or hard enough to get. I want stuff like Carsomyr +5 (BG2). You had to kill one of the hardest enemies in game for it, and only a specific class could use it, but once you get it - it makes a huge difference, (and then you can go after Kangaxx! :P). Here - i got so many clutter drops from enemies and every once in a while there was a small upgrade but it never really made a big enough impact.
Anyway, overall this is not a bad game, and if Steam used a number rating i'd give it a 7 out of 10 maybe. But i didn't love it, i have no desire to replay it, and i wouldn't recommend it to any of my friends. It was like going to steak and shake late at night. Nothing else is open, and the milkshakes are good, but the service was mediocre at best and if I had a choice - i would have gone somewhere else.

WARNING BEFORE YOU BUY THIS GAME;
TL;DR - Incredible gameplay and story, with heartbreaking loading times FOR SOME COMPUTERS. Download a third-party mod to disable auto-saving for a semi-fix.
Due to the auto-save feature requiring the saving of extremely large file sizes (gets worse as the game progresses) each time you load up a new or old area or even a house within that area there is a 1-2min load time. Sounds small, but there are a lot of areas in this game.
This is so bad that there is a fairly successful mod designed to simply enable the ability to turn off the autosave feature - this mod has been updated 73 times (upon writing this). A simple fix of allowing the option disable the auto-save feature would make this game playable without mods.
Note that mods are made redundant with each new update to the game - avoid updating the game until the mod is updated...
THIS DOES NOT APPLY TO ALL COMPUTERS - check online first to see if someone else has had this problem with your system. I experienced this on a fairly old Mac, however I've read this happens with better systems as well. A quick bit of research could save you 20-50 bucks.

When I first played Sonic CD a little more than a year ago, I disliked it and wrote a negative review. The reason for my disliking of the game stemmed from the fact that I thought that Sonic CD had some of the worst level design of any of the 2D Sonic titles. While I still find the general level design to be lacking, I decided to give the game another shot recently and found it to be enjoyable.
Pros:
- Features some of the best music of any Sonic game
- The special stages are a lot of fun and really unique
Cons:
- The level design is all over the place and feels a bit "gimmicky"
- With just one or two exceptions, the bosses are all humorously easy to defeat
The game is pretty short. I finished it in about two hours, but you could finish it even sooner depending on how well-versed you are with classic Sonic titles. It took me about 10 hours total to unlock all of the achievements, so your mileage may vary depending on how much of an achievement hunter you are.
In short, Sonic CD is a fun game, but sports inconsistent quality of level design. Still, if you're a Sonic fan like I am, you're likely to have a good time if you give this game a chance.

Dark souls is a brilliant game. It's a wee bit clunky if you're coming from DS3 or Buldgeborn but once you get back into it, it's still as good as ever. Beautifully varied areas, enemies, weapons and armours all painted with a delicious blend of historical realism and high fantasy, bathed in a bleak light for about 4 hours.
I could prattle on about "muh difficulty" but everyone's done that for me. I'd seriously recommend this game to anyone who wants a decent challenge all the while exploring a seemingly barren and twistedly beautiful fantasy world.
The replay value, I find, is immense due to how many different builds you can try out each time just for aesthetic appeal, challenge or just for the chance to have a different perspective on the gameplay. Some of the clues and areas are a bit more cryptic than later games and can be a bit frustrating, but I still think it's worth it.
It's not perfect, but there's definetely a reason such a large and dedicated fanbase has sprouted up around this game and its sequels (prequels too if you count demon souls)

Wow. I would enjoy liking this game, but they make it SO hard to even practice, it's a complete turn-off.
So it's a dogfighter like War Thunder, but you can hover. The two different "modes" of flight are just hover and boost from what I can tell, so it's not really difficult to learn that. However, boost flight is so unstable and cumbersome, and the tutorials just dump you in to figure out flight and weapons yourself. The tutorial is truly just a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ campaign with no voice acting, and the only tips come up on the side. Because when I'm flying at 2000 near-deaths per second, I'm capable of reading these tips on the far side of the screen.
Weapons aren't introduced in any way, and it seems pretty clear that lock-on is the way to go. Maybe there's counters to that, but it seems like slow-firing precision weapons aren't going to work well when everyone is boosting around. And then someone gets on your tail, and you can't shake them. The hover ability is kinda pointless, as everyone that has played a shooter of any kind knows, standing still is standing dead. Mobility is survival, so you need to keep agile. But other shooters with feet, ground, and gravity at least let you turn around to fire at your chaser while you both jump and dodge off walls as fast as possible.
I know I didn't put much time into the game, but it was just a major turn-off. It's trying to evoke Unreal Tournament, War Thunder, or even Planetside, and it just makes me want to play those. And come on, did Quake or UT have a massive learning curve? Even Tribes was fair to pick up and play, and the worst player of the bunch could at least pick up some kills. Why even bother putting in a tutorial if it's intentionally going to be♥♥♥♥♥♥ So many other games offer the feeling of mastery and improvement mentioned in the description, but don't do so in a manner to turn players away immediately.
Maybe games were this bad and unwelcoming back in the day, but we didn't have masses of alternatives available. Simply, there are so many better games than this. Maybe it improves with dedication, but why waste $5 or more along with many hours on a game that has maybe 100 players? It's dead in under a year, for these very problems of never attracting people and turning the few interested players away. Yes, some people will praise it for not being CoD or Battlefield; I have news, there are many other shooter games out there that are also not CoD. I'll be enjoying some classic FPSs instead, since I could play 10 FPS games from 10 years ago with larger populations than this game has DURING FREE WEEKEND.

SC:Blacklist combines the finest elements of the previous titles of the series, and for me it is the best Splinter Cell so far, even topping Chaos Theory.
The enemy AI is wonderful, for example I really liked how the enemies notice if one of their  teammate gets missing. If you get noticed, the enemy squad will switch to patrol mode permanently, and the only way to reset the situation is to move on to the next area, which is really neat and refreshing compared to normal 'alert mode and cooldown' -system. The AI perception gets quite sensitive on harder difficulties, but the cover diving mechanic exploits the sightlines compared to how the enemies would normally see you, you can do a cover dive right next to an enemy and he doesn't necessarily get to react to it at all.
The cover and climbing system is not the simplest one; during the first missions you will probably do some shenanigans you weren't intended to do, but shortly Sam will start to follow your orders as you want him to. More complex than in Assassin's Creed, but due to that it's very reliable once you get a hang of it.
Stun weapons were overpowered, there was no need for a gun once you got the gas and electricity based weapons that were silent, accurate and reliable one hit KOs. The strenght of the gadgets would be okay if the ammo was scarce, but it's plenty since many different tools contain similar gas and electric properties, for example you can have both gas grenades and a rifle with a gas grenade thrower with you at the same time. It is even possible to restock all your ammo and gadgets in certain drop-off points during the missions. Due to this the first couple of the missions were the most exciting to go through 'cause your weapons and tools were limited. You're not forced to equip the best stuff, but the temptation is still there.
The Perfectionist difficulty denies the restocking during missions, so if you're looking for the best experience and don't mind the harsh difficulty, go for that.
The huge list of keyboard bindings might be overwhelming at first, but since a lot of functions overlap each other, not many keys are needed. Several keys have a double function whether the key is either tapped or held down (which is logical and clever btw), but it just gives you an option to bind it individually. Just let the game teach you first and change the buttons as it's telling you the control system.
Base menus could be clearer, story is meh, characters are memorable though.

Hello all ! Lemme first start of by telling you that I have been a fan of the Warriors series (Samurai, Dynasty and Orochi) by the same developers for about 7 years now. So lemme just assure this to fellow fans of the series. This game is right at home among the other games. Just graphically superior and Liu Bei is even more annoying now. Now for rest of you,kiddies....
Pros
- Rush of adrenaline as your scythe your way through 1000's of normal enemies till your fight an officer. I kid you not. 1k KOs per each stage, I promise you.
- Game set in romanticised ancient China. A refreshing setting to be sure.
- Hypothetical maps which can be unlocked if you against the historical facts and fulfill certain conditions.
- Ambition mode, higher difficulties and weapons collection adds to a lot of replayability.
- Pick up and play style of game. Very easy to get into and get out in 10 mins time.
- FINALLY A LU BU CAMPAIGN!
Cons
-Ambition mode is grindy. Very much so.
- No straight forward descrtiption  on how to complete optional challenges for the stages. Alt-tabbing to a WIki (or the logical equivalent) very much needed.
- Ranged weapon attacks (knives and Lianshii's) suck unless upgraded.
- Weapon Fusion is more costly now and requires 'Gems' instead of money. Which you will receive from slogging through Ambition mode. Speakin of which...
- Ambition Mode is a pain to play continuosly through. Enemies just get tankier, requiring more time.
- No way to bring a horse into Story Mode unless you play certain characters.
- A CONTROLLER IS AN ABSOLUTE MUST! Doesnt matter which (i use a cheap 4$ gamepad,I should know!)
In Summary
Fans of the series have nothing to fear. BUY THE GAME
However, if the rest of you desire high skill gameplay, accurate history and very involving storylines, better search elsewhere.

Well lets start off with the Groupie fan base we got going on for this game, you got to hand it to the select die hard ones. At the drop of a hat some of the adolescent teens living in their mothers basement will attack you for disagreeing with their ideologies and their obsessive love for this lack luster game. But the base line of my honest review starts out like this....
Games been out for 2 years as Early Access (EA) title. Still no major improvements to the wonky but vast map to include AI, gun play is lackluster (5+ shots with a handgun, 3-4+ shots with rifles even head shots, and 2 mind boggling head shots with a shotgun at point blank range to kill someone). The loading and swapping of ammo is unique in this game which is also its downfall as you have to find ammo and magazines for use in said weapons (standard) but you have to drag and drop them into the gun slot and if not done even when the magazine is in your inventory you will not be able to shoot.
While roaming through the maps and towns the landscape is well done and even some of the developments/towns, but it still isn't enough to overlook the interiors of said areas and the lack of AI. Around 50-60% (which is decent amount) of interiors are finished but the remainder are vast empty rooms with no loot and bad textures. To further elaborate on the loot, most areas and buildings have little to no loot in them and most of what you find is useless at begining stages (very limited space). You can only carry so much in the game slot and weight wise (which makes finding a backpack crucial) but what you do find is a tedious chore to swap out and or drop as it can still be buggy when doing so.
AI and hit registration is very very horrible when fighting mutants, wolves (that look like a really bad "Miscreated dogs"), successful hits on the wolf/dogs do not register 70% of the time, bullets go right through them and even their behavior is erratic and confusing. Most wolf/dogs run in gigantic circles and terrible loops that make it seem like they're completely lost in the sauce and code, they dont attack in packs or succession just sporadic bursts and most of the time overshoot their attacks (just like most of your attacks are unsuccessful when trying to kill them). Mutants feel like clunky big blocks of meat that do decent amounts of damage but have horrible animations when doing so.... I can literally go on but this has taken enough of my time.
Oh, and PVP would be great in the game with some updates to hit registration for weapons and actual damage to reflect weapon types correctly, but once again it falls flat just like the game...
Best part of the game... Great Running simulator, but a big waste of time even with a group.
Still would give the game a 10/10 just for the mess that they call their down syndrom wolf/dogs

This game has some potential, and I really hope the developers can pull it off. But, honestly, in its current state, this game sucks. There's really nothing much to do in it, and there are a lot of fundamental problems with pacing and gameplay. Islands are much too far apart, too small, and virtually identical. The inventory is also much too small to want to bother with crafting. And crafting itself is annoying and currently involves throwing a group of random items on the ground and hoping you come up with a recipe.
There also currently only seems to be one enemy in the game, the sharks, which are buggy. After being chased to land, the sharks began swimming through the sand, fins flying up the beach and through the foliage. I know there are bound to be a lot of bugs at this stage of game development, but with only one enemy in the game, I would expect the sharks to have proper collision and clipping with the islands.
I'll try this game again later in its development cycle, but as it stands, it is just not fun to play.

I was sick of zombie games, the last one I played was the reddead zombie dlc. They put zombies in my war games and western games, they're everywhere so I swore them off....until now! A Zombie survival RPG/Sim done right was exactly what the genre needed.

There's Terraria, which is a great game.
Then Starbound came along to be greater in all respects. There were amazing promises about all the features and so on and it sounded like it would be like Terraria, only better. The problem is that Starbound never got even good at what it wanted to be. Even worse - they changed their goals, tweaked them and so on. The development seemed extremely unfocused and so it went nowhere.
In the mean time Terraria got patches over patches and got better then Starbound at pretty much anything. Starbound was very ambitious, but never reached any of its goals. It took years and years between meaningful updates and even through those the game always just got something added which changed the game, but it didn't enrich the game.
The combat is very ambitious, but it never quite worked. The idea with various planets with various perils and dangers and things to discover is a great idea, but ultimately it's different colours for the very same biotopes over and over.
I gave this game a go several times, and it never was much fun. It disappointed in all things which were meant to elevate it over other games of the genre and what was there for basics other games did better. I don't suggest buying this.

State of Decay is a thirdperson Zombie-Survival game where you have a base.
You can move your base to another location if needed. You can build some buildings like watchtower and a kitchen for bonuses or defense. You have to scavange for supplies for your group in town. Once you cleared a house you can build an outpost in almost every kind of house. An outpost kills incoming zombie hordes and there spawn less zombies in the range of the outpost. You can find other survivors and if you help them they are more likely to join you. When you killed all zombies in a house and it is marked as "safe" then you can call for scavangers so you dont need to do it yourself. The game makes fun but it gets boring after you completed the story. The Breakdown DLC is is the same as the story (without storytelling) and each level it gets harder. The Lifeline DLC brought good changes. A new map and a new story and new missions.
The game is running smoothly but the Ai has sometimes problems like being stuck at the fence of your base (i was able to push the character in the right place to get him moving correctly).
All in all i would say that everyone who likes Zombie-Survival and base-building should buy the game!

A great RPG, firmly rooted in the old-style glory years of PC gaming,

The combat intially was confusing for me. Endurance is used in a strange way; damage reduction is very mathematical; four base stats for deflecting damage, But once that's sorted out, and you get a team with different abilities, it was tactical bliss -- perhaps a tad too easy on normal difficulty.

The first "Xtreme Legends" title that released for PC, and I think it did very good  job.
Gameplay is similar like previous Warriors series from KOEI: beat up hordes of enemies using combos, finding rare weapons/animals, or leveling character to max level. About character, some of them have their "old" weapon back, e.g. Xiahou Dun using scimitar again instead of mace like in DW6. And new characters that added in DW8 or DW8: XL are quite good, their weapons, movesets, and personalities are unique and give new atmosphere to Dynasty Warriors series (my favorite new characters are Guan Yinping and Lu Lingqi).
Another new addition in this title is Ambition Mode: build a Tongquetai and raise all the facility to attract the Emperor to visit it. Ambition Mode also one of the feature that makes me hard to put this game down :D.
Besides the good points, there are also some points that still need improvement from my point of view:
1. The button prompt still using keyboard icon even if we play using controller.
2. Most of the DLC are purely cosmetic, and yet they are overpriced. That's why I only pick Japanese Voice Option for the DLC, which is free.
Overall, despite some flaws, KOEI did a good job by porting this game to PC.

I bought this game because of the good reviews, and that I heard that it was "the spiritual successor to BG" and the infinity engine. It sort of is and it isnt at the same time. The environment, puzzles, and story feel like something out your classic DnD IE game. The gameplay has a lot of new elements that don't seem similar, and I outline the most apparent of these here.
Firsr combat and fighting in this title is mostly useless. That took some getting used to. If you can stealth your way through the entire game and never fight a single monster, you could and would be almost the same level at end game. There is no xp from fights, which is hard to believe because many of the fights in this game are ridiculous hard.
Then there is the engagement system. It is kind of like attacks of opportunity but I would argue that it is still different. Once something runs into range of your character, your character gets locked down and stuck and cannot move. Pretty much any character, even your tank, that tries to disengage after that will die instantly. Enemies have unlimited number of attacks of opportunity (literaly 3 or 4 from the same target in under a second is possible), and enemies seem to have a bonus to hit when you disengage. This kind of sucks, but you learn to work with it after grueling hours spent playing and learn that there are some mechanics to manipulate it (like running around targets but not disengaging).
Lastly abilities synergize but at first dont seem to at all and seem clunky. Abilities at first to me seemed detached from one another. I'm not sure how exactly to explain this. It was like a group of individuals playing side by side instead of a team. As the game went on this feeling goes away as you get more abilities with more uses (and even some group oriented abilities!).
My conclusion, is that if you are BG1 & BG2 fan this game will hit you in the facve hard, and you will wonder what the hell is going on for the first few hours. I hated this game for the first 10 hours I played it (I even wrote a negative review initially). I kept rerolling and starting again (Wizard -> Cipher -> Min Maxed Cipher -> Chanter) until I found something I was ok playing with. This game has definetly grown on me and I enjoy it, but it took a while to get over the new mechanics and gameplay style. Still, it is a worthy buy, and a lot of fun.

It says I have 200 hours but believe me I have way more than that because I tend to play this in offline mode a lot.
The game's a large sandbox-like story based game where you have three different paths: The Prajna, The Shogunate and the Foreigners. Each one has their own assortment of interesting and layered characters and the cast usually has very many over the top and hilarious moments including moments of grim and seriousness which the game pulls both of these kinds of moments off very well. The writing of the characters, their dialogue and story is done extremely well. Hell, even the side characters are extremely well written.
The combat on the other hand has its mixture of ups and downs. On the upside it can feel satisfying to murder many of the locals with your own set of combos from the style of fighting you made or one you've found. It relies heavily on pulling off combos and launching enemies to combo into more things. The problem becomes all the enemies are literally the same and I don't mean that in the sense of there's a small pool of enemies you fight I mean all the enemies are pretty much the exact same (except for the unkillable dogs in that one side mission, they're the real final boss of this game)and the fact that they like to hold block a lot instead of attacking doesn't help either. Likewise the game starts to turn into a grind fest of getting enough scrap and gold to max out the stats on your weapon and leveling up your combat styles. Or you can do what I did after I (accidentally) deleted my save data and just cheat a bunch of money and buy move scrolls.
As for some of the pros and cons I've made a short list
(+) Very well made story
(+) Incredibly well written characters
(+) Fun combat
(+) Enslaving the locals to run laps eternally at your dojo
(+) Hardcore BDSM if you're into that
(+) Bitesized Solid Snake levels to find your one night stand
(+) Best sex scene in all of game history
(+) Replayability
(+) Kicking children
(+) Going to school with your edgy friend and be obnoxious (Hey, it's just like middle school all over again)
(+) Trust no one, not even yourself
(+) There's a character called megamellons
(+) Sensei best girl
(+) Moro is secretly best character
(-) Combat gets repetative
(-) Additionally, some missions just become kill a bunch of dudes which gets really boring
(-) Becomes a grind game if you're going to master all the styles and what not
(-) Animations look pretty janky
(-) Sometimes your immersion will just break
(-) Crashes sometimes and it becomes a real pain in my crotch
(-) Game's locked at 30fps but that should be obvious
(-) Samurai police are a pain in the behind
(-) Okay seriously the one submission with all the dogs is a special kind of hell
(-) Old man needs to pay his god damn tax
(-) Don't romance the loli or I'll call the police

Incredibly Satisfying and Amazingly Tense.
When you first see Throne Of Lies, it intrigues you. It looks interesting, but you don't know if you'd like it. Well I can tell you, you will like it.
The game is great and supported by an even greater community. Many players get extremely immersed in the role play this game has to offer. I've had Kings speaking with a 16th centure tounge, People slagging each other off in shakespearen - the lot. On the screen where you're choosing a custom name to use within the game you can often create a small group of 'related meme players' as I call them. For example:
A player called themselves Bread.
I called myself Toast.
Someone else called themself Bread Crust.
And so on. The community is truly one of a kind.
Playing as the Blue Dragon (Or BD for short) is very satisfying in most cases. Finding that one cultist, Unseen or Neutral Killer and telling everyone else about it can feel awesome - especially when you're right. When you're not right you'll feel awful and usually get executed straight after. But you can't blame 'em, In this game you can't trust anyone. Unless you're evil:
Playing as the Unseen, Cultists or as a Neutral Killer can be great. As the Unseen or Cultists you can see directly who is with you as you will gather at night and can communicate in private. As the Unseen or Cultists your objective is to: "KIll all members of the Blue Dragon / Convert members of the blue dragon and remove any neutrals that wish to harm you." This objective is awesome. It allows for many, many varities of playing ensuring that no game is either the same. Winning a game will make you feel like a true leader, assassin or just plain killer. It's great.
While you're playing the other neutral roles the game can be very tense. The same goes for most Blue Dragon roles such as the Knight or Sheriff. As the Sheriff you need to work as fast and as well as possible to discover members of the Unseen or Cult - if you don't you may look suspicious to others as you have no proof to back up your claim of being a sheriff. As the neutral roles you will usually try your best in order to make yourself look good. Fail, and you get executed - it's very tense. However, you win as long as you've completed your objective.
Lastly, the price of this game is perfect. It allows players in who really want to play - and keep the vast majority of griefers and trollers out (Unless that's your role :D). It's really a one of a kind game and can be compared to the hugely popular Town Of Salem - the only thing is that Throne Of Lies has WAY more depth than Town Of Salem ever did. For the developers I only hope that this game gets more popular, it is a great one.
If you're unsure, just try it - You won't regret it.

I was a hard sell, since I played Town of Salem and I was very skeptical this would be worth the money. But I can honestly say this game is a much better version of Town of Salem. Unlike Town of Salem there are no 'dead weight' roles who have nothing to do every day/night.
Lets compare Town of Salems 'Jester' to Throne of Lies' 'Fool'. They have the exact same win condition, they want to be executed during the day. The 'Jester' has no abilities and has to resort to trying to either be annoying or overly suspicious to get lynched. Most of the time this means you just get killed by evils at night. In Throne of Lies however, the Fool has the ability to 'Trollbox' a player. This sends a message during the day as another player and that player doesn't see the fake message. This can be very fun and useful to convince everyone you're dangerous; especially if he's a confirmed role. The 'Fool' can also appear guilty at night(2 uses) to investigative classes and hide(2 uses) to be immune.
This is a very basic example of how the game has stepped up and genuinely impoved upon the playability of the various classes.

If you like Werewolf, Mafia, or any other hidden role game, you'll love Throne of Lies. The pace moves just quick enough through the phases to keep interested and the roles vary enough to make false claims more powerful. Love the Journal/Deathnote/Private note parts of it as well.

Throne of Lies is a game about lying, funnily enough. But also about determining whether or not others are lying.
Lying well in this game requires knowledge of the classes and their abilities, since if you are evil, you must try convince the Blue Dragon (the good guys) that you're one of them.
Each class (1 of which you are randomly assigned at the start of the game) has abilities, and some limited in the amount of times they can be used. Most abilities are used during the night, such as trying to kill people, or jailing them etc. Some characters have day abilities, too.
Each player must keep a nightly journal of their activities, but of course anyone evil has to fabricate their journal so that they appear innocent when asked to hand over their logs.
During the day, if someone gets a majority "treason" vote, they get put up on trial and must quickly defend their case, which includes pasting their logs into the chat for scrutiny. You live or die here depending on your ability to lie, if bad, or others vouching for your claimed actions, if you're good. There's also the fact that the King may be evil, and he influences votes here. Many people will vote how the King says to (although you do not have to).
There's also a neutral faction, who have their own goals. Such as the Fool, whose win goal is to be put on trial and voted for execution.
I recommend this game a lot. Once you've learned the mechanics, it can become quite thrilling as you watch your web of lies grow to the point where innocents are being offed and you still aren't a suspect...
The graphics are pretty terrible (apart from the art of the character info pages). This doesn't matter for a game like this, but it's my only real complaint.
It's constantly being updated, with tweaks to abilities and new classes being introduced.
Do you like lying to people and getting away with it, in a situation that will do no real life harm? Or testing your investigative abilities? Get this game.
