Toxic Bunny is a good-looking platformer, but that is all that's positive I have to say about it. The controls are incredibly unresponsive (and the tutorial was broken) and the way the enemies work is simply absurd - I could actually just WALK by them without really suffering any damage, at least at the beginning of the game. And if you do decide to fight them, you will notice that some of them do not really care for you, while others try to attack you so furiously that their animations almost break. Not a polished title, to say the least. Which is noticeable even more when you get stuck on a normal ground and have to jump over, well, nothing.
The game also does a terrible job when it comes to telling the player what he or she should do. While the giant green arrow points toward a boss, I had no idea I should drop of freakin' anchor on him. Sure, my character would say earlier that I should find someone to drop it on, but I did try to attack other enemies in this fashion and it didn't work. I'm still not sure what was the point of it. Cool concept, bad execution. And the difference between the difficulty levels is absurd - on normal, not having dropped the anchor, I hardly scratched the boss in a fight mano-a-mano. On easy - I shot it three times and bam, boss dead. Only after that I figured out I should have dropped the anchor on him. Needless to say I was confused. And still am.
To add insult to injury, although the game looks good, the world itself is ugly. Sure, it's a TOXIC, BAD bunny, so it has to look like that, but it's ugly nevertheless. Like one of those cartoons that are supposed to be "edgy" and aimed at "bad" kids who don't do their homework, and all the jokes revolve around barfing and farts. Which brings me to my next point - the humour. While the jokes in Toxic Bunny are not as crude as in the aforementioned example, they are a) scarce, b) have hardly anything to do with Looney Tunes or Monty Python (both are mentioned in the description, and both I adore).
To sum up, the game has clunky controls, looks ugly (though it is well drawn), and the humour - and the whole game - is simply bland. It is not really worth its price, especially since there are virtually billions of better (both modern and remakes) platformers. Unless you have played them all. Or you have always dreamed of a game about an unpleasant rabbit.

As someone who loves plattformers, I thought I'd give this game a try, so I did just that and here are my first impressions.
First off: The game is a HD remake, but it is not a case of just having its resulution upped. Sprites, backgrounds etc. were updated so it looks like a relatively modern title now.After taking a look at gameplay footage of the original game though, the animations, the physics, as well as the soundtrack are the exact same, as far as I can tell. You can call it staying true to the original or developer laziness...whatever you want to call it, I won't judge you.
Before we go into the game itself, we take a look at the options first, which provide us with fully rebindable controls. The audio options are fairly standard with seperate sliders for music, sound effects and ambient sounds. The graphics options are Unity standard: Low, Medium and High as well as standard resolutions are avaiable to chose.
Another thing I'd like to mention that, even though it is stated on the store page that this game has full controller support, I couldn't get my XBOX Controller to work with this game. So that is a big issue, at least for me, because I like to play plattformers with a controller better.

As we get into the game the first thing many people will notice is that the way the momentum as well as the physics feel in that game is quite odd. So might take a little time getting used on the "oldschool" style of movement and momentum there. After playing the first level my experience with the combat is that is very shallow, which is good for new players, but it hurts the longevity of the game. Since it only  has 4 levels and I have been through the first level within 30 minutes it is safe to assume that the game lasts about 2-3 hours.
If you are an achievementhunter you might go back to some levels, but at this point I'd like to point out an issue which might take you your completionist enthusiasm. Sometimes, mostly when collecting a lot of stuff at once, it seems to me that the game is not recognizing you picking up items. Some items even take 3-4 attemps to count as collected, even though you've clearly hit it the tries before that.
Speaking of hitbox issues, the hitbox of walls as well as the ground when you try to shoot enemies takes a lot of getting used to.
For both issues you'll see examples in the video, I've made.
Another issue I've encountered is that I don't see what potion currently is active, which was the case when playing the tutorial. In the game itself it is not shown though. It seemed to me that the potion mechanic is not working properly, but this could be my mistake.
Other than that I have to say that the potion mechanic sounds nice in theory and it's a shame, I couldn't see it in action.
Finally the question of questions: Is the game worth it?

I've been playing this game since it first appeared on Steam and I still find myself returning to it on a regular basis. State of Decay is a game in a very over-saturated genre. We live in the age of the zombie and everywhere you look there are zombie films, TV shows and games. However, SoD is not just another survival horror game, in fact... it's not really survival horror at all. I would classify this game as an "action, zombie-apocalypse simulation" game. What do I mean by simulation? Well, in this game you are given the task of joining a group of survivors in the early days of a zombie outbreak and it is up to you to ensure their survival. To that end you have to establish a home-base, contact survivors to join your group and scavenge for food, medicine and other vital supplies. You can build facilities at your base such as a workshop to craft useful items, a medical lab to care for your sick and injured survivors and a library to research new survival techniques. But it's not all home-on-the-prairie, you will have to complete missions ranging from clearing out zombie infestations to trading goods with other survivors. Zombies abound in this game, the streets are filled with undead heads to bash in, but the zombies while numerous, are no push-overs. Get surrounded and you are in real danger and there are times when it's better to err on the side of caution and run away, or find a big bush to hide in. The recent DLC adds a lot of replayability to the game, meaning that after you've finished the main story, you can dive into a mode where the game progressively becomes harder and harder, as if it wasn't hard enough.
There are some downsides to this game however. It would benefit enormously from a multiplayer component. Playing alongside a friend would create all kinds of fun gameplay moments and it is a mystery why Undead Labs didn't find a way to accomodate this. Especially in today's gaming environment where almost every game has at least some multiplayer aspect. Also, the one map, while large and detailed, will eventually feel stale if you play the game for longer than a couple of weeks. I have reached the point now where I can almost navigate the game-area blindfolded.
So in summary, if you're looking for a fun, visceral, zombie-filled escape, then look no further. State of Decay stands out in an over-saturated genre and I can't wait for more from the developers. There's definitely room to improve, but what is there is very satisfying.

Update: decided to modify my review a bit, since it is now possible to get all the achievements in the game with the help of steam console, redownloading some files using it and a guide by one of the players. Keep in mind that it is still an unoficial way (since the game wasn't patched since i posted my review), so i can't change my attitude towards this game. All the points about bugs remain the same, just ignore the broken achievement ones.
Not sure where to start from. It's just a generic horror game with a monster and notes, but with a bit more effort put into it (it's not complete garbage). Collecting notes is optional, but they help understand the plot. Although i found at least 2 spots in chapter 3 near one of the chess pieces where picking up notes is impossible. I can see the notes but they are glued to the table and it won't let me pick them up. The solution to this is simple: die and hope the note spawns on another table where you can pick it up from. But that shouldn't be the way to solve problems in a GOOD game.
What is unique about this game is that it's constantly shifting/looping corridors, which is interesting and perhaps even fun at first, but becomes annoying and tedious later on in the game (especially when you know what you must do, but the game thinks you need to visit THAT location for the 5th time).
Another mechanic in this game is called "insanity" which makes your screen blurry/wobbly/colorful unless you take your pills. Pills spawning areas are randomly generated of course, so inattentive players may find themselves in a constant state of drunk camera. It's not an annoying effect, although some parts of it literally made my eyes hurt, especially the blurry vision.
Did I mention the game length? Well it's roughly 2 hours (blind playthrough) and less than an hour if you are speedrunning. As for me it's rather short, especially for the price it's sold, but you can always refund it if you don't like it.
The monster...Well it is there and not really annoying, but the game is atmospheric enough and doesn't need a constant threat in my opinion, but of course it is an artificial way of prolonging the game. Without it the game would be even shorter, so it's up to you to decide whether it's a good feature or a bad one.
Now for the painful part...Achievements. One of the achievements requires you to beat the game without using any light source (lighter and flashlight). Do you understand what it means? Yep 2+ hours of bumping into walls and hoping to stumble upon a door. Of course you can adjust your in-game gamma to the max, increase monitor brightness/contrast, but that barely helps and even when it does, it still hurts the eyes and is just a poorly designed achievement.
So overall i can say that this game has its flaws and bugs but a casual player might even enjoy it, especially since it's so short.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Glad I bought it and played it, but I don't think I can really recommend this to others.
* Camera effects are completely nauseating. I went to the Options to tone it down, but the Options don't really work. It wouldn't save my changes. Furthermore, you are supposed to be able to take benzos to calm the screen down, but even taking multiple pills didn't seem to have any impact. I found myself trying to get killed just to clear the screen.
* The monster materializes out of nowhere. I don't mind a tough game, but I don't want it artificially difficult. Just walking down a hallway, a sound plays, and then there he is right in front of you, completely out of nowhere. However, as I said above, it was almost a reward to get killed so the character would regain his sanity.
* I had to close and restart the game several times to allow myself to progress due to glitches; for instance, once I got trapped on the wrong side of an NPC and there was just nothing I could do.
* Due to the nature of the game (routes sometimes change) you have to walk through the same areas over and over.
Now I did think there were some nice things. Overall, I thought the sound design was nice, and I enjoyed the monster character models. The graphics, as a whole, were just average, though. I did get scared a few times by noisy jump scares, and a number of scenes made me tense, particularly BEFORE the monster was introduced.
Anyway, I did end up enjoying it, but there are just too many problems to really recommend it.

This is a great game. It allows for very fast paced RTS gameplay with up to 4 players. The campaign is nicely challenging for those who are RTS veterans yet also has enough early missions that are easy to bring players who are new to the genre up to speed. The multiplayer is fairly well rounded allowing for eaven 1v1 and 2v2 matches as well as less even 1v3 matches or 1v2 matches. There are even options to do humans vs AI. This game does of course need some work. For one, there doesn't seem to be any real reward asside from steam achievements for doing the challenges on each campaign mission. Also it would be nice if for the campaign there were options to make the AI harder or easier. There also of course needs to be some balancing especially with the map generation. Off of the many maps I have played there is generally a bias towards victory depending on where you start. Sometimes you start and have two or three gristmill expansions all very close to your first base and sometimes you have to go very far just to find one. It would be nice if the maps were more balanced so that victory didn't depend so much on where you start. Also the unit types need some balancing. Some of the units are very useful while others just don't seem worth the time. Even with all these issues however, I would still reccomend this game to any RTS enthusiast or anyone looking for a good place to learn more about the genre. The fast pace of games mean that it is great for beginners to learn about micro and macro management tactics and it acts as a good polishing stone for veterans.

This port is fantastic, and certainly better than the original PC version. This game was ported by the almighty Christian Whitehead, the guy who is currently working on Sonic Mania! He's also made two other Sonic ports for iOS and Android, and this game is also available on mobile platforms. If you are a fan of the original SegaCD version, this game is definately for you. With the new-style spindash and Tails, as well as a much better engine, this is pretty much an upgraded version of the SegaCD game! As you probably know if you've played Sonic CD on the Sega/MegaCD, it has two different soundtracks; US and JP. This game allows you to swap between them at the main menu, and also features controller support!

My favorite Sonic game of them all is the good half of Sonic Unleashed (Might be overtaken by Generations but I've only played the 3DS port). This game is now a CLOSE second. I'm not too fond of the slower pace and platforming focus of the original games but this one I love.
If you somehow didn't know, this game was made for the Sega CD add-on for the Geneses and is a real overlooked gem of the system. I had an early PC port of this as a kid but we gave it away with our old desktop but it barely works on modern computers anyways. This is the definitive version you should play because the porter, "TAXMAN", done a great job with it. You can change spin dash physics, graphics filter, and regional soundtrack (JP is better and more fitting) plus being able to play as Tails when you beat the game. There's also a save system now (I don't remember if that was in the original; I think not). So, yes, you can emulate it but it'll have problems and crap so just get this cheap but wonderful port.
The game starts with a nicely animated cutscene, that bugged out and started flickering on me, showing sonic arriving at this tiny planet that's been roboticized and chained to the ground, before dropping you off on the first level. This game plays like the other original Sonic games but now with the ability to look up and use this new kind of figure-8 dash that's way faster than the spin dash but leaves you defenseless. This new layer of speed makes this one of the fastest sonic games in that era and is very fun.
I remember, back when I had that old port, that I couldn't beat the game because I was stuck at the Metal Sonic boss and could not get past it. Now, I beat the final boss in under 30 minutes my first casual playthrough. One gripe with this game is that it's pretty short. It has over a dozen levels but they all feel short compared to the numbered games and the bosses were lame (except for the first one and Metal Sonic). Because levels are so short, the level design is more compact, clustered, and is pretty bad at points (wacky workbench is crap incarnate)  and you can usually get through them in a minute and a half BUT, if you can "crack" the stage, you can blaze through them around 30-40 seconds.
As said, this is the fastest classic Sonic game and is, without a doubt, my favorite one to do the time attack and speedrun on. This is exactly what I want out of a Sonic game: a great sense of speed that tests your memory and reflexes and make you play a stage over and over again to see if you can shave off seconds on your records. This game delivers that on almost all the levels.
Back to level design, a potential reason why they're short and whatever is because there's a future, present, and past version of each level. There's this weird time travel mechanic where you touch a future or past pole then go "88 miles per hour" for a few second before transferring to that version of the act. Sounds cool and all but it's pretty mishandled here. You have absolutely no reason to go to the future. What you're supposed to do to get the good ending in this game is to find the rarer past pole and go to the past and destroy a Metal Sonic hologram projector and a Badnick generator to create a good future (and also collect 50 rings to activate a special stage to get the Time Emeralds). Really wished this was explained in the game itself. I had to look it up on the internet. I'm currently doing all of this on my second playthrough with Tails whilst time attacking.
Other bad bits about the game would be that the menu interface are annoyingly not convenient enough (why is there no restart level button on the pause screen?). If you take the game at a slower pace, you'll find some glitches with clipping. Sonic feels a bit more slippery than the other ones. The level design loves to troll you with dead ends, loops, bait, and soullessly placed enemies and spikes. Surprisingly, there are barely any bottemless pits in this game; the only one I found was in the final few levels (which I fell into, of course).
Pro tips: I recommend playing with a controller (though the keyboard layout is solid). Also, if you're about to lose a special stage: return to main menu and the save will restart it! When you're going superspeed, jump right on upward facing curves or whatever and you can get launched into the air skipping chunks of stages. At the soundtest, place the first number at 12 and the second one at 25 and see what happens.

As good as this port is in terms of new features and accuracy in recreating the original game's physics, this isn't a very good port on PC; its interface is annoyingly slow, with transitions that take too long to begin, drag on needlessly, and hinder the player's ability to quickly navigate the menus. The game also runs very poorly in windowed mode; I'm not entirely sure why, but I experience way too much slow down in windowed mode that isn't present when in full screen. I run all the games I can in windowed borderless mode, so it's incredibly annoying to have the choice of either not being able to alt-tab and play the game normally, or to have unplayable frame rates. If you just want to play the game without interruption, this port is fine. However, if you expect to have the conveniences of having quick, responsive, and permissible interfaces most PC games give you, you're out of luck. Hopefully Sonic Mania won't have these issues, and perhaps an update could fix this title.

Are you a fan of FMV adventure games? Do you like a certain type of cheese to go along with all the puzzles? Well then, Tesla Effect: A Tex Murphy Adventure could be a worthy addition to your Steam library. It’s filled with jokes, a sarcastic protagonist, plenty of puzzles, puns, and green screen FMVs.
The store page already has a very good summary about the intro, so I’ll just mention that the game is one of those Kickstarter projects that actually made it to release and is a sequel to an old series of adventure games starring our favorite P.I., Tex Murphy. It’s also not a point-and-click style game as it makes use of a first-person camera and 3D environments.
I’d like to point out the game’s biggest weakness immediately. The graphics of the game outside of the UI and FMVs are not easily digestible for the eyes. They look very dated for a title that came out in 2014 and the first-person view lets you occasionally see some horrible textures on certain objects. The good thing is that the graphics don’t interfere with navigation or the puzzles at all. You can also rest assured that the kooky FMVs are where the game shines. Talking to the various people and seeing their reactions are a highlight of Tesla Effect and the FMV cut-scenes have a certain style to them that make me chuckle. They certainly know how to utilize that green screen and their actors.
I appreciate the game’s sense of humor and my fondness of puns increased my enjoyment. I’ve seen some humorous green screen gags, glorious overacting, and witty observations. Tex has something to say about all the observable items in the environment and his trademark sarcasm can be found everywhere. Even the vague dialogue choices during some cut-scenes will sometimes try and make you laugh. Don’t worry, the extremely important choices that can alter the path of the game and possibly the ending are usually very clear.
The game is split up into twelve days, each with their own set of puzzles. The puzzles usually involve putting items together using the Smart Alex UI (, using the correct items on objects in the environment (firewood on fireplace), or a special kind of puzzle that changes the camera angle so that you can have a better look at it. The latter has a bunch of different types of puzzles that can involve logic puzzles or inputting passwords that you’ve figured out from gathering clues. It also has its own symbol which is a puzzle piece when you move your camera over it. You can right click on it to back away or click on a “?” symbol which makes Tex explain what the goal is.
Some of the negative aspects of the gameplay can mostly be found in Day 5. Even with an item highlighting flashlight (I picked Casual mode), I had trouble locating all the tiny items that you have to find in that area. Small items can be easily missed, especially if you’re running around everywhere with Shift. Now what’s an adventure game without a notoriously bad puzzle? Tesla Effect has one of those in the form of a sliding puzzle involving two rows with ten spots and nine pieces. I managed to solve it on my own, but holy smokes, what a time consuming and boring experience.
I found the hint system to be pretty useful. It’s set up to keep track of your current, unsolved objectives which helped me remember what I was doing. You can also purchase solutions with Detective Points that you earn by examining items and exhausting topics of conversation with people. I like those type of conveniences and the puzzles I needed to buy solutions for gave me that, “Oh darn it, I should have known that.” feeling which is a good thing. I didn’t run into anything that was painfully elaborate or obtuse.
I can completely understand some people being driven away by the mediocre 3D graphics, but Tesla Effect is still one of the best modern FMV adventure games I’ve experienced. To be fair, the only other one I’ve played myself was Contradiction. Still, I enjoyed my time spent with this goofy game and had fun as a sly sci-fi P.I. guy in a world gone awry.

If you were both a mystery lover and a PC Gamer in the early 90s, the name Tex Murphy must certainly make you smile. His games felt real, the stories were fantastically well-crafted and mysterious, the characters were all engaging, sometimes funny and other times intimidating, and the puzzles made your head spin. Sadly, these games were casted into oblivion by modern pop-style blockbuster video games, were the "X" that marked the spot was as big as a planet. When I heard that the team that made the Tex Murphy adventures was back, I gave them my support, and thank god I did! Tesla Effect is certainly not a game for everyone, it has its flaws and its virtues, and that's quite alright. Do yourself a favor and play this game for all those times you wished you could live inside a futuristic dystopian movie. Put on your fedora hat and live a Tex Murphy adventure!

This is one of the most endearing games I've ever played. Some games have so much polish and feel absolutely sterile. Dragon's Dogma is a game with a boatload of flaws and almost feels like more of a fun experience for it.
This is a western-style RPG in a western setting that is unmistakeably made by Japanese people, from the unconvincing accents and manners of speaking to the goofy yet at the same time super-serious dialogue to the fact that practically everything is a reference to Berserk.
I'll start out with the good parts before I get into the flaws. There are a lot of good parts and a lot of flaws.
+This is a big game that offers a lot of exploration. If you're one of those people who rabidly dislikes the open-world craze that's sweeping through the game industry like a big, expansive virus, suck it up and play it anyway.
+The atmosphere is brilliant. You'll be running through gorgeous rolling hills (before a griffin swoops down and ruins your day), exploring dark, dripping caverns (before an ogre comes and ruins your day), and walking verdant forests (before a drake runs up and ruins your entire weekend).
+As I so subtly alluded to, there are lots of battles with enormous monsters. This game came out when Monster Hunter was huge, and you can see influences everywhere. Each battle with a really big foe feels like a genuine challenge for the first little while, and once you kill them you will hear the best quest-over music you've ever heard. There are loads of these big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s scattered throughout the landscape, and encountering them (again, on the first playthrough) will feel somewhat organic, like they're hunting in this area and you're just unlucky enough to be on their list.
+This game has a great final boss and the best endgame content I've ever seen. Unfortunately, I will not expand upon this for the purpose of avoiding spoilers.
+This game has a great soundtrack, although it's been lessened slightly on this port because it no longer has Into Free as its menu music like the PS3 version did.
However, it does have
+Bitterblack Isle. The single greatest dungeon in any game I've ever played. Every inch of this place feels permeated with danger and death. I have not yet finished it, but I will. Once you're a smug SOB who's conquered the rest of the game and feels invincible, Bitterblack Isle will smack you until you learn some goddamn humility.
+Innovative online content. This game essentially has you pimping out your follower (your Pawn, a member of a race of high-functioning autistics who follow the Arisen -you- around) to other players. You never see these players, but the adventures they have with your pawn allow him or her to gain knowledge about areas and monsters you may not have fought yet, leading your pawn to spout "helpful" hints about the beasts and areas they've encountered, even if you haven't.
+The magic system is pretty cool and in some cases fairly innovative. Yes, you have the standard fireball and lightning bolt spells, but then you have more advanced spells that use lightning as a whip your character can attack with or that creates a wall of fire that launches enemies. You can also summon a bigass tornado or a herd of meteors. This is as awesome as it sounds.
+Probably the best dragon in any piece of media I've ever played, read, or watched. Grigori is one of the coolest characters I've ever seen, and he's almost portrayed as more of an event than a character.
Now we get on to the flaws.
-The game does a really bad job of informing you about some of its key mechanics. There's a romance system in this game. I did not know that until the "final boss" (in quotation marks for a reason. Sorry, won't expand upon that), because there was little to no indication the system existed. I was "romancing" someone I had spoken to maybe four times, apparently. But more aggravating than this is that it gives you no indication of how its stat growths work. You cannot just level up your skills and class levels. As you level up, the class you're playing as at the time you level up determines what stats get the boosts. The game (to the best of my knowledge) gives you no information about this at all. So if you play to level 100 with a sorcerer and then try to play as a warrior, you will be a terrible warrior and there is no way to reverse this without deleting your save file. Did I mention you only have one save file?
-You only have one save file. This is a bit aggravating. Either you have a way to respec your class-based stat growths somehow or you have multiple save files.
-You will sometimes notice some technical issues. For example, if you're running around, you will be in a specific area before all the NPCs are loaded. This is really not that much of an issue, though.
-The pawns never shut up. This is charming for a bit, but trust me, it absolutely will get on your nerves. They only have about three different things to say about each specific enemy and situation. That doesn't seem so bad. That's a lot of lines, when you really think about it. But given the fact that you'll be fighting a lot of these enemies throughout the entire game, it doesn't seem like a lot. Yes, you can make your pawn say less through the magical behaviour modification chair (this is sounding a lot like my childhood...), but you cannot just say "almost never talk unless you have something really important to say." You can either have them say everything or say nothing.
-Not a lot of the characters are all that likeable, in my opinion. Except Grigori. That sex beast right there.
+/- This game is cheesy as hell in terms of dialogue and voice acting.
CONCLUSION:
This is a very flawed game you should definitely play, particularly if you like dragons, western RPGs, or Berserk.
Sound: 7/10 A pretty good original score with some really great and meaty sound effects (especially the ones to do with arrows hitting monsters).
Gameplay: 8/10 A bit repetitive at times, but I will never get tired of the giant monster battles, and the exploration aspect is absolutely nailed in this game. You really feel like you're exploring a dangerous frontier.
Replay value: 9/10. The endgame content, as I've mentioned, is absolutely stellar. I wish I could expand upon it, because I could write an essay on why it's so good.This is also an obsessive collector's wet dream. You can find so many weapons and pieces of armour, and lots of quests that unlock vast amounts of gold as well as golden versions of regular weapons you already have.
Plot and writing: 6/10 Honestly, it's nothing too special. The plot is kind of a vehicle that facilitates super happy adventure fun time and leads you to new areas, but sometimes it does seem like the writers pulled certain things out of their♥♥♥♥♥to make that happen.
Overall: 8/10. I may give some other games higher scores even if I don't like them as much simply because, while this is not necessarily the best of games on all of its technical aspects, it is just so goddamn charming that I can't help but consider it one of my favourites.

Pillars of Eternity was expressly created as an homage to the Infinity Engine games; the interface and beautiful painted backgrounds definitely make it look the part.  But what made games like Baldur’s Gate, Icewind Dale, and Planescape so special was more than just an aesthetic: they were vast, sprawling settings with epic stories that delivered engaging tactical encounters.  And when judged by those criteria, I feel that Pillars of Eternity is a worthy successor to carry on the legacy of the Infinity Engine.  Though the loss of the AD&D engine and settings does take some getting used to, the mechanics are solid and the world is compelling and fun to discover.  It’s an easy recommendation for fans of of the Infinity Engine and I’d also recommend it for anyone interested in an engrossing quest through a fantastic land.

This is a neato platfomer that especially since it was made by one person has a lot going for it
the good
-some really catchy music (especially when you get a powerup)
-interesting platforming
-good asthetics
-each orb to collect has a timer when you collect it to escape 1) if you lose it can be reset 2) it's a good difficulty not too hard but hard enough that some levels I had to retry (so usually timed events I hate but these were actually bearable because it wasn't too punishing if you lose)
the ok
-a lot of the levels are translucent which both makes it easy to see where to go but sometimes makes it harder to see where you need to jump to
-level size, its both a plus and minus the plus is that sometimes hitting a huge jump has you clenching your muscles and makes it a bit more tense the minus is that it takes longer to get from point A to point B
-the platforming - later on in the game you basically fly espcially if you have a power orb
the bad
- as the clock ticks down in the timed events everything gets brighter and combining that brightness with the translucent blocks there were 2-3 times I was down to the last 5-10 seconds left and I was basically blind and was guessing my jumps to escape the level
one thing that I was kinda dissapointed about but understand is that in the beginning levels you will use 1-2 types of orbs in a level but later on you use only 1 type of orb per level because they become so overpowered
oh one thing to realize that took me a bit to figure out because I went into this game blind is that there are levels within levels kinda like when you go to find a file location on a computer and you have to go into a few folders in order to find it that information should give you the mindset to help you navigate your way around to your objectives much easier (so while there are 16 orbs to collect there is more like 40ish levels in total in this game)
so yeah other then that this is a solid platformer (if you like platformers you are likely to like this one)

I have never quite played a game like this before.  Everything is about knowing when to lie and what to lie about, while untangling the web of lies that everyone else might be telling.

Think of a social deduction game like Mafia, Werewolf, Resistance, or Town of Salem, that has a medieval kingdom theme, gets consistent character/feature/cosmetics/balance updates every few days, has an awesome community and a dev team, and worth every penny of its full price. That is Throne of Lies. Is it flawless though? I can only say not yet, but it is pretty close.
There are some bugs here and there, which are getting fixed every patch. There are a few imbalanced classes as of this review's date, such as Inquisitor. This is likely to change though because if you take a look at updates section of the game, you can see the number of patches they've made thus far and see how much effort they put to make the game better.
So all in all, it's a highly addictive super fun game which has a wonderful community and hard working devs that are trying to make the game even better. 10/10 would buy at the full price again.
Edit: I recommend watching some gameplays or streams before playing though. There are 42 classes, and it is kind of hard to grasp everything before seeing how a game usually plays.
Update 13.12.2017: Inquisitor has been nerfed, and Sorcerer got a buff. It feels a bit more balanced now but we'll see.

It seems every time Dynasty Warriors join another console Techmo Koei try to start the series again from scratch by experimenting with new gameplay mechanics with often disastrous results. It's predecessor Dynasty Warriors 7 completely lacked any free flowing story, unlock-able content and was at best one dimensional. Dynasty Warriors 8: The Complete Edition however has absolutely outdone itself in terms of entertainment. The stages in the game give the player the Freedom to move around on the battlefield and use their own style of play with the characters and their Weapons for jam packed action.
The game is relentlessly entertaining allowing players to experiment with a massive veriety of Weapons, Items & Characters on every level which seems more fluid than ever thanks to a much improved graphics engine and a more diverse plot line. Unfortunately however the game does have it's flaws such as the new Storm Rush system which is based on a weapons attribute (Heaven, Earth or Man) and gives a player an advantage in battle by allowing them to endlessly spam attacks on their opponent and doesn't seem to have any real benefit besides looking like an excuse for the players to use the feature to cycle through weapons. Ambition Mode too while it contains a lot of content can get very repetitive, very quickly which is unfortunate for those wishing to unlock animals or that illusive Platinum Trophy but even taking those minor issue's aside doesn't take away the shine from what is one of the best Warriors games to date.
If you've ever been curious about the Dynasty Warriors series then there is no better game to get you started then the complete edition as it gives the full true Dynasty Warriors experience. Honorable judge, a great game.

Cons: Slightly dated graphics, and the main story line is kind of weak.
Pros:
Excellent game. It starts off feeling sort of liner, because the quests available and the path to the 'greater world' sort of is. But once you get to the capital the world branches out into several directions, and you start getting access to higher level mosters and quests at a relatively low level. I would consider this the perfect balance of hand holding and 'getting thrown into the deep end'.
The pawn system is weird. You have a main pawn that gains experience and levels, and can take equipment and skill/class customization almost identically to your main character. On top of this, you can recruit other pawns. These other pawns do not level up, and you cannot customize them. You can give them stuff/gear, but in doing so you forfeit them. As you progress in the game you generally need to replace your non-primary pawns as the level of monsters and your own level increases.
The mosters start off as very boring and not requiring much thought to defeat. But gradually, they start having elemental and physical immunities and vulnerabilities that require you to understand each monster to dispatch it quickly, or at all.
Many of the quests are indeed formulaic, like fetch, escort, and monster-quota type quests. But the escallation of reward for even these makes them engaging enough to want to tackle. On top of these formulaic quests, there are also some more intreresting quest structures that involve multiple ways to succeed, the possibility of losing the quest forever by, for instance, accidentally/intentionally killing someone, and even oblique/secret quest resolution routes that are not obvious from the quest description. There is also just a massive amount of side quests, so I feel like I will be playing this game for quite a while to come.
There seems to have been an issue with fast travel being prohibitively expensive in the past, but that's been resolved.  That they did not over-correct in their effort to make it more accessible is comendable. Fast travel is essential to a good open-world game, but the gathering and spending of money and other resources are essential to a good RPG. They did not sacrifice the one for the other.
I would rate this an 8.5/10. It could be better, but not by much. It would be worth the cost at twice its current 30 USD price.

Side missions a plenty, various types of zombie, lookout points that enable you to identify surround buildings and enemies, scavenging missions from abandoned buildings.... loads....
however, it feels clunky, and a bit dated in the gameplay. Your characters are all a bit lame, and the graphics just dont look at all like a 2013/14 title. It plays in a similar manner to grand theft auto, but the mechanics for controlling the character feel a little sludgy, slow and unresponsive. Driving cars has this annoying "zoom - in" of the screen area as you accellerate which distorts your view as you set off leading to all sorts of driving errors, its like someone takes your glasses off for a second and then puts them back on just as you are about to crash! helpful feature!
One thing i also noticed is you get offed a lot of side missions but, you dont get  a single clue as to WHERE the side mission is, and by the time you have any idea you even have one you are told you were too late. Its a bit odd not having the option of "accepting" side missions, maybe your RADIO OPERATOR could ask you if you want to check it out, then give you the co-ordinates or something so that you can see the location on map??
I dont know it just feels like it needs another look over the whole game. Great idea, poor execution. Hopefully the team will produce a sequel or something :)?
Worth a play - but a bit frustrating that it could have been so much better.

Construct: Escape the System is a first person platformer. It's almost as if Distance and Portal had a malformed child. It starts as a relaxing, actually even a bit boring easy stroll across some simple platforms. After gaining new abilities the game starts to hook you up nicely. Suddenly, though, everything turns into a tedious mess.
The one specific level that got me was the D3 system core orb. There's a 150 second time limit to escape the level. The visuals are somewhat special and nice looking, but in that specific area there are way too many transparent objects and figuring out the direction is almost just guesswork. On my third try, I missed the one last critical jump by only a few pixels, but I'm not going to try it again. Why? Because each time you screw up, you have to wait for the timer to end. This means that if you accidentally miss one jump or go to the wrong direction in the beginning of the run, you sometimes have to wait e.g. 140 seconds until the next try. It's almost like in Super Meat Boy instead of immediately respawning after dying, you'd have to wait for a minute. It quickly becomes super tedious and I'd like to play, not wait. It might be that the other end-game levels are really cool and everything, but I'm not taking the risk of wasting time anymore.
It's a shame, really. The game has a lot of potential. For the levels as they currently stand the controls should be a bit "tighter", now it most of the time feels like the player is just floating around. There should be the possibility of instant retry when escaping. Also, traveling back and forth between core levels and hubs should be cut away, it adds nothing to the game after you've once passed through and becomes just a boring time waster.
Technically it's a job well done. I played on Gentoo Linux with no problems whatsoever. I got the game on sale for three euros. For that price I can recommend it for the few hours before things turn tedious, but hopefully there will be a patch to address the problems. Then I will give it a thumbs up review.

I'm still getting started with this game, but I'm absolutely loving the simple, yet well-done scenery. Like Kairo or NaissanceE, it mixes platforming with wonderful eye-candy so just looking around is an experience by itself.
It runs very well on weak hardware. I'm enjoying the game on a laptop with a Celeron N2920 (aka an Atom), 4GB RAM, and Ubuntu when playing on 1024x600 resolution.
Starts a bit slow but once you unlock some of the movement upgrades the game really takes off.

Although I'm not a huge fan of platformers that feel like you're jumping through treacle, Construct's romp through vast, cybertronalien (only way I can describe it) environments manages to stay fresh and interesting throughout, with the gameplay-altering ability orbs shaking levels up, the intense escape sequences and the gradual collection of power orbs in order to...well, escape the system.
With its semi-open-world style - having multiple hubs and worlds within worlds - you might assume it's easy to get lost. However, the developer has done a brilliant job of putting in as much anti-frustration as possible. Don't know what to do in a certain section? Bright lights hover over areas of interest. Don't know where to go next? You're never too far away from a little terminal that will tell you the location of your next upgrade.
The sound design and very Unity-esque graphics reflect its independent origins, but for the most part if you like either platformers or the aesthetic in general, this game is well worth the price.
Also that ending was great. Just thought I'd mention.

I got Star Saviors in a very low bargain priced multipack bundle. I never would have bought this game on its own even at a low price because its just not my sort of game at all - or so I thought. Yeah, the criticism that the character portraits are ugly is fair. They're all ugly, like uncanny valley to the max ugly but that's the only bad thing I have to say. But even that is kind of charming in its own way I suppose, simply because of the sci-fi feel of the game. I like to imagine these characters aren't entirely human.
The gameplay is really smooth, fluid and fun. Its also something I can reasonably play, while still being challenging enough to not be boring (I wear braces so anything that's really stressful for my fingers and wrists are pretty much not possible for me to play). Granted the difficulty might spike too much for me, even on easy, in future levels but I wouldn't take points off for this since I don't have the endurance most people would.
And if you're afraid this means the game won't be challenging enough for you, don't be. There are several difficulty settings, including one that pretty much says you're dead meat.
The game is tons of fun, I'm digging the perks upgrade menu where you can choose how to boost your ship, and the fact that all weapons get more powerful as you gather new ones so you can pick what you like without it being totally obsolete to the newer ship equipment.
Also I'm the type that frequently turns off the game music and just has sound effects so I can play my own music while gaming but I actually love the soundtrack for this game, a lot. It seems to vary from nice and chill space electro to an interlude you'd find on a gothic power metal cd.
This game is good on its own but if you compare it in terms of value, its amazing for its price tag.

Welp, first review I've done in years so I'll try to keep it simple.
Way of the Samurai 4 is one of those games you can really enjoy, despite its many flaws.
From the trailer and images alone its easy to say that its graphics are outdated by a wide margin, but any long-term gamer knows that graphics don't make the game.
Sound design? Don't know if its for anyone else but large portions of cutscenes seem eerily quiet, especially considering how action-packed they're supposed to be at times. I'll get into the voice acting later on while discussing characters and story, but let's just say that from an industry stand-point it isn't the best.
The setting is condensed and easy to move around, once I got a hang of which area led where there were no issues with getting misdirected or anything. Similar to the graphics you shouldn't really expect epic scenery and all.
I hear many other reviews talk about how much the game crashes, personally I haven't had this problem. My computers nowhere near High-Grade material and the only times I've experienced crashes is when a slip of the hand opens another window. Accidentally opening up say tech support or the windows menu will always crash for me, but I've never experienced random crashes at all. Maybe I'm just lucky in that regard and mght come back later if I start experiencing it en masse or something.
The story is solid, cheesy to the nth degree but so hilarious that you can't help but enjoy it. The voice acting ties into this because every character soundscomically stuck to their intended tropes that you can't help but smirk every time something serious sounds hilarious due to the way its said. Due to certain dialogue options I've found in the game, I'm nearly certain the guys who made this know exactly how ridiculous this story can be at times and embrace it wholesale. I have to respect that.
The Replay value in this title puts quite a number of triple A titles to shame, with how many choixes you can make and how many endings there are to find you can easily find a day or two's worth of content in here. But the main stories aren't even all that's there. The side missions, jobs you can take, the character customization is suprisngly versatile. Although I will admit that the clothing options can be quite limmited, especially for female characters, what's there is shockingly abundant.
Combat has many features, and there's a good variety of blades and customization for you to choose from. I will say here that despite loving the fact that you can use guns in a samurai game, the guns do feel a bit like a gimmick compared to the army slaying power you can build into your swords and even spears if you feel up to it. Almost any blade can be dissassembled and mixed with others to create your killing machine of choice. The same can be said with your fighting styles. After finding a blank book (Or buying it) you can take the various moves you've learned in thevast array of fighting styles the game has, then mix and match them together until you have your ultimate move set.
With all this variety in themechanics expect to find a learning curve, not a big one but an initially daunting one. Couple this with the fact that on harder difficultioes this game can get infuriating, no surprise that I initially forgot about and left it lying in my library for over a year. But while waiting for a certain game to get released I decided to give this another try and actually muscled my way into greatly enjoying this.
One thing I especially found delightful was the whole 'Fight your previous character' thing.
Its a small touch but a well enjoyable one where if you make a new character to start another playthrough, whether to get another ending or farm side missions for money, there's a chance you'll run into the character you used for the last playtrough walking around as an NPC. Bump into them or draw a weapon in front of them and they immediately go on the attack using the weapon style you used for them. They'll be allied to whatever faction you got the ending for with them, and members of that faction will come to aid them in battle.

So yeah, if you can handle the negatives this game will offer days of gameplay, so if your feel like taking a crack at itfor whatever reason be it on sale or just liking the concept then pick it up.

I'd love to recommend this game, but it's full of bugs and it's dead. The game itself is actually very good!
I like to think of this game as a modern day Descent
game. It has a very similar 6DOF feeling to it, but combat is speeded up by the advanced movement mechanics, weapons-balance is
better and it has very impactful soundeffects. It evolved the genre where, whereas Descent 3 highlighted all its faults, which the first 2 Descent games have hidden so well.
Thanks to the movement and weapons, the game allows for far more variety in maps - having maps with large empty space was usually a bad idea in Descent multiplayer, because all projectiles were slow and easily dodged. Throne of Lies is a good game for anyone who likes the "Werewolf" or "Mafia" genre of Social Deduction games. Who are your friends? Who are your enemies? Should you make unsavory alliances with filthy Neutral people? You never really know who to trust, and that is the strength of Throne of Lies.
I've been playing for about 2 weeks now, and I must say that I enjoyed pretty much every hours. There are enough classes to keep you interested for a while, trying out new classes every now and then. All classes have their quirks, and their details you can use to either fool your adversaries, or make your allies trust you. I personally come from Town of Salem, a game I played quite a bit and at first, I was afraid that Throne of Lies would feel the same, but with less features.
But I was wrong, while Town of Salem is a good game in itself, I must say that Throne of Lies succeeds at being different, while keeping everything we love about these kinds of games. Every game in Throne of Lies starts with various members of the Blue Dragon Faction (BD) and either the Unseen or the Cult. To spice things up, there are various Neutral classes that are added to every game. The Unseen&Cult have the ability to CONVERT Blue Dragon members, which is a very important part of the social deduction gameplay that takes place in Throne of Lies. Someone who was a friend yesterday, could be your worst enemy today. This contributes greatly to the ever present tension that is there in every single game you play.
Now, of course Throne of Lies is not without issues. A lot of users are reporting crashes, some classes feel quite lackluster and the lack of a more serious Ranked Mode might turn some people off. But the positive thing about all of this is that the developers are extremely transparent and are always keeping in touch with the community. So you k now what's going on, what's going to happen and how they are going to fix it.

I've played through and beaten this game four times now, between PC and console. That is to say, I enjoyed it so much I bought it twice. It's a perfect bridge between old-school Morrowind and a more structured, story-driven experience. There's New Game+, character customization, upgrades, skills to buy, an enormous amount of equipment and fashion, some of the most intense magic I've ever seen, and a lot of love in this game. I probably spent 200-300 hours on the console version of this, and the PC port is even better.
First you make your character. Then you make your AI companion, or "Pawn". Then you go out and learn about the world and all the things in it that want to kill you. When you learn, your companion learns too. Shoot a Cyclops in the eye and your Pawn learns that a cyclops' eye is vulnerable. If you give them a bow or a ranged spell to use, they'll try to target the eye when they can from then on. If you and your Pawn discover that skeletons are weak to holy damage, they will buff the party with holy magic if they have it whenever you encounter skeletons later on. If you and your companion are both archers, your Pawn will pay attention to what skills you use on what and when, and eventually start to copy you. Over time, you will either purposefully or inadvertantly teach your Pawn all of your habits, both good and bad.
There are a number of classes to choose from, both for yourself and your Pawn, and you can swap whenever you like. In fact, it's important to level multiple classes as you go, since passive skills are shared between them, and your permanent attributes are determined by what class you were when you gained a level. You can be any of the basic fantasy archetypes: Fighter, Mage, and Rogue, as well as their specialized versions, like the Warrior, which uses two-handed weapons instead of a sword and shield. The main character (and only the main character) can also access hybrid classes, like the Magick Archer, a bowman who shoots auto-tracking beams of energy instead of arrows. All of the classes are viable and useful in their own ways. For example, a Sorcerer is a more specialized Mage, with huge, flashy, apocalyptically powerful spells, but they pay for those spells by being unable to cast healing magic. So while a Mage can't summon meteors from the heavens to blast apart the entire field in front of them, they can heal their companions and keep them fighting ten times longer.
The world reacts fairly intelligently to what you do. For example, did you know you can use resurrection items on NPCs? Named NPCs, even. And the game will actually react to it in some cases. You also can pay someone to make forgeries of items. Keep a magical artifact and give the questgiver a fake. Everyone's happy! For now, anyway. You can change things, like killing off (or befriending) a bandit clan, or clearing monsters out of an old trade route to make it viable again, or helping to set up new shops.
The world is large, and there's a lot of items, monsters, traders, and quests to ferret out. The main town, Gran Soren, has a lot of people to talk to and quests to pick up throughout the game. Different merchants sell different items, and will even sell extra things if you butter them up with gifts. You can miss things. Quests may only activate at certain points in the story, or you may fail an objective - and then the game carries on, paying attention and modifying the world based on what you did or what choices you made.
Even now, years later, I could boot it up and get lost in it for another 100 hours. I fully recommend this game. It really is a classic.

This is done by either finding the exact angle you are allowed to walk waya from the cover, this will let go of the cover and let you walk towards the guard. The gameplay is freeroam the moment you start, but, for newcomers, following the tutorial until you meet your second group will definately improve your skills. Elements like fatigue, serious injuries, or sickness keep the rotation of characters smooth, but until you start pulling in more than a few survivors, you'll notice that most characters are going to be too tired to go adventuring. One tip is to definately not put all your eggs into one basket with character selection, I made the mistake of sticking to three primary survivors that would switch out every so often, and then lost the character to a 'Big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥' type zombie. There are special class zombies, but they are usually rare. Killing them is simple, some have less health than the others, but I've noticed the best way to deal with a crowd is to ram them with your car. That applies to all except for the 'BB' his health is tremendous and is completely offset to whatever skills aquired and weapon you have in your hands. Unloading twenty headshots from a shotgun, point blank will still cause frustration as you realize that the only way to get around it is to blow up your car with it pinned against a wall. And going in for a melee is outrageously insane unless you want to see your character ripped in half. This is only one of the two unfair advantages you will have during the game, the other is the mutant zombie that is definately faster than you, and will definately take out a large chunk of your health. It has just a little bit more health than normal zombies, but it means you'll have to be faster on the swing, or quicker on the draw because these things will tackle you, leaving you defenseless.
The gameplay gets a little repetitive, especially when you have to save a group member every other time you send them out for scavenging. Or, constantly getting calls about hunting a special zombie type that will penalize your morale and inventory if you don't get around to it. The driving is a bit tricky at first, moreso since none of the fences are breakable nor are you able to run over them in your car. This can lead to some massive detours or a serious ding in the paint job. The spawn rate of enemies can be a bit annoying as well, having just cleared out an area, passing through a minute later, and there are two herds closing in from both directions.
The instructions for leveling up and choosing a skill that gives you a bonus are for you to figure out on your own, meaning there will be some time spent in your inventory/journal looking for a way to do so. Some more instruction would've been a bit more useful, but aside from the setbacks, the game concept is quite good and yet to be done elsewhere. I would probably be interested in a sequel, fan of zombie games as I am, but I would need to see some improvements on house layout diversity, side mission necessity, spawn rate of enemies, and difficulty scaling. A system that tracked and monitored zombie prescene in an area would be a welcome addition.
The collision mechanics are a far cry, and there's never a moment of rest for your character, so I recommend the game at a 6/10.

The Tesla Effect sees the return of fan favourite detective, Tex Murphy for the first time in years. The last game ended on something of a cliff hanger so it was a long wait to find out what happened.
The game is a real throwback to the days when FMV was considered the future, and we all saw how that turned out. Even at the time though the Tex Murphy games stood out for having way better than average stories and really solid adventure game puzzling.
Tex is basically your stereotypical hard boiled detective straight out of a 1940's detective film, only living in a futuristic dystopia version of San Francisco, complete with flying cars and hideous mutants. Part of the reason that the old games succeeded so well was that the actors revelled in hamming up their roles and chewing the scenery. The games for the most part, don't take themselves too seriously and there is plenty of humour. That said, Tex himself is a likeable guy and he ends up in pretty dark situations that despite their over the top nature, you actually care about the outcome of, simply because Tex is such a fun lead character.
The game itself is very solid, in between FMV scenes where you will converse with characters in the usual "pick a menu option for what you want to say" style, you wander around in a 3D world, finding clues, looking for items and solving puzzles. The FMV is as fun and campy as ever, though your mileage may vary. The actual 3D itself looks pretty dated, with low poly count models and so so textures. It does the job though and the plot and puzzles carry it.
If you are a fan of the originals you probably already own this, if not you should definitely pick it up as it captures the spirit of the originals. I still don't think its as great as my favourite entry, The Pandora Directive, its still a welcome return of a beloved character.
If you aren't a fan, this is a solid puzzle based adventure game. Watch one of the trailers to see whether you are going to like the FMV bits or not, but honestly, the grow on you.
Recommended 7.5/10
Edit: Oh, I got the really sucky ending somehow. I ended up having to watch the good ending online.

So, at the moment of writing this I have about an hour and a half into the game, right where most people will decide to ask for a refund or keep playing.  Perfect time for a review I think.  To add my own, admitadly simple, survival background into the review I have gone through USAF SERE school and a bunch of camping as a boy scout, just so you know what frames a bit of my opinions later on.  A simple pros, cons to start with:
Pros:
1.  It's beautiful for an early access game.  I played Rust quite a while ago and I remember what that looked like, There are moments where the game messes itself up, like tree not quite meeting the ground, but for every one of those I've stared out at a sunset over the Pacific or staring up at one of the nicest night skies I've seen.
2.  Single player option.  Actually at the moment it's the only option, but so many survival/crafting games lately are multiplayer and when people's default setting seems to be griefer it's nice to just be able to try to compete only with mother nature.
3.  There are no zombies.  Another default setting these day it seems.  Again, zombies are fun, I love them, but as unforgiving as mother nature herself can be it's nice to see something other than zombies as the primary antagonist.  This could be improved in the future, for example in the future rain could have more effect on the player than simply obscuring the vision.  It's a mixed blessing, a chance for fresh water to be collected without having to boil it, but also a harsh physical challenge.
4.  Sharks.  I guess this will take some explaining.  I left my first island on a run to what looked like a close island (more on that later), I was dogged the whole way by a tiger shark that kept bumping my raft.  I don't even know if it's the same shark that followed me towards the shore the first time I paddled ashore, but I feel this sort of dogged antagonism from something that's probably not even the same shark.  The attitude seems about right, this coming from someone who's never seen a shark out of an aquarium, almost a sort of aggressive curiosity.  Sharks are just one of many, many things that can kill you in this game but they somehow top the list of what I don't want to see show up.
5.  Atmosphere.  At least to a point.  The game does an amazing job of dropping you into the situation, but it also, at the moment, leaves you wondering why no one has noticed you're missing.  In the futuer a "winning" possibility has been promised, but for now you start as what appears to be a fairly rich guy on a private plane,  and no one seems to notice, or care, that you're missing.  That being said, the game puts you into a beautiful, but utterly hostile, environment.  Taking too long to appreciate it feels like something else is sneaking up on you.  I can't explain it to well, but it's a strange mix of excitment, anticipation, and utter fear as you sit in your raft picking out what island to paddle to next.
Cons:
-Crafting system.  This will be a long explanation and forms my one big gripe for the game, if you don't want to read it all, there will be times you feel like you can/should be able to do something but just can't because you haven't figured out how the developer wanted to do it.  I don't mean this as an argument that it shouldn't have one, but that the introduction to it is insufficent.  The player is literally just dropped on an island only having made a martini beforehand and you can die horribly still trying to figure out how to make a fire.  This is more of gripe when the player has collected a pile of sticks and has a lighter, the average person will  figure they can make a fire.   This in addition to the fact that the player has a knife to start with.  With sticks, a lighter and knife I know I could get a fire going with no problem.
There's more to this, recipies need ingredients that you may not know how to get, if I hadn't known what a yucca plant looked like I'd have never found lashing, and for some reason the axe creates almost everything, despite the fact you could smash a rock with a hammer just as easily.  Without spending some significant time with a wiki or a youtube walkthrough you'll be left staring at what seriously seems like the answer to a crafting question and it just won't work.  This extends to weird solutions to crafting problems, things like simply boiling a bucket of sea water causes it to suddenly be fresh water, which is something that simply doesn't work without a few extra steps.
Also, some ideas you may have with any survival training, like setting an empty bucket out in the rain, just don't seem to work.  In additon certain items that should be one use only, like a flare, are somehow infinate use, while others that should be fine for years, like a stainless steel survival knife, somehow fall apart in after a few days of use
2.  Some items don't do what they should.  Antibiotics don't cure poison, duct tape is somehow useable after what looks like years under water, it's minor but it breaks the feeling.
3.  This doesn't quite feel like it takes full advantage of its environment.  The South Pacific has had years of ships, planes, war and such that could have delivered supplies of some sort to the area.  Every ship seems to be a fishing trawler, every plane is  a small prop plane.  A few years of war would have delivered warships and fighter aircraft of the Empire of Japan, the United States and United Kingdom to the area for World War II alone.  That doesn't even count numerous civilian wrecks and ships that have gone missing through the years.  I just feel like it would give some character.
4.  Navigation through the world.  The first island you start on will probably be ungodly small, and every island seems to be the same way.  They're a few trees, a few rocks, maybe some lashing and the random ship or aircraft wreck.   Each of these takes several minutes to navigate through, the entire time of which you will seemingly be shadowed by a shark with the raft constantly bumped.  The shark I'm ok with, as I stated earlier, but the reason I bring it up is because the risk doesn't ever seem to fit the reward.  I risked several long journeys across hostile waters for a few more sticks and rocks.  I never managed to find a bigger island or some sort of cache of supplies that seemed to make it worth it.  Maybe it's random bad luck,  but I just never felt like my expeditions really paid off.
5.  Set character.  I know for a game like this it seems like a minor gripe, but being able to be something other than a random white guy would be nice, I'm assuming this will change in the future so for now, no real complaint that would have kept me from buying the game.
All in all, I'm certain I'm keeping the game, despite having to look up crafting and spend some time with tutorials, I've enjoyed my time with it so far.  That isn't so much based off my satsisfaction with what it is right now, rather it's based off the potential I see in the game, and potential the developers could take advantage of to create something other than the same old post-apocalyptic suvival MMO where every random person tries to kill you.

CONSTRUCT
Oliver Boyce
Immanitas Entertainment
Abstract
The Unity 5 Engine shows its potential once again, in the hands of a creative developer (at the start of his career, no less!) that manages to add another fine title to Steam’s growing collection of indie abstract games. CONSTRUCT has indeed a clearly defined gameplay design but the clever use of shapes and effects in motion, do provide for an intriguing first person platforming experience that still manages to stand out. Officially described as “sci-fi”, I firmly believe that tag doesn’t do it justice the way “abstract” fits the bill.
Divided into 4 Hubs, each with its own distinct theme, you will not get bored by this game at any point as long as you enjoy a more slow-paced approach to platforming. It is by no means as difficult as some similar titles I tried in the past, but still requires more patience than quick reflexes and that is fine by me. Taking in the sights will be combined with object-based puzzles that involve finding and using orbs to power up/light the next areas ready for exploration. Reaching them will not be much of a challenge, but the presence of gameplay upgrades does offer a sense of progression. It’s only natural that you jump higher and run faster as per level advancement.
I absolutely love video games that both offer the chance and make it easy for me to take as many and diversified screenshots as I please. CONSTRUCT, perhaps initially for the sake of ensuring even more replay value, has integrated multiple visual filters such as Monochrome and Negative. You’re able to freely switch between these chromatic modes by just pausing the game and entering the Options tab. It goes without saying that as simple as this feature might sound, changing the color gamut on abstract objects and backgrounds does present the opportunity for some surreal screenshots, just to my liking. I would suggest the developer to implement the option of hiding the entire User Interface, thus allowing users an even better chance at making fantastic wallpapers from their own game progress. I’m sure that in a future update this small but significant change, could become reality.
From a technical perspective, I’m certain that you don’t require a powerful PC to run the game maxed out. And Unity as a whole, never gave me any issues or crashes in the countless games running its assests, that I have play tested and reviewed over the past few months. I’m not exaggerating one bit in calling the union between Steam indie games and the Unity Engine, a “match made in heaven”. A development kit that offers potentially anyone’s dreams and ideas to materialize, represents much more than just an affordable medium to express their creativity. To all detractors who complain about Steam “opening the floodgates” to all sort of software detritus, I can point out as many quality titles released in the same timeframe and all of it is made possible by Steam’s freedom of expression rather than alleged greed and lack of proper QA. It is ultimately up to the customers (and hopefully, my readers) to decide which independent games released daily on this platform are worth their hard-earned cash.

On the surface CONSTRUCT is very easy to pick up and play.
Once I got into the game I was drawn in to its impressive and surreal visuals.  And solving the puzzles were both challenging and rewarding.  There is some backtracking and exploring because there are places the player cant reach until discovering a particular upgrade.  Double jump, tripple jump, gravity manipulation and teleportation powers are among the upgrades you can find.
This makes for very interesting and sometimes mind bending 3 deminsional puzzles.  Where you must think creatively to discover the solution.
The graphics for CONSTRUCT are simple and well made, making the game both interesting to look at and easy to run.
The enviornments are often stunning and very large.  Making for some vast puzzles where you cant always see where you are supposed to be going because its so far away.
The music and sound are both well done, with the right music for the particular setting.  Sometimes you get mellow and relaxed tunes, then when things are tense, the pulse accelerates pushing you to the edge of your seat.
So the plot of CONSTRUCT... well there really isnt one.  Basicly the player goes through a tutorial and you are just thrown into a computer system and told to escape.  Thats it... really.
So the plot or story is seriously lacking, but that seems to me  to be the only thing missing from an overall enjoyable experience.
I recommend CONSTRUCT for those that enjoy puzzle games or platformers, but also to those looking for something a little different from the everyday.
So why not treat yourself to an enjoyable experience that is a little out of the ordinary?
