Omg, I have not stop playing this game for the past week. I'd like to say that this game is truly unique and has some really good things to offer. Though I will definitely not give it a 10/10, I do know that I will recommend this game. Middle Earth: Shadow Of Mordor is an action adventure open world stealth based game that takes place in the world of LOTR. It features an amazing and unique nemesis system, and the game borrows much from both the Batman Arkham City series and the Assassins Creed franchise.
Lore: It pays its respect to the LOTR saga, by giving importance to storytelling and lore. To sum up, the story: You are a Ranger named Talion, who's family (wife and son) are murdered along with you. You are brought back by a Wraith(Ghost) who is now part of you. So right off the bat you play as two characters, merged into one person. The Wraith tells him he has to kill the man who killed him, to bring himself back to life along with his family. The Wraith remembers nothing about himself. So you go on a journey to learn about the Wraith. The game pays respect to LOTR. You'll meet characters from the actual book series and movies, both LOTR and Hobbit.
Visuals: The game itself looks gorgeous, and cutscenes are on my list of best cutscenes ever. The environment makes me immersed and makes me feel as if I'm actually in one of the movies. Though I did sometimes feel there could have been more work done on the textures. But I barely ever feel the need to address the issue, cause most textures look good. The orcs though sometimes look similar when there should be more variety other than the 25 or more faces. The humans in these game make me mad. They look all the same, and another issue, which might sound as if I'm nitpicking at this point, but I'm not... The humans are very similar looking and short. There's a variety of orcs and Talion is tall, so is the other characters, but the humans same looking and short. I really do hope Monolith addresses this and fixes this for the next game.
Combat: I love how they combined the Arkham series combat to this game because it really does work. It's not exactly button mashing. But honestly when you're fighting massive troops of them, more than like 50, yea I just smash my keyboard or my Xbox One controller, in hopes of survival. Combat gets repetitive when you're on your some what 100 hours into the game, where you have all upgrades for both Wraith and Talion and you're a pro. There are these things called Runes which you can get by killing a Captain. Runes can be put into Rune Slots, which can make weapons better and stronger. You can grind for the best Runes by making one Captain super strong and then kill him, or you can just play the game. Another thing I appreciate is the strong holds. You can find stronghold everywhere. There basically headquarters for Captains and Warcheifs with a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of Urks. You can try to kill off the archers and then kill slowly pick out the people around the Captain. Then make your move on the Captain. The Captain or war chief also has weakness and strengths. Which you can get by interrogating Urks with Intel. Forcing them to spill♥♥♥♥♥♥can tell you how to kill a Captain or Warcheif. You can send Death threats, and awww yea sexy slo mo archery makes me feel like a complete badass... AWWWW YEAAA!!!
Nemesis System: The thing everyone talks about when they talk about this game the ''Nemesis System" Basically you're this guy who can't be killed cause your cursed from death, so you magically come back alive aka Respawn. So when anybody kills you, the person that kills you gets promoted. So that person can be a Captain, a War chief, a random Urk whos supposed to be keeping his eye out for Ranger. AWWW YEAAA, make that arrow go in Urk. Once someone gets promoted you can go kill them. A random Urk can become a captain. A captain can become War chief. A random war chief can increase in power level etc.
Cons: - AI is sometimes dumb af, not a consistent bug though
- Humans are short and look alike
- Not a lot of RPG elements other than leveling up, power levels, ability points etc. No crafting or etc
- You use the same three weapons, sword, dagger, and bow and arrows
- Not a lot to expect from the open world (the world is too small) It's just two massive area's Mordor and Sea of Nurnin.
- Not a lot of plantlife or animals, I want more!

So WHO SHOULD GET THIS GAME?!: Anyone really. You like LOTR, you like assassins creed, you like Batman Arkham City.

A pleasant surprise for a cheap horror game from a bundle. Generally I don't expect much from those but play them for the laughs. But there were no laughs here, only chills. With generally decent visuals and a slow pace that builds creep factor well, it stands above the usual standard of "it's dark and there are sounds" games.
Hektor keeps things simple, and at times comes close to walking simulator horror as you progress from one hallway to the next. Under the hood, the levels are randomly generated, and can change themselves around on the fly. There are puzzles to solve along the way, so it's not just a matter of walking forward. Sometimes you'll find yourself looping through the same few rooms, which means there's something for you to find in one of them.
Unlike other similar horror games though, there are actual threats in the twisting corridors. There's nothing to be done about them but avoid them, and they don't feel especially necessary, but they're there and they have some creepy sound design to go with them. There are no game overs, only setbacks, so they're not a huge obstacle.
The story isn't exactly easy to follow, but it drops enough hints to build a good sense of mystery and spookiness. There's some exposition through voiced notes, which feature surprisingly good voice acting for a cheaper title. They don't get in the way too much though, and it does come to a conclusion even if it's a bit sudden.
It's adjustable, but by default your ever-lowering sanity meter can create some wobbly screen effects if it gets low that are pretty nauseating. You get plenty of pills to stave it off, but when I ignored it for a while I actually got motion sickness, which isn't common for me and games. Might wanna check out that option before you start.
By now, Steam has hundreds of games like this, to be sure. It's dark, your light is limited, you can only run and hide from the monsters. And so on. But where many of them are half-finished railroads from one jump scare to the next, Hektor isn't afraid to let you explore and take it at your own pace. Nor does it feel the need to scream in your face every five minutes. If you're a genre fan always looking for more to satisfy your craving, then this might be your next snack. Just don't expect too much beyond the usual.

RTS hardcores will probably find the core gameplay mechanics of Tooth and Tail aggravating but, if you're like me and you're far out of season, there's a good chance you'll be like someone picking up TnT as their first RTS: appreciating the mechanical limitations of the game as fuel for strategic and tactical decisions.
Those who have reached the top levels of Starcraft or Warcraft ladders or tournament play, you might not find TnT to be a breath of fresh air as much as a gimmick. But statistically, if you're reading this, you'll never reach the game's reasonably high skillcap anyway, so you can reap the rewards of the lower skill floor.
The game also has a small community (140ish concurrent players at the time of writing), so you will have difficulty finding games off peak hours, and even during peak hours, will probably be doing some rematches. But it's a fairly devoted community as far as I can tell, and the total death of the game is unlikely before you get your money's worth of entertainment and challenge.

Sonic CD is a classic game that doesn't get quite as much attention as the main series, but is still pretty solid in its own way.
The level design is based less around speed and more around exploring, which is all well and good, but looking for the "Past" sign, gaining enough speed to go there, searching for the robot-making machine, and destroying it in every single level to get the good ending can be extremely tedious at times. Less tedious is clearing the special stages to get the time stones, which also unlock the good ending, but it's still quite difficult. As a whole the levels in the game aren't as polished as Sonic 2 and 3K, either. They feel rather scatterbrained in the way they're laid out.
The music in the levels is delightful all around, though. The game gives lets you choose between the more atmospheric and moody US soundtrack or the upbeat and peppy JP soundtrack. My personal favorite is the US one, but I'm clearly in the minority on that.
The port job in this version is fantastic, also. Not being one to simply emulate a game, Christian Whitehead rebuilt the game practically from scratch in order to pack it chock-full of bonus features and settings, such as unlocking a new character after being the game. I can't remember ever playing a more polished port of a classic game in my life. Seriously, I can't stand the original version of this game after having played this one. This one is just that good.

Become your own Head of State while knocking zombies around and organizing survivors into a successful community that lives to fight and scavange another day. The gameplay is freeroam the moment you start, but, for newcomers, following the tutorial until you meet your second group will definately improve your skills. Elements like fatigue, serious injuries, or sickness keep the rotation of characters smooth, but until you start pulling in more than a few survivors, you'll notice that most characters are going to be too tired to go adventuring. One tip is to definately not put all your eggs into one basket with character selection, I made the mistake of sticking to three primary survivors that would switch out every so often, and then lost the character to a 'Big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥' type zombie. There are special class zombies, but they are usually rare. Killing them is simple, some have less health than the others, but I've noticed the best way to deal with a crowd is to ram them with your car. That applies to all except for the 'BB' his health is tremendous and is completely offset to whatever skills aquired and weapon you have in your hands. Unloading twenty headshots from a shotgun, point blank will still cause frustration as you realize that the only way to get around it is to blow up your car with it pinned against a wall. And going in for a melee is outrageously insane unless you want to see your character ripped in half. This is only one of the two unfair advantages you will have during the game, the other is the mutant zombie that is definately faster than you, and will definately take out a large chunk of your health. It has just a little bit more health than normal zombies, but it means you'll have to be faster on the swing, or quicker on the draw because these things will tackle you, leaving you defenseless.
The gameplay gets a little repetitive, especially when you have to save a group member every other time you send them out for scavenging. Or, constantly getting calls about hunting a special zombie type that will penalize your morale and inventory if you don't get around to it. The driving is a bit tricky at first, moreso since none of the fences are breakable nor are you able to run over them in your car. This can lead to some massive detours or a serious ding in the paint job. The spawn rate of enemies can be a bit annoying as well, having just cleared out an area, passing through a minute later, and there are two herds closing in from both directions.
The instructions for leveling up and choosing a skill that gives you a bonus are for you to figure out on your own, meaning there will be some time spent in your inventory/journal looking for a way to do so. Some more instruction would've been a bit more useful, but aside from the setbacks, the game concept is quite good and yet to be done elsewhere. I would probably be interested in a sequel, fan of zombie games as I am, but I would need to see some improvements on house layout diversity, side mission necessity, spawn rate of enemies, and difficulty scaling. A system that tracked and monitored zombie prescene in an area would be a welcome addition.
The collision mechanics are a far cry, and there's never a moment of rest for your character, so I recommend the game at a 6/10.

Such a beautiful and amazing game. So many places to explore, so many new things to find, so many random little side quests and occurances that just come up. Starbound is more than just "Terraria in space." It has a lot of great ways to build and design and is very well thought out. Although it may get a bit redundant with similar planets and similar things and limited levels on biomes, the community workshop keeps things fresh and the game continues to grow.

If you've played Minecraft, if you you've played Terraria, or other of the myriad of craft/build sims that have been coming out in the last few years, you're by now probably assuming if you've played one, you've played them all, or close enough. I would have been inclined to agree with you before this game. Something truely special in a sea of sameness, Starbound manages to take what you think you know about these types of games and wrap it around a simple, but decent story, while placing it into a sea of multiple worlds. Like most of these types of games, it really shines in multiplayer, with company on the journey easily multiplying the fun factor as you explore your world, their worlds, and take the best from all around the universe. This isnt a game that makes the world your oyster, it makes the GALAXY yours to explore, to build, to fight, to say screw it all and be a farmer if you want. It's a bit hard to truely put into simple words what makes this game special versus it's family of titles, but the obvious thought, love and detail into every bit makes for a far greater whole.

This is hands down the best RPG I have ever played in my life. It has everything.
Story is deep and engaging, with all the interesting twists and turns, exciting NPC stories, darkness, magic, difficult choices you have to make on every step you make, exciting places to explore... The world of Pillars is vibrant, magical and complete. The background: lore (gods, monsters, cities, woods, villages), huge green crystals of Adra growing everywhere in the world, it all creates a unique fantasy experience.
Music is just great, visuals are top-notch and I'm really glad they went with hand-drawn environments instead of going for clunky 3D style of of contemporary RPGs go with. The game is extremely pleasant to watch and experience on the sensual level.
Now to the meta side of the game. Character creation is excellent (the game also allows you to create a full party of your own!) with plenty of classes, races, skills and traits to choose from. Combat is really difficult on Path of the Damned level if someone likes challenging encounters (I do!), there is also a 15-level megadungeon with plenty of loot and gold to be found (and many dangerous foes). Character progression is great and rewarding. Itemization is another huge thing in PoE. There are countless items you can find granting you stats, special traits, passive bonuses, on-hit effects and so on. It's really great!
It's a must-play for every RPG fan.

Strike Vector is a fusion of space combat game (Freespace, Descent etc) and FPS with a high skill ceiling. If you've played Strike Suit Zero this game is sort of similar, but more hardcore (no autoaim, faster paced, easy to crash, etc.) and designed for multiplayer.
In the game your ship has a flight mode and a hover mode. Flight mode gives you superior speed but you cannot turn quickly. Hover mode allows you to hover in place and aim like you would in an FPS, you are able to turn 180 degrees instantly if you turn fast enough.
Learning to switch between the modes effectively is key to getting good with the controls, since there is no delay in changing modes since hover mode is excellent for aiming shots and stopping momentum.
Navigating the maps which have a lot of complexity and various hidden paths is a skill in itself. Flying through complex paths at max speed while trying to flee enemy fire can feel very rewarding in a way I can't really remember experiencing in any other game, usually space combat or mech games don't have this complex environments. Powerup and healing items are also hidden in difficult places to encourage exploring, similarly to many old school FPS games.
The maps are well designed and really bring out the potential of the combat. For beginners the complexity can be a turnoff since it can be easy to crash into walls, but on the flipside this makes you learn the controls very quickly if you have some patience.
There are a wide variety of weapons which all have their own strengths. Though as of the current patch (1.0.4008) missiles and the LMG are pretty useless, but apart from those it feels very balanced. There are a variety of game modes that are typical for FPS games but they all work quite well with the maps.
My biggest negative point in the game is the games graphics settings, which are pretty much nonexistent ingame. It's very easy to manually set various detail settings just by editing a text file with false/true entries, but that makes it even more confusing as to why it isn't implemented ingame. With default settings the system requirements can be very high but at low settings you should be able to reach constant 60fps on a mid-tier system.
A lot of people have complained about the lack of players, but at least from my experience in the european servers there are always at least 20-30 people playing which isn't bad at all unless you want to avoid expert players or tend to switch servers a lot.
The developers are releasing updates for the game every few months to polish features and add new maps/modes which is very nice to see. I think this could really be a big cult classic if they keep it up.

I only played for amount of time, but it had some problems that immediately made a bad impression on me. I did get to encounter a bit of the nemesis/warleader system and it was cool, and the game really does have that going for it.
I personally had quite a bit of trouble playing the game with a mouse and keyboard though. There were a lot of different button binds you have to manage. It felt more like I was fighting to control the game as opposed to fighting off the orcs. I did some rebinding but it didn't help much. The combat is similar to the Batman games where you spam counter and get a few hits in before you hit counter again. It's honestly pretty easy and the only real "difficulty" comes from fighting the warleaders. Even then the difficulty lies in reading what their weakness is and exploiting that.
I did get killed a few times but it was just from getting attacked by like 4+ of the named orcs at once (I think I was close to a fortress or something, but I was in the first area of the game). I killed most of those orcs, but they don't remain dead if you die in the battle, which was a little upsetting but understandable I guess. The game doesn't have much of a tutorial, but I assume you learn more as you do the story missions. However I personally like to do a bit of running around when I first get tossed into an open world but I only got punished for doing that.
The stealth is also incredibly simple, but seems to one of the big points of the game. You can assassinate orcs feet away from their allies, and so long as you are a little behind them they won't notice. I also see the movement praised by some people, but it is as simple as "hold _ button and run toward a wall".

If you are looking for games that requite deduction and logic, this is the exact game for you. Throne of Lies (ToL) is a variation of the popular Mafia social game whereby you will either be on the side of the Blue Dragon (Good), Cult/Unseen (Evil) or the forsaken Neutrals. ToL is also often compared or described as Town of Salem (ToS) in 3D, which I can agree to a certain extent as they have the same core gameplay but currently ToS has much more content in terms of roles and meta.
The gameplay for ToL is extremely addictive, provided that you are willing to commit mistakes and learn more about the game as the games could be tainted with toxicity due to salty/stupid players at times (I admit I do get salty too). Winning the game is very satisfying as you tend to be emotionally invested into the game as you could be wrongly framed, caught out being as an evil but turning it around etc etc.
However, a word of warning for beginners who are new to the Mafia game genre, you could try out ToS on the web browser for free before jumping into ToL. This allows you to understand the overall mechanic of Mafia games and provide a smoother transition into ToL as the players in this game could be quite unforgiving towards newbies.
As of 18/11/2017 and being a player for a month, I would recommend this game because the developers are consistently updating the game and tweaking the "unfun" classes like Court Wizard/Noble from the feedback of the players. This shows that the dev team are listening to the players and making positive changes to the game in order to better the gaming experience for the players. $10 for possibly hundreds of hours in gameplay is very much a steal, even more if you are looking to make a purchase during sales.
EDIT: I voted this game for the "The World Is Grim Enough Let's Just All Get Along" Steam Award

Hektor is not your run-of-the-mill type survival horror game, each time you move your environment might change even a little bit which can cause the feeling of being lost in a maze where you have to go forwards to go back and sometimes backwards to go forwards. The lure of the game is simple, escape Hektor, a maze-like underground military base without going insane from the maze like architecture of the underground base. Not all of the game takes place underground, (or does it?) as sometimes you can really lose your head and start hallucinating to the point where you are in a room with nothing but red curtains to guide your way. At other points you might get the feeling like you might lose your lunch as at points there are times where the game forces you to play the game like it was a fun house mirror creating a distorted view of your surroundings. Hektor never quite makes you feel comfortable and to me, that is the only thing that can make a survival horror game a great game, if I’m on the edge of my seat all the time, then the game is worth the price of admission.
This is what everyone wants to know, just how scary is it? Well, in all honesty it is hard to put into words as each player might play the game a little differently depending on how the levels are generated, one person might find the game baron and lacking substance as they go through maze after maze while others might find solace in the fact that we are guessing until the very end. One thing I truly loved about Hektor was it’s attention to detail, a little into the story I had to find a certain object (no spoilers here, don’t worry) and I was gong through room after room that felt exactly the same for about 20 minutes, “What am I doing wrong?” I asked myself as my pulse was rising, then I wondered, what exactly would happen if I tuned around and went backwards? I will stop there, but sometimes the most obvious decision is the best decision.
Hektor doesn’t have what we would call mind-blowing graphics by any sense, but it does wonders for what it has, you will notice many different settings and places, that… or some reason.. You feel like you have seen before. Every room might feel or look the same, but different at the same time. Which, in Hektor’s case is a huge step up from games like Daylight, as both games are procedurally generated but Daylight felt like each room was baron until you could find your next objective, heck, even finding a video tape in Hektor caused me anxiety until I found it randomly laying on a shelf. Hektor comes out at just under 1 gb once downloaded and I really couldn’t believe how wonderful the graphics really were for how small the game file was. Hektor really does an excellent job with what it has.
One of the highlights of the game would have to be the sound effects and music. Simply put, a horror game just HAS to have these two things if they want to survive in the horror genre. A scary game is nothing without that screeching violin effect that puts shivers up even the toughest person’s spine. Thankfully, Hektor hits both of these points in stride. Not only did the music raise my pulse but it made me feel like I had to run as only my lighter show the way while swallowing my pills for psychosis, (if you don’t take the pills in Hektor regularly the world starts to change color and have odd effects.) Rubycone did a fantastic job creating sound effects and music that fit perfectly in the realm of Hektor’s world.
Let’s face it, odd effects and nice music doesn’t quite make the game a survival game, “where are the monsters?” you might ask. Well, we definitely have a monster for you and that is in the form of a huge modified human like character that comes after you forcefully. The first few times, I nearly jumped out of my chair, run out of my house and down the street screaming, (admittedly a slight bit of hyperbole), but once seen a few times, it becomes less scary and instead turns into a game of cat and mouse, Hektor’s monster is generated when you are going too far into the story too quickly, making you slow down a bit making it much harder to complete the game in any fashion that makes you feel like your in control of it and that is what makes this game a masterpiece to me, Hektor never makes you feel comfortable and many games not even Outlast made me feel that way. Which is saying a lot since it is still my favorite horror game I have ever played.
Overall, Hektor is a nice game with a short but scary story. Admittedly I would have liked for it to be a little longer and have more of a back end to the plot, but all can be forgiven for just how scary the game can be at points. Will it knock Outlast off of it’s perch? For me, unfortunately not, but for many people, Hektor will be the only game they need to fulfill there nightmarish dreams as the “predator” comes after you with force. I leave you with this, when you get stuck and are not sure what to do, sometimes you have to go backwards to go forwards.

My background for social deduction games of this sort comes from Resistance/Avalon board games, although I've played a bit of One Night Werewolf and Coup as well. ( I haven't played ToS, the obvious game everyone compares it to)
The game is very addictive, and a lot of fun. It's very frequently updated with patches ( too frequently, if you can imagine that ), so it keeps constantly changing - it really brings out the sentiment that devs are intent on improving it.
There is a great variety of classes you can end up getting, with various powers and win conditions, most of which are quite fun, with a couple of boring ones. Most of the game is about being either good at lying, or at catching other people in a lie. Communicating and deducing information quickly as well, of course. Being a fast typist helps too.
Some gripes I have with the game:
- The game is a bit nonintuitive at first in terms of how night abilities interact, and what interactions return which messages. It will take a while to learn those, and even when you do, they are constantly being changed with patches.
- As with every game of this sort I imagine, you cannot really play them together with your friends if you intend on sharing information before the game is finished, since that would be cheating. It's also kinda impossible to catch this type of cheating, so that's why I feel you can't take this game too seriously.
- Some players will disconnect from the game, leave on purpose, out their teammates because they didn't want to be converted, all of which can ruin it for the other 15. I am not sure how serious the team behind the game is about punishing this behavior yet - they say they are on discord, but I would love to see some public announcements on how people are being punished.
----
Currently there is only one mode of play, unranked, but at least the waiting queues are short since there seem to be a lot of players at all times.
9/10, easily worth $10, even at this stage with all its warts, and I imagine it will only be getting better since devs seem to be very active.

10/10

+ Fluid third person combat.
+ Tactical combat. Using correct elements against enemies makes combat easier and fun. Against huge enemies, you even have to climb and attack parts of their body first to make it weaker.
+ Class based stats and skills system. Can switch classes quickly to experiment with playstyles.
+ Interesting party system. The party members in this game are called 'Pawns'. You get to create your main pawn and then recruit two others and go adventuring. As the pawns see you fight enemies and employ tactics, they will learn to you use it by themselves.
+ Online component. The pawns you hire are actually the main pawns that other people have created. Your pawn is available for hire as well and after they are released from service, the main pawns come back with exp, rift crystals (currency to buy or improve some of the best gear) and items if gifted.
+ Huge open world to explore.
+ Interesting lore.
+ Minimal handholding. Information about area and quests are given by pawns who are familiar with this quest from their run in their game. which is quite nice!
- Very convoluted quest pathing. You will miss some of the interesting side quests if you do the story mission at the wrong times. Some of these quests involve apperance of NPCs that sell good gear. Which you will miss because somehow you are supposed to guess a new quest has appeared at that one village you passed. Use of one of the guides here in Steam is almost a must,
- Class switching is a cool feature. However, what they fail to mention is that stats you gain are according to the class you were when you gained that level. Therefore, the melee damage, health, defense etc are purely dependant on that. Which sucks when you want to play as a shield heavy fighter, but you have to switch to other classes just before level to gain enough melee dmg or stamina.
- Grinding and RNG are pretty much intergral to the game. If you want good loot or enhance the said loot, you need monster parts and certain items that you will need to go out and farm and kill diffcult enemies in hopes of that one item dropping from them. This is especially true of qutting-loading again when certain chests dont have that 2% chance of good loot appearing. (cue traumatic flashbackls to Final Fantasy XII)
- 90% of the sidequests and fetch/kill quests which you will soon tire of and abandon.
- Pawn A.I, while mostly competent, sometimes go full mentally challenged and refuse to do that one thing you desperately need. Like when my healer decided that casting one more spell at a nearby trash mob is a better choice than healing me.
- Some of the fetch quests are unclear and you will definitely will have to consult a wiki.
- Too many monsters are reskinned, increased stat versions of their lower forms. Want to make a new mob? Paint a goblin white and give it some muscly damage and hitpoints.

I am a longtime RTS player having played many games in the genre including all the games from the Age of Empires and StarCraft series, and I have to say I love this game.
Other players have said in reviews that the distilling of the RTS experience in this game has limited certain strategic abilities and challenges. While I can't entirely disagree with this statement I think that what this game has to add to the genre more than makes up for what it takes away.
At first the simplicity of the game, and the limitations in the ability to strategically multitask and micromanage like a traditional RTS game seemed to be a major drawback. Until I realized that in this case simplicity does not by any means equal easy, and the limitations in strategically multitasking actually opened up for different and more unique strategic challenges than the ones in more traditional RTS games.
On top of the unique gameplay mechanics, this game has a rich story driven single player campaign, fun multiplayer (including an offline mode against AI), cool stylized graphics, a great musical score (recorded with real instruments which is always a plus) and much more.
A far as I know, this is a completely new and original type of RTS game almost in its own subgenre. I foresee it becoming much more popular as time goes on and that future games will influenced by its gameplay.

Omega Force's trademark Warriors franchise has developed a sort of immunity to typical criticism.
"Why don't the enemies attack?"
"All you do is press one button repeatedly."
After 20 or 30 games, you'd think the average reviewer would get the hint. This is a franchise very much set in its ways, and as long as it remains appealing to its sizable fanbase, then I see no reason to complain. There isn't a shortage of videogames in the world, so it's not like gamers don't have a choice. Although, it's possible I'm just saying this, because I'm a huge fanboy when it comes to Musou. If I were to list all of the games I played in this genre, the Steam servers would crash harder than during the Winter sales.
Anyway, DW8:XLCE is a ginormous helping of 3rd Century slaughter. In the story mode, you can determine the fates of the Three Kingdoms, follow Jin to conclude the era, or side with the great hero Lu Bu. Each storyline has an optional path, which is unlocked by helping certain "doomed" heroes in their respective stages. Assisting Guo Jia's recovery from his illness, or keeping Sun Jian from taking an arrow in the face, could be keys to accessing these hypothetical stories. These "what-if" routes are pretty entertaining, even if they lack the drama that the Three Kingdoms is well-known for.
The free mode allows players to use any hero on any stage. Yet more stages are unlocked by completing the story mode and its many routes. These stages also have a ranking system. It's a neat idea, but some ranks are determined by completing specific goals. One such goal might be "kill 200 soldiers with EX attacks". EX attacks are charge-attack follow-ups such as X X Y (Y), if the enemy dies before you press Y a second time, then it doesn't count. By the time I got around to this mode, most of my enemies died as soon as I pressed X! While it's not all that well thought-out, at least this addition gives added value to free mode. There's also a challenge mode, which might be worth checking out... once.
When you want to conquer China in the name of the Emperor, then you'll want to play Ambition mode. This is also a fine way to grind out the experience levels of your favorite heroes. At first, your goal is to raise a hamlet into a city fit for an Emperor. This involves a ton of farming missions, and the only real challenge is to not lose your mind. Once that's over and done with, then you get to unify China. By the way, if you managed to recruit all 80+ warriors in part 1 of Ambition mode, then congratulations! In part 2, you get to do it all over again! Better yet, it's a far more painful task! Hurray!
In Ambition mode part deux, in order to win battles, you have to defeat leaders. This involves taking control of nearby bases. It's similarly to DW5, although a bit more repetitive. You also have to account for nearby enemy soldiers, as they will retake bases if given the opportunity. Playing on harder difficulties and capturing more bases before winning battles will allow you conquer lands more quickly, which is great. However, this mode gets very old and extremely dull, if you try to re-recruit everyone. Only the enemy leaders of these battles tend to be playable characters. My advice is to separate the wheat from the chaff, and use a guide to find out where your faves are in each land.
While all of this recruiting, farming, and conquering is going on; you'll also do a little bonding. After every mission, one of the heroes you recruit will have something to say. This can involve everything from "I respect your abilities" to "You're a good friend" to "Please! Wife me this instant!" It's very odd that Dong Zhuo comes off as not the biggest creep in these one-sided conversations. Earlier, Zuo Ci, who must be 300 years old, called me the "epitome of feminity". There's a line I'm going to try the next time I'm at a bar.
The presentation is great, although the voice-acting is still suspect. Overall, it's an improvement over the Playstation 2 days, but some characters sound extremely bored. Then again, I guess if I was stuck voicing a plank of wood like Yue Jin, I wouldn't sound very enthused either. I also still have a soft-spot for DW3's classic "You flaming idiots! Take this!" voice-acting. The cut-scenes are all pretty good, though I tend to skip the in-between story chapters commentary. That's just me, I'm on my fourth reading of the Three Kingdoms novels, I already know the story.
As for the rest of the game, it's altogether very solid. This entry is more dynamic and versatile than DW7, which was already a massive jump over DW5. Almost all of the weapons are fun to use, and the heroes have more interesting EX attacks, which definitely helps in terms of variety. The harder difficulties are fair enough, provided you're a high level, and there are plenty of secrets and awesome items to acquire. Although in standard DW fashion, finding the best weapons pretty much requires a guide. Outfitting these weapons with powerful skills and obliterating hundreds of soldiers in seconds, will never cease to be enjoyable for me.
As far as the port is concerned. I got this game back when it first came out*. At the time, I considered it an okay port. The assets are lower quality than I would have liked, and the lack of online multiplayer is definitely a head-scratcher. On the bright side, at least it runs well on a lower-end PC, the load-times are superior to the console versions, and sweetfx does wonders with the colors. I gave Tecmo/Koei a pass then, because I figured they would deliver improved Omega Force ports in the future.
Oops?
With that in mind, I still recommend this version... at least when it's on sale. DW8XLCE is overall a fantastic entry. It has a ton of content, and I believe the game-design, controls, and other elements are the best the series has seen to date. There are the issues that I mentioned earlier in the review, but it's not really problematic. If anything, I respect that Omega Force continues to throw around ideas. Despite countless sequels and spin-offs, this is a franchise that I can go back to again and again, because it has so many appealing qualities. These "comfort" games are perfect to come home to after putting myself through the grinder that is 2D shootemups.
*I probably could have gotten this review out *a little* sooner.

This game is awesome and a must-have!

I am a big fan of Tex Murphy, Louie, Chelsea, Rook, Taylor and all the other characters that make up Tex's world. I have played each Tex Murphy game as they came out starting with Meanstreets and I was thrilled to find out that Tex and crew was back in the Tesla Effect. The game did not disappoint. In two words, it was cinematic Tex.
The video quality was excellent with highly detailed FMV that looked great on a big screen. The sound and music were excellent, The acting carried the story and humour along well with the varied characters convincing in their roles with only a couple of missteps. Although they don't reach Crysis levels of reality, the 3D environments were detailed, varied and atmospheric. The interface was clean, elegant and easy to navigate. Through all of it there was the great mix of humour and depth. Tex wants to find out what happened and he does it only as Tex can: sticking his fingers where they shouldn't go, always making a wry quip, and in the end doing the right thing with a little bit of luck, heart and battered thick-headed determination.
The only drawbacks for me were the usual problems for an adventure game: occasionally spending an excess of time searching for a small clue in all the detail and some puzzles which are only very loosely tied to the story. That and the flow-breaking vagueness of the dialogue choices titles.  But for all the rest, the puzzles are finding and assembling the clues to tell the story, which is as it should be.
I'm into the game for the story and the fun of it, so I played in casual mode and took my time to explore eveything I could. In honour of it being a new chapter in Tex's life, although I wanted to stay true to Chelsea, on my first run through, I thought Tex deserved to make the most of what his circumstances had granted him, and went with Taylor. Making those choices, Taylor vs Chelsea vs Ariel, was agonizing, in a good way.
If you are a fan of Tex you'll enjoy the game. If you are a fan of Noir, Science Fiction, quirky characters, and a silly but heartfelt homage to hard-boiled detectives, you will not regret the experience of Tesla Effect: A Tex Murphy Adventure. And if you are new to  Tex, and enjoyed this game, all the previous ones are available too for a retro-adventure gaming time and a Big Finish Games blessed fan remake of Overseer is in production as "The Poisoned Pawn"
projected for release in fall 2017.

Before you read further, I am a "Tex Murphy Newbie" so this was my first exposure to the series... and if this is my first exposure then I sure do love what I have played. A suprisingly well written and well acted and entertaining game that should serve as a template for future adventure games.
I don't want to spoil much but Tex Murphy wakes up with a case of amnesia... sounds boring right? A lot of games have done this but I feel that Telsa Effect does this in a unique way. Instead of it just being a plot device for the sake of helping players learn what is going on, it serves as an integral part of the plot that isn't intrusive and actually makes the story even more interesting as it goes on. As the story does seem confusing at first, the game surprisingly does an excellent job of giving just enough exposition for it to makes sense, and to not bring down the pace. The twists aren't hamfisted and are very well put (and once you replay the game the twists definatly help you enjoy it even more because you can see a scene again and say "yep makes sense, the twist."
This is unlike any other Adventure game I have ever played... It is basically what i'd call a FPPC (First-Person Point and Click) it has the idea of a first person shooter, without the shooting,  and makes you explore to solve puzzles... and it works too very well. It is the adventure game genre in the modern age and it plays great. Sure the enviroments look like they came from the early 2000s, but it runs great and honestly it didn't hinder my enjoyment.
Surprisingly the puzzles are very intuitive and never get on my nerves (except for the Sliding puzzle... I always hate those) if a puzzle seems confusing then you can press the help button and Tex will tell you, basically, what to do to solve the puzzle (not the answer or correct way... but an instruction) which makes puzzle a lot more tolleratable (looking at you Nancy Drew)
Since this is an adventure game the characters play a major role... and I have a soft spot for every single one of them... they are all surprisingly entertaining to watch and complement off of each other fairly well. The only character I could not stand was the guy who you meet at the BBQ place (can't place his name) he was just obnoxious. The ner stereotype that doesn't work and only serves as a plot device. (Literally he does one thing and then he is basically worthless besides a few "nerd" jokes)
The pacing is where my first fault with the game comes. The game is split up into 12 days and each day acts as an "episode" with two amusing pun names to introduce them. My problem with the day system is sometimes you will have a crap load of stuff to do and could total to around an hour of game time... but then the next "day" could only be a puzzle and a cutscene totaling to about 12 or so minutes. This is especially evident in the final few days where it just flys by as though the writers were like "oh we are at the end but we are schedualed to do 12 days... oh well rush the next 2 days" It didn't hinder my enjoyment much (besides me being sad that the game would end) but it was definalty something I noticed. Day 8 took me a good hour and a half while the following day only took me about 30 minutes. Either way the whole
segment besides creeping me out badly with its use of Bee and Spiders really drug REALLY badly.
From jazzy noir styled tunes to an epic orchestral ending this game's soundtrack is REALLY good. It may not be something you'd listen to all the time, but I'd be damned if I didn't enjoy everytime I heard the Chandler Avenue theme or feel a sense of bombast and dread when I hear the
Theme. Very well done. And the opening song is freaking fantastic! Just
Some graphical glitches here and there (which didn't affect my liking) and a few green screen errors (artifacts were definalty noticable) and there was an exchange with one of the characters where the background behind them shifted all around. Again it didn't hurt the enjoyment at all.. but they were noticable. Also that sneak area was balls. Should be been developed much more.
Is this the end for Tex Murphy? Honestly, if this game's quality speaks for the series I say I hope it isn't. Well acted, very entertaining, and a surprisingly excellent story helps Tex's newest adventure (and my first) become one of the best adventure games I have played ever. Sure there may never be another game with this being a "reunion" game, but for what is here it is certainly worth the 15 dollar price tag. And now I am off to play the other 3 FMV Tex Murphy games I have missed..
Oh and yes, there are MT3K references, rejoice!

This is a very solid game.

The game is immersive enough so you won't get bored reading the fortresses of text it has, and some of which are actually voice-acted, which is pretty good.
You start from scratch. Get on your feet. Get allies. Build a fortress if you so desire. Become a
of society.
The interactions you're able to have depending on your status are also a very nice feature. This makes you want to explore the possibility of different builds and possible outcomes of certain situations.
Sometimes, less than I'd like to be honest; you're able to use your party members to use their statuses to do tasks. This feels fresh and natural as it would feel in a good ol' D20 tabletop session.
Fights are mostly well thought and challenging, requiring you to pay attention on what's going on.
Upon the release of the DLC (The White March) party members (and yourself) can have some settings for automate actions. Originally, the game is primarily intended for you to pause and issue actions to your party, and, I found myself doing just that. The automate settings are very lackluster and could use a total overall.
The game has pretty OK graphics that look good enough, with decent sound design and likewise alright special effects, nothing too amazing to be pointed out, things fit well, but they don't stand out from other games.
I was deeply in love with this game for the first 50 hours. However,... at some point. Something really put that relationship at a definite stop. It... simply feels like something is missing.
I've been trying to find out what really bothers me, but it's weird.
It's not the absurdity of enemies spamming "Charm", "Mind Control", "Confusion" or "Paralyze" spells on the fly with no limits of use [this little annoying nuisance I overcame with lots and lots of raw Will force. Rolling a paladin for my second play through really made me enjoy the game much more].
It's not the grand majority of characters being uninteresting at all, save a few like Aloth and... Iselmyr? Really... the rest of them is pretty forgettable. I also found myself enjoying the game more by making a full custom party. I did miss the voice acting though.
It's not the dragging out of certain areas that bothers me... not the most though. The Endless Paths (this is largely arguable I guess) fits the lore somewhat, but it's just too long and has some pretty absurd stuff. Not to mention its impossible-to-hit-or-apply-negative-status-except-petrify-building-sized-boss.
Maybe... it's that... in the end, nothing really matters. It doesn't matter how much you have grown in the game. It feels like an empty victory, since I couldn't care less about the game's main plot been the plight of the people and a forced-relationship with the game's antagonist, who tries very hard to be a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bag, but really never earns his right to be hated.
After the meeting with the gods, which was pretty damn sweet, I found myself plowing through the game not caring at all with the outcome, it just felt dragged out and the outcome didn't really matter.
On my second play through I went through everything, including the DLC, and upon its completion, I lost all desire to keep playing the game.
The way the game is built makes replayability very limited to the point of slightly different outcomes while you have to see the same things play out the same way they did before, making it more of a struggle to the point that you want to see instead of a fresh new experience.
What I really would like to see, though, is a Map Creator feature where players can create whatever the hell they want with the various creatures the game provides and play it out with their friends. (Even if it's just the repetitive dungeon layouts).
I give this game a solid 7/10.
It's worth a shot if you got some spare money and your hankering for a decent tabletop session is becoming too much to handle.

Pillars of Eternity is a very well done game. It's got a lush, rich world teeming with life and history and to compare it to games like Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale is to rob this game of it's ability to stand on it's own.
This game would be amazing even if the world had never heard of an isometric RPG before, it's one of Obsidian's first truly original ideas and it's wonderful to see a game that doesn't have its own history precede it. It stands beautifully on it's own with it's history on spirits and animancy. Obsidian has made some truly amazing games over the years with other people's ideas and I'm proud to see their own flourish so well.
It's taken the concepts that have come before it and refined them, the classes are wonderfully thought out and unique and it's got a lof of quality of life perks that most other isometric RPGS have needed.
That being said, my one issue is that the classes are so lush and unique, I feel like it'd be better suited to a turn-based system so one could get the full flavor. It's great as is, but I feel like I just automate the AI on everyone so I can focus on one or two characters at a time.

One of my favorite Sonic games, right next to Sonic 1, 2, 3 & Knuckles, and Generations. Sonic CD was one of the definitive titles for the Sega CD add-on for the Genesis, and was re-released quite a few times. What you are looking at is the remastered edition of Sonic CD, and it's quite special!
Many of us have played Sonic before, so you pretty much know what to expect here. What makes this game unique to other games in the Sonic series is time travel. You can go to the past or future, and the levels' layouts change depending on the time frame. Though the future's gonna look ugly when you're just aiming to finish levels - that's why you can attempt to make a good future! There's also F-Zero-esque special stages where you're running around destroying UFOs to collect Time Stones to get the game's good ending. They're pretty sweet, but be warned, they're hard. Thankfully, in this version of the game, you can return to the main menu when time's running out, so you'll be able to try the special stage again. Sonic CD also marks the debut of Amy Rose and Metal Sonic. Perhaps the most memorable part of the game is where you're racing against Metal Sonic, while Dr. Eggman's closing in on Sonic with his laser that takes him down in one hit! It's also famous for its incredible music, especially when it comes to the Japanese soundtrack!
The remastered edition has some new features that weren't available in versions prior to this one. It has both the Japanese and US soundtracks. Yes, you read that correctly. Both! You can switch between the two in the main menu, as well, depending on which soundtrack you like more or you just wanna listen to both soundtracks. (I like the Japanese soundtrack more, but I like the US soundtrack too, and it's more nostalgic for me. I've played Sonic CD since I got it for PC way back in 2002.) You can also play as Tails after beating the game, and there's also achievements and leaderboards. Also, unlike previous versions, the special stages in the remastered version run in 60fps, and you can use the spin dash just like you would in Sonic 2 (you can change the spin dash to charging it like in the original, if desired). It's easily the definitive version of Sonic CD if you ask me.
Sonic CD does have one major flaw though: the boss battle for Collision Chaos Zone is AWFUL. You are always bouncing all over the place when all you're trying to do is get to the freaking top where Eggman is. The checkered floor that makes you bounce really high in Wacky Workbench Zone can be a nuisance too, but not as bad as that friggin' Collision Chaos boss imo.
Definitely get this game if you're a Sonic fan. If you've never played Sonic CD on the Sega CD, PC (well, before it came out on Steam), or Sonic Gems Collection, give it a shot if you're into platform games - it's not too expensive for what it is. There's no other Sonic game quite like this one.

Just finished this game yesterday, really a good experience. It brought back memories of Elder Scrolls Oblivion thanks to the environment and equipment weight mecanics, the game play is kinda like Shadow Of The Colossus, and Spartan (ps2 game).
Sadly the main story is short and can be finished in 20 hours, but if you like doing lots of side quests and exploring the map and dungeons, you might take 100 hours just like i did.
, and that is a great time for you to go around the world map and have some fun, also do some monster hunting quests from the boarders since new monsters will appear you will have plenty of more quests from them.
Pros:
-  Hydras, Chimeras, Cyclops, Dragons, Goblins, Cockatrices, Gargoyles and all those fu**ers will be in this game
-  Very good combat system, so you fans of Dark Souls and Elder Scrolls will be blown away by this game. It's much better than both in this aspect. Every class feels different to play with, if you don't care about the op dungeon, you might find fun to start all over again from zero just to play a different class.
-  A lot of replayability, thanks to hard mode and overpowered dungeon called Bitterblack Island which will give you strong af items.
-  Great graphics (except for your main character facial expressions, they look bad...)
-  Nice character customization, and character weight and height will influense some aspects of the game play, like how easily he can go out of balance from enemy attacks, pass through the lags of cyclops and other monsters, how far his weapon swings will reach the enemies and etc.
-  Great interaction with companions (pawns), your pawns and other people's pawns will always be talking about the place, the quest you have active, they will also be screaming the monsters weaknesses when you're in battle, the AI from pawns is really great and the way they talk to you can be customized to your likings. When someone gets your pawn to side with them, they will return with the knowledge they got from the quests, monsters, or areas they got involved there.
Cons:
-  Short main story, and not really good plot overall. (The end kinda gave me some insights about humanity, good and evil, yng-yang stuff, meaning of life if there's one... but still, the story is badly developed until then)
-  Main world monsters and bandits are too weak, you reach level 40 or 50 and the main world can't stop you anymore, the only challenge then becomes the Bitterblack Island dungeon and a mutated version of The Everfall which is accesible way in the end of the main story.
-  Hard Mode is retardly hard when you're starting, but in new game plus, it feels like a joke just like normal mode, the only challenge is bitterblack island at this point... and a hell of challenge i might say.
It's worth full price if you like action rpg's, and character customization, party-based combat. Really a great game.

This is a game that many will overlook, due to it not being very famous, but I think Way of the Samurai 4 is a very good game in many ways.
The story is not long at all, you could complete a play through in like 3-4 hours, but there are 10 endings, where if you want to know the full picture, you have to achieve most of them. The true ending is more difficult to achieve, which I presume total play time will be like 40+ hours. Although the story is not very long, but interesting regardless, the story took place in last days of the Shogunate, where foreign culture (British) are trying to blend/mix with the Japanese. Creating conflicts between the town, Shogunate and the British Empire.
The structure of the story is like a combination of Visual Novel with Action game, where you make important decisions, and walk down the path, see a few bad ending and normal endings, then you work your way to true (happy) ending.
The combat system is superb, basic but fun. I can clearly see that the developers have put a lot of effort into researching different combat styles and moves, especial in Samurai Swords, they know how one draw and stash (put in to Saya) a sword properly. There are 55 Swordfighting styles, 8 Spear styles, 9 Dual sword styles, 7 Hand-to-Hand styles and even 3 gun styles. The way they portray a sword hitting and slashing again human body, the movement of the sword with the body, and stops between each move shows strength in the movement, sharpness of the sword, I really like this kind of action games where you can 'feel' the sword slash. Unlike many other 'action' games I have played. (Yeah, Batman, new DMC, shadow of Mordor, looking at you guys.)
The graphic is not very good, even for PS3 generation, but hey Japanese games were never known for their graphics.
Overall I think this game has a very interesting idea/core, executed pretty well, definitely good combat animation and system.
8/10

Sweet holy Moses, get this game.
Okay, lemme qualify two things real quick:  1) I'm a pretty big Asiaphile (mostly China, but Japan, too, duh; I DID grow up on an SNES alongside DOS), and 2) my brother got me this game cuz he saw it on my wishlist and I was havin' a rough time of things lately, so I didn't pay anything for it, technically (though I hit him back the 25 bucks because I felt like it was a good thing to do and I would totally buy this game for 25 anyway).  I knew I wanted this game from the doofy Two Best Friends playthrough of it; I did not know I would like it THIS HARD.
You start off as a ronin coming to a new town, which is apparently how the other three start (have not played them, and probably won't; they'd be hard to go back to, I feel, after this).  You show up right when a brawl has jumped off in the streets.  Do you get involved?  Congratulations, the story just forked. If you did, who of the three groups, if any, do you side with?  Another story fork.  This is the main draw of WotS4: you can beat it in about 5 hours your first time through, if you're really being thorough in side stuff to do, but it's insanely replayable.  It should tell you something that you can beat it that quickly and I'm just shy of 40 hours at time of writing. This game is ALL I have done in the week since I got it. It's that engaging.  There are ten different endings, the characters are likeable/relatable, and the dialogue is better than you might expect.
The gameplay is tons of fun; the combat system is VERY detailed.  There are 108 fighting styles, but that number is kinda ♥♥♥♥ing with you; there's five or six STANCES that each fighting style falls under one of.  Different styles in the same stance will have the same basic attack structure, but unique attacks bound to individual buttons (i.e., if two given Iai styles, for instance, both have the basic X-X-X three-hit combo, it will be the exact same move, but Kasshin style has a Y attack that's a quick doublestrike, while Perfect style has a stronger, slower, upward slice).  Styles will also combo differently, if they combo at all (it is possible to find styles that are built entirely out of discrete, individual moves, but I don't recommend them; you're gonna want a bread-and-butter at the very least).  As you master styles, you can eventually make your OWN style that is a mishmash of styles you've mastered, meaning you can take your favorite style of your favorite stance, take out moves you don't like and replace them with maybe those one or two good moves you really liked from a style that was otherwise inferior.
The fighting is surprisingly technical, with pushing, pulling, parries, counters, and overall a lot more strategy than I expected to find in the game, and while there is a very basic tutorial, you will figure out a lot of it just by playing and having it emerge over time.
That SAID, this IS a "wiki game". You're gonna want a guide out for the more arcane parts of the game. I had to look up how to get a few super-well hidden extras, a shinobi-stance style I really wanted, what the Hell the "Crime Rate: Great!" pop-up meant, how the forge worked, and a few other things. It didn't detract from the experience for me, but it may for you, so it merits mentioning.
Sound design's a bit weak; slashes and slices don't have a lot of impact to them, and characters running at each other can sometimes take place it cutscenes with no sound effects; no yelling, no foot steps, one or two sounds of steel hitting steel, if any, that kind of thing. That can come off as janky, but don't let it dissuade you; it does very little to devalue the game. The spoken dialogue is all very good, though. It's in Japanese, subtitled, but it's very good.
This game is translated BEAUTIFULLY. If you're familiar with the term "Woolseyism", this game is chock full of them. That's basically where puns, cultural references, jokes and the like are translated in such a way that the characters make an equivalent reference that would make sense to your culture, rather than just spelling out what they said in English. Characters may make puns based on alternate readings of Japanese characters or make references to Japanese history that would be considered an impenetrably-deep cut for foreigners, but the translation team reworked the dialogue (and a number of item names) so that it all fits, characterization remains the same, but the jokes and comments themselves will scan for a foreign audience.  This to a degree that I don't see very often, even in other, well-translated games, but it made me smile a number of times (again, gotta qualify, maybe part of the pleasure there comes from knowing the language and seeing that captions wrote something markedly different from what the character actually said, but did so in the name of including people with no outside knowledge and I KNOW I sound like a prick but I'm very much not trying to; I just think it's really neat and very admirable).
The game is also surprisingly irreverent. People call it "Demented" fairly often, and with good reason; there is a LOT of goofy♥♥♥♥♥♥in here, and a lot of deconstructions of the Jidai Geki (famous samurai films, like 47 Ronin, Zatoichi, etc) genre.  There are a number of silly moments and a lot of times serious characters will be made to look like fools, either for humor's sake or for the sake of not being a cliche', this-is-grimdark-serious-feudal-Japan malarky. That said, when it wants to, the game can be very powerful.  One of the endings I got siding with the rebels was actually really profound and moved me, while the golden ending, which I busted my♥♥♥♥♥to get, was one of THE more fulfilling video gaming experiences I've had since I was a kid.  You will almost certainly get a bad ending the first time you play, but it doesn't suck because the game is brief, and it's done in the name of setting up the big bad as a complete monster piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥that you want to see dead. And boy, when you finally get the best ending, it is climactic, rewarding, dramatic, epic and some other nice words.
On another note, the character customization is straight-jacket-wearing insane. Dynasty Warriors 8 Xtreme Legends is my favorite Dynasty Warriors game since Dynasty Warriors 4 on the PS2. The game has an absurd amount of content for us Warriors fans, from the large cast of characters to the combat system. It also has the Ambition mode, where you try to conquer and unite the nation.
The story mode is much the same as usual. The major story doesn’t change for each faction, as, well, it’s based on history. However, the game has hypothetical routes in each of the game’s stories. It’s a genius way to refresh the game’s story while staying true to the history. It added a much needed boost to the original story mode. I don’t recall if this was in any of the more recent previous versions, but then again, Dynasty Warriors 7 was forgettable. I hardly remember a thing about it.
The ambition mode gives you a taste of Dynasty Warriors: Empires. It’s essentially a simpler version of the same mode. I enjoyed it. I hesitate to say such. The mode was such a grind, and I’ve gotten to the point where I simply stopped playing through it because it takes so long with so little payoff. In this mode you can upgrade and fuse weapons to give them customizations that suit you perfectly. While a good idea in theory, I find that the lack of customizability on the 5-star and 6-star weapons renders it much less exciting than it should be. It would take a significant amount of effort to have the upgraded weapons surpass the 6-star special weapons, and all that means is much more grinding. There’s other items you can unlock which require just as much grinding throughout the mode. Seriously, it’s ridiculous. Bonding with other officers was interesting, but the appeal wore off after about the 9th officer.
Challenge mode? Eh. I never understood the appeal. I believe I beat two before I was bored out of my mind and never touched those modes again.
This is the first Warriors game where I felt as if every character was unique. Before, you’d get a few officers with the same move set, and that was damn disappointing. I didn’t see such in this game, and the ex-attacks contributed further to it. I won’t say they’re all likeable (freaking Han Dang), but they’re different.
In regards to the game’s flaws, the most obvious is the lack of create-a-character. It’s in Empires, of course, but not here. As it is in every iteration of the game, the fan-service is a bit annoying. Lastly, despite the game’s mediocre graphics, the game ran with a weird issue. Many times when I would strike, I’d teleport backwards ever so slightly as if knocked back. I’ve watched videos of other people playing, and it did not exist for them. I fiddled with a few settings, and did bing searches, both to no avail. It wasn’t too bothersome for warriors like Lu Bu, but the characters with shorter ranges (ex: Cao Cao), it was completely and utterly annoying to attack twice and the teleporting pushing me back enough to where my target was out of my range.
Overall, a wonderful addition to the series. I loved it. Daqiao was a monster. Best character in the game.

Starbound is a game set in the future, where you must stop an evil creature that was locked away years ago from returning, and destroying everything everyone holds dear. (Mainly, the ability to live.)
I have only played Starbound for five hours at this time, but I think I know enough about it to give a decent review. Not to say that Starbound is simple, by all means no. It is incredibly detailed and incredibly well thought out.
Let's start off with the graphics. Starbound takes Terraria style graphics and builds on them, making them more detailed and better looking. The graphics in the game Stardew Valley are also similar because both games are made by Chucklefish. The blend of weaponry and tech make for a stunning, Star Trek style journey. It features assault rifles, laser guns, swords, hammers, bigger swords, weapons you cannot even imagine at the present moment, and more.
Now for the gameplay. Starbound has been likened to Terraria in many ways, since it is a 2D, sidescrolling adventure with pixel graphics where you can craft stuff, the ususal. But I've got to say that Starbound outdoes Terraria by miles. Here's why: first, the building system. I got Terraria on the Xbox and then on the PC, and I think it is very enjoyable, but it isn't a pick up and play kind of game. If you want to play it right, if you want to build the best homes and have all the NPCs come and live in your house and you want to be prepared to fight all the awesome bosses, you need to do some homework. Starbound is nothing like that. It sets you off with a 'save the universe' ordeal as your main quest. If you do some thourough looking throughout your environment, you can find stuff fairly quickly. The second point I would like to mention is the building/combat system. In Starbound, you have a plethora of weapons, but only one tool for digging/mining/chopping: The Matter Manipulator, which can be upgraded throughout the course of the game. This not only makes collecting materials simpler, it also makes building things simpler, with selected blocks shown being placed by the MM and nothing else.
Finally, let's look at the value. Starbound is a game that I will come back to for quite some time. It has multiplayer support, so if you want to hop into a friend's world, or vice versa, then go do it! Nobody's stopping you. Starbound provides a lot of content that may seem daunting at first, but is so well organized and simple that with a little thinking, you can surely go and conquer the galaxy, save humanity, and the like.

I felt the need to capitalize it, because, frankly, who wouldn't want to capitalize aesthetics based on early Russian communist propaganda posters mixed with the setting about Orwellian animals' revolutionary fighting for cannibalistic privileges? Tooth and Tail has simple mechanic to it. In fact, it is probably the first strategy game that works really well with a gamepad. It offers only one type of resource, only six units/structures per game that you get to pick before the match, only four players max per map. Yet it is surprisingly brutal and fast-paced with ranked (1v1) matches rarely going for more than 15 minutes and a simple and minor miscalculation being your fatal mistake that would cost you the match.
I wonder if this game is Pocketwatch`s wicked way of celebrating the centenary of 1917, a year when Russian empire saw two revolutions, and a civil war later. The carnivorous beasts use some sort of a made-up Slavic-sounding language to communicate, refer to their state leader as Tsarina, and have an overall early 20th century aesthetic to them whether it comes to music or characters. And, of course, it has an indie 8-bit touch to it. Can be a turn-off for some, understandable.
However, this gem hides a vibrant world full of different characters past its blocky visuals. While not being rich for cutscenes the game explains most of its lore through peaceful locations between the missions where your leader can interact with different objects and characters.
The leader of the faction is the only unit you directly control: building, issuing orders to others, and scouting. The unit does not attack and has to be in the location to issue out an order to go somewhere or attack something. Also, and I wonder if it’s a feature, you can only issue commands either to all units or one unit type which can be a bit frustrating seeming how it makes tactical positioning more difficult. However, it works well with the overall “think fast” approach that the game is implementing.
The player is presented with a variety of units loosely divided into 3 tiers based on strength and the last tier being defensive structures, like mines or machine gun nests. You can pick out 6 different units for each game as you want.
The game randomises almost any map it can. Campaign maps are random, and ranked maps are random which makes them really difficult to predict and master. The developer has introduced seeds and pre-built maps with one of the updates, but only for non-ranked matches.
Tooth and Tail stands out due to its unusual mechanics, amazing soundtrack, and a fast paced approach. It may not be something that turn-based or grand strategy lovers would appreciate, especially due to its 8-bit coating. Yet for me it`s a thumbs up all the way.

After a frustrating 15 year hiatus, Tex Murphy finally returns to resolve the cliffhanger seen in Tex Murphy: Overseer. I remember how outraged I felt after seeing that cliffhanger at the end of Overseer, and the subesequent hiatus in the series only served to further justify that anger. However, Tesla Effect makes up for the wait with its cinematic production quality (filmed in 2K video) and its solid classic FMV adventure-puzzle gaming experience. You can tell the developers put their heart and soul into its development, and were anxious to please their fan base with a quality sequel that was highly improbable ever to happen, and yet greatly desired and made possible only with a wildly successful (by adventure gaming standards) Quickstarter campaign. Since watching the story unfold is one of the most satisfying parts of the gaming experience, I won't spoil it for anyone with further details, other than to say it has a multipath story with different possible endings based on your choices (akin to Pandora Directive). Fortunately, most of the actors were able to reprise their roles in this sequel. Overall, everyone really delivered the goods, which is a rarity in and of itself these days. Suffice it to say that veteran adventure gamers like myself, or anyone with a desire to see a good "interactive" story with puzzles will want to play this game. Best of all, it ends with a true sense of closure, with just an open-ended allusion to another possible sequel in the future. Please make another sequel possible by supporting this game with your friends, because this is the kind pf gaming experience we need to see more!
