What a brilliant game. Tex is back in a brand new adventure about 15yrs or so after the last game came out. This one is set 7yrs after the events of Overseer and Tex has lost his memory after some shady events went down at his apartment block. Now he has to get his memory back and find his girlfriend Chelsee which ends up drawing him into the world of Nicola Tesla and his disciples.
After playing the original Tex games back in the 90s it was amazing to play this game and it doesn't disapoint for old fans. All the old characters are there and being back on Chandler Ave is like coming home. Not much has changed since those previous games. You still move around the world in a first person view, clicking on things, picking up objects, solving puzzles and questioning characters. When you trigger a cut scene or talk to a character the 3D world switches to FMV footage. This technique was all the rage for awhile back in the 90s but hasn't really been used since then until now. The team at Big Finish have done a really good job with the quality of the FMV here. It's hi-def, the acting is pretty good (in a Tex way) and it fits pretty seamlessly into the rest. As with all the prior Tex games the humour is a big part and it's still here. Gotta love those eye rolling Tex jokes.
The story is not bad, puzzles are pretty decent and gameplay is pretty easy to get a handle on. There were a couple of times in later sections of the game I found myself wandering around for ages trying to work out what to do next but I was playing on Gamer difficultly with no hints or guides. Luckily they also have a hint system and a Casual difficulty which will highlight objects if you get stuck.
I've played this one through twice now and really enjoyed it. There is a team also working on remaking Overseer (the game that is a prequel to this one). Check out the site.
Will be looking forward to playing that one to.

Ahh, Tesla Effect. How hard it is to review it. One one hand, this is AMAZING reboot of a FMV adventure series. On the other hand... its a FMV adventure, packed with some of the same issues it used to have back then, and a few new ones packed in. Yes, we still have some amateurish acting in here. Yes, we still have bad looking rendered backgrounds that don't mesh too well with the characters. And we also have another issue here: after 16 years, the actors aren't exactly at their prome. Hell, one of the main characters looks so old (and fatter) compared to his/her last game that it kinda ruined some scenes in the game. And that's one of the main issues with the FMV genre...
As an adventure game, Its a great entry. It does have a few casual puzzles (you know, the ones you usually find in hidden object games - sliding, jigsaw, etc), but there are also some amazingly designed ones, and the detective stuf is till top notch. You can open every drawer, you can look at every corner of the maps, you can still click in everything just to hear Tex cracking some jokes... Fact is: even if the game is indeed flawed, its easy to forget about the issues when you have a game that delivers EXACTLY what the fans where looking for: an answer to the question that has been living on our brains ever since we saw the end of Overseer. And unlike most recent adventure games, you DO have a nice inventory management, including the ability to combine items. Yeah, like the classics. ^^
Much like Pandora Directive, Tesla Effect features two things that are usually NOT found in FMV games: branching dialogue trees and multiple endings. This is nice, because it gives you a reason to replay the game. The story will be the same, but you'll be able to see different dialogues, different scenes and different endings (there are 5 of them, BTW). The story, BTW, is, in my opinion, amazing. Very complex, very detailed and very creative. It VERY fictional, but not absurd. While it continues from the cliffhanger ending presented in Overseer, it also features a new plot, involving Nikola Tesla's inventions and some urban legends around it. In fact, the connections between all the older games and this new plot are so natural that you REALLY have to congratulate Chris Jones for its amazing writing.
The gameplay is actually quite good. You still are able to navigate full 3D backgrounds in first person view, but all dialogues and most actions are presented in FMV scenes with branching  dialogues. You don't really choose WHAT Tex is gonna say, but HOW he will deliver his next line (sarcastic retort, weird PI humor, change subject, etc). This is nice, since you never know what he is gonna say until he does. This game has two difficulty settings, but unlike the older games, you can select between casual, which is VERY easy, and gamer, which is just "normal". Yeah, this game doesn't present too much challenge for classic adventure players. But it's still harder than most adventure games coming out nowdays, and still feels like a real game, not an interactive movie, which is nice.
The graphics are ok. For some lame reason, they decided to use Unity (YUCK!), so expect unstable framerates, VERY low res textures and weird 3D models. But the game doesn't really look BAD. Hell, for a budget game, some places are actually quite pleasing to the eyes. The FMV scenes are fantastic though. Not only they are in a very high resolution (blu-ray quality!), but most of them are quite well produced (the ending scenes specially have amazing special effects!). The sound department is perfect. The sound effects are realistic and VERY atmospheric and the musics are great and always set the right mood to most scenes. I have nothing to complain about the soundtrack. Heck, they even put the UAKM day transition song in here!! :p
Anyway... Tesla Effect isn't perfect. It doesn't poop on Tex Murphy's name, and actually make it even stronger. In fact, its a better game that most people expected, and considering how dead the FMV genre is, its amazing that we got a new game that feels so similar to the older ones. It's a game that REALLY delivers to fans of the series. If you are not a fan though... well, I recommend that you try the demo first, because this game is aimed at the fans.
I give this game an 9/10. And I REALLY hope they do a new one in the near future. At least before the actors get even older. :p

There is a lot of emphasis on the "full motion video" part, but in the end, it's a point & click adventure in a 3D engine. The 3D environments could be better, though -- but the cutscenes are what you'll be hoping for anyway. And while it's not an hundreds of million dollars movie production, they are quite nice.
Tex also doesn't get boring when examining stuff, unless you count the repeats when clicking on the same kind of item in the same environment and get the same comment again.
The gameplay isn't too bad. I wasn't a big fan of some areas, when they put a timer on things or made you sneak around stealthy, but it could be worse. Playing in "casual" mode lets you skip some puzzles if you want to -- it will cost you some points, just like getting yourself killed does, but points don't matter anyway.
Likewise, there's supposed to be multiple endings, but I doubt they are THAT different. You'll complete the objective, so what? Options in dialogues are usually vague, so you never know what you're saying or where you're heading; I just randomly clicked an answer. I still liked the game -- again, not much of a difference compared to a game where the outcome is fixed anyway.

Tesla Effect is the latest game in the Tex Murphy series, a first person point and click adventure game with a heavy emphasis on FMVs (full motion video). FMVs were quite popular in the early nineties because computer graphics still weren't able to provide a good character representation. However they fell out of favour because most of them had bad gameplay and even worse acting. The only games I played which really used FMV effectively were the Command & Conquer games. The FMVs there felt like a reward for progressing through the story.
In Tesla Effect I get a similar feeling, I enjoyed most of the FMV sections. Mostly because of the protagonist Tex Murphy, who is played in a very self aware manner, the game knows it's cheesy and doesn't take itself too seriously. And if you strip away all the videos there's still a pretty good game underneath it all. While the 3D graphics certainly aren't anything to special (they look like something out of a decade old game) they were actually better than I expected, especially since the levels themselves are reasonably large. I am pleased with the size of the world they constructed, there isn't that much of revisiting the same locations and they are quite varied as well. However pretty much the whole 3D world is dead, there are very few encounters with living beings outside of the FMVs.
The story itself is cheesy and by the end of the game I felt it became pretty much ridiculous. The game played much better when it wasn't focusing on the main premise of the game. It would have been nice to have some side quests, but in true adventure game fashion every single thing is connected and you can not progress without doing everything. I wouldn't fault most other adventure games with this, however as I mentioned I felt the game was best when it wasn't focusing on the main story.
The videos themselves are quite well made, the acting is cheesy but not bad. There are barely any real world objects, almost everything besides the characters themselves is CGI, which is on par with the rest of the game. So, not great, but considering the budget they had to work with I think it's good enough.
As an adventure game there are quite a lot of puzzles, I was OK with most of them, however I certainly needed help sometimes. Thankfully there's an optional help system included in the game and an option to skip the puzzle mini game sections, which I used once because the puzzle itself made absolutely no sense to me.
Tesla Effect is not an easy game to recommend, it's a throwback to a type of game which existed for a very short amount of time, due to limited technical capabilities of the time. And the series from which it comes is probably one of the best of its type. When I played the game I took it as such and mostly enjoyed what I got, so if you do the same you can go ahead and try this out. I hope the series continues, as I think a really good game can be made from this, with the right story.

Traditional Rating - 79
Recommendation - cRPG fans, put this on your shortlist
cRPGs have made a triumphant return in recent years. From the Baldur's Gate Enhanced Editions to successful(ly kickstarted) revivals of popular franchises like Wasteland, Torment, Sword Coasts, and even some new ones, there has been more than enough quasi-turn-based party management fantasy to sink your teeth into.
Most of those games have been (or will be) fairly modernized versions of the genre, but Pillars of Eternity is the first one to REALLY bring to mind the original Baldur's Gate, in all its pock-marked glory. In fact, if I didn't know any better, I might even be convinced into believing this was just a thoroughly well-done mod pack.
It's obviously not, though. This game was built from the ground up in the Unity engine by Obsidian Entertainment who, as you might know, were instrumental in designing everything from Baldur's Gate, to Planescape Torment, to Fallout 2, and even Fallout New Vegas. These are some genre (and industry) veterans, and it shows. Every aspect of this game is well-polished. Stability is rock-solid, the graphics are beautiful and well-optimized, sound and music is fantastic, voice acting is solid, there are lots of interesting NPCs, and the story is interesting.
This game is a shining example of the genre, and if you're looking for a cRPG and you loved Baldur's Gate 1, you absolutely cannot overlook Pillars.
Over the course of the 50+ hour journey, you'll be exploring numerous towns/caves/ruins/forests, battling evil monarchs and quashing uprisings, helping secure lineages, rooting out corruption, and slaughtering enemies by the hundreds. You'll make friends in one town, enemies in another, and something in between on more than a few occasions. This is a game where your choices can have a profound impact on the world, and the consequences of those decisions will be summed up in brutally painful clarity during the ending.
It's hard to know what exactly to start talking about, so I'll choose story. In my 60 hours spent playing, most of my time was spent away from the main quest line, but the game did a pretty good job of tying everything in together. A game like Divinity: Original Sin (D:OS) will have a large series of self-contained quests, each of which you earn exp for, but Pillars' quests are all inter-related. Some will earn you reputation which you can use to persuade other quest-givers, some will enable or lock out other quests entirely, and some will either please your companions into confiding in you or anger them into leaving. The Baldur's Gate games did this too, and it's refreshing to see Pillars keep the tradition alive. I will say I wish there was more clashing between the various personalities within the party (everyone got along a little too well), but your actions can and do have an impact on their opinion of you. The main quest itself twists and spirals around, and while it does ramble quite a bit (and start to go off the rails) towards the end, I thought it came together nicely.
Going back to NPCs, I thought that overall, they were really well-done. There's close to 10 of them, and they each have their own quests/goals/personalities, most of which develop quite satisfyingly. It was a source of slight frustration that I had to leave a few of them behind at my citadel to watch over things, but I was able to dispatch them on missions remotely, so it was OK. Interacting with the NPCs all felt very organic, too. Sometimes they would want to talk to you about important things, but otherwise it was up to you to initiate conversations. You'd have to build up trust with them before they would open up to you, and they wouldn't shy away from telling you "that's enough for now". I got along with certain NPCs better than others, and certain ones were stronger than others, but at least they were always interesting. Speaking of talking, not all of this game is voice-acted, and the transitions can be distracting.
One area this game differs noticeably from Baldur's Gate is in combat. It's still the same pause-when-you-want, micromanaging type of party control, but they eased back a bit on the brutal realism. Don't get me wrong, there are a LOT of tough fights (adra dragon, for one), but when each battle is over, you don't need to use all your healing spells and camp twice to recover. That was one thing I always hated about the BG games, and thankfully it wasn't a sore spot here. In battles, you have health and endurance (800 health and 160 endurance, for example). When damaged, you take equal hits to both health and endurance, and if endurance drains to empty (in this example, you'd have 640 health and 0 endurance), you are knocked out (in BG, you'd be dead). If the surviving team members win the battle, that knocked out character will stand back up, and endurance will regenerate (health will not). This allows you to fight several battles in between resting/camping sessions, which speeds the game up DRASTICALLY. Obviously there are spells that can heal endurance inside battle, but you will need to rest/sleep to recover any health. If health ever runs out, a character is either maimed or killed. I had a few characters get maimed (temporary stat debuff until they rest), but never had one get killed, thankfully. Resting is always 8 hours, and always fully heals/recovers.
I only really had a few sore spots about combat. The first problem is that this game falls prey to the classic Baldur's Gate slog, where it will sometimes take you 40 minutes spread across 6 different boring battles to cover a single screen. Battles here resolve quite a bit quicker than they ever did in BG, but it can still sometimes be laborious. Take step, fight Xaurips, more steps, more Xaurips, etc. I call this Baldur's Gate syndrome because parts of that game were absolutely filled to the rafters with it, so if you played that, you know what to expect. Just remember to take breaks when you start feeling weary, and it should be fine. The second problem I had is classic party management frustration. Giving orders to melee characters quite often ends with them ignoring the orders and continuing with their regularly scheduled programming. This can REALLY be a problem when my priest is getting turned into cheesecloth by archers. My warriors acknowledge my order to disengage and cross the room, but instead take 2 steps, get punished with a disengagement strike, and then turn around to continue attacking their original target again, ignoring my order and letting the priest die. So what you have to do is either re-issue orders every 2 seconds, baby-stepping the warriors across the room while they suffer 8 disengagement strikes BECAUSE THEY KEEP RE-ENGAGING, or just let the priest die. If there are 2 or 3 enemies clustered together tightly, it can be literally impossible to pull a warrior away. This is with the default NPC non-AI, so maybe there's a way to wipe them completely clean or something. As with many other party management games, the AI here is just "smart" enough to screw with my orders.
Going along with the slog, I should talk about backtracking. There is a lot of it in this game. The world itself is smallish, and there's a lot of content crammed into it, so quests (which you will have 11 of at a time) will have you heading to A, talking to B, killing C and his friends, returning to D, and turning the quest in to E. It gets rather repetitive, but luckily a lot of side quests are not only unnecessary but also pointless (max level is 12, which completionists will hit early).
Overall, I found Pillars game to be a great love letter to Baldur's Gate and its ilk. It certainly has some problems, but it's meaty and satisfying, and as long as you don't mind some momentary bits of repetition and tedium, you should find it enjoyable too. I was ready for it to be over a few hours before it actually was, but it didn't overstay its welcome too much, and I'm glad I visited.

As you can see from my hours played I tried greatly to enjoy this game.  Whilst this game attempts to harken back to the "good ole days" of Baldur's Gate and other isometric crpgs, Pillars of Eternity feels bland and suffers from some major game breaking bugs cropping up in each patch cycle.
With each patch cycle Obsidian makes changes to the stat, ability and buff/debuff mechanics in what is an already convoluted system, not to mention the myriad of bugs that such a cycle brings.   Having to thoroughly read through patch notes to understand what over-the-top changes have been made can be frustrating.  Obsidian also seems to make changes to mechanics and systems that work fine whilst seemingly ignoring broken classes and abilties.
The combat becomes tedious very quickly, usually involving bottling up your adversaries in a choke point and autoattacking them until dead.  When you do decide to use spells or abilities you will quickly find that a majority of them are completely useless, whilst those that cause stun or knockdowns to be king.
At those times that you are unable to keep your enemy hemmed in, you will find those carefully crafted tank characters will be next to useless in keeping the enemies of your squishy damage dealers.  The fault here is with the poorly implemented engagement system.  A tank has the ability to 'engage' an enemy and should that enemy leave the area from the tank they will take a hit.  Of course this hit does nothing to actually stop an enemy from casually walking over and making paste of your rogue or wizard.   I won't detail the number of enemy creatures in this game that can just bypass the engagement system by teleporting straight into your group's back ranks and perma-stunning or killing them in two or three hits.  This problem has only gotten worse with the new expansion.
The itemization for character equipment is dull.  After a lengthy dungeon crawl of tedious fights to find items that are mostly yawn worthy was very disappointing.
The writing in the game seems to peak and trough.  The companions and their storylines seem to vary from interesting to just mind numbling boring.  The lore itself comes at your thick and fast with exposition upon exposition though with the latter it takes too many liberties by assuming you already know some hidden but integral world lore.  This can affect your conversation choices, though admittedly that is not a big deal as your choices in the end really mean nothing.  The authors are telling a story and be damned if you are going to have really influence on how that is going to be told.
On a few positive notes the graphics are very good and I absolutely adore the music.  Many times during my day I've caught myself humming the music from the game.
If you want to try the game, do so!  Just wait until it is on sale.  The price for non backers is astounding when you compare it other rpg styles games released in the same time that offer a whole lot more.

This is great. The best time I've had with a fantasy RPG since, I think, the first Dragon Age. A lot of games of this sort, like ShadowRun or Divinity, end up losing me with their convoluted, doofy, or wink-wink storylines. So far, this one has stayed focused and interesting. A 'Children of Men'-style curse on the population's reproduction is a great premise for this sort of game: emotionally unsettling, but not too immediate or urgent that you don't feel you can take your time in exploring the world. The writers have also struck a nice balance between making your character special (your soul is 'awakened' so that you can perceive your past lives, and those of others), while managing to avoid all the 'chosen one/prophesy/most important person ever' garbage that often flatlines fantasy stories. I feel like an ordinary person, but an influential one.
Prose-wise, the writing is confident and detailed. In converstaions, the writers do a good job of adopting the attitudes of each character without resorting to too many gimmicks such as corny accents. "I'll 'ave yer 'ead for this, I will!" doesn't happen too often. In describing the setting, they focus on brief, telling details. Consider this description of a table: "A dozen tiny somethings squirm within a pot of rice." A lazier writer would have said, "The table is strewn with rotten food and utensils." Little touches like this are important, because the game is one-third combat, two-thirds fantasy novel.
As far as combat and character systems go, I don't really know how to critique them except to say they work for me. It's a nice update of the old AD&D games; less cryptic and arbitrarily roadblocking, but still complex enough to reward good decisions. I was happy to find I could reroll my character for a few hundred coppers at any inn.
There are lots of nice 'atmospheric' systems too, such as recruiting custom adventurers and refurbishing a ruined castle. Importantly, these support the main plot instead of detracting from it. In Dragon Age 3, I thought the castle was an annoying gimmick; here, it's built into the plot in a satisfying way and doesn't overstay its welcome.
In all, the game has something that's rare to this genre: consistency. Its atmosphere, combat, characters, plot, and systems are all ticking nicely together to deliver an original story that is itself intriguing. I'm only about halfway through, but I recommend it.
PS: My enjoyment of the game went up a lot when I turned off all the voice-acting. No offence to the actors, but the mix of fully-voiced and silent dialogue was annoying to me, and I didn't expect my Inuit-inspired huntress companion to talk like a southern belle. I find reading more immersive; your mileage may vary.

Mass Effect is the first game in a series that has captivated me since I first discovered it on Playstation 3 years and years ago.  I would consider it a role playing game with shooter/action elements because although the primary method of combat is over-the-shoulder third-person shooting, the biggest and most important element of the game is the story, and your interactions with the characters in the universe.  I'll try to break this review down into a couple of different parts; graphics/visuals, audio and voice acting, gameplay, story, and technical stability.  With regard to any technical aspects of the game, you should know that I played the game at 1080p with every setting turned as high as it can go on the following hardware:
CPU: AMD FX 8370
GPU: MSI Radeon RX 480 8GB Gaming (overclocked to 1,303 Mhz)
RAM: 16 GB Corsair Vengeance DDR3 1,866 Mhz
First the graphics/visuals.  Today is 27 December 2017, and this game was released in 2008, so it's almost 10 years old, so don't come into this expecting to be blown away by the graphics.  That being said, in my opinion, the visuals have aged VERY well, especially compared to some other games that were released around that same time.  The character and facial models in particular look surprisingly good.  Animations look fluid and natural, particle effects add a little extra bling to certain events in the game such as an enemy disintegrating when you finish them off with incendiary rounds.  Lighting looks very good and natural and does a very good job of setting the mood.  The pre-rendered cutscenes are lower resolution than I played the game at, and you'll occasionally notice a low resolution texture on somebody's clothing, but generally speaking the game's visuals still hold up pretty well nearly 10 years later.
The audio and voice acting is really good.  The background music does a good job of matching what's going on around you and setting a mood.  The voice actors did a very good job of portraying their characters.  The game's audio did a good job of hitting some low bass frequencies when you were supposed to feel like the thing going on around you was incredibly large, and it works.
The gameplay consists of 3 major elements; interactive conversations where you'll choose what you want to say to advance the conversation along, boots on the ground walking around and/or fighting, and driving what is called the "Mako" vehicle on the surface of various planets.
The story is advanced mostly through the use of interactive conversations with various characters in the game.  Depending on the choices you make in those conversations, and your actions during combat missions, you will accrue either "Paragon"(Good) or "Renegade"(Evil) points, and those points open up other options in conversations.  Some outcomes in the story can only be accomplished if you pass a speech check by having a high enough Paragon/Renegade rating and enough points allotted to either Charm or Intimdate in your skill tree.  The conversations can be advanced with other choices, but if you don't have enough points, those options will be grayed out in your dialog wheel.
The combat is over-the-shoulder third person shooting.  You have 4 weapon types and various abilities that can be unlocked and taken into combat with you.  Each of your 3 party members (you can only take 2 people with you when you leave your ship) has their own separate loadout of 4 weapons, armor, and assistive device like grenades, etc.  You carry a pistol, assault rifle, shotgun and sniper rifle with you at all times.  You will constantly find increasingly better variations of items littered all around the galaxy, and it will benefit you to spend some time paying attention to the gear your party members are wearing.  Certain characters also have biotic or tech abilities that allow you to do things like throw people into the air, short circut their shields, etc.  Your other two party members can be commanded individually or as a group.  You can have them follow you, attack a specific enemy on screen, take cover, or you can even manually select a weapon or ability you want them to use.
The "Mako" is a 6 wheeled vehicle used to traverse the surface of various planets and moons you find throughout the galaxy.  It can drive, jump, and fire two different types of weapons.  In the event that the planet you are on has a particularly inhospitable environment, it offers protection from the elements.  It is primarily used to travel from one point of interest to another on the surface, but it can also be a useful tool for taking out enemies that would be difficult to handle on foot.  If you choose to complete side quests, you will spend a lot of time in the Mako.
You are command Shephard; backstory, gender, etc. to be chosen by you when you start your game.  Through the discovery of some ancient ruins on Mars, humans were able to advance their own technology and eventually make contact with other species of intelligent life.  However, not all is well in the Milky Way; evidence of mass extinction events have lead to the discovery of an ancient race of sentient machines that systematically wipes out all intelligent life in the galaxy on a regular basis, and it's up to you to stop it.  The story, overall, is really good.  It's not just the big, major arc that's interesting, it's all of the little details in between, the relationships you build with the people you meet.  You can even form romantic, even sexual relationships with certain people, and there's always more to learn about the galaxy by talking to your friends, helping them out with their side quests, exploring the planets and moons of the galaxy (there's lots of content on them that has nothing to do with the main story line), or even reading the codec and journal entries you accrue as you perform certain actions in the game.  Whether you place humanity first, or wish to solidify our alliances with the other races of the galaxy, whether you give everybody a fair shake at justice, or kill everybody who crosses you, or somewhere in between, the story is a fun ride that I thoroughly enjoyed.
Generally speaking, the game is rock solid and ran great, never dropping below the refresh rate of my monitor (60hz) when I had VSync enabled and never crashing.  There were some things to take note of though.
- With certain newer AMD processors that do not have the "3DNow" instruction set (FX / Ryzen), character models turn into black, pixellated blobs at two locations of the game.  There is no official fix for this, and using the console to change the lighting made the game look terrible.  I eventually found a community mod that fixed the issue without bothering the lighting.
- There are occasional pauses or pops in the audio, almost as if it's taking a split second to swap between audio files.  Not game breaking, and not common, but noticeable when it does happen.
Overall, I love the game.  It's one of the greatest games, and series of games around.  It's an adventure, a space odyssey that places you in the driver's seat.  The visuals and audio work were great in 2008, and are still good enough by today's standards to help you suspend your disbelief and engross yourself in this universe that has been created.  The characters are fleshed out, believable, and by the end of it all you legitimately care about what's going on around you.  A LOT of the major story events can be directly influenced by your choices throughout the game, and it's really cool that your save game can be imported into Mass Effect 2 so that your choices in this game continue to influence events, people and attitudes in the 2nd game.  It provides a consistent, continuous experience that really helps make you feel like you're a part of the story.  I highly recommend this game and series to people who love a good story and the idea of space exploration.

Well, what can I say?
In a few words: it sucks, and in and of itself it's pretty useless and bland, unless you plan on using its last save to import your character into ME2.
First of all, I have to say: I seriously do not understand why all those people were so enthusiastic about it back in 2007. I think it's no better than the first KOTOR game, or the second one. In fact, I think KOTOR I is vastly superior to this one. I remember lots of people used to say one of these two (ME1 & 2) made Gears of Wars look like just a bunch of pixels by comparison but...that is such a bizarre claim. I have Intel HD 4000 graphics, and even at maximum settings, I am definitely not impressed. The one thing that did impress me though was the way your character moves on the ship: it feels real, it feels like you're carrying around a few pounds of (m)@ss, the animation is that good. And what a glorious (m)@ss it is! Your character feels heavy. As far as graphics go, it's not that bad, but there is a definite lack of options here: for instance, I see no 'antialiasing' option in the menu.
Just like with Jade Empire, I feel like they did not really bother with side quests; besides just being boring, they lack personality and it does not feel like the developers put much effort into them.
It's always the same f*cking thing: shoot your way past a bunch of armed hostiles in the usual, generic compound...and what a horrible f*cking mess combat is. You try to position yourself and your companions in a "strategic" way, but the enemies just rush at you, almost always overwhelming you in a matter of a couple of minutes, maybe less. The best way to deal with the enemies in this game is to basically run around the compound like an idiot, trying to pick them off one by one, hoping to finally find a spot where no one can flank or go around you; and I mean, what you do is basically just intentionally backing yourself into a corner, with no place or possibility of retreat. What the f*ck. I mean, this is the opposite of what one would do in a real life combat situation: you find a cover, but you make sure that somebody has your back and you can retreat if things get too dicey. But no. The enemies just run and swarm around you. And they only decide to take cover when there are barely 3 or 4 of them left, when that is basically useless anyway. And there are some bizarre moments, too. I remember there was this group of three Krogans in a narrow passage. So I decided to equip a shotgun; I wanted to get a little closer, but I was still too far away for it to be a real, much bigger danger. Makes sense, right? After all, if an enemy is not a total jackass, he will try not to let you close to him if he sees you and your team all have a shotgun in your hands, and will attempt to keep you at bay and will go to close quarters combat only as a last resort. But no. As soon as I switched to a shotgun, the f*ckers charged at me and my team. What the f*ck. You'd think this is normal, seeing as how Krogans are tough but...they stopped doing that as soon as I went to a much weaker assault rifle. And what I mean by "as soon as I went..." is that I got killled, and killed, and killed, and had to reload at least 3 or 4 times, before I tried another weapon. So combat is pretty random to me.
Now, the worst thing about combat in this game is that there is no easy way to enter a cover and exit it. You first have to draw a weapon, and grabbing a cover by mistake simply because you already have a weapon in your hands occurs from time to time, but often enough that you're annoyed by it. WHAT WERE THEY THINKING??? Was assigning a button to such a simple function that difficult? Brothers In Arms: Hell's Highway does this. A lot of other games do this. It's not a difficult solution. The worst thing about it is disengaging from the cover, and going to another one, which basically requires either tapping the S key twice or just holding it long enough for the character to quit it. It is possible there is a button that does that...but I was not able to find it, which amounts to the same thing. This makes combat annoying or awkward at best, and this is the single, worst flaw in the game. Oh, but they fixed it in ME2. How f*cking nice. Did they even adequately test this game? A game usually takes 1 or 2 years to develop. It boggles my mind that such a fatal flaw could escape their attention for so long, or that it was intentionally left there, which is even WORSE.
Other awkward or JUST PLAIN F*CKING ANNOYING moments include telling you to order a character under your command to use a power when that character is already down; leaving you utterly perplexed and p*ssed off, because these were basically the initial moments of the game used as a tutorial of sorts. I f*cking hate when game developers do this thing. They throw you in the middle of the action, causing you so much stress and anxiety. I mean, what the f*ck, do I look like an Alliance soldier to you? I did not grow up in the universe this is all taking place in, wouldn't it at the very least be nice to make you go through some sort of skippable boot camp or target practice? And as for ordering your followers to do something, why in the unholy mother of f*ck isn't there some kind of reticule you need to tap with your mouse, just like this was done in KOTOR I & II? That would have been much easier, less confusing and made you feel more in control of things. The fact is, I still don't exactly know how to properly target enemies; and this after playing this game for 34 hours.
Next, the confusing menu. You have a limit of 150 items you can carry: it would have certainly been nice if there was an indication of that somewhere; and, as an aside, have an on-board container to store items you don't need and are not sure what to do with. The only moment you get notified of it is when you're at 135 items, and when you hit the 150 number, you get invited to "omni-gel" some of those items: the problem with this is that this usually happens when you have opened or broken into an otherwise locked container and...mòtherf*ck3r surprise, you cannot exit this menu and come back to those items later, which means items you don't even know anything about get turned to omni-gel. And you can have funny situations of this kind, which are only funny in retrospect, because when they do happen, they simply make you want to scream in rage or frustration (pick one). Suppose you attempted manual override on a locked container; it failed, so now you have to use 20 or, more commonly, 25 omni-gel units to unlock the f*cker. Ok, you decide you want to do this; but upon opening it, you discover you forgot to omni-gel those other items you had in your menu, so that means...you omni-gel the new ones since you cannot exit it and come back to it later, and since the operation ALWAYS gives you 4 omni-gel units, no matter the level or complexity of the thing you're turning to gel (another thing that pisses me off), if you happen to have just three items in that container, you get 12. While spending twice as many. What a f*cking cruel joke. This is seriously one of the most backasswards and poorly thought out things I've seen in a videogame, I SWEAR.
Then there's the confusing inventory. Was the multiple weapons thing necessary? Was not separating the equipped\selected item thing, or making them look a little bit different, necessary? I was always a little bit confused about what kind of item was selected, also because the items are not shown with an actual image, they are shown inside some generic, boring case, or at the very least they are when you are buying them, and if you want to see what they look like, you have to first equip them, unholster
Are you serious? Even Skyrim does it better.

8/10 for an in-dev game that seems largely complete
This game has a very beautiful atmosphere, and an even more beautiful menu tune. The graphics are extremely well done for a game with a fraction of the funding of DayZ, and the surroundings in the towns and forests are outstanding.
The game runs surprisingly well for its level of detail. I can hold a solid 60 frames on medium settings, and 32 on max. The only issue that it has with performance is that sometimes frames will drop when entering or leaving a town for me, but otherwise it stays steady.
The gameplay whilst alone is rather simple, but that's to be expected from a game requiring human interaction to really get going. Loot is easy enough to find to entice the player to search for more, but rare enough that people will attempt to rob you for pieces of clothing or food. There is incentive to find other players and either work together or ruin their survival for your own gain. Ammo is very rare, even in the military base, and so players with guns and ammo are valuable to any groups that may form.
The community is what made me rate 8/10 instead of 9/10. My first hour and a half was spent on a normal public server, where I met a few people that were working together. We met an ax murderer halfway through my time on the server that killed everyone, and then hunted down everyone while they were still freshly spawned-- no weapons, clothes, ammo, food, or drink yet, so no incentive to hunt down and kill them other than for sport. There were people with some very obnoxious names spamming the chat and calling everyone inappropriate names the entire time. We also met someone who spammed screaming and yelling through the microphone.
I then joined a non-PvP, PvE only server to cool off a little bit and see if I could find anyone willing to join me on a regular server later. I spent about 45 minutes on that server looting up the airfield and the military base there. I did manage to find a shotgun and some ammo, as well as some military clothes. Immediately after I found the ammo for the gun, a man who was screaming into his microphone ran up behind me. I turned just in time to move out of the way and avoid being shot three times by a 9mm. He did not think I had ammo for my shotgun, which I only know because he yelled it into his microphone along with three or four curses. Fortunately, I managed to kill him in self defense and take his pistol.
If you enjoy good survival games with reasonably rare loot and a bit of difficulty but not a huge learning curve, Miscreated is for you. You can find good people with excellent intentions and gaming sense if you look hard enough, but half of the people you meet (even on RP and PvE servers) will spam on the microphone, try to kill you on sight, or kill you when you have no gear. I recommend getting a friend to join you on the game or finding and sticking with a group of people who you trust as quickly as possible, because strangers tend to lean toward hostility.

Just finished this game yesterday, really a good experience. It brought back memories of Elder Scrolls Oblivion thanks to the environment and equipment weight mecanics, the game play is kinda like Shadow Of The Colossus, and Spartan (ps2 game).
Sadly the main story is short and can be finished in 20 hours, but if you like doing lots of side quests and exploring the map and dungeons, you might take 100 hours just like i did.
, and that is a great time for you to go around the world map and have some fun, also do some monster hunting quests from the boarders since new monsters will appear you will have plenty of more quests from them.
Pros:
-  Hydras, Chimeras, Cyclops, Dragons, Goblins, Cockatrices, Gargoyles and all those fu**ers will be in this game
-  Very good combat system, so you fans of Dark Souls and Elder Scrolls will be blown away by this game. It's much better than both in this aspect. Every class feels different to play with, if you don't care about the op dungeon, you might find fun to start all over again from zero just to play a different class.
-  A lot of replayability, thanks to hard mode and overpowered dungeon called Bitterblack Island which will give you strong af items.
-  Great graphics (except for your main character facial expressions, they look bad...)
-  Nice character customization, and character weight and height will influense some aspects of the game play, like how easily he can go out of balance from enemy attacks, pass through the lags of cyclops and other monsters, how far his weapon swings will reach the enemies and etc.
-  Great interaction with companions (pawns), your pawns and other people's pawns will always be talking about the place, the quest you have active, they will also be screaming the monsters weaknesses when you're in battle, the AI from pawns is really great and the way they talk to you can be customized to your likings. I played this back on ps3 when it ran below 25fps and even then it was probably one of my favourite titles. It needs so much more recognition.
It's like all of my favourite games rolled into one tasty treat. Sure it has its drawbacks compared to some games like say Dragon Age, it's story simply doesn't compare.
But you won't be playing this for story anyways. It's the combat, and how goddamn satisfying it is. Not to mention some of the beautiful spells that can be cast. The mage classes in this are very fun to play and completely over the top with the spells.
Some of the fights can be dragged on like in Monster Hunter, which makes the payout all the more exciting. I was exploring a region in early game as a magic archer and I came across a golem. I was not prepared at all, but I wasn't just gonna run away. So this fight took place over like two ingame days. Non stop. We were doing so little damage. But through reading the enemies attacks and dodging accordingly and figuring out how to cause the thing to trip to get that one last weak spot we finally defeated the damn thing. The next golem I encountered lasted nowhere near as long thankfully. But that first fight was memorable and so damn satisfying.
Did I also mention this game has a climbing system? Tell me one other game where you can set yourself on fire grab a griffon, climb unto its back and set its wings ablaze, rendering it unable to fly for some time.
If you can get past the initial washed out visuals you're in for a treat.
And I haven't even brought up the Bitterblack Isles content, which is much, much darker than the base game. It's also very unforgiving, so be prepared.
I would recommend this game wholeheartedly if you're at all a fan of rpgs, there are so many aspects I haven't even touched on, like loot and gear. Hell even character creation is open enough to create some true monstrosities.
I hope to all that's good that capcom sees the potential in this series and we see a sequel, just imagining a Dragon's Dogma 2, with all these systems in place built upon and fleshed out even more is like a dream come true. Hell I'd love to see true co-op as well.

This game is a fresh take on RTS games. Instead of controlling mass quantities of units by scanning the entire battlefield, you control a single mouse, who acts as your cursor. You can cycle your units and control specific units or control all units. This simplification of controls lets you play with either a mouse and keyboard, or even a controller. Something that can be viewed negatively is the maps. The maps are randomly generated each time you start a game, meaning that you can't memorize the best choke points and locations to fortify. Instead, players have to figure it out on the fly. However, this does leave potential for bad starting locations. Cute characters and an interesting art style make this game fun to look at.
TLDR: Fun, pretty, and simplified enough for an RTS noob to understand :D

Tooth and Tail is a fresh, breakneck take on the RTS genre, as well as an intriguing story about civil war and cannibalism. While it doesn't spend a lot of time (about five missions?) with each viewpoint character, the world is set up beautifully. And I mean beautifully in many ways -- the spritework in this game is some of the most gorgeous I've seen when put together in full ensemble.
Controlling your armies with a player avatar helps with how much of a blitz each game is. While the randomly generated maps were a pain in the main campaign, the multiplayer benefits greatly from how important scouting is.
Overall, if you like freakishly cruel animals and thinking on your feet, Tooth and Tail is accessible to any interested. It doesn't matter if you're into RTS games or not.

RTSs are a genre that has always engaged me thematically and in their spectacle, yet mechanically they never clicked for my younger self. As someone who dabbled in RTS games like Halo Wars and who enjoyed the original Starcraft only with cheats as a teenager, Tooth and Tail is the entryway I always needed to master these games. What always deterred me away from RTSs was the complexity and the dexterity required, and T&T manages to take both qualities, simplify them, and retain all their flavor. In short, what Skullgirls is for fighting games is what Tooth and Tail is for RTSs, or as the tagline says “real-time strategy distilled” like a fine wine.
Where games like Starcraft: Brood War are as taxing of athleticism due to UI oversights and micromanagement as strategic with their unit/building tactics, T&T manages to level the skill-floor enough to demand players to truly understand the mechanics. There are four major overhauls of RTSs that make the game both accessible and more demanding of skill. If the developers truly sought to emulate Hearthstone/Blizzard for accessibility, then it’s safe to say they have succeeded in making a game casual enough with its changes to enjoy and dedicated enough at its core for the hardcore base.
The first major overall is the controls themselves that turns players into cursors. While controls are perfectly acceptable on a mouse-and-keyboard, the controller scheme is more ideal with how players maneuver general units as visible (and killable) cursors. All actions from base-building, unit direction, targeting, etc. are all coordinated with general units, which allows players not only the means to see what their enemies are planning but also offer offensive/defensive roles as unit direction is their sole role. This takes away the unknowns of gauging the enemy’s movements from RTSs where hotkeys, clicks and other unseen factors cannot be taken into account. It further enhances the need for strong map control and the coordination of battles as generals can move specific units (Rally Group) or entire armies (Rally All) along with burrowing home or to another location to redirect them.
Resources are also used more thoughtfully than other RTSs as it’s not simply a number to build up a base, unit, etc. but also a factor that must be considered everywhere. Food is intrinsically tied to base/unit building as players can easily starve themselves into defeat if they waste resources by the accumulation of errors. Food is used for everything from building new farms to harvest more food, from refilling lost units at bases, and from determining what structures/spawn-camps are worth keeping. Having too many tier one units could be good for a while until they begin dying in mass numbers to the player’s demise. This also rewards good defenses as they can be cheaply made and cause more harm for the other player.
Opportunities and mistakes are more vital than ever as the length of a match now cuts out a lot of the fattier aspects of RTS. The average time for a match, single-player or multiplayer, is between five to twenty minutes per session. Think of Starcraft 2’s rhythms of playing versus the original game’s crawl of every match. As a result of this condensed focus, every minor mistake can quickly build into failure, and it’s mainly knowing how to quickly solve a problem that will prevent defeat. Even in defeat, it’s not as much of a time-commitment to make learning not as fun as eventually winning against the odds.
The last of these major changes is unit synergy. RTSs often focus on asymmetrical armies to establish how they should play as well as offer different means of engaging different players. Instead of different armies, T&T allows players to choose five types of units from four tiers (three infantry; one defenses) out of 20 options. None of these options are useless, and if a certain unit type has a counter then attrition will often make up for a defect. (The game doesn’t limit you on each tier, but it’s best not to spend all in one place.) Aside from certain meta strategies, if you were to play the game with bots for 1v1, 2v2, or free-for-all, there is a huge potential for versatility, especially team-play where players can make up for any defects.
All these factors are what makes the initial buzz stave off the hangover moments where defeat sometimes was never in your favor no matter how hard you try. Even in these small sobering moments of T&T’s faults, the best solution is simply to play another round.
If I were to come up with a made-up probability to showcase how often victory feels, then there would be two general statements made of Tooth and Tail. For multiplayer, which the only matches I lost were during Free for All, it often feels like there is an 85% chance of winning with the rest of the odds determined by the randomized map, the units chosen and the mistakes that often come back to bite you. In the campaign, it often feels like there is a 75% chance of winning as some of the more demanding/restricting missions, excluding the finale which is meant to be brutal, required multiple attempts even when I knew what to do.
T&T attempts to solve a problem of memorization to get more players to think about their strategies at the cost of properly teaching the player how to execute them. The most obvious omission is the difference from Rally Group vs. Rally Army as it’s not immediately obvious what it does—at first, I thought it was a local rally with no indication of its range—until I learned it is dependent on the unit you have selected. This was a lesson I had to learn on my own when using special units like the Fox for more efficiency. In comparison to SC1, T&T’s missions do teach players techniques, unit synergies and other necessary tidbits to master the gameplay. This is what often the Heroic achievements are meant to do as they steer the player on the intended path of victory for certain missions, which depending on the RNG of the maps, they can make missions more difficult than intended.
Now most players would argue that additional difficulty modes are needed, which isn’t an absurd claim when bots have different AI levels, but I think overall the game’s difficulty is warranted to appreciate its depth. RTSs themselves are not about solely optimal strategies but knowing how to adjust to new challenges when things don’t go according to plan. The RNG of maps could be tweaked further, especially for 2v2 and FFA modes, or the campaign can have preset-maps for lower challenges—along with the system that is in place—to make it more approachable for newcomers. However, the low time for commitment of each map and the thrill of overcoming success after a dozen failures makes the campaign something worth overcoming for a real sense of pride and accomplishment.
Perhaps what makes me more critical of the campaign mode’s faults is that the campaign is what initially drew me into getting over my gripes with RTSs and learning how to appreciate them. There is a lot of atmosphere, attention to detail in art, character and world-building as well as the overall dark comedy of T&T’s narrative that manages to make Animal Farm look tame in comparison with its level of violence and of its sociopolitical commentary. (It’s not as deep of a commentary but the effectiveness of its message is what makes it more impactful.) Even in the finale, which is purposely so unfair that defeat is not intended, makes for one of the most memorable RTSs to date, mechanically and thematically.
If you can overcome Tooth & Tail’s moments of despair into your personal triumph, then you not only have the hundreds of other victories to look forward to but all the games that inspired it now to explore.

So I decided to buy Tooth and Tail because I needed a new RTS game that didn't make me micromanage to death and want to rip my eyeballs out because I just get rushed with units anyway.
Turns out, Tooth and Tail fills the niche of "RTS that isn't bullcrap micro all the time" quite well. In fact, there's no micromanaging at all! Thank god! Instead, I get to focus on my tactics and play up my army, keep it supplied, and hit strategic targets all while evading the enemy's eyes. Playing multiplayer allowed me to customize my army to exactly which units I liked during the campaign, which lead to some swift victories in multiplayer since my tactics were superior to my enemy's.
On top of the gameplay, though, don't shy away from this game's lore! It has one of the most macabre ideas I've come across for a game that has such a calming soundtrack: Essentially, you fight against your enemy knowing all the while that you will consume their flesh after they fall. The characters in the story mention over and over the idea of "POW meat" versus the "Swine", which appear to be docile pigs that don't mind being slaughtered for food.
Talking to folks around town reveals little juicy tidbits like the fact that the Civilized apparently chopped off Hopper's arm and ate it.
All in all, well worth the money, even if I didn't buy it on sale. If you already own Monaco, you can pick it up as a bundle for a bit cheaper than full price!

Brilliant game. You'll see complaints here about the randomised maps, which can be a bit of an annoyance, but that should not put you off the game as a whole.

But that is what makes the game interesting and unique. If you only play RTS's to micromanage then this will not be the game for you.
It's got a fab soundtrack and atmosphere, and a surprising amount of depth and variety for such a simple strategy title.
If you're getting frustrated because it is sometimes very difficult, then I feel you. But have a few more goes, try out a few different strategies, watch a playthrough of the level you're on, or just give yourself away from the keyboard/controller. You'll get there. I did and I'm really not a particularly great quick thinker.
Some of the levels area bit like puzzles, where you have to work out how the enemy side works. If you're having trouble then a bit of trial and error will show you the way. There's not much hand-holding but that means you'll feel super powerful when you finally beat the level!

Such a beautiful and amazing game. So many places to explore, so many new things to find, so many random little side quests and occurances that just come up. Starbound is more than just "Terraria in space." It has a lot of great ways to build and design and is very well thought out. Although it may get a bit redundant with similar planets and similar things and limited levels on biomes, the community workshop keeps things fresh and the game continues to grow.

If you've played Minecraft, if you you've played Terraria, or other of the myriad of craft/build sims that have been coming out in the last few years, you're by now probably assuming if you've played one, you've played them all, or close enough. I would have been inclined to agree with you before this game. Something truely special in a sea of sameness, Starbound manages to take what you think you know about these types of games and wrap it around a simple, but decent story, while placing it into a sea of multiple worlds. Like most of these types of games, it really shines in multiplayer, with company on the journey easily multiplying the fun factor as you explore your world, their worlds, and take the best from all around the universe. This isnt a game that makes the world your oyster, it makes the GALAXY yours to explore, to build, to fight, to say screw it all and be a farmer if you want. It's a bit hard to truely put into simple words what makes this game special versus it's family of titles, but the obvious thought, love and detail into every bit makes for a far greater whole.

THIS REVIEW IS FOR THE ENTIRE TRILOGY, NOT JUST THIS GAME
After playing Mass Effect, I was left with the very definite impression that I would never, and could never, play a better game. The worldbuilding, soundtrack, characterisation, the feeling of exploring a huge galaxy, and plot were all incredible. Sure, the combat was clunky, the graphics weren't great, but those were products of its time rather than developer oversight. Anyway, I was sure nothing could top it.
Then I played Mass Effect 2. The game begins in such away that your attention is immediately grabbed, and it isn't let go of until the game is complete, by which point you're hungering for 3. The graphics and combat are greatly improved, for those of you who care about such things, and the worldbuilding is still top notch, showing a darker and seedier side of the galaxy. The range of characters is also expanded, and they have even greater development than those is Mass Effect 1, except one, who was dreadfully boring and dull. The plot itself is weak, but you'll be so engaged by the characters and world that it doesn't matter, and it has the best ending to any videogame I have played.
Mass Effect 3, then. This one is infamous for its sub-par ending, and I must admit that it furstrated me a great deal, to the extent at which I made up my own one (but that's a different story, literally). As such, playing with the Extended Cut DLC is absolutely essential. It's also the only game in the series not available on Steam, so whatever your thoughts on EA are, you'll need an Origin account. Bar the ending, it had a very good plot, and introduced a few new and well loved characters as well. Though the paid DLC are pretty pricy, I'd recommend the Citadel and From Ashes expansions, they're both very good, Citadel probably being the best piece of DLC I've ever played.

Way back when I was a wee tot, I got the original PC port of Sonic CD. It was actually the very first game I ever owned for myself (all the others, I shared with my brother). Even now, I still have the disc, and I'll probably never get rid of it.
Sonic CD needs very little introduction, as it's one of the most heavily praised classic Sonic games, and with good reason... it is truly a classic and embodies everything great from the era of platforming games.
This remake? This is everything great about Sonic CD evolved. As per the American theme song to this game... this is the REAL Sonic Boom.
A friend gifted this to me for Christmas, and... honestly, it's one of the best Christmas gifts I'd ever recieved (why am I only now reviewing it in June? ...'Cuz I'm an idiot, that's why).
It's still the same game despite being rebuilt from the ground up (if everything I've read is to be believed). It feels just like it did back in the day, except even better. In fact, it might even be faster than the original, regardless of the original PC port of the SEGA CD original, and the improved Spin Dash is a godsend, although the original style Spin Dash is still present if you so desire.
Additionally, the anime-style opening and ending have been brought back, and have never looked better. They also give the option of either the Japanese or American soundtracks, although the Japanese opening and endings are sadly missing their lyrics, which is probably my only gripe about this remake... and it's so minor a nitpick that it's not a big deal.
On top of that, Tails has been added as a playable character as a bonus for beating the game.
Sonic CD is understandably a great classic Sonic game. This HD remake takes the classic, and adjusts it just enough to improve on it, without losing any of what made the original fantastic. Whether you want to call it a remake, or simply a remaster, the fact is if you haven't played this, you are missing out.

Sonic CD is the summary of what made the original Sega Genesis Sonic games... well, good. The same mechanics as before,  with a completely new move altogether - just hold up and mash the Spin-dash button - and the same sort of level design, but... bigger. A LOT bigger. Plus the four different versions of each stage, that can be achieved with TIME TRAVEL - weird concept in Sonic, I know.
The music, the bloody music, my god is it good. I didn't play the original, but it gives you the choice of the two different soundtracks between each region version - Japan/Europe on one hand and the US in the other. Personally I much, MUCH prefer the JP/EU one, except for Palmtree Panic, then the US one is better for that round. Plus, the infamous US boss theme has returned ladies and gentlemen, so be prepared to♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself, it really is ♥♥♥♥ing creepy. All in all the soundtrack is my favourite thing in thes game (not that the rest of it is bad, ♥♥♥♥ing far from it), and it's better than most music nowadays in my opinion.
A fantastic game for a fantastic price. Would recommend this to hell and back.

They're all a ton of fun, whether you're a mountain crushing powerhouse like the warrior, the nimble and sly Strider, or the hell-raising apocalypse bringing Archmage. Melee and ranged combat feel good, which is good, but for the first time in an RPG playing a mage is a blast. Unleashing the higher spells feels gatdam incredible.
The large enemy encounters in this game are some of the best. You'll be clinging for your life if you're a melee character and trying to strike their weak spots by getting up close and personal, or you'll be slowly disabling them as a ranged or magic user.
The party setup in the game is really interesting. Basically when you start the game you make your character. Neat, that's to be expected. There's a lot of neat options in there even including your character's posture and how they carry themself.  Soon after beginning the game you make another character. This second character is your Pawn, who is basically your new best friend and traveling companion. Your other two party slots are consisted of OTHER player's pawns. So basically everyone is sharing these secondary create-a-characters who actually learn strategies by adventuring with other Arisen (player characters). They can also form their own behaviors in combat which can range from life-saving to complete dummy.
This game is incredible overall, despite its many foibles. I plea to Capcom that they make a sequel fitting of a sleeper hit such as this.

Dragon's Dogma is a fantastic game. Your character isn't set to one play style, being able to change classes at just about every town. You originally start with 3 base classes, covering the standard archtypes of warrior, mage, and archer. These each have their own playstyle, focusing on either ranged or melee combat. Yet each of these classes can be mixed with another when you pick an advanced class. These are things like Mystic Knight or Assassin. Of course you can also just choose to upgrade your current class into an advanced form. A Mage can become a Sorcerer, or a Fighter to a Warrior.
But you aren't in this alone. You create not just your own character, but a pawn as well. A pawn's class is set when created, but you can have up to 3 pawns with you at a time. Have friends that play this? Well you can summon their pawns to your world to help you out. Create a merry band of warriors to fight back massive beast and creatures of the night.
Climb up the back of a cyclops or hydra. Climbing has many uses in combat, and this game gets some great moments from climbing atop different monsters.
This version of the game has a neat dlc dungeon that is way harder than the base game, and will really be a challenge to most players. I highly recommend that you try it out once you've beaten the base game. Of course, you can just enter New Game +, keeping your gear and levels. New Game + adds more challenges, and gives you a better chance to do storylines that you missed previously.
An important note is that you CAN FAIL QUEST by not doing them in a timely manner. Certain quest are time sensitive, and require you to go to areas you might not be leveled for. These usually lead to how your ending will occur. Completing certain quest will raise your affinity with other npcs, which will change your ending. Theres a total of 3 or so endings involving different people you meet.
All in all, I highly recommend Dragon's Dogma. It's a fun game with a ton of replayablility. In total, between the PS3, Steam, and PS4 release I've put in well over 80 hours.

Spoilers are found below! Proceed with caution!
1853. American Commodore Matthew Perry anchors his warships off the coast of the capital of a Japan that has been closed for more than two centuries. This event, followed up by another visit in January 1854, forced the doors of Japan open to the west and caused a huge uproar among the people of Japan. They were forced to side with the xenophobes who hated the western intrusion, the Tokugawa shogunate who had ruled the nation since 1603 and cooperated (albeit at gunpoint) with the westerners, and the Emperor who supported Japanese values and tradition, but had allied with the British to meet this end.
This backdrop is necessary to understand the context of Way of the Samurai 4, a game released in March 2011 in Japan and August 2012 in America. You take the role of a samurai, newly arrived to the fictional island of Amihama, who finds himself dragged into a battle between the idealist terrorist Prajnas and the shogunate forces. A very young girl who wants nothing more than for the two nations to get along leads the British consulate in the area.
Though the game itself is not a bad one (an overall “not awful”), the writing is where the game seems to fall short. The humor in the game is incredibly Japanese, which in itself is fine for a game produced and fully voiced for and by Japanese. Unfortunately, a lot of it is lost in translation. In the very beginning for example, a young, defenseless girl is threatened with♥♥♥♥♥♥by who appears to be a major threat. A man appears to lay down the law and detain the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ The game has started off on a very serious note. The battle is about to begin! The law-bringer literally jumps into battle, only to comically fall flat on his face off camera with a cartoony noise to indicate what has happened. At this point, I was a bit confused, but just chalked it up to how I was supposed to view the man. He must be a bumbling officer who simply wants to do his job right and fails at every attempt. He’s Barney Fife! However, when the man stands, he ignores his blunder as no one seems to notice. Enter a British commander. She’s clearly stylized on a knight, carrying a large, western sword and wearing gold armor. She has a serious look on her face and means business. As a well-intentioned Brit, she won’t have anyone being assaulted on the streets. Melinda Megamelons joins the fray. At this point, I literally hung my head. No, her breasts were not huge. They seemed decidedly average (which, granted, is probably large to Japanese eyes). Perhaps this is the comic-relief character I was expecting? No… she’s just a commander who wants her men to stand just as firmly as any samurai. This scene seems to sum up my feeling as a whole for the game. In one word, “huh?”
I played through the game multiple times (the New Game+ is this Way of the Samurai 4’s shining point), each time trying to pick a new faction. The first time I chose and succeeded with beating the game while siding with the British (because there is no Emperor faction). I got my jailbait ambassador and sailed to Britain with her! Fin, roll credits. The second time I played through, I chose to side with the shogunate forces as the magistrate in the area, our lovely Barney Fife, was a very well-intentioned man. As I played through this line, I became more confused in regards to the first scene. Not once he play the comic relief roll again. He’s played straight as an arrow, believing the evil Prajnas must be brought to justice. I found myself siding against the shogun in the end, as the shogun’s chief minister who is brought to the area is a complete and utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, choosing to boil innocent citizens alive to send a message to a terrorist organization. This led me down (what I believe to be) the most moral path. I defeated the evil Prajnas along with a man close to the magistrate. This man was probably the most well-written character in the game. He cares for his nation, but isn’t a jerkass to the foreigners. He is played as a lazy, nonchalant man who will always eventually get the job done. After this playthrough, I returned to the consulate, this time failing to save the ambassador and  heading off in the end to Edo on a warpath to destroy the evil chief minister, the credits claiming that my actions were lost to time. After a replay of the first, I reluctantly joined the Prajnas on my last playthrough.
Strap yourselves in. Almost the entire scenario♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. With the exception of one mission where you stop drunken marines from♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥a young shopkeeper, you do nothing redeemable. You go on with the Prajnas to hide in a cave and plot an overthrow of the government while stealing arms from the constabulary, killing off my favorite character as he collects a shipment of bolts (the Prajnas had some bad information that they were illegal arms), and, eventually, invade the British consulate. Not once during these missions did I feel like anything but a complete and utter d-bag for being a “patriot in support of expelling the foreigners.” The game punishes you in the end for siding with a group whose leader wanted to♥♥♥♥♥♥the British ambassador by having you die in a slow-motion shot of the last remaining Prajnas being mowed down by a group of shogunate soldiers carrying western rifles. I assume this was meant to be an allegory for history in which the Japanese who were in support of banning all foreign influence were mowed down in the wake of western expansion. I, however, was livid. No, the main character does not deserve this cinematic end for terrorizing an entire city. No, you don’t get to have a sad, emotional death because you sided with a xenophobic jerkbag. As an alternative, perhaps this ending could have been used for the “I-tried-and-failed-to-stick-to-my-ideals-and-not-be-a-total♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ending. What should have been used for this ending is one in which you confront the vile chief minister for selling out aboard a Black Ship that is fully implemented into the game yet I never once found myself entering. You cut down a hoard of British soldiers, each time the flames of passion burn ever stronger and threaten to consume you. You reach the innards of the ship to find the despicable chief minister already and an assload of British and shogunate elite forces thirsty for revenge. They get their revenge, sailing out a ways and dumping your body into the ocean within a barrel full of scrap metal. Fin, roll credits.
Also, I’d like to mention that the voice acting for the Japanese is great, but the British are played so horribly stereotypically that it hurts. People who clearly do not speak English as a first language were fed lines in a studio. The pronunciation is wrong, as are any emphases used. It deeps very heavily into the uncanny valley and I’m left not laughing at the strange foreigners or understanding how the Japanese saw them, but with an uncomfortable feeling whenever I see them.
I was a bit confused at the writing in this game and I never once knew how to feel at anything. The whole experience tried to do several 180s, failing each time. There is not one morally ambiguous character in the game. The Prajnas are bigoted jerks, the British are moral paragons trying to bring modernity to a backwards nation, and the shogunate is corrupt on top and just on the bottom, ruling its people through fear and nice lower-ranking officials. I would certainly recommend this game, though I’d say its $25 price tag is $5 overpriced (I believe it is because Way of the Samurai 3 is $20). Pick it up for a few days of fun, but don’t expect to be blown away by the amazing story.

This is the long awaited sequel to the hit game, State of Emergency. Although it veers strongly from the establish plotline of the State of Emergency series, it manages to stay connected, and even throws out oblique references. For example, the main character of the story mode is black. So was one of the main characters in State of Emergency, and they were both similarly named. Many parallels can be drawn to State of Emergency, such as The Law mission.
However, this is where the review becomes negative. I was disappointed at how different the game felt and played from the original. The forumla for the first game worked pretty well, and there wasn't much of a reason to change it. This seems to be a total redesign in the wrong direction.
Although open-world, there is now a resource-collecting and base-building sidegame, which adds to the confusion. Most of the additions seem tacked-on, and pointless. Zombies, while a welcome addition, provide nothing more than cannon fodder. Although cops served a similar purpose in the first game, in that game their A.I. was more advanced, and were generally more interesting to fight.
Overall, I can't really recommend this game for State of Emergency fans. I was disappointed.
